answer:
Above the so‐called critical velocity, bonding in cold spray is driven not by melting but by intense, high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at the particle–substrate interface.  In practice this proceeds in three linked steps:

1. Impact pressure exceeds the dynamic yield strength of the materials (>1 GPa), producing very high strain rates (10^6–10^7 s^–1).  
2. Severe plastic flow at the particle edge generates a supersonic “jet” that shears off oxides and other surface films, exposing fresh metal.  
3. The now oxide‐free metal surfaces are pressed together under extreme pressure and local temperature rise (due to adiabatic heating), permitting atomic‐scale contact and metallic bonding (cold welding), aided by mechanical interlocking and, in some alloys, dynamic recrystallization.  

It is this combination of jet‐cleaned, oxide‐free surfaces plus intimate, high‐pressure solid‐state contact (often enhanced by localized adiabatic shear softening) that produces the strong bonds in cold spray once the critical impact velocity is exceeded.

Key to cold‐spray bonding is that a particle’s impact velocity must exceed a material- and process-specific “critical velocity,” vcrit, sufficient to generate the adiabatic shear and jetting needed to break oxides, produce fresh metal–metal contact, and plastically deform both particle and substrate.  In practice vcrit depends on a combination of  
 1. Particle and substrate material properties  
    • Density (ρ), yield strength (σy) and hardness (H)—higher strength or lower ductility raises vcrit  
    • Strain-rate sensitivity and work-hardening behavior  
    • Thermal properties (conductivity, specific heat)—which govern adiabatic heating and shear localization  
    • Stacking-fault energy (in metals) and fracture toughness  
 2. Particle characteristics  
    • Size and size distribution—smaller particles have less momentum and thus require higher velocities  
    • Shape and morphology—sharp or irregular shapes can initiate jetting more readily  
    • Initial temperature—hotter particles need less additional heating to reach shear instability  
    • Surface condition—thick oxide or contaminant layers must be disrupted, which raises vcrit  
 3. Propelling gas and spray parameters  
    • Gas species (molecular weight)—lighter gases (He) give higher exit velocities but can alter shock structure  
    • Gas temperature and pressure—higher T and P increase particle velocity  
    • Nozzle design (converging–diverging geometry, throat diameter)  
    • Stand‐off distance—too long and particles slow by drag; too short and jet structure is underdeveloped  
    • Mass flow rate and carrier‐gas velocity distribution  
 4. Impact conditions  
    • Impact angle—normal incidence minimizes vcrit; oblique impacts require higher speed  
    • Substrate temperature—preheating lowers yield strength and raises the degree of plastic flow, reducing vcrit  
    • Substrate roughness—appropriate roughness aids mechanical interlocking but large asperities may raise local stress requirements  
 5. Cumulative/“snowball” effects  
    • Priorly deposited layer temperature and stress state—subsequent particles may bond at slightly lower velocities  

Taken together, these factors define the process window in which cold spray yields good adhesion.  In design or simulation one often tunes gas species/temperature/pressure, nozzle geometry, stand-off distance and preheating to achieve particle velocities just above the critical value for the chosen materials.

Gas temperature is one of the key “tuning knobs” in cold spray.  By raising or lowering the gas preheat you change the particle’s velocity, temperature and deformability at impact—and that directly controls bonding, microstructure, residual stress, porosity and hardness in the as‐sprayed deposit.  In broad strokes:  

1. Particle velocity and critical‐velocity threshold  
   • Higher gas T → higher gas enthalpy and speed of sound → generally higher peak particle velocities (up to an optimum)  
   • As velocity rises, more particles exceed the critical velocity for effective jetting and metallurgical bonding  
   • Below a minimum gas T you under‐shoot critical velocity and get poor deposition efficiency and weak, porous coatings  

2. Plastic deformation, bonding strength and deposition efficiency  
   • Gas‐preheated particles are hotter and have lower flow stress on impact  
   • They deform more extensively, form larger interfacial jets, close up native oxides and bond more completely to substrate and to each other  
   • Deposition efficiency climbs with gas T until you reach the point where extra heating no longer yields higher velocity or you begin to overheat the build  

3. Porosity, microstructure and hardness  
   • As gas T increases (and particle velocity/deformation goes up), residual porosity falls—densification improves  
   • Severe plastic deformation at optimal T can induce adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement in the deposit, raising hardness  
   • Overheating (very high gas T) may soften the deposit via thermal annealing or promote oxide formation on particle surfaces, both of which can reduce hardness and bonding  

4. Residual stresses and substrate heating  
   • Low‐T sprays (large ΔT between cold substrate and room‐temperature or marginally heated particles) tend to generate tensile residual stress in the deposit  
   • Higher gas T “warms up” the substrate and deposit so thermal‐mismatch stresses drop or even go compressive, improving fatigue resistance  

5. Oxidation and process window  
   • Higher gas T (especially with oxygen‐bearing carrier gases) can oxidize particle surfaces in flight, raising critical velocity again or embedding oxide stringers in the deposit  
   • There is therefore an optimum gas‐temperature window that maximizes particle velocity and plasticity while minimizing in‐flight oxidation and excessive substrate heating  

Practical takeaway:  
– Low gas T (<300–400 °C in most metal systems) → insufficient particle velocity, poor bonding, high porosity, weak deposit.  
– Medium gas T (400–800 °C, depending on material and nozzle design) → peak deposition efficiency, dense microstructure, high hardness, low residual stress.  
– Very high gas T (>800–900 °C) → marginal velocity gains, risk of oxidation or thermal softening, possible drop in hardness and bond strength.

Key to cold‐spray’s ability to yield dense, low‐oxide coatings is that it is a solid‐state, high‐velocity “peening” process rather than a thermal spray.  The principal features are:

1. Solid-state deposition  
   • Powder particles never melt, so there is no oxide formation during melting/solidification.  
   • Thermal input is low and very brief, greatly reducing in-flight and in-coat oxidation.

2. Supersonic particle impact  
   • High gas pressures (up to 3–6 MPa) and moderate preheat (usually < 600 °C) accelerate particles to 500–1200 m/s.  
   • On impact, particles undergo extreme, high-strain‐rate plastic deformation.

3. Adiabatic shear and jetting  
   • Localized adiabatic shear at the interface generates “metal jets” that scour away native oxide films and surface contaminants.  
   • The fresh metal at each impact bonds by cold welding, leaving virtually no entrapped oxide.

4. Mechanical interlocking and pore closure  
   • Repeated high‐pressure impacts press particles together and plastically close any voids.  
   • Layer-by-layer buildup leaves < 1% residual porosity in properly optimized systems.

5. Inert or reducing carrier gas  
   • Helium or nitrogen carrier gases have very low oxygen partial pressures.  
   • Minimal in‐flight oxidation further ensures the deposit’s metal remains oxide-free.

By combining supersonic, solid-state particle bonding with oxide‐film disruption and inert environment, cold spray produces coatings of exceptionally low porosity and oxide content.

Compared to an air-plasma spray, detonation gun (D-gun) coatings are markedly denser (porosities down in the 0.5–1 % range versus the 3–10 % often seen in APS), typically reaching 98–100 % of theoretical density rather than the 90–95 % you get with APS.  The fundamental reason is that in D-gun spraying the powder is picked up in a detonation‐driven shock wave and launched at supersonic speed, so the particles hit the substrate with much higher kinetic energy (and attendant impact pressure) than in an APS torch.  That ultra–high impact pressure promotes extensive plastic deformation, splat interlocking and void closure, giving you a virtually pore‐free deposit.

Compared to air‐plasma spray (APS) and wire‐arc, both HVOF and cold spray give you markedly denser, less‐oxidized deposits.  In rough terms you see the following trends:

 1. Coating density (porosity by volume)  
    • APS (atmospheric plasma‐sprayed): typically 2–10 % porosity  
    • Wire‐arc: 3–8 % porosity  
    • HVOF: 0.5–3 % porosity (often 1–2× denser than APS/wire‐arc)  
    • Cold spray: <0.5–2 % porosity (approaches full theoretical density)  

 2. Oxide content (by weight or area fraction)  
    • APS: 5–20 % oxides (depends on plasma gas composition, spray distance)  
    • Wire‐arc: 3–10 % oxides (molten metal is exposed to ambient O₂ briefly)  
    • HVOF: 1–5 % oxides (fuel‐rich/neutral flame chemistry limits re‐oxidation)  
    • Cold spray: ≪1 % oxides (particles never fully melt, reaction time is very short)  

Underlying reasons:  
– HVOF’s supersonic, relatively reducing flame both densifies the splats and suppresses oxidation.  
– Cold spray is solid‐state; particles plastically deform on impact without melting, so you get near‐fully dense, virtually oxide-free coatings.

In cold spray the single‐most important velocity is the particle’s normal‐to‐substrate component (Vₙ), because only when Vₙ exceeds the material’s critical velocity (V_c) will you get the high‐strain, adiabatic shear and metallurgical bonding you need.  But two other “directions” of velocity also matter:

  •  Tangential (or in‐plane) component, Vₜ  
     – Drives the lateral shear that flattens the particle and helps “wipe” fresh metal onto the substrate.  
     – Too much Vₜ (high glancing angle) and you can get sliding, erosion, or particle rebound instead of bonding.  
  •  Radial (off‐axis) component  
     – Mostly redistributes particles away from the beam center and can cause oblique impacts that reduce effective Vₙ.  

In practice one starts with the nozzle‐axis velocity (u_z) and resolves it at each point on the substrate into Vₙ and Vₜ by using the local surface normal n:

  Vₙ = U·n  
  Vₜ = √(U²–Vₙ²)  

where U is the magnitude of the particle’s incoming velocity vector.

How surface morphology influences these components
  1.  Local incidence angle.  Rough or textured substrates present a distribution of micro‐facets whose normals are tilted toward the spray centerline.  On a small ridge angled toward the jet you actually boost the local Vₙ even though the global U is unchanged.  Conversely, facets tilted away suffer lower Vₙ and more glancing blows.  
  2.  Mechanical interlocking.  Valleys and pits can trap rebounding or slowly moving particles, giving a second chance at impact.  Once lodged, subsequent impacts on those “anchors” are effectively normal and weld more easily.  
  3.  Flow perturbation.  Sharp edges and deep textures induce local shock expansions, micro‐jets and vortices in the gas stream.  These accelerate some particles (raising local Vₙ or Vₜ) and slow others, broadening the velocity distribution and shifting more particles above V_c.  
  4.  Effective “surface-normal” distribution.  A polished flat gives a single, uniform incidence angle.  A blasted or laser‐textured surface gives a spread of angles; statistically more peaks will intercept the jet under near-normal incidence, improving overall deposition efficiency.  

Bottom line
  – You need primarily to maximize the normal‐component Vₙ of your particles above V_c.  
  – You want enough tangential Vₜ to flatten particles without causing erosion.  
  – By tailoring surface roughness (amplitude, wavelength, feature shape) you reshape the local incidence‐angle distribution, concentrate impinging momentum into normal components, trap incoming particles, and generate helpful microscale flow structures.

Cold spray relies on particle impact velocities exceeding a material‐specific “critical velocity” (Vcrit) to produce the severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear bonding you need. Stronger alloys (high‐yield‐strength Al, Cu, Ti, Ni‐base, etc.) have higher Vcrit because they resist deformation. Raising your gas pressure or temperature helps in two key ways:

1. Increasing Gas Pressure  
   • Higher stagnation (manifold) pressure → higher mass flow and dynamic pressure → greater particle acceleration → higher particle exit velocity.  
   • A higher velocity margin above Vcrit boosts deposition efficiency (higher build rates, denser coatings, lower porosity).  
   • Typical pressures for high‐strength alloys run 4–6 MPa (30–90 bar) in He or Ar systems.

2. Increasing Gas Temperature  
   • Warmer gas raises the local speed of sound and thus the Mach number for a given nozzle geometry → higher particle velocity.  
   • It also imparts some thermal softening to particles (lower yield stress), reducing Vcrit.  
   • Above about 600–800 °C (for N2/Ar) you get diminishing returns: gas density drops, momentum flux falls, and oxidation or grain growth can set in.

Practical outcome for strong alloys: by combining high gas pressures (4–6 MPa) with elevated temperatures (400–800 °C), you push particle velocities past the ~800–1 200 m/s needed to bond Cu, Ti, Ni‐based alloys. You’ll see greatly improved deposition efficiency, denser microstructures, and stronger interparticle and particle–substrate bonding.

Critical velocity (Vc) in cold spray is the minimum impact speed a powder particle must reach on striking the substrate so that it undergoes sufficient plastic deformation to bond rather than rebound.  Below Vc, particles simply ricochet or erode the surface; above Vc, the kinetic energy and the associated jetting at the interface expel oxides and contaminants, expose fresh metal, and create metallurgical bonds.

Key points:

1. Definition  
   – Vc depends on the materials pair (particle vs. substrate), particle size and morphology, gas type, gas temperature and pressure.  
   – Typical Vc values for common metals range from ~500 to 1200 m/s.

2. Mechanism  
   – At velocities ≥ Vc the local pressure and strain rate at the impact point exceed the material’s dynamic yield strength.  
   – A supersonic microjet forms around the particle perimeter, cleaning and pressing the surfaces together.

3. Importance  
   a. Deposition efficiency:  Only particles reaching or exceeding Vc contribute to buildup; sub-critical particles waste carrier gas and powder.  
   b. Coating quality:  Vc governs the onset of full-density deposits with high bond strength and low porosity.  
   c. Process window:  The operating gas pressure/temperature must be set so that the bulk of the particle velocity distribution exceeds Vc but stays below the erosion velocity (above which substrate damage or particle fragmentation dominates).  
   d. Material compatibility:  Determines which alloys or ceramics can be successfully cold-sprayed onto given substrates.

In practice, establishing Vc experimentally (often via “stop-and-capture” tests or incrementally increasing gas pressure) is a crucial first step in cold-spray process development.

The single biggest “knob” you have in cold‐spray to move particles faster or slower (at a given gas temperature and pressure) is the molecular weight (M) and thermodynamic properties (k = cₚ/cᵥ) of your propellant gas.  In simple terms the jet—and therefore your particles—can only accelerate up to a few times the local speed of sound, a, where  
a = √(k·R·T/M).  

• Lower M ⇒ higher a ⇒ higher achievable Mach number for the same nozzle geometry and stagnation conditions ⇒ higher particle velocity.  
• Higher k also gives a small boost to a (H₂ and He have k≈1.4–1.67 versus ≈1.4 for N₂/air).  

Typical ballpark values at 800 K stagnation, 3 MPa inlet:  
  – Helium (M=4) ⇒ a≈1700 m/s ⇒ particle V≈800–1100 m/s  
  – Hydrogen (M=2) ⇒ a≈1940 m/s ⇒ V≈900–1200 m/s (but highly flammable)  
  – Nitrogen (M=28) ⇒ a≈540 m/s ⇒ V≈500–800 m/s  
  – Air (M≈29) ⇒ similar to N₂  
  – Argon (M=40) ⇒ a≈430 m/s ⇒ V≈400–700 m/s  

In practice:  
  – He (or He/H₂ blends) give the highest velocities (best for very hard or high‐melting materials),  
  – N₂/air are cheaper and give moderate velocities,  
  – Ar/CO₂ give the lowest velocities and are used only for softer or highly ductile powders.

Nozzle design is one of the most critical factors in cold spray because it directly controls the gas‐dynamic environment the particles “ride” in.  Key points are:  

1. Converging–Diverging Geometry (de Laval Nozzle)  
   • Convergence section accelerates the gas toward sonic at the throat.  
   • Throat diameter sets the mass flow rate and the local sonic condition (Mach 1).  
   • Divergence angle and expansion ratio (exit area/throat area) determine the supersonic Mach number at the exit and thus the peak gas velocity. Higher Mach numbers → higher drag forces on particles → greater particle velocities.  

2. Pressure Ratio and Critical Flow  
   • The ratio of plenum pressure to ambient (or vacuum) must exceed the critical value for choked flow at the throat.  
   • Above this ratio, exit velocity is dictated by nozzle geometry; alterations in expansion ratio fine-tune exit Mach number.  

3. Length and Divergence Angle  
   • A longer divergent section gives particles more distance (and time) to accelerate but at the cost of added wall friction and weight/size.  
   • Too sharp an expansion angle causes boundary‐layer separation and shock formation, lowering both gas and particle velocities. Angles of 5°–15° are typical.  

4. Internal Surface Finish and Cooling  
   • Smooth, erosion-resistant coatings (e.g. tungsten carbide, silicon carbide) minimize flow turbulence and wear.  
   • Active or passive cooling can stabilize throat temperature to keep gas properties consistent.  

5. Multi-Channel and Curved Nozzles  
   • Multiple small throats can boost total mass flow while keeping each channel in an optimal Reynolds‐number regime.  
   • Curved or offset nozzles help with robot‐arm clearance but must be designed to avoid flow separation.  

By tailoring throat diameter, expansion ratio, length and surface quality, nozzle designers set the gas velocity profile, residence time and shock‐structure locations—and thereby control the maximum particle velocities and impact energies achievable in a cold spray system.

Increasing the cold‐spray gas pressure raises the particle velocity (and mass flux) entering the nozzle, and that in turn governs both how much material “sticks” per pass (coating growth rate and final thickness) and the microstructure/mechanical integrity of the deposit.  Key effects are:

1. Particle Velocity and Deposition Efficiency  
   • Velocity boost above the material’s critical velocity (Vc) is needed for plastic deformation and interparticle bonding.  
   • At low pressures (below or just around Vc), deposition efficiency is small, coatings grow very slowly (thin) and tend to be porous and poorly bonded.  
   • As pressure—and thus velocity—increases above Vc, deposition efficiency (mass of metal adhered per unit powder delivered) rises steeply, so thickness per pass jumps.  
   • Beyond an optimum pressure, further velocity gains give diminishing thickness benefits (efficiency plateaus) or even drop if excessive rebound or particle fracture occurs.

2. Coating Thickness  
   • For a fixed traverse speed and powder feed rate, raising gas pressure typically increases thickness roughly linearly up to the optimal point.  
   • Higher pressure also allows higher feed rates while maintaining good bonding, enabling faster build‐up of thicker coatings.  
   • Below optimum pressure you get thin, patchy films; above it you achieve target thickness in fewer passes.

3. Coating Quality: Density, Porosity, Adhesion, and Residual Stress  
   • Density/Porosity: Higher particle impact energy at elevated pressure leads to better particle flattening (“splat”), fewer voids, and densities approaching wrought metal.  
   • Bond Strength: Improved metal–metal intimate contact and jetting at the interface increases tensile and shear adhesion.  
   • Surface Roughness: Moderate pressure yields a balance—enough peening to smooth peaks and fill valleys. Too much can over‐peen, roughen or work‐harden the top surface.  
   • Residual Stress and Cracking: Very high pressures drive high strain rates and embed residual compressive stresses that can improve fatigue life—but if excessive, can induce microcracks or even delamination under service loads.  
   • Oxidation and Gas Entrainment: Higher flow rates can entrain more oxygen (if shielding is poor) and trap gas at interfaces; proper nozzle design and shielding are critical at high pressures.

4. Practical Trade-Offs and Limits  
   • Nozzle Wear: Elevated pressures accelerate erosion of nozzle inserts (especially with ceramic powders).  
   • Gas Consumption & Cost: Higher pressures mean higher gas flow, energy and operating cost, especially with helium.  
   • Substrate Damage: Very high velocity impacts can erode or over‐work substrates, so pressure must be tuned to the substrate hardness and thickness.

Summary:  
Raising the cold‐spray gas pressure boosts particle velocity and deposition efficiency, so you get thicker, denser, better‐adhered coatings per pass—up to an optimum. Beyond that point, returns diminish or reverse, and you risk substrate erosion, nozzle wear, residual‐stress–induced cracking or powder rebound. Properly optimized pressure is thus a balance between thickness growth rate and coating quality.

Critical velocity (Vc) in cold spray is the minimum impact speed a particle must reach to plastically deform, jet at the interface, and form a metallurgical bond with the substrate.  It is not a fundamental constant but depends on  
 • particle and substrate mechanical properties (yield strength, hardness, work-hardening rate)  
 • particle size and temperature  
 • gas density, temperature, and chemistry  
 • spray standoff distance and nozzle design  

Typical Vc values range from roughly 400–600 m/s for soft metals (Al, Cu) up to 800–1 200 m/s for harder alloys and ceramics.

Effect on deposition efficiency (DE):  
 1. Below Vc: particles rebound elastically or plastically without bonding, so DE ≈ 0.  
 2. Near Vc: a narrow “activation” window opens; a small fraction of particles bond and DE climbs steeply with velocity.  
 3. Above Vc: most particles bond and DE approaches a plateau (often 50–90 %, depending on material and conditions).  
 4. Far above Vc: excessive impact energy can induce substrate erosion, particle fracture, or over‐deformation, which can actually reduce DE.  

In practice, one tunes gas pressure and temperature (and thus particle velocity) to just exceed Vc for the material system in order to maximize DE while minimizing erosion or powder wastage.

In cold spray the “deposition efficiency” (DE) is simply the fraction of powder you actually get to stick to the substrate versus the powder you feed into the gun.  It is almost always quoted as a percentage and may be expressed in one of two equivalent ways:

1. Mass‐based definition  
   DE (%)  =  (mass of powder deposited on the part ÷ mass of powder fed into the spray gun) × 100  

2. Rate‐based (instantaneous) definition  
   DE (%)  =  (deposition rate, e.g. g/min ÷ powder feed rate, g/min) × 100  

In practice you determine it by weighing the substrate before and after spraying (and carefully removing any loosely attached material) to get the deposited mass, and by metering the total powder consumed over the same time interval to get the fed mass.

Typical cold‐spray particle velocities (Vp) fall in roughly the 300–1,200 m/s range, with most metallic systems operating between 500 and 900 m/s.  How that high-speed window drives consolidation:  
1. Overcoming the critical‐velocity threshold  
   • Each material has a “critical” impact velocity (Vc)—below Vc particles simply ricochet; above Vc they plastically deform and stick.  
   • Soft metals (Al, Cu) have Vc ≈400–600 m/s; harder alloys and ceramics may require 700–1,000 m/s.  
2. Severe plastic deformation  
   • Kinetic energy (½mv²) converts to localized plastic work at the particle–substrate/interface.  
   • Strain rates up to 10⁶–10⁹ s⁻¹ produce adiabatic shear instabilities and dynamic recrystallization in a narrow jet zone.  
3. Oxide disruption and fresh‐surface welding  
   • High‐velocity “microjets” at the leading edge remove surface oxides and contaminants.  
   • Exposed metal-to-metal contact under extreme pressure (~GPa) promotes true solid-state bonding without melting.  
Together, these effects turn the 500–900 m/s window into the sweet spot where particles deform, jet off oxides, cold‐flow, and weld into a fully consolidated coating.

Key hardware modules in a cold-spray deposition system are:

1. High-pressure gas supply  
   • Industrial compressor or bottled gas (He, N₂)  
   • Pressure regulators, safety relief valves  

2. Gas-heating package  
   • Electric or combustion heater (resistive coils, gas burner)  
   • Temperature sensors and PID control  

3. Powder feed system  
   • Hopper or magazine for powder storage  
   • Metering feeder (vibratory, auger-type)  
   • Carrier-gas injector to transport powder into the gas stream  

4. Spray gun (deposition head)  
   • Mixing/injection chamber (where powder meets the hot high-pressure gas)  
   • Converging–diverging (De Laval) nozzle to accelerate particles to supersonic speed  
   • Cooling/jacket circuits to protect gun internals  

5. Motion and fixturing  
   • Articulated robot arm or multi-axis CNC gantry  
   • Part fixturing/positioning table (often with rotary axes)  

6. Control system  
   • PLC or industrial PC running process recipes  
   • Human–machine interface (HMI) for gas pressure, temperature, feed rate, gun motion, etc.  

7. Exhaust and powder‐recovery  
   • Local exhaust ventilation with cyclone or bag filters  
   • Powder reclaim cyclone (optional)  

8. Safety & utilities  
   • Interlock enclosures or blast cabinet  
   • Gas‐detector panels, emergency shutdowns  
   • Cooling-water chiller (for gun and heater)  

Together, these modules deliver, heat and accelerate powder to produce high-velocity impact deposition with precise, programmable motion control.

In cold spray you only get good bonding if each particle arrives just above its “critical velocity” Vc.  In practice one defines the velocity ratio VR = Vparticle/Vc and finds three regimes:

 1. VR < 1  
    • Insufficient plastic deformation on impact → particles rebound or simply bounce off the substrate.  
 2. 1 ≤ VR ≤ 2  
    • Particle kinetic energy is high enough to induce adiabatic‐shear instabilities at the interface, jet the oxides off, and create intimate metal–metal contact → high deposition efficiency, good coating build-up with moderate residual stress.  
 3. VR > 2  
    • You begin to overdrive the interface.  Substrate erosion (grit-blasting), particle fracturing or excessive heating occur → coating porosity rises, particles break up, residual stresses and nozzle wear go up, and overall deposition efficiency actually falls.  

Thus by keeping VR between about 1 and 2 you ensure every particle carries just enough energy to bond, but not so much that it damages the growing coating or substrate.

In cold spray the solid particles are accelerated to high speeds (typically 300–1200 m/s) and bond to the substrate (or to previously‐deposited particles) almost exclusively by plastic deformation rather than by melting.  The key role of impact velocity can be summarized in three points:

1. Kinetic Energy and Plastic Deformation  
   – The particle’s kinetic energy Eₖ = ½ m·v² must exceed a threshold so that, on impact, the local stress state exceeds the material’s dynamic yield strength.  
   – Above this “critical velocity” (v_c) the particle undergoes intense adiabatic shear deformation at its front face and at the substrate interface.  This creates a high‐strain‐rate plastic flow field rather than elastic rebound.

2. Adiabatic Shear Instability and Jetting  
   – At velocities above v_c, the interface experiences adiabatic heating in a very thin shear band.  The temperature rise there softens the metal instantaneously, driving a lateral “metal jet” that strips away surface oxides and contaminants.  
   – Once oxides are disrupted and fresh metal is in atomic contact, a metallurgical bond forms under the high local pressures (on the order of GPa).

3. Bonding Window and Erosion Regime  
   – Below v_c: insufficient deformation, particles simply rebound or adhere weakly by mechanical interlocking.  
   – Between v_c and some upper limit v_max: stable bonding regime; deposition efficiency and bond strength rise steeply with velocity.  
   – Above v_max: excessive kinetic energy causes substrate erosion, particle rebound, or severe work‐hardening and cracking—bond strength and deposition efficiency can actually decrease.

Factors that set v_c (and v_max) include particle and substrate yield strengths, hardness, density, and thermal properties.  Empirically, v_c typically scales as roughly   
   v_c ∝ √[Y/ρ]  
where Y is a characteristic dynamic yield stress and ρ is density.  Hard, high-strength alloys demand higher velocities to achieve the necessary adiabatic shear for bonding; softer metals bond at lower velocities.

In practice, optimizing the spray gas pressure, temperature, nozzle design, and standoff distance tunes the particle velocity into the narrow window that maximizes deposition rate and bond strength without causing damage.

Key differences between cold‐spray and conventional thermal‐spray processes arise from whether particles are melted (or semi-melted) and how they bond to the substrate.  

1. Deposition Mechanism  
  • Thermal spray (plasma, HVOF, flame):  
    – Feedstock is heated into a molten or semi-molten state.  
    – High-velocity droplets impinge, flatten (“splat”), solidify rapidly, and build up a lamellar coating.  
    – Bonding relies on mechanical interlock plus some metallurgical diffusion at splat interfaces while cooling from the melt.  
  • Cold spray:  
    – Feedstock particles remain solid (T ≪ Tm) and are accelerated to 300–1200 m/s by a high-pressure gas jet.  
    – Upon impact, severe plastic deformation (strain rate ~10^6–10^9 s^–1) creates adiabatic shear instabilities at particle/substrate interfaces.  
    – Dynamic recrystallization and metallic bonding occur without melting.  

2. Defect Formation  
  • Porosity  
    – Thermal spray: 5–15 % porosity typically arises from entrapped gases, unmelted particles, and incomplete splat coalescence.  
    – Cold spray: very low porosity (<1–3 %) if particle velocity exceeds the critical bonding velocity; otherwise you get isolated unbonded particles or inter-particle voids.  
  • Oxides and inclusions  
    – Thermal spray: high flame/plasma temperatures promote oxidation of metal, incorporation of oxides and inclusions at splat interfaces.  
    – Cold spray: minimal thermal input keeps oxides from forming or growing; as-sprayed coatings are often oxide-free at interfaces.  
  • Microcracking and residual stress  
    – Thermal spray: rapid solidification and thermal cycling induce tensile residual stresses, interlamellar cracks, and brittle phase formation.  
    – Cold spray: impact-induced plasticity generates compressive residual stresses (good for fatigue resistance) and ultrafine grains; cracking is rare unless substrate bonding is poor.  
  • Phase transformations  
    – Thermal spray: possible partial vaporization, phase decomposition, grain coarsening, and amorphous phase formation.  
    – Cold spray: original feedstock microstructure is largely retained, apart from work-hardening and nanocrystalline layer formation at interfaces.  

In summary, cold spray’s solid-state, high-velocity impact route yields dense, low-oxide coatings with compressive stress and little thermal damage, whereas thermal spray relies on melting/splatting and typically exhibits higher porosity, oxide entrainment, lamellar interfaces and tensile residual stresses.

In cold spray AM, particles bond to the substrate not by melting but by extreme plastic deformation and the high‐strain‐rate mechanics of their supersonic impact.  The key steps are:  

1. Particle Acceleration  
   • Micron‐sized feedstock particles are accelerated to 300–1,200 m/s in a supersonic gas jet.  

2. High-Velocity Impact and Plastic Deformation  
   • Upon striking the substrate (or previously deposited layer), each particle experiences very high local pressures (on the order of GPa) and strain rates (10^6–10^9 s^–1).  
   • The kinetic energy is dissipated almost entirely into plastic deformation rather than heat (temperatures rise only locally and briefly).  

3. Adiabatic Shear Instability and Oxide/Contaminant Removal  
   • At the particle–substrate interface, the combination of high pressure and strain rate induces adiabatic shear bands.  
   • These shear bands fracture and jet away native oxides or surface contaminants, exposing fresh metal.  

4. Jetting and Surface Flattening  
   • Material jetting at the leading edge of the impact flattens the particle, increases real contact area, and further strips surface films.  

5. Solid-State Metallic Bonding  
   • Once oxide layers are broken and intimate, atomically clean metal surfaces meet under GPa‐level pressure, enabling metallic bonding (interatomic attraction) across the interface.  
   • Mechanical interlocking from the deformed particle geometry also contributes to bond strength.  

Because there is no bulk melting, the result is a fully consolidated, low‐oxidation deposit whose adhesion and cohesion originate in severe plastic deformation, oxide removal by adiabatic shear, and subsequent solid‐state metallic bonding.

Cold‐spray deposition efficiency and coating quality are overwhelmingly governed by the particle impact velocity (and hence the gas jet conditions), with a secondary but still important role played by powder feed and geometrical parameters.  In rough order of influence you get:

1.  Particle impact velocity  (the single most critical factor)  
    – Controlled by:  
      • Gas temperature (T) – higher T → lower gas density → higher sound speed → higher particle vₚ  
      • Gas pressure (P) – higher P → higher mass flow → higher vₚ  
      • Gas species (He > N₂ > Ar for the same P,T because of molecular weight)  
      • Nozzle geometry (throat diameter, area‐ratio, length, divergent angle)

2.  Powder feed rate/carrier‐gas flow  
    – Too low: poor deposition efficiency  
    – Too high: strong particle–particle collisions, jet choking, velocity drop

3.  Stand-off distance (SOD)  
    – Affects gas expansion, jet divergence and particle deceleration  
    – Typically 10–40 mm, optimized for each nozzle/power configuration

4.  Spray incidence angle  
    – Best at 90° to substrate; deviations reduce normal component of vₚ and bonding

5.  Traverse speed (scanning or raster rate)  
    – Governs local mass build‐up, layer thickness uniformity and thermal buildup

6.  Powder size distribution & morphology  
    – Smaller powders accelerate faster but carry less momentum; wide size spreads broaden velocity distribution and can hurt DE

7.  (Less directly, substrate preparation: roughness, temperature and cleanliness)

In practice, you tune T and P first (to meet a target vₚ), then adjust powder feed, SOD and angle to maximize deposition efficiency and coating cohesion.

Adhesion in cold spray is governed almost entirely by getting particles to exceed a material-specific “critical velocity,” above which impact causes the severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear‐induced jetting needed to clean oxide films and forge a metallurgical bond.  In practice this means:

 1. Particle velocities above about 400–1 200 m/s  
    – Al-alloys in N₂: vc ≈ 500–700 m/s  
    – Cu in N₂: vc ≈ 700–900 m/s  
    – Ti and steels: vc ≈ 900–1 200 m/s  
  These are achieved by expanding N₂ or He through a De Laval nozzle at inlet pressures of 3–8 MPa and temperatures up to ≈ 600 °C, yielding Mach 1.5–3 jets (gas exit ~600–1 000 m/s).  

 2. Particle sizes in the 5–50 µm range (optimum ~10–30 µm)  
    – Small enough to accelerate to high velocity over a short nozzle length  
    – Large enough to carry sufficient momentum to plastically deform on impact  

Below these velocity/size windows particles simply rebound or erode the substrate; above them you get the jetting, oxide‐stripping and high-strain deformation essential for cold-spray bonding.

In low‐pressure cold spray you often cannot get metal particles to deform and weld to each other or to the substrate unless you “help” the process by adding a population of very hard, brittle particles (typically ceramics such as Al₂O₃, SiC or glass beads). These serve principally as in-situ shot peening media:

  •  Oxide‐film disruption.  Ceramic “shots” impact first, crack or spall off the thin, tenacious oxide on both the substrate and previously deposited metal, exposing fresh metal surfaces.  
  •  Micro‐peening/hammering.  Even at lower gas pressures, the hard ceramics introduce additional localized plastic deformation (“hammer blows”) that drive the metal particles past their critical bonding velocity and into intimate contact.  
  •  Compressive residual stress.  Repeated micro-peening helps close porosity, refines grain size at the interface, and can introduce light compressive stresses that improve adhesion.

Drawbacks of introducing ceramic shot-peening particles:

  1.  Non-bonded inclusions.  Because the ceramics do not plastically deform or metallurgically bond, they remain as hard islands or interfacial particles. These raise stress‐concentrators, reduce ductility and toughness, and can initiate cracks under fatigue or impact.  
  2.  Increased porosity/heterogeneity.  By volume they displace metal–metal contact, so if the ceramic fraction is too high you can actually end up with a more porous, lower‐density coating.  
  3.  Degraded functional properties.  Embedded ceramics often reduce electrical or thermal conductivity, hamper corrosion resistance (through galvanic effects or crevice sites), and make post‐spray finishing (grinding, polishing) harder.  
  4.  Process and equipment wear.  Abrasive particles accelerate nozzle and fixture erosion, contribute to powder‐handling wear, and impose tighter maintenance and filtration requirements.  

In practice you balance just enough ceramic shot‐peening additive to recover deposition efficiency at low pressure without compromising the coating’s ductility, integrity or service properties.

Substrate pre-treatment by grit-blasting with coarse ceramic particles (for example, angular alumina, 50–150 µm) is one of the most widely used ways to boost adhesion in cold spray.  The principal effects are:

1. Increased surface roughness and anchor profile  
   • Blasting creates under-cut “peaks and valleys” (Ra typically rises from <1 µm to 3–10 µm), which gives sprayed particles mechanical interlocking sites.  
   • Pull-off and tensile-adhesion tests typically show a 20–50 % increase in bond strength versus polished or lightly abraded substrates.

2. Oxide and contamination removal  
   • The high-velocity impact of hard ceramic grains strips off native oxides, mill scale and oils, exposing fresh metal and raising surface free energy.  
   • Cleaner surfaces facilitate closer metal-to-metal contact in the severe, adiabatic-shear bonding zones of cold spray.

3. Substrate work-hardening and strain hardening  
   • On ductile substrates (Al, Cu, steels), grit blasting induces a thin, work-hardened layer.  That layer can absorb impact energy more uniformly and reduce substrate deformation under the cold spray jet, helping more particles to reach the critical velocity for bonding.

4. Caveats of “over-blasting”  
   • If the abrasive is too large or the blasting pressure too high, you can embed ceramic debris into the substrate.  These hard inclusions act as brittle interlayers, interrupting metal–metal contact and locally preventing the adiabatic shear bonding mechanism.  
   • Excessive roughness (Ra ≫10 µm) may also trap spray powder in voids rather than producing load-bearing interlocks, and can lead to higher porosity in the coating’s base.

Guidelines for best results:  
- Use angular alumina around 80–120 µm at pressures of 4–6 bar (depending on nozzle distance) to achieve Ra ≈5–8 µm.  
- Follow immediately (within minutes) with cold spray to avoid re-oxidation or contamination.  
- Inspect by microscopy or X-ray to verify that blasting has not embedded abrasive fragments below the critical bonding zone.  

In practice, this kind of pre-treatment routinely lifts static adhesion values from the low tens of megapascals into the 30–50 MPa range (pull-off or tensile).  Beyond that, bond strength gains asymptote—and risks of brittle inclusions or excessive porosity rise—if the blasting becomes too aggressive.

High particle velocity is the defining feature of cold spray—and it is essential because only when powder particles impact at very high speed do they acquire enough kinetic energy to cold-weld rather than merely bounce or fracture. Here’s how it works:  

1. Kinetic energy and critical velocity  
  •  Kinetic Energy (KE) ∝ ½·m·v².  Only when particle velocity v exceeds a material-specific “critical velocity” (typically 300–1200 m/s for metals) is KE sufficient to generate the local stresses needed for bonding.  
  •  Below that threshold, particles simply rebound or form a weak mechanical interlock; above it, they adhere and consolidate into a dense deposit.  

2. Impact-induced plastic deformation  
  •  At v ≥ vcrit, the instantaneous impact pressure can reach the gigapascal range. This drives extremely high strain rates (10⁶–10⁹ s⁻¹) in the near-surface of both the particle and the substrate.  
  •  Such severe plastic deformation cleans and breaks up surface oxides, oxide films and adsorbates, exposing fresh metal.  

3. Adiabatic shear and jetting  
  •  The high-strain-rate region undergoes localized adiabatic heating and shear instabilities, which eject a thin metallic “jet” at the interface.  
  •  This jetting action mechanically interlocks the two surfaces and creates intimate metal-to-metal contact on a microscopic scale.  

4. Metallurgical bonding  
  •  Once oxide barriers are disrupted and fresh metal surfaces are pressed together under high pressure, atomic diffusion and metallic bonding take over—even at temperatures well below melting.  
  •  Dynamic recrystallization in the plastically deformed zone refines the grain structure, further improving bond strength and coating density.  

In short, high particle velocities in cold spray convert kinetic energy into the mechanical work needed to (a) rupture surface films, (b) generate extreme local pressures and shear, and (c) create clean, high-pressure metal contacts that cold-weld into a solid, low-porosity deposit.

Key Concept  
In cold spray, bonding occurs when impacting particles deform plastically enough—often via adiabatic shear instability—to jet away oxides/contamination and forge‐weld to the substrate. The “critical velocity” is the minimum particle speed at which this happens. It is not a universal constant but depends on a host of interrelated material, particle, substrate, and process parameters.

1. Material Mechanical Properties  
  • Yield strength and hardness – Higher strengths require more kinetic energy (i.e. higher velocity) to achieve the critical plastic strain.  
  • Strain‐rate sensitivity and work‐hardening – Materials that harden rapidly under high‐strain‐rate loading demand higher impact velocities.  
  • Ductility/toughness – More ductile alloys absorb deformation more readily, lowering the critical velocity.  
  • Density – Affects momentum (½mv²), so heavier particles at the same speed carry more energy.  
  • Thermal properties (conductivity, specific heat) – Control heat buildup in the shear zone; high conductivity can bleed off heat needed to trigger adiabatic shear, raising the critical velocity.

2. Particle Attributes  
  • Size and size distribution – Smaller particles accelerate faster in the gas stream but carry less energy per particle; larger ones require higher gas pressures/velocities to reach bonding-threshold energy.  
  • Shape and surface condition – Irregular shapes or rough surfaces promote localized strain and jet formation; thick oxides or adsorbed contaminants raise the barrier to metal-to-metal contact.  
  • Temperature – Particles preheated by the gas are softer and need somewhat lower velocities.

3. Substrate Characteristics  
  • Hardness/strength – A harder substrate opposes deformation, pushing the critical velocity upward.  
  • Surface preparation – Roughening promotes mechanical interlocking; oxide or contaminant films must be disrupted for metallurgical bonding.  
  • Temperature – Preheating the substrate reduces its yield strength and oxide cohesion, lowering the required particle velocity.

4. Process Gas and Nozzle Parameters  
  • Gas species (He vs. N₂ vs. Ar) – Lighter gases (He) achieve higher sound speeds and particle exit velocities at a given pressure, lowering the critical impact speed requirement.  
  • Gas temperature and pressure – Higher gas temperatures reduce particle strength (thermal softening) and increase exit velocity; higher pressures accelerate particles more.  
  • Nozzle geometry (throat diameter, length, expansion ratio) – Controls the velocity profile and temperature of the gas, hence particle speed and heating.

5. Spray Configuration  
  • Stand-off distance – Too close and particles haven’t fully accelerated; too far and they decelerate or cool before impact. There is an optimal distance for peak velocity.  
  • Spray angle – Off-normal impact can increase the effective critical velocity by reducing normal strain on impact.  
  • Traverse speed and overlap – Affect cooling, reheating, and work‐hardening of the growing deposit and local substrate.

6. Environmental and Statistical Factors  
  • Chamber pressure (vacuum or ambient) – Influences gas expansion and particle deceleration.  
  • In-flight collisions and clustering – Can broaden the velocity distribution, meaning only a fraction of particles exceed the critical threshold.  

Design Implication  
To minimize the critical velocity—and thus energy consumption—one typically preheats gas and/or substrate, selects the lightest practicable gas (He when budget allows), optimizes nozzle geometry for maximum particle acceleration, and chooses or conditions feedstock (size, shape, surface) to be as oxide‐free and ductile as possible.

Post‐deposition heat treatments (HTs) are routinely used to “activate” and strengthen cold‐sprayed coatings by evolving residual stress states, microstructure and interface chemistry.  In broad terms, HT affects adhesion in three ways:

1. Stress relief and densification  
   • As‐sprayed coatings carry high compressive and tensile residual stresses from particle impingement.  A moderate HT (typically 0.3–0.6 T m.p. for 1–4 h) relaxes those stresses, reduces microcracking, and allows slight plastic creep under the constraint of neighboring particles.  
   • This creep closes nano‐voids at interparticle and substrate–coating boundaries, raising the true contact area and mechanical interlock.

2. Interdiffusion and metallurgical bonding  
   • At elevated temperatures atoms diffuse across oxide‐free metal–metal contacts formed by adiabatic shear.  Even small diffusion distances (tens of nanometers) can turn a mechanical joint into a metallurgical one.  
   • In alloys such as Al, Cu, Ni or Ti, HT can dissolve thin oxide films or redistribute them to grain boundaries, exposing fresh metal for bonding.  On steel substrates a thin interdiffusion zone (e.g. Fe–Ni solid solution) will form, boosting adhesion.

3. Microstructural evolution (pros and cons)  
   • Recrystallization and grain growth lower the hardness of highly cold‐worked splats, improving ductility and the ability to accommodate mismatch strains at the interface.  
   • If too aggressive (T > 0.7 T m.p. or very long times) grain coarsening reduces strength, and thick intermetallic or oxide layers can form at boundaries.  Large CTE mismatches during cooling may then crack or delaminate the coating.

Optimal adhesion gains are therefore seen at intermediate HT temperatures and times—enough to relieve stress and drive short‐range diffusion, but below the regime where deleterious coarsening or oxidation dominates.  Typical example windows are 300–400 °C/1 h for Al, 400–600 °C/1–2 h for Cu and Ni, or 500–700 °C/1 h for Ti‐based coatings, always tailored to substrate compatibility.

Key factors controlling particle velocity in a cold‐spray process fall into four broad categories—gas properties and conditions, nozzle design, powder characteristics, and process setup.  

1. Gas properties and operating conditions  
  • Gas type—helium has a higher speed of sound and lower molecular weight than nitrogen, so for a given pressure and temperature it accelerates particles to higher velocities.  
  • Gas stagnation pressure (P0)—higher feed pressure raises the jet’s momentum and exit Mach number, increasing drag acceleration on particles.  
  • Gas stagnation temperature (T0)—preheating lowers gas density and raises Mach number; too much heating, however, can soften or oxidize particles and reduce drag.  
  • Back‐pressure (ambient or chamber pressure)—in a pressurized enclosure or against residual pressure the expansion ratio is reduced, slowing particles.  

2. Nozzle geometry and flowpath  
  • Converging–diverging profile—throat diameter, diverging‐section half‐angle and length define the achievable Mach number and expansion ratio.  
  • Nozzle length—longer diverging sections allow particles more residence time to accelerate but can increase wall friction.  
  • Throat aspect ratio and surface finish—a rough or partially choked throat can induce shocks or turbulence that reduce effective particle acceleration.  
  • Standoff distance—excessive distance lets the jet spread and decelerate; too short and particles may impinge improperly.  

3. Powder properties  
  • Particle size and size distribution—smaller particles accelerate more easily (higher drag‐to‐mass ratio) but also decelerate faster in the free jet.  
  • Particle density—the denser the material, the greater its inertia, so heavier particles reach a lower terminal velocity under the same drag force.  
  • Particle shape and surface roughness—irregular or rough particles have higher drag coefficients and may heat or erode more in the jet.  
  • Powder feed rate (mass loading)—high feed rates can “steal” momentum from the gas, reducing the achievable velocity; optimum loading balances throughput and velocity.  

4. Process setup and injection strategy  
  • Injection angle and position—axial versus radial injection or multi‐port feed alters particle residence time in the high‐velocity core of the jet.  
  • Carrier‐gas versus direct injection—direct (pneumatic) injection into the throat gives better velocity control than simple carrier‐gas entrainment.  
  • Preheating of powder—raising particle temperature (within limits) can reduce yield strength, improving deformability at lower impact speeds but may slightly change their drag response.  
  • Chamber environment—vacuum or inert‐gas chambers reduce drag losses from ambient air entrainment and can raise effective particle speed.  

By tuning these interdependent parameters—gas choice and thermodynamic state, nozzle design, powder size/shape/density, feed strategy and standoff—you optimize particle acceleration and hence impact velocity and coating quality.

One of the simplest, equipment‐free ways to get your particles to deform more in cold spray is to tailor the powder itself rather than the gun.  In practice that means switching to a bimodal (or even trimodal) feedstock mix and/or using a finer size fraction of your existing powder.  

How it works:  
•  Fine particles (say 5–15 µm) in the mix act as “momentum carriers” and fill the interstices between the larger particles (30–75 µm or whatever your coarse fraction is).  
•  On impact, the fines plastically deform first, generating localized heating and shear bands at the substrate interface.  That pre-softens or “lubricates” the bond area, so when the large particles arrive they undergo a higher strain before rebounding.  
•  The result is a flatter, more spread‐out “splat” for each large particle, fewer voids in the deposit and better overall deposition efficiency—yet you haven’t changed your hardware at all, only the powder feedstock.  

In short, by optimizing your powder size distribution and morphology you can boost particle deformation, bond strength and build rate without ever touching the cold‐spray gun.

Key points for surface finishing of cold‐spray coatings when fatigue life is critical:

1. Minimize surface roughness  
   • Rough peaks and valleys act as crack‐initiation sites.  
   • Target Ra ≤ 1 µm (or as dictated by application); Ra < 0.5 µm for high‐cycle fatigue.  
   • Typical route: light grinding (200–400 grit), finish‐grinding (600–1200 grit), then polishing if needed.

2. Remove lamellar ridges and overspray  
   • The stacked “splats” in as‐sprayed coatings form intersplat ridges that concentrate stress.  
   • Use controlled grinding, honing or superfinishing to level the top surface without inducing heat damage.

3. Control induced residual stresses  
   • Cold spray coatings inherently have compressive residual stress, which is beneficial for fatigue.  
   • Aggressive machining or grinding can relieve or even flip to tensile.  
   • Use low-feed, high-speed grinding with coolant; check residual stress (e.g. X-ray diffraction) post-finish.

4. Avoid heat build-up  
   • Excessive heat from grinding or polishing softens or over‐ages the coating/substrate interface.  
   • Use coolant or intermittent grinding, keep surface temperature < 100 °C where possible.

5. Ensure uniform thickness and eliminate geometric notches  
   • Variations in coating thickness change local stiffness and stress distribution.  
   • Precision machining or CNC grinding helps maintain uniform section modulus.  
   • Chamfer edges smoothly rather than leave sharp termination.

6. Seal pores if corrosion-fatigue is a concern  
   • Even a small open pore can be a fatigue‐crack origin under corrosive environments.  
   • Options: resin impregnation, low‐temperature diffusion sealing, or thin conformal convert‐coating.

7. Validate finish quality  
   • Measure surface profile (stylus or optical profilometry), residual stress (XRD, hole‐drill) and inspect for microcracks or delamination (dye‐penetrant, ultrasonic).

By combining a judicious grinding/polishing schedule, tight control of induced stresses, and verification of roughness and coating integrity, you can safeguard against surface‐initiated fatigue failures in cold-spray coatings.

Key distinctions between cold spray and conventional (“thermal”) spray arise from whether particles are melted prior to impact and how bonding is achieved:

1. Particle State and Temperature  
   • Thermal spray (plasma, HVOF, flame, arc): feedstock is heated above or near its melting point. Molten or semi-molten droplets travel to the substrate.  
   • Cold spray: feedstock remains solid (typically <0.5Tm); gas temperatures are well below melting, and particles gain kinetic—not thermal—energy.

2. Driving Force for Deposition  
   • Thermal spray: surface wetting and fusion–solidification. Droplets flatten on impact (“splats”), solidify rapidly, and build up in layered lamellae.  
   • Cold spray: purely kinetic. Particles accelerate to supersonic velocities (300–1,200 m/s) and bond by severe plastic deformation, adiabatic shear instabilities, and the formation of localized metallic jets.

3. Bonding Mechanism  
   • Thermal spray: metallurgical bonding via fusion between splat and substrate or between splats. Residual oxides can form at splat boundaries.  
   • Cold spray: solid‐state bonding. Intimate atomic contact results from mechanical interlocking, disruption of surface oxides by jetting, and dynamic recrystallization at high strain rates (10^6–10^8 s^–1).

4. Microstructure and Defects  
   • Thermal spray: rapid solidification can yield metastable phases, internal microcracks, unmelted particles, lamellar porosity, and oxide films.  
   • Cold spray: highly dense deposits (>99% theoretical density), minimal oxidation, preserved feedstock phase, but pronounced work hardening and grain refinement near interfaces.

5. Residual Stress and Adhesion  
   • Thermal spray: stresses from cooling and phase changes can be tensile or compressive; adhesion relies on mechanical keying plus fusion.  
   • Cold spray: predominantly compressive residual stresses (from impact peening), high adhesion via plastically deformed interfacial zone, seldom requiring post-treatment.

6. Process Windows and Materials  
   • Thermal spray: wide temperature range suits ceramics, refractories, polymers (all melted or partially so). Oxidation-sensitive metals can degrade.  
   • Cold spray: best for ductile metals and alloys (Al, Cu, Ni, Ti) that respond to high-strain bonding; ceramics and hard phases are difficult to deposit unless co-sprayed with ductile carriers.

In essence, thermal spray fuses molten droplets into a layered structure, whereas cold spray relies on supersonic, solid‐state particle impact to plastically weld coatings without melting.

Cold‐spray additive manufacturing (also called cold spray or gas dynamic spray) deposits metal coatings by purely solid-state bonding of high‐velocity particles. Its operating principle can be summarized as follows:

1. Powder acceleration  
   • A carrier gas (N₂, He or air), often preheated to 200–800 °C, is expanded through a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle to supersonic speeds (300–1 200 m/s).  
   • Metal powder (typically 5–50 μm) is injected into the high–speed gas jet and accelerated to velocities above a material-specific “critical velocity.”

2. High-strain‐rate impact  
   • Each particle impacts the substrate (or previously deposited layer) at speeds high enough to induce severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear instabilities in a very short time (µs).  
   • Impact pressures locally exceed the flow stress, breaking up surface oxides and contaminants.

3. Solid-state bonding  
   • The combination of extreme plastic flow, dynamic recrystallization at the interface and the removal of intervening films allows fresh metal–metal contact and metallurgical bonding without melting.  
   • Subsequent particles build up layer by layer to form a dense, cohesive coating or bulk structure.

Key advantages  
– Minimal thermal input avoids melting, oxidation and distortion.  
– Retains feedstock microstructure and mechanical properties.  
– Enables thick, high-quality coatings or freeform builds with low residual stresses.

The cold-spray process can be understood as three coupled gas-dynamic and particle-deposition stages:  

1. High-pressure gas expansion and jet formation  
   • A light carrier gas (N₂, He or H₂) is pressurized (10–40 MPa) and optionally preheated (300 – 800 °C).  
   • This gas expands isentropically through a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle.  Across the throat and into the diverging section the local Mach number M rises according to  
     A/A* = (1/M) · [ (2/(γ+1))·(1 + (γ–1)/2·M²) ]^((γ+1)/[2(γ–1)])  
   • The exit Mach number and corresponding jet velocity u  ≈ M·(γ·R·T₀)½ can exceed 500–1 500 m/s, producing a collimated supersonic jet.  

2. Particle entrainment and acceleration  
   • Powder (2–50 µm) is injected just upstream of the throat.  Particles accelerate in the supersonic stream under drag:  
     F_d = ½·C_d·ρ_g·A_p·(u_g – u_p)²  
   • Given enough nozzle length, particles reach a large fraction of the gas velocity.  Their trajectory stays within the Mach disk region for uniform acceleration.  

3. Impact, plastic deformation, and bonding  
   • Particles strike the substrate at velocities above a material-specific “critical velocity” (300–1 000 m/s).  Below that they tend to rebound.  
   • Upon impact the kinetic energy is converted to plastic work in a micron-scale region.  Extremely high strain rates (10⁶–10⁹ s⁻¹) and adiabatic shear cause localized heating, oxide-film disruption, surface freshening, grain refinement and dynamic recrystallization.  
   • Fresh metallic surfaces come into intimate contact under high pressure and microscopic interlocking.  This yields a predominantly solid-state, oxide-free bond with minimal feedstock heating, avoiding melting, oxidation or undesirable phase changes.  

By repeating this bombardment, a dense, high-adhesion coating builds up with little heat input to the substrate (typical substrate temperatures < 500 °C).

In aluminum cold-spray the metal powders are carried at very high speed in a hot, supersonic gas jet.  What you discover in practice is that aluminum particles are very “sticky” to conventional cold-spray nozzles (steel, tungsten, even ceramics), so you get rapid build-up, clogging, frequent shutdowns, nozzle machining or replacement, and sometimes unwanted iron contamination of your coating.

High-temperature plastics (for example PEEK, PEK, Torlon®, Ultem®) offer a surprisingly elegant solution.  Their key advantages are:

1. Low surface energy/non-wetting.  Aluminum doesn’t cold-weld to the polymer the way it does to steel or tungsten, so you do not get the same hard, adherent build-up of particles inside the throat or on the exit lip.

2. Lower thermal conductivity.  A plastic nozzle holds heat in the gas stream instead of bleeding it off into a metal body.  That translates into slightly higher gas/particle temperatures and velocities at the exit plane, improving deposition efficiency without extra power.

3. Electrical insulation.  By preventing particle charging on the nozzle walls you reduce powder‐flow instabilities and “sticking” due to triboelectric effects.

4. Cost, weight and manufacturability.  Polymer nozzles can be injection-molded or 3D-printed in complex, optimized profiles at low cost.  They’re lighter to handle, quick to swap, and you avoid expensive precision machining and the downtime associated with metal or ceramic replacements.

5. Noise dampening and wear resistance.  The inherent damping in a polymer body can reduce jet noise, and because aluminum simply doesn’t “bite” into the plastic nearly as aggressively, these nozzles often last longer in run‐hours before you even consider swapping one out.

In short, plastic cold-spray nozzles for aluminum combine non-stick behavior, thermal advantages, lower powder charging, and much lower life-cycle cost—all of which translate directly into higher uptime, more consistent coating properties, and less maintenance than you get with conventional metal or ceramic nozzles.

Particle impact velocity is one of the primary knobs in cold spray.  As you raise the velocity across the critical-velocity threshold for a given material, you progressively move from “no deposition” through marginal bonding to full, high-quality coating.  The key microstructural effects are:  

1. Critical-velocity threshold  
   • Below VCrit: particles rebound or fragment; essentially no plastic deformation or bonding takes place.  No coating, intact oxide films, coarse original microstructure.  

2. Just at or slightly above VCrit  
   • Partial bonding.  Particles flatten but only modestly, producing lamellae with gaps and oxide remnants at interfaces.  
   • Plastic strain localizes in narrow shear zones; little or no dynamic recrystallization (DRX) beyond the immediate contact.  
   • Resulting microstructure: mixed zones of deformed parent grains and some subgrain formation near the interface; moderate porosity.  

3. Moderate over-velocity (optimum window)  
   • Severe plastic deformation (strain rates ~10^6–10^8 s–1) drives adiabatic shear and high‐strain‐rate DRX.  
   • You see an ultrafine to nanocrystalline layer (10–500 nm grains) at particle/substrate and particle/particle boundaries.  
   • Oxide films are fragmented and dispersed; lamellae weld into a near‐fully dense, equiaxed or elongated fine-grain structure.  
   • Mechanical properties (hardness, bond strength) peak; porosity falls below 1–2 %.  

4. Very high velocities (≫ optimum)  
   • Further intensification of DRX and adiabatic shear bands can cause localized heating, microcracking, or even particle erosion.  
   • Excessive residual tensile stresses may develop in the deposit.  
   • Deposition efficiency can drop as particles begin to shatter or erode the substrate rather than plastically weld.  

Material dependence  
• Soft alloys (Al, Cu): VCrit ~300–500 m/s, optimum ~600–800 m/s  
• Ti, stainless steels: VCrit ~700–900 m/s, optimum ~900–1200 m/s  
• Hard ceramics (WC, oxides): require still higher velocities or specialized carriers  

In summary, increasing impact velocity up through the material’s optimum window systematically increases particle flattening, strain-rate–induced recrystallization, oxide fragmentation and lamellar bonding, yielding a denser, ultrafine-grained coating.  Pushing past that window risks erosion, embrittlement and loss of deposition efficiency.

The glass‐transition temperature (Tg) of a polymer powder is in effect the dividing line between its “glassy,” brittle state and its “rubbery,” viscoelastic state at room (or spray) temperature.  In cold spray, particles need to deform plastically on impact in order to wet and bond to the substrate.  If the polymer is still well below its Tg when it hits, it behaves like a little shard of glass—fracturing or rebounding instead of spreading—and you get very low deposition efficiency.  Conversely, if the particle temperature (either ambient plus any modest adiabatic or preheater boost) exceeds Tg, the particles will flatten, flow, and coalesce on impact, giving much higher deposition rates.

Key points:  
• Tg ≫ spray temperature → particles stay glassy → brittle fracture, poor deposition efficiency.  
• Tg ≲ spray temperature → particles enter rubbery/viscoelastic regime → plastic flow on impact, good adhesion and efficiency.  
• In practice you can either choose polymers with inherently low Tg (e.g. polyethylene grades with Tg well below 0 °C) or preheat the gas/powder so that higher‐Tg polymers (e.g. PMMA, PEEK) soften during flight.  
• Be wary of going too far below Tg: if the powder is too soft at feeding temperature it may agglomerate in the hopper or nozzle, leading to clogging or uneven powder delivery.  

So in short, the closer the powder’s Tg is to or below its actual spray/impact temperature, the easier it will plastically deform on impact and the higher the deposition efficiency in cold spray.

Powder morphology is one of the single most important “knobs” you can turn in cold spray.  In practice it dictates both how well the powder flows through feeders and hoses and how efficiently the particles convert propellant‐gas energy into bonded coatings.  Key effects are:

1. Sphericity and surface finish  
   • Spherical, smooth‐surfaced powders (sphericity >0.8) exhibit low interparticle friction and cohesion.  Hall‐flow rates are high, angles of repose are low, and feeders deliver a uniform, pulse-free mass flow.  
   • Irregular, plate‐like or dendritic morphologies interlock and bridge, causing erratic feed rates or blockages.  

2. Particle size distribution (PSD)  
   • A narrow, well-graded PSD limits segregation in the hopper and the feeder and prevents fine fractions from filling interstices and raising cohesion.  
   • Very broad or bi‐modal PSDs can lead to inhomogeneous feeding and localized overdosing of fines, spiking gas-solid momentum transfer.  

3. Porosity and internal structure  
   • Highly porous or spongy particles have lower true and bulk density, higher effective drag area, and trap gas pockets.  They accelerate more slowly, reach lower impact velocities and require higher driving pressure or temperature.  
   • Fully dense, gas-atomized powders accelerate more efficiently and deliver higher average particle velocity.  

4. Satellites and surface roughness  
   • Small satellites on larger particles raise the drag coefficient, broaden the particle‐velocity distribution, and reduce the fraction above critical velocity.  The result is lower deposition efficiency and often rougher coatings.  

5. Impact on deposition efficiency (DE)  
   • DE scales roughly with the fraction of particles exceeding critical velocity and with their momentum (ρV²).  Spherical, smooth, dense powders minimize in-flight drag and scatter, so more particles arrive above Vcrit and bond.  
   • Irregular or porous powders demand higher gas pressure/temperature to achieve the same DE and often still yield lower cohesion, higher residual stress and rougher microstructures.  

In short, to maximize flowability and deposition efficiency you want a narrow, fully dense, near-spherical powder with smooth surfaces and minimal satellites or internal porosity.

In cold spray you “glue” particles to a substrate by ramming them at supersonic speed so that they deform plastically, dissipate most of their kinetic energy at the impact interface, and build up a true metallurgical bond.  Non‐deforming ceramics simply can’t do that:

1. No plasticity → no intimate contact  
   • Ductile metals squash, spread, cold‐weld and create fresh, highly reactive surfaces that bond to the substrate or to each other.  
   • Ceramics (high hardness, high elastic modulus, low fracture toughness) rebound or shatter instead of flowing, so they never develop the large real contact area needed for strong adhesion.

2. High coefficient of restitution → most of the impact energy is retained or returned  
   • A hard, brittle particle bounces off (high e) or fractures, rather than “sticking” as a flattened splat.  
   • Metals have a much lower e, so they dissipate more energy at the interface and stay put.

3. Much higher critical velocity  
   • To force a ceramic to stick you need velocities well above those already sufficient for metals. In practical cold‐spray rigs you rarely exceed the critical velocity for ceramics, so very few particles ever reach the bonding threshold.

As a result of all three effects, the fraction of ceramic powder that actually deposits under the same conditions is far lower than that of a ductile metal powder.

Low‐pressure cold spray (typically 3–7 bar gas pressure, gas temperatures ≲350 °C) is almost always chosen for metallizing polymers because it:  

 1. Minimizes thermal load  
    • Keeps nozzle and spray gas temperatures well below the glass-transition or melting points of most common polymers.  
    • Avoids polymer softening, melting, scorching or outgassing that would lead to poor adhesion or surface damage.  

 2. Limits mechanical damage  
    • Generates particle impact velocities (300–600 m/s) high enough to plastically deform ductile metal particles but low enough to prevent brittle fracture, cracking or “pitting” of the much softer polymer.  
    • Reduces substrate erosion, recoil (particle bounce), and delamination that are common when using high‐pressure, high‐velocity sprays on low‐strength materials.  

 3. Provides sufficient adhesion on low‐energy surfaces  
    • Relies on mechanical interlocking: metal particles embed in the microscopic surface asperities and “bite” into the polymer without needing substrate pre-heating or aggressive surface abrasion.  
    • In many cases a light plasma or corona pretreatment is enough to raise surface energy for even better coating wettability and bond strength.  

 4. Lowers equipment complexity and cost  
    • Uses smaller compressors or shop air rather than the large, high‐pressure booster systems required for 30–40 bar “high‐pressure” cold spray.  
    • Makes bench‐top or portable systems feasible for in-field repairs, shielding‐critical parts, plastic housings, and lightweight assemblies.  

Together, these factors let you build up dense, adherent metal films on temperature‐ and impact‐sensitive polymer parts without thermal degradation, substrate fracturing, or excessive setup costs.

In cold spray the spray angle (θ) is the angle between the particle jet and the substrate surface normal.  It exerts a first‐order control on deposition efficiency (DE = mass deposited/mass sprayed) because it directly governs the normal component of the particle’s impact velocity and hence its ability to plastically deform and bond.

1. Normal‐incidence optimum  
   – At θ ≈ 90° (jet aligned with the surface normal) Vnormal=V · cos 0°=V, so kinetic‐energy transfer is maximized.  
   – DE reaches its peak—often 60–80 % or more for ductile metals (Cu, Al) at optimized gas pressures.

2. Oblique‐incidence drop‐off  
   – As the angle tilts away from normal (θ decreases from 90° toward the surface) the normal velocity falls as Vn=V·cos(90°–θ), reducing plastic deformation.  
   – Particles increasingly glance off or rebound; lateral momentum can even erode the deposit.  
   – Empirically, DE often scales roughly with the normal‐velocity fraction, DE(θ) ≈ DE(90°)·cos^n(90°–θ), where n≈1–2 depending on material and particle size.

3. Critical angle  
   – Below a certain spray angle (typically 60–70° from the normal, i.e. 20–30° above the surface plane) Vn drops below the material’s critical deposition velocity.  
   – DE falls toward zero; no net build‐up occurs.

4. Material and process dependence  
   – Softer, more ductile powders tolerate larger angular deviations before DE collapses; harder or smaller particles are more sensitive.  
   – Higher gas pressures (hence higher V) can shift the critical angle lower, improving off‐normal deposition.

Practical implication: to maximize DE you aim to keep the nozzle within ±10–15° of normal incidence or compensate (higher pressure, reduced standoff) when coating complex geometries.

In cold spray additive manufacturing (CSAM), particle velocity is the single most important parameter controlling whether—and how well—particles bond to the substrate (and to each other).  Here’s why:

1. Kinetic energy and critical velocity  
   • A particle of mass m traveling at velocity v carries kinetic energy Ek = ½ m v².  Only above a material‐dependent “critical velocity” (typically 300–1200 m/s for most metals) does the particle have enough energy to plastically deform and bond.  
   • Below this threshold the particle simply bounces (rebound) or sticks weakly via mechanical interlocking; above it, bonding becomes metallurgical.

2. Severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear  
   • When v ≥ critical velocity, impact generates very high local strain rates (10⁶–10⁸ s⁻¹).  
   • This leads to adiabatic shear instabilities at the interface, producing a thin jet of material that expels surface oxides and contaminants.  
   • The result is intimate metal‐to‐metal contact, fresh surface exposure, and dynamic recrystallization—key steps in forming a strong, oxide‐free bond.

3. Deposition efficiency and coating quality  
   • As v increases above the critical value, deposition efficiency (the fraction of particles retained) rises sharply and then plateaus.  
   • Overly high velocities, however, can cause particle erosion of previously deposited layers, increased residual stress, or substrate damage.  
   • The optimal window of particle velocity yields dense, low‐porosity builds with fine microstructures and good mechanical properties.

4. Process control and materials tailoring  
   • Nozzle design, gas type and temperature, and standoff distance are adjusted to achieve the desired velocity distribution for a given powder–substrate pair.  
   • Tuning v allows engineers to balance deposition rate, bond strength, residual stress, and thermal effects without melting the powder.

In summary, reaching and controlling particle velocity around—and just above—the critical threshold is essential in CSAM. It governs the transition from mere mechanical contact to true metallurgical bonding through extreme, localized plastic deformation and oxide disruption, thereby determining coating adhesion, density, and overall part performance.

Increasing the stand‐off distance (SOD) in a cold‐spray process generally drives down both deposition efficiency (DE) and the internal cohesion of the deposit.  The root causes are:

 1. Particle‐gas dynamics  
    • As the powder–gas jet expands and entrains ambient air, shock cells break down and the supersonic core shrinks.  
    • Drag and turbulent mixing slow the particles, and in some gas chemistries they cool slightly.  
    • A larger SOD means more distance over which particles decelerate, so fewer particles reach or exceed the critical velocity for bonding.  

 2. Impact energy and plastic deformation  
    • Bonding in cold spray relies on high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation and adiabatic shear instabilities at the interface.  
    • With reduced impact velocity, particles deform less on impact, flatten less, and do not weld fully to the substrate or to each other.  
    • Internally, this shows up as higher porosity, more inter‐particle voids, poorer “splat” interlocking and lower cohesive strength.  

Practical effect:  
– DE typically peaks at some “optimum” SOD (often 20–40 mm for many systems) and then drops off sharply as SOD increases further.  
– Cohesive/tensile strength of the spray builds falls off in parallel—measured bond strengths can drop by 20–50 % if you double the SOD beyond its optimum.  

In short, once you move beyond the optimum spray distance, particle velocity and deformation both fall, so fewer particles stick and those that do stick form a weaker, more porous coating.

Below is a concise overview of the principal thermal-spray families and where cold spray fits in:

1. Combustion/Flame Spraying  
   • Process: A combustible gas (acetylene, propane or natural gas) is burned with oxygen. Powder or wire feedstock is entrained in the flame and propelled onto the substrate.  
   • Typical particle temperatures: 1,500–2,500 °C  
   • Typical particle velocities: 50–200 m/s  
   • Common coatings: metals (Cu, Al), ceramics (Al₂O₃), polymers  

2. Wire-Arc Spraying  
   • Process: Two consumable metal wires are electrically arced at their tips; molten droplets are atomized and directed by compressed air.  
   • Particle temperatures: 1,600–1,900 °C  
   • Particle velocities: 100–300 m/s  
   • Common coatings: steels, Ni alloys, Zn, Al  

3. Plasma Spraying (APS)  
   • Process: A non-transferred arc between a cathode and anode generates a plasma jet (argon, hydrogen, sometimes helium). Powder is injected axially or radially into the plasma and accelerated.  
   • Particle temperatures: 10,000–15,000 °C core (feedstock heats to 2,000–12,000 °C depending on dwell time)  
   • Particle velocities: 150–350 m/s
