   • Common coatings: ceramics (ZrO₂, Al₂O₃), carbides, cermets, refractory metals  

4. High-Velocity Oxy-Fuel (HVOF)  
   • Process: A high-pressure oxy-fuel combustion (propane, kerosene, hydrogen) produces a supersonic jet; feedstock powder is injected into this jet.  
   • Particle temperatures: 2,500–3,100 °C  
   • Particle velocities: 500–1,200 m/s  
   • Common coatings: WC–Co, NiCr, stainless steels, superalloys  

5. Detonation Gun (D-Gun) Spraying  
   • Process: Repetitive detonations of acetylene/oxygen in a barrel accelerate powder to extremely high velocities.  
   • Particle temperatures: 2,000–3,500 °C (very short exposure)  
   • Particle velocities: 1,200–1,500 m/s  
   • Common coatings: WC–Co, Ni alloys, ceramics  

6. Warm Spraying  
   • Process: A variant of HVOF or plasma where the gas temperature and pressure are adjusted to give intermediate particle velocities and temperatures between HVOF and cold spray.  
   • Particle temperatures: 200–700 °C  
   • Particle velocities: 300–700 m/s  

Cold Spray in Context  
• Mechanism: Particles (typically 1 – 50 µm) are entrained in a high‐pressure, supersonic gas jet (He or N₂), accelerated to 300–1,200 m/s, and deposited by plastic deformation on impact. There is little or no melting of the feedstock.  
• Unique features versus “thermal” spray:  
   – Minimal oxidation, phase transformation or residual stress from melting/re‐solidification.  
   – Very high bond strengths (often > 85 MPa) via metallurgical jetting and mechanical interlocking.  
   – Capability to deposit oxygen-sensitive alloys (Al, Cu, Ti) and nanostructured powders without degradation.  
• Relationship to other methods:  
   – Whereas flame, arc, plasma and HVOF rely on high temperatures to melt or semi-melt powders, cold spray relies on kinetic (rather than thermal) energy to consolidate powder.  
   – Particle velocities in cold spray overlap or exceed those of HVOF/D-Gun but particle temperatures remain near or below the substrate’s temperature capability, enabling coatings on heat-sensitive substrates.  

In summary, the “classic” thermal-spray family (flame, arc, plasma, HVOF, detonation) all use heat to melt feedstock and kinetic energy to propel droplets, whereas cold spray decouples these two functions—providing ultra-high velocity impact at low temperature—opening up coating possibilities for temperature-sensitive materials and applications requiring minimal oxidation or phase change.

Typical powder particle size ranges in cold spray AM  
• Fine‐feed systems (high pressure; low enthalpy): 5–25 µm  
• Standard‐feed systems (medium pressure; medium enthalpy): 15–45 µm  
• Coarser feedstocks (low‐pressure; high enthalpy or specialized nozzles): up to 50–100 µm  
(Note: optimal D₅₀ is often in the 20–40 µm range for most metals to balance flowability and deposition efficiency.)

Common carrier gases  
• Nitrogen (most widely used; lower cost; good for steels, Cu, Ni alloys)  
• Helium (light molecular weight ⇒ higher jet velocities; used for Al, Ti, superalloys)  
• Compressed air (very low cost; used for some steels but gives lower deposition rates)  
• Gas mixtures (e.g. N₂–He blends to trade off cost vs. velocity)  
• Occasional use of hydrogen or H₂–N₂ mixtures in research systems to boost velocity further  

Typical operating pressures are 10–40 bar and gas preheat temperatures of 200–1000 °C, depending on powder and desired impact velocity.

Key reasons why atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) of WC–Co powders is much harsher on the carbide than HVOF or lower-energy processes are:

1. Extremely high particle temperatures and long dwell times  
   • In a plasma torch particles can reach 12 000–15 000 K (vs. 3 000–4 000 K in HVOF), and they travel through the hot core for hundreds of micro- to milliseconds.  
   • WC is thermodynamically unstable at these temperatures; it decomposes by  
      WC → W2C + C or WC → W + CO/CO₂.  
   • The higher the particle temperature and residence time, the more extensive the decomposition.

2. Oxidizing and reducing species in the plasma plume  
   • Common plasma gases (Ar/H₂, Ar/N₂, sometimes air entrained) carry both oxygen and atomic hydrogen.  
   • Oxygen (even in ppm) oxidizes carbon to CO/CO₂.  
   • Atomic hydrogen attacks WC, stripping carbon to form CH₄ or H₂O and releasing free W.

3. Carbon solubility in the molten Co binder  
   • As WC particles partially or fully melt, carbon dissolves into the liquid Co.  
   • Upon rapid solidification, binder-lean and binder-rich regions form, leading to inhomogeneous microstructure.

4. Formation of brittle sub-carbides and free tungsten  
   • Decarburized regions renucleate as W₂C or metallic W, which are harder and more brittle than WC.  
   • These phases tend to form at splat boundaries and in the intersplat regions, embrittling the coating.

5. Consequences for coating microstructure  
   • Higher porosity and microcracking due to stresses from phase changes and volume contraction.  
   • Coarser grains (complete melting–solidification) rather than the finer, partially melted WC seen in HVOF.  
   • Binder-starved zones next to binder-rich areas, giving up to a 50 % drop in toughness.

In short, the very high thermal energy, the oxidizing/reducing chemistry of the plasma jet, and the long particle residence times combine to strip carbon out of WC, form brittle carbide/W phases, and yield a more porous, cracked, and compositionally inhomogeneous coating.

Deposition efficiency (DE = mass deposited/mass sprayed) in cold spray is governed almost entirely by whether particle impact velocity exceeds the material’s “critical velocity.” Propellant gas temperature (T0) and pressure (P0) set the gas‐jet Mach number, gas density and mass flow, which in turn determine how fast and how efficiently powder particles can be accelerated through the nozzle.  Key effects are:

1. Gas Temperature (T0)  
 • Higher T0 raises the local speed of sound (a0 ∝ √T0), so for a given nozzle pressure ratio you get a higher jet Mach number and jet exit velocity.  
 • Because the drag force on a particle Fdrag ∝ CD · ρg · A · (vg−vp)^2, the larger vg speeds particles up more rapidly and closer to vg over a shorter nozzle length.  
 • As particle velocity vp approaches or exceeds the critical velocity, DE rises sharply. Below critical velocity DE ≈ 0; above it DE climbs toward a plateau (70–90 % typical).  
 • Downside of excessively high T0 (> 600–800 °C on steel powders): oxidation of powder or feedstock, partial agglomeration, nozzle throat wear.

2. Gas Pressure (P0)  
 • Higher P0 (or higher P0/Pback) yields a stronger pressure drop through the converging–diverging nozzle, higher mass flow, and higher jet exit velocity.  
 • Higher gas density at higher absolute pressure gives more drag force for a given velocity differential and thus faster particle acceleration.  
 • DE rises with P0 until most particles reach or exceed critical velocity. Beyond that “saturation,” further pressure increases give only marginal DE gains and may lead to substrate erosion (over‐peening).

3. Interplay and Optimums  
 • You can trade off T0 and P0: raising T0 can allow operation at lower P0 for the same DE, and vice versa.  
 • Each material has its own critical velocity (e.g. ~500–600 m/s for Al, ~800–1000 m/s for Cu or Ni, 1000–1200 m/s for steels). You choose T0 / P0 so that the modeled particle velocity profile at your powder size reaches ~1.1–1.3 × critical velocity before impact.  
 • Too low T0 or P0 → vp < critical → almost zero DE.  
 • Too high T0 or P0 → possible erosion of deposits or substrate, nozzle wear, powder oxidation—DE plateaus or even falls.

Practical ranges  
 • Nitrogen runs: P0 = 20–40 bar, T0 = 300–800 °C.  
 • Helium runs (for very high critical‐velocity materials): P0 = 10–30 bar, T0 = 500–900 °C.

In summary, raising gas temperature and/or pressure boosts particle velocity (and thus DE) up to the point where particles reliably exceed their material’s critical velocity. Beyond that optimum window, further increases offer diminishing DE gains and introduce unwanted side effects.

Increasing the propellant gas temperature and/or pressure in a cold‐spray process drives down coating porosity almost invariably—up to a point—by boosting particle impact velocity, particle temperature (hence ductility), and dynamic pressure on impact.  In more detail:

1.  Effect of Temperature T₀  
    – Raising T₀ increases the total enthalpy of the gas.  Upon expansion through the nozzle this converts into greater exit velocity (v ≃ √[2·cₚ·T₀·(1–(pₑ/p₀)^((γ–1)/γ))]) and also warms the particles en route, lowering their yield strength and promoting plastic flow.  
    – Result: particles deform more readily on impact, fill voids more completely, and form stronger metallic bonds → lower porosity.

2.  Effect of Pressure p₀  
    – Increasing the supply pressure p₀ raises the pressure ratio p₀/pₑ and inlet gas density.  Both drive up Mach number and mass flow, so particles accelerate to higher velocities and experience higher drag‐force heating in the jet.  
    – Result: again, greater particle kinetic energy and ductility at impact → denser coatings.

3.  Quantitative trends  
    – At low T₀/p₀ (e.g. 300 °C, 20 bar He) porosities of 5–15 % are common.  
    – At moderate conditions (500–600 °C, 30–40 bar) porosity falls below 2 % and can approach 0.5 % in optimized runs.  
    – Beyond ~600 °C or ~40–50 bar one sees diminishing returns: porosity asymptotes as velocity well exceeds the critical velocity for deformation, and excessive velocity can even introduce microcracks or substrate erosion.

4.  Practical takeaway  
    – To minimize porosity, raise T₀ and/or p₀ until you reach the velocity window where particles plastically deform fully but do not over‐impact.  In most metal systems that window lies around 500–650 °C and 30–50 bar (with He or N₂), yielding porosities <1 %.

Post‐deposition heat treatments (furnace anneals, hot isostatic pressing, etc.) are almost invariably applied to cold–sprayed coatings because the as‐sprayed deposit, though well attached, is held together largely by mechanical interlocking and adiabatic‐shear welds rather than true metallurgical fusion.  In practice this leaves the coating with some combination of  

 •  residual dislocation‐rich, strain‐hardened microstructure  
 •  incomplete inter‐particle bonding and interfacial micro‐voids (porosity)  
 •  high tensile residual stresses at and near the substrate interface  
 •  only nascent (or absent) diffusion bridges across oxide films  

A carefully chosen post‐spray thermal cycle remedies these issues by:  

1.   Driving boundary and grain‐boundary diffusion so that neighboring particle surfaces “neck” and sinter  
2.   Healing micro‐voids and reducing open porosity to improve density, strength, and impermeability  
3.   Relaxing or redistributing residual stresses and enabling partial recrystallization for more uniform mechanical properties  
4.   Converting the predominantly mechanical/adiabatic‐shear bonds into true metallurgical bonds across oxide–metal interfaces  
5.   (When desired) Precipitating or coarsening secondary phases (e.g. γ′ in Ni‐base alloys) to restore or enhance high‐temperature strength  

The net result is a coating that is more ductile, tougher, better adhered and far less permeable (improved corrosion and wear resistance) than the as‐sprayed material.

The process gas in a cold‐spray system governs two key things: the maximum jet (and hence particle) velocity you can attain, and the kinetic‐energy‐driven bonding that closes pores in the deposit.  In practice the molecular weight, heat‐capacity ratio (γ), gas constant (R), viscosity and thermal conductivity of the gas enter into the isentropic nozzle‐flow equations and set the sonic velocity, Mach‐number trajectory and momentum flux through the nozzle.  Here’s how it breaks down:

1. Gas properties → jet & particle velocity  
   • Sonic (jet) velocity vj ≈ sqrt[γ·R·T0] at the throat and then accelerates to high Mach numbers in the diverging section.  
   • Light gases (low molecular weight) have a higher R and often a higher γ, so they give a higher speed of sound at a given T0 and P0.  
   • Helium (Mw≈4 g/mol, γ≈1.66) → vj up to ~1 400 m/s and particle speeds of 1 200 m/s+  
   • Nitrogen (Mw≈28 g/mol, γ≈1.40) → vj ~900 m/s, particle speeds 700–900 m/s  
   • Argon (Mw≈40 g/mol, γ≈1.67) → vj ~800 m/s, particle speeds 600–800 m/s  

2. Particle velocity → porosity  
   • There is a critical velocity Vc for each material below which particles rebound (no deposit) or bond weakly (porous).  
   • Above Vc, increasing velocity drives more adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization and “splat” welding, collapsing voids.  
   • Helium sprays typically produce deposits with porosity < 1% (often < 0.5%), even at moderate stand‐offs.  
   • Nitrogen/argon sprays often yield porosities of 1–5%, unless you compensate with higher pressures, higher T0 or shorter standoffs.  

3. Trade‐offs and tuning  
   • Helium is expensive but gives the lowest porosity and highest deposition efficiency on hard or high‐Vc materials.  
   • Nitrogen or argon is cheaper; mixed He–N blends can be used to trade off cost vs. velocity.  
   • Raising gas temperature or stagnation pressure can partially make up for a heavier gas, but you never quite reach the same particle KE that pure He delivers.  

Bottom line: lighter, higher‐γ gases accelerate particles to higher velocities, which in turn drives stronger plastic deformation and metallurgical bonding—and therefore lower porosity—in the cold‐sprayed deposit.

Raising the temperature of the propellant gas in a cold‐spray system has two primary, closely related effects on the as‐sprayed coating:

1. Higher deposition efficiency  
   • As the gas temperature T increases, the local speed of sound rises (c ∝ √T) and for a given nozzle geometry and pressure ratio the peak jet Mach number (and hence particle impact velocity) goes up.  
   • Faster particles exceed their material’s critical bonding velocity more readily, undergo more intensive plastic deformation on impact, and adhere more completely to both the substrate and previous splats.  
   • The net result is a marked increase in “hit‐and‐stick” probability and hence overall deposition efficiency (DE) up to an optimal temperature.

2. Lower porosity (denser coatings)  
   • Higher impact velocities produce flatter, better interlocking splats, closing up interparticle voids.  
   • More vigorous plastic flow on impact squeezes entrapped gas and eliminates gaps between splats.  
   • Porosity typically falls as T goes up, reaching a minimum once you have saturated the velocity–bonding relationship.

Caveats/optimum range  
– Once you heat beyond the point at which gas density (and thus mass flow) drops too far, the net momentum transfer to the particles can level off or even decline, so DE may plateau or drop off.  
– Excessive gas temperatures can also promote oxidation (for reactive materials) or overheating of the substrate, which can reintroduce defects or residual stress.  

In practice you therefore tune the gas‐heater so as to reach just above the critical velocity window for your powder–substrate pair, maximizing DE and minimizing porosity without sacrificing throughput or inducing unwanted thermal effects.

In cold spray the only way two metal surfaces “wet” and weld to each other is by extremely high‐strain, adiabatic shear and plastic flow that shatter and eject the native oxide films and expose fresh, clean metal.  The thicker (or harder) that oxide film on the powder surface is, the more energy—and hence the higher particle impact velocity—is needed to fracture that film and entrain it into the shear flow, so that metal‐to‐metal contact can occur.  

Key points:  
1.  Oxide as a barrier.  A continuous oxide layer (Al2O3 on Al powders, Cr₂O₃ on stainless steel, etc.) must be broken up before bonding.  Thicker layers require larger stresses to initiate and propagate cracks.  
2.  Stress needed to fracture the oxide film scales (to first order) with its thickness δ and its fracture toughness KIC.  In simple fracture‐mechanics or beam‐bending models of a skin–core particle, the critical bending stress σc to crack an oxide film of thickness δ is proportional to √(E oxide·KIC/δ).  To achieve that stress in the particle particle, you need a higher impact velocity v.  
3.  Empirical trends.  – If you compare two batches of Al feedstock, one with a 20 nm native oxide and one with a 200 nm thermal oxide, you will typically see the thinner‐oxide powder reach appreciable deposition at ~450 m/s, whereas the thick‐oxide powder may not deposit until 650–750 m/s.  – Stainless‐steel powders with 10 nm of spinel‐type oxide will cold‐spray at 500 m/s, but if an additional 50 nm liver‐of‐sulfur scale is present you may have to push >700 m/s.  
4.  Limits.  Once the oxide layer becomes too thick (> 500 nm or so for many systems) the oxide simply cannot be fully broken up or entrained into the shear jet at any practical velocity, and deposition efficiency collapses.  

Practical takeaways:  
– Pre‐treatment (acid etch, plasma cleaning, controlled atomization) that keeps oxide thickness below ~50 nm can lower the critical velocity by 100–200 m/s.  
– If your powder has a meter‐scale oxide (e.g. polycrystalline MnO on Cu), cold spray will never work, period.  

In short, oxide‐scale thickness is one of the primary knobs for shifting the critical velocity: thicker/harder oxides → higher vcrit to achieve the same degree of plastic flow, oxide fracture, and ultimate bonding.

Particle size enters the cold‐spray bonding problem in two competing ways:

 1. Kinetic‐energy (and momentum) delivery  
   – At a given impact velocity v, particle mass m∝d³, so the kinetic energy per particle E=(½mv²)∝d³ and the energy per unit contact area E/A∝d (since contact area ∝d²).  In other words, larger particles deliver more energy (and higher pressure) into the substrate over a longer contact time, which tends to promote the intense plastic deformation and adiabatic shear that underlie cold‐spray bonding.  

 2. Aerodynamic acceleration and threshold effects  
   – In the supersonic nozzle the drag force F_d∝d² but the particle’s inertia∝d³, so its acceleration ∝F_d/m∝1/d.  Small particles accelerate almost instantly to the gas speed, whereas large ones never quite catch up in the nozzle and emerge at reduced velocity.  Moreover, if a particle gets too big the impact becomes so energetic that you can get substrate erosion, particle fracture or rebound instead of bonding.  

The net result at fixed gas/exit velocity is a “bell‐shaped” curve of deposition efficiency (and hence adhesion capability) versus particle diameter:  
 • Below a minimum size (~2–5 µm for most metals) the mass is too small to reach the critical impact energy, so particles simply rebound or wash away.  
 • In the intermediate range (roughly 10–50 µm, depending on material and spray conditions) you have enough mass for good local pressure and heating, and still high enough exit velocity.  This is where adhesion is maximized.  
 • Above the optimum (>50–75 µm) the particles are under‐accelerated in the nozzle and/or deliver so much energy that you tend to get substrate cratering or particle shatter rather than a coherent deposit.  

In practice, each material/gas combination has its own “sweet spot,” but the generic trend is:  
  – Adhesion capability rises with increasing diameter up to an optimum (where E/A and contact time are large enough for good interfacial bonding),  
  – Then falls off at still larger diameters because of incomplete acceleration and erosion/rebound effects.

Standoff distance (often abbreviated SOD) in cold spray is simply the gap between the exit plane of the spray nozzle and the surface of the substrate being coated.  It is typically on the order of 10–50 mm (exact optimum depends on gas pressure, nozzle design, powder type and particle size).

General effects of SOD on coating formation  
1. Particle velocity and temperature at impact  
   • Too short a SOD: particles have not yet fully accelerated in the gas jet; impact velocity (and thus kinetic energy) can be sub‐optimal.  
   • Optimum SOD: particles reach their peak velocity and temperature before impact, maximizing deformation and bonding.  
   • Too long a SOD: particles decelerate (and cool) in the expanding jet, reducing impact energy and lowering deposition efficiency.  

2. Deposition efficiency and build rate  
   • Peaks at the optimum SOD (where the greatest fraction of particles deform and adhere).  
   • Falls off at both extremes—too close (jet impingement/erosion effects, particle rebound) and too far (particle deceleration & miss‐rate).  

3. Coating microstructure and properties  
   • At optimum SOD you generally get the highest density, lowest porosity and strongest bond.  
   • Short SOD can cause substrate erosion, high residual stress, surface roughness and non-uniform thickness.  
   • Long SOD leads to poor packing, elevated porosity, weaker interparticle and particle-substrate bonds, and thinner coatings.  

4. Spray plume characteristics and coverage  
   • Short SOD concentrates the plume (narrow spray footprint, risk of “hot spots”).  
   • Long SOD broadens and cools the plume (wider but weaker spray footprint), which can help coat complex geometries at the cost of lower local deposition rates.  

In practice one tunes SOD—along with gas pressure, temperature and feed rate—to hit the sweet spot where particle kinetic energy is maximized on impact, for best coating density, adhesion and build rate.

1. Definition of fluence in laser processing  
Fluence (often denoted F) is the laser energy delivered per unit area, typically expressed in joules per square centimeter (J/cm²). For a pulsed laser it is defined as  
  F = Epulse/Aspot  
where  
  • Epulse is the energy in one pulse (J)  
  • Aspot is the cross‐sectional area of the laser spot on the workpiece (cm²)  

For a continuous‐wave or quasi‐CW beam scanned at speed v, average fluence can be written as  
  Favg = Pavg/(v · h)  
where Pavg is the average power (W), v is the scan speed (cm/s), and h is the hatch distance or effective line width (cm).

2. Why fluence matters in laser post‐treatment of cold-sprayed coatings  
Cold spray produces a highly porous, mechanically bonded deposit of metal particles (“splats”). Laser post‐treatment seeks to locally remelt, reflow, or sinter the upper layer of that coating to:  
  • Close pores and cracks  
  • Improve inter-splat cohesion and adhesion to the substrate  
  • Refine microstructure (grains, phase distribution)  
  • Adjust residual stresses and hardness  
  • Smooth the surface finish  

Fluence is the single most important parameter because it directly controls the peak temperature and molten depth in the coating:  
  – Below a threshold fluence Fth, no melting occurs and the coating remains porous.  
  – Near Fth you achieve a shallow molten pool just deep enough to seal pores without overheating the substrate.  
  – Above an optimum fluence range, you risk excessive melting, substrate damage, keyholing, vaporization, cracking, or oxidation.  

3. Practical implications  
  • Process window: Identifying the fluence window that produces sufficient reflow without deleterious effects is critical.  
  • Scan speed/spot size trade-off: For a given laser power, reducing spot size or scan speed raises fluence; increasing either lowers fluence.  
  • Uniformity: Maintaining a constant fluence across the surface (constant speed, overlap, beam profile) ensures uniform densification and properties.  
  • Quality metrics: By correlating fluence to metrics such as porosity reduction, microhardness, and bond strength, one can optimize the laser post-treatment recipe.  

In summary, fluence governs the thermal budget imparted by the laser, which in turn dictates the microstructural healing and property enhancement of cold-sprayed coatings. Choosing and maintaining the correct fluence is therefore essential for achieving reliable, high‐performance post-treated surfaces.

Key gas‐property differences  
1. Molecular weight (M): He ≈4 g/mol vs. N₂ ≈28 g/mol  
2. Specific‐heat ratio (γ): He ≈1.66 vs. N₂ ≈1.40  
3. Gas constant (R): He ≈2077 J/kg·K vs. N₂ ≈296 J/kg·K  

These feed directly into the isentropic relations for a converging–diverging nozzle:

  a) Sound speed at stagnation temperature T₀:
     c₀ = √(γ·R·T₀)  
     → He has a much higher c₀ than N₂ for the same T₀.  

  b) Exit Mach number Mₑ set by the nozzle area ratio and γ.  
     Typical cold‐spray nozzles run Mₑ(He) ≈3.5–4.5 vs. Mₑ(N₂) ≈2.0–3.0.  

  c) Exit velocity Vₑ:
     Vₑ = c₀·Mₑ  
     → He jets typically reach 1 000–1 500 m/s; N₂ jets 600–1 000 m/s under comparable pressure (20–30 bar) and T₀ (400–800 °C).  

  d) Exit (static) temperature Tₑ:
     Tₑ = T₀ / [1 + (γ – 1)/2·Mₑ²]  
     → He jets cool much more strongly in expansion (Tₑ often 150–300 °C), whereas N₂ jets remain hotter (Tₑ ≈300–600 °C).  

Consequences for particle heating and acceleration  
– Particle acceleration F_d ∝ C_d·ρ_g·(V_g–V_p)²; helium’s low density ρ_g partially offsets its higher V_g, so you typically need a longer nozzle or higher pressure to reach peak particle velocity, but in practice helium still produces ~20–80 % higher V_particle.  
– Convective heating ∝ h·(Tₑ–T_p), where h ∼ k_g. Helium’s thermal conductivity is higher than N₂’s, but because its jet Tₑ is much lower, the net powder heating is usually less with He.  

Typical experimental numbers (P₀ ≈30 bar, T₀ ≈650 °C, powder ∼20 μm):  
– With He: V_particle ≈900–1 200 m/s, particle temperature rise ΔT_particle ∼50–150 °C  
– With N₂: V_particle ≈600–800 m/s, ΔT_particle ∼150–300 °C  

Practical trade-off  
– Helium maximizes particle velocity (good for high‐strength alloys requiring high kinetic energy).  
– Nitrogen gives higher particle and substrate surface temperatures (useful for softer materials or when some thermal softening aids bonding).

Critical velocity (Vc) in cold spray is the minimum particle impact speed required to achieve plastic deformation–driven bonding of feedstock particles onto a substrate. Below Vc particles tend to rebound or erode the surface; at or above Vc they undergo intense, localized deformation (often with adiabatic shear instability), fracture oxide films, and form strong mechanical–metallurgical interlocks.

Why it’s essential for coating formation  
1. Bonding threshold: Only above Vc do particles deform enough to breach surface oxides and create intimate contact.  
2. Deposition efficiency: Vc marks the knee in the deposition-efficiency vs. velocity curve. Below it, yields are near zero; above it, efficiency rises steeply.  
3. Coating cohesion and adhesion: Sufficient impact energy (½ m·V²) ensures interparticle and particle–substrate bonding, leading to dense, well-adhered coatings.  
4. Process window control: Knowing Vc allows optimal gas pressure/temperature and nozzle design to reliably produce coherent coatings without substrate damage or particle erosion.

Vc depends on  
• Particle material (strength, hardness, melting point)  
• Particle size and shape  
• Substrate properties (hardness, surface roughness, oxide layer)  
• Gas temperature, pressure, and nozzle geometry  

Typical ranges (approximate)  
• Al alloys: 450–550 m/s  
• Cu: 550–650 m/s  
• Ti alloys: 800–1 000 m/s  

In practice, cold spray systems are tuned (gas type, pressure, temperature, nozzle design) to exceed Vc by 10–20 % to ensure reliable, high-quality coating formation.

Gas temperature in a cold‐spray system enters principally via two linked effects on particle kinetic energy and thus on coating density:

1. Particle velocity and deposition efficiency  
   – Raising the stagnation (heater) temperature at fixed pressure ratio increases the gas’s total enthalpy and its speed of sound.  In a converging–diverging nozzle this means a higher Mach number and therefore higher exit velocity.  Since particle impact velocity is the single most important parameter for getting above the material’s “critical velocity,” the coating becomes denser and better consolidated as Tgas rises.  

2. Momentum flux and density trade-off  
   – Higher T reduces gas density (ρ∼p/T), so although V increases, the momentum flux ρV² eventually plateaus or even falls off at very high temperatures if V can no longer rise proportionally.  In practice there is an optimum window (often 300–800 °C with N₂, up to 1 000 °C with He) beyond which further heating gives no real benefit in density.

Operational constraint on maximum gas temperature  
  • Heater and hardware limits: the electrical or gas‐fired heater, the feed lines and especially the nozzle material have maximum service temperatures (creep, oxidation, thermal shock).  You must stay below those to avoid damage or warping.  
  • Powder‐preheat/softening threshold: powders begin to oxidize, sinter or even melt if you overheat them in the carrier gas, leading to injector/nozzle clogging.  
  • Choked‐flow requirement: to maintain a supersonic jet, the stagnation‐to‐ambient pressure ratio must exceed the critical ratio, which itself rises with temperature.  At very high T you must boost chamber pressure (and hence compressor size/cost) just to stay in choked flow.

In short, hotter gas generally yields higher particle speeds and denser coatings, but the upper temperature is capped by heater/nozzle material limits, powder stability and the need to sustain choked supersonic expansion.

The “critical velocity” in cold spray is simply the minimum particle impact speed below which no net deposition occurs.  Physically it is the speed at which the particle‐substrate impact pressure and attendant plastic deformation (and any adiabatic shear/jetting) just become sufficient to break through surface oxides, generate fresh metal–metal contact, and produce a metallurgical bond.  Below that speed the particles rebound or erode; above it they adhere.

Although its numerical value must be determined experimentally for each material pair and spray gas, typical ballpark figures are:

 • Aluminum on aluminum: 450–550 m/s  
 • Copper on copper: 600–700 m/s  
 • Stainless steels: 750–900 m/s  
 • Titanium alloys: 650–800 m/s  
 • Hard alloys/ceramics: 900–1 200 m/s  

Key parameters controlling the critical velocity are:

1. Particle and substrate mechanical properties  
   – Yield strength and hardness (including strain-rate sensitivity)  
   – Density (ρp for the particle; ρs for the substrate)  
   – Elastic modulus (which influences the impact pressure profile)  
   – Melting point and thermal softening behavior (affects adiabatic shear)  

2. Particle characteristics  
   – Size and size distribution (smaller particles accelerate faster but store less kinetic energy)  
   – Shape and surface roughness/oxide thickness (oxide films raise the bonding threshold)  

3. Spray‐gas properties and state  
   – Gas molecular weight (helium vs. nitrogen) and ratio of specific heats (γ)  
   – Stagnation pressure (P0) and temperature (T0) in the plenum  
   – Nozzle geometry (expansion ratio, length, throat diameter)  

4. Process parameters  
   – Stand‐off distance (affects cooling/drag of the particles)  
   – Gas flow rate (throughput)  
   – Substrate temperature (preheating lowers yield strength, reducing the critical velocity)  
   – Impact angle (normal incidence maximizes the effective pressure)  

A rough scaling law can be written (for ductile metals) as  
   v_c ≈ √[2·σ_y/(C·ρ_p)]  
where σ_y is the dynamic yield strength of the softer partner, ρ_p the particle density, and C a dimensionless factor encapsulating jetting/geometry effects.  In practice one calibrates v_c via single‐particle or “speed‐window” tests for each powder‐substrate–gas combination.

Increasing the gas temperature (T₀) at fixed stagnation pressure (P₀) always boosts the nozzle exit velocity and therefore the particle speed in cold spray.  The key points are:

1. Isentropic‐flow scaling  
   For an ideal (or near-ideal) gas expanding through a converging–diverging nozzle under constant P₀ and fixed exit pressure P_e, the exit velocity uₑ is  
   uₑ = √[2·c_p·T₀·(1 − (P_e/P₀)^((γ−1)/γ))]  
   ≃ Mₑ·√(γ·R·T₀)  
   where  
     • γ = gas specific‐heat ratio  
     • R = gas constant  
     • Mₑ = Mach number at the exit (fixed by P_e/P₀)  

   Since P₀ and P_e are unchanged, Mₑ remains essentially constant, so uₑ ∝ √T₀.  In other words, raising the stagnation temperature by 20 % raises the exit velocity by about √1.2 ≈ 10 %.

2. Speed of sound and Mach number  
   A higher T₀ raises the local speed of sound a₀ = √(γR T₀).  For the same exit Mach number Mₑ you get a proportionally higher uₑ.

3. Particle acceleration  
   Particles riding in the gas jet are accelerated by drag and pressure forces.  Higher gas velocity gives them more momentum transfer, so their impact speed—and hence coating quality—goes up.

4. Trade-offs  
   • Gas density ρ₀ = P₀/(R T₀) falls as T₀ rises, so mass‐flow rate decreases.  
   • Too high a T₀ can start to approach powder material softening or oxidation limits.  

In practice you’ll see roughly uₚ ∝ √T₀, so moderate heating at constant pressure is an effective way to push particle speeds higher.

Preheating the substrate is one of the most straightforward “knobs” for improving bond quality in a cold‐spray process, especially when you’re trying to get very small (nm‐scale) particles to stick.  In essence, a warmer substrate

  • softens the target locally (lowers its yield strength),  
  • reduces the thermal sink effect so that the particle’s own adiabatic‐shear hot spot is maintained longer, and  
  • gives the particles a little extra thermal energy on impact for enhanced plastic flow, interfacial mixing and—even at modest temperatures—some short‐range diffusional bonding.  

Mechanisms in more detail  
  1.  Reduced critical velocity.  A preheated substrate has a lower dynamic hardness than room-temperature steel or aluminum, so the gas-jet velocity needed to exceed the “critical impact stress” for particle embedding goes down by 5–15 %.  
  2.  Deeper adiabatic shear and jetting.  When a high-speed nanoparticle strikes a “hotter” surface, its local deformation zone heats up and flows more readily, generating a stronger metallic jet at the interface that removes oxides/contaminants and promotes intimate metal‐to‐metal contact.  
  3.  Enhanced mechanical interlocking.  Softening of the substrate means each particle embeds more deeply, roughening the interface and increasing the area available for load transfer.  
  4.  Faster sintering/diffusion at nanoscale.  Even a few hundred °C can activate surface diffusion in nanoparticles, healing inter‐particle boundaries and eliminating voids in the as-sprayed layer.  
  5.  Lower residual stresses.  Because the temperature rise from room temperature to the spray temperature is smaller, the thermal‐mismatch stresses on cooldown are reduced, cutting residual tensile stresses at the interface.  

Practical notes  
  – Typical preheat ranges are 100–300 °C for aluminum and copper alloys, 200–400 °C for steels.  
  – Beyond ~400 °C you risk growing oxide layers on both substrate and feedstock, or sintering/agglomerating the nanoparticles in flight.  
  – Uniform heating is important—hot spots can lead to local over‐softening and poor dimensional control.  

In practice you’ll see 20–50 % gains in deposition efficiency and 20–30 % increases in tensile bond strength by preheating into the 150–300 °C window versus room temperature.

In cold spray the particle velocity at the nozzle exit is set by the balance of drag‐driven acceleration in the expanding supersonic gas and the particle’s own inertia.  In compact form one can write for a spherical particle:  
   mₚ·dvₚ/dt = F_d = ½·C_d·ρ_g·Aₚ·(v_g–vₚ)²  
with mₚ = ρₚ·(πdₚ³/6), Aₚ = πdₚ²/4.  From this form the key gas and particle‐side parameters emerge:

1.  Gas‐phase properties  
   •  Stagnation pressure p₀ and temperature T₀ – these set the mass flow, Mach number and exit velocity v_g via the isentropic nozzle relations.  
   •  Gas density ρ_g (∝ p/T) – directly proportional to the drag force.  
   •  Specific‐heat ratio γ = c_p/c_v and molecular weight M – control the speed of sound a = √(γ R T) and hence the attainable Mach number and v_g.  
   •  Viscosity μ_g (and thermal conductivity) – enters C_d through the Reynolds number Re = ρ_g·dₚ·v_rel/μ_g and modifies the boundary‐layer thickness and shock structure in the nozzle.  
   •  Nozzle geometry (expansion ratio, throat diameter) – determines the pressure‐ratio needed for a given exit Mach number and v_g.  
   •  Gas species choice (e.g. He vs N₂): He has lower density but much higher sound speed, permitting higher Mach at the same pressure ratio; N₂ is denser but slower.

2.  Particle characteristics  
   •  Diameter dₚ (or size distribution) – since mₚ ∝ dₚ³ but drag area ∝ dₚ², smaller particles accelerate far more rapidly (τ_acc ∝ dₚ·ρₚ/ρ_g).  
   •  Density ρₚ – higher‐density particles have more inertia, so accelerate more slowly toward v_g.  
   •  Shape factor and surface roughness – enter the drag coefficient C_d (non-spherical or rough particles yield higher drag).  
   •  Knudsen‐number effects (particle diameter vs gas mean free path) – at very small dₚ slip corrections (Cunningham factor) alter the effective drag.  
   •  Injection conditions and mass loading – radial position in the nozzle throat, injection angle, and high particle flux all modify local v_g (momentum coupling and particle–particle collisions can slow the gas).  
   •  Initial particle temperature (very minor effect on density) and any preheating (mainly affects deformability upon impact, not the flight speed).

In practice you optimize the cold‐spray gas (choice of He vs N₂, p₀, T₀) and nozzle design to deliver the desired v_g and density, then select or mill your powder so that dₚ and ρₚ give you the accelerator time‐constant τ = mₚ/(½ C_d ρ_g Aₚ v_g), ensuring that vₚ approaches v_g before exit.

High‐pressure, “cold” gas jets are the heart of cold spray because they turn powder particles into hyper-velocity projectiles without ever melting them.  Below are the two parts of your question answered in turn:

1. Why high pressure at sub-melting temperatures?  
   • Kinetic‐energy driven bonding:  By expanding a high‐pressure gas (typically 20–50 bar inlet) through a converging–diverging nozzle, particles reach supersonic speeds (300–1200 m/s).  Their kinetic energy (½mv²) is then converted on impact into severe plastic deformation at the particle/substrate interface.  
   • Avoidance of melting and oxidation:  Keeping the gas temperature well below the powder’s Tm (often 0.3–0.6 Tm in absolute terms) prevents any liquid phase, oxidation or phase transformations, preserving the original powder chemistry and microstructure.  
   • Substrate safety:  Low bulk temperatures mean that heat-sensitive substrates (e.g. Al alloys, polymers, composites) are not thermally damaged or distorted.  

2. How this choice influences coating integrity  
   • Solid-state metallurgical bonding:  Extremely high local strains and adiabatic shear at the interface produce intimate metal-metal contact, often assisted by dynamic recrystallization, yielding bond strengths close to or above the parent metal.  
   • Low porosity and oxide content:  No melting → no splat boundaries or re-oxidation zones.  Coatings typically achieve porosities <2 % and very few oxide inclusions.  
   • Refined microstructure and residual stress state:  Impact‐driven grain refinement near the interface imparts high hardness and strength.  Coatings often exhibit beneficial compressive residual stresses that improve fatigue and wear resistance.  
   • Minimal dilution and thermal cracks:  Because there is no molten pool, there is essentially zero mixing (“dilution”) with the substrate and very low risk of thermal cracking or warpage.  

In short, high‐pressure, sub-melting‐temperature gas jets enable purely mechanical, solid‐state bonding with excellent adhesion, low defects and preserved feedstock/substrate integrity—key to the high performance of cold-sprayed coatings.

A principal microstructural benefit of cold‐spray coatings is that, because the powders never melt, you end up with an almost fully dense, oxide-free deposit made up of plastically sprayed particles rather than the “splat” lamellae you get in thermal spray.  In practice that means  
 • porosities often below 1 % (vs. 5–15 % or more in thermal spray)  
 • virtually no oxide or nitride films at particle boundaries  
 • retention of the feedstock’s fine‐grained structure (or even further grain refinement by severe plastic deformation)  
Together, these features give cold‐spray coatings higher cohesive strength, better ductility and corrosion resistance than conventional thermal‐sprayed layers.

Nozzle geometry and powder‐injection location together set the gas flow field that “drags” particles to their impact speeds.  In cold spray, particle velocity is almost entirely controlled by the momentum transfer from a high‐velocity carrier gas in a converging–diverging (de Laval) or straight‐diverging nozzle. Here’s how each factor plays a role:

1. Nozzle geometry  
  • Throat diameter and expansion ratio  
    – The throat sets the minimum flow area, determining the Mach number at the start of the divergent section.  
    – A larger expansion ratio (exit area ÷ throat area) generally yields higher exit Mach and gas speed, up to the point where shock formation or flow separation occurs.  
  • Divergence angle and length  
    – Too steep an angle (>5–7° for most supersonic nozzles) can cause boundary‐layer separation, flow distortions, and local Mach drop, lowering net drag on particles.  
    – A longer, gently expanding diverging section gives particles more “runway” to accelerate.  
  • Converging section (when present)  
    – Improves uniformity of gas velocity profile entering the throat.  
    – Can smooth pressure gradients that otherwise create secondary shocks.  

2. Powder injection location  
  • Axial position relative to the throat  
    – Upstream (in the converging section) gives maximum acceleration length but risks particle–wall impacts and nozzle wear if too close to walls.  
    – At or just upstream of the throat is most common: particles see supersonic drag immediately downstream but are sheltered from direct wall erosion.  
    – Injecting downstream in the diverging section shortens acceleration path—lower peak velocities—but reduces nozzle erosion and simplifies feed design.  
  • Radial offset and injector design  
    – Center‐line (axial) injection aligns particles with the gas core for maximum axial drag, yielding higher mean particle speeds and tighter velocity distributions.  
    – Radial or angled ports enhance mixing but introduce swirl or off‐axis momentum, broadening the velocity distribution and lowering average axial speed.  
  • Number of injectors  
    – Multiple ports around the circumference can give more uniform particle loading but must be symmetrically arranged to avoid jet asymmetry and local velocity deficits.  

In practice, you tune nozzle geometry and injection location together to maximize the drag force (which scales roughly with ρgas·(Vgas–Vparticle)²·projected area), while avoiding shocks, flow separation, and nozzle wear.  Optimal designs deliver the highest possible gas Mach number with a clean, centered jet and give particles the longest uninterrupted path in that jet—producing the highest and most uniform impact velocities.

Increasing the particle velocity in a cold‐spray process has two principal, and interrelated, effects on the target substrate and on how many particles actually stick (deposition efficiency):

1. Greater plastic deformation and interfacial bonding  
   • Kinetic energy (∝ ½mv²) rises steeply, so each impact imparts much more strain energy into particle and substrate.  
   • Very high‐strain‐rate deformation (10⁵–10⁶ s⁻¹) breaks up surface oxides, generates adiabatic shear instabilities at the interface, and produces a high‐velocity metal jet that “wets” and mechanically interlocks the particle to the substrate.  
   • The substrate beneath each impact develops a highly deformed, work-hardened layer (thickness typically 5–20 µm) whose flow accommodates and locks in the splat.  
   • As velocity rises from below the critical velocity (Vc) toward ~1.1–1.3 Vc, the flattening ratio of particles increases, interface porosity falls, and true metallurgical bonding steadily improves.

2. Improved deposition efficiency up to an optimum  
   • Below Vc particles rebound or shatter; effective deposition efficiency is near zero.  
   • Once Vc is exceeded, deposition efficiency climbs rapidly with velocity. Typical S-curve behavior shows a sharp “turn-on” near Vc and a slower rise toward an asymptote of 90–98% efficiency.  
   • Higher velocities also allow smaller particles (which inherently carry less momentum) to stick, broadening the usable particle‐size window.

3. The erosion/damage trade-off at very high velocities  
   • Beyond some optimum (often in excess of ~1.3 Vc), further velocity increases can begin to erode or even micro-fracture the substrate rather than build up a coating.  
   • Excessive impact stress and localized heating can (a) generate tensile residual stresses in the deposit, (b) initiate interfacial cracking or delamination, and (c) roughen or pit the substrate so severely that new particles rebound again.  
   • In practice one tunes gas pressure, temperature, and nozzle geometry to stay in the “high‐efficiency, low‐damage” window.

Summary  
– At low velocities (<Vc): little deformation, no bonding, near-zero efficiency.  
– Between Vc and ~1.3 Vc: sharply increased plastic deformation, oxide disruption, adiabatic‐shear bonding, rising flattening ratio, and rapidly climbing deposition efficiency.  
– Above the optimum velocity: substrate erosion, crack initiation, and spallation compete with bonding, causing efficiency to plateau or even fall.

Particle velocity in cold spray is the single most important parameter controlling whether a powder particle will bond (via severe plastic deformation) or simply erode (bounce off) the substrate, and it also dictates how much plastic deformation the particle (and substrate) undergoes on impact.  In essence, as you raise velocity you move through three regimes:

1.  Sub-critical (v < vcrit)  
    – Kinetic energy is too low to trigger the adiabatic shear and interfacial jetting needed for bonding.  
    – Particles largely rebound, causing only mild micro-cutting and pitting of the substrate (low erosion rate).  
    – Particle deformation is minimal (flattening ratio H/D ≈ 1–1.2).

2.  Near-critical (v ≈ vcrit)  
    – Erosion of the bare substrate peaks.  Particles still fail to bond but carry enough energy to plastically remove or micro-cut substrate material.  
    – Erosion rate scales strongly with velocity (roughly E ∝ v^2–v^4 for ductile impact erosion).  
    – Particle flattening begins (H/D ~ 1.2–1.5), but rebound is still predominant.

3.  Supra-critical (v > vcrit)  
    – Impact pressure and localized adiabatic shear exceed yield strengths of both particle and substrate.  An interfacial jet forms, oxide films are expelled, and metallic bonding occurs.  
    – Particles deform severely into “pancakes.”  Typical flattening ratios rise with velocity (e.g. H/D ≈ 0.3–0.5, or diameter expansion of 2×–4×).  
    – Strain rates reach 10^6–10^8 s–1, promoting dynamic recrystallization in the impact zone.  
    – Once a coating is established, subsequent particles see a softer, more ductile surface and net substrate erosion drops sharply; further deposition dominates.  
    – If velocity is pushed excessively above bonding-optimum, you can re-introduce erosion of the nascent coating and induce cracks or excessive roughness.

Typical critical velocities (vcrit) depend on material:  
– Aluminum alloys: ~550–700 m/s  
– Copper alloys: ~700–850 m/s  
– Titanium alloys: ~900–1100 m/s  

In practical cold spray additive processes you tune carrier gas pressure/temperature and nozzle geometry to exceed vcrit for your powder–substrate pair by a modest margin.  That maximizes bond strength and particle deformation while minimizing unwanted substrate erosion once the coating starts building up.

In cold spray you control porosity principally by the particle‐impact velocity (and hence deformation) and by how well small particles can fill the voids left between larger ones in a broad PSD.  Two of the easiest “tuning knobs” are the powder feed rate and the gas pressure (or equivalently the gas mass flow and temperature).  Their effects may be summarized as follows:

1. Powder feed rate  
  • At fixed gas conditions, increasing the feed rate raises the total mass flux of powder through the nozzle.  That means the same gas momentum must be shared by more particles, so the average particle velocity (and kinetic energy) drops.  Lower particle velocity → poorer deformation on impact → higher residual porosity.  
  • High feed rates also increase particle–particle collisions in the nozzle throat and shock‐cell region.  This broadened velocity distribution further reduces deposition efficiency and leaves more inter‐particle gaps.  
  • Conversely, if you back off the feed too far you get excellent particle acceleration but low deposition efficiency (thin coatings).  In practice there is an optimum feed rate that balances throughput against densification.  

2. Gas pressure (or total gas mass flow)  
  • Raising the gas pressure (for a given gas temperature and nozzle geometry) increases the peak supersonic jet velocity and the gas density at the throat.  Both effects boost particle acceleration, especially for the coarser fraction of a broad PSD.  Faster, heavier particles deform more plastically on impact, filling voids and welding better to neighbours, so porosity drops.  
  • If the pressure is too low, only the finest fraction reaches critical velocity.  Coarse particles tend to rebound, build up spalls, and create large voids.  
  • There is again an optimum: at very high pressures you may over‐accelerate fines so they fracture or erode already deposited splats, actually opening up new porosity.  

3. Interaction with broad PSD  
  • A mixed distribution can help by having small particles lodge in the interstices between larger ones, but only if all size fractions exceed their critical velocity.  
  • At too high a feed rate the fines “crowd” the jet; they collide with each other and with the coarse particles, slow them down, and can rebound around pores—raising porosity.  
  • At too low a feed rate you waste the large particles’ ability to build the “backbone” of the coating and lose the filling benefit of the fines.  

In practice you map out a small matrix of feed‐rate vs. pressure runs, looking for the region where deposition efficiency and porosity both plateau.  For broad PSDs that typically means moderate to high gas pressures (to get the coarse fraction moving fast enough) and intermediate feed rates (to avoid jet loading and maintain particle velocity), yielding the lowest porosity.

When you cold‐spray oxygen‐sensitive metals (Ti, Nb, Al, certain superalloys, etc.) you need a process gas that (a) won’t oxidize or nitrify the powder or newly formed deposit, (b) will let you generate very high particle velocities, and (c) won’t introduce safety or contamination issues of its own. Inert gases—typically helium or argon—meet all three requirements:

1. Chemical inertness  
   • No free O₂, H₂O or other reactive species to form oxides, nitrides or hydrides on the powder surfaces or in the deposit.  
   • Keeps particle surfaces “fresh” so that when they impact at high velocity the clean metal–metal contact can bond by severe plastic deformation.

2. Velocity performance  
   • Helium (low molecular weight) gives a high speed of sound in the nozzle, so at a given pressure ratio you reach higher Mach numbers and particle velocities (often ≫600 m/s).  
   • Argon is denser (heavier), so it produces somewhat lower velocities but is far cheaper than helium. You trade off cost vs. achievable particle speed.

3. Safety and cleanliness  
   • Inert gases eliminate the fire/explosion risk associated with fine metal powders in O₂ or air.  
   • They do not leave reactive residues (chlorides, oxides) that would later degrade mechanical properties or complicate post‐treatment.

If you tried to spray in air (or even dry nitrogen with trace O₂), you’d end up with thick oxide films that act like a lubricant at the particle interfaces, preventing true bonding, raising porosity, embrittling the deposit and drastically reducing strength and ductility. By contrast, an inert propellant gas keeps powders oxide‐free right up to impact, maximizes bonding, and protects both the feedstock and the growing part from unwanted chemistry.

In cold‐spray you improve the “hit-to-stick” window either by pushing the actual particle speed higher or by pulling the critical speed lower (or both).  Below is a summary of the most widely used levers:

1. Raising the Actual Particle Velocity  
  a. Higher gas pressure/stagnation temperature  
     – Increase supply pressure (2–5 MPa typical) and pre‐heat the gas (up to 800 °C) to raise Mach number and flow velocity.  
  b. Choice of carrier gas / gas mixtures  
     – He gives ~1.0–1.2 km/s, N₂ ~0.6–0.8 km/s.  
     – He–H₂ blends or pure H₂ boost speed further by lowering molecular weight and increasing sound speed.  
  c. Nozzle geometry optimization  
     – Higher expansion ratios, optimized throat and exit diameters, longer “de Laval” diverging sections, shallow divergence angles (~4–6°) to sustain supersonic core.  
  d. Powder feed conditions  
     – Optimum stand‐off distance and injection angle (typically 10–30 mm and 0–10° off normal).  
     – Narrow size distribution (10–50 µm for most metals) and high sphericity minimize drag and maximize acceleration.  

2. Lowering the Critical (Minimum) Velocity  
  a. Surface conditioning  
     – Grit-blasting or shot-peening to introduce surface roughness (~2–5 µm) and work‐hardening eases metal flow/bonding.  
     – Substrate preheating (100–300 °C) softens the surface, lowering the plastic‐deformation threshold.  
  b. Powder modification  
     – Use purer, finer, or more ductile powders (e.g. gas‐atomized vs water‐atomized).  
     – Grain-refined or nanostructured powders have lower flow stress upon impact.  
  c. Interlayer or seeding powders  
     – A thin “soft” buffer (Cu on steel, Al on Ni, etc.) forms a compliant under‐layer that bonds at lower velocity, then you over‐spray your harder material.  
  d. Oxide/contaminant removal  
     – Small additions of reactive gases (e.g. H₂ or tiny O₂) can chemically strip surface oxides in‐flight and reduce the critical threshold for bonding.  
  e. Powder metallurgy routes  
     – Mechanically alloyed powders containing a ductile second phase or precursor milled powders can plastically deform more easily on impact.  

3. Combining Both  
  – In practice you often raise gas pressure and temperature AND pre‐blast/pre‐heat your substrate.  You may choose He–H₂ at 4 MPa/600 °C, grit‐blast the target, spray a ductile seed layer, then build your final coating.  That multi-pronged approach typically drives vactual/vcritical well above unity and maximizes deposition efficiency.

Cold-sprayed and LPPS coatings look quite different under the SEM or profilometer because one is built up by high-velocity, solid-state impacts and the other by successive splatting of molten droplets.  In practice you observe:

1. Cold-sprayed coatings  
   • “Pebble-like” or “bowl-shaped” lobes of plastically-deformed feedstock.  Individual particles remain recognizable, but are heavily work-hardened and cold-welded together.  
   • A high-roughness, jagged topography (typical Ra ≈ 5–20 µm) reflecting powder size and shape.  
   • Virtually no splash, oxides, or “pancake” splat features – all the deformation is mechanical, so there are no melt-solidification artifacts.  
   • Very low oxide content at the surface; pores, if any, are narrow interparticle boundaries.  

2. LPPS coatings  
   • “Pancake” or “splatted” morphology: droplets impinge in the molten state, spread into thin lamellae, then solidify.  You see smooth, disc-shaped splats, often with concentric ridges or intersplat voids.  
   • A somewhat smoother surface (Ra ≈ 2–8 µm) and clear lamellar stacking with distinct intersplat boundaries.  
   • Some degree of re-oxidation or trapped gas pores along splat interfaces, though low-pressure operation reduces these compared with APS.  

In short, cold spray leaves you with a rough, particle-based surface of mechanically deformed lobes, whereas LPPS produces a smoother, layered splat architecture characteristic of molten, re-solidified droplets.

Key distinctions between cold spray and (molten-state) thermal spray come down to the maximum particle temperature in flight and the microstructural consequences of that temperature:

1. Particle temperature  
  • Cold spray  
    – Gas temperature typically 200–600 °C, well below most metal melting points.  
    – Powder particles remain fully solid; no melting or resolidification.  
  • Thermal spray (e.g. plasma, flame, HVOF)  
    – Gas temperatures from ~2 000 up to >10 000 °C.  
    – Powder particles are heated to, or above, their melting point and typically deposit as molten or semi-molten droplets.

2. Oxidation  
  • Cold spray  
    – Low in‐flight temperatures + short residence time = minimal oxidation beyond the native surface oxide.  
    – Resulting deposit can contain <0.1–0.5 vol% oxides.  
  • Thermal spray  
    – High temperatures and reactive plume gases promote oxide formation in flight and on impact.  
    – Deposits often contain several vol% oxide stringers and lamellae, degrading ductility and conductivity.

3. Phase transformation  
  • Cold spray  
    – Solid-state jetting preserves the original crystal structure and any metastable phases in the feedstock.  
    – No melting means no solidification microstructures (e.g. none of the quench-hardening or phase‐decomposition features you see in molten deposits).  
  • Thermal spray  
    – Melting and rapid solidification lead to phase transformations (e.g. martensite in steels, amorphous phases in alloys, nitrides/oxides if reactive gases).  
    – Can see oxide precipitates, decarburization, vaporization of low‐boiling constituents, and other heat‐driven reactions.

In short, cold spray is a solid-state process (low particle T, minimal oxidation/phase change), whereas thermal spray is a molten-state process (high particle T, significant oxidation and melting-related transformations).

Raising the carrier‐gas temperature in a cold‐spray process (at fixed supply pressure and nozzle geometry) systematically alters the conditions under which powder particles are accelerated and strike the substrate.  The key effects are:

1. Higher gas exit velocity  
   – For a supersonic nozzle of fixed geometry, the exit Mach number is essentially set by the pressure ratio.  Since the local speed of sound a = √(γ R T₀), increasing the stagnation temperature T₀ raises a and thus the gas velocity Vg ∝√T₀.  

2. Modified drag‐force history  
   – Particle acceleration is governed by Fd = ½ Cd ρg (Vg–Vp)².  
   – Gas density ρg ≃ p₀/(R T₀) falls as T₀ rises, but the increase in (Vg–Vp) more than compensates over typical temperature ranges, so the net drag impulse (and hence the terminal particle speed) goes up.  

3. Particle pre‐heating and softening  
   – Convective heat transfer from a hotter gas raises particle temperature during flight.  
   – Elevated particle temperature lowers its yield strength and flow stress, so on impact it plastically deforms more readily.  

4. Impact‐zone temperature rise  
   – A hotter gas can transfer more energy into the near‐surface layer of the substrate (and into the bow shock), increasing local substrate temperature and further easing the formation of a metallurgical bond.  

5. Lowered critical velocity and improved deposition  
   – The combination of higher particle velocity, greater particle/substrate temperature, and reduced flow stress all serve to reduce the material’s “critical velocity” for bonding.  
   – As a result, deposition efficiency and bond quality typically improve with an increase in carrier‐gas temperature (up to limits set by material oxidation or gas‐phase dissociation).  

In practice, one observes (for a given nozzle and powder) that boosting gas temperature raises particle exit speed, softens both particles and substrate on impact, lowers the threshold speed needed to weld, and thereby increases the build rate and coating adherence—so long as you stay below temperatures where undesirable chemistry (oxidation, nitriding or gas breakdown) begins to dominate.

Because cold spray is a solid‐state, velocity-driven process rather than a melt-and-solidify one, each powder component must individually achieve sufficient impact energy and plastic flow to bond. If two constituents in your feed mix have different mechanical or aerothermal properties, they will generally have different “critical velocities” and thus different deposition efficiencies (DE). Those differences lead directly to compositional drift in the build. Key reasons are:  
1. Critical velocity mismatch  
  • A harder or higher‐yield‐strength phase (e.g. a ceramic or high‐strength alloy) needs a higher impact velocity to generate the adiabatic shear and plastic deformation required for bonding. A softer phase may deposit at lower gas pressures or shorter spray distances.  
  • Spray conditions optimized to deposit one phase may lie below the critical velocity of the other, so that second phase simply bounces or erodes away.  
2. Density/size/shape effects on particle acceleration  
  • Lighter or smaller particles accelerate more quickly in the gas jet and may exceed their critical velocity even when coarser or denser particles of another phase remain below it.  
  • If the two constituents have different size distributions (e.g. one is fine and one is coarse), the fine fraction will reach bonding speed more readily, enriching the deposit in that phase.  
3. Differential rebound and re-entrainment  
  • Particles that do not plastically deform sufficiently will rebound; they may then be re-entrained in the gas stream and either strike again (delaying or reducing overall DE) or be lost. If one material rebounds more often, its DE is lower.  
4. Substrate and spray‐built morphology  
  • Early‐arriving particles condition the substrate surface. If the first phase wets and cold welds well, it can create a surface to which the other phase has more difficulty adhering (or vice versa).  

All of these factors cause the mass fraction of each phase in the coating to differ from the feed ratio unless the spray parameters (gas pressure, temperature, nozzle stand-off, powder blend, etc.) are carefully tuned to give both constituents high and nearly equal deposition efficiencies.

The critical velocity in cold‐gas spraying is not a single “universal” number but rather the outcome of a number of coupled material, gas‐dynamics and interfacial factors that together determine whether a particle will plastically deform, shed its oxide and produce the high‐strain‐rate shear needed to jet material at the interface.  The principal factors are:

1. Particle material properties  
   – Dynamic yield strength and flow stress (which set the stress/strain‐rate threshold for adiabatic shear)  
   – Hardness and work‐hardening rate (higher values → higher v₍c₎)  
   – Thermal properties (thermal conductivity and specific heat govern how much of the kinetic energy goes into local heating)  
   – Oxide or surface film thickness and toughness (must be stripped away at impact)

2. Particle geometry and size  
   – Diameter (smaller particles heat and accelerate more easily, lowering v₍c₎)  
   – Shape (non‐spherical particles may have localized stress concentrators)

3. Gas parameters and process conditions  
   – Gas species (He vs. N₂: lighter gases reach higher exit velocities at the same pressure)  
   – Gas stagnation temperature and pressure (sets the maximum achievable particle velocity)  
   – Nozzle design and expansion ratio (controls Mach number and particle acceleration)  
   – Standoff distance (too short → incomplete acceleration; too long → gas/particle cooling and dispersion)

4. Particle–substrate interaction  
   – Substrate hardness and roughness (harder substrates require higher v to achieve the same plastic deformation)  
   – Substrate temperature (pre-heating lowers its yield strength and thus v₍c₎)  
   – Impact angle (normal impact maximizes the normal stress required for jetting)

5. Adiabatic heating and jet formation  
   – At impact the balance between kinetic energy density, plastic work and heat generation determines if a high‐strain‐rate shear instability (jet) will form and break the oxide layer  
   – Strain‐rate sensitivity and thermal softening of the materials control the onset of the adiabatic shear necessary for bonding

In practice, the “critical velocity” for a given particle–substrate pair is found empirically by mapping deposition efficiency vs. carrier‐gas pressure/temperature (and thus particle velocity). That empirical v₍c₎ scales with the material’s dynamic yield strength, thermal softening behavior, and surface condition, all modified by the acceleration and heating history imparted by the gas‐dynamic spray conditions.

Key gas properties in cold spray are molecular weight (M), specific‐heat ratio (k), gas constant (R), density (ρ) and thermal conductivity (λ).  Through these properties, the choice of gas controls the achievable gas (and thus particle) velocity and the thermal/mechanical history of particles en route to—and upon impact with—the substrate.  

1. Gas sonic speed and exit velocity  
  • Sonic speed c = √(k·R·T/M).  Lighter gases with high k (H₂, He) have much higher c than heavier gases (N₂, Ar).  
  • For a fixed pressure ratio, highest Mach numbers—and thus highest jet velocities—occur with H₂ ≈ He > N₂ > Ar.  
  • Typical cold‐spray exit velocities (at ~1.5–3 MPa stagnation, 500–800 °C) run roughly:  
     – H₂: 1 400–1 700 m/s  
     – He: 1 200–1 450 m/s  
     – N₂:   800–1 050 m/s  
     – Ar:   700–    950 m/s  

2. Gas density and particle acceleration  
  • Drag force Fd ∝ ρ·v²·Cd·A.  Higher‐density gases (Ar > N₂ > He > H₂) transfer momentum more readily per unit velocity but usually can’t reach as high v.  
  • There is a trade‐off: Ar’s density helps accelerate heavy particles, but its lower sonic speed limits the peak velocity.  Hydrogen and helium excel at accelerating small/medium particles to very high speeds.  

3. Thermal conductivity and particle heating  
  • λ(H₂) ≫ λ(He) > λ(N₂) > λ(Ar).  Higher thermal conductivity gases heat particles more effectively in the nozzle, boosting their ductility and lowering the critical velocity needed for bonding.  

4. Effects on deposition quality  
  • Particle velocity vs. critical velocity:  
     – Under-velocity → poor bonding, high porosity, low cohesion.  
     – Near-optimal velocity → good deformation, metallurgical bonding, low porosity, high adhesion.  
     – Over-velocity → erosion of coating or substrate, particle rebound, excessive work‐hardening.  
  • Gas choice shifts the achievable velocity window:  
     – H₂/He allow higher safe operating velocities → denser, harder coatings of high-strength or high-melting alloys.  
     – N₂ or Ar often suffice for softer materials (Al, Cu), lower cost, and non-flammable operation.  
  • Oxidation and contamination:  
     – Inert gases (Ar, He) minimize in-flight oxidation versus N₂ or H₂ (when not pure).  
     – High thermal conductivity (H₂) can drive off surface oxides more effectively but requires careful handling due to flammability.  

Summary of trade‐offs:  
  – Highest particle velocities and best deformation (hence dense, well-bonded coatings): H₂ > He.  
  – Good performance for many alloys, lower cost, inert: N₂.  
  – Best momentum transfer for large-particle/high-density feeds but lower top speed: Ar.  
  – Safety/cost considerations often drive a blend (e.g. He/N₂) or pure N₂ systems when ultra-high velocity is not required.

In cold spray the non-dimensional “velocity ratio” η is simply a way of measuring how fast your powder is moving compared to the flow that is carrying it (or to the minimum (“critical”) speed you need to get it to stick).  In most of the recent literature you will see it defined one of two ways:

  1.  η = vparticle/vgas–jet  
     –  vparticle is the particle impact velocity on the substrate  
     –  vgas–jet is the local gas‐jet velocity (e.g. the nozzle-exit or post-Mach–disk velocity)  

  2.  η = vparticle/vcritical  
     –  vcritical is the empirically determined threshold velocity below which no net deposition occurs  

Either way η is zero when the particles haven’t picked up any speed, it rises through unity at the onset of deposition, and approaches one (or above one, in the vparticle/vcritical form) as you drive the particles ever harder.  

What everybody observes, whether you plot tensile‐bond strength, shear‐cohesive strength or deposit porosity, is that  

  •  η < ≈0.5  ⇒  poor or zero cohesion and adhesion  
  •  η in the range 0.6 – 0.8 (or in vparticle/vcritical terms, roughly 1.1 – 1.5)  ⇒  maximum cohesive and adhesive strength  
  •  η > ≈0.9 (or vparticle/vcritical > ≈2)  ⇒  you begin to see re-erosion of your deposit and diminishing returns on bond strength  

So as a practical guideline you aim your process settings (gas pressure, gas temperature, nozzle geometry, powder feed rate, standoff distance, etc.) so that the powder arrives at the substrate with η on the order of 0.6–0.8 (or vparticle/vcritical ≃1.2–1.5).

In cold spray the two single most important “knobs” for driving particles into a near‐fully dense coating are (1) particle impact velocity and (2) particle (and gas) temperature.  Broadly speaking:

1. Particle impact velocity  
   • Below a material‐specific critical velocity (Vcrit) particles simply rebound or erode the surface; porosity is high and bonding is negligible.  
   • As you approach and exceed Vcrit, plastic deformation at the impact sites becomes sufficient to break up surface oxides, produce jetting and mechanical interlocking, and the coating porosity drops precipitously.  
   • Typical Vcrit’s are on the order of 300–600 m/s for soft alloys (Al, Cu), 900–1200 m/s for harder alloys and steels, and even higher for refractory metals.  
   • Further increases in velocity (up to about 1.2–1.3 × Vcrit) continue to raise density toward 98–99 % of theoretical. Above that range you risk substrate erosion, particle rebound and microcracking, which can actually increase porosity again.

2. Particle (and gas) temperature  
   • Preheating the carrier gas raises the static gas temperature, which (for a fixed pressure ratio) raises the sonic velocity in the nozzle and thus the terminal particle speed.  
   • Higher particle temperatures also soften the feedstock, lower flow stress, and so further reduce the required Vcrit for adhesion.  
   • In practice raising gas temperature by a few hundred °C can boost coating density by 5–10 % (for example from ~90 % to ~98 % theoretical density on Al alloys), or allow you to run at lower gas pressures for the same density.  
   • Beware overheating: excessive gas/particle temperatures promote oxidation, grain growth or even localized melting, any of which can introduce porosity or weaken the bond.

Putting it together, the highest‐density cold‐sprayed coatings are obtained by tuning gas temperature and pressure to accelerate particles just above their material‐specific Vcrit, and—if necessary—by preheating the feedstock or substrate to lower the required critical velocity.

Key morphological features of individual splats differ markedly between high-velocity, solid-state sprays (e.g. cold spray) and conventional thermal sprays (HVOF, plasma, flame):

1. Splat outline and edge  
   – Cold spray: very flat, nearly featureless “pancakes” with sharp, well-defined edges and no peripheral rim or splash fingers.  
   – Thermal spray: thicker, cup-shaped splats often with a raised “rim” or micro-craters, fine satellite droplets, and “finger‐like” splashes around the rim.

2. Surface texture  
   – Cold spray: smooth, mirror-like core with occasional radial “jetting” ridges or fold lines due to high-strain plastic flow. No evidence of solidification microstructures.  
   – Thermal spray: rough, often dimpled or nodular surfaces marked by dendritic or cellular solidification patterns, oxide “stringers,” and surface porosity.

3. Cross-sectional microstructure  
   – Cold spray: heavily deformed, ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains near the interface (due to adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization), intimate mechanical interlocking, virtually no oxides between particle and substrate.  
   – Thermal spray: characteristic columnar or dendritic grains growing inward from the splat’s periphery, oxide films or entrapped gas pores at boundaries, and evidence of resolidification fronts.

What these differences indicate about the particle state on impact  
– In cold spray the particle remains solid; it bonds by extreme plastic deformation and adiabatic shear without ever melting. The flat, un-splashed morphology and absence of solidification features testify to a fully solid-state, high-strain-rate impact.  
– In conventional thermal spray the particle is molten or partially molten at impact; it spreads as a liquid drop, wets the substrate, and then solidifies. The presence of splash rims, dendritic microstructures, and oxide networks is diagnostic of post-impact solidification of a liquid (or semi-liquid) droplet.

Increasing the process‐gas temperature in cold spray almost always raises deposition efficiency, and here’s why in brief:

1. Higher particle velocity  
   • At fixed stagnation pressure, raising T₀ boosts the speed of sound and hence the gas exit velocity (Vexit ≃ M·√(γR T₀)).  
   • Particles entrained in the jet therefore attain higher impact speeds and carry more kinetic energy (KE∝½mV²), making them more likely to exceed the material’s “critical velocity” for bonding.

2. Lower critical velocity  
   • A hotter, lower‐density carrier gas reduces aerodynamic drag during flight and can slightly soften the particle surface on impact, which further lowers the threshold velocity needed to achieve plastic deformation and bonding.

3. Net effect on efficiency  
   • Because more particles reach or exceed critical velocity, the fraction that actually adheres (the deposition efficiency, DE) increases sharply with temperature at first.  
   • Beyond some point you usually see diminishing returns or possible downsides (e.g. increased particle oxidation or reduced momentum flux from the lower gas density).

Bottom line:  
Raising process‐gas temperature → higher particle speeds and lower effective bonding threshold → higher deposition efficiencies up to an application‐specific limit.

Key to why an Archimedean spiral is so widely used in cold spray is that its “pitch” – the radial distance between one turn and the next – is a true constant.  That one feature immediately delivers several practical benefits over other spiral or raster‐like patterns:

1. Uniform overlap and powder flux  
   •  Because the spacing equals the spray plume’s width (or an integer fraction of it), each new pass overlaps the last by a fixed amount.  
   •  No zone is “double-dosed” or “skipped,” so the particle impact density remains constant over the whole build.

2. Even coating thickness and microstructure  
   •  Constant overlap = constant local deposition rate.  
   •  You avoid ridges in the center (where turns bunch up) and thin edges (where they spread out), both of which plague logarithmic or variable-pitch spirals.

3. Consistent thermal input and residual stress  
   •  Every point on the substrate sees the same dwell time under the spray plume, so the local heating and cooling rates are reproducible.  
   •  This uniformity suppresses gradients in microstructure, porosity, and residual stress.

4. Fluid, low–stress motion for the robot or gantry  
   •  The motion law is simple (r = a + b·θ with b constant), so acceleration and jerk profiles are smooth.  
   •  That translates into fewer dynamic transients in the nozzle feed, reduced mechanical wear, and cleaner spray plume dynamics.

5. Easy CAM/G-code implementation and parameter tuning  
   •  You choose one spacing parameter b to dial in your overlap; there’s no need to adjust spacing as the spiral grows.  
   •  Fine-tuning coating thickness is a matter of tweaking a single variable (scan speed, plume width, or spiral pitch).

In contrast, non-Archimedean spirals (e.g. logarithmic) have spacing that grows or shrinks with radius, so you end up with nonuniform overlap, variable dwell times, and zones of over- or under-deposition.  By locking in a constant turn-to-turn offset, the Archimedean spiral guarantees the most reproducible, homogeneous coating possible with a single continuous motion.

Key factors influencing cold spray deposition quality can be grouped into powder, gas/jet, process and substrate variables:

1. Powder properties  
  • Material ductility and hardness – ductile metals (Al, Cu) deform readily, while harder alloys may require higher impact velocity.  
  • Particle size and distribution – typically 5–50 μm; narrow distributions improve velocity uniformity.  
  • Morphology and flowability – spherical, oxide‐free powders feed more consistently and cold spray with fewer defects.  

2. Gas/jet parameters  
  • Gas species – He yields higher particle velocities than N₂ but at greater cost; mixtures balance performance and economy.  
  • Gas temperature and pressure – higher stagnation temperature and pressure raise jet velocity and particle impact energy.  
  • Nozzle design – converging–diverging geometry, throat diameter and length determine Mach number, jet profile and spray pattern.  

3. Process conditions  
  • Stand‐off distance – too short induces overheating and erosion; too long reduces velocity and deposition efficiency.  
  • Spray angle – 90° to substrate maximizes normal impact; oblique angles can increase shear bonding but may raise porosity.  
  • Traverse speed, pass overlap and powder feed rate – control deposit thickness uniformity and residual stress.  

4. Substrate preparation and properties  
  • Surface roughness – a grit‐blasted profile (Ra ~3–10 μm) enhances mechanical interlocking.  
  • Hardness and yield strength – softer substrates can deform under impact, improving adhesion; very hard substrates may require preheating.  
  • Preheating – moderate substrate heating (up to 200–300 °C) lowers critical velocity threshold and reduces residual stresses.  

Optimizing these interrelated factors to exceed the critical particle velocity while avoiding substrate damage is the key to high‐quality, dense, well‐bonded cold spray coatings.
