Cold spray builds coatings by propelling hard metal/ceramic particles at supersonic speed onto a substrate; on impact they deform (the metals plastically, the ceramics by brittle fracture) and interlock with one another. Because the surface topography is simply the “mosaic” of these flattened and fractured particles, you can tune roughness in‐situ by adjusting:

1. Particle impact velocity  
   – Gas pressure, temperature, nozzle design and standoff distance set the particle speed.  
   – Higher velocities → greater plastic flow of metal particles → flatter “splats” → lower Ra.  
   – Lower velocities → less deformation and more unmelted facets or ceramic fractures → higher Ra.

2. Feedstock characteristics  
   – Particle size distribution: finer powders pack and fill gaps more completely, giving smoother surfaces; coarser powders leave more pronounced peaks and valleys.  
   – Metal-to-ceramic ratio: metals deform and smooth out, ceramics crack and protrude; increasing ceramic content drives up microroughness.

3. Traverse speed, feed rate and number of passes  
   – Faster nozzle traverse or lower feed per pass deposits thinner, more uniform layers → smoother finish.  
   – Slower traverse/higher feed builds thicker lobes and higher asperities → rougher finish. Multiple low-feed passes can “feather” the surface smoother.

4. Spray angle and nozzle path  
   – Perpendicular impacts maximize deformation and flattening.  
   – Off-angle shots or steep overlap patterns introduce ridges and re-entrant features that increase roughness.

By selecting the right powder blend, particle size, spray velocity and movement strategy, you can dial in surface profiles from very smooth (Ra ≤1 µm) up to deliberately rough (Ra >10 µm) without any post-spray machining. This tunability is critical for implants, where submicron smoothness improves wear resistance in articulating parts, and controlled microscale roughness promotes bone ongrowth and soft-tissue integration.

Key points  
1. Basics of cold spray acceleration  
   - Particles are carried in a high-speed jet by a pressurized carrier gas flowing through a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle.  
   - The final particle velocity vₚ depends on the gas exit velocity v_gas, the particle–gas drag, the nozzle geometry, and the run‐through distance.  

2. Effect of gas molecular weight  
   - Lighter gases (He, H₂) have higher sound speeds (a = sqrt(γ·R·T/M)), so for the same stagnation conditions they reach a higher Mach number and a higher jet exit velocity.  
   - Typical ranking of achievable exit velocities at 20 °C and 3 MPa: He (≈ 1 200 m/s) > H₂ (≈ 1 000 m/s) > N₂ (≈ 550 m/s) > Ar (≈ 400 m/s).  
   - In practice helium jets yield solid‐particle speeds up to 800–1 000 m/s, nitrogen up to 500–700 m/s, argon up to ~400–550 m/s.  

3. Effect of stagnation pressure  
   - Raising the stagnation (or feed) pressure increases the total enthalpy in the gas, which boosts both the mass flow rate and the jet velocity.  
   - Particle drag acceleration ∝ (ρ_gas·C_d·A_p/2·m_p)·(v_gas–vₚ)². Since ρ_gas grows with pressure, the drag force grows, pushing particles faster.  
   - Empirically particle speed rises sub‐linearly with pressure: doubling from 1 to 2 MPa might increase vₚ by ~20–30%; going from 3 to 4 MPa yields smaller marginal gain and risks nozzle wear.  

4. Temperature–pressure interplay  
   - Most spray systems also heat the gas (300–800 °C). Higher temperature lowers gas density but raises sound speed and the available enthalpy, so vₚ still increases.  
   - The net result is optimum pressure-temperature pairs for each gas. Exceeding them risks particle overheating or nozzle erosion without much velocity gain.  

5. Practical considerations  
   - Nitrogen at 3–4 MPa and 450–500 °C is the industrial workhorse, giving 500–700 m/s.  
   - Helium (or He/H₂ mixes) at similar conditions hits 700–900 m/s—needed for high‐hardness materials (Ti, Ni alloys), but at 5–10× gas cost.  
   - Argon is cheap and inert but slow; used mainly for very soft metals or where reactivity of N₂/He is a concern.  

Summary  
- Lighter molecular‐weight gases → higher jet Mach number → higher particle velocity.  
- Higher stagnation pressure → higher gas density and mass flow → stronger drag → higher vₚ, but with diminishing returns and potential nozzle wear.  
- Heated gas magnifies the effect, so in practice you tune gas type, pressure, and temperature as a set for your material system.

In cold spray the powder never melts. Instead, particles are accelerated (typically 300–1200 m/s) in a heated gas and impact the substrate so violently that they undergo severe plastic deformation in the solid state.  Two features govern the resulting microstructure and properties:

1.  Low‐temperature deposition  
    •  No melt means virtually no oxidation, evaporation or phase transformations of the feedstock chemistry.  
    •  Native grain structure is retained in the particle cores, so there is little or no heat‐affected zone in the substrate.  

2.  High‐velocity impact plastically consolidates the powder  
    •  Adiabatic shear instabilities and extreme strain rates at the particle–substrate (and particle–particle) interface produce dynamic recrystallization in a very thin surface layer (typically <1 µm).  That layer is composed of ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains and very high dislocation densities.  
    •  The interior of each particle remains largely as in the feedstock (coarser grains), giving a “core–shell” or “onion‐ring” morphology when you cross‐section the deposit.  
    •  Particles squeeze out any entrapped gas or oxide at their peripheries, yielding coatings with very low porosity (<1–2 vol %) and strong metallurgical bonds.  

As a result of this microstructure you get coatings that combine:  
  – High bond and cohesion strength (>300–500 MPa in many systems)  
  – High residual compressive stress (improving fatigue and crack‐arrest behavior)  
  – Elevated hardness (strain‐hardening plus grain‐refinement hardening in the interface layers)  
  – Excellent corrosion and wear resistance (dense, oxide‐free metal and compressive surface stress)  
  – Little or no substrate heat damage, so dimensional tolerances and underlying microstructure remain intact.  

In short, cold‐sprayed coatings are dense, strongly adherent, strain‐hardened and often nanostructured in the interface region—all achieved without melting or high‐temperature oxidation.

In cold spray the degree to which a metallic particle “pancakes” on impact—usually quantified by the spread factor, S = Dfinal/D0—depends almost entirely on how much kinetic energy it carries into the collision and how easily it can plastically flow on impact.  Two of the easiest levers to pull on are (a) the impact velocity, v, and (b) the particle temperature, T, on impact.

1. Impact velocity  
  • Kinetic‐energy driving force.  Kinetic energy per unit volume scales as ½ρp v².  Above a material‐specific “critical velocity” vc (just enough energy to initiate bonding), any further rise in v quickly produces more plastic deformation and thus more spreading.  
  • Flattening trend.  Empirically one observes roughly  
     S ∼ A·v^m  
    with m typically in the range 0.5–1.0 (m depends on the material’s work‐hardening behavior and strain‐rate sensitivity).  In finite‐element or analytical “energy‐balance” models one often ends up with  
     S ∼ v/√(Y(T)/ρp)  
    or some variant thereof, so that doubling v almost doubles the spread factor (up to the point where geometric constraints or rebound effects begin to set in).

2. Particle temperature  
  • Lowered flow stress.  Heating the particle (via a hotter carrier gas or in‐flight plasma heating) reduces its yield strength Y and flow stress: for many metals Y drops by 10–30% for every 100–200 °C rise in T.  Lower Y means the same kinetic energy produces a larger plastic strain field and hence more pancake spreading.  
  • Effect versus velocity.  In practice raising T by a few hundred degrees C will boost S by perhaps 10–30%, whereas doubling v can boost S by 50–100% or more.  In other words, velocity is the dominant knob; temperature is a powerful secondary knob for fine‐tuning.

3. Critical‐velocity crossover and “optimum” flattening  
  • Below vc no coherent deposit forms—particles tend to rebound or fragment.  
  • Just above vc you get partial flattening and limited adhesion.  
  • As v increases well above vc, S grows rapidly until either:  
    – the particle is so thin that substrate contact area saturates, or  
    – very high strain‐rates cause local heating, dynamic recrystallization, or even jetting/splat detachment.  

Practical implications  
– To maximize spreading (and hence bonding area), you usually set the gas pressure and temperature to get particles just above vc at the nozzle exit, then trade off additional preheat or pressure vs. feed rate.  
– If you overheat particles you risk oxidation in flight or unwanted phase changes; if you overspeed them you risk substrate damage or particle erosion rather than net deposition.

Summary  
– Impact velocity v drives flattening most strongly (spread factor roughly ∝ v^0.5–1).  
– Higher particle temperature T lowers yield stress, giving an additional boost to flattening (∼ 10–30% per few‐hundred °C).  
– There is a material‐specific vc below which no effective flattening/adherence occurs, and at very high v or T you begin to see diminishing returns or damage.

Typical carrier gases in cold spray are  
  • Helium (He)  
  • Nitrogen (N₂)  
  • Argon (Ar)  

Air (i.e. compressed shop air) is sometimes used in place of—or in combination with—these inert gases for three main reasons:

1. Lower cost and ready availability  
   - Helium is expensive and in short supply.  
   - Nitrogen (liquid- or cylinder-sourced) and argon both carry handling and storage costs, whereas plant‐compressed air is “free,” continuous, and on-demand.

2. Acceptable performance with ductile alloys  
   - Many common feedstocks (soft copper, aluminum, stainless steel, nickel alloys) tolerate a small amount of surface oxidation and only need moderate gas velocities to achieve the critical deposition velocity.  
   - Air (M ≈ 29 g/mol) can accelerate particles fast enough for those alloys, especially when pre-heating the gas to 300–800 °C.

3. Simplified logistics and safety  
   - Eliminates gas‐manifold changeovers and leak-checking inert gas piping.  
   - No risk of asphyxiation from inert gas leaks in confined spaces.  
   - In applications where a thin surface oxide is not detrimental—or is even beneficial to corrosion resistance—air is a pragmatic choice.

Limitations of air:  
  • Oxygen and moisture can promote oxide formation on particle surfaces, raising the required impact velocity.  
  • Not suitable for reactive powders (e.g. pure titanium or high‐strength aluminum alloys) unless very tight process control and pre-heating are employed.

In a cold‐spray system the powder never “flies itself” – it is simply carried by a high‐velocity gas jet that has been driven to supersonic speed by a de Laval (converging–diverging) nozzle.  In outline the steps are:

1.  A carrier gas (usually N₂ or He) is compressed to 15–40 bar and preheated to 300–900 °C.  
2.  It is then expanded isentropically through a converging–diverging nozzle.  As the gas accelerates from the throat to the exit its pressure energy is converted into kinetic energy, producing a Mach > 1 jet.  
3.  Powder is injected just upstream of (or at) the nozzle throat and becomes entrained in this jet.  
4.  Within a few nozzle diameters the particles experience large aerodynamic drag forces   
      Fₙ ≃ ½ C_D ρ_g A_p (v_g–v_p)²  
   and are accelerated toward the gas speed (2–3 times the local speed of sound).  
5.  On exiting the nozzle the particles impact the substrate at 600–1200 m/s, deform plastically, and bond without melting.

In short, it is purely the momentum transfer (drag) from a supersonic, isentropically expanded gas flow that accelerates the particles to high speed.

In cold spray the carrier‐gas exit speed is set by the isentropic expansion through the nozzle, which to a good approximation obeys  

vexit = √[2γRT0/(γ–1) · (1 – (pexit/p0)^((γ–1)/γ))]  

or, if the flow is choked (pexit/p0≤(2/(γ+1))^(γ/(γ–1))),  

vexit = √[γ R T0]·(2/(γ+1))^((γ+1)/2(γ–1)).  

Key points:  
• R = Ru/MW, so a low molecular weight directly raises R and hence raises vexit roughly as v∝1/√MW.  
• γ (the specific‐heat ratio c p/c v) appears under the radical and in the pressure‐ratio exponent. A larger γ gives a steeper, more energetic expansion and thus higher Mach—and exit—velocity.  

In practice this means:  
– Monatomic gases (He: γ≈1.66, MW=4 g/mol) produce exit speeds up to ~1.5–2 km/s under typical cold‐spray pressures and temperatures.  
– Diatomic gases (N2 or air: γ≈1.4, MW≈28–29 g/mol) yield exit speeds more on the order of 600–900 m/s under the same conditions.  

Bottom line: in cold spray you maximize exit velocity (and hence particle impact velocity) by choosing a carrier gas with as low a molecular weight as feasible and as high a γ as feasible.

Below is a concise summary of the principal strategies for reducing porosity in cold‐sprayed deposits, followed by why it is essentially impossible to drive porosity to zero.

1. Spray‐process optimization  
 • Gas temperature & pressure – higher gas temperature or pressure increases particle velocity and plastic deformation, improving interparticle bonding.  
 • Stand‐off distance and traverse speed – tuned to give particles just enough dwell time and impact energy. Too close or too slow → particle rebound; too far or too fast → insufficient deformation.  
 • Powder size distribution – narrower, finer powders deform more uniformly and fill gaps.  

2. Substrate and powder pre-treatments  
 • Substrate preheat – raises substrate temperature to reduce thermal mismatch and increase particle “weldability.”  
 • Powder surface conditioning – mechanically or chemically remove oxide films, apply low‐melting or ductile “binder” layers (e.g. Cu on Al particles) to promote bonding.  

3. Post-spray thermal/mechanical densification  
 • Annealing – elevated‐temperature dwell drives diffusional healing of small voids at particle interfaces.  
 • Hot isostatic pressing (HIP) – high temperature + high isostatic gas pressure collapse and close nearly all internal pores.  
 • Laser or electron‐beam remelting – localized melting of the top‐coat to fill open pores, though this changes microstructure and sometimes properties.  
 • Severe‐plastic-deformation treatments (SMAT, shot‐peening, roller‐pressing) – impose secondary cold working to close voids by plastic flow.  

4. Infiltration and sealing  
 • Metal or polymer infiltration – low-viscosity infiltrants (e.g. molten metals, polymers, ceramic slurries) fill residual open porosity.  
 • Post‐coat sealants or diffusive coatings – pores plugged by CVD/ALD layers.  

Why you cannot drive porosity to zero  
 1. Line-of-sight and shadowing – some voids become fully enclosed during build-up and cannot be accessed by subsequent sprays or infiltrants.  
 2. Oxide/contaminant films – even thin oxide layers on powder or substrate surfaces inhibit 100% intimate metal–metal contact.  
 3. Non‐uniform deformation – at the very high strain rates of cold spray, some particles “splat” more than others, creating microgaps.  
 4. Entrapped gases – air or process‐gas pockets get sealed inside before they can escape.  
 5. Equipment limits – practical bounds on gas temperature, pressure, standoff, and post-treatment severity constrain how much densification is feasible without degrading the coating or substrate.  

In practice, combining spray‐parameter optimization with post‐spray HIP or laser remelting plus infiltration can routinely reduce porosity below 0.5–1 vol. % in many alloys, but reaching truly zero pores is precluded by a combination of inaccessible enclosed voids, residual oxides, and process trade-offs.

In most cold-spray additive-manufacturing systems you feed powders whose particle sizes lie roughly between 5 and 50 μm (in some cases 5–75 μm, with the most common grades in the 10–40 μm range).  That window is important because:  
• Acceleration and impact velocity  –  Particles must be small enough for the supersonic carrier gas to drag them up to (or above) their critical velocity in the nozzle, but not so small that they simply follow the gas streamlines around the part or bounce off.  
• Deposition efficiency  –  Too-large particles won’t reach impact velocity and either erode the coating or build up porosity; too-small particles have poor momentum and low adhesion.  
• Feed reliability and wear  –  A controlled size distribution prevents nozzle clogging and minimizes erosion of internal hardware.  
• Feature resolution and microstructure  –  Finer powders make thinner, higher‐resolution layers; coarser powders speed bulk build‐up but give rougher surfaces and more heterogeneity.

Key defining features of cold spray in terms of particle and thermal state are:

1. Solid‐state deposition  
   • Powder particles remain entirely solid—they are never melted.  
   • Bonding occurs by severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at impact.  

2. High kinetic, low thermal energy  
   • Gas pressures of 1–5 MPa and temperatures typically 150–800 °C accelerate particles to supersonic speeds (≈300–1 200 m/s).  
   • Particle kinetic energy far exceeds any thermal energy input; thermal softening is limited and always below the alloy’s melting point.  

3. Minimal substrate heating  
   • Since particles do not melt, and gas temperatures are well below Tm, substrate temperatures remain near ambient.  
   • Very low heat‐affected zone, minimal oxidation and thermal stresses.  

4. Critical‐velocity requirement  
   • Each material has a threshold impact velocity (≈500–800 m/s for many metals) above which intimate, oxide‐disrupted, plastic‐flow bonding occurs.  

In sum, cold spray relies on supersonic, solid particles plastically deforming on a “cold” surface, achieving metallurgical bonding with negligible melting or bulk heating.

Below is a concise comparison of helium versus compressed air as cold‐spray carrier gases, organized by the key trade-off categories.

1. Gas‐property fundamentals  
   – Molecular weight (M): He ≈ 4 g/mol vs air ≈ 29 g/mol  
   – Ratio of specific heats (k): He ≈ 1.66 vs air ≈ 1.40  
   – Speed of sound (a): He ≈ 970 m/s vs air ≈ 347 m/s  
   – Result: At the same stagnation pressure and temperature, a He jet reaches much higher sonic and supersonic velocities.  

2. Particle acceleration & deposition efficiency  
   – Higher gas velocity → higher particle velocities, so materials with high critical velocities (e.g. Cu, Ti, stainless steels) can be reliably deposited with He.  
   – Air yields lower maximum particle speeds (≈ 350–450 m/s), so deposition is limited to softer/low‐critical‐velocity powders (e.g. Al, Zn, low-alloy steels).  
   – He typically gives superior deposition efficiency (up to 90–100%) and denser, better‐adhering coatings; air sprays often show lower build‐up rates and higher porosity.

3. Oxidation & microstructure  
   – Helium is inert—minimizes in-flight or in-deposit oxidation. Ideal for oxygen-sensitive alloys (e.g. Ti, Ni superalloys).  
   – Compressed air contains O₂ and H₂O (even after drying), which can form oxide shells on particles or in the deposit, degrading cohesion, ductility, or corrosion resistance.

4. Economic & practical considerations  
   – Helium  
      • High gas cost (several dollars per m³) plus need for recovery/recycling systems to control operating expense.  
      • Cylinder logistics, potential supply constraints.  
   – Compressed air  
      • Nearly “free” on site (electricity to run shop compressors).  
      • No special storage or recovery hardware required.  
      • Must invest in reliable dryers/filters to remove moisture, oil, particulates.

5. Equipment & safety  
   – Heat capacity: He cools less on expansion (higher T₀ required for same gas jet temperature), but in practice cold‐spray systems are designed for either gas.  
   – Leak safety: He is non-toxic/inert; air poses no unusual hazards but O₂ enrichment is a consideration in confined spaces.  

6. Hybrid & intermediate solutions  
   – N₂ or Ar blends with He (e.g. 50:50 He/N₂) can cut gas cost while retaining much of He’s velocity advantage.  
   – Pure N₂ is sometimes used as a lower‐cost inert alternative but has only marginally better performance than air and still carries the oxidation/moisture issue.

Summary  
– Use helium when maximum particle velocity, high build-efficiency and oxide‐free deposits are required—especially for high-critical-velocity or oxidation-sensitive alloys.  
– Use compressed air when cost or equipment simplicity is paramount, and when you are spraying low-critical-velocity, oxidation‐tolerant materials (or when you have robust filtration/drying in place).

In cold spray the single most important “knobs” for tuning particle velocity are those that set the gas‐jet’s Mach number and the coupling between the gas jet and the particles.  In practice that means:

 1. Carrier‐gas stagnation pressure (P₀)  
  • Higher P₀ ⇒ higher gas‐jet velocity ⇒ higher drag on the particles.  
  • Limited by compressor/tank capacity and nozzle strength.  

 2. Carrier‐gas stagnation temperature (T₀)  
  • Raising T₀ lowers the gas density at a given pressure, raises the speed of sound and boosts jet velocity.  
  • Must balance against powder thermal sensitivity.  

 3. Nozzle geometry (area ratio, convergence/divergence angles, length)  
  • A properly designed De Laval nozzle converts P₀ and T₀ into a supersonic jet.  
  • Exit Mach number (and thus velocity) is set by the ratio of exit area to throat area and by the pressure ratio P₀/P_back.  

 4. Gas species  
  • Light gases (He, H₂) have higher speeds of sound and reach higher jet velocities than heavier gases (N₂, Ar) at the same P₀/T₀.  

Secondary effects:  
  • Powder feed rate: too high a feed rate starves the gas of momentum (drops particle velocity); too low a rate wastes jet energy.  
  • Standoff distance and nozzle alignment: optimal distance (~20–50 mm) and normal incidence ensure maximal acceleration and minimal jet expansion losses.  
  • Particle size and shape: smaller particles accelerate faster (lower inertia), very large particles may never reach critical impact velocity.  

In summary, P₀, T₀, nozzle design (area ratio and pressure ratio), and gas species are the primary levers for controlling particle velocity; powder feed rate, standoff distance, and particle size then fine-tune the actual velocities achieved.

In cold‐spray, raising the propellant‐gas temperature drives the particle impact velocity higher (both by increasing sound speed and reducing gas viscosity), which in turn:

1. Lowers porosity by  
   • boosting particle kinetic energy above the critical velocity for the metal, so that particles plastically deform more on impact and “fill in” voids,  
   • improving interparticle bonding and reducing interstitial gaps.

2. Shows diminishing returns above a certain temperature  
   • once velocities well exceed the critical threshold, further T increases give only marginal porosity gains,  
   • excessively high T also lowers gas density (so momentum transfer per unit pressure drops) and can promote surface oxidation, both of which can slightly degrade densification.

Typical examples (argon propellant, Al or Cu alloys, 40–60 μm powder size):  
– At 350 °C you may see 3–5 vol% porosity.  
– By 550–600 °C porosity often falls below 1–2 vol%.  
– Beyond ~650 °C the porosity curve flattens out or can even creep up if oxidation becomes severe.

In practice you select the minimum temperature that reliably puts your particles above their material-specific critical velocity—this maximizes densification (minimizes porosity) without over‐heating or oxidizing the feedstock.

Mixing a hard, brittle phase (e.g. WC, SiC, Al₂O₃, diamond) into a ductile cold‐spray powder will almost always drive the as-sprayed coating density down unless you compensate by boosting particle velocity or re-optimizing the process.  The mechanisms are:

1. Impeded plastic flow  
   •  Hard particles act as rigid inclusions in the deforming metal matrix.  Under impact they do not cold-weld, so they locally block the extrusion and inter-particle flow that normally closes pores.  
   •  Stress concentrations at the hard/soft interfaces induce micro‐voiding or even micro‐cracking during deposition.  

2. Reduced deposition efficiency  
   •  At typical cold‐spray velocities many hard particles simply rebound instead of embedding, leaving gaps in the buildup.  
   •  The overall mass of ductile material delivered per pass drops, so more void space remains.  

3. Poor packing and interstitial filling at higher loadings  
   •  At low volume fractions (≈5–10 %) a very fine hard phase can actually lodge in the tiny interstices between ductile particles and marginally improve packing.  
   •  Beyond ~20 %–30 % hard‐phase by volume, however, particles begin to agglomerate and inhibit closing of larger voids, driving porosity—and thus 1–15 % density loss—up sharply.  

In practice you see typical cold‐spray composite coatings (20–30 vol% hard phase) run at 85–95 % of theoretical density, versus 98–100 % for the pure ductile powder.  To claw back density when adding hard particles you must increase particle velocity (higher gas temp/pressure or lighter carrier gas), optimize the powder size ratio (large ductile core + very fine hard shell), or apply a post-spray densification treatment.

Laser power in a laser‐assisted cold‐spray system is essentially the “thermal knob” that controls how much of the particle and/or substrate you soften before impact.  By tuning the laser power you directly affect:

 1. Particle temperature rise and softening  
    – Higher laser power → more energy absorbed by the particle (and a thin surface layer of the substrate) → greater reduction in yield strength and hardness → particles plastically deform more easily on impact.  
    – Lower laser power → insufficient softening → particles behave more like in conventional cold spray and need very high impact velocities to bond.

 2. Critical velocity for deposition  
    – As you increase laser power and thus thermal softening, the minimum gas velocity (or particle impact velocity) required to achieve metallurgical bonding goes down.  
    – This allows deposition of harder alloys or larger particles at lower gas pressures or temperatures.

 3. Deformation, flattening (“splat”) geometry, and bonding  
    – Moderately high laser power promotes greater spreading (higher “flattening ratio”), intimate substrate contact, dynamic recrystallization at the interface, and stronger metallic bonding.  
    – Too little laser power → poor splatting and weak mechanical interlocking.  

 4. Avoiding undesirable melting or oxidation  
    – If laser power is pushed above a certain threshold, particles begin to melt.  You lose the benefits of “cold” spraying (minimal oxidation, low residual stress) and risk an inhomogeneous, thermally sprayed coating with oxides, porosity, or resolidified globules.  
    – In practice there is an optimal power window: high enough to plasticize, low enough to stay below the melting point.

In short, laser power controls the balance between purely kinetic (cold), mixed thermo-kinetic, and fully thermal spray regimes by setting the amount of pre‐impact thermal softening.  Optimizing it is key to lowering required velocities, improving deposition efficiency, and retaining the microstructural advantages of cold spray.

Particle shape is one of the single biggest factors controlling how tightly powder can pack both in the feed‐tube and, ultimately, in the deposited cold-sprayed layer.  In broad terms:

1. Spherical particles  
   • Pack most efficiently (theoretical random‐close packing ≈ 0.63 by volume; ordered packing up to 0.74)  
   • Good flowability and uniform density in the feed line  
   • Tend to give the lowest residual porosity in the coating  

2. Angular/Irregular particles  
   • Interlock and “bridge,” creating larger voids and a lower overall tap or packing density (often < 0.60)  
   • Poorer flow in the supply system but can enhance mechanical interlocking at the substrate  
   • Typically lead to higher porosity in the as-sprayed deposit  

3. High-aspect-ratio (platelet or flake) particles  
   • Pack in strongly anisotropic ways  
   • Can lie flat and form lamellar voids, or stand on edge and form columnar porosity  
   • Lowest volumetric packing (often < 0.50) unless deliberately aligned during spraying  

4. Effects on the cold-spray deposit  
   • Lower‐packing powders leave more interstitial space in the pre-impact particle bed; unless fully collapsed by plastic deformation on impact, those voids become porosity in the coating.  
   • Highly spherical powders promote the highest deposition density and lowest porosity.  
   • Irregular/rough particles may give slightly thicker, more mechanically interlocked coatings but at the expense of higher residual porosity and less uniform density.  

In practice, one often trades off the excellent packing and flow of spherical powders against the enhanced bond strength sometimes achieved with angular or irregular powders—recognizing that the latter will always pack less densely and yield a higher-porosity deposit unless compensated by higher impact energy or post-spray densification.

Cold‐spray (“kinetic spray”) additive manufacturing builds metal parts by accelerating micron- to sub-millimeter powder particles to very high velocities and relying on their solid-state impact to create a dense deposit.  Its key steps are:

1. Gas acceleration  
   • A high-pressure, typically inert gas (He or N₂), is heated (but kept below the powder’s melting point) and expanded through a converging–diverging (De Laval) nozzle.  
   • Expansion converts gas enthalpy into kinetic energy, driving particles entrained in the flow to supersonic speeds (300–1200 m/s).  

2. Particle impact and bonding  
   • Upon striking the substrate (or previously deposited layer), each particle undergoes extreme, localized plastic deformation—often with adiabatic shear instabilities.  
   • This deformation “breaks through” native oxide films, fresh‐metal contact is established, and bonding occurs by a combination of mechanical interlocking and solid‐state metallurgical adhesion.  

3. Layer build-up  
   • Repeated high-velocity impacts bury earlier particles and fill interstices, producing a dense (> 99% theoretical density) structure without ever melting the feedstock.  
   • The process requires that each particle exceed a material-specific critical velocity; below that threshold, particles rebound rather than adhere.  

Because no melting or solidification is involved, cold spray preserves the starting material’s fine microstructure, avoids oxidation and thermal distortion, and enables rapid, low-heat input additive manufacturing of metals and metal composites.

As you move the nozzle farther away than the length of the “acceleration window” in a cold-spray jet, the particles begin to slow down rather than pick up any more speed. In practice what happens is:

 1. Gas‐stream velocity and density are already declining beyond the optimal stand-off.  
 2. The particles see a “tail‐end” jet whose drag force now exceeds its accelerating force.  
 3. Net drag decelerates the particles, so their velocity—and hence their kinetic energy (½mV²)—falls off with increasing distance.  
 4. Some of the lost kinetic energy is dissipated as heat in the gas and in interphase shear/turbulence; the particle temperature also drops.  
 5. If the stand-off becomes too large, most particles will dip below the critical velocity for bonding and either rebound or generate a very poor deposit.  

In short, once you push past the gas stream’s optimum acceleration zone, particle KE decays rapidly with further increase in stand-off distance, degrading deposition efficiency.

Below is a summary of the most common approaches used in cold‐spray research and commercial systems to lessen the bow‐shock slowdown of powder particles:  

1. Nozzle‐geometry optimization  
   • Contoured (“smooth”) convergent–divergent profiles with low exit angles (1–5°) and carefully shaped throat fillets delay or weaken normal shocks.  
   • Extended diverging sections or modular barrel‐extensions shift the bow shock downstream, giving particles more residence time in the near‐isentropic core.  
   • Larger exit‐to‐throat area ratios run the nozzle at a lower exit Mach number (M≈2–2.5 instead of M≈3–4), reducing shock strength.  

2. Particle‐injection strategies  
   • In-nozzle (down‐the‐throat) injection places particles inside the supersonic core before any shock forms.  
   • Aerodynamic focusing rings or convergent particle‐lens inserts align and center the powder stream on the axis, keeping particles out of peripheral shocks.  
   • Adjustable powder-feeder feedrates and carrier-gas pressures can be tuned so that peak particle concentration coincides with the nozzle’s shock‐free region.  

3. Coaxial/shroud‐gas curtains  
   • A low‐velocity, co‐axial “sheath” gas enveloping the supersonic core cushions and smoothes pressure gradients, blunting the bow shock.  
   • Shroud gases can be the same species at reduced pressure or a heavier gas (e.g., Ar around He) to tailor the mixing layer and shock stand-off distance.  

4. Gas‐type and thermodynamic control  
   • Mixing He into N₂ (or switching entirely to He) raises the speed of sound, lowering the nozzle’s exit Mach number for a given pressure ratio, which softens shocks.  
   • Preheating the propellant gas reduces its density and increases its sonic speed; this also weakens and pushes the bow shock farther downstream.  

5. Spray‐parameter and stand-off tuning  
   • Operating at lower total pressure ratios (just above the nozzle’s critical ratio) can eliminate strong normal shocks at the exit.  
   • Optimizing the stand-off distance so that the spray toe is just beyond the natural shock stand-off point avoids the stagnation region.  

6. Active and passive shock‐manipulation  
   • Small wedges or “shock‐train” spoilers placed off‐axis can split or deflect the bow shock away from the particle path.  
   • Acoustic or pulsed-flow actuation has been investigated (in research) to periodically break up the shock, giving particles shock-free windows.  

By combining several of these strategies—most often: a well-contoured long diverging nozzle, in-nozzle powder injection, a coaxial shroud gas, and gas‐composition/temperature control—commercial cold-spray systems push the strong bow shock well downstream or soften it sufficiently so that particles remain at near-free-jet velocities upon impact.

Key points  
1.  Standoff distance (SOD) controls how far the gas–particle jet expands and decays before it impacts the substrate.  That, in turn, determines particle velocity, particle momentum on impact, and hence both deposition efficiency (DE) and film‐build rate.  
2.  In virtually every cold‐spray system there is a “sweet spot” SOD at which the supersonic core is fully developed (maximizing particle acceleration) but drag‐ and mixing‐induced decay have not yet had time to rob the particles of too much momentum.  Too short or too long an SOD both reduce DE and film thickness.  

Detailed description  
1.  Very short SOD (< 5–10 mm, nozzle dependent)  
   •  The shock‐cell structure and barrel shock are still forming out of the nozzle – the jet has not yet reached its peak velocity profile.  
   •  Particles have not attained their maximum attainable velocity, so their impact kinetic energy is sub‐optimal.  
   •  The jet is highly underexpanded and high‐pressure, which tends to erode as well as deposit; the deposition footprint is narrow and may be erosive.  
   → DE is moderate (often < 40 %), film thickness per pass is low and nonuniform; residual stress and substrate damage can be high.  

2.  Optimum SOD (typically 10–30 mm for common nozzles and gases)  
   •  The supersonic core has fully formed, particles have reached near‐maximum velocity (e.g. 500–1200 m/s depending on gas and pressure).  
   •  Gas–particle mixing with ambient air is still minor, so drag‐induced deceleration is low, and particle momentum is maximized at impact.  
   •  The deposition footprint is well defined, and particles deform plastically on impact to form a dense, adherent coating.  
   → DE peaks (often 50–70 % for ductile metals like Cu or Al), film growth rate is high (tens of microns per pass), and thickness uniformity is good.  

3.  Long SOD (> 30–50 mm)  
   •  The jet has begun to decay: shock‐cell strength weakens, turbulent mixing with ambient air increases, gas temperature and velocity fall off, and packeted particles begin to slow down via drag (drag force ∼ρgas·v²·Cd·A).  
   •  Particles lose momentum en route and some even scatter outside the main plume, so fewer particles reach the critical impact velocity needed to bond.  
   •  The deposition footprint broadens and thins.  
   → DE drops sharply (often < 30 %), film thickness per pass decreases roughly linearly with SOD, and coatings become more porous and rough.  Beyond ~50–80 mm the DE can approach zero.  

Qualitative curves (for a fixed spray pressure, powder loading, traverse speed)  
   – DE vs. SOD: bell‐shaped, peaking at the “optimum” SOD.  
   – Film thickness per pass vs. SOD: roughly constant near the optimum, then falling off monotonically at longer SOD.  

Mechanistic summary  
   – At very short SOD the jet is underexpanded (particles under‐accelerated).  
   – At the optimum SOD the supersonic core is mature, drag is minimal, and particle momentum at impact is maximal.  
   – At long SOD particle velocity decays due to aerodynamic drag, jet turbulence, and thermal losses; fewer particles reach the critical velocity for deposition.

Increasing the “dwell” between cold‐spray passes has one simple, dominant thermal effect: it gives the substrate more time to dump heat and therefore lowers its surface temperature before the next pass.  In practice this shows up as:

  1.  Reduced heat‐build-up (thermal-accumulation) from pass to pass.  If your inter‐pass interval Δt is short compared with the substrate’s thermal time‐constant τ (τ∼L²/α for a characteristic thickness L and diffusivity α), the surface continues to climb.  As Δt grows toward or beyond τ, convective (and radiative) cooling lets the surface decay nearly back to ambient temperature.
  2.  An exponential “cool‐down” curve:  
     Tsurf(t) = Tambient + (T0 − Tambient)·e^(–t/τ)  
     so doubling or tripling your wait time cuts the residual ΔT by the same exponential factor.
  3.  Consequences for coating: cooler surfaces give less adiabatic heating of particles on impact, reduce local plastic deformation and bonding, and lower residual stresses—whereas very short waits drive up Tsurf and can improve bond strength (but risk overheating or oxidation).

In short, the longer you wait, the more nearly your substrate returns toward ambient between passes, and the lower its mean and peak surface temperature will be.

In shot‐peening–assisted cold spray the depth (or “thickness”) of the plastically deformed surface layer is set by two things: (1) the indentation depth produced by each shot, and (2) the number of overlapping indentations per unit area.  Pressure, flow rate and shot size each play a role in one or both of those.  A very good way to see their relative influence is to write the peening‐induced layer thickness H simply as  
   
 H ≃ N·δ   
   
where N is the number of impacts per unit area (coverage) and δ is the plastic indentation depth per impact.   

1.  Indentation depth δ per shot  
   •  δ scales with the kinetic energy of a single shot and the shot diameter D:  
     –  m ∼ ρ·D³  (shot mass)  
     –  KE ≡ ½ m v²  (v = shot speed set by gas pressure)  
   •  In elastic–plastic contact models (Hertzian→plastic transition) one finds empirically  
     δ ∝ (m v²/σy²)^(1/3)  ∝  D·v^(2/3)/σy^(2/3)  
   •  Thus increasing D at fixed v boosts δ linearly; increasing v (by raising gas pressure) boosts δ with a ∼v^(2/3) law.  

2.  Number of impacts N (coverage)  
   •  N ∝ mass flow rate (F) × t / m  ∝  F/D³     (for constant shot material density)  
   •  In practice, raising the flow rate increases the overlap of indentations; past a certain point the surface “saturates” (nearly full coverage) and further increases of F give diminishing returns.  

Putting these two together, the peened‐layer thickness scales roughly as  
   
 H ∝ N · δ  ∝ (F/D³) · (D v^(2/3))  
   = F · v^(2/3)/D².   
   
From that relation you can see:  
 •  Flow rate F enters linearly: double F, and at low coverage you roughly double the final layer thickness until you hit full coverage.  
 •  Shot diameter D enters as 1/D² in coverage but also linearly in δ.  In practice moderate increases in D give a modest net gain in H, but very large pellets can lead to surface roughening and lower coverage efficiency.  
 •  Pressure controls v, and since δ∝v^(2/3) and also higher v improves per‐particle adherence/overlap, pressure ends up being the single most powerful “tuning knob.”  

Which is most influential?  
 •  In the typical operating window for cold‐spray peening (gas pressures from, say, 3 to 6 bar, shot sizes from 200 to 600 µm, flow rates from 10 to 40 g/min), changes in gas pressure (and thus particle velocity) systematically drive the largest change in plastically deformed thickness.  Raising pressure not only boosts per‐shot indentation depth, but also sharpens each shot’s impact footprint so you get better coverage—even before you crank up the flow rate.   

Bottom line  
 •  Pressure (via shot velocity) is the most influential parameter for controlling the depth of the plastically deformed layer in shot‐peening‐assisted cold‐sprayed coatings.  •  Shot diameter is the next most important (it governs per‐shot mass and indentation size).  •  Flow rate is largely a coverage/throughput parameter and, beyond the low‐coverage regime, has the least leverage once you approach saturation.

Substrate roughness boosts cold‐spray deposition efficiency almost entirely by altering how particles impact, deform, and stick, as follows:

1. Mechanical anchoring of early particles  
   – Peaks and valleys act as “micro‐pockets” in which the very first particles lodge rather than ricochet.  
   – Once these anchor points form, subsequent particles can build up more readily, reducing the critical velocity needed for bonding.

2. Concentration of impact stresses and local plasticity  
   – Sharp asperity tips focus the impact load into very small areas, raising local pressure and strain rates.  
   – This encourages adiabatic shear and large plastic deformation at the particle–substrate interface, which is key to bonding in cold spray.

3. Increased true contact area and frictional dissipation  
   – A rough surface has much greater real surface area than a polished one, so more of each particle’s kinetic energy is spent deforming and “wedging” into those asperities rather than bouncing off.  
   – Higher friction at the interface further dissipates impact energy and promotes particle accommodation.

4. Progressive surface “self-roughening”  
   – As the first few particles deform against the asperities, they flatten and create a new, conformal rough surface.  
   – This evolving topology even more effectively traps and deforms later particles, giving a positive feedback that sharply raises deposition efficiency for the growing layer.

In combination, these effects lower the effective critical velocity for deposition, reduce particle rebound, and convert a larger fraction of the spray’s kinetic energy into the plastic work and interfacial bonding that build up the coating or part.

Key points  
1.  Gas temperature (Tg) and powder‐injection point jointly set the particle’s in-nozzle trajectory, its exit velocity and temperature, and hence its impact energy, plasticity and bonding.  
2.  Higher Tg → higher particle velocity (Vp ∝√Tg) and more thermal softening (flow stress ↓) → stronger bonding, lower porosity, higher electrical conductivity.  
3.  Axial (on-axis) injection places powder in the supersonic hot core, maximizing Tg and Vp; lateral (off-axis) injection feeds powder into cooler, slower boundary layers → lower Vp, less plastic deformation at impact → higher porosity, poorer conductivity.  

Mechanisms in detail  
1.  Aerodynamic acceleration and gas thermodynamics  
 •  In a converging–diverging nozzle the Mach number M at the throat and exit grows with stagnation temperature T0 (i.e. Tg) via  
  Mexit≈[(P0/Pback)^((γ–1)/γ)–1·2/(γ–1)]^½,  
  Vp≈Mexit·√(γ·R·T0)  
 •  Because Vp∝√T0, raising Tg by e.g. 100 °C typically boosts Vp by ~5–7 %. Even small uplift in Vp can push particles past their “critical velocity” for bonding.  

2.  Particle heating and softening  
 •  Particles entrained in hot gas pick up heat; their surface temperature rises, reducing flow stress σy≈σ0+K·ε^ n. Lower σy at the moment of impact allows deeper plastic flow, jet formation at particle–substrate interfaces, and adiabatic‐shear‐instability bonding.  

3.  Injection position effects  
 Axial (on-axis)  
  – Powder enters the high‐momentum, high‐temperature core  
  – Long residence time in core → maximum Vp and particle‐surface temperature  
 Lateral (off-axis)  
  – Powder injected into cooler boundary layer or mixing region  
  – Lower local gas velocity and temperature → reduced Vp and less heating  
  – Possible wall‐collisions or interparticle collisions in the nozzle → agglomeration, satellites, or clogging  

4.  Porosity  
 •  If Vp<Ecrit or particles remain too “cold,” they rebound or only lightly plastically deform → incomplete interparticle bonding → voids.  
 •  Off-axis injection raises porosity at a given Tg because more particles travel in low‐energy flow.  
 •  Raising Tg shifts even off‐axis‐injected particles closer to Ecrit, reducing void fraction but never quite matching on-axis performance.  

5.  Electrical conductivity  
 •  In metallic cold‐spray deposits electron transport is dominated by percolation through particle–particle contacts.  
 •  Voids act as insulating gaps; interfacial oxides (if any) further block conduction.  
 •  Lower porosity and better metallurgical bonding (via adiabatic shear and oxide‐film disruption) restore conductivity toward bulk metal values.  

Interaction summary  
– At low Tg, both axial and lateral injection yield high porosity and poor conductivity, but lateral is worse.  
– As Tg rises, axial injection quickly reaches the critical zone for dense, well‐bonded deposits; conductivity climbs steeply.  
– Lateral injection shows a more gradual improvement with Tg: porosity falls and conductivity rises, but even at high Tg remains inferior to axial injection.  
– Thus, powder‐injection position dictates how effectively particles “see” the hot, fast core flow that Tg defines. Proper alignment (axial feeding) plus elevated Tg gives the lowest porosity and highest electrical conductivity.

Gas temperature (Tg) and pressure (Pg) in cold spray act almost entirely through their effect on particle impact velocity and on the instantaneous temperature of both particle and substrate surface.  On polymer substrates this has three, inter-related consequences:

1. Particle deformation  
  • Raising Pg (i.e. the stagnation pressure upstream of the nozzle) directly increases gas mass flow and density in the diverging section, which accelerates the particles to higher velocities.  
  • Raising Tg reduces the gas density but increases its exit Mach number; in practice that too boosts particle velocity, and it pre-heats the powder so its yield strength drops slightly, making it easier to plastically deform on impact.  
  • Higher impact velocity plus mild thermal softening means each metal or ceramic particle “splat” spreads more, giving you a larger, flatter footprint and thinner residual thickness per particle.  

2. Splat cohesion (interlamellar bonding)  
  • Good cohesion in a cold-sprayed coating depends on intimate, oxide-free metal–metal (or metal–ceramic) contact under very high local pressure. Higher impact velocities (from higher Pg or Tg) drive adiabatic shear instabilities at the particle–substrate and particle–particle interfaces, breaking up surface oxides and generating fresh metal surfaces that weld together.  
  • On polymers, a modest rise in local surface temperature (from Tg and the heat deposited by successive particle impacts) softens the polymer just enough to conform to the incoming splat without bulk melting.  This compliance enhances mechanical interlocking and intimate metal-polymer contact, which boosts overall coating adhesion and inter-splat cohesion.  

3. Porosity  
  • At low Pg/Tg (i.e. sub-critical particle velocity) particles either rebound or impinge without full plastic flow.  You end up with poorly deformed “ballistic” deposits, large gaps between splats, and porosity often in the 10–20 % range.  
  • In the optimal window (particle velocity just above critical velocity for your powder/substrate combination—typically 500–900 m/s for metals, reached at ~30–40 bar He or 50–100 bar N₂ and Tg ≈200–400 °C) you get full splat deformation, oxide-breaking shear, strong metal–metal welds, and mechanical interlocking into the polymer—porosity can drop below 2–5 %.  
  • If you drive Pg or Tg too high you overshoot: particle velocities become so large that (a) you begin eroding or crazing the polymer surface rather than embedding, (b) you trap gas or generate microcracks from substrate recoil, and (c) you can even thermally degrade the polymer.  All of that drives porosity back up and can weaken interlamellar bonds.  

Practical take-home:  
– Use just enough Pg and Tg to exceed the critical velocity of your powder/substrate system so you achieve full splat deformation without bouncing, but stop short of the regime where you damage or melt the polymer.  
– Monitor in-situ particle velocity (e.g. with light‐gate diagnostics) and substrate temperature.  
– Aim for a porosity-minimizing window (often at 50–70 % of your maximum Pg and Tg capability), and verify by cross-sectional microscopy and helium pycnometry.

Spraying a metallic‐glass powder so that its particle temperature upon impact falls into the supercooled liquid region (i.e. between its glass transition temperature Tg and its crystallization onset Tx) is critical to getting a dense, pore‐free, amorphous deposit and a strong bond to the substrate.  Here’s why:

1. Viscous flow and plasticity  
   • Above Tg the amorphous alloy suddenly softens by orders of magnitude—its viscosity drops from ~10^12 Pa·s to 10^8–10^4 Pa·s depending on how far you are above Tg.  
   • Particles arriving in this “warm” but still‐amorphous state can deform and “wet” the roughness of the substrate under the combined action of their kinetic energy and residual heat.  They flatten and coalesce rather than simply bouncing or fracturing.

2. Elimination of porosity  
   • Viscous flow allows the particles to fill voids and to recrystallize around surface oxides or contaminants, squeezing them out or trapping them at grain boundaries.  
   • Repeated impacts of softened particles builds up a laminate of well‐sealed layers.

3. Atomic‐scale bonding without crystallization  
   • In the time window between impact and cooling back below Tg (often milliseconds), atomic diffusion across the newly formed metal–metal interface is fast enough to form metallic bonds, but not so long or hot that nucleation of crystals can proceed to any appreciable extent.  
   • Once the local temperature falls back below Tg (thanks to the high quench rate of the spray process), the deposit “freezes in” its fully amorphous structure.

4. Process control  
   • If you overheat past Tx you push the particles into the crystallization regime: you lose the glassy structure and get embrittling nanocrystals or intermetallics.  
   • If you underheat (below Tg) you have a classic “cold‐spray” situation: insufficient softening, poor wetting, high porosity, and weak bonding.

In practice, one carefully tunes the spray‐jet gas temperature, the powder feed rate, and the standoff distance so that—at the very instant of particle–substrate contact—the particles are in that narrow Tg–Tx window.  The result is a dense, amorphous coating that is metallurgically bonded to the substrate without the porosity or crystallinity you would get outside the supercooled liquid region.

In cold spray the only “engine” that drives particles onto the substrate is the high‐velocity gas jet, so both the gas stagnation pressure (P₀) and stagnation temperature (T₀) in your high‐pressure supply bottle or heater block have a first‐order influence on whether particles (a) reach a velocity above the critical deposition velocity v_c and (b) arrive hot and soft enough to deform.  Below is a concise breakdown:

1. Gas dynamics and particle acceleration  
   • Stagnation pressure P₀ sets the mass density in the nozzle throat and diverging section.  Higher P₀ ⇒ higher ρgas ⇒ larger drag force on a particle of cross‐sectional area A:  
      Fdrag = ½·C_d·ρgas·A·(v_gas–v_p)²  
     so v_p accelerates faster toward v_gas.  
   • Stagnation temperature T₀ controls the available enthalpy that can be converted into kinetic energy.  In an isentropic expansion through a deLaval nozzle, the exit velocity u_gas scales roughly like  
      u_gas ≈ √[2·γ/(γ–1)·R·T₀·(1–(P_exit/P₀)^((γ–1)/γ))]  
     so higher T₀ ⇒ higher u_gas ⇒ greater (u_gas–u_p) driving force for acceleration.  
   • There is a mild trade‐off: at fixed P₀, raising T₀ lowers the gas density ρgas=P/(RT), which slightly reduces drag.  In practice, however, the gain in exit‐jet velocity (∝√T₀) outweighs the density reduction.

2. Particle thermal state  
   • As particles race down the nozzle and through the supersonic jet (residence times ~0.5–2 ms), they pick up only a thin, hot boundary layer.  Their core temperature stays near the feedstock temperature, but local surface heating ΔT ~ (h·A·ΔT_gas–T_p)·Δt can be enough to soften the surface oxide and lower yield strength.  
   • Higher T₀ and higher u_gas both increase convective heat transfer coefficient h (h∝k_gas·Re^0.6/Pr^0.3), so particles arrive at the substrate slightly warmer—and thus more deformable—without ever melting.  

3. Deposition window and bonding probability  
   • Critical velocity v_c is the minimum impact speed needed to generate the high strain‐rate plastic flow and adiabatic shear that break up surface oxides and create metal‐to‐metal contact.  
   • By increasing P₀ and/or T₀ you raise the particle velocity toward (and above) v_c.  
   • If v_p < v_c, particles rebound or form a dusting (“under‐bonded”) regime.  
   • If v_p ≫ v_c by too much, you can enter an erosion regime (particles fragment or substrate is eroded).  
   • Likewise, if particles are too cold (low T₀), their yield strength is high and bonding is less likely even at v_p≥v_c.  Conversely, too high T₀ risks excessive oxidation in the nozzle or partial softening that leads to nozzle clogging.

Practical take‐home:  
• Raising P₀ boosts ρgas and mass flow, accelerating particles more sharply;  
• Raising T₀ raises the jet’s sonic throughput and exit velocity, plus the heat‐transfer rate that softens particles;  
• Both knobs must be balanced so that particle impact velocity just exceeds v_c without inducing erosion or nozzle fouling.

Increasing the Reynolds number of a metallic-glass powder in a cold-gas‐spray (CGS) system is almost always tied to increasing the gas (and hence particle) velocity and to thinning the gas‐particle boundary layer.  That in turn has three linked consequences:

1. Deformation  
   • Higher Re ⇒ higher particle velocity ⇒ higher impact kinetic energy.  Metallic glasses have no dislocations, so they accommodate impact by adiabatic shear-banding and local softening.  As velocity rises you get:  
     – More extensive shear‐band formation, splat flattening, and larger contact footprints.  
     – Greater local heating (both by gas‐to‐particle convection—Nu∼Re^0.5Pr^0.33—and by adiabatic work) which further softens the glass and promotes shear‐flow rather than brittle fracture.  
   • Beyond a certain velocity (very high Re) you begin to see particle fragmentation or excessive rebound—too much strain‐rate heating can even induce partial devitrification/crystallization, embrittling the splats.

2. Deposition efficiency  
   • At low Re many particles never reach the “critical velocity” needed to stick, so deposition efficiency (DE) is very low.  
   • As Re increases toward and just above the critical‐velocity regime, DE climbs steeply: more particles impact with enough energy to form adherent splats.  
   • Past an optimum Re DE levels off and then can fall off because:  
     – Particles begin to erode or crack upon impact rather than adhere.  
     – Very high‐speed particles can sputter or rebound substrate material.  
     – Turbulent gas flow can fling newly deposited material off the surface.

3. Bonding strength  
   • Up to the optimum Re, bond strength rises in parallel with DE:  
     – Larger, flatter splats give more mechanical interlocking and higher real contact area.  
     – Better oxide‐film scouring under higher shear cleans both particle and substrate surfaces.  
     – Slightly elevated interfacial temperatures can promote solid‐state atomic bonding (diffusion across the glass interface is still limited but improved by the high‐energy, clean contact).  
   • Beyond the optimum Re, bond strength can degrade due to  
     – Excessive residual tensile stresses (from very rapid quenching of highly deformed splats) leading to crack nucleation at interfaces.  
     – Fragmentation of particles and formation of porous or microcracked zones.  
     – Possible embrittlement if local temperatures exceed the devitrification threshold.

In practice one tunes the gas‐pressure and nozzle geometry to hit an Re (and corresponding particle velocity) just above the critical‐velocity window for metallic glass, thereby maximizing deformation, deposition efficiency and interfacial strength, but avoiding the high-Re regime where erosion, fragmentation or devitrification kick in.

Cold spray onto metals is usually limited only by a “no‐bounce” critical velocity from below, but on stiffer polymers you often see a second, upper‐velocity bound beyond which deposition actually falls off.  That upper limit is not simply “too much heat,” but rather a stress‐wave and strain‐rate–driven failure of the polymer surface and loss of intimate contact.  In brief:

1.  At very high particle speeds (often >1 – 1.5 km/s) the impact stress pulse in the polymer far exceeds its strain‐rate–dependent yield strength.  
2.  Instead of flowing plastically to engulf and weld the particle, the polymer surface undergoes adiabatic shear localization, brittle cracking or spallation when the reflected tensile wave at the free surface exceeds its fracture/tensile strength.  
3.  The surface is eroded or craters form, and the particles rebound from the hard, damaged layer rather than adhere.  

Thus the “upper velocity limit” on harder polymer substrates is set by the onset of strain‐rate stiffening plus stress‐wave–driven fracture/spall of the polymer, which destroys the compliant, freshly deformed interface needed for good bonding.

In cold spray the coating porosity is governed almost entirely by how well individual particles plastically deform and “weld‐together” when they hit the growing deposit.  Raising the working‐gas temperature and pressure both serve to boost particle impact velocity and ductility, which in turn drives down porosity:

1. Higher gas pressure ⇒ higher stagnation pressure ⇒  
   • greater gas density through the nozzle throat and exit  
   • higher mass‐flow rate and momentum flux on the particles  
   ⇒ particles accelerate more and arrive at the substrate with greater kinetic energy.

2. Higher gas temperature ⇒ higher stagnation temperature ⇒  
   • higher speed of sound in the gas ⇒ higher achievable Mach number in the supersonic jet  
   • warmer particles (they spend time in hotter flow), so their yield strength and work‐hardening rates are reduced  
   ⇒ particles deform more easily and more completely on impact.

3. Consequences of increased impact velocity and ductility:  
   • More intense plastic flow at each particle–substrate and particle–particle interface, flattening particles into thinner “pancakes.”  
   • Collapse of interparticle voids as metal streams flow laterally to fill gaps.  
   • Stronger mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding with fewer unbonded or only lightly bonded spots.  
   • Decreased shadowing of low spots—high‐momentum particles can “hammer” into recesses and further consolidate the deposit.

Net result: coatings sprayed at higher gas pressure and temperature show dramatically lower porosity because each incoming particle arrives with enough velocity and softness to plastically weld and fill any microscopic voids in the growing layer.

The “window of deposition” in cold spray is simply the range of particle impact velocities over which you get net build-up of material rather than rebound or erosion.  It is bounded on the low side by the critical velocity, Vc, and on the high side by the erosive velocity, Ve:

1.  Critical velocity (Vc)  
    – Minimum impact speed needed to force sufficient adiabatic shear and plastic deformation at the particle–substrate (or particle–particle) interface so that metallurgical bonding occurs rather than rebound.  
    – Depends on material properties (yield strength, hardness, thermal softening behavior), particle size and temperature, gas species and stagnation temperature, and substrate roughness.  
    – Heating the gas (and thus the particles) lowers the yield strength at impact and so reduces Vc.

2.  Erosive velocity (Ve)  
    – Upper limit beyond which additional kinetic energy no longer produces better bonding but instead causes substrate or deposit erosion, particle fracturing, or back-scattering.  
    – Governed by the same material properties plus the relative hardness of particle vs. substrate and the local strain‐rate sensitivity.  

Net deposition only occurs for  
     Vc  <  Vparticle  <  Ve  

– Below Vc: particles simply rebound or cold-spray “dust” with no build-up.  
– Above Ve: excessive impact energy damages the previously deposited layers or the substrate, leading to removal rather than addition of material.  

In practice you map out Vc and Ve as functions of gas pressure, temperature, and particle size/distribution so as to choose spray conditions that deliver particle velocities squarely inside that window.

Increasing the gas stagnation temperature (T₀) in a cold‐spray system boosts deposition efficiency primarily by raising the achievable particle impact velocity.  Here is how it works, in three steps:

1.  Higher T₀ ⇒ higher gas exit velocity  
   •  For an ideal, isentropic expansion through the nozzle:  
     v_g ≃ sqrt[ 2·k/(k–1) ·R·T₀ ·(1 – (p_exit/p₀)^((k–1)/k) ) ]  
   •  Since T₀ appears under the radical, v_g ∝ √T₀ (all else equal).  
   •  Example: raising T₀ from 800 K to 1 200 K can boost v_g by ∼22%.

2.  Higher gas velocity ⇒ stronger drag and faster particle acceleration  
   •  Particle acceleration a = (F_drag/m_p) = (½ ρ_g v_rel² C_d A_p) / (ρ_p V_p)  
   •  Although ρ_g at the exit falls with T₀, the increase in v_rel² more than compensates, so the net drag force—and therefore the asymptotic particle speed—goes up.  
   •  Typical cold‐spray particles accelerate over O(10–50 cm) to within 90 % of the carrying‐gas speed.

3.  Faster particles ⇒ higher deposition efficiency  
   •  Each material has a “critical velocity” v_crit below which particles rebound or erode rather than bond.  
   •  Deposition efficiency η can be modeled empirically as a sigmoid of (v_p – v_crit):  
     η ≃ 1/[1 + exp(–α (v_p – v_crit))]  
   •  By increasing T₀ you raise v_p, shifting more particles above v_crit and thus sharply increasing η.

In practice, boosting T₀ by a few hundred degrees can increase peak particle speeds by tens to hundreds of meters per second—enough to turn a low‐efficiency spray into one with > 90 % deposition efficiency.

In cold spray, you are literally “blasting” metal or ceramic powders into a substrate at velocities typically between 300 and 1,200 m/s.  Two of the chief levers for getting particles up into that speed range are the stagnation (or total) gas pressure p₀ and stagnation temperature T₀ you feed into the nozzle.  Here’s why you run both of them high, and how that practice drives up deposit density:

1. Getting Above the Critical Velocity  
  • Every powder material has a critical impact velocity (v_c) below which particles simply rebound or cold-weld poorly, leaving a spongy, porous deposit.  
  • Raising p₀ increases the gas’s density and its mass-flow rate through the nozzle.  That translates directly into more aerodynamic drag on each particle, and therefore a higher terminal speed.  
  • Raising T₀ increases the local speed of sound in the gas (a = √(γ·R·T₀)), which in a converging–diverging nozzle gives you a higher Mach number (M) and thus a higher exit velocity (v_exit ≈ M·a).  

2. Balancing Density vs. Velocity  
  • A higher stagnation pressure alone would push you toward higher v_exit, but gas density and viscosity matter too: at fixed T₀, boosting p₀ thickens the gas, increasing particle drag.  
  • A higher stagnation temperature thins the gas (lower ρ) but raises the sound speed and permits a higher Mach number at the same pressure ratio.  In practice you pick T₀ and p₀ together to maximize particle velocity without starving momentum transfer.  

3. How Particle Velocity Controls Deposit Density  
  • Particle impact density—and hence deposit density—depends strongly on plastic deformation at the impact zone.  Above v_c, particles “jet” and mechanically interlock, collapse porosity, and rupture surface oxides.  
  • Too little velocity ⇒ incomplete deformation ⇒ interparticle voids, poor bonding, high porosity (low deposit density).  
  • Sufficiently high velocity ⇒ full deformation into pancake shapes, minimal entrapped voids, strong metallurgical or mechanical bonding ⇒ densities routinely 95 – 99+ % of theoretical.  

4. Secondary Effects of High p₀ and T₀  
  • Higher mass flow (from p₀) means more powder throughput, higher build rates, and a denser spray plume.  
  • Higher T₀ can limit chilling of the gas by the cold substrate and reduce nozzle freezing, but it also risks any temperature‐sensitive powders—so one tunes T₀ to just above the minimum needed for velocity gain.  

In short:  
  – High stagnation pressure gives you the raw gas density and drag force to shove particles fast.  
  – High stagnation temperature boosts the achievable Mach number (and so v_exit) without excessively raising flow resistance.  
  – High particle velocity above the material’s critical velocity is what collapses porosity and maximizes deposit density.

In cold spray additive manufacturing the particle‐impact conditions—and therefore both how many particles actually stick (“deposition efficiency”) and how well they forge a metallurgical bond at the interface—are set largely by what happens to the powder in the supersonic jet once it leaves the nozzle.  You can think of the region outside the nozzle in three zones—(1) the expansion/shock‐cell region, (2) the supersonic core with shear layers, and (3) the eventual mixing/decay zone—and each of these governs particle trajectories, speeds, and impact angles.  

1. Expansion and Shock-Cell Region  
  • Immediately past the nozzle throat a sequence of expansion fans and compression (shock) waves forms “shock diamonds.”  
  • Particles crossing a compression wave can lose momentum, and off-axis shocks scatter smaller or lighter particles into the shear layers.  
  • Strong shock interaction broadens the plume and creates radial velocity components that reduce the fraction of particles striking the substrate at normal incidence.  

2. Supersonic Core and Shear Layers  
  • In the core the gas (and ideally most of the powder) maintains near‐exit Mach number and a narrow cone angle. Particles in this region achieve their maximum velocity.  
  • In the surrounding shear layers, mixing with ambient air and turbulence grow, decelerating both gas and entrained particles.  
  • Particles in the shear are slower, travel at oblique angles, and often erode deposited material or simply rebound—both effects lower deposition efficiency.  

3. Mixing/Decay Zone  
  • Beyond an optimal stand-off distance (typically 20–40 mm for most nozzles) the supersonic jet entrains ambient gas so strongly that the core collapses into a subsonic, turbulent plume.  
  • Particle velocities drop below the material’s critical bonding velocity; impact energy falls off and both deposition efficiency and interfacial bonding strength deteriorate rapidly.  

Net Effects on Deposition Efficiency  
  – Only those particles that remain in the high-velocity core and impinge near normal to the surface can exceed the critical velocity for plastic deformation and cold welding—thus maximizing the mass loading rate.  
  – Off-axis or decelerated particles either bounce (wasting powder) or strike deposited material at shallow angles, promoting erosion rather than net build-up.  

Net Effects on Interfacial Bonding  
  – Well-centered, high-velocity particles produce very high strain rates on impact, disrupting oxide films and creating localized adiabatic heating, which allows metal–metal contact and dynamic recrystallization. That’s the basis for strong metallurgical bonding.  
  – Particles that have traversed shocks or shear layers generate lower “impact pressures” and strain rates, so oxides are not fully broken up, leaving weak mechanical interlocks or merely adhesive contact.  

Practical Implications and Control Strategies  
  • Nozzle design and pressure ratio should be tuned to minimize the strength and extent of shock waves inside and immediately outside the nozzle.  
  • Stand-off distance must be chosen to intercept the dense, Mach-disc–less core region. Too close and the jet may damage the substrate mechanically; too far and the particles slow down or spread out.  
  • Powder feed positioning (radial or axial injection) can bias particles into the core rather than the shear layers. Aerodynamic focusing inserts or tailored converging–diverging profiles help focus the particle stream.  
  • Schlieren imaging or CFD can be used to map the shock structure and identify the true high-velocity core length, ensuring that the workpiece sits in the optimal zone for both deposition efficiency and bonding integrity.

In cold spray the stagnation temperature (T₀) of the process gas governs two of the most important drivers of bond strength – the particle kinetic/thermal energy available for intimate metal–metal contact and the magnitude and sign of the residual stresses locked into both the coating and the substrate when everything cools back down to ambient.  In a nutshell:  
1.  Stagnation temperature → particle velocity & deformability  
   •  T₀ = T_gas·(1 + (γ–1)/2·M²)  
   •  Higher T₀ (and hence higher gas velocity) means particles travel faster and undergo more adiabatic heating on impact.  That in turn gives you:  
     –  More plastic deformation at the interface, jetting of oxide films, higher dislocation density, mechanical interlocking  
     –  Greater “peening”–induced compressive residual stresses in the outer layers of the deposit (good for fatigue and crack‐closure)  

2.  Thermal mismatch on cooling → interface tensile stresses  
   •  Even though the sprayed metal is called “cold,” in most systems it still arrives at several hundred °C and cools to room temperature, contracting by ΔL/L ≈ α·ΔT.  
   •  If the coating’s coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) differs from that of the substrate, or if layers of the coating see different ∆T, you generate thermal residual stresses.  Typically:  
     –  If CTE_coating > CTE_substrate: the coating goes into tension upon cooling (peeling‐type stress at the interface)  
     –  If CTE_coating < CTE_substrate: the coating is left under compression (helpful, up to a point, for adhesion)  

3.  Net effect on adhesion  
   •  Below the critical velocity/energy (too low T₀), you get barely any plastic deformation, a sparse “splat” coverage, low dislocation density, and essentially no mechanical interlocking → LOW adhesion.  
   •  As T₀ rises above the critical regime, particle flattening, oxide‐film jetting, vacancy‐driven metallic bonding and compressive peening stresses ramp up, producing HIGH adhesion.  
   •  If you push T₀ excessively high you still get excellent deformation but you introduce large thermal‐mismatch tensile stresses on cooling, which can nucleate interfacial cracks or drive delamination → adhesion BEGINS TO DROP.  

4.  Design implications  
   •  Choose a stagnation temperature/pressure combination that just exceeds the critical velocity for your powder‐substrate pair.  
   •  If thermal‐tensile stresses are a concern, consider:  
     –  Substrate preheating (shrinks ΔT on cooling)  
     –  Using a “warm spray” approach (intermediate between cold and HVOF)  
     –  Matching CTEs via interlayer materials or by selecting powders/alloys with closer CTE to the substrate  

Summary:  stagnation temperature is the “throttle” that sets your impact energy and plastic‐deformation‐induced compressive stresses (both beneficial to adhesion), but it also widens the temperature swing between deposit and room temperature, which generates thermal‐mismatch tensile stresses (detrimental to adhesion).  Optimal bond strength is found at a T₀ (and particle velocity) high enough to ensure full particle deformation and mechanical‐metallurgical bonding, yet low enough (or thermally managed) to limit harmful tensile residual stresses at the interface.

In a cold‐spray system the converging–diverging (De Laval) nozzle is nothing more than a gas‐dynamics accelerator that converts the gas’s enthalpy into kinetic energy while actually cooling the flow.  Here is how it works in practice:

1. Gas pre‐heating and pressurization  
   • You feed an inert carrier gas (typically N₂ or He) at high stagnation pressure (15–50 bar) into the spray gun.  
   • The gas is only moderately heated (200 °C–800 °C), well below the melting points of most metals, so its total (stagnation) temperature T₀ stays low.

2. Converging section to the throat  
   • As the high‐pressure, moderate‐temperature gas enters the converging portion of the nozzle its static pressure p and temperature T rise slightly, but its velocity remains subsonic.  
   • At the throat (the minimum‐area section), the flow “chokes” at Mach 1 if the upstream/downstream pressure ratio exceeds the critical value,  
     p₀/p_exit ≥ (2/(γ+1))^(γ/(γ–1)).  

3. Supersonic expansion in the diverging section  
   • Beyond the throat, the nozzle area increases.  Isentropic expansion drives the Mach number above unity.  In going from the throat to the exit:  
     – Static pressure p and static temperature T fall according to p/p₀ = (1 + (γ–1)/2·M²)^(–γ/(γ–1)) and  
       T/T₀ = (1 + (γ–1)/2·M²)^(–1).  
     – The loss in thermal energy shows up as a gain in kinetic energy, so the jet speed can reach 600–1200 m/s even though T_exit can drop below T₀.

4. Particle injection and acceleration  
   • Metal powders are injected just downstream of the throat (or in the converging section) so they see the steepest pressure‐gradient and highest accelerating forces.  
   • Because the jet temperature—both stagnation and static—remains well below the metal’s melting point, the particles stay solid.  They pick up momentum from the gas via drag and reach velocities of 300–1200 m/s over only a few centimeters of nozzle length.

5. Impact and bonding  
   • On striking the substrate at these high speeds, the particles undergo severe plastic deformation.  Local adiabatic heating at the impact site promotes metallurgical bonding, but the bulk of the deposit never melts, preserving the cold‐spray signature:  
     – Dense, oxide‐free coatings  
     – Minimal heat‐affected zone in the substrate

Summary  
By using a De Laval (converging/diverging) nozzle, cold spray converts moderate gas temperatures into very high velocities via nearly isentropic expansion.  The drop in static temperature during expansion ensures that even though the gas carries high kinetic energy, it never gets hot enough to melt the feedstock.

Carrier‐gas parameters (type, temperature, pressure and flow) control the momentum and thermal state of the spray jet, and hence govern particle velocity, particle temperature, in-flight particle–particle interactions and impact deformation.  All of those in turn set the degree of particle consolidation (porosity, bonding) and the microstructural refinement in the deposit.  In practice you see the following trends:

1. Gas type (molecular weight, γ and Cp/Cv)  
   • Helium (M≈4 g/mol) gives the highest jet speed (c ∝ √(γRT/M)), hence the highest particle velocities and best densification (porosity <1 %, strong metallurgical bonding).  
   • Argon (M≈40 g/mol) and nitrogen (M≈28 g/mol) yield lower jet speeds; particle velocities are 10–30 % lower than with He, porosity typically rises to 1–5 % and interparticle bonding is weaker.  
   • H2 additions can boost sound speed and improve velocity but raise safety concerns and oxidation risk.

2. Stagnation (supply) pressure  
   • Raising the carrier‐gas pressure increases the pressure ratio P₀/Pₐmb across the nozzle, elevates Mach number in the supersonic section and thus increases both gas and particle velocities.  
   • Higher particle velocities → larger plastic deformation on impact → more extensive adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization and interface jetting → denser, finer‐grained deposits.  
   • Typical cold-spray operating window: 2–6 MPa; beyond ~6 MPa diminishing returns and more nozzle wear or powder “back-flow.”

3. Gas temperature  
   • Preheating to 200 – 600 °C raises sound speed and particle temperature.  Hotter particles deform more readily on impact (lower flow stress), improving interparticle bonding and filling of microvoids.  
   • Very high gas temperatures (> 600 °C) can promote surface oxidation of feedstock, embrittlement of ductile metals and undesirable microstructures (e.g. grain growth).  

4. Gas flow rate and nozzle design  
   • Higher mass flow rate improves powder entrainment and stabilizes the supersonic jet but can also increase interparticle collisions in the barrel, broadening the velocity distribution and slightly raising porosity.  
   • Nozzle geometry (converging–diverging profile, length) dictates the optimum flow rate for a given gas; off‐design flow causes shock diamonds, velocity nonuniformity and higher deposit porosity.

Resulting effects on coating microstructure and density
