– Particle velocity governs impact kinetic energy (E ∼ ½mv²).  Above a material-specific critical velocity, particles undergo severe plastic deformation, interfacial jetting and metallurgical bonding.  Below it, they rebound or bond weakly, leaving microvoids and poor cohesion.  
– Higher gas pressures/temperatures and lighter gases raise vparticle, lowering porosity (down to < 1 %), refining dynamically recrystallized grains at splat boundaries (< 1 μm) and increasing hardness/toughness.  
– Lower gas pressures/temperatures or heavier gases produce vparticle near or below critical velocity, yielding higher residual porosity (1–10 %), incomplete splat flattening, coarser recrystallized structure and reduced mechanical properties.

In short, to maximize coating density and achieve a fine, ultrafine or nanocrystalline microstructure, one chooses the lightest practical carrier gas (He or He-rich mixtures), the highest feasible stagnation pressure and a moderate preheat temperature, all balanced against cost, oxidation risk and equipment constraints.

Cold spray deposits depend critically on accelerating particles to—and embedding them at—velocities just above their material-specific “critical velocity.”  Small shifts in any spray parameter can tip the balance from good bonding to a high-defect microstructure and hence to degraded mechanical performance.  

1. Gas temperature and pressure  
   •  Too low → particles never reach critical velocity → weak or no bonding, high interparticle porosity.  
   •  Too high → excessive gas heating can oxidize powder surfaces or overheat substrates, forming brittle interfacial oxides or scale that inhibit metallurgical bonding.  

2. Powder feed rate and particle size distribution  
   •  Over-feeding the nozzle → gas energy is shared among too many particles → average particle speed drops below the critical threshold → more “cold” particles that simply pile up, boosting porosity.  
   •  Wide size distributions → large particles under-accelerate (weak bonding) while fines may overheat, erode the substrate, or rebound, all raising porosity and nonbonded fractions.  

3. Nozzle geometry and stand-off distance  
   •  Off-design expansion ratios or wrong nozzle throat–exit profile → nonuniform jet, so parts of the spray stream under- or over-accelerate particles, leading to local zones of poor bonding and residual stress concentrations.  
   •  Stand-off too large → gas jet diffuses and cools → particles slow, yield porosity; too small → crowding of splats, substrate erosion, and trapping of debris or oxide films at interfaces.  

4. Spray angle and substrate condition  
   •  Spray angles >20–30° off normal reduce the normal component of particle velocity → shallow embedment → more interlamellar gaps and lower cohesive strength.  
   •  A cold, smooth, or contaminated substrate resists particle deformation and bonding → poor nucleation of plastically deformed splats → high initial porosity and weak adhesion.  

Resulting microstructural defects  
   – Porosity and interparticle voids (5–15 volume % if outside the ideal window)  
   – Unbonded or weakly adhered particles (“white fields” or unmelted islands)  
   – Oxide or contaminant films trapped at splat interfaces  
   – Microcracks from excessive residual tensile stresses or substrate erosion  

Mechanical‐performance consequences  
   •  Tensile and shear strength fall off roughly in proportion to bonded area; 10 % extra porosity can cut cohesion by 20–30 %.  
   •  Fatigue life plummets because pores and microcracks act as stress concentrators and crack‐initiation sites.  
   •  Reduced hardness and wear resistance—unbonded islands are easily plucked out under sliding or abrasion.  
   •  Lower corrosion resistance—porosity and oxide-film channels let corrosive species penetrate deeper.  

In practice, one tunes gas pressure/temperature, feed rate, stand-off, angle, and substrate prep to hit the narrow window that yields severe plastic deformation, adiabatic shear bonding, and dynamic recrystallization at each particle interface.  Deviations from that window directly translate into higher defect levels and degraded coating performance.

Agglomerated/porous ceramic powders are almost indispensable to getting dense, well‐bonded cold‐spray coatings because they overcome ceramics’ intrinsic brittleness and lack of plasticity.  The key reasons are:

1. Impact cushioning and pore collapse  
   – The internal porosity in each agglomerate acts like a “shock absorber.” Under high‐velocity impact the pores collapse, converting kinetic energy into local compaction and micro‐scale crushing rather than simply shattering the particle outright.  
   – Pore collapse promotes adiabatic shear and generates localized plastic flow zones—even in intrinsically brittle ceramics—helping fragments to embed and weld.

2. Controlled fragmentation and fresh‐surface generation  
   – Weakly bonded primary particles within the agglomerate break apart on impact, creating fresh, clean surfaces that can cold‐weld (mechanical interlock or form metallurgical bonds if there’s a ductile phase present).  
   – The resulting fine debris fills gaps between larger fragments, raising the coating’s green density.

3. Enhanced particle–particle contact and interlocking  
   – Irregular agglomerate shapes and internal voids provide multiple contact points and “nooks and crannies” for mechanical interlocking as fragments collapse and reorganize.  
   – This widens the range of impact angles and velocities over which bonding is effective, boosting deposition efficiency.

4. Lower effective strength and density  
   – Porous agglomerates have lower bulk density and reduced effective yield strength compared to solid particles, so they require less kinetic energy to deform.  
   – Lowering the critical velocity for bonding means more particles deposit successfully, which in turn fills pores and densifies the coating.

In sum, by tailoring powder agglomeration and porosity you create a fracturable, compactive feedstock that (a) breaks and plastically flows on impact, (b) generates fresh bonding surfaces, and (c) mechanically interlocks to build up a high‐density ceramic layer in atmospheric cold spray.

Traverse-speed (the nozzle’s lateral sweep rate) has a very direct effect on coating porosity because it controls how many particles strike any one spot per unit time, how much local heating/preheating accumulates, and how much severe plastic deformation (and attendant dynamic recrystallization) can occur.  In practice one almost always sees:

 1.  Slower traverse speeds → lower porosity  
    •  Higher particle‐impact density per unit area (more “hammering” of the same spot)  
    •  Greater local substrate and deposit preheating → the yield stress of both substrate and deposited layer is reduced, so subsequent particles plastically deform and bond more easily  
    •  More adiabatic shear at particle/substrate and particle/particle interfaces → dynamic recrystallization produces ultrafine, high‐angle grain‐boundary networks that weld lamellae together and collapse voids   
    → Result: porosity can fall to well under 1 % in many alloys if the speed is sufficiently slow.  

 2.  Faster traverse speeds → higher porosity  
    •  Fewer particles impacting per area (lower mass flux) → thinner passes and more unfilled interstices  
    •  Less local heating → higher flow stress, so particles do not spread or interlock as fully  
    •  Incomplete or absent adiabatic‐shear zones → fewer recrystallized bridges at interfaces, leaving microvoids at particle boundaries  
    → Result: porosity may rise to several percent or more, and one often observes lamellar gaps and unmixed cores of original powder.  

Microstructurally, the key bonding mechanism in cold spray is impact‐induced severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear, which produces a nanocrystalline interface layer that metallurgically welds the particles together.  As traverse speed goes up you simply don’t get enough cumulative deformation and thermal softening at each spot to form a continuous such layer—and the trapped pores and incomplete interfaces translate directly into higher macroscopic porosity.

Nanopowders (d < 1 μm) almost invariably hurt cold‐spray efficiency because…  
• Cohesion & agglomeration: Very high surface‐area–to–volume gives huge van‐der‐Waals and capillary forces, so the particles form hard agglomerates that don’t feed or accelerate uniformly.  
• Poor flowability: Fine powders bridge in hoppers, cake on feeder walls and nozzle throats, and fluidize poorly under the carrier gas; mass‐flow rate into the jet becomes erratic or too low.  
• Momentum transfer: Individual nanoparticles have very low mass, so even if dispersed by the gas they carry little kinetic energy; blistering or rebound dominates rather than plastic deformation and bonding.

To restore good feed and boost deposition efficiency you must rebuild them into coarser, free‐flowing “granules” while retaining their nano‐scale substructure. Common approaches:  
1. Spray‐drying or freeze‐granulation: Atomize a nanopowder slurry (often with a small polymer or ceramic binder) and dry to yield 20–50 µm spheroidal granules.  
2. Plasma or flame spheroidization: Pass nanopowder through a high‐T zone so it melts/spherodizes into larger beads.  
3. Roller compaction + milling: Lightly compact the powder into flakes, then gently mill to break them into uniform granules.  
4. Surface coating or “gluing”: Adsorb a thin polymeric or silane layer on the nanopowder to reduce surface energy, then break up the clusters in a low‐energy mill.  
5. Carrier‐particle blending: Coat or embed the nanoscale phase onto coarser (> 10 µm) ductile particles so the composite feeds and accelerates like a standard feedstock.  

All of these methods increase the true powder size (improving angle of repose, lowering Hausner ratio), cut interparticle cohesion, and give you stable mass flow into the cold‐spray gun—so you regain the high deposition rates and efficiencies you see with conventional (5–50 µm) powders.

Increasing the process‐gas temperature in a cold-spray system promotes denser coatings almost entirely by enhancing inter-particle bonding.  Mechanistically, the effects are:

1. Higher particle velocity and impact energy  
   • Because the expanded gas carries more enthalpy, supersonic jets accelerate particles to higher terminal speeds.  
   • Impact kinetic energy (≈½mv²) scales roughly with the gas enthalpy, so particles impinge with more energy, driving deeper plastic flow and larger contact areas.

2. Reduced particle yield strength (thermal softening)  
   • As gas temperature rises, particles heat up in flight.  Even a few tens of degrees of surface warming can cut the flow stress of most metals by 10–20%.  
   • A softer particle plastically deforms more readily on impact, improving mechanical interlocking and increasing the intimate metal–metal contact area.

3. Enhanced adiabatic shear and oxide disruption  
   • Higher kinetic energy promotes the very high strain rates (>10⁴–10⁶ s⁻¹) needed for localized adiabatic shear instabilities at the interface.  These instabilities eject surface oxides (“jetting”) and expose fresh metal, enabling true metallurgical bonding.  
   • Greater jetting also helps fill small voids and level surface roughness, reducing porosity.

4. Net effect on coating density and integrity  
   • The combination of higher impact energy and softer particles lowers the critical velocity for deposition and yields coatings with fewer inter-particle voids and higher cohesive strength.  
   • In practice one observes a steady rise in deposited density, bond strength, and microhardness up to an optimum gas temperature.

5. Practical limits and trade-offs  
   • Excessive gas temperatures can encourage oxidation in transit or, for very ductile powders, localized melting that may lead to pore formation on re-solidification.  
   • There is therefore an optimum gas temperature (and pressure) window that maximizes plastic deformation and jetting while minimizing in-flight oxidation or thermal damage to substrate and powder.

In summary, raising gas temperature improves coating density by (1) accelerating and softening particles so they deform more, and (2) fostering adiabatic-shear-driven cleaning and metallurgical bonding at every impacting interface—up to the point where thermal side effects begin to degrade coating quality.

Key points  
1. Stagnation pressure (p₀) and powder mass-loading (β=ṁp/ṁg) act in opposite ways on particle exit velocity vₚ:  
   – Raising p₀ boosts the maximum gas‐phase Mach number and thus the drag force available to accelerate particles.  
   – Raising β at fixed p₀ steals gas momentum to accelerate more powder, lowering both gas velocity v_g and per‐particle acceleration.  

2. Isentropic expansion gives the unloaded gas‐phase exit speed  
   Vg0 ≃ √[2 γ/(γ–1) · R·T₀ · (1 – (p_e/p₀)^((γ–1)/γ))]  
   where γ, R, T₀ are the gas constants and p_e the nozzle exit pressure.  

3. With powder the coupled gas–particle mixture obeys momentum balance:  
   ṁg·Vg0 ≃ ṁg·v_g + ṁp·vₚ  
   ⇒ when β increases, v_g and vₚ must fall if p₀ (and hence ṁg·Vg0) is held constant.  

4. 1D drag‐law integration along the nozzle (length L) predicts vₚ more quantitatively:  
   vₚ = ∫₀ᴸ [F_d(mp,ρg(ξ),v_g(ξ)–vₚ(ξ)) / m_particle]·dτ  
   with F_d ≃ (πd²/8)·C_d·ρg·|v_g–vₚ|(v_g–vₚ).  
   – Raising p₀ raises ρg(ξ) and v_g(ξ) ⇒ larger F_d ⇒ higher vₚ.  
   – Raising β lowers v_g(ξ) (and ρg only weakly if total pressure is fixed) ⇒ smaller F_d ⇒ lower vₚ.  

5. Practical trends  
   – At low β (< 5–10 %), vₚ scales almost with the unloaded gas speed Vg0 (i.e. roughly with √p₀).  
   – Beyond β≈10–20 %, gas‐momentum depletion accelerates more particles than the gas can sustain, so vₚ falls off rapidly.  
   – Higher stagnation pressures push the “knee” to higher β, allowing greater powder throughput before vₚ drops below the critical deposition velocity.  

Design implications  
– To maximize vₚ for a given powder: use the highest p₀ you can afford, then choose β just below the point where measured vₚ (by PIV or time‐of‐flight) begins to roll off in your specific nozzle.  
– If throughput must rise (higher β), compensate by raising p₀ (or T₀) so that net gas momentum ṁg·Vg0 keeps pace with the larger powder flow.

Polymeric particles behave very differently from metals in cold spray. Because they soften—but do not fully melt—near their glass‐transition (Tg) or melting temperature (Tm), the key to good deposition is to make them sufficiently ductile at impact while avoiding excessive kinetic damage or rebound. That is why combining higher particle temperatures with lower impact velocities works best:

1. Reduced yield stress and viscosity at high T  
   – Heating the polymer particles up toward (but below) their Tg/Tm causes a dramatic drop in yield strength and a large increase in molecular mobility.  
   – Upon impact, the softened particles flow plastically (or viscously) rather than fracturing or rebounding.  

2. Lower critical velocity for bonding  
   – In cold spray the “critical velocity” v_c scales roughly with (σ_y/ρ)^½ (σ_y = yield stress).  By reducing σ_y via heating, v_c drops, so you no longer need very high velocities to achieve adhesion.  

3. Minimized particle damage  
   – At very high impact speeds polymers can shatter, form debris, or undergo chain scission from excessive shear.  Slower impacts preserve chain integrity and maintain molecular weight.  

4. Enhanced contact time and interfacial wetting  
   – Softer, tack-like particles spread more completely on the substrate, increasing the real contact area.  The longer deformation time at lower speeds also allows any surface additives (plasticizers, tackifiers) to help form a mechanically interlocked or even partially interdiffused bond.  

5. Avoidance of thermal degradation  
   – Staying below the decomposition temperature while just above Tg/Tm gives you enough softening without chemical breakdown.  

In short, heating polymer particles close to their softening point lowers their resistance to deformation so that even moderate‐speed impacts produce large‐area, plastically deformed splats that adhere strongly. Trying to compensate only with high velocity would either exceed the particle’s strength (causing fragmentation) or require discharge energies that risk thermal damage.

Reducing the gun’s traverse speed increases the local coating build-up, while increasing it thins the deposit.  Two linked effects govern this:  

1. Particle‐impact density  
   • At slower traverse speeds more powder passes over the same substrate area, so the shot‐to‐area flux is higher.  More impacts per unit area per pass mean more material accumulates.  
   • At higher traverse speeds fewer particles strike each spot, so less material sticks and more is lost to rebound.  

2. Impact‐induced plasticity and substrate softening  
   • Every high-velocity particle impact generates severe plastic deformation (and a little heat) in both the deposited splat and the immediate substrate.  At slower traverse speeds those thermal spikes accumulate, locally lowering the substrate’s yield strength and hence its “critical velocity” for bonding.  Particles thus penetrate and adhere more readily via adiabatic‐shear‐driven bonding and mechanical interlock.  
   • At faster traverse speeds the substrate remains colder, its strength stays higher, more particles rebound rather than plastically deform and bond, and deposition efficiency falls.  

In practice you tune the traverse speed to hit a balance between deposit rate, coating density, and thermal loading of the substrate.

The key role of the nozzle’s expansion ratio (Ae/At, exit area divided by throat area) in a cold‐spray system is that it fixes the peak Mach number and gas exit velocity for a given stagnation pressure and temperature.  Because particle kinetic energy (KE ∝½ m v²) and final particle velocity are almost entirely determined by the drag acceleration they experience in that supersonic jet, the expansion ratio ends up directly controlling both the particle KE and the likelihood that particles will stick (deposition efficiency).

1.  How Ae/At controls gas and particle velocity  
   •  In a choked (throat-limited) supersonic nozzle, the local Mach number M at the exit plane is given by the isentropic area–Mach relation:  
      Ae/At = (1/M)·[(2/(γ+1))(1 + (γ–1)/2·M²)]^((γ+1)/(2(γ–1)))  
   •  Larger Ae/At ⇒ higher exit Mach ⇒ higher gas velocity (vgas ≈M·√(γRT0)).  
   •  Particle acceleration is by drag: dvp/dt ≈ (CD A/2m)·ρgas·(vgas–vp)², so a higher vgas over a longer acceleration length almost always pushes vp higher.

2.  Deposition efficiency and the “velocity window”  
   •  Below a critical velocity vcrit, particles simply rebound or erode—DE≈0.  
   •  As vp passes vcrit, DE rises steeply toward a plateau (ideal “sticking” window).  
   •  Above a second (higher) velocity, particles may shatter, create tensile rebound, or locally harden the substrate—DE can fall again.  

3.  Why there is an optimum range of expansion ratios  
   A. Undersized expansion (Ae/At too low)  
      – Exit Mach is modest ⇒ vp < vcrit ⇒ little or no deposition.  
      – Even if vp slightly exceeds vcrit, you are not maximizing DE or density of the deposit.  
   B. Oversized expansion (Ae/At too high)  
      – Unless you simultaneously boost stagnation pressure, you begin to over-expand the flow:  
         •  Internal oblique shocks, boundary‐layer separation, increased turbulence, and total‐pressure losses.  
         •  Reduced core velocity or nonuniform velocity profile—particle acceleration suffers.  
      – Nozzle becomes very long/heavy with diminishing returns in exit velocity vs. length and weight.  
      – Particles can enter the “over­velocity” regime—erosion, fragmentation, substrate damage, reduced DE.  

4.  The net result—an optimum AoT  
   •  For a given gas (γ, R), stagnation pressure P0 and temperature T0, and a desired target vp just above vcrit, there is a narrow band of Ae/At that:  
      – Yields the highest usable jet velocity with minimal shock losses,  
      – Provides the right acceleration length,  
      – Keeps particles in the “high‐stick” window without causing rebound/erosion.  
   •  In practice, for cold‐spray with nitrogen or helium at 3–6 MPa, optimum Ae/At typically falls in the 8–20 range (exact value set by P0, T0 and particle size/density).  

Bottom line  
Increasing Ae/At raises exit Mach and particle KE—improving DE up to the point where either (a) the flow becomes overexpanded and shock-loss dominated or (b) particles exceed their upper “stick” velocity and begin to rebound or erode.  That trade-off creates a finite window of expansion ratios that delivers the best combination of particle velocity, deposition efficiency and process stability.

Carrier‐gas pressure in a cold-spray gun is really the “throttle” that determines particle velocities—and it is the particle’s kinetic energy on impact that controls both how many times it must hit the substrate before it sticks, and by what physical mechanism it ultimately bonds.  In practice you see three regimes as you raise the gas pressure (and thus the jet’s stagnation pressure and exit Mach number):

1.  Sub-critical regime (low gas pressure)  
    •  Particle velocity v < critical velocity for that material.  
    •  Almost no metallurgical bonding on first impact: most particles rebound or merely plastically indent the substrate.  
    •  Bonding can only build up by repeated impingements. Each impact gradually roughens and work-hardens the interface, breaks up oxides, and builds up a mechanical “interlock” layer.  
    •  Deposition efficiency is low; you may need hundreds or thousands of particle collisions (and many passes of the spray gun) to build a coherent coating.

2.  Near-critical regime (moderate gas pressure)  
    •  v approaches the material’s critical velocity.  
    •  A fraction of particles begin to undergo severe plastic deformation on first impact: you see incipient jetting at the particle–substrate interface, partial oxide fracture, and localized adiabatic shear bands.  
    •  Deposition efficiency rises steeply with small increases in pressure. You still rely on a mix of mechanical interlocking and nascent metallurgical bonding, so some repeated impingements remain necessary to “condition” the surface.

3.  Super-critical regime (high gas pressure)  
    •  v well above critical velocity.  
    •  Particles plastically flow almost immediately upon impact, driving a high-speed microjet that strips oxides, generates heat/adiabatic shear, and forges true metal–metal contact.  
    •  Single impingements can produce a metallurgical bond; deposition efficiency is high and only a handful of passes are needed to reach coating thickness targets.  
    •  Beware of overshooting—excessive velocities can erode the substrate or induce tensile residual stresses in the deposit.

In summary: raising carrier-gas pressure raises particle velocity, which reduces the number of impacts required for a given particle to stick, and shifts the dominant bonding mechanism from slow, build-up by mechanical interlocking to rapid, jet-assisted metallurgical bonding via adiabatic shear.

Key differences between cold‐gas spray (CGS) and high‐velocity oxy‐fuel (HVOF) arise from whether the feedstock ever melts—and hence from how it cools on impact—and these in turn control the coating’s grain size, defect structure and oxide content.

1. Cold‐gas spray  
  • Solid‐state deposition: particles are never molten but are accelerated (500–1 200 m/s) by adiabatic expansion of a preheated/pressurized gas.  
  • Minimal thermal input: particle temperatures typically stay well below the melting point. The only “heating” comes from plastic‐work and localized shear‐heating on impact.  
  • Cooling mechanism: the jet and substrate act as a heat sink, but there is no liquid‐to‐solid phase change. Deposited material cools essentially by conduction into the substrate and by the cold jet.  
  • Resulting microstructure:  
    – Severe plastic deformation at strain rates >10^6 s–1 causes adiabatic shear bands, dislocation tangles and dynamic recrystallization.  
    – Ultrafine to nanocrystalline grains at particle boundaries.  
    – Very low porosity and almost no oxides (no exposed liquid during flight).  
    – Predominantly compressive residual stresses from peening.

2. HVOF  
  • Melt or semi‐melt deposition: fuel (kerosene, propane, H₂) combusts with O₂ to generate a ~2 500–3 000 K gas stream; powders injected into the hot jet partially or fully melt.  
  • Cooling mechanism: upon impact on a relatively cool substrate each molten or semi-molten droplet rapidly quashes—cooling rates on the order of 10^3–10^6 K/s—via conduction into the substrate and convective mixing with the ambient.  
  • Resulting microstructure:  
    – “Splat” or lamellar morphology with splat boundaries defined by rapid solidification fronts.  
    – Within individual splats, fine dendritic or equiaxed grains form, their scale set by the local solidification rate.  
    – Oxide stringers or oxide‐rich layers can develop at splat interfaces (from in‐flight oxidation).  
    – Some residual porosity and tensile stresses (from differential cooling) remain trapped between lamellae.

In summary, CGS coatings inherit a heavily deformed, ultrafine‐grained, oxide‐free microstructure produced by adiabatic deformation and rapid conductive cooling, whereas HVOF coatings show classical rapid‐solidification features—lamellae, fine dendrites/equiaxed grains and inter-splat oxides—dictated by fast quenching of molten droplets.

In most cold‐spray systems the carrier gas flow is deliberately kept at a very high mass‐flux and pressure so that particles “ride along” in a dilute two‐phase stream.  Up to moderate solids‐to‐gas ratios (say a few percent by mass, or even as high as 10–20 % in some setups) two things happen:

1. Gas‐phase momentum dominates  
   – The gas mass flow rate is much larger than the particle mass flow rate, so adding particles up to moderate loading does not appreciably change the overall momentum or pressure drop in the nozzle.  
   – Because the gas expansion and acceleration through the converging–diverging nozzle remain essentially the same, the exit velocity and temperature fields barely shift.

2. Particle–particle and particle–gas coupling remain weak  
   – At low to moderate loadings the average distance between particles is large enough that collisions and wake interference are rare.  
   – The drag force on each particle comes from nearly the same local gas velocity regardless of how many neighbor particles are present.  

As a result, each particle experiences almost the same acceleration history and reaches nearly the same impact velocity and temperature, even when you double or triple the feed rate—provided you stay within the “dilute” regime.  Only when the particle mass flux approaches the gas mass flux (i.e. very high loadings) does the gas slow down, cool appreciably, and start to alter particle impact conditions in any significant way.

Laser‐preheating in laser‐assisted cold spray (sometimes called LACS or LP‐CS) is used to raise the temperature of the feedstock particles and/or the substrate immediately ahead of impact.  By doing so you substantially change the impact plasticity of the particles, the substrate’s ability to deform, and hence the bonding/coating buildup.  The key effects are:

1. Reduction of flow stress in the particles  
   • Raising the particle temperature even a few hundred degrees (200–600 °C, depending on material) cuts its dynamic yield strength via the Johnson–Cook (or similar) constitutive law.  
   • Lower flow stress means that, at a given impact velocity, particles deform more (larger flattening ratios), generate wider “splat” footprints, and dissipate their kinetic energy more readily into plastic work rather than bouncing off.  
   • Practical upshot: the critical velocity needed to achieve bonding drops (often by 50–100 m/s), and deposition efficiency goes up.

2. Enhanced adiabatic shear and localized plastic flow  
   • In conventional cold spray, bonding often relies on adiabatic shear instability at the particle/substrate interface.  Preheating brings the particle/substrate temperatures closer to the regime in which shear‐localization can initiate at lower impact velocities.  
   • You get a more pronounced shear jet and jetting of surface oxides or contaminants, further cleaning and metallurgically bonding the interface.

3. Substrate softening and increased interfacial accommodation  
   • Laser‐heating the substrate just ahead of the spray stream lowers its hardness and yield stress locally.  
   • A softer substrate can accommodate the incoming particles by deforming plastically, embedding them more deeply and promoting mechanical interlocking.  
   • The combination of substrate softening plus a hotter, more ductile particle tends to broaden the cohesive zone and reduce residual tensile stresses in the deposit.

4. Resulting improvements in coating structure and properties  
   • Higher deposition rates and efficiencies (more mass actually sticks, less rebounding).  
   • Denser coatings with lower porosity and fewer unbonded interfaces.  
   • Improved adhesion strength and cohesive strength—metallurgical bonding becomes more uniform.  
   • Finer microstructure in the deformed zone (dynamic recrystallization can be modulated by the starting temperature).

5. Caveats and limits  
   • Over‐heating the powder (or substrate) risks surface oxidation, sintering of the powder stream, or unwanted phase changes.  
   • Too large a temperature gradient in the substrate can induce thermal stresses or even melting.  
   • Optimal laser power, spot size, and scanning speed must be tuned for each powder alloy and substrate material.

In summary, laser preheating tailors the temperature state of both particles and substrate so that at identical or even reduced gas‐jet velocities you get dramatically better particle flattening, higher bonding efficiency, denser coatings and stronger adhesion than in “cold” cold‐spray alone.

In cold spray, particles are accelerated in a supersonic gas jet (typically 500–1,200 m/s) so that upon impact they carry very high kinetic energy but remain solid.  The key adhesion mechanisms are:

1. Instantaneous high‐pressure impact  
   • At velocities above the material’s “critical velocity,” interfacial pressures on impact can exceed 1 GPa—comparable to explosive or magnetic pulse welding.  
   • This pressure drives intimate, atom‐to‐atom contact across the interface.

2. Severe plastic deformation and jetting  
   • Impact strain rates on the order of 10^6–10^9 s^–1 cause intense adiabatic shear at the particle–substrate interface.  
   • A lateral “jet” of metal is expelled from the contact zone, carrying away oxides and adsorbed contaminants and exposing fresh, clean metal.

3. Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement  
   • The combination of high strain and localized heating (below the melting point) refines grains at the interface to the nanoscale, increasing dislocation density and driving further plasticity.  
   • These ultrafine grains help accommodate residual stresses and lock the particle to the substrate.

4. Cold welding (solid‐state bonding)  
   • With oxides stripped away and surfaces pressed together under gigapascal pressures, true metallic bonds form by atomic diffusion over the deformed, freshly exposed surfaces.  
   • No melting means there is minimal dilution or heat‐affected zone, preserving feedstock and substrate properties.

Because every impacting particle undergoes this sequence—extreme pressure, oxide‐free contact, mechanical interlocking and solid‐state bonding—the resulting coating is highly dense, exhibits strong adhesion (often exceeding substrate tensile strength), and retains the metallurgical integrity of both coating and substrate.

Cold gas‐dynamic spraying (CGDS) is fundamentally a solid‐state process: powders never melt during deposition, and the bulk substrate temperature remains well below the melting point of the sprayed material.  That low thermal input governs both the phase‐transformation behavior of the deposit and its mechanical properties:

1. Suppression of high‐temperature phase changes  
   • No melting → no solidification microstructures, no thermal cracking or re‐solidification porosity  
   • Minimal diffusion → original crystal structure (e.g. FCC Al, HCP Ti) and any metastable or amorphous phases in the feedstock are largely retained  
   • Negligible formation of intermetallics, carbides or oxides that would require prolonged high temperature

2. Localized adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization  
   • Particle impact at velocities >500 m/s generates a very high, sub‐millisecond temperature spike in the shear zone—often on the order of a few hundred °C—but only over a few microns of material  
   • This extreme, high‐strain‐rate deformation produces very high dislocation densities and, in many alloys, ultra‐fine‐grained or nanocrystalline layers via dynamic recrystallization  
   • The result is a marked increase in hardness and yield strength in the interfacial region (Hall–Petch strengthening), even though the bulk remains “cold.”

3. Work hardening and residual stresses  
   • Severe plastic deformation induces compressive residual stresses in the deposit, which improve fatigue and corrosion‐fatigue resistance  
   • The overall coating is stronger and harder than the feedstock powder but can have reduced ductility unless post‐spray annealing is applied

4. Preservation of oxidation‐sensitive chemistries  
   • Low gas and part temperatures minimize on‐route oxidation of alloying elements (e.g. Ti, Cu, Al), preserving ductility and toughness  
   • No thick, brittle oxide skins at particle boundaries means better interparticle bonding and lower coating porosity

5. Tailoring through post‐spray heat treatment  
   • Because few or no high‐temperature transformations occur during spraying, it is possible to carry out controlled, subsequent anneals or aging treatments to precipitate strengthening phases (e.g. Al–Cu T‐phase, Ni‐based superalloy γ′) without contaminating the deposit  

In sum, the low thermal exposure in cold spraying freezes in the feedstock phases and microchemistries while relying on impact‐driven, solid‐state deformation to refine grains, introduce work hardening, and generate residual compressive stresses. The outcome is a coating that combines high strength and hardness with minimal thermal damage or unwanted phase transformations.

Key consequences of cold‐spray’s low thermal input (typically < 600 °C metal “surface” temperature on impact) for coating microstructure and performance are:

1. Preservation of Feedstock Microstructure  
  • No melting or solidification → original powder phases, grain sizes, and metastable/amorphous structures are retained.  
  • Avoidance of oxidation, nitride or carbide scale formation that you see in thermal sprays.  

2. Impact‐Driven Microstructural Refinement  
  • Severe local plastic deformation at particle–substrate and interparticle interfaces produces very high dislocation densities, subgrains, and in many alloys even dynamic recrystallization in a narrow shear zone.  
  • Grain sizes in the interfacial region can drop to submicron or nanometer scale, boosting hardness (Hall–Petch effect).  

3. Low Thermal Residual Stresses and Heat‐Affected Zone  
  • Because particles never melt, the thermal gradient between coating and substrate is small.  
  • Minimal shrinkage on cooling and little or no HAZ in the substrate leads to low tensile residual stresses. Often slight compressive stresses remain beneficial for fatigue and crack‐growth resistance.  

4. Bonding Mechanisms and Cohesion  
  • High‐velocity impact generates adiabatic shear instabilities and “jetting” of surface oxides, enabling clean metal–metal contact and cold‐welding.  
  • Mechanical interlocking plus metallurgical bonding yields coating cohesive strengths often above 90% of wrought material tensile strength.  

5. Resultant Mechanical Integrity  
  • High hardness and yield strength from work hardening/grain refinement without embrittling intermetallics.  
  • Good ductility and toughness compared with fusion‐sprayed or thermal‐sprayed coatings (no crack networks).  
  • Excellent fatigue performance (low crack‐driving stresses), wear resistance, and corrosion behavior (minimal oxide pores).  

In short, cold spray’s low heat input avoids melt‐related defects and leverages impact‐induced plasticity to produce dense, strongly bonded, fine‐grained coatings with high strength, good toughness, low residual stresses, and superior wear/corrosion resistance.

In cold spray the powder‐size enters twice: first in the gas acceleration stage, and second in the impact/bonding stage.  In very broad strokes:

1. Acceleration in the nozzle  
   – Drag vs. inertia:  a=Fdrag/mp ∝d²/(ρp d³)=1/(ρp d).  All else equal, smaller particles accelerate more rapidly toward the carrier‐gas speed.  
   – Nozzle length limit:  a small particle can almost “catch up” to the supersonic gas; a large particle carries so much inertia that over the finite nozzle length it never reaches high velocity.  
   – As d increases, terminal particle velocity Vp falls off (for a given gas pressure, temperature, and nozzle geometry) roughly as Vp≈Vgas·[1–exp(–const/(ρp d))].  

2. Bonding on impact  
   – Critical velocity Vc(d):  any given material has a minimum impact velocity needed to induce sufficient plastic flow at the interface.  For smaller particles Vc rises because their mass (and thus kinetic‐energy per particle) is lower, so you need higher velocity to get the strain work required.  
   – Momentum and energy:  PR ∼mp Vp must exceed a threshold to produce jetting, substrate erosion and adiabatic shear instabilities that lock the particle in place.  Too little momentum → rebound or powder “pop‐in.”  

3. Putting the two together: the “Goldilocks” window  
   – If d is too small (<≈3–5 µm for most metals) you can exceed Vc but mp is so low that the energy‐density delivered on impact is marginal.  Also very fine powders tend to agglomerate, get caught in boundary layers or build up on the nozzle walls.  
   – If d is too large (>≈50–80 µm for many ductile metals) the particle never achieves Vc before exiting the nozzle.  You end up with high‐mass but sub‐critical‐velocity particles that simply bounce or erode the deposit.  
   – In practice for common ductile metals (Al, Cu, Ni alloys) the optimum size range is roughly 10–40 µm.  Within this range you attain a high fraction of particles above Vc and you carry enough per‐particle energy to form dense, well‐bonded coatings.  

4. Fine tuning  
   – Harder alloys or higher‐density materials shift the window downward (e.g. 5–20 µm for steels, WC‐Co).  
   – High‐pressure He or H₂ carriers and optimized nozzle designs can push the upper limit up by giving larger particles more acceleration length and higher drag forces.  

Summary  
Accelerate small enough to outrun inertia but keep large enough to carry sufficient momentum.  That compromise—typically a mean particle size of 10–40 µm for ductile metals—delivers the highest deposition efficiency and bonding quality in cold spray.

Electrostatic‐assisted (ESA) cold spray differs from a conventional (purely aerodynamic) cold spray in that the powder particles carry net charge and fly through an imposed electric field on their way to the substrate.  Two things happen simultaneously:

 1.   An additional field‐induced acceleration along the spray axis (E∙q/mp) raises every particle’s axial velocity  
 2.   The non‐uniformity of the field near the nozzle and around the spray plume imposes radial forces that tend to steer (“focus”) or defocus particles depending on polarity and electrode geometry  

The net effect on the radial profile of impact velocity and on the footprint of the deposit can be summarized as follows:

 •  “Flattening” of the axial‐velocity profile  
    –  In a pure gas jet the axial impact speed Vz(r) is highest on axis and falls off quickly with increasing radial distance r (roughly Gaussian or parabolic).  
    –  The ESA field adds essentially the same axial boost at all radii.  Since the off‐axis gas‐only speed is lower to start with, the *percentage* gain in Vz is larger at large r than on axis.  The result is a flatter Vz(r) curve (the standard deviation of Vz across the jet shrinks).  

 •  Reduction of radial divergence (plume focusing)  
    –  Close to the nozzle exit the electric‐field lines are not purely axial (they “wrap” from the nozzle lip to the substrate).  This produces a weak inward radial force on negatively charged particles (assuming a positive substrate or vice-versa).  
    –  That radial component pulls outward‐traveling particles back toward the centreline, so the half‐angle of the spray plume shrinks.  

 •  Consequences for the deposition footprint  
    –  Because more of the off‐axis particles now exceed the critical bonding velocity, the *overall* diameter of the region where you actually build a coating can increase by 10–30 %.  
    –  At the same time, the narrowing of the plume angle means that the “high‐velocity core” is more tightly localized.  In practice one sees a deposit whose edges are pushed out farther than in conventional cold spray but whose central thickness peak is narrower and higher.  
    –  As you increase the applied voltage the peripheral boost dominates at low fields (wider, more uniform coating) but at very high fields the focusing effect overtakes and the entire footprint can actually shrink again (giving a small, very high‐velocity core).  

Quantitatively you will often observe, for a given gas condition and powder, a rise in on-axis particle speed of ∼5–10 % and a ∼15–50 % speed increase at r near the original spray edge.  The critical–velocity contour therefore moves outward, enlarging the deposition zone, while the spray‐half‐angle can drop by 10–20 %, steepening the radial thickness profile.

In cold spray, two things happen in concert to give you very dense, very clean metal coatings:  

 1. High-pressure gas acceleration  
   • You feed metal powder (typically 5–50 µm) into a converging–diverging (De Laval) nozzle.  High-pressure gas (N₂, He or even H₂ at up to 5–6 MPa and temperatures of 300–800 °C) expands through the nozzle and converts almost all of its enthalpy into kinetic energy, propelling each particle to supersonic speeds (300–1 200 m/s).  
   • At those velocities the particle’s kinetic energy (½mv²) massively exceeds the threshold needed to cause intense, localized plastic deformation when it strikes the substrate (or previously deposited particles).  That plastic flow at the impact face produces ultra-high strain rates and adiabatic shear instabilities, jets off any existing oxide film, and forges metal-to-metal intimate contact at the interface.  
   • The result is a “solid‐state” weld between particles and substrate, with mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding.  Because every incoming particle is essentially hammered flat into the layer beneath, porosity drops to well under 1 % and the coating builds up into a fully consolidated, high-density deposit.  

 2. Low thermal input  
   • Unlike thermal spray, cold spray never melts the powder.  The bulk gas temperature may be a few hundred degrees, but particles never reach their melting point—there is simply not enough dwell time or heat input.  
   • Because there is no liquid metal, you avoid oxidation or nitride formation in flight or upon solidification.  You also avoid segregation, phase transformations, and excessive residual stresses.  The chemical composition of your feedstock is preserved in the coating, giving you near-100 % purity.  
   • The only heating is extremely localized and transient at the micro-impact sites (enough to plasticize the metal but not to melt it), so the as-sprayed microstructure—often with refined grains in the shear zones—remains very clean and largely unaltered from the feedstock.  

Together, the supersonic “cold hammering” of particles (high kinetic energy) plus the fact that you never cross the melting point (low thermal input) yield coatings that are both extremely dense (very low porosity) and extremely pure (minimal oxides or secondary phases).

In cold spray the carrier gas is not just a conveyor—it sets the maximum particle velocity and thus controls how much plastic deformation (and hence bonding) each particle undergoes on impact.  Three key gas properties come into play: molecular weight (M), specific‐heat ratio (γ), and viscosity (μ), plus the operating temperature (T₀) and pressure (P₀).  

1.   Gas velocity and particle acceleration  
     •  Speed of sound c₀=√(γ·R·T₀) (R=gas constant/M).  For a fixed P₀∕P_exit, a higher c₀ gives a higher nozzle Mach number and hence a higher jet velocity V_g≈M·c₀.  
     •  Molecular weight: lighter gases (He) have a larger R and often a larger γ, so c₀(He)>c₀(N₂)>c₀(Ar) at the same T₀.  That is why helium jets can exceed 1 200 m/s, nitrogen ~800–1 000 m/s, argon even less.  
     •  Drag acceleration:   
        m_p·dV_p/dt ≈ C_d·A_p·½·ρ_g·(V_g–V_p)²  
       – ρ_g scales with P₀/T₀ and M; a higher ρ_g at the same V_g boosts the drag force.  
       – μ determines the boundary‐layer thickness in the nozzle and the fine structure of the supersonic jet (shock cells), which in turn affect how efficiently momentum is transferred to each particle.  

2.   Particle velocity → kinetic energy → deformation  
     •  Kinetic energy per particle ∝½·m_p·V_p².  Small increases in V_p give large gains in impact energy.  
     •  Below a material’s critical velocity V_cr the particle simply bounces or lightly “peens” the surface; little or no metallurgical bonding occurs.  
     •  Above V_cr plastic deformation is intense: oxide layers crack, fresh metal surfaces flow together, adiabatic shear bands and dynamic recrystallization form, and inter‐particle/substrate bonds nucleate and grow.  

3.   How gas choice affects coating quality  
     •  Helium (low M, high γ) produces the highest particle velocities and is often required for high‐strength alloys (stainless steels, Ni‐based superalloys) whose V_cr can exceed 1 000 m/s.  
     •  Nitrogen offers a balance of cost and performance for lower V_cr materials (Al, Cu, some softer steels).  
     •  Argon, with the highest M and lowest c₀, gives the lowest velocities, and so is used only when very low impact energies are needed (e.g. embedding soft powders).  

4.   Gas temperature and pressure  
     •  Raising T₀ boosts c₀ and lowers ρ_g, yielding a higher Mach‐number jet but slightly reduced per‐particle drag; the net effect is usually a higher V_p.  
     •  Higher P₀ increases ρ_g and the available pressure ratio P₀/P_exit, both of which push V_g (and hence V_p) up.  

In practice you choose the gas type, temperature and pressure to achieve a particle exit velocity just above the critical velocity of your feedstock material.  That ensures sufficient plastic deformation for metallurgical bonding without over‐driving into substrate erosion or particle rebound, and thus maximizes coating density, adhesion and mechanical properties.

Cold spray is a solid‐state, high‐velocity impact process. Rather than melting the powder, it uses a supersonic gas jet (typically N₂ or He at 500–1,200 m/s) to accelerate particles so that, upon striking the substrate, they undergo:

  • Severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear instabilities at the interface  
  • Microjetting that strips oxides and contaminants    
  • Mechanical interlocking and true metallic contact at asperities  
  • Localized dynamic recrystallization, promoting fresh metal–metal bonding  

Because the feedstock never reaches its melting point, cold-sprayed coatings exhibit:

  • Very low oxidation and oxide‐inclusion levels (oxide films are fragmented and “jet‐cleaned” away)  
  • High coating density (porosities often <1 %) and near‐100 % deposition efficiency  
  • A fine, work-hardened, dynamically recrystallized microstructure in both particles and interface  
  • Compressive residual stresses that improve adhesion, fatigue life, and wear resistance  
  • No heat-affected zone or distortion in the substrate, making it ideal for heat-sensitive materials  
  • Preservation of feedstock chemistry (no detrimental phase transformations or grain coarsening)

Together, these effects yield thick, tough, corrosion-resistant metal or composite layers with bond strengths often exceeding those of thermal-sprayed or weld-deposited coatings—but without melting-related defects.

In cold spray the ultimate density of the deposit is set by how completely each incoming particle plastically deforms and “wets‐out” against its neighbors.  Two material parameters dominate that behaviour: the particle’s momentum (m·v) at impact, which sets the dynamic pressure driving deformation, and the particle’s hardness (or, more strictly, its dynamic yield strength), which controls how much pressure is needed to force that deformation.  

1. Momentum → driving pressure  
  • On impact at velocity v a particle of mass m delivers a pressure on the order of Pd ≃ ½ρp v² over its contact area (or, equivalently, momentum flux m·v per collision time).  
  • If Pd falls below the particle’s dynamic yield strength Y, it rebounds elastically: no bonding, high local porosity.  
  • Once Pd ≳ Y, plastic flow localizes at the interface (often via adiabatic shear), removing surface oxides and allowing metal‐to‐metal contact and jetting.  

2. Hardness (dynamic yield strength) → resistance to deformation  
  • Harder materials (higher Y) require a higher Pd (hence higher v or bigger m—i.e. larger or denser particles) to produce the same flattening.  
  • Soft, low-hardness powders deform readily at lower velocities and yield high flattening ratios (wide “splats”), producing dense, low-porosity coatings—provided the momentum is still above the critical threshold for jetting.  

3. Joint effect on coating density  
  a) Below critical momentum (Pd < Y): particles rebound → no deposition, or very porous “cake.”  
  b) Near critical momentum (Pd ≃ Y): barely sufficient plastic flow → partial flattening, interparticle gaps remain → moderate porosity.  
  c) Above critical but below erosion limit (Pd ≫ Y but below substrate‐erosion pressure): good plastic deformation, extensive splatting, oxide‐free contact → high coating density (porosity < 1 %).  
  d) Excessively high momentum (Pd >> Y of substrate): substrate erosion and particle shattering → poor adhesion and again increased porosity.  

4. Practical implications  
  • For a given powder material (fixed Y), one tunes gas pressure, temperature and nozzle geometry to achieve v just above the material’s critical velocity vcr ∝ √(Y/ρp).  
  • Harder alloys and intermetallics shift vcr upward, narrowing the “dense‐deposition window.”  
  • Pre-heating powders or substrates can lower apparent Y, widen the deposition window and improve deposit density.

In summary, coating density in cold spray is maximized when particle momentum is high enough to exceed the particle’s hardness-controlled yield stress (so the particle plastically spreads and bonds) but not so high as to erode substrate or shatter the particle. Harder powders simply move that optimum momentum (velocity) higher, and if you don’t hit that window you end up with a porous, poorly bonded coating.

In cold spray the “workhorse” of bonding is plastic deformation of your ductile metal particles; the ceramic particles are essentially passengers that can only become trapped if they hit a freshly deformed metal bed at a high enough velocity.  When you raise the ceramic fraction in your feedstock you therefore see two linked effects:

 1.  Drop in embedded‐ceramic fraction  
    •  Fewer metal particles ⇒ fewer plastic–metal collisions to build up the rough, high-surface-energy bed that can mechanically lock in the hard ceramic grains.  
    •  More ceramic–ceramic collisions, which tend to rebound or shatter the ceramics rather than bond them.  
    •  Beyond some “saturation” of the metal layer thickness, additional ceramic simply bounces off instead of embedding.  

 2.  Drop in overall (relative) deposition efficiency  
    •  Ceramics have a much higher critical velocity for bonding.  As you add more ceramics, the proportion of particles that ever reach their critical velocity (and impact on a ductile target) falls.  
    •  You dilute out the metal “glue,” so not only do fewer ceramics stick, you also build up the coating more slowly.  Thus the mass of feed that actually ends up on the substrate goes down.  

In short, increasing ceramic in the feed robs the spray of its ductile, energy‐absorbing phase and so both the fraction of ceramics that get entombed in the growing metal matrix and the total mass of powder that deposits successfully are reduced.

Cold‐sprayed Al coatings almost always show an apparent “dead time” at the very start of a spray run—in other words, you get essentially zero net buildup until you’ve sprayed for some finite dwell time, and only after that do you begin to see measurable thickness.  That behaviour comes almost entirely from the fact that cold spray bonding is not an instantaneous, single‐impact phenomenon but an accumulation of:  

 1. Oxide fracture and removal.  Aluminum particles carry a 50–100 nm Al₂O₃ shell.  Until you’ve impacted the substrate (and early‐arriving particles) enough times to crack and disperse that shell, you never get fresh Al–Al contact and hence no metal–metal bond.  

 2. Substrate surface conditioning.  The very first handful of impacts simply plastically deform (and even work‐harden) the substrate, roughening it, building up local dislocations, and heating it slightly by adiabatic shear.  None of that by itself produces a stable, bonded layer, but it does raise the probability that subsequent particles will meet the critical velocity/strain‐rate conditions for jet‐formation, shear‐instability, and metallurgical bonding.  

 3. Heat build‐up and yield‐strength reduction.  Aluminum’s high thermal conductivity means that a single particle impact sheds most of its heat into the bulk substrate.  It takes a train of impacts on the same spot to raise the local temperature enough that the flow stress drops to the point where you can get the adiabatic shear bands and dynamic recrystallization needed for true bonding.  

Only after a critical number of impacts (i.e. a critical spray‐time or dwell‐time on each point) do you have:  
 • Most of the Al₂O₃ removed or fragmented,  
 • A roughened, slightly work‐hardened‐and‐heated substrate, and  
 • The local conditions (stress, strain‐rate, temperature) for impact‐driven bond formation.  

Below that dwell‐time you simply accumulate bounced or shallowly‐embedded particles whose net contribution to measured thickness is essentially zero.  Once you exceed the threshold, deposition “turns on” and you begin to see a linear (or near‐linear) build‐up of coating thickness with further spray time.

Increasing the gas temperature in a cold-spray system affects all three of the key steps—particle acceleration, impact deformation, and deposition efficiency (DE)—and does so in a mechanically coupled way.  A handy way to see why is to write out the two governing formulae:

 1. Gas (and hence particle) exit velocity,  
    v_g ≃ √{(2γ/(γ–1)) R T₀ [1 – (p_back/p₀)^((γ–1)/γ)]}  
    ∝ √T₀  (for fixed pressure ratio and nozzle geometry)  
 2. Drag acceleration on a particle,  
    a_d = (3 C_d ρ_g)/(4 ρ_p d_p) · (v_g – v_p)²  

where  
• γ = gas heat capacity ratio  
• R = gas constant  
• T₀, p₀ = stagnation (heater) temperature and pressure  
• p_back = chamber pressure  
• ρ_g, ρ_p = gas and particle densities  
• C_d = drag coefficient, d_p = particle diameter  

From these you can see:

1. Particle velocity increases roughly with √T₀.  
   – Higher T₀ raises the gas sound speed and thus the achievable Mach number and exit velocity.  
   – In practice you see 10–30 % higher particle speeds for a few hundred‐degree Celsius rise in T₀.

2. Particle deformation on impact grows strongly with velocity and with any softening of the particle by pre‐heating.  
   – Impact kinetic energy ∝ v_p². More KE in the same mass → more plastic strain at the interface.  
   – Meanwhile the hot carrier gas also heats the particles in flight, reducing their yield strength and raising their strain‐to‐failure.  That both lowers the critical velocity for bonding and enlarges the contact area when they hit.

3. Deposition efficiency climbs as more particles exceed the (now lower) critical velocity and deform sufficiently to bond.  
   – Below the critical velocity almost every particle rebounds or erodes the substrate; above it DE typically jumps from single‐digit percent to 50 – 90 %.  
   – You do eventually reach diminishing returns (and you can even get erosion or oxidation penalties at very high T₀), but in most metals the “sweet spot” is a few hundred degrees above ambient.

In short, raising the spray‐gas temperature:  
– accelerates particles to higher speeds,  
– softens them so they deform more readily at impact, and  
– therefore shifts more of the powder into the deposit rather than rebound or erosion, usually boosting deposition efficiency dramatically until other side‐effects (e.g. oxidation, gas‐density drop or nozzle wear) become limiting.

In conventional cold spray the particle jet and substrate are both essentially isothermal and the nozzle–substrate axis is the only symmetry axis. You therefore impinge a nearly uniform, axis-symmetric momentum flux and get a symmetrical “footprint” (track cross-section). By contrast, in supersonic laser-assisted deposition you superimpose a high‐power diode or fiber laser onto that jet, and that upsets every symmetry:

1. Off-axis heating and melt‐pool dynamics  
   • The laser is often angled or laterally offset from the spray axis so one side of the spray sees more thermal input.  
   • Localized melting of the substrate (or the impacting particles) creates a directional (“down-stream”) flow of molten material, so more deposit builds up on one side of the scanning direction.

2. Non-uniform thermal gradients  
   • The leading edge of the melt pool is hotter and more plastic than the trailing edge, biasing where particles stick and where the pool flows under surface tension.  
   • Steeper temperature gradients also drive thermocapillary (Marangoni) flows that pull molten metal toward cooler regions—typically the sides or the rear of the laser spot, not symmetrically around it.

3. Supersonic shock‐cell and pressure‐profile distortion  
   • At Mach ≥ 2 the jet encloses a series of barrel shocks and Mach diamonds that already shift the peak stagnation pressure off–center.  
   • Adding a laser thermal boundary layer modifies the local gas density and pressure field, further skewing the particle momentum distribution.

4. Scan‐direction vector addition  
   • Unlike a “static” cold‐spray spot, you are continuously moving the laser+nozzle over the substrate. The in-plane translation velocity vector adds to the particle impact velocity to give a net impingement angle that varies across the track width, favoring one side.

Taken together, these effects break the simple conical‐nozzle symmetry of conventional cold spray and produce lopsided, asymmetric deposits in supersonic laser deposition.

Nozzle traverse speed controls the local particle flux (particles · mm⁻² · s⁻¹) that impinges on the polymer.  Because cold‐spray embedding into a soft polymer relies on repeated high-velocity impacts to produce local plastic flow (and modest thermal softening), slowing the traverse (i.e. spending more spray‐time per unit area) raises:

 1. Peak local pressure and strain per unit area  
 2. Cumulative particle count impacting the same spot  
 3. Local temperature (from adiabatic heating)  

All of these lower the polymer’s yield stress in the impact zone and allow deeper, higher-density particle embedding and therefore higher mass loading.  Conversely, a faster scan spreads the same powder over more area, so each point sees fewer impacts and carries less embedded mass.

Mass loading versus traverse speed typically follows an inverse trend:  
  • At high speeds (e.g. > 50 mm/s) you get light, patchy coverage and low weight gain.  
  • As you slow the scan toward an optimum (often 5–20 mm/s, depending on the system), embedding becomes continuous and mass gain per pass rises steeply.  
  • Below that optimum speed further slowing gives diminishing returns and can even be counterproductive.

The practical ceiling on weight gain (and layer thickness) arises when:

 1. Polymer saturation and work-hardening The local polymer can only flow so much. Once the surface is “jammed” with particles it stops conforming, and fresh particles simply bounce or abrade the deposit.  
 2. Deposit-deposit impacts New particles predominantly strike existing particles (rather than bare polymer), which reduces impact pressure at the particle–polymer interface and lowers bonding efficiency.  
 3. Thermal and mechanical damage Excessive heating can soften or char the polymer bulk; thick particulate layers build residual stresses that promote cracking or delamination.  
 4. Substrate viscoelastic recovery Polymers relax stresses over time; repeated passes can allow “spring-back” of the matrix, squeezing out loosely held particles.  

In short, slowing the nozzle increases embedding and mass gain up to the point where the polymer’s capacity for plastic flow, the changing nature of impact events (particle-onto-particle rather than particle-onto-polymer), and thermal/mechanical limits cause the deposition efficiency to plateau.

Under a fixed laser‐energy density (i.e. fixed power/scan‐speed), raising the powder feed rate drives three linked trends:  
1. Coating (clad) thickness rises.  You are dumping more metal into each melt pool, so you build height faster.  
2. Substrate dilution falls.  A larger fraction of the melt‐pool mass comes from powder rather than remelted substrate, so the clad‐substrate mixing ratio decreases.  
3. Track width stays about the same or shrinks slightly.  Because more powder cools the pool and less substrate is melted, the melt pool spreads less laterally, so you often see a modest narrowing of the clad bead.  

In practice, if you push the feed rate too high you can also begin to get poor powder melting, porosity, or lack of fusion defects.

Adding ceramic particles (Al₂O₃, SiC, TiC, etc.) into a ductile metal powder feedstock (Al, Cu, Ni alloys) converts a pure‐metal cold‐sprayed coating into a metal–matrix composite (MMC). The main effects on microstructure and adhesion are:

1. Microstructure refinement and phase distribution  
  • Severe plastic deformation of the metal binder upon impact drives dynamic recrystallization, producing a submicron or even nanocrystalline metal matrix.  
  • Dispersed ceramics act as Zener-pinning sites, inhibiting recrystallized grain growth and further refining the metal grain size.  
  • Ceramic volume fraction and particle size control how uniformly they distribute: too high a loading (> 30–40 vol %) or large (~10 µm+) particles lead to clustering and increased porosity.

2. Splat deformation and pore formation  
  • Pure metal particles flatten readily, promoting dense, interlocked lamellae. Ceramic inclusion reduces the overall ductility of each splat, limiting flattening.  
  • At moderate ceramic loadings (10–20 vol %), the metal binder still flows around the stiff inclusions and “solders” splats together, preserving ~95 %+ relative density.  
  • Excessive ceramic content increases unmelted “rigid” islands, creating microvoids around them and ultimately raising coating porosity.

3. Coating–substrate and intra‐coating adhesion  
  • Bonding in cold spray is purely solid‐state: metal plastically flows and mechanically interlocks at the substrate interface. Ceramics do not plastically deform and therefore do not directly bond metallurgically to the substrate.  
  • A continuous metal binder at the substrate interface is essential. If ceramics reach the interface (e.g. from poor feed staging), they reduce the real contact area and can act as crack-initiation sites, lowering adhesion strength.  
  • Optimized process windows (higher particle velocities, substrate pre-heating) help the metal “wet” both substrate and ceramic surfaces, enhancing matrix continuity and thus both interfacial adhesion and cohesive strength of the composite coating.

4. Mechanical‐property trade-offs  
  • Hardness, wear resistance, and stiffness rise with ceramic content as the second phase carries load and impedes plastic flow.  
  • Fracture toughness and adhesion (both cohesive and adhesive) tend to decrease if ceramic fraction is too large or poorly dispersed, because of stress concentrations around hard inclusions and incomplete splat bonding.

Practical guidelines:  
- Keep ceramic loading to ~10–25 vol % for a balance of hardness and adhesion.  
- Use fine (< 5 µm) ceramic powders to promote even dispersion and help the metal binder flow around particles.  
- Increase spray temperature/pressure to raise impact velocity, ensuring sufficient metal deformation to encapsulate ceramics and maintain good mechanical interlock at the substrate.

In cold spray the process gas (typically N₂ or He) is first brought to a high stagnation pressure (10–40 bar) and temperature (300–800 °C) in a plenum, then expanded through a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle to generate a supersonic jet. Because the expansion is (to a first approximation) adiabatic, the gas does work accelerating itself and its static temperature drops; in fact  
  T_exit = T₀·[1 + (γ–1)/2·M²]⁻¹  
where γ is the specific-heat ratio and M the Mach number. At typical M≃2–3, the static exit temperature can be 30–50 % below the plenum (stagnation) temperature.

Impact on cold spray  
• Lower gas temperature means particles receive less convective heating prior to impact.  
• If the exit temperature falls too low, particles may not reach the softening or “incipient plasticity” window needed for good bonding.  
• Reduced temperature also increases gas density at fixed pressure, slightly lowering exit velocity (and thus particle speed).

Compensating measures  
1. High stagnation temperature  
   – Preheat the gas (electric or gas-fired heaters) so that even after adiabatic cooling, T_exit remains above the particle softening threshold (usually 300–500 °C for metals).  
2. Gas selection  
   – Use gases with higher γ (e.g. He or H₂) to reduce the fractional temperature drop for a given Mach number, and to raise the speed of sound (thus achievable jet velocity).  
3. Nozzle design  
   – Optimize the expansion ratio (exit area/throat area) so that M is enough for high velocity but not so large that T_exit falls below the required process window.  
   – Employ stepped or multi-throat nozzles to tailor the local Mach distribution and minimize excessive cooling.  
4. Multi-stage or bypass heating  
   – In some systems a secondary heater surrounds the nozzle throat, or hot “bypass” gas is injected downstream, to reheat the core flow.  
5. Thermally insulated plumbing  
   – Minimize heat losses between the heater and the nozzle throat (e.g. ceramic insulation, low-conductivity supports).  

By combining sufficiently high stagnation temperatures, judicious gas choice, and carefully engineered nozzle geometries (with optional secondary heating), cold-spray systems ensure that—even after adiabatic expansion—gas temperatures remain high enough to soften and accelerate particles into the high-velocity, high-strain‐rate regime required for metallurgical bonding.

Substrate roughness plays several complementary roles in boosting particle deformation, adhesion and overall deposition efficiency in cold spray:  
- Stress concentration at asperities  
  • High‐velocity particles impacting sharp peaks locally exceed the material’s yield strength more readily, promoting intense plastic flow and splat formation.  
  • These localized “hot spots” can trigger adiabatic shear instabilities that aid metallurgical bonding.  
- Increased real contact area  
  • Valleys and crevices multiply the true bonding area compared with a flat surface, allowing more material-to-material intimate contact.  
  • More contact area lowers the effective critical velocity required for bonding.  
- Mechanical interlocking  
  • Deformed particles flow into valleys and lock behind asperity peaks, creating a dovetail-type anchoring that resists tensile and shear loading.  
  • This geometric interlock supplements any metallurgical bond.  
- Frictional energy dissipation  
  • Rough surfaces impede lateral sliding and rebound of newly arrived particles, converting more kinetic energy into plastic deformation rather than elastic rebound.  
  • Reduced rebound directly raises deposition efficiency (ratio of adhered to injected powder).  
- Mitigation of tensile stresses  
  • Particles lodged in valleys act as crack‐arresters for interfacial tensile stresses, improving coating cohesion and adhesion.  

Optimizing roughness amplitude—typically on the order of a few micrometers up to a fraction of the particle diameter—strikes a balance between providing sufficient anchoring sites and avoiding excessive trapping of powder. In practice, grit-blasting or controlled etching is used to achieve the desired roughness profile, leading to higher bonding rates, stronger coatings and improved material utilization.

Key mechanisms  
‐ In cold spray the gas stagnation temperature (T₀) and pressure (P₀) set the nozzle exit Mach number and the gas–particle drag—and thus control particle exit velocity, particle heating, and ultimately the degree of particle deformation (“splatting”) on the substrate.  

1. Particle velocity (and critical velocity)  
  • Mach number M ≃[(2/(γ–1))·((P₀/P_back)^((γ–1)/γ)–1)]^½; exit velocity v = M·√(γ·R·T₀).  
  • Raising P₀ increases the pressure ratio P₀/P_back, so M↑ and v↑.  
  • Raising T₀ increases the local speed of sound √(γRT₀), so v↑, but at the same time gas density ρ_gas ∝ P₀/(R·T₀) drops, slightly reducing drag.  
  • Net effect up to an optimal T₀: higher T₀ and P₀ → higher v_particle → greater plastic deformation, better bonding as long as v_particle exceeds the material’s critical deposition velocity.  

2. Splat morphology  
  A. Low T₀ or P₀ (sub-critical v_particle):  
    – Particles rebound or only lightly indent; splats are irregular, non-pancake, high porosity, poor adhesion.  
  B. Moderate-high T₀ & P₀ (v_particle slightly above critical):  
    – “Pancake” splats with high flattening ratio, radial flow, metallurgical bonding.  
    – Uniform rims, low oxide entrapment, near-full density splats.  
  C. Excessive T₀ or P₀ (v_particle ≫ critical):  
    – Very high impact energy → substrate erosion, particle shattering, localized heating.  
    – Can produce microcracks at splat edges or re-entrainment of fragments.  

3. Coating uniformity  
  • Deposition efficiency (DE) rises with v_particle (above the critical threshold) until erosion or particle rebound balances further gains.  
  • At too low P₀/T₀ the spray plume is “starved” toward the edges: thinner, patchy deposits, high roughness.  
  • At optimal P₀/T₀ the plume impinges uniformly; layers build up evenly, low intra-coat porosity, consistent thickness.  
  • If P₀ is too high or T₀ too hot, increased gas turbulence widens the spray cone and can cause excessive overspray or edge-bead buildup; substrate erosion may introduce topography that disrupts uniformity.  

4. Practical tuning  
  – For ductile metals (Al, Cu): moderate T₀ (350–550 °C) and P₀ (3–5 MPa) usually suffice.  
  – For harder alloys or intermetallics: higher T₀ (600–800 °C) and P₀ (4–6 MPa) push v_particle over the higher critical velocity.  
  – Fine-tuning of stand-off distance, nozzle geometry, and gas composition (He vs. N₂) further refines splat shape and layer homogeneity.  

Summary  
  Gas pressure primarily drives particle velocity via increased stagnation pressure ratio, while gas temperature both raises the speed of sound (boosting velocity) and softens particles (enhanced flattening). Together they set whether particles stick and how they deform—hence controlling splat shape, inter-splat bonding, porosity, and overall coating uniformity.

You can think of “layer separation” in sprayed graphite as simply another “bond–formation” criterion: the particle must impact at or above a certain critical velocity Vc so that its kinetic energy and associated shock‐driven stresses exceed the interlayer shear strength of graphite.  Empirically one almost always observes that larger particles require slightly lower critical velocities than smaller ones.  In practice the size–dependence is captured by a simple power‐law of the form  
   
   Vc(d) = A · d ^(–n)  

where  
•  d is the particle diameter,  
•  A is a material- and system-specific coefficient (with the dimensions of velocity × length^n),  
•  n is an empirically determined exponent (typically between 0.1 and 0.3 for many cold‐sprayed metals and ceramics, and for graphite n often falls in the 0.1–0.2 range).  

How to use this in your graphite deposition:  
1.  Gather or generate a data set of critical velocities (layer separation thresholds) for a range of smaller graphite particle sizes d₁, d₂, … dₖ.  You can do this by performing single‐particle impact tests in your kinetically sprayed system (e.g. with laser‐Doppler velocimetry or high-speed imaging).  
2.  Fit the Vc vs. d data to the power law Vc = A·d^(–n).  A simple log–log linear regression will give you ln Vc = ln A – n ln d.  From that fit extract A and n.  
3.  Extrapolate to your target larger size dL by plugging into the same formula:  
   
      Vc(dL)  =  A · (dL)^(–n)  

   Let’s say your fit gives n = 0.15 and A = 1.3 × 10^4  (with d in microns and V in m/s).  If your existing data are around d ≃ 10 μm, you might have found Vc(10 μm) ≃ 800 m/s.  For dL = 50 μm  
   
      Vc(50 μm)  = 1.3 × 10^4 · (50 μm)^(–0.15)  
                 ≃ 1.3 × 10^4 · (50^(–0.15))  
                 ≃ 1.3 × 10^4 · 0.71  
                 ≃ 920 m/s.  

   So you’d predict that 50 μm graphite particles must strike at roughly 900–950 m/s to achieve the same degree of interlayer separation (and bonding) that 10 μm particles did at 800 m/s.  

Caveats & checks:  
•  Particle shape, porosity, and orientation effects can perturb A and n, so it’s wise to validate the extrapolation with a few trial runs at the predicted Vc for the large fraction.  
•  Gas temperature and pressure also shift A slightly, so if you change spray conditions re-calibrate.  
•  Most graphite flakes are highly anisotropic: if you switch from equiaxed powders to platy particles, you may observe a different exponent or prefactor.  

But in every cold‐spray system the key steps are the same: measure Vc vs. d at small scales, fit a power law, then use Vc(d_target) = A·d_target^(–n) to predict your critical velocity for larger, microscale particles.

In the cold‐spray process the “sticking” of a powder particle to the substrate is entirely a momentum‐transfer event.  Since the particle leaves the nozzle at velocity Vi and comes to rest on the substrate (Vf≈0), the impulse imparted to the substrate–particle system is simply  
ΔP = mi Vi – mf Vf ≃ mi Vi.  

Thus, to improve deposition you must maximize the particle’s incoming momentum mi Vi.  Vi itself is controlled by the drag-acceleration that a particle experiences in the supersonic jet, namely  

 mi dVp/dt = Fd = ½ Cd ρg Ap (ug – Vp)²,  

where  
  • ρg is the local gas density,  
  • ug is the gas velocity,  
  • Cd and Ap are the particle’s drag coefficient and cross‐sectional area.  

Both ug and ρg at the nozzle exit depend on the carrier‐gas stagnation pressure P0 and temperature T0 via the isentropic expansion relations:  

 ug ≃ √[2 cp T0 (1 – (pe/P0)(γ–1)/γ)]  
 ρg ≃ pe/(R Te)   with  Te = T0 (pe/P0)(γ–1)/γ  

1. Raising the stagnation pressure P0  
   – Increases the pressure ratio P0/pe through the converging–diverging nozzle, boosting the jet Mach number and thus ug.  
   – Increases the exit‐plane gas density ρg (at fixed T0), which strengthens the drag force Fd and accelerates the particles more rapidly.  

2. Raising the stagnation temperature T0  
   – Increases the total enthalpy cp T0 available for conversion to kinetic energy, which raises the gas exit speed ug ∝ √T0.  
   – Decreases the gas density ρg at fixed P0 (ρ ∝1/T0), so drag per unit Δu is somewhat lower, but in practice the velocity gain usually dominates for particles in the 5–50 μm size range.  

By judiciously balancing P0 and T0 you thus shape both ρg and ug to achieve a target Vi (and hence ΔP) that exceeds the material’s critical velocity for plastic flow and bonding, but does not overshoot so far as to cause substrate erosion or particle fracture.  In practice:  
  • Too little gas pressure or temperature → Vi < Vc → particles bounce or erode the surface → poor deposition.  
  • Too much pressure (very high ρg) at low temperature → particles may not reach their momentum potential before exiting (drag saturates), or agglomerate in the duct.  
  • Too much temperature at low pressure → gas is “thin,” acceleration is slow, and large particles never catch up to the jet velocity.  

Optimal cold‐spray performance is therefore found in the regime where P0 and T0 jointly maximize mi Vi, deliver ΔP above the critical bonding threshold, and produce a high‐density, well‐adhered coating.

In most of our VPSC models of cold‐sprayed deposits the extra “hardness” you see at the inter-splat boundaries is introduced simply by raising the initial CRSS of every slip system by a Hall–Petch term whose characteristic length is the powder (or splat) size.  In other words you start with your bulk (or long-range dislocation) CRSS, τ0,bulk, and then add  
     
   τHP = kHP · dpowder^–1/2  
     
so that for each slip system i your VPSC input uses  
     
   τ0,i = τ0,bulk,i + kHP · dpowder^(–½)  
     
Here  
• τ0,bulk,i is the intrinsic (bulk) CRSS for slip system i  
• kHP is the experimentally fitted Hall–Petch coefficient for inter-splat boundaries  
• dpowder is the nominal particle (or splat) diameter.  
     
If you like to think in terms of polycrystal yield stress, you would write  
     
   σy(d) = σ0 + kHP d^(–½)  
     
and then convert to CRSS by dividing by the appropriate Taylor factor, M.  Either way, the effect is that as you reduce your powder size you automatically make the intersplat CRSS go up in exactly the 1/√d–fashion you observe in hardness measurements.

In one‐dimensional, steady, isentropic flow the exit velocity vₑ of a perfect gas expanding from stagnation (total) conditions (P₀, T₀) down to an ambient or back‐pressure Pₑ is given by:  

 vₑ = √[2·γ/(γ–1) · R·T₀ · (1 – (Pₑ/P₀)^((γ–1)/γ))]  

where  
• γ = ratio of specific heats (cₚ/cᵥ)  
• R = specific gas constant  
• T₀ = stagnation temperature  
• P₀ = stagnation pressure  
• Pₑ = static (ambient) pressure at the exit
