1. Influence of stagnation temperature (T₀)  
 – vₑ scales as √T₀. Raising T₀ (e.g. preheating the carrier gas) directly increases the available enthalpy and thus the maximum achievable exit velocity.  

2. Influence of stagnation pressure (P₀) and ambient pressure (Pₑ)  
 – The term (Pₑ/P₀)^((γ–1)/γ) quantifies how “far” the gas can expand.  
 – A higher P₀ (at fixed Pₑ) drives the pressure ratio P₀/Pₑ up, reducing the bracketed term and boosting vₑ.  
 – Conversely, a higher ambient Pₑ (smaller P₀/Pₑ) leaves less expansion headroom and lowers vₑ.  
 – Once the pressure ratio P₀/Pₑ exceeds the critical choke ratio (P₀/Pₑ > [(γ+1)/2]^(γ/(γ–1))), flow at the throat becomes sonic (M=1) and further increases in P₀ do not raise the throat Mach number (though they can affect the downstream expansion pattern and the overall mass flow rate).  

3. Particle acceleration  
 – In cold spray, particles are entrained in this high‐speed jet and accelerated by drag. A simple first‐order model gives  
  duₚ/dt ≈ (3 Cᴅ ρ_g |u_g–uₚ|)/(4 dₚ ρₚ) · (u_g–uₚ),  
 where uₚ is particle velocity, u_g ≈ vₑ is local gas velocity, dₚ and ρₚ are particle diameter and density, ρ_g the gas density, and Cᴅ the drag coefficient.  
 – The higher vₑ and the lower ρ_g (at a given upstream mass flow) the larger the drag forcing, but heavier/larger particles take longer to accelerate.  

4. Limitations of the 1‐D isentropic model in real cold‐spray nozzles  
 a) Non‐isentropic losses:  
  – Viscous friction and boundary‐layer growth in the nozzle reduce total pressure and alter the effective γ.  
  – Heat transfer to nozzle walls can cool or heat the gas non‐uniformly.  

 b) Two‐phase coupling:  
  – High particle loadings modify the flow (momentum and energy exchange) and generate local shocks or wakes.  

 c) Three‐dimensional and transient effects:  
  – Real nozzles can have complex geometries (curvatures, area‐changes, roughness) and may exhibit flow separation, shock‐cell structures, and unsteady pulsations.  

 d) Gas property variations:  
  – At very high temperature or pressure the perfect‐gas assumption and constant γ start to break down.  

 e) Choked‐flow behavior downstream of the throat:  
  – If the exit section is in a region of over‐expansion or under‐expansion relative to ambient, oblique or normal shocks form and reduce the usable jet velocity.  

In practice, CFD or semi‐empirical correlations that include frictional losses, real‐gas effects, particle–flow coupling, and geometry‐specific shock patterns are used to predict more accurately the gas jet and particle velocities in cold spray systems.

The key point in all flash‐temperature (ΔT) models (Brinkman, Jaeger, Archard, etc.) is that the local temperature rise at an asperity contact is controlled by the rate of frictional heat generation and the ability of the solid to conduct that heat away before it accumulates.  In its simplest sliding‐wear form one often writes for a single circular contact of radius a moving at speed V under local shear stress τ:  

 ΔT_max ≃ (τ·V)·a  / (k·√π·a·√(V/α))  

or, more compactly,  

 ΔT_max ∝  (µ·P·V)  /  [ k·√(a·V/α) ]  

where  
 • µ·P·V  is the frictional power per unit nominal area,  
 • a is the asperity‐contact radius,  
 • k is the thermal conductivity,  
 • α = k/(ρ·c_p) is the thermal diffusivity.  

From this expression you can see two orthogonal “handles” on ΔT_max:  

1) Increasing yield strength (or hardness)  
   –  For a given normal load P, the real contact area Ar scales roughly like P/H.  Thus as H (hardness) goes up, Ar and hence a shrink.  
   –  At the same time the local contact pressure (and hence τ ≃ µ·P/Ar) actually rises or at least stays high until yielding.  
   –  Smaller a and higher local τ both concentrate more frictional heat into a smaller region.  
   ⇒  ΔT_max goes up with increasing H.  

2) Increasing thermal conductivity k  
   –  A larger k directly enters the denominator of the flash‐temperature expression.  
   –  Heat is conducted away faster into the bulk, lowering the temperature gradient at the surface.  
   ⇒  ΔT_max goes down as k increases.  

In plain English:  
– A harder (higher‐yield‐strength) coating forces the same load through smaller, more highly stressed micro‐contacts, boosting the local flash temperature.  
– A more thermally conductive coating shunts frictional heat away more effectively, reducing peak flash temperatures.

You generate the spindle‐rpm and the axial‐traverse as nothing more exotic than the kinematics of a helix on a cylinder.  In practice you do this in three steps:

 1.  Pick your tube OD (D) and the axial “pitch” per revolution (P) that gives you the overlap you want.  
    •  D in mm (or m)  
    •  P in mm /rev (or m /rev) → usually chosen so that P ≤ nozzle jet width for the desired % overlap  

 2.  Compute the length of one turn of the helix (L):  
      L = √[(π·D)² + P²]  [units the same as D and P]  
     L is in mm/rev (or m/rev).  

 3.  From your desired helical spray speed Vₕ (the speed of the nozzle relative to the surface, measured along the helix) you get:  
    •  N (revolutions per minute) = Vₕ / L  
         – If Vₕ is in mm /min and L in mm /rev → N in rev/min  
         – If Vₕ is in m /min and L in m /​rev → N in rev/min  
    •  Axial (nozzle) traverse Va = P × N  
         – Va in mm /min (or m /min)  

Put another way, in symbols (all mm/min):  
   let Vₕ = your target helical speed  
       L = √[(π D)² + P²]  
   then  
     N = Vₕ / L           [rev/min]  
     Va = P · N           [mm/min]  

If you prefer to work in seconds:  
   N [rev/s] = Vₕ [mm/s] / L [mm/rev],  
   rpm = 60·N,  
   Va [mm/s] = P·N.  

Equivalently you can introduce the helix‐angle α where tan α = P/(π D).  Then  
   Vcirc = Vₕ·cos α = π D·N  
   Va    = Vₕ·sin α  

but you end up with exactly the same two results:  
   N = Vₕ cos α/(π D)  
   Va = Vₕ sin α  

All of these formulations are algebraically equivalent.  In practice you:  
  •  Choose P for the overlap you need  
  •  Calculate L  
  •  Divide your target helix speed by L to get the spindle speed  
  •  Multiply that rpm by P to get the nozzle feed rate.

In cold spray you are essentially “shooting” solid powder particles at a substrate so fast that, upon impact, they plastically deform and weld to it rather than rebound.  The key to success is to operate inside the so-called velocity window, which sits between two material‐dependent limits:

  1. Critical adhesion velocity (Vcrit)  
     – the minimum particle speed needed to generate enough plastic deformation on impact for bonding rather than elastic rebound.  
  2. Erosion or damage velocity (Verode)  
     – the speed above which impact energy is so high that it either fractures the particles, pitting or eroding the substrate, or causes substrate spallation.  

Graphically you can think of a band on a velocity axis:
  
     rebound        ←––––– [ Vcrit ]–––––→   adhesion   ←––––– [ Verode ]–––––→   erosion  
  particle speed  

Goal: keep particle speed Vimpact between Vcrit and Verode.

Because Vcrit and Verode depend on:
  •  powder and substrate material (hardness, yield strength, work-hardening behavior)  
  •  powder size and morphology  
  •  substrate temperature and microstructure  

you generally characterize Vcrit and Verode in preliminary trials (often via single‐particle impaction tests or thin‐film build rate vs. jet Mach number).

Once you know your window, you tune your process parameters—most importantly carrier gas temperature and standoff distance—to land your particle velocities squarely in that band.

1. Carrier‐gas temperature  
   – Raising the gas temperature Tgas (for a given pressure) increases the local speed of sound a=√(γ·R·Tgas/M), so for the same nozzle geometry and pressure ratio you get a higher jet Mach number or a higher jet exit velocity.  
   – Higher Tgas also softens particles slightly (reduces yield strength), lowering Vcrit so you can achieve bonding at slightly lower speeds.  
   – Too high Tgas, however, reduces gas density, shortening the jet’s momentum and potentially making it more susceptible to shock‐train instabilities (flapping shocks inside the nozzle) that widen the particle velocity distribution.  

   Tuning rule‐of-thumb:
     •  if Vimpact < Vcrit → raise Tgas by 50–100 °C steps until buildup begins  
     •  if Vimpact approaches or exceeds Verode → back off Tgas or switch to a heavier gas (e.g. Ar→N₂ or He blend)  

2. Standoff distance (SOD)  
   – Shortly after exiting a converging–diverging nozzle, the supersonic jet goes through an expansion region, a potential core, and then shock‐cell structures. The particle speed peaks somewhere in or just beyond the potential core.  
   – If SOD is too short (<10–15 mm), particles haven’t fully accelerated to their peak velocity. Also the jet may impinge too close for full expansion, giving a broad velocity spread.  
   – If SOD is too long (>40–60 mm), aerodynamic drag, shock‐cell mixing, and boundary‐layer growth on the jet axis slow particles down, possibly dropping them below Vcrit.  

   Typical optimum SOD is in the 15–40 mm range (depending on nozzle throat size, powder size, and gas).  

   Tuning rule-of-thumb:
     •  start at SOD≈20 mm  
     •  if deposition efficiency is low but no erosion, reduce SOD in 5 mm steps to raise Vimpact  
     •  if you see substrate damage or powder fracturing, increase SOD to allow some jet decay  

Combined tuning strategy  
  1.  Fix gas pressure at a level giving good jet shape (e.g. 3–5 MPa for many metals).  
  2.  Set an initial Tgas (e.g. 400 °C) and SOD (20 mm).  
  3.  Run a short “shot” and examine the substrate (SEM cross-section, microhardness, surface finish).  
  4.  If no deposit forms, increase Tgas or reduce SOD; if you see substrate pitting or cracked particles, reduce Tgas or increase SOD.  
  5.  Iterate until you find a stable build rate with no signs of rebounding or erosion.  

By balancing carrier‐gas temperature and standoff you essentially “dial in” the average particle impact velocity so it stays between Vcrit and Verode, giving you high deposition efficiency without substrate damage.

In cold spray the “no-inclusion” shot peening window is simply a restatement of the same ballistic-penetration balance that governs particle bonding in the spray gun: you must impart enough momentum to the surface to yield and close porosity, but not so much that your peening media themselves puncture, dig in and become second-phase inclusions.  In practice that means:

1.  Choose a relatively low-density, moderately hard peening media rather than heavy steel balls.  
    – Glass or ceramic beads (alumina, zirconia, soda‐lime glass) at ρ≈2.5–3.5 g/cm³  
    – Hardness only a few hundred MPa above the yield strength of the coating, not GPa‐class carbides, so you won’t gouge or fracture the spray material.  

2.  Keep the diameter below the “ballistic” critical size.  
    – From the simple scaling V^2·ρ·d ≈ constant for penetration, you see that for a given shot velocity V the penetration risk grows linearly with ρ and d.  
    – In practice that puts most effective peening media in the 20–80 μm range.  Below ~20 μm they lose peening efficiency, above ~80 μm you risk embedding.  

3.  Insist on a smooth, spherical morphology.  
    – Sharp or angular edges concentrate stress, locally exceed yield and bite into the surface.  
    – Spheres spread the load, give uniform compressive residual stress and roll across asperities rather than dig in.  

4.  Adjust your peening intensity (shot velocity and flow) so that the average kinetic‐energy‐per‐area (½·ρ·d·V²) lies above the coating yield criterion for pore collapse, but below the threshold for metallic‐particle penetration.  

By staying in that narrow 20–80 μm, ρ≈2.5–3.5 g/cm³, moderate‐hardness, spherical bead regime you get maximum work hardening/densification of the cold-sprayed layer with essentially zero shot-inclusion.

In Cold Spray Additive Manufacturing (CSAM) the particles are accelerated by a supersonic jet issuing from a de Laval nozzle.  Although in practice there are losses (friction, heat transfer, shock waves, particle loading) the core of the acceleration mechanism can be understood with the inviscid, isentropic flow relations for a converging–diverging nozzle:  

1.   Isentropic exit velocity  
     For a perfect gas with stagnation (total) pressure p₀ and temperature T₀ expanding to ambient pressure pₑ through a nozzle whose exit‐to‐throat area ratio is Aₑ/A* the exit Mach number Mₑ satisfies  
       Aₑ/A* = (1/Mₑ)·[(2/(γ+1))·(1 + (γ–1)/2·Mₑ²)]^((γ+1)/(2(γ–1)))  
     and the corresponding exit velocity is  
       Vₑ = √[2·cₚ·T₀·(1 – (pₑ/p₀)^((γ–1)/γ))]  
     where γ is the gas heat‐capacity ratio and cₚ the specific heat at constant pressure.  

2.   Role of nozzle geometry  
   •  Area ratio Aₑ/A*:  A larger diverging‐section area ratio drives a higher Mₑ (up to the limit set by p₀/pₑ) and thus a higher ideal exit speed.  If Aₑ/A* is too large relative to p₀/pₑ, the jet never reaches design Mach, or it overexpands and incurs shocks that diminish Vₑ.  
   •  Throat size A*:  The throat area fixes the mass flow ṁ = ρ₀·A*·M*·a* (with M* =1 at choking).  A smaller throat chokes at lower total mass flow, which can reduce jet density (and so drag force on the particles) even though the ideal Vₑ from the isentropic relations is unchanged.  
   •  Divergence angle and length:  Steeper angles or too‐short nozzles promote boundary‐layer separation and shock formation in the diverging section, both of which reduce the realized jet velocity and uniformity.  

3.   Role of carrier‐gas properties  
   •  Molecular weight and gas constant R:  Vₑ scales as √(R·T₀).  Lighter gases (e.g. helium, hydrogen) have a larger specific gas constant R = Rₘₒₗ/M_w and so higher sound‐speed a = √(γ·R·T) and higher achievable jet velocity at given T₀.  
   •  Heat‐capacity ratio γ:  A larger γ increases the thermodynamic “work” extractable in the expansion (through the factor 2·cₚ·T₀ = 2·γ/(γ–1)·R·T₀) and sharpens the dependence of Mach on area ratio (makes the nozzle more “efficient” at converting enthalpy into kinetic energy).  
   •  Stagnation pressure p₀ and temperature T₀:  Higher p₀/pₑ gives a higher pressure‐ratio term (1 – (pₑ/p₀)^((γ–1)/γ)) so more enthalpy converts to velocity.  Higher T₀ directly raises the available enthalpy.  

4.   Particle acceleration  
   The particles do not instantaneously reach Vₑ.  They accelerate under the drag force F_D ≈ ½·C_D·ρ·A_p·(V_g–V_p)² over a characteristic “momentum‐coupling” or stopping distance.  Thus:  
   –  High‐velocity, low‐density (light) gases yield the largest V_g and thus the greatest driving force on small to moderately sized particles.  
   –  Too much particle loading, or too large particles, reduces the jet Mach number via two‐phase losses and prevents full conversion of enthalpy to kinetic energy.  

Summary  
––––  
•  Nozzle geometry (exit‐to‐throat ratio, throat area, divergence angle and length) fixes the ideal Mach number and mass flow.  
•  Carrier gas properties (molecular weight, γ, stagnation pressure and temperature) set the maximum attainable jet velocity via the isentropic expansion law.  
•  The actual particle velocity is then governed by the drag‐mediated coupling to that jet, so higher ideal Vₑ, higher ρ·Vₑ, and better nozzle flow quality all lead to higher particle speeds in CSAM.

The key point is that in the simple estimate 

  Vcr/C₀ ≃ (2/k)·(P­s/B)

all parameters except the strength P­s or the stiffness B remain fixed.  Therefore:

1. Doubling the spall strength P­s → P­s′=2·P­s  
   – The ratio P­s/B doubles  
   – ⇒ Vcr/C₀ doubles  
   – ⇒ Vcr roughly doubles (you’d need about twice the particle velocity to achieve bonding)

2. Increasing the bulk modulus B by 50% → B′=1.5·B  
   – The ratio P­s/B falls to 1/1.5≃0.67 of its original value  
   – ⇒ Vcr/C₀ falls to ≃0.67 of its original value  
   – ⇒ Vcr drops by ≃33% (you’d need only two-thirds the original velocity)

In other words, strengthening the material raises the critical bonding velocity linearly, whereas stiffening it (higher B) lowers the required velocity by the inverse of that stiffness increase.

In cold spray, whether a powder particle “sticks” or bounces is governed primarily by its impact velocity relative to a material‐specific critical velocity Vc. Two key concepts capture this behavior across different alloys or composites:

 1.  Normalized Velocity Ratio η  
    •  Definition: η = Vp/Vc, where Vp is the particle’s impact velocity (often taken as the velocity at the nozzle exit or at stand‐off) and Vc is the minimum velocity needed to plastically deform and bond that material.  
    •  Thresholds:  
       –  η < 1: almost no deposition (all particles rebound)  
       –  η ≃ 1…1.1: onset of “incipient” deposition; bonds are weak and build‐up is uneven  
       –  η ≃ 1.1…1.3: stable, high‐quality buildup; deposition efficiency peaks  
       –  η > 1.4…1.6: risk of substrate/powder erosion, overspray, poor part quality  
    •  Material Differences: harder or higher‐yield materials (e.g. Ni-based superalloys, ceramics) have higher Vc, so for a given spray gas condition, η is lower and DE will be poorer versus a ductile metal with low Vc (e.g. Cu, Al).

 2.  Particle Velocity Distribution  
    •  In reality, not all particles travel at exactly Vp; you have a statistical distribution f(V). Its shape and width depend on particle size, shape, gas conditions, and nozzle design.  
    •  Deposition Efficiency DE is essentially the fraction of that distribution above Vc:  
       DE ≃ ∫[Vc to ∞] f(V) dV  
    •  Broader distributions allow some high‐velocity “tail” particles to deposit even if mean η < 1, but you also get more low‐velocity particles that never stick. Narrow (tight) distributions give more predictable, reproducible DE once their mean exceeds Vc.

Putting it together for two materials A and B sprayed under the same conditions:  
  • A has Vc,A = 400 m/s, B has Vc,B = 600 m/s.  
  • If your gas/particle setup yields a mean exit velocity of 550 m/s with ±50 m/s spread, then ηA ≈ 550/400 = 1.38 (high‐efficiency regime) but ηB ≈ 550/600 = 0.92 (no net buildup).  
  • The DE ratio roughly equals [area of f(V) above 400 m/s] divided by [area above 600 m/s], showing A might achieve ~80–90 % DE while B sits near zero.  

In practice you plot DE vs. η for each material and see S-shaped (sigmoidal) curves that collapse many data sets. The steeper the rise at η=1 and the higher the plateau before erosion sets in, the more “spray-friendly” the material. Adjusting gas pressure, temperature, nozzle geometry or powder size shifts the velocity distribution (and thus the effective η) to optimize DE for each alloy or composite.

In cold spray the single most important driver of deposition efficiency (i.e. the fraction of particles that exceed their critical‐impact velocity and actually bond) is the particle exit (or “impact”) velocity.  That velocity in turn is set by the drag acceleration the carrier gas can impart over the nozzle length.  Both the stagnation pressure (P₀) and stagnation temperature (T₀) at the nozzle inlet control the gas‐dynamic state in the converging–diverging jet and therefore control that drag acceleration.  

1. Nozzle inlet pressure P₀  
  • Higher P₀ ⇒ larger mass‐flow rate through the throat ⇒ higher static gas density ρ_g at any point in the nozzle.  
  • At fixed nozzle geometry the Mach number distribution M(x) is set by the pressure ratio P₀/P_∞, so boosting P₀ increases M at the exit slightly, but more importantly raises ρ_g almost in direct proportion.  
  • Drag on a particle of diameter d is  
     F_d ≃ ½ C_D ρ_g A (V_g–V_p)²   with A∝d²,  
    so larger ρ_g (and slightly larger V_g) directly increases the drag force, shortens the aerodynamic “time constant” τ≈(4 d ρ_p)/(3 C_D ρ_g V_g), and lets the particle reach a higher fraction of V_g over a given nozzle length.  
  ⇒ Higher inlet pressure → higher final particle velocity → more particles above the critical velocity → higher deposition efficiency.  

2. Nozzle inlet temperature T₀  
  • Raising T₀ at fixed P₀ raises the stagnation enthalpy and thus the local speed of sound a=√(γ R T).  For a given M(x) this pushes up the local gas velocity V_g=M a∝√T.  
  • However, at the same time the static gas density at a given pressure drops as ρ_g∝1/T.  
  • Because the dynamic pressure that drives drag is q=½ ρ_g V_g²∼½ γ M² P₀ (independent of T₀), the gross drag force changes little with T₀ if the nozzle were infinitely long.  In practice, two secondary effects appear:  
     – Short‐nozzle or limited‐residence‐time regimes benefit from the higher V_g (since particles see a larger V_g–V_p over the available length) and so can reach higher V_p with higher T₀.  
     – Gas viscosity μ rises with T, which lowers the particle Reynolds number and can slightly reduce C_D and thus F_d.  
  ⇒ Overall the deposition efficiency is much more sensitive to P₀, but at fixed P₀ one often finds a mild increase in particle velocity (and deposition efficiency) with T₀ in short or moderate‐length nozzles, up to the point where reduced density and drag begin to dominate.  

In summary:  
– Increasing inlet pressure directly increases gas density and mass flow, boosting drag acceleration and particle velocity—and so deposition efficiency—in a nearly monotonic fashion.  
– Increasing inlet temperature raises the gas velocity potential but lowers density; the net effect on drag is small in a long nozzle (dynamic pressure ∼P₀), yet in practical (finite‐length) systems higher T₀ can give particles that extra burst of velocity early on and thus modestly improve efficiency—until the density drop and viscosity effects begin to counteract it.

In cold spray you accelerate particles by entraining them in a high‐speed jet.  Two simple 1–D models explain why raising the *stagnation* (total) temperature of your drive gas always increases the *exit* jet velocity, and through it the particles’ speed.

1.  One‐dimensional isentropic nozzle flow  
   – For an ideal gas with ratio of specific heats k and gas constant R, the local velocity u at any point in the nozzle is given by energy conservation from stagnation conditions (p₀,T₀) down to static conditions (p,T):  
     u² = 2·cₚ·T₀·[1 – (p/p₀)^((k–1)/k)]  
     where cₚ = kR/(k–1).  
   – In particular the *exit* Mach number Mₑ is set by the pressure ratio p₀/pₑ and the area ratio of the nozzle, so  
     uₑ = Mₑ·√(kR Tₑ)  and  Tₑ = T₀/[1 + (k–1)/2·Mₑ²].  
   – Both forms show that for fixed p₀/pₑ (and hence fixed Mₑ), uₑ ∝ √T₀.  Doubling T₀ raises uₑ by √2, etc.

2.  Drag‐force acceleration of a particle  
   – A particle of diameter dₚ, density ρₚ in a gas of local density ρ_g experiences a drag force  
     F_D = ½·C_D·A·ρ_g·(u_g – vₚ)²  
     where A = πdₚ²/4.  
   – Its equation of motion along the jet axis is  
     mₚ·dvₚ/dt = F_D  ⇒  dvₚ/dt ∝ ρ_g·(u_g – vₚ)².  
   – Since u_g at the exit has grown like √T₀, the *driving term* (u_g – vₚ)² grows roughly ∝T₀.  Particles therefore accelerate faster and reach a higher asymptotic speed within the same nozzle length.

Putting it all together: by raising the stagnation temperature you increase the total enthalpy available for conversion into kinetic energy in the nozzle.  This boosts the exhaust gas speed in direct proportion to √T₀, and because the drag force scales with the *square* of the gas–particle velocity differential, the particles pick up significantly more speed as well.

In most of the semi‐empirical and phenomenological models for cold spray bonding the critical velocity comes out as a weak power‐law of the particle density, strength and melting‐point and an inverse power‐law of the “undercooling” (T m–T 0).  A compact way to see the trends is to write, for example, the common fourth‐root form (Fenner/Guile/Trudeau etc.)  

   v c  ≃  K [ σ u 2  /  { ρ C p ( T m – T 0 )} ] ^1/4  

where σ u is the ultimate (or yield) strength, ρ the density, C p the specific heat (assumed constant here), T m the melting temperature and T 0 the initial particle temperature.  From that form you immediately read off:  

 1. Density ρ ↑  ⇒  v c ↑   
    (heavier particles need more KE to generate the same jetting pressure)  

 2. Melting point T m ↑  ⇒  v c ↑  
    (more thermal energy is needed to reach the softening/jetting regime)  

 3. Strength σ u ↑  ⇒  v c ↑  
    (stronger materials require more mechanical work to deform/jet)  

 4. Initial temperature T 0 ↑  ⇒  v c ↓  
    (pre‐heated particles start closer to T m, so require less kinetic‐to‐thermal conversion)  

If you ignore C p or absorb it into the constant K, the pure dependences become  
   v c  ∝  ρ^¼ · σ u ½  · (T m)^¼  · (T m–T 0)^–¼  

so in all cases density, melting temperature and strength drive v c upward, while raising the particle’s initial temperature drives it downward.

First, let’s recall the three numbers and how they relate in a simple Maxwell‐type viscoelastic picture of a metallic glass just above its glass transition:

  • Reynolds number  
    Re   = ρ U D/η  
      – measures the ratio of inertial to viscous stresses  
      – U = impact velocity, D = particle diameter, η = shear viscosity at the shear rate of impact  
  • Weissenberg number  
    Wi   = λ γ̇ ≃ λ (U/D)  
      – ratio of elastic (memory) to viscous effects  
      – λ = characteristic relaxation time of the glass, γ̇ ≃ U/D  
  • Elasticity number  
    El   = Wi/Re = (λ η)/(ρ D²)  
      – ratio of elastic to inertial forces, independent of U for a linear Maxwell fluid  

Qualitative chain of effects as Re is raised (i.e. as U goes up):

1.  Higher impact velocity ⇒ higher shear rate γ̇ ≃ U/D.  
2.  Metallic glasses near T g are strongly shear‐thinning: both η(γ̇) and λ(γ̇) decrease with increasing γ̇.  
3.  Even though in a linear Maxwell fluid El is formally U-independent, in our real shear-thinning glass  
       η↓(γ̇),  λ↓(γ̇) ⇒  El = λ η/(ρ D²)  falls off as shear rate (and thus Re) rises.  
4.  A smaller El means inertia (and viscous dissipation) overwhelms elastic memory: the glass layer on the particle and substrate cannot store much elastic energy to drive a rebound.  
5.  Instead, most of the kinetic energy is funneled into viscous/plastic flow right at the interface, promoting intimate contact and mechanical interlocking.  

Bottom line: by increasing Re (raising U), you push the local shear rate up, shear-thin the glass (η and λ drop), drive the elasticity number El down, and so suppress elastic rebound in favor of dissipative deformation that “wets” and bonds the particle to the substrate.

In cold spray, it is the normal (i.e. perpendicular) component of a particle’s impact velocity that produces the high‐pressure, high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation needed to weld metal particles together.  If you tilt the nozzle off of normal you can resolve the particle velocity vector V into two pieces:  
• Vn = V·cos θ (normal to the surface)  
• Vt = V·sin θ (tangential or shear)  

Where θ is the angle between the spray axis and the surface normal.

1. Reduced normal momentum and impact pressure  
   – The kinetic energy driving deformation is ½ m Vn² = ½ m (V cos θ)².  
   – As θ increases, Vn falls off with cos θ, so peak pressures at the particle–substrate (and particle–particle) contacts drop below the critical value needed to initiate the adiabatic shear instabilities that produce metallurgical bonding.  

2. Increased tangential sliding and rebound  
   – The Vt component rises with sin θ, so particles hit the surface with more lateral velocity.  
   – Instead of “stamping” in place and flowing plastically, they tend to skid, plough out previously deposited material, or outright rebound.  

3. Net effect on porosity  
   – Lower normal deformation → fewer metallurgical bonds → more unbonded interfaces.  
   – More shear/rebound → gaps and voids left behind at the deposit surface.  

Thus, as you tilt away from normal, the loss of effective perpendicular impact energy and the rise in sliding/rebound combine to reduce interparticle bonding and compaction, and the deposit’s porosity goes up.

Carrier‐gas choice and spray parameters control the kinetic and thermal state of powder particles at impact, and hence the coating’s microstructure, residual stress state, porosity and hardness—all of which set its resistance to cavitation erosion.  Below is how the key gas‐property and process‐setting levers map through impact mechanics to cavitation performance:

1. Carrier‐Gas Physical Properties  
  • Speed of sound (a) and molecular weight (M)  
    – He: a ≈ 1000 m/s, low M → highest achievable peak particle velocities (>1000 m/s).  
    – N₂: a ≈ 350 m/s, intermediate performance.  
    – Ar: a ≈ 320 m/s but heavy → higher momentum at a given velocity but lower max velocity.  
  • Heat capacity ratio (γ), thermal conductivity, viscosity  
    – Gases with higher γ (He>Ar≳N₂) yield higher jet Mach numbers and more adiabatic cooling—so particle heating/time‐at‐temperature can be tuned.  

2. Main Process Parameters  
  a. Supply pressure (Psup)  
    –↑ Psup raises stagnation enthalpy → higher jet velocity and particle kinetic energy per impact.  
  b. Gas preheat temperature (Tg)  
    –↑ Tg lowers powder yield strength at in‐flight, promotes particle deformation/bonding.  
    –Too hot → agglomeration, nozzle fouling or partial melting can reintroduce porosity/oxides.  
  c. Nozzle geometry & expansion ratio  
    –Controls the shock‐cell structure and length of the high‐velocity core.  
    –Optimized for each gas to maximize particle acceleration zone.  
  d. Stand‐off distance  
    –Too short → unsteady flow & poor spreading; too long → particle deceleration, cooling → lower impact efficacy.  

3. Particle Impact Mechanics → Coating Microstructure  
  • Critical particle velocity (Vc) must be exceeded for each alloy powder to achieve  
    – Severe plastic deformation (adiabatic shear instabilities, dynamic recrystallization)  
    – Oxide‐film fracture and oxide‐free metallic bonding  
  • Impact energy (½mv²) and work‐hardening determine local grain refinement and residual compressive stress  
  • Temperature rise at the interface drives dynamic recovery or grain‐boundary healing  

4. Microstructure & Properties Governing Cavitation‐Erosion Resistance  
  a. Porosity and interparticle cohesion  
    – Dense, well‐bonded coatings deflect or blunt cavitation jets; porosity concentrates stress and initiates cracks.  
  b. Hardness vs toughness balance  
    – High hardness (from grain refinement, work‐hardening) resists repeated jet impingement.  
    – Adequate toughness prevents brittle spallation under cyclic loading.  
  c. Residual compressive stress  
    – Suppresses crack opening and growth during bubble‐collapse impacts.  
  d. Grain structure and phase distribution  
    – Ultrafine, equiaxed grains and a homogeneous phase distribution deflect or arrest propagating microcracks.  

5. Putting It All Together  
  – Helium at high preheat and pressure → highest particle velocities → maximum adiabatic shear, lowest porosity, highest hardness and compressive stress → best cavitation‐erosion resistance (but highest gas cost).  
  – Nitrogen offers a cost/benefit compromise: moderate velocities, good deformability, slightly higher porosity than He but much lower gas cost.  
  – Argon can yield greater momentum transfer to heavy particles but lower max velocity and more limited grain refinement. It is sometimes chosen for very ductile powders or when minimal powder heating is required.  
  – Fine‐tuning nozzle geometry, stand‐off, and powder feed rate for the chosen gas maximizes particle impact efficiency and hence yields coatings with the dense, work‐hardened, compressively stressed microstructure needed to resist cavitation erosion.

Pure‐ductile metals in cold spray reach a “ceiling” in build rate at high gas temperatures because once you exceed the critical velocity (Vc) and sufficiently soften the powder to plastically bond, additional kinetic energy (from still hotter gas) either

  •  Gives diminishing gains in particle velocity (nozzle flow and gas‐viscosity effects limit acceleration beyond a certain Tgas),  
  •  Drives more particle rebound or mild substrate erosion (you’re well above Vc, so excess energy doesn’t improve adhesion),  
  •  Can even promote oxide breakup and surface re-oxidation or local adiabatic shear instabilities that don’t translate into greater net deposit.

In practical terms, DE (deposition efficiency) for a ductile metal asymptotes once you’ve just passed the plastic‐bonding threshold. The system ceases to lay down any extra material even if you heat the gas further.

By contrast, metal–ceramic blends keep “growing” in thickness because the hard ceramic fraction fundamentally alters the deposition mechanics:

  1. Mechanical-interlock sharpening  
     Ceramic particles (or fragments) act like micro-abrasives on the substrate and on preceding layers, ramping up surface roughness and producing new undercuts into which the metal can flow and lock.

  2. Progressive strain hardening and dislocation trapping  
     The ceramic phase impedes dislocation motion in the metal binder, so each subsequent spray pass still finds “work to do,” and additional kinetic energy (from hotter gas) goes into fresh plastic deformation and bonding rather than mere rebound.

  3. Elevated effective critical velocity  
     A metal–ceramic composite particle must reach a higher Vc for the ceramic to adhere, so raising Tgas and thus particle velocity continues to translate into steadily improving DE.

  4. Synergistic binder reinforcement  
     Even if some metal alone would have saturated, it still flows around and encapsulates ceramics. Those ceramics, in turn, lock the binder into a growing porous–dense architecture that never quite hits a hard “plateau.”

As a result, while pure metals top out once you’ve passed their simple plastic‐bonding regime, metal–ceramic mixes keep converting added gas‐temperature (and velocity) into fresh anchoring, so coating thickness rises continuously.

Below is the sequence of “cause → effect” steps in the Alkhimov isentropic‐nozzle model showing how your two operating knobs, stagnation pressure P₀ and preheat (total) temperature T₀, end up controlling the powder velocity vₚ:

1.  Stagnation conditions  
    – P₀ and T₀ set the total (stagnation) enthalpy h₀ and density ρ₀ = P₀/(R T₀).  
    – T₀ also fixes the stagnation speed of sound a₀ = √(k R T₀).  

2.  Mass flux through the throat  
    – The ideal (choked) mass flow ṁ/A* = ρ₀ a₀.  
    – Raising P₀ at fixed T₀ increases ρ₀ and so ṁ; raising T₀ at fixed P₀ decreases ρ₀ but raises a₀, so has a more modest net effect on ṁ.  

3.  Isentropic expansion in the diverging section  
    – From the known pressure ratio P₀/P(x) one obtains the local Mach number M(x) = f[P₀/P(x), k].  
    – Local static temperature T(x) = T₀/[1 + (k–1)/2 M²], and density ρ(x) = P(x)/(R T(x)).  
    – The local gas velocity Vg(x) = M(x)·a(x) with a(x)=√(k R T(x)).  

4.  Free‐jet (post–nozzle) region and possible shock  
    – Downstream of the exit plane the jet rapidly expands (or may form a normal/barrel shock).  
    – Still use local isentropic or shock‐corrected relations to get P, T, ρ, Vg in the supersonic plume.  

5.  Particle drag‐force acceleration  
    – A single spherical particle of diameter dₚ, density ρₚ feels  
       Fd = ½ C_d(Re,Ma) ρ(x) Aₚ [ Vg(x)–vₚ(x) ]², with Aₚ=π dₚ²/4.  
    – Hence the axial acceleration  
       dvₚ/dx = Fd/(mₚ) = (3 C_d ρ(x) [ Vg–vₚ ]²)/(4 ρₚ dₚ).  

6.  Integration → final particle speed  
    – Integrate dvₚ/dx from the throat exit to the stand‐off distance past the shock (or until drag and vₚ≈Vg equilibrate).  
    – Since P₀ and T₀ set ρ(x), Vg(x), T(x) profiles, they directly control the drag history and thus the final vₚ.  

In plain terms:  
– Raising P₀ boosts mass flow and static gas density, increasing drag force on each particle.  
– Raising T₀ raises the available enthalpy and speed‐of‐sound, tending to push Vg higher for the same pressure ratio (though it slightly lowers ρ₀).  
Together they produce a faster, denser supersonic jet and hence a larger drag impulse on the powder, delivering higher particle exit velocities.

Because in a cold‐spray system the drag force per particle goes roughly as Fdrag∼A⋅Δv^2 (A∝d^2) while the particle’s mass m∝d^3, the acceleration a=F/m ends up scaling about a∝1/d.  In practice that means very small particles reach very high speeds (good for exceeding the material’s critical deposition velocity) but they carry little momentum (and oxidize or scatter more easily), whereas very large particles carry plenty of momentum but simply never accelerate enough to stick.   To hit the “sweet‐spot” you therefore choose a powder fraction just small enough to exceed the critical velocity for that metal, yet large enough to carry sufficient momentum and to maintain a useful mass‐flow rate.  

1.  Determine the material’s critical velocity Vc (for Cu in N2 it’s roughly 500–650 m/s; for Ti more like 700–900 m/s).  
2.  Use either published nozzle flow/drag models or empirical calibration curves to find the maximum particle diameter dmax that will accelerate to Vc in your chosen gas, pressure and temperature.  
3.  Specify a powder size distribution that sits below that diameter but is not so fine that yields collapse:  

   •  Copper (N2, 3–4 MPa, ~900 K):  
      – d10≈5 μm, d50≈15–25 μm, d90≈30 μm  
   •  Titanium (He, 3–5 MPa, ~1000 K):  
      – d10≈10 μm, d50≈25–40 μm, d90≈45–50 μm  

In most industrial cold‐spray trials you’ll see commercial Cu powders in the 10–30 μm range and Ti powders in the 20–50 μm range.  That sizing gives you a high fraction of particles that can exceed the critical velocity (because a∝1/d) without losing so much feed‐rate or mechanical integrity that efficiency collapses.

Increasing the propellant‐gas temperature in a cold-spray system raises deposition efficiency by two linked mechanisms: (1) boosting particle velocity so more particles exceed the critical velocity for bonding, and (2) softening both particle and substrate so the critical velocity itself is lowered.  Mechanistically:

1.  Gas expansion and particle acceleration  
    •  Stagnation (total) temperature T₀↑ → local speed of sound c = √(γR T) ↑  
    •  For a given nozzle pressure ratio, nozzle exit Mach number M and exit velocity v₉ ≃ M·c both increase roughly with √T₀  
    •  Although higher T reduces gas density (ρ₉ ∼ p₉/R T₉), the v₉² term in the drag force F_D ≃ ¼ C_D ρ₉ (v₉–v_p)² d_p² dominates, so particles accelerate more strongly and reach a higher terminal velocity v_p at the substrate  

2.  Impact temperature rise and yield‐strength reduction  
    •  Particles entrained in hotter gas enter the nozzle at a higher starting temperature T_p0  
    •  Upon impact, plastic work converts a fraction of ½ m_p v_p² into heat, raising the local contact temperature T_imp even further.  Because plastic work ∼∫σ_y dε, warmer particles/substrate require less stress before yielding  
    •  Yield strength σ_y(T) falls with temperature (typical metals lose 20–50 % of σ_y between room temperature and a few hundred °C)  

3.  Critical velocity reduction  
    •  The classical estimate for the critical velocity V_c for bonding scales like  
        V_c ∝ √[σ_y(T)/ρ_p]  
    •  As σ_y(T_imp) drops when T_imp is elevated, V_c decreases.  Meanwhile actual v_p has gone up because of the higher gas exit speed.  

Net effect: more particles arrive at the surface with v_p > V_c, deform plastically on impact, and cold–weld to the substrate.  Raising the propellant‐gas temperature therefore widens the “deposition window” (v_p – V_c), giving higher overall deposition efficiency.

In virtually all of the semi‐empirical cold‐spray models the critical velocity, Vc, enters in essentially the form

  Vc ≃ [ 2·σy(Timpact) / ρ ]½

or more generally as an inverse‐square‐root dependence on whatever resistance to deformation (σy, flow stress, hardening term, etc.) the particle still exhibits when it strikes the substrate.  Since σy (T) falls off with temperature, the net result is that raising the particle’s impact temperature lowers the critical velocity.  

Put another way:

  ∂Vc/∂Timpact = ½ [2/ρ·σy]–½ · (dσy/dTimpact)  < 0

because dσy/dTimpact < 0.  In practice this means:

• The hotter the particle at impact, the softer it is,  
• the less kinetic‐energy per unit mass it needs to exceed the yield threshold,  
• and the lower Vc becomes.  

As a rough rule of thumb for common metals (Al, Cu, Ni alloys) you will typically see a 5–15 % drop in Vc for every 100 °C increase in particle (or substrate) temperature prior to impact.

Annealing at T ≥ 0.5 Tm is in effect a solid‐state sintering step: at these homologous temperatures the self‐diffusion coefficients in most metals rise by orders of magnitude, grain‐boundary and bulk diffusion become rapid enough that atoms can migrate across the cold‐spray particle–particle contacts on laboratory timescales.  In practice this does four things simultaneously:

1. Vacancy‐ and grain‐boundary diffusion heal microvoids at the interfaces, growing “necks” between particles and closing porosity.  
2. High dislocation densities introduced during deposition provide fast “pipe” diffusion pathways that further accelerate mass transport across contact patches.  
3. Recrystallization and recovery remove the extreme work hardening imparted by the supersonic impact, lowering residual stresses and allowing more intimate surface contact.  
4. Grain‐boundary migration and subgrain coarsening reduce the high‐energy boundaries left over from the plastic fragmentation of the feedstock, stabilizing the new, bonded microstructure.

Below ~0.5 Tm the diffusion rates are simply too low to accomplish significant neck growth, pore elimination and stress relief in reasonable annealing times, so the interparticle bonding remains weak. By going above that threshold you essentially trigger the same diffusion‐driven densification and bonding mechanisms exploited in conventional powder‐metallurgy sintering, but without ever reaching the melting point.

In cold spray the ultimate microstructure (and hence strength) is governed by the particle–substrate impact velocity, which in turn is set by the carrier‐gas velocity and by the drag‐law acceleration of the powder.  Two key relationships are:

 1. Isentropic nozzle flow (ideal gas approximation)  
    vg = √[2·k/(k–1) · Rspec · T0 · (1 – (pe/p0)^((k–1)/k))]  

    •  k  = Cp/Cv of the gas (≈1.4 for diatomics)  
    •  Rspec = Runiv/M  (specific gas constant; M = molecular weight)  
    •  T0,p0 = stagnation temperature and pressure upstream of the throat  
    •  pe     = exit pressure  

    ⇒  Because Rspec ∝1/M, a lighter gas (smaller M) directly raises vg.

 2. Particle acceleration by drag  
    mp·dv p/dt  = ½·Cd·A·ρg·(vg – vp)^2  

    •  mp, vp = particle mass and velocity  
    •  Cd, A   = drag coefficient and cross‐sectional area  
    •  ρg      = local gas density  
    •  vg      = local gas velocity  

    Over the nozzle length L one obtains an exit particle velocity  
      vp(exit) ≃ vg·[1 – exp(–β·L)]  
    with β ∝ (Cd·ρg·A)/(mp)  

Since vg is higher with lower‐M gas, vp(end) rises as well.  Higher vp at impact means:

  •  Greater plastic strain and strain‐rate in the substrate and in the particle  
  •  Adiabatic shear‐induced dynamic recrystallization, producing ultrafine and equiaxed grains  
  •  Smaller final grain size d

By the Hall–Petch relation  
   σy  = σ0  + kHP/√d  
smaller d ⇒ higher σy.  In practice He (M = 4 g/mol) or H2 (M = 2 g/mol) streams give vg ~ 2–3× that of N2 (M = 28 g/mol), driving vp > 1 km/s and producing submicron grains and dramatically increased yield strength in the deposit.

Key Points

1. Isentropic‐nozzle exit velocity  
   For a calorically perfect gas flowing from stagnation conditions (P0, T0) to an exit/back pressure Pe, the exit velocity u_e is given by  
     u_e = √[2·c_p·T0·(1 – (Pe/P0)^((γ–1)/γ))]  
   or, using c_p = γ·R/(γ–1),  
     u_e = √[ (2·γ)/(γ–1) · R · T0 · (1 – (Pe/P0)^((γ–1)/γ)) ].  

   • T0­–dependence: u_e ∝ √T0.  Raising the gas temperature directly increases the available enthalpy that can be converted into kinetic energy.  
   • Molecular properties:  
     – R = R_u/M: lighter gases (smaller molecular weight M) have larger R, so u_e ∝ √R.  
     – γ = c_p/c_v: monatomic gases (γ≈1.66) convert stagnation enthalpy to kinetic energy slightly differently from diatomics (γ≈1.4); the factor γ/(γ–1) enters the velocity expression.  

   In practice the R‐effect dominates: at the same T0 and pressure ratio, helium (M=4 g/mol, R≈2.08 kJ/kg·K) can produce 2–3× higher u_e than argon (M=40 g/mol, R≈0.208 kJ/kg·K), even though argon’s γ is somewhat lower.

2. Effect on particle acceleration in cold spray  
   Particles are accelerated by the drag force in the supersonic jet.  A one‐dimensional drag law gives  
     m_p·dv_p/dt = ½·C_d·A_p·ρ_g·(u_g – v_p)^2,  
   or along the nozzle axis x  
     dv_p/dx = [3·ρ_g·C_d/(4·ρ_p·d_p)]·(u_g – v_p)·|u_g – v_p|.  

   • Higher u_g → larger (u_g – v_p)^2 → stronger drag.  
   • ρ_g at the exit scales as P_e/(R·T_e), so lighter gases have lower density but much higher u_e.  
   • Net momentum flux ∼ρ_g·u_g^2 is the figure of merit for particle acceleration.  Helium jets have lower ρ_g but much higher u_g, so they often yield higher particle exit speeds than argon or nitrogen.  

3. Practical consequence  
   – Raising T0 (e.g. hotter preheat) boosts u_e and gas momentum, accelerating particles more strongly and shortening the required nozzle length to reach critical bonding velocity.  
   – Switching to a lower–M gas (He > N2 > Ar in that order) raises u_e (and momentum flux) for the same P0, also increasing particle throughput and achievable particle velocity.  

Summary  
Gas exit velocity in an isentropic model scales as √(R T0) modified by the factor γ/(γ–1) and the pressure‐ratio term.  Higher T0 and lower molecular weight give higher u_e; in turn, higher u_e (and resulting gas momentum flux ρ_g u_e^2) strengthens drag on micron‐scale powders, raises their acceleration, and helps achieve the critical impact speeds required for successful cold‐spray deposition.

In hexagonal‐close‐packed (HCP) Mg alloys the typical sequence under sliding abrasive wear can be summarized in four overlapping stages:

1. Two-body micro-ploughing and cutting  
   – At the onset, hard asperities or abrasive particles indent into the relatively soft Mg matrix (low hardness, limited slip systems).  
   – Plastic flow is highly anisotropic: shear localizes on basal and prismatic planes, producing shallow grooves and wedge-shaped chips.  

2. Debris formation and third-body transition  
   – Detached chips, intermetallic particles (e.g. Mg17Al12 in AZ-series alloys) and nascent MgO quickly accumulate in the contact zone.  
   – These fragments become secondary abrasives, transforming the contact into a three-body abrasion regime.  

3. Subsurface deformation, crack initiation and delamination  
   – Repeated cutting and pressure cycles induce subsurface shear bands and tensile cracks along basal planes and slip‐band interfaces.  
   – Cracks coalesce and lead to spallation of flakes or lamellae (delamination wear), which in turn feed the debris population.  

4. Steady‐state wear with oxide/debris layer  
   – Frictional heating accelerates oxidation; a mixed Mg/MgO debris mat can form a pseudo‐protective film.  
   – Its toughness and thickness control whether it reduces metal-on-metal cutting or simply serves as a reservoir of hard oxide fragments that perpetuate abrasion.  

Key points  
 • Limited ductility of the HCP lattice focuses deformation at the surface and just beneath it, making micro-cutting and shallow delamination especially aggressive.  
 • Hard second phases or oxides exacerbate three-body wear once they are liberated.  
 • A quasi‐steady state often establishes in which an oxide/debris layer partly shields the metal but also continuously supplies fresh abrasives.

In particulate‐reinforced metal‐matrix composites (MMCs), the ceramic particles themselves and their bond to the metal matrix both evolve systematically as you change particle size.  Two key size‐dependent mechanisms are:

 1.  Ceramic‐particle “intrinsic” strength  
    •  Griffith‐type flaw scaling: real ceramics contain microcracks, porosity or other flaws whose critical half‐crack length c controls failure strength by  
         σf ≃ √(2E·γ/πc).  
       If particles are ground or milled down to diameter D, the largest flaw size c cannot exceed D.  In practice one finds roughly  
         σf ∝ 1/√D.  
       Thus smaller particles (submicron to a few microns) are intrinsically stronger—flaw sizes are limited by the particle dimension itself.  
    •  Weibull scaling: the probability of finding a critical defect decreases with volume.  Thus for a Weibull modulus m, the characteristic strength σc∝D^(–3/m).  Again smaller D raises σc.  

 2.  Particle–matrix interfacial behavior  
    A.  Interface area per unit volume  
       •  Specific surface area scales as 1/D.  Halving D doubles the total interface area at a given volume fraction.  
       •  More area ➔ more sites for chemical bonding (wetting, intermetallic formation, metallurgical reaction layers) and mechanical load transfer.  
    B.  Reaction‐layer thickness effects  
       •  Most wetting or reaction layers (e.g. Al4C3 on SiC/Al systems, spinel on Al₂O₃/Al) grow to a roughly size‐independent thickness t.  
       •  If D≫t, the reaction zone is a thin “glue,” often beneficial.  If D approaches t, the reaction zone may consume a large fraction of each particle and embrittle it or lead to early decohesion.  
    C.  Thermal‐mismatch stresses  
       •  The local thermal stress σ_Δα≃E_m·|α_m–α_p|·ΔT/(1–ν) is set by the mismatch in expansion coefficients and temperature change ΔT, not by D.  
       •  But crack‐nucleation from these stresses still obeys Griffith scaling: smaller D means shorter surface cracks and higher stress required to propagate them across the particle–matrix interface.  
    D.  Mechanical‐anchorage and stress transfer  
       •  For rough or faceted particles, mechanical interlocking scales with facet size—smaller particles can present more facets per unit volume and thus higher net shear‐transfer capacity—up to the limit where reaction layers or oxide coatings smooth them out.  

Putting it all together:  
–   As you decrease D from tens of microns into the submicron range, the particles themselves become stronger against crack‐driven failure, and you gain interface area that boosts load transfer—so the composite’s yield and ultimate strengths rise.  
–   If D becomes too small (often below 0.1–1 µm, depending on the system), undesirable effects set in: particle agglomeration, thick reaction layers relative to D, and excessive matrix hardening around each particle that can embrittle the composite and impair ductility.  
–   Conversely, when D exceeds a few tens of microns the intrinsic particle strength drops (larger flaws), interface area shrinks (weaker load transfer), and stress‐concentrating particles can crack the matrix or pull out prematurely.  

In practice most particulate MMCs target a “sweet‐spot” in the 1–10 µm range (or sometimes 10–30 µm for lower‐temperature applications) where particles are small enough to be strong and well bonded yet large enough to avoid overgrowth of brittle interface layers or processing issues such as powder handling, agglomeration and viscosity rises in semi‐solid processing.

Cold spray is classified as a solid-state deposition process because the powder particles never melt. Instead they are entrained in a high-pressure carrier gas (typically nitrogen or helium), accelerated to supersonic/hypersonic velocities, and plastically deform upon impact with the substrate.  Bonding occurs by severe localized plastic flow and intimate metal-to-metal contact rather than by fusion and solidification.

Key advantages for metal powders:

 1. No melting, so very little oxidation or gas entrapment  
    • Oxide films remain thin and are broken up mechanically, allowing fresh metal-metal contact.  
    • No vaporization of low–boiling-point alloying elements.  

 2. Minimal thermal input  
    • Virtually no heat-affected zone—no grain coarsening, phase transformations, or residual‐stress–driven cracking.  
    • Substrate distortion and shrinkage are negligible.  

 3. Retention of feedstock microstructure and properties  
    • As-atomized powders (even nanostructured or oxide-dispersion-strengthened) deposit with their fine grains and second phases intact.  
    • Hard or refractory alloys that crack if melted can be built up reliably.  

 4. High deposition rate and build-up efficiency  
    • Thick, dense deposits (typically >98 % theoretical density) with low porosity.  
    • Layer‐by‐layer building with minimal post-heat treatment.  

 5. Dissimilar metal joining  
    • Because there is no intermetallic melt, you can build bimetallic structures with sharp compositional transitions and little brittle intermetallic formation.

Together, these attributes make cold spray uniquely capable of producing high-integrity, high‐performance metal builds and coatings in the solid state.

Key distinctions between cold‐gas‐dynamic spraying (“cold spray”) and conventional thermal spraying center on the particle’s state at impact and how the coating builds up:

1. Particle state at impact  
   • Cold spray  
     – Particles remain solid (gas temperatures typically <800 °C, well below the alloy’s melting point).  
     – Very high particle velocities (500–1 200 m/s) impart kinetic energy without melting.  
   • Thermal spray (e.g. plasma, HVOF, wire arc)  
     – Particles are molten or semi-molten (gas/plasma temperatures exceed the feedstock’s melting point).  
     – Moderate velocities (50–800 m/s) carry hot droplets to the substrate.

2. Bonding and coating formation  
   • Cold spray  
     – Upon impact, particles undergo extreme plastic deformation and adiabatic shear.  
     – Bonding is primarily solid‐state mechanical interlocking and metallurgical adhesion via dynamic recrystallization at interfaces.  
     – Results in near‐fully dense, low-oxide coatings with minimal thermal damage.  
   • Thermal spray  
     – Molten droplets flatten into “splats” on impact and quickly solidify.  
     – Coating builds up as a stack of lamellae.  
     – Typically higher oxide content and porosity; some residual stresses and heat-affected zones are common.

3. Consequences for microstructure and performance  
   • Cold spray yields fine, work-hardened grains at interfaces, very low oxidation, and high bond strengths—ideal for ductile metals (Al, Cu, Ni, some soft alloys).  
   • Thermal spray can process ceramics and hard alloys but produces more oxide interlamellar films, higher porosity, and coarser, heat-affected microstructures.

In short, cold gas dynamic spraying is a solid-state, high-velocity process that relies on plastic deformation to bond powders, whereas thermal spraying melts the powder and deposits it as a lamellar, splat‐based coating.

Cold‐gas spraying (CGS) is a solid‐state deposition process, so the metal or alloy particles never melt. That is the key reason CGS preserves the as‐manufactured (or “feedstock”) crystalline phases, whereas high‐temperature thermal sprays (plasma, HVOF, flame spray, etc.) rely on partial or full melting and rapid resolidification, which invariably alters phase chemistry, grain size, oxide content, and residual stress.  In more detail:  
1. Sub‐melting‐point gas temperatures  
   • Typical gas preheat in CGS (300–1 000 °C) is deliberately kept below the melting point of the powder.  
   • Particles retain their original microstructure and phase constitution.  
2. Extremely short thermal exposure  
   • Powder acceleration and impact take place in milliseconds; any particle heating is almost entirely adiabatic and dissipates on impact.  
   • No-time (or very limited time) for diffusion‐driven solid‐state transformations or grain growth.  
3. Solid‐state bonding by plastic deformation  
   • Upon hypervelocity impact (300–1 200 m/s), particles undergo severe plastic flow and interfacial jetting, creating fresh metal–metal contact.  
   • No liquid phase means no solidification microstructures (e.g. dendrites), no resolidification stresses, and minimal oxide entrapment.  
4. Minimal oxidation and contamination  
   • Lower gas and particle temperatures translate to much lower overall oxidation kinetics than in plasma or flame sprays.  
   • Original alloy chemistry and oxide dispersoids (if present) remain essentially unchanged.  
5. Retained mechanical and functional properties  
   • Because grain size, precipitates, intermetallics, and phase distributions are preserved, coatings often show higher ductility, toughness, and fatigue performance than their thermally sprayed counterparts.  

In contrast, high‐temperature thermal sprays melt or semi‐melt the feedstock. Melt‐pool chemistry, rapid solidification rates, thermal gradients, and ensuing quench all drive phase transformations, precipitate dissolution or re-formation, oxidation, and grain coarsening. Cold gas spray sidesteps these by never crossing the melting line.

Key to the very low friction of cold‐sprayed amorphous‐metal coatings under sliding is the formation, in situ, of a thin, strongly adherent oxide tribofilm whose structure and chemistry combine to give “self‐lubrication.”  Two broad classes of features are critical—(1) how the film is built and bonded to the substrate, and (2) why it shears so easily:

1. Formation and adhesion of the oxide film  
  • Tribo-oxidation of the amorphous alloy: mechanical mixing, local flash heating and high free‐volume in the glassy feedstock drive rapid diffusion of O₂ and selective oxidation of B, Si, Cr, Fe, etc.  
  • Nanocomposite/glassy structure: the film is typically a mixed network of amorphous oxide (e.g. B₂O₃-rich or silicate glassy phase) plus nano-crystalline Fe/Cr oxides (Fe₃O₄, Fe₂O₃, Cr₂O₃) with grain sizes <10 nm.  
  • Strong anchoring: under the repeated hammering of the cold spray process the substrate retains residual compressive stress and high free‐volume; nascent oxide grows into the plastically deformed interfacial region so the film “locks” mechanically and chemically onto the glassy alloy.  

2. Low‐shear, self-lubricating behavior  
  • Weak ionic/liquidlike bonds: the glassy borate or silicate network has no long‐range order and a high concentration of network‐modifying cations and oxygen vacancies; it yields by viscous flow or intergranular sliding at very low shear stresses.  
  • Nanograin‐boundary sliding: the crystalline oxide particles are embedded in an amorphous matrix so that under shear the dominant deformation mode is grain‐boundary or amorphous‐phase sliding rather than dislocation glide.  
  • In situ renewal and transfer-film formation: as wear proceeds portions of the oxide film are continually stirred out, fill surface asperities and redeposit on the counterface; this regenerating transfer film maintains a low‐shear, lubricious interface.  
  • Reduced metal-metal contact: the tribofilm smooths the mating surfaces and sustains a continuous load‐bearing film, preventing direct adhesion of the harder substrate and dramatically lowering friction and wear rates.  

In sum, the self-lubricating oxide is a thin, tightly bonded, nanocomposite/glassy layer whose amorphous network and grain-boundary structure shear at very low stresses and which is continually refreshed under sliding, giving highly stable, low‐friction performance.

Primary advantages of solid-state supersonic (cold spray) deposition versus fusion-based thermal spray are:

1. No melting of feedstock  
   – Particles remain in the solid state, so you avoid melting-related oxidation, decomposition or phase transformations (e.g. carbide dissolution, oxide spinels).  
   – Retains original powder microstructure and chemistry.

2. Low thermal input to the part  
   – Substrate heating is minimal (typically <100 °C rise), so there’s negligible thermal distortion, low residual stresses, and no heat-affected zone.  
   – Enables coating of heat-sensitive substrates (polymers, composites, thin sheets).

3. High material utilization and deposition efficiency  
   – Typical powder utilization >80–90 % (versus 50–70 % in many HVOF/plasma processes).  
   – Low overspray and minimal “blow-back” waste.

4. Dense, oxide-free microstructure  
   – Coatings exhibit very low porosity (<1 %), negligible interparticle oxides, and strong particle–particle bonding via severe plastic deformation.  
   – Yields high cohesive strength and good fatigue/erosion resistance.

5. Enhanced mechanical properties  
   – Work hardening of ductile metals in situ produces fine grain/subgrain structures, boosting hardness and wear resistance without brittle phases.  
   – Tensile and fatigue properties closer to bulk material than in fusion‐sprayed coatings.

6. Versatility for temperature-sensitive or novel materials  
   – Can deposit oxygen‐sensitive alloys (e.g. Ti, Al, Zr), composites (metal-polymer), or nanostructured powders that would degrade in a thermal spray plume.

Key points  
1. Solid‐solution strengthening  
   – In martensite, carbon sits in octahedral interstices and distorts the b.c.t. lattice.  The lattice distortion raises the yield strength and hardness by impeding dislocation motion.  
   – Empirically, quenched martensite hardness (in HV) rises roughly linearly with wt.% C up to about 0.6–0.7 %:  
     • ~350 HV at 0.2 %C  
     • ~550 HV at 0.4 %C  
     • ~700–800 HV at 0.6–0.7 %C  

2. Tetragonality and retained austenite  
   – Higher C lowers Ms/Mf temperatures.  Below ~0.4 %C nearly all austenite transforms to hard martensite; above ~0.6 %C a significant fraction may remain as retained austenite, which can slightly reduce “as‐quenched” hardness unless subsequently tempered.  
   – The carbon‐induced increase in c/a ratio of martensite (tetragonality) levels off above ~0.7 %C, so further C adds diminishing hardness returns and more retained austenite.

3. Carbide precipitation and tempering response  
   – In powder form, very high C (≥0.8–1.0 %) can promote MC‐type (V, Mo) carbides during atomization or heat treatment, leading to local brittle phases and microcracking.  
   – Optimal powder blends for cold spray or sintering typically use 0.3–0.6 % C to balance high martensitic hardness and good powder ductility/sinterability.

4. Practical guidelines for powders  
   – 0.2–0.4 % C martensitic powders: 300–550 HV; easy deformation on impact, lower residual stress.  
   – 0.4–0.6 % C: 550–750 HV; peak strength/hardness, moderate fracture toughness.  
   – >0.6 % C: up to ∼800 HV as‐quenched, but more retained austenite, lower impact deformability, risk of cracking.

Bottom line  
Increasing carbon content in martensitic steel powders raises as‐quenched hardness by solid‐solution strengthening and increased lattice tetragonality, up to about 0.6–0.7 wt.% C. Beyond that, retained austenite and carbide precipitation reduce net hardness gains and may compromise ductility and powder integrity.

When you disperse graphene or graphene oxide (GO) flakes into a polymer‐based corrosion coating, their main “magic” is simply physical: they are essentially impermeable, atomically thin sheets of carbon that force any corrosive species (H₂O, O₂, Cl–, etc.) trying to reach the metal to weave a much longer, zig-zag (tortuous) route through the coating.  Key points:  
1. Impermeability of the sp² network  
   • Perfect graphene is almost totally impermeable to gases and liquids.  
   • Even GO, despite its oxygenated defects, presents a far lower permeability than most polymers.  
2. High aspect‐ratio platelets  
   • Nanometer‐thin but microns wide platelets overlap in the matrix.  
   • They seal off straight‐through diffusion channels.  
3. Tortuosity effect  
   • By increasing the effective path length that water/oxygen/ions must travel, they slow down the ingress rate by orders of magnitude.  
The net result is a dramatic drop in permeability of corrosive agents, postponing the onset of substrate corrosion.

Under Archard’s law the wear volume V is given by  

   V = K·L·s / H  

where  
• K is the dimensionless wear coefficient,  
• L is the normal load,  
• s is the sliding distance, and  
• H is the hardness of the softer material.  

Thus V is inversely proportional to H.  In practical terms, if you double the hardness of the softer partner (all else equal), you roughly halve the wear volume; if the material is softer (lower H), its wear volume rises proportionally.

Key distinctions of cold spray versus conventional thermal-spray methods (flame, HVOF, plasma, wire-arc) stem from its bonding mechanism and thermal input:

1. Bonding by Plastic Deformation  
   • Particles remain solid (below their melting point) and impact the substrate at 300–1 200 m/s.  
   • High-strain–rate deformation creates mechanical interlocking and adiabatic shear instabilities that form a metallurgical bond.  

2. Low Process Temperature  
   • Gas (typically N₂ or He at 20–50 bar) is heated only enough to reduce its density and viscosity—particle temperatures stay well below melting.  
   • Substrate sees minimal heating, preserving its microstructure and preventing heat-affected zones.  

3. Reduced Oxidation and Phase Changes  
   • Absence of a molten state minimizes in-flight or splat oxidation, decomposition, and undesirable phase transformations.  
   • Coatings retain the feedstock’s original microstructure and chemistry.  

4. High Coating Density and Low Porosity  
   • Supersonic impact expels entrapped gas and closes voids, yielding typically > 98 % theoretical density.  
   • Resulting residual stresses are often compressive, enhancing fatigue and corrosion resistance.  

5. Materials and Applications  
   • Enables spraying of temperature-sensitive alloys, nanostructured powders, composites (e.g. metal–ceramic), and even polymers—materials that would degrade or vaporize in high-heat systems.  

In contrast, other thermal-spray processes melt or partially melt the feedstock—bonding by splat solidification—which inherently introduces higher thermal loads, oxide formation, phase changes, and typically higher porosity.

Carbon nanotubes (CNTs) enhance the hardness of ceramic nanocomposites by introducing several simultaneous reinforcement and microstructural‐control mechanisms:

1. Load transfer to high‐strength reinforcements  
   • CNTs have tensile strengths >50 GPa and Young’s moduli ∼1 TPa.  
   • When well bonded to the ceramic matrix (e.g. by carbide‐forming interlayers or functionalization), applied loads are shared with the CNT network rather than borne solely by the brittle ceramic.

2. Grain‐boundary pinning and Hall–Petch refinement  
   • Dispersed CNTs at grain boundaries inhibit grain growth during sintering.  
   • Finer ceramic grains raise hardness via the Hall–Petch relation (H ∝ G^–1/2), because smaller grains block dislocation motion more effectively.

3. Crack‐bridging and pull-out toughening  
   • Upon indentation or crack initiation, CNTs spanning crack faces carry load, blunt crack tips, and increase the energy required for crack propagation.  
   • CNT pull-out (or fracture) during crack advance contributes additional resistance, effectively raising the composite’s indentation hardness.

4. Crack deflection and branching  
   • High‐aspect‐ratio CNTs force propagating cracks to kink or branch, further dissipating energy and reducing the stress intensity at crack tips.

Key factors for maximizing hardness gains:  
– Uniform dispersion of individual or small CNT bundles (avoiding agglomerates)  
– Strong but not overly rigid CNT–matrix interfaces (to allow pull-out)  
– Control over processing routes (spark plasma sintering, hot pressing) to preserve CNT integrity and distribute them at critical grain boundaries.

In the purely elastic part of a spherical‐indenter indentation experiment the load–displacement curve is governed by Hertz’s solution:

  F = 4  3 E* R_eff^1/2 δ^3/2   

where  
 • F is the applied load,  
 • δ is the indentation depth,  
 • E* is the reduced modulus of indenter–specimen pair,  
 • R_eff is the effective radius seen in contact.  

If you indent a rigid sphere of radius R_i into a nanoparticle of radius R_p the two‐sphere Hertz formula gives  

  1 / R_eff = 1 / R_i + 1 / R_p.  

Key consequences of changing the indenter radius R_i are:

1. Elastic stiffness (dF/dδ) ∝ E* R_eff^1/2 δ^1/2.  
   – A larger indenter radius → larger R_eff → steeper initial slope in F–δ.

2. Contact area radius a ∝ (R_eff δ)^1/2.  
   – For a given δ the contact area grows with R_eff, so the mean contact pressure p_mean = F/(π a^2) ∝ δ^1/2 / R_eff^1/2 is smaller when R_i is larger.

3. Onset of yield.  
   – Plasticity begins when the peak Hertzian pressure p_max ≃1.5 p_mean reaches the yield strength σ_y of the metal.  Since p_max ∝ δ^1/2 / R_eff^1/2, a larger R_i requires a larger δ (and a larger F) to reach σ_y.  Equivalently, the “elastic regime” (the Hertzian F∝δ^3/2 region) extends to higher loads and depths when the indenter radius is larger.

Putting it all together:

– Small‐radius indenters concentrate stress into a small contact; you get a relatively shallow elastic regime, a low initial stiffness, and you hit yield at a low load and depth.  
– Large‐radius indenters spread out the load, raise the initial stiffness, lower the contact pressure for a given δ, and therefore delay the transition to plasticity, lengthening the Hertzian (purely elastic) portion of the F–δ curve.

In cold spray the particles never melt; instead bonding is achieved by converting their kinetic energy into extreme, highly‐localized plastic deformation at the particle/substrate (or particle/particle) interface.  The key mechanisms are:

1. Severe Plastic Deformation  
   • At velocities typically 300–1200 m/s a solid particle impacts the substrate and is almost instantly decelerated over a microscopic contact zone.  
   • Strain rates of 10^6–10^9 s⁻¹ produce very high dislocation densities, grain subdivision, and local work-hardening.  

2. Adiabatic Shear Instability & Jetting  
   • The intense, localized shear heats a narrow band so rapidly that heat cannot dissipate (adiabatic heating), softening the metal in that band.  
   • A thin “jet” of oxide, contaminants and surface asperities is expelled from the interface, exposing fresh metal surfaces.  

3. Dynamic Recrystallization & Grain Refinement  
   • The combination of high strain and temperature promotes dynamic recovery and recrystallization in the shear zone, forming ultrafine equiaxed grains.  
   • These new grains have high boundary energy and short diffusion paths, which accelerates atomic bonding.  

4. Mechanical Interlocking  
   • Beyond the metallurgical bonds, the heavily deformed shapes of neighboring particles interlock physically, giving the coating immediate cohesion even before full metallurgical bonding matures.  

Together these effects—oxide-free metallic contact, ultrafine‐grained interfacial layers, and mechanical interlocking—produce a solid‐state bond almost as strong as the parent metal, all without ever reaching the melting point.

In most solid-state AM processes (cold spray, friction-based deposition, ultrasonic consolidation, etc.), the material in the deposit experiences extremely high strains at elevated but sub-melting temperatures.  That combination of severe plastic deformation and adiabatic heating drives dynamic recrystallization (DRX) in the deposited zones, which in turn produces a very fine, equiaxed grain structure.  The consequences for microstructure and properties are:

1. Grain‐refinement via DRX  
   • Discontinuous DRX (d-DRX) or continuous DRX (c-DRX) at splat or stir‐zone interfaces breaks up the initial cold-worked or parent grains into submicron‐ to low‐micron‐size equiaxed grains.  
   • High dislocation densities and stored energy in the plastically deformed regions provide the driving force for nucleation of new, strain‐free grains.  

2. Microstructural homogeneity  
   • Fine grains are distributed uniformly through the build (e.g. within the “nugget” in friction-stir AM or the bonded particle regions in cold spray).  
   • Elongated or columnar grains common to fusion processes are largely eliminated, reducing texture and anisotropy.  
   • Pores and interparticle voids are more effectively closed, since recrystallized material can “flow” into defects during deformation.  

3. Mechanical property effects  
   • Strength/hardness up → by Hall–Petch strengthening (σy≈σ0+k·d–½).  Typical grain sizes drop from tens of microns to 1–5 μm in friction-stir AM or even <1 μm in cold spray, producing 20–50 % higher yield strength and 30–60 % higher hardness versus non-refined material.  
   • Ductility/toughness maintained or improved relative to a coarse‐grained state, because equiaxed DRX grains blunt crack initiation sites and accommodate plasticity more uniformly.  
   • Fatigue and wear resistance improve as fine, homogeneous grains reduce crack nucleation sites and hardening is uniform throughout the deposit.  

4. Process‐ parameter sensitivity  
   • Too little strain/heat → incomplete DRX, leaving high dislocation density, anisotropy, and residual stresses.  
   • Too much heat (or slow cooling) → secondary grain growth, loss of the beneficial ultrafine structure, and drop in strength.  

In sum, solid-state AM leverages in-process DRX to convert highly deformed feedstock into a fine, equiaxed microstructure that combines high strength (via grain-boundary strengthening) with good ductility and fatigue performance—advantages rarely obtainable in fusion-based builds without extensive post-processing.

Key XRD indicators of residual stress and microstrain in cold‐sprayed coatings are (1) shifts in peak positions (macro‐ or “residual” stress) and (2) broadening (microstrain and grain‐size effects), often accompanied by asymmetry or shoulders on individual reflections.  

1. Peak‐position shifts (residual stress)  
   • Tensile residual stresses stretch lattice planes, increasing d‐spacing, so peaks move to lower 2θ.  
   • Compressive stresses shorten d‐spacing, shifting peaks to higher 2θ.  
   • The shift Δ2θ can be related to an average stress via the sin²ψ method or single‐exposure geometry:  
     σ = (E / (1 + ν))·(Δd/d)/sin²ψ (approximately),  
     where Δd/d ≈ −Δ2θ·cotθ/2.  

2. Peak‐width broadening (microstrain and small domains)  
   • Increased full‐width at half‐maximum (FWHM) indicates a distribution of d‐spacings (microstrain ε) and/or reduced coherent domain size D.  
   • In a Williamson–Hall plot (β·cosθ vs. 4 sinθ), the slope gives the microstrain ε, and the intercept gives the size contribution (β in radians).  
   • Pure microstrain broadening scales as βstrain ≈ 4ε·tanθ; size broadening scales as βsize ≈ λ/(D·cosθ).  

3. Peak asymmetry or shoulders  
   • Severe plastic deformation in cold spray can produce subgrain structures or overlapping zones of different local stress (e.g. particle–substrate interface vs. coating interior), giving rise to shoulders or asymmetric tails on peaks.  
   • A high density of dislocations and planar defects can yield a “Lorentzian” component in the peak shape.  

Causes in cold spray  
   • Intense, high‐strain‐rate impact of particles → large plastic deformation, high dislocation densities, subgrains, and grain refinement to ultrafine or nanocrystalline scales.  
   • Rapid solid‐state deposition traps non‐equilibrium stresses—compressive in the near‐surface of particles, tensile between layers or at boundaries.  
   • Texture development and anisotropic strain fields from repeated impacts yield crystallographic orientation‐dependent d‐spacing variations.  

In practice, therefore, observing systematic peak shifts versus ψ‐angle and quantifying FWHM increases versus θ (or through Williamson–Hall or modified Warren–Averbach analyses) provides a direct measure of the residual stress state and internal microstrain in cold‐sprayed coatings.

Powder sphericity in PREP (Plasma‐Rotating‐Electrode Process) is controlled by a race between (a) capillary‐driven shape relaxation of a liquid metal droplet, (b) droplet cooling/solidification and (c) aerodynamic and inertial disturbances (including collisions and satellite coalescence).  As the droplet size increases each of these factors works against forming a perfect sphere:

 1.  Capillary relaxation time grows as r 1.5 (tcap ∼√(ρ r^3/σ)), whereas the convective solidification time only grows roughly linearly with r (tsol ∼ρ cp r/h).  Above a critical diameter tcap exceeds tsol, so large droplets begin to freeze before they can fully round‐out under surface tension.

 2.  Larger droplets carry more inertia (higher Weber number) in the high‐speed rotation spray and are more prone to shape‐distorting aerodynamic shear and deformation.

 3.  The in-flight collision probability (and satellite‐droplet attachment) rises with droplet size and concentration, producing rough surfaces and “lumps” that further degrade sphericity.

In contrast, small droplets (tens of microns and below) solidify so fast relative to their very short capillary relaxation time that they “snap” into nearly perfect spheres before freezing.  Once you exceed that size window, you see a gradual drop in powder sphericity.

In essentially every cold‐spray system studied to date the deformation is far from uniform – the vast majority of the plastic strain is confined to the immediate particle–particle (or particle–substrate) interfaces, while particle interiors remain comparatively lightly deformed.  A few representative numbers (all in true‐strain) are:  

 • Interface region (first few microns from the contact face)  →  ε_p ≈ 2 … 10 (i.e. 200 % … 1 000 %)  
 • Mid‐thickness of a flattened particle                       →  ε_p ≈ 0.5 … 3 ( 50 % … 300 %)  
 • Particle core                                           →  ε_p ≈ 0.05 … 0.3 ( 5 % … 30 %)  

Put another way, the interfacial zones routinely carry an order of magnitude (or more) higher plastic strain than the particle interiors.  This localization is what drives the high dislocation densities, dynamic recrystallization and nanostructuring observed at the bonded interfaces, while the grain structure in the particle cores remains largely un‐refined.

Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) is a dynamic plastic‐flow phenomenon that occurs when a metal is deformed so rapidly that the rate of heat generation by plastic work greatly exceeds the rate of heat conduction away from the deforming zone.  In practice this means:  
  • under very high strain rates (typically >10³–10⁴ s⁻¹),  
  • work‐hardening is outpaced by thermal softening,  
  • local temperature rises nearly “adiabatically” (i.e. without heat loss),  
  • strain localizes into narrow shear bands, often only a few micrometers wide.

In a cold‐spray impact event each powder particle strikes the substrate (or underlying layer) at several hundred m/s.
