The contact pressure can exceed the material’s yield strength by an order of magnitude, producing strain rates high enough to trigger ASI in a ring‐shaped zone around the particle’s edge.  That shear‐banding accomplishes several critical things for bonding:  
  1. Extreme local softening lets the particle “flow” onto the surface rather than rebound.  
  2. Plastic‐work heating and shear eject a peripheral micro–jet that scrapes off oxides and surface contaminants.  
  3. Fresh, metal‐to‐metal contact under high pressure and temperature gradients promotes intimate atomic contact or localized dynamic recrystallization at the interface.  

In short, adiabatic shear instability in cold spray:  
  • cleans the interface by jetting away surface films,  
  • generates the localized thermal and mechanical conditions needed for metallurgical bonding,  
  • and defines the critical impact velocity below which particles merely embed mechanically but do not form a strong bond.

Both finer crystallites and higher dislocation densities toughen (i.e. harden) a metal by the same basic mechanism—both impede further dislocation motion—so in cold‐sprayed coatings you almost always see higher hardness as grain size goes down and ρ disloc goes up.  In fact you can think of the hardness (or yield strength via Tabor’s relation) as the sum of a Hall–Petch term plus a dislocation‐strengthening term:

   H ≃ H₀  +  kHP·d^(–½)  +  α·G·b·√ρ

where  
 • H₀ is the “base” hardness of a very large‐grained, low‐strain‐material  
 • kHP is the Hall–Petch coefficient (typically 0.1–0.2 MPa·m^½ for steels, smaller for softer metals),  
 • d is the (crystallite) grain size,  
 • α is a constant on the order of 0.2–0.5,  
 • G is the shear modulus,  
 • b is the Burgers vector, and  
 • ρ is the dislocation density.

Key take-aways:  
 • Halving the grain size raises the Hall–Petch term by about √2, i.e. ≃ 40 % harder contribution from that term.  
 • Doubling the dislocation density raises the Taylor term by √2 as well.  

Overall therefore, as you refine the microstructure down to the submicron or nanocrystalline regime and trap ever more dislocations in the sprayed metal, you systematically increase its hardness by tens or even hundreds of MPa.

Cold‐sprayed deposits almost always show a porosity gradient, with the highest void fraction at the unconfined (free) surface, because of the way particles hammer and “peen” the growing layer.  The key reasons are:

1. Hammering/Peening Effect  
   – Every new particle impact delivers a high‐strain, high‐pressure spike that plastically deforms and densifies the previously laid material.  
   – The first few layers (right on the substrate) are “hammered” by every subsequent particle and see the highest cumulative compressive (hydrostatic) stresses, which close up inter‐particle voids.  
   – The very top layer, by contrast, sees only one generation of impacts (itself), so there is little post‐deposition plastic flow to collapse its pores.

2. Boundary‐Condition Effects  
   – Near the rigid substrate the stress waves reflect and superimpose, boosting local compressive pressure.  
   – At the free surface there is no reflecting boundary, so peak compressive stresses are lower and any tensile components can even re‐open small voids.

3. Impact Kinematics and Aerodynamics  
   – As the spray builds up, particles must traverse an increasingly thick jet of carrier gas and previously deposited material; they lose some velocity and kinetic energy before reaching the top surface.  
   – Lower impact velocities mean less local plastic deformation and worse inter‐particle bonding at the very top.

4. Gas Entrapment  
   – High‐speed entrainment of carrier gas into surface asperities is less easily expelled at an open boundary, leaving behind micro‐voids.

In practice all of these combine to give a densest, lowest‐porosity region adjacent to the substrate and a looser, higher‐porosity “skin” at the free surface.

Key distinctions between cold spray and conventional thermal spray lie in how the feedstock particles are heated (or not) and how they bond to the substrate:

1. Particle Heating  
   – Conventional thermal spray (plasma, HVOF, flame, detonation) heats particles above—or very near—their melting point. Particles are molten or semi-molten on impact.  
   – Cold spray heats only the carrier gas (typically to a few hundred °C), keeping particles strictly in the solid state (well below melting).

2. Deposition Mechanism and Adhesion  
   – Thermal spray: Molten or semi-molten particles (“splats”) impact, spread, cool and solidify. Bonding is by rapid solidification, mechanical interlocking, some interdiffusion, and sometimes the formation of oxide films between splats.  
   – Cold spray: Solid particles are accelerated to high velocity (300–1 200 m/s). On impact they undergo extreme plastic deformation, adiabatic shear instabilities and localized metal jetting that expel surface oxides, exposing fresh metal. Bonding arises from intimate metal-to-metal contact and high-strain–rate plastic flow, producing a predominantly oxide-free, wrought‐like microstructure.

3. Consequences  
   – Cold‐sprayed coatings feature low oxidation, minimal heat‐affected zones, high density and high cohesion/tensile strength.  
   – Thermally sprayed coatings can be more readily melted and alloyed in flight, but often contain splat boundaries, oxide inclusions, and higher residual stresses from rapid solidification.

Surface oxides on feedstock particles are almost always detrimental to cold‐spray bonding because they sit between two deforming metal surfaces and must be disrupted before true metal–metal contact can occur.  Key effects are:

1. Barrier to plastic flow and interfacial shear  
   • Oxide films (Al2O3, TiO2, native iron oxides, etc.) are much harder and more brittle than the underlying metal.  Under impact they tend to crack or spall, but until they do they prevent the clean, high‐strain‐rate jetting and adiabatic‐shear instabilities that create fresh metal surfaces and forge a weld.  
   • A thicker or more coherent oxide layer raises the critical velocity needed for rupture and bonding; below that velocity particles simply rebound or form mechanically mixed, poorly bonded “oxide sandwiches.”

2. Reduced interdiffusion and weld formation  
   • Even after oxide fracture, residual oxide fragments can become entrapped at the splat interfaces and inhibit atomic diffusion across the boundary.  
   • The result is lower interfacial strength, higher porosity, and a deposit with reduced cohesive strength and potentially lower fatigue life.

3. Increased porosity and defects  
   • Fractured oxide platelets often remain as interlamellar inclusions, acting as stress concentrators.  
   • Local oxide debris also prevents full particle deformation and intimate contact, increasing void content.

4. Higher powder velocities or pre‐treatments required  
   • To overcome an intact oxide barrier one must raise gas temperatures and pressures (to boost particle velocity) or reduce the oxide thickness beforehand (e.g. H₂ reduction annealing, chemical etching, or mechanical polishing).  
   • In practice most successful cold‐spray processes for easily oxidized metals include an oxide‐removal or oxide‐reduction step on the powder.

Summary  
Unbroken oxide layers act as a hard, brittle interlayer that must be cracked and cleared before metallic jetting and true metallurgical bonding can occur.  They therefore increase the required impact energy (critical velocity), degrade deposit density and interfacial strength, and lead to higher porosity and weaker cold‐spray deposits unless mitigated by powder pretreatment or more aggressive spray parameters.

Key factors that make metallic‐glass (MG) particles attractive as reinforcements in composite coatings (including cold‐sprayed or thermal‐sprayed systems) are:  

1. Amorphous (grain‐boundary‐free) structure  
  • No crystalline defects ⇒ very high yield strength (1–3 GPa) and hardness (800–2 000 HV)  
  • Extremely uniform chemistry ⇒ outstanding corrosion and oxidation resistance  

2. High elastic strain limit (~2 %)  
  • Can elastically accommodate more load before plastic flow, raising composite stiffness and toughness  

3. Tunable glass‐transition (Tg) and crystallization (Tx) temperatures  
  • Process windows exist wherein particles remain glassy during deposition (preserving hardness)  
  • In situ partial devitrification at impact/anneal can form nano‐crystals, improving interparticle bonding  

4. Unique deformation mechanisms  
  • Shear‐banding in the MG phase absorbs impact energy, promotes interparticle welds in cold spray  
  • Nano‐scale shear bands or nano‐crystals at interfaces enhance load transfer into the hard phase  

5. Powder morphology and flowability  
  • Spherical, mono-modal MG powders can be produced by gas‐atomization  
  • Narrow size distribution ensures uniform dispersion and consistent coating microstructure  

6. Thermal and residual‐stress advantages  
  • Low coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) helps manage thermal mismatch with metal matrices  
  • Amorphous particles introduce beneficial compressive/toughening residual stresses around impact zones  

By combining these attributes, MG reinforcements deliver coatings with markedly higher hardness, wear resistance, fatigue life, and corrosion protection than coatings reinforced with crystalline hard phases alone.

Cold spray is fundamentally a solid‐state, high-velocity impact process. Because particles never melt—only deform plastically on impact—there is negligible thermal input to drive melting, evaporation, or solid-state phase transformations. Key points:  
1. No melting means no liquid-phase solidification or associated segregation.  
2. Thermal exposure is low (particle temperatures typically remain well below their melting point), so diffusion-driven composition changes and oxidation are minimal.  
3. Bonding occurs by adiabatic shear and severe plastic deformation at the particle–substrate interface, locking in the original crystal structures and chemistries of the feedstock.  
As a result, deposits essentially preserve the feedstock’s phases and elemental distributions.

Because cold spray relies on ultra-high-strain‐rate plastic deformation of the *particles* (not the substrate) to generate the interfacial jetting and adiabatic‐shear bonding that weld them on, you want the substrate to act rigidly compared with the particles.  If the substrate is softer than the powder:  
• Most of the kinetic energy goes into deforming or denting the substrate rather than the particle.  
• You lose the high local shear in the particle–substrate interface that strips oxides and creates the “jet” needed for cold welding.  
• Particles tend to embed or rebound instead of plastically flowing and bonding.  
• The critical impact velocity for deposition rises (lower deposition efficiency and poorer bond strength).  

By using a substrate whose yield strength or hardness exceeds that of the powder, you force the incoming particles to take up almost all the plastic deformation.  That concentrates shear at the interface, promotes oxide‐free metal‐to‐metal contact through jetting, and maximizes bonding efficiency.

The single biggest hurdle when trying to load graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) into a ceramic matrix is simply that the platelets want to re‐stack into big, inert agglomerates.  Their atomically flat faces engage in very strong van der Waals/π–π stacking, they are essentially hydrophobic, and they wet poorly (if at all) with typical ceramic slurries or sols.  If you pour in a handful of GNP powder you almost always end up with flakes floating on top or massive clumps buried in the fired piece—in neither case do you get the uniform, exfoliated network you need to tap graphene’s mechanical or functional benefits.

How it’s commonly addressed  
1. Surface-chemical pretreatment  
   • Oxidation to graphene oxide (GO) introduces –OH, –COOH, epoxy groups that render the platelets hydrophilic and allow them to be dispersed in water- or alcohol-based ceramic sols.  After shaping or presintering you can thermally or chemically reduce GO back toward graphene for electrical or mechanical performance.  
   • Silane coupling agents or polymer “brushes” graft covalently to the graphene surface, tailoring its interfacial energy to match that of the ceramic precursor.  

2. Use of dispersants and high-shear/ultrasonic mixing  
   • Small-molecule dispersants (e.g. surfactants like SDS, SDBS, polycarboxylates) adsorb on the graphene faces, imparting electrostatic or steric stabilization.  
   • Ultrasonication or three-roll milling in the presence of a dispersant breaks up agglomerates and peels off individual platelets.  

3. In-situ or freeze-dry approaches  
   • Co-precipitating or sol–gel processing a ceramic precursor around exfoliated GO sheets can lock the platelets apart from one another.  
   • Freeze-drying a mixed GO/ceramic precursor gel can “freeze” graphene in an open, porous network that redistributes uniformly when subsequently sintered.  

By combining a surface-functionalization step with vigorous mechanical de-agglomeration (ultrasound, milling) and/or a templated in-situ route, one can achieve a stable, homogeneously dispersed graphene network in the final ceramic composite.

Bulk metallic glasses (BMGs) are metal alloys that solidify without long-range crystalline order.  Their amorphous structure gives rise to a set of properties not found in conventional crystalline metals:

1. Extremely high strength and hardness  
   • Yield strengths often in the 1–2 GPa range (roughly twice that of common steels)  
   • Hardness typically 400–800 HV

2. Large elastic strain limit and high elastic energy storage  
   • Elastic strains up to ~2 % (approaching theoretical limits)  
   • Young’s moduli of 80–160 GPa combined with high strength ⇒ exceptional specific stiffness and energy density as springs

3. Corrosion and wear resistance  
   • Lack of grain boundaries and segregations suppresses localized attack  
   • High hardness and isotropic atomic structure yield low friction coefficients and excellent wear behavior

4. Soft magnetic behavior (for Fe-, Co- or Ni-based BMGs)  
   • Very low coercivity (<1 A/m)  
   • High initial permeability (10^4–10^5) and low core losses

5. Thermoplastic formability in the supercooled liquid region  
   • Well-defined glass transition temperature Tg and onset of crystallization Tx, with ΔT = Tx–Tg often >100 K  
   • Viscosity drops to 10^1–10^3 Pa·s between Tg and Tx ⇒ net-shape molding, microreplication, foaming, and joining like polymers

6. Isotropic physical and thermal properties  
   • No texture or grain anisotropy  
   • Uniform thermal expansion, conductivity, and elastic response in all directions

7. High resistance to radiation damage (in certain compositions)  
   • Amorphous structure better accommodates point defects without swelling

Limitations include limited sample ductility in tension (shear-band–driven failure) and size constraints tied to cooling-rate requirements, but composite or gradient strategies can enhance plasticity and increase casting thickness.

In cold‐spray you are essentially “drag‐accelerating” a solid particle of mass m through a high‐speed gas stream of fixed velocity Vg and density ρg.  The higher the particle’s inertia (i.e. the larger m or the larger its diameter d or density ρp), the more slowly it will pick up speed from the gas and the lower its exit velocity will be for a given nozzle length (or acceleration distance).  

Why?  Because the acceleration of the particle is set by the drag force divided by its mass:  
   a = dvp/dt = Fdrag/m ≃ (½ Cd ρg Ap (Vg – vp)^2)/m  
where  
  • Cd is the drag coefficient,  
  • Ap ∼ πd^2/4 is the particle cross‐section,  
  • m ∼ ρp πd^3/6.  

Rewriting,  

   dvp/dt = (3 Cd ρg/(4 ρp d)) (Vg – vp)^2.  

Two things jump out:  
  1. The “response time” or acceleration constant τ ∝ ρp d/Cd ρg grows with particle size and density.  
  2. For a fixed gas acceleration distance L (or fixed residence time t≈L/Vg), vp asymptotically approaches Vg according to  
      vp(t) = Vg [1 – exp(−t/τ)]  
   so a larger τ (higher inertia) means a smaller fraction of Vg is reached in the available time.  

In plain terms:  
  – Small, low‐density particles (low inertia) accelerate very rapidly and can reach nearly the gas speed.  
  – Large or high‐density particles (high inertia) accelerate more slowly and will exit the nozzle at a noticeably lower velocity.  

Because impact velocity is critical to deposition efficiency in cold spray, one must therefore choose particle sizes and materials (densities) that strike the right balance between “easy to accelerate” (low inertia) and “sufficient mass to carry momentum” into the substrate.

Both PM sintering and any “sintering” you get in cold spray rely on solid-state diffusion and neck growth between particles below the bulk melting point, but the way you supply the driving force, and the time-temperature-pressure regimes, are very different.

1. Driving forces  
  • Powder-metallurgy (PM) sintering uses a furnace heat cycle (typically 0.5–0.9 Tm), sometimes with applied pressure (hot pressing, HIP), to activate grain‐boundary and lattice diffusion over minutes to hours.  The result is neck growth, pore shrinkage, densification and often measurable dimensional shrinkage.  
  • Cold spray “sintering” (or more precisely in-situ bonding) comes from the extreme plastic deformation, adiabatic shear heating and interfacial jetting that occur during high‐velocity impact.  Local interface temperatures may spike to a few hundred °C and dislocation densities reach 10^15–10^17 m–2, greatly accelerating diffusion—but only over microseconds and confined to thin boundary regions.

2. Bonding mechanism  
  • In PM sintering, particles adhere by thermally activated diffusion across clean or oxide-reduced surfaces, forming true metallurgical necks.  Growth of those necks and redistribution of porosity is thermally controlled.  
  • In cold spray, initial bonding is mechanical (metal flow and interlocking) plus solid-state welding when fresh metal is exposed at the interface.  Any diffusion–driven necking that follows is extremely localized and limited by the short time and absence of a bulk thermal soak.

3. Porosity & densification  
  • PM sintering aims for near‐full density (ρ ≥ 99 %) through prolonged high-temperature dwell and/or pressure.  
  • Cold‐spray deposits typically run 85–98 % density as-sprayed; without a post‐spray sintering step (anneal, HIP) you will retain residual porosity and zero or negative macro shrinkage.

4. Post-processing synergy  
  • One route is to use cold spray to build a “green” or semi-dense preform, then follow with a PM-style sinter/HIP step to close the remaining porosity.  You combine the near-net geometry freedom of cold spray with the high final density of PM sintering.

In summary, both processes generate solid‐state, diffusion‐based bonds below melting.  Powder-metal sintering supplies that diffusion thermally over long times (and often pressure), whereas cold‐spray sintering is driven by impact‐induced plasticity and adiabatic heating in microseconds.  If ultimate density is required, cold‐sprayed components can be subjected to a conventional PM sintering or HIP cycle as a post-treatment.

In cold spray, three “cluster‐scale” phenomena combine to weld powder particles and build a coating:  
1.   Mechanical interlocking  
2.   Metallurgical bonding (solid‐state joining)  
3.   Tribo‐physical/chemical effects  

Briefly:  
•  Mechanical interlocking  – Particles impact at high velocity (300–1200 m/s), plastically deform, and “hammer” themselves into surface asperities and into previously deposited particles. Deformation creates micron‐scale hooks, folds and undercuts that lock particles together.  
•  Metallurgical bonding  – Impact pressures (on the order of GPa) and adiabatic shear locally breach the oxide film, bring fresh metal into intimate contact, drive severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization, and form a true solid‐state bond.  
•  Tribo‐chemical effects  – At the extreme shear rates and temperatures of the jetting/peening zone, oxide fragments can be dispersed or chemically altered, aiding fresh‐metal contact. Van der Waals forces or tribo­chemical reaction layers may contribute at the atomic scale.

Enhancing mechanical interlocking  
1. Substrate pretreatment:  
   • Grit-blast or laser‐texturize the substrate to create deep, angular undercuts and a high‐aspect‐ratio roughness.  
   • Acid or alkaline etching to produce nanoscale pits.  
2. Powder shape and size distribution:  
   • Use angular or irregularly shaped powders (e.g. gas‐atomized “snowflake” or water‐atomized powders) rather than spherical powders—corners and edges dig in more effectively.  
   • Broaden the size distribution so fine particles can fill the interstices between larger ones.  
3. Process parameters:  
   • Raise particle velocity (gas pressure, temperature, smaller nozzle throat) to increase plastic flow and substrate erosion, deepening undercuts.  
   • Optimize standoff distance so particles strike at the peak of their kinetic energy.  
   • Multi‐pass strategies: rougher first pass, subsequent “sealing” passes.  
4. Additive strategies:  
   • Co‐deposit a small fraction of hard, fragmentation-prone particles (ceramic whiskers, carbides) that embed and act as micro-anchors.  
   • Use ductile–brittle mixed powders so some fragments shear off and fill undercuts.

By combining a deliberately roughened substrate, appropriately shaped powders, and high‐velocity impacts you maximize the plastic deformation and anchoring geometry that define mechanical interlocking—and hence the build rate, bond strength and coating cohesion in cold spray.

Cold‐spray coatings adhere by solid‐state “impact welding,” i.e. by the extreme plastic deformation and adiabatic shear that each particle undergoes on striking the substrate at high velocity.  In that process:  
• The oxide films are fractured and expelled, exposing fresh metal surfaces.  
• Intimate, oxide‐free metal–metal contact is established under very high pressure.  
• Severe plastic flow (and local adiabatic shear instabilities) causes mechanical interlocking and rapid dynamic recrystallization at the interface.  
• Atomic‐scale bonding (diffusion and metallic bonding) then locks the particle in place—all without melting.

During moderate‐temperature annealing of cold‐sprayed metallic coatings (typically 0.3–0.5 Tm of the metal), the following microstructural evolutions are routinely observed:

1. Recovery  
  • Dislocation rearrangement and annihilation within the heavily work-hardened, ultra‐fine grains created by the cold spray impact.  
  • Formation and coarsening of subgrains bounded by low‐angle grain boundaries (LAGBs).  
  • Relaxation of residual compressive stresses, particularly near particle–particle interfaces.

2. Static recrystallization  
  • Nucleation of strain‐free, equiaxed grains—often at original particle boundaries or other high‐energy sites (triple junctions, oxide films).  
  • Transformation of LAGBs into high‐angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) as recrystallized grains consume the deformed matrix.  
  • Local reduction in microstrain and elimination of the nanolamellar or fibrous deformation features imparted by the spray process.

3. Grain growth and boundary migration  
  • Modest coarsening of the newly formed equiaxed grains; grain‐boundary migration may bridge across former particle boundaries and help heal inter‐particle voids.  
  • Overall grain‐size increase is usually limited under “moderate” annealing to preserve refined microstructure.

4. Densification and pore shrinkage  
  • Grain‐boundary‐ and lattice‐diffusion–driven closure of nanovoids and microcracks along prior particle interfaces.  
  • Enhanced metallurgical bonding as grains grow across original splat interfaces.

5. Precipitation/coarsening (alloy‐specific)  
  • In age‐hardenable alloys (e.g. Al – Zn – Mg, Ni – Cr), dissolution or coarsening of supersaturated precipitates formed during rapid impact.  
  • Possible re‐precipitation of strengthening phases upon further aging, altering hardness and ductility.

Macro‐scale consequences of these changes include a drop in microhardness and yield strength (due to lower dislocation density), improved ductility and electrical/thermal conductivity, and better cohesion between splats.

Typical microstructural observations at the substrate–coating interface in a cold-sprayed deposit fall into three categories:  

1. A wavy, intimate bonding line  
   • SEM or optical micrographs show the particle edges embedded in a sinusoidal or “wavy” interface.  
   • In many cases you see thin, jet‐like protrusions of both substrate and particle material that grew out of the impact zone.  
   • That topology is a signature of high-velocity, high-strain-rate impact and local adiabatic shear at the moment of bonding.  

2. A highly deformed, ultrafine-grained interfacial layer (1–20 µm thick)  
   • TEM reveals extremely high dislocation densities, formation of subgrain and cell structures, nano-twins, and dynamically recrystallized equiaxed grains (often down in the 100–500 nm range).  
   • In Ni- or Al-based systems one often sees “onion‐shell” layering in the outer few hundred nanometers of particles near the interface—each ring marking a burst of severe shear and recovery.  
   • Microhardness across this zone jumps sharply, reflecting the work hardening and grain refinement.  

3. A narrow, work-hardened zone in the underlying substrate  
   • Immediately beneath the interface (usually <10 µm) the original substrate grains are elongated or kinked, with a high density of dislocations but not fully recrystallized.  
   • Hardness here is elevated relative to the bulk substrate but lower than in the ultrafine-grained coating layer.  

Causes:  
– Supersonic impact drives strain rates of 10^5–10^7 s^–1, creating local adiabatic heating and shear instabilities that lead to jetting. That jet scours off oxides and leaves a clean metallic contact.  
– The same extreme plastic deformation introduces very high dislocation densities; when the instantaneous temperature rise crosses a dynamic recovery threshold, subgrains form and can recrystallize into nanoscale grains.  
– The wavy interface and mechanical interlocking arise because each particle “ploughs” into the substrate under high pressure, then rebounds slightly, arresting in a corrugated shape.  

In sum, the interface in cold spray is characterized by an oxide-free, wavy metallurgical bond underpinned by an ultrafine-grained, heavily strained layer on the coating side and a thinner work-hardened zone on the substrate—all produced by the extreme, localized plasticity of particle impact.

As the particle’s impact speed is ramped up through and beyond the “critical velocity” for bonding, a single metal microparticle will pass through a well‐documented sequence of deformation modes.  In rough order of increasing velocity these are:  

1. Elastic-dominated (rebound)  
   • Impact below the plastic threshold (v < ~0.5 vcrit)  
   • Recoverable (elastic) deformation, little or no dislocation motion  
   • Particle bounces from the substrate, no adhesion  

2. Onset of plasticity (partial flattening)  
   • Speeds approach ≈ 0.8 vcrit  
   • Local slip, single dislocations, limited dislocation cell structure  
   • Shallow “dimple” or slight pancake, but still often rebounds  

3. Full plastic spreading (pancake splat)  
   • Near critical velocity (v ≈ vcrit)  
   • Homogeneous plastic flow, Von Mises strains of order 1–3  
   • Particle flattens into a “pancake” and begins to bond  

4. Shear localization and jetting  
   • Slightly above vcrit (1–1.1 vcrit)  
   • Extreme strain rates (10^6–10^9 s⁻¹) drive adiabatic shear instability at the periphery  
   • High-speed “solid-state jet” expels surface oxides and contaminants  
   • Clean metal–metal contact, strong bonding  

5. Adiabatic shear bands & local softening  
   • v > 1.1 vcrit  
   • Narrow shear bands with local temperature rise (but below melting point)  
   • Dynamic recovery and/or incipient recrystallization in the jet and band zones  

6. Dynamic recrystallization & ultrafine grains  
   • At still higher velocities  
   • Subgrains break up into nanoscale grains via dynamic recrystallization  
   • Yields extremely hard, refined microstructure in the bonded splat  

7. Over-driven fragmentation/erosion  
   • v ≫ vcrit  
   • Particle shattering or spallation instead of coherent spreading  
   • Substrate erosion or pitting may dominate over net deposition  

Because each material (Al, Cu, Ni, Ti, etc.) and substrate will have its own critical velocity and strain‐rate sensitivity, the precise vcrit and the widths of these regimes vary, but the sequence from elastic rebound → limited plastic flattening → full pancake deformation → shear‐induced jetting → adiabatic banding/dynamic recrystallization → eventual fragmentation at extreme speeds is a universal roadmap in cold‐spray impact mechanics.

Cold gas (or “cold”) spraying is fundamentally different from conventional thermal‐spray processes in three respects:  

1. Process temperature below the melting point  
   • In cold spraying, powders are entrained in a high‐pressure gas (often N₂ or He), heated only to a few hundred °C—well below the metal’s melting point.  
   • Particles remain solid throughout acceleration and impact, so there is no melting or re‐solidification.  No melt pool means no thermal‐cycle‐driven oxidation or phase transformations.  

2. Extremely short dwell time at elevated temperature  
   • Particles zip through the gas at 500–1,200 m/s and spend only milliseconds in the hot zone.  
   • Even if the gas is oxygenated, the brief exposure time and moderate gas temperature limit oxide‐scale growth.  

3. Mechanical bonding via high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation  
   • Upon impact, particles undergo intense adiabatic shear at the interface, forging a bond without liquid films.  
   • Because bonding is driven by mechanical work instead of solidification, there is no opportunity for thermal‐induced phase changes (e.g. grain coarsening, intermetallic formation).  

In contrast, thermal sprays (HVOF, plasma, flame) melt or partially melt the feedstock. Melted droplets oxidize in-flight and upon impact, then rapidly solidify—locking in oxides, porosity, and high‐temperature phases. Cold spraying sidesteps those issues entirely by keeping the material in the solid state.

Solid‐state metallic bonding (often called “solid‐state welding”) requires that two metallic surfaces be brought into intimate, oxide‐free atomic contact under conditions that allow interatomic forces (metallic bonds) to form without bulk melting.  In practice the key requirements are:  

1. Surface Cleanliness and Oxide/Contaminant Removal  
   • Even thin native oxides, adsorbed water or hydrocarbons will block atomic contact.  
   • You must generate enough shear and pressure at the interface to fracture or jet away these films (mechanical “cleaning”).  

2. Intimate Atomic Contact under High Pressure  
   • Surface roughness (asperities) must be plastically flattened to expose fresh metal.  
   • Contact pressures must exceed the yield strength (often several GPa locally) so that metals flow and conform.  

3. Sufficient Atomic Mobility (Diffusivity)  
   • Although bulk temperature stays below melting, local adiabatic heating and very high dislocation densities boost diffusivity.  
   • Even at T/Tm ≈ 0.2–0.3, diffusion and/or short‐range ordering in heavily sheared, ultrafine‐grained zones can form metallic bonds.  

4. Maintenance of Pressure until Bonding Proceeds  
   • Once intimate contact is achieved, the interface must remain under pressure long enough for diffusional or displacive rearrangement of atoms.

How Cold Spray Uses Plastic Deformation to Meet These Conditions  
Cold spray propels powder particles at supersonic velocities (300–1200 m/s) so that upon impact:  
 • Peak stresses well above the bulk yield strength are generated in micro‐seconds.  
 • Very high strain rates (10^5–10^8 s^–1) produce adiabatic shear bands at the particle/substrate interface.  
 • These shear bands “jet” away surface oxides and contaminants, mechanically clean and flatten asperities, and expose fresh metal.  
 • The enormous local deformation refines the grain structure (dynamic recrystallization) and builds up ultra‐high dislocation densities, both of which accelerate short‐range diffusion.  
 • The combination of mechanical interlocking, fresh‐metal contact, adiabatic warming, and enhanced diffusion across ultrafine grains completes the metallic bond—solid‐state—without ever melting the material.  

In short, cold spray achieves solid‐state bonding by harnessing extreme plastic deformation to (1) remove oxide films, (2) force intimate atomic contact under GPa‐level pressures, and (3) generate the local heat and defects needed for rapid bonding at temperatures well below the bulk melting point.

In cold‐gas spray the metallic bond is not formed by melting and solidification but by extreme plastic deformation and the intimate, high‐pressure contact it creates.  Four interrelated phenomena are routinely cited as the “bonding mechanisms” in cold spray:  

1. Severe plastic deformation and oxide‐layer disruption  
   – Particles striking at 400–1200 m/s plastically flow and “jet” at the leading edge, tearing and scouring off surface oxides and contaminants.  
   – That leaves fresh, highly stressed metal surfaces in direct contact.  

2. Interfacial jetting and adiabatic shear instabilities  
   – Impact generates a very narrow, high‐strain‐rate shear zone at the particle–substrate (or particle–particle) interface.  
   – Material is expelled in a jet that further cleans and pre-loads the interface under dynamic pressure (up to several GPa).  

3. Mechanical interlocking and asperity collapse  
   – High‐velocity flattening of particle asperities produces intimate surface conformity, locking particles together mechanically even before true metallurgical bonding begins.  

4. Localized, high‐strain heating and dynamic recrystallization  
   – Although bulk temperatures remain well below melting, plastic work at the interface can raise the local temperature (and defect density) enough to induce dynamic recrystallization or short‐range diffusion.  
   – These fine, ultrafine, or nanocrystalline grains weld together across the cleaned interface via metallic (interatomic) bonds.  

In practice all four act in concert.  The result is a dense deposit of particles that are metallurgically fused, with bond strengths often approaching those of wrought materials without ever exceeding a fraction of the melting temperature.

A cold‐sprayed Ni/Al₂O₃ “metal–ceramic” coating is, in essence, just a plastically deformed nickel binder with embedded corundum particles.  In practice you will find:

1. FCC nickel  
   – The ductile “matrix” phase, heavily work‐hardened and grain‐refined by the high‐velocity impacts.  
   – Often contains a very high dislocation density and subgrain structure.  

2. α‐Al₂O₃ (corundum)  
   – Essentially unchanged from the feedstock ceramic—hard, brittle particles dispersed throughout the Ni.  

3. Surface/Interfacial oxides (minor)  
   – Thin NiO layers on the nickel powder surfaces (from pre‐existing native oxide or slight oxidation during spraying).  
   – In some cases, very thin NiAl₂O₄ (spinel) can form at the Ni/Al₂O₃ interface if local frictional heating briefly exceeds ~500–600 °C.  

You will *not* normally see intermetallics such as Ni₃Al (there is no free Al) or any new bulk compounds—cold spray is a solid‐state process, so essentially all you get is a two‐phase Ni + Al₂O₃ composite, with only trace oxides/spinel at the interfaces.

In cold spray, particles impact the substrate (or earlier‐deposited layers) at high velocities (300–1200 m/s), undergoing extremely high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation at the interface.  That impact produces a thin, localized jet of material that (a) strips away surface oxides and adsorbates, (b) brings fresh metal surfaces into intimate atomic contact, and (c) drives an adiabatic‐shear‐instability zone.  The result is a solid‐state, metallurgical bond—often called “cold welding”—rather than a fusion weld.

Because cold spray deposits particles entirely in the solid state (no melting), it offers several key benefits when you need to coat or consolidate powders that are either highly oxygen‐sensitive or that owe their properties to metastable or nanocrystalline structures:  

1. Negligible oxidation or contamination  
   • Process temperatures are typically 0.2–0.5 Tmelt of the feedstock metal, so there’s no molten metal–air interface.  
   • Native oxides or surface coatings remain intact rather than being blown off and re-oxidizing.  

2. Preservation of metastable or nanostructured phases  
   • Absence of a liquid phase means you avoid grain growth, phase coarsening, or transformations (e.g., amorphous → crystalline).  
   • Metastable chemistries (like supersaturated alloys, hydrides, nitrides) survive the impact event unaltered.  

3. Minimal thermal damage to encapsulated or composite powders  
   • You can embed temperature-sensitive additives (e.g., energetic materials, polymeric binders) without thermally decomposing them.  
   • No heat-affected zone in the substrate or the particles, so residual stresses are lower.  

4. High compositional fidelity  
   • Since you never go through a liquid, there’s no risk of elemental segregation, evaporation of low–melting‐point constituents, or pore formation from gas evolution.  
   • All alloying elements (even very reactive ones like Al, Mg, Ti) stay exactly where you put them.  

5. Fast build-up with intact functionality  
   • You can co-spray oxygen-scavenging alloys or passivation agents directly onto the sensitive powder surface.  
   • For energetic or catalytic powders, the preserved surface area and active sites mean you retain full reactivity or catalytic performance.  

In short, cold spray lets you make dense, adherent coatings (or near‐net shapes) of oxygen‐sensitive and metastable materials without the usual drawbacks of high‐temperature, melt-based processes.

In cold‐spray additive manufacturing the “welding” of powder particles into a coherent solid is achieved almost entirely in the solid state and arises from two—and in practice interlinked—mechanisms:  
1. Severe plastic deformation (mechanical bonding)  
   • Upon impact at velocities above a material‐specific critical velocity, particles undergo extremely high strain (104–105 s–1) and spread into thin “splats.”  
   • This creates mechanical interlocking at particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces and breaks up surface oxides or contaminants.  
   • Localized adiabatic‐shear instabilities at the periphery of the splat further enhance material flow and interface conformity.  

2. Metallurgical/atomic bonding  
   • Plastic‐deformation–induced fracture of the native oxide film exposes fresh metal–metal contact, allowing metallic bonding.  
   • High dislocation densities and temperatures approaching but below melting point drive dynamic recrystallization—grain subdivision into ultrafine or nanocrystalline structures—and solid‐state diffusion across interfaces.  

Characterization of these bonding mechanisms is typically carried out by a combination of microstructural, chemical, and mechanical methods:  
A. Microstructural and crystallographic probes  
   – SEM (backscatter and secondary‐electron) on polished cross sections to assess particle deformation, interparticle boundaries, pore distribution and oxide remnants.  
   – EBSD to map grain‐size refinement in the spray deposit and misorientation distributions at former interfaces (evidence of recrystallization).  
   – TEM (on focused‐ion‐beam lamellae) to reveal dislocation networks, subgrain structures and ultrafine grains at splat boundaries.  

B. Chemical/oxide analysis  
   – EDS/EELS line‐scans or maps across interfaces to confirm oxide‐film disruption or absence, and to detect any alloying elements or contamination.  
   – XPS or AES depth profiling of fracture surfaces to assess the degree of metal‐metal contact.  

C. Mechanical testing  
   – Macro‐ and micro‐tensile or lap‐shear tests to quantify bond strength; comparison of cohesive (within particles) vs. adhesive (interface) failure modes.  
   – Microhardness or nanoindentation across the build height and at interfaces to track work‐hardening, strain‐ageing and recrystallization effects.  

D. Porosity and defect inspection  
   – X‐ray microtomography or optical image analysis for volumetric porosity and defect size distribution.  
   – Ultrasonic C‐scan for planar flaws.  

By correlating (a) the degree of plastic deformation and grain refinement seen in EBSD/TEM with (b) the completeness of oxide‐film breakup (EDS/EELS) and (c) the ultimate bond strength from mechanical tests one builds a consistent picture of how mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding jointly produce a high‐integrity, nearly fully dense solid in cold‐spray AM.

In the first‐order shear‐deformation (Reissner–Mindlin) layerwise plate model the following two assumptions are made regarding the thickness (z) behavior:  

1. Transverse normal strains vanish  
   – εzz≡0 everywhere.  In other words, normals to the midsurface remain straight (no stretching or contraction in the z‐direction), although they are allowed to rotate.  

2. Transverse shear strains are taken as constant (per layer) through the thickness  
   – γxz and γyz do not vary with z within each layer.  Equivalently, the in‐plane displacements vary linearly in z, w is z‐independent, and each layer carries a uniform shear strain (often corrected by a shear‐correction factor to compensate for the true parabolic shear‐stress profile).

Passive oxide scales (e.g. Cr₂O₃, Al₂O₃) protect alloys in many oxidizing atmospheres by forming a continuous, adherent barrier. In high‐temperature molten salts, however, that barrier often breaks down for several interrelated reasons:

1. Chemical dissolution (“fluxing”)  
   • Many molten salts (chlorides, nitrates, fluorides) react with the protective oxide to form soluble metal salts (e.g. Cr₂O₃ + 6 NaCl → 2 Na₃CrO₃ + 3 Cl₂).  
   • Halide ions (Cl–, F–) dissolve oxide ions from the scale, forming oxy‐ or halometallate complexes that diffuse away into the bulk salt.

2. Chloride‐induced inward corrosion  
   • Chlorides transport through nano-defects in the oxide and react at the metal/oxide interface to form volatile metal chlorides (e.g. FeCl₂, NiCl₂).  
   • These chlorides migrate back to the oxide/gas interface, oxidize to reform the oxide, and release Cl₂ (the “chlorine cycle”), thus continuously consuming metal and scale.

3. Low oxygen activity  
   • Molten salt environments generally maintain oxygen partial pressures well below those required to stabilize dense, protective oxides.  
   • If pO₂ drops below the stability limit of Cr₂O₃ or Al₂O₃, the scale either cannot reform after damage or transforms into nonprotective spinels.

4. Mechanical degradation (spallation and cracking)  
   • Thermal‐expansion mismatch between metal and oxide at high T induces stresses that crack the scale.  
   • Molten-salt penetration into these cracks promotes under‐scale corrosion and rapid scale detachment.

5. Pitting and localized attack  
   • Grain-boundary or compositional heterogeneities in the oxide give preferential ingress paths for salt.  
   • Once pitting begins, local acidification (e.g. from dissolved metal chlorides) accelerates corrosion.

Taken together, these effects mean that, unlike in dry oxidizing gases, oxide scales in molten salts are continually attacked, dissolved, and mechanically disrupted, so they cannot form a stable, self-healing corrosion barrier.

During a cold‐spray impact (particle velocities typically 300–1200 m/s, strain rates 10^5–10^7 s^–1, pressures of several GPa), plastic deformation and eventual bonding are controlled almost entirely by dislocation‐based and shear‐localization processes at the atomic scale.  The primary mechanisms are:

1.  Dislocation nucleation and slip  
    •  Extreme contact stresses at the front (up to a few GPa) drive homogeneous emission of dislocations from the free surface and the particle–substrate interface.  
    •  Frank–Read sources multiply dislocations rapidly; forest interactions raise the local flow stress.  
    •  Cross‐slip (in fcc/BCC metals) and limited climb at the shear‐heated interface allow dislocation redistribution.

2.  Adiabatic shear localization and jetting  
    •  The combination of very high strain rates and poor heat conduction confines plastic work to a thin interfacial zone, causing a local temperature spike (“adiabatic shear band”).  
    •  Shear‐induced jetting of surface oxide/contaminant layers exposes fresh metal surfaces to bond.  

3.  Mechanical twinning (in low stacking‐fault‐energy or HCP/BCC alloys)  
    •  Under the extreme shear stress, {101¯2} or {112} twins form and accommodate additional strain when dislocation slip alone cannot.  

4.  Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement  
    •  The ultra‐high dislocation densities in the shear zone drive continuous dynamic recrystallization (CDRX): subgrains rotate and coalesce into new, ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains.  
    •  This grain refinement stiffens the interfacial region and contributes to a strong, defect‐tight metallurgical bond.

5.  Interface mixing and atomic‐scale bonding  
    •  Ballistic mixing: atoms from particle and substrate interpenetrate over a few nanometers.  
    •  The localized heating plus high defect densities greatly enhance short‐range diffusion—solid‐state “cold” welding occurs without bulk melting.

Together, these mechanisms—dislocation‐dominated plasticity, shear‐driven jetting/oxide removal, twinning in certain alloys, and dynamic recrystallization combined with atomic mixing—govern how particles deform, clean, and metallurgically bond into a coherent cold‐sprayed film.

Smaller ceramic or oxide reinforcements show much higher retention in cold‐sprayed metal matrices than large ones for three main reasons:

1. Higher attainable particle velocity  
   - Under a given gas pressure and nozzle geometry, drag acceleration ∝ area/mass favors small particles.  They accelerate more quickly and so reach or exceed the critical velocity for embedding.  Large particles, by contrast, accelerate more slowly and often never hit the speed needed to overcome their own rebound tendency.

2. Lower energy threshold for mechanical entrapment  
   - Embedding a hard, non‐deformable particle requires that the particle “punch” into a plastically deforming metal splat or underlying substrate by supplying enough kinetic energy (½ m v²) to create a local crater and lock itself in.  Because smaller particles have lower mass m, their required v is less, so at the same gas conditions they more readily meet this criterion.

3. Better mechanical interlocking and frictional retention  
   - Small particles have a higher surface‐area‐to‐volume ratio and tend to lodge within the interstices of a growing metal splat network, where they’re gripped by the plastic flow of the metal around irregularities.  Large particles, when they do impact, create oversized craters, bounce more readily, and are less effectively “clamped” by surrounding metal.

Taken together, these effects mean that under typical cold‐spray conditions small reinforcements both reach embedding speed more easily and once they hit the substrate are far less likely to rebound or roll off, leading to significantly better incorporation into the coating.

Substrate temperature is one of the most important “process knobs” in cold spray because it directly controls (a) the thermal and mechanical state of the substrate at impact, (b) the propensity for adiabatic shear, and (c) the interfacial chemistry and diffusion.  In broad terms:  

1. Reduced Critical Velocity  
  • Raising the substrate temperature lowers both its yield strength and that of the impacting particles in the vicinity of the interface.  As a result, particles require a lower impact velocity to achieve the same degree of plastic deformation and bonding.  

2. Enhanced Plastic Deformation and Adiabatic Shear  
  • A warmer substrate is less of a heat sink.  The localized temperature rise at the particle–substrate contact zone persists longer, promoting adiabatic shear band formation in the particle.  This facilitates extreme plastic flow, jetting at the periphery of the impact site, and mechanical interlocking.  

3. Improved Interfacial Bonding  
  • Elevated substrate temperature accelerates atomic diffusion across the interface and can activate thin‐film tribochemical reactions (oxide disruption, local micro‐welding).  The net effect is higher interfacial strength and coating cohesion.  

4. Lower Residual Stresses  
  • Preheating the substrate to an optimal temperature reduces the thermal gradient between the bulk substrate and the deposited material.  This softens the substrate, decreases quench‐induced tensile stresses, and mitigates crack formation or delamination.  

5. Trade­offs and Limits  
  • Too low a substrate temperature (< ambient or highly heat‐sinking) means particles cool and “freeze” on impact—poor deformation, high critical velocity, weak bonding, high porosity.  
  • Excessive substrate heating can accelerate oxidation of both substrate and particles, promote grain growth in sensitive alloys, and eventually degrade coating hardness or corrosion resistance.  

In practice, preheat temperatures of 100–400 °C (dependent on material) are often used to optimize deposition efficiency, adhesion, and final coating properties without crossing oxidation or grain‐growth thresholds.

Ball milling refines powder to a nanocrystalline state by subjecting particles to repeated high‐energy impacts that produce very large plastic strains.  The key steps are:

1. Severe Plastic Deformation  
   – Each collision of balls with powder particles imposes intense shear and compressive strains.  
   – Dislocation densities rise rapidly, and dislocations rearrange into cell walls and low‐angle boundaries.

2. Fracture–Cold‐Welding Cycles  
   – Hard particles fracture along these newly formed boundaries, breaking large grains into smaller fragments.  
   – Softer fragments cold‐weld under pressure and are then re-fractured in subsequent impacts.  
   – This continual cycle thins lamellae and reduces subgrain sizes.

3. Subgrain Refinement and Dynamic Recovery  
   – As dislocation cells evolve into high‐angle grain boundaries, true grains form in the 10–100 nm range.  
   – Recovery processes are suppressed by low local temperatures and high strain rates, preventing extensive grain growth.

4. Steady-State Nanocrystallinity  
   – Eventually a balance is reached between defect generation and annihilation: grain size saturates in the nanometer regime.  
   – Further milling only refines porosity and disperses any second phases or oxides uniformly.

Process variables such as ball size and material, ball-to-powder ratio, milling speed, atmosphere, and total milling time control the rate of deformation, fracture–welding cycles, and final grain size.

Adding brittle ceramic particulates (e.g. Al₂O₃, SiC) into an otherwise fully‐ductile cold‐spray powder almost invariably drives down the deposition efficiency of the metallic fraction.  Three principal mechanisms are at work:

1. Kinetic-Energy Partitioning  
   • In a binary blend the total particle momentum is shared between metal and ceramic.  Because ceramics do not plastically deform on impact, they absorb (and then rebound) a larger fraction of the incoming kinetic energy.  That leaves less energy available to drive the high‐strain adiabatic shear and jetting required for metallic bonding.  
   • The effective critical velocity for the ductile metal goes up.  Even if the nominal gas conditions (pressure, temperature) are unchanged, fewer metal particles can exceed the new, higher threshold.

2. Interfacial Shielding and Mechanical Impedance  
   • Ceramic splinters or whole grains tend to lodge at the metal–substrate or metal–metal interface and act as rigid spacers.  This “third‐body” effect blocks the intimate metal‐to‐metal contact needed for metallurgical bonding.  
   • The extra hardness also raises the local contact stiffness, reducing the true contact area during impact.

3. Powder‐Flow and Nozzle-Wear Effects  
   • A harder, mixed‐size feedstock abrades the nozzle walls more aggressively, which can alter the local gas flow pattern and further reduce particle velocities.  
   • Ceramics often have a lower density than many ductile metals (Al alloy blends being a common exception), but their rough surfaces and irregular shapes increase powder cohesion.  That can lead to poorer acceleration and more flow instabilities in the spray jet.

Quantitatively, a typical Al‐based powder might spray at 70 – 80 % deposition efficiency on steel.  Introducing 10 – 15 vol % Al₂O₃ can drop that to 50 – 60 %.  Beyond 20 – 30 vol % ceramic loading the metallic fraction often falls below 30 % unless one compensates by raising gas pressure/temperature or switching to a lighter carrier gas (e.g. He).

In practice, you can partially offset the efficiency loss by  
• Limiting ceramic loading to the minimum needed to achieve the desired composite properties,  
• Using bimodal or multimodal size distributions so the ductile metal fills the interstices around the hard grains,  
• Optimizing nozzle design to minimize premature ceramic–wall impact, and  
• Tweaking spray parameters (higher P, T or He content) to restore the metal’s critical‐velocity margin.

In cold spray the particles never melt – they bond by extreme high-strain‐rate plastic deformation at impact.  At several hundred to over 1,000 m/s the particle–substrate interface undergoes adiabatic shear, oxide breakup and “jetting” of surface films, and intense mechanical interlocking.  That jetting removes oxides, fresh metal-to-metal contact is established, and local dynamic recrystallization at the interface locks the particle in place.  In short, it’s a solid-state bond formed by severe plastic deformation (adiabatic shear + metal–metal intimate contact), not by fusion or melting.

Cold spray is a solid‐state process in which metal powders are accelerated to high velocity (300–1200 m/s) in a supersonic gas jet and bond to the substrate by adiabatic shear and severe plastic deformation—never by melting. Because:

1. Operating temperatures are well below the melting point, there is no liquid metal exposed to oxygen, so thermally driven oxidation is essentially eliminated.  
2. Residence times at elevated temperature are very short and the carrier gas (often N₂ or He) is inert, so there is negligible oxygen available to form new oxides.  
3. Any native oxide films on the powder particles are shattered during high‐velocity impact, mechanically dispersed (or entrapped at interparticle boundaries), and fresh metal–metal contact is formed.  

The net effect is a metallurgically bonded coating with virtually no newly formed oxide phases.

In Al–Mg alloys the very thin (2–10 nm) “native” film that forms on exposure to air is an amorphous alumina that contains dissolved magnesium (and, in humid air, Mg‐hydroxide or hydrated oxy-hydroxide).  On heating, that film undergoes the following broad sequence of transformations:

1.  RT→150 °C  
    – Loss of adsorbed water and dehydroxylation of any Mg‐OH.  
    – Film remains mostly amorphous Al₂O₃ with Mg²⁺ in solid solution.  

2.  200 °C→400 °C  
    – Onset of crystallization of γ-Al₂O₃ (and/or transition aluminas such as δ or θ).  
    – Mg²⁺, being more mobile than Al³⁺, begins to diffuse and nucleate spinel‐type domains.  
    – Small amounts of MgO may also precipitate if local Mg supersaturation occurs.  

3.  350 °C→550 °C  
    – Rapid growth of MgAl₂O₄ spinel crystallites at the γ-Al₂O₃/metal interface and throughout the oxide.  
    – Coarsening of γ-Al₂O₃ and incipient transformation toward θ-Al₂O₃ or δ-Al₂O₃.  

4.  600 °C→1 000 °C  
    – γ, δ, θ transition aluminas progressively convert to the thermodynamically stable α-Al₂O₃.  
    – MgAl₂O₄ spinel remains stable and grows at the expense of the transition aluminas.  
    – If the alloy is Mg-rich or if the oxide film is thick enough, discrete MgO particles may coexist with spinel and α-Al₂O₃.  

5.  Above ∼1 000 °C  
    – Fully crystalline α-Al₂O₃ matrix laced with MgAl₂O₄ spinel grains (and MgO if present).  
    – Further coarsening of all phases; eventually grain-boundary diffusion can lead to islanding or fracture of the protective scale.

Summary of key phases and their approximate appearance temperatures:  
• Amorphous Al₂O₃ (RT→200 °C)  
• γ-Al₂O₃ (onset ∼200 °C)  
• MgAl₂O₄ spinel (200–350 °C nucleation, rapid growth 350–550 °C)  
• MgO (locally, 200 °C and up, if Mg supersaturates)  
• Transition aluminas δ/θ (through 600 °C)  
• α-Al₂O₃ (600 °C→1 000 °C and above)

Low‐volume fractions of plate‐ or sheet‐like reinforcements (e.g. graphene, h-BN, MoS₂) in a cold‐sprayed metal matrix can be essentially “invisible” to laboratory XRD for several interrelated reasons:  

1. Low signal intensity  
  • XRD phase detection limits for well‐crystallized minor phases are typically in the 1–5 wt% (≈1–3 vol%) range.  Anything below that contributes very little coherent scattering compared with the bulk metal peaks.  
  • Two-dimensional reinforcements have very little thickness and therefore a very small diffracting volume per unit area, further reducing peak intensity.  

2. Peak broadening and overlap  
  • If platelets are only a few nanometers thick they produce very broad, low‐intensity 00ℓ reflections that can merge into the background.  
  • Their principal diffraction angles often coincide with or lie close to strong matrix peaks.  e.g. graphene’s 002 reflection around 26° 2θ overlaps with background and weak Al peaks, making it impossible to resolve.  

3. Turbostratic or poorly ordered structure  
  • Exfoliated or cold‐sprayed 2D layers often lose long‐range registry (turbostratic disorder), which further broadens and weakens their Bragg peaks.  
  • If the reinforcement is partially amorphous (edge‐oxidized graphene, defect‐rich h-BN), its diffraction signature may be a broad hump rather than sharp peaks.  

4. Preferred orientation and surface layering  
  • Cold spraying tends to align platelets with their basal planes parallel to the substrate surface.  That orientation may not satisfy Bragg’s condition for the strongest reflections in a θ–2θ scan.  
  • Many flakes may lie near the surface or be shielded by oxide films or splat boundaries, reducing their contribution to the bulk diffracted signal.  

5. Matrix strain and background noise  
  • Severe plastic deformation of the metal splats broadens and shifts the substrate peaks, raising the background under the weak reinforcement peaks.  
  • Instrumental and fluorescence backgrounds in a lab diffractometer can further mask any tiny, broad features from 2D reinforcements.  

Taken together, these effects drive the reinforcement‐to‐background ratio below the practical detection threshold of conventional XRD.  Complementary techniques (Raman spectroscopy, TEM‐EDS/EELS, GIXRD, synchrotron XRD, or thermal analysis) are usually required to confirm the presence of sub‐percent 2D phases in cold‐sprayed coatings.

Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) in cold spray is a highly localized, rate‐driven softening and flow phenomenon that occurs in metallic particles (and often in the substrate) when they impact at very high strain rates (typically 10^5–10^7 s^–1). Because the deformation happens so quickly, thermal energy generated by plastic work cannot diffuse away—hence it is “adiabatic.” Temperatures in the narrow shear bands can rise by hundreds of degrees over micro‐ to millimeter length scales, dramatically reducing flow stress and producing ultra‐fine, highly strained zones.  

How ASI contributes to bonding in cold spray  
1. Localized softening and jetting  
   - The softened shear bands act almost like a viscous fluid, permitting a high‐pressure lateral “jet” of metal to expel surface oxides, adsorbates and entrapped gases at the particle–substrate interface.  
   - This jetting cleans the contact surfaces and spreads fresh, oxide‐free metal over both the particle and substrate.  

2. Mechanical interlocking and metallurgical contact  
   - ASI‐induced plastic flow creates very high true strains (>200 %) in the impact zone, producing tight interfacial conformity and mechanical interlocking at micro‐ and nano‐scales.  
   - As oxides are stripped away, intimate metal–metal contact allows for solid‐state diffusion and metallurgical bonding—even at temperatures well below the bulk melting point.  

3. Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement  
   - The extreme strain rates and temperatures within the adiabatic shear bands drive dynamic recrystallization, leading to ultra‐fine grains.  
   - These fine grains enhance bond strength by increasing the density of grain boundaries (paths for diffusion) and by providing barriers to crack propagation.  

In sum, adiabatic shear instability is the trigger for the cleaning, extreme plastic deformation, jet‐formation and grain refinement that collectively enable the high‐strength, oxide‐free solid‐state bonds characteristic of cold‐sprayed coatings.

In cold spray the particles never melt; instead the high‐velocity impact (300–1200 m/s) produces extreme, localized plastic deformation and adiabatic shear right at the particle/substrate (or particle/particle) interface.  That shear:

  • Fractures and jets away the native oxide layers,  
  • Exposes fresh metal surfaces under ultra–high contact pressures, and  
  • Drives dynamic recrystallization in a thin interfacial shear zone  

The net result is true solid‐state (cold) welding: intimate metal–metal contact on the atomic scale and the formation of a metallurgical bond without bulk melting.

Particle density enters the cold‐spray deformation process almost entirely through its effect on the particle’s kinetic energy and momentum at a given impact speed.  At fixed impact velocity v, a spherical particle of density ρ and volume V carries  
  – kinetic energy Ekin = ½ ρ V v²  
  – momentum p = ρ V v  
Both of these scale linearly with ρ (for constant V and v), so higher‐density particles will impart larger stresses, higher strain rates and more adiabatic heating on impact.  In practice this means:  
  1. Higher peak contact pressure:  σmax ∼ p/Acontact ∝ ρ v, so denser particles drive the local stress above the yield strength more deeply.  
  2. Greater plastic work (Wp ∼ ∫σ dε ∼ Ekin), so they spread and flatten out more (higher “flattening ratio”) and develop more pronounced shear instabilities.  
  3. Lower effective critical velocity for bonding: many models (e.g. Assadi’s critical‐velocity theory) give vc ∝ √(Y/ρ), so higher‐ρ particles will reach the regime of full plastic flow—and hence metallurgical bonding—at a lower v.  

Conversely, low‐density particles carry less energy per impact, produce smaller stresses and strain rates, deform less, and may even rebound if v is below their (higher) critical velocity.  

In formula form one often writes the approximate “impact pressure” or shock amplitude as  
    P ≃ k ρ v²  
and the average plastic strain in the particle (or substrate) scales as  
    εpl ∼ P/Y ∼ (k ρ v²)/Y,  
where Y is the dynamic yield strength and k a constant of order unity.  Thus, at fixed v and Y, εpl (and hence the extent of deformation) grows linearly with particle density.

Severe plastic deformation (SPD) at the particle–substrate interface in cold spray is the key driver of both bonding and the emergence of an ultrafine-grained interfacial layer.  In a nutshell, the impact of each high-velocity particle (strain rates often ≥10^6 s⁻¹) produces:  

1. Intense strain localization and adiabatic shear at the immediate interface  
2. Dislocation multiplication and formation of cell/block/subgrain structures  
3. Continuous or geometric dynamic recrystallization (CDRX/GDRX) in both the coating and the disturbed substrate surface  

The net result is a pronounced grain-refinement “gradient” spanning typically 1–20 µm from the interface:  
• At the very interface (≲1 µm): equiaxed ultrafine-/nanocrystalline grains (often 50–300 nm), very high dislocation density, strong misorientations.  
• A transition zone (1–10 µm): residual subgrains and partly refined parent grains (0.2–1 µm).  
• Beyond ~10–20 µm into the coating or substrate: the original (coarser) spray-deposited or wrought microstructure (1–10 µm grains) is largely recovered.  

Consequences  
– Higher hardness and strength near the interface (Hall–Petch strengthening)  
– Improved mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding  
– Residual compressive stresses that retard crack initiation  

In short, the severe plastic deformation inherent to each particle impact shatters and dynamically recrystallizes the local microstructure, driving a steep grain-size gradient that underpins the excellent adhesion and mechanical performance of cold-sprayed coatings.

Key points  
1. Drag‐to‐inertia scaling  
   – A particle of diameter d and density ρ_p moving through a carrier gas of density ρ_g and bulk velocity V_g is driven by a drag force  
     F_D ≃½ C_D ρ_g V_rel² A  , A=πd²/4.  
   – Its acceleration a=F_D/m so its characteristic response (acceleration) time τ scales as  
     τ ≃ m/(C_D ρ_g A V_g) ∝ (ρ_p/ρ_g)·(d/(C_D V_g)).  
   – Smaller d ⇒ smaller τ ⇒ particle velocity v_p(t) = V_g[1–exp(–t/τ)] approaches V_g more rapidly. Larger d ⇒ long τ, large inertia, v_p≪V_g in the finite nozzle length.  

2. In–flight velocity  
   – Small particles (sub-micron to a few µm) see high drag-to-mass ratio ⇒ v_p→V_g (say 500–1200 m/s) over typical spray lengths.  
   – Large particles (tens of µm) have low drag-to-mass ⇒ v_p remains well below V_g (sometimes only a few hundred m/s).  

3. Kinetic energy scaling  
   – KE = ½ m v_p² ∝ d³ v_p²(d).  
   – Very small d ⇒ v_p≈V_g but m∝d³ so KE is low.  
   – Very large d ⇒ m∝d³ high, but v_p(d) falls off strongly so KE again is low.  
   – Intermediate sizes often maximize KE (and thus impact stresses), typically in the few‐micron range for ceramic powders in common cold‐spray setups.  

4. Practical implications for ceramic reinforcements  
   – If d is too small (< 1 µm): excellent acceleration but too little KE to embed or fracture.  
   – If d is too large (> 30–50 µm): too slow, low KE and poor bonding.  
   – Optimum d (often 2–10 µm) balances mass and velocity to exceed the critical velocity for embedment into the metallic matrix.

Mechanical‐interlocking bonding in cold spray is simply a “key‐and‐lock” type of attachment that arises when high‐speed particles plastically deform and mechanically anchor themselves into the microscopic valleys, undercuts, and asperities of the substrate (or previously deposited particles) rather than forming a true metallurgical (diffusion or metallurgical‐shear) bond.  

How it occurs, step by step:  
1. Particle acceleration: Particles are gas‐accelerated to velocities near or just above the material’s critical bonding velocity (typically 300–1200 m/s depending on material).  
2. Impact and plastic flow: Upon impact, the particle’s front face and the underlying substrate experience extremely high local pressures (GPa scale), producing intense, ultrafast plastic deformation.  
3. Filling of asperities: The plastically flowing metal extrudes laterally and forward, literally flowing into and around microscopic surface roughness—valleys, pits, undercuts, grit‐blast peaks, etc.  
4. Mechanical anchoring: Once the material has deformed into those asperities, it “locks” in place when the stresses relax, resisting pullout or shear. If enough particles interlock, a cohesive coating builds up.  

Key points  
• It does not require melting or significant interdiffusion—only solid‐state plastic deformation.  
• It is most pronounced on rough or grit‐blasted substrates, where deeper undercuts are available.  
• At higher velocities or with more ductile materials, mechanical interlocking can be supplemented (or overtaken) by metallurgical bonding via adiabatic shear and oxide‐film disruption, but mechanical interlocking is often the first bond to form.

Because metal cold‐spray particles are so small and highly conductive, they internally equilibrate thermally much faster than they exchange heat with the gas or substrate.  In practice:  
•  Particle diameter D is O(1–50 µm) and metal thermal diffusivity α is O(10⁻⁵ m²/s), so the internal conduction time τ_cond ~ D²/α is on the order of 10⁻⁷–10⁻⁵ s.  
•  The convective time scale τ_conv ~ (ρcpV)/(hA) (where h is the gas–solid h­eat‐transfer coefficient, A the surface area) is longer—by about one to two orders of magnitude—than τ_cond.  
•  Equivalently, the Biot number Bi = h·(D/2)/k_metal ≪ 0.1, so temperature gradients inside the particle are negligible.  

Under those conditions the entire particle can be treated as a single (uniform) temperature node.  This “isothermal‐particle” assumption greatly simplifies the thermal model with very little loss of accuracy for cold‐spray simulations.

In most cold‐spray CFD studies the goal of the “acceleration” simulation is simply to predict the particle exit (or impact) velocity and temperature at the nozzle outlet (or a short distance downstream), not to model the actual deposition process.  For high‐density powders in particular, the substrate itself has a negligible effect on those upstream quantities for three main reasons:

1.   Inertia Dominance  
     •  Metal and ceramic powders (densities 5–20 g/cm³) have such high particle mass that once they leave the nozzle throat their trajectories and speeds are overwhelmingly governed by the drag history inside the nozzle and in the near‐jet plume.  
     •  The short “jet–substrate” gap in a typical spray set-up is traversed so rapidly that any disturbance of the carrier gas by the substrate cannot propagate upstream far enough (especially in supersonic jets) to affect the acceleration phase.

2.   Computational Economy and Modeling Strategy  
     •  Explicitly meshing the substrate (and the spray gap around it) would vastly increase cell count, introduce very thin boundary layers, require wall‐treatment models, and add particle–surface interaction physics (rebound, splash, thermal contact) that are irrelevant to the acceleration phase.  
     •  Most practitioners therefore truncate the domain at or just past the nozzle exit (orifice), apply appropriate pressure or velocity outflow conditions, track particle velocities in that truncated plume, and then hand those velocities off to a separate impact/deposition model.

3.   Decoupling of Acceleration and Impact  
     •  The cold‐spray process is typically analyzed in two steps:  
       a)  Nozzle flow + particle acceleration (Euler–Lagrange CFD, no substrate) → particle exit velocities T(x), v(x)  
       b)  Particle‐substrate impact (discrete element, FEM, or analytical jetting models)  
     •  In step (a) you only care about how the gas accelerates the powder; in step (b) you add surface compliance, adhesion work, and plastic deformation.  

Because high‐density powders have short response times (τp=ρpdp^2/μg) relative to their flight time, any back-pressure or recirculation caused by the target plate is confined to a very small region right at the surface.  That region does not affect the gas–particle coupling upstream, so it is routinely omitted in acceleration‐only simulations.

Oxide layers on powder particles are one of the principal barriers to achieving high‐strength metallurgical bonding in cold spray.  Because cold spray relies entirely on plastic deformation—and not on melting—to join particles to themselves and to the substrate, any hard, brittle or poorly deformable surface film will tend to:

  •  Limit intimate metal–metal contact at the particle/substrate interface  
  •  Suppress the jetting and adiabatic shear localization that drive bonding  
  •  Act as a crack-initiation site in the built‐up coating  

How oxide films are dealt with in cold spray  
1.	In-flight particle deformation and jetting  
    – At the moment of impact (typically 300–1200 m/s), the particle’s leading edge undergoes extremely high strain rates (>10^6 s⁻¹).  
    – Adiabatic shear bands form at the interface and shear out—i.e. “jet”—the oxide film, redistributing it into fine fragments at the periphery of the splat.  
    – This jetting both physically carries oxide fragments away from the bonding front and freshens the exposed metal surface to enable metallic bonding.  

2.	Oxide fragmentation and dispersion  
    – The oxide does not entirely vanish; it is broken into sub‐micron particles that tend to disperse in the interparticle boundaries or become entrapped as oxide stringers.  
    – If the initial oxide is thin (a few nanometers), the fragmentation is sufficient to leave large areas of clean metal–metal contact.  

3.	Feedstock pre‐treatments  
    – Mechanical: ball‐milling, attritor milling or shot peening to crack or thin the native oxide prior to spraying.  
    – Chemical: acid or alkali etching to remove or reduce oxide thickness, followed by controlled passivation to prevent re-oxidation.  
    – Thermal or hydrogen reduction: heating powders in a reducing atmosphere to convert oxides back to metal or sub‐oxides.  
    – Surface functionalization: depositing a thin, more ductile “seed” layer (e.g. Zn on Al) that fractures more readily than the native oxide.  

4.	Process atmosphere and nozzle design  
    – Using inert (Ar, N₂) or reducing (H₂–Ar) carrier gases to minimize further oxidation in the hot gas stream.  
    – Tailored nozzle geometries to maximize particle acceleration (and thus impact kinetic energy), ensuring oxide‐fracturing strain rates are reached.  

5.	Material choice and allowable oxide  
    – Some alloys (e.g. Ni, Co) form adherent, ductile oxides that do not catastrophically inhibit bonding.  
    – For highly reactive metals (Al, Ti), stringent pre‐cleaning and higher spray pressures are often needed.  

In sum, oxide layers are an inevitable but manageable obstacle in cold spray.  The primary removal mechanism is high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at impact—which fractures and jets the oxide film away—supplemented by feedstock conditioning and optimized process parameters to minimize oxide thickness and maximize metal–metal contact.

In cold spray, particles ride a high‐velocity gas jet and build up a coating only where they impact with sufficient normal momentum. On non-flat or profiled substrates any “upstream” feature casts a geometric shadow onto downstream areas, so that those regions see fewer—or even no—particle impacts. That phenomenon is called the shadow effect.

Key points:  
1. Line-of-sight process  
   • Particles travel nearly straight from the nozzle; they do not wrap around corners.  
   • Raised or inclined features block the particle stream for areas lying “behind” them.  

2. Consequences in the shadow zones  
   • Reduced or zero deposition—thinner, porous, or missing coating.  
   • Poor adhesion, since the local particle velocity and impact density fall below the critical threshold for bonding.  
   • Increased risk of erosion or corrosion at uncoated spots.  

3. Common locations  
   • Deep grooves, holes, undercuts, recesses in complex shapes.  
   • Areas on the leeward side of weld beads, ribs, or stepped geometries.  

4. Mitigation strategies  
   • Re-orient the part or use multi-axis/robotic motion so that no feature remains permanently shadowed.  
   • Employ multiple spray passes at different angles.  
   • Use nozzles with wider spray patterns or multi-nozzle arrays to broaden the effective coverage.  
   • In some cases, introduce secondary gas jets or swirling flow attachments to deflect particles into sheltered regions.  

By recognizing the shadow effect and tailoring part handling or nozzle strategy accordingly, one can achieve more uniform thickness and consistent adhesion even on complex, non-planar substrates.

Key distinctions between low‐pressure (LP, roughly 0.5–1.5 MPa) and high‐pressure (HP, roughly 3–5 MPa and up) cold spray lie in equipment requirements, operating costs, spray patterns, and substrate impact.  The main advantages of LP cold spray are:

1. Lower capital and operating costs  
   • Smaller compressors (often air‐powered boosters rather than multi-stage high-pressure units)  
   • Reduced gas heating requirements (lower preheat temperatures or even unheated gas)  
   • Lower overall energy and consumable (gas) consumption  

2. Simpler, more compact equipment  
   • Fewer stages in the pressure booster and simpler plumbing  
   • Reduced need for high-pressure fittings, safety interlocks, and shielding  
   • Easier maintenance, less wear on nozzles and seals  

3. Portability and on-site flexibility  
   • Lighter, more compact spray guns and boosters  
   • Suited to field repair, coating of large or awkwardly shaped parts, weld seam build-up  

4. Gentle spray impingement  
   • Lower particle velocities (350–600 m/s vs. 700–1 200 m/s) reduce risk of substrate erosion or heat-sensitive part distortion  
   • Lower residual stresses in the deposit and substrate, useful on thin or delicate substrates  

5. Wider and more uniform spray patterns  
   • Larger nozzle diameters and broader divergence angles  
   • Faster coverage of large areas (e.g. corrosion protection, large‐area cladding)  

6. Improved handling of fine or soft powders  
   • Reduced powder fracture and embrittlement in the feeding line  
   • Better deposition of ductile or nano-structured materials that might over‐work in HP lines  

7. Lower noise levels and reduced shock waves  
   • Lower supersonic jet intensities translate to less shop-floor noise and vibration  

While LP cold spray typically yields lower peak particle velocities and can produce coatings with slightly higher porosity than HP processes, its cost, simplicity, and flexibility make it the preferred choice for many large-area, on-site, or heat‐sensitive applications.

Cold‐sprayed metal coatings almost never look like cast or spray‐plasma microstructures.  Instead you get  

1. A “bed” of plastically deformed particles, each one radially flattened (“splat‐like”), overlapping its neighbors  
2. Inside each particle the original grains are heavily work‐hardened and elongated in the direction of material flow  
3. Right at the particle–particle (and particle–substrate) interfaces you often see ultrafine or even nanocrystalline grains formed by dynamic recrystallization—driven by very high strain rates and local, adiabatic heating (shear instabilities) on impact  

Why this forms  
— Impact velocities (300–1200 m/s) impose strains of several hundred percent in microseconds.
