— The kinetic energy dissipates partly as heat in micron‐thick zones at the interface (“adiabatic shear”), briefly raising the temperature enough for recrystallization, but not long enough to coarsen the grains.  
— The result is bonded particles whose interfaces are finely recrystallized, surrounded by bodies of heavily deformed, dislocation‐rich metal.

Typical strain‐rate levels in cold spray are extremely high, owing to the very short impact/deformation times (t ≈ 10–100 ns) of high‐velocity particles (v ≈ 300–1200 m/s) over O(10–50 μm) deformation zones.  Roughly speaking you see:

1.   Bulk‐particle deformation  
     – Average strain rates on the order of 10^3–10^5 s^–1 when you average over the entire grain or particle volume.  
     – Localized “hot spots” inside the particle (e.g. cell/subgrain regions) can briefly reach 10^6–10^7 s^–1.

2.   Interfacial/shear‐jet region  
     – The very thin bonding zone (the “jet” and adiabatic‐shear layer at the particle–substrate or particle–particle interface) experiences the highest rates, typically 10^6–10^8 s^–1.  
     – In some materials (especially hard alloys) localized peaks may even exceed 10^8 s^–1 over a few nanoseconds.

These numbers shift somewhat with particle size, material, gas type, pressure and stand‐off distance, but 10^4–10^6 s^–1 (bulk) and 10^6–10^8 s^–1 (interface) are representative “rules of thumb.”

Among the three common crystal‐lattices (FCC, BCC, HCP), face-centered cubic (FCC) metals generally have the lowest resistance to deformation in cold spray.  Their high atomic packing density and 12 primary slip systems give them a relatively low critical resolved‐shear stress at room temperature, making FCC alloys (e.g. Al, Cu, Ni) the easiest to plastically deform and bond under cold‐spray impact.

Ceramic‐particle reinforcement in cold‐sprayed metal coatings arises from a combination of classic composite‐strengthening mechanisms plus the special microstructure inherited from the high‐strain, low‐temperature deposition process.  In practice you see five principal contributions:  

1. Load transfer to the hard particles  
   – Stiff ceramics carry a larger share of an applied load, unloading the softer metal matrix.  
   – If the particle–matrix bond is good, tensile or shear stresses transfer efficiently and raise the macroscopic yield strength.  

2. Orowan (dispersion) strengthening  
   – Nanometric or finely dispersed particles present obstacles to dislocation glide.  
   – Dislocations bow between particles (“Orowan loops”), adding a strength increment Δτ ≃ (Gb/λ)·ln(r/b), where G is shear modulus, b Burgers vector, λ inter‐particle spacing, r particle radius.  

3. Thermal‐mismatch induced dislocations  
   – Cooling from the (locally elevated) spray temperature creates differences in thermal contraction between metal and ceramic.  
   – These mismatches generate geometrically necessary dislocations concentrated around particle–matrix interfaces, boosting strain hardening.  

4. Grain‐refinement (Hall–Petch) via Zener pinning  
   – Ceramics pin grain‐boundary motion during the severe plastic deformation of cold spray, suppressing dynamic recrystallization and impeding grain growth.  
   – Finer grains in the metal matrix raise strength ∝ k·d^(–½).  

5. Work‐hardening and residual stresses  
   – The high‐velocity impact of powder particles produces very high local strains in the metal, pumping in dislocations even before any ceramic effects.  
   – In many systems a compressive residual stress field around the particles further retards crack initiation and dislocation motion.  

Taken together, these mechanisms can double or triple the hardness and significantly improve wear and fatigue resistance compared with the unreinforced cold‐sprayed metal.

Typical residual‐stress patterns in welded or laser‐glazed steels can be summarized as follows:

1. Welding  
   • Macrostress (Type‐I) in the longitudinal (along-weld) direction is tensile in the weld metal and heat-affected zone (HAZ), often peaking at or above the yield strength (σy×0.7–1.2) at the surface.  
   • Transverse (across-weld) stresses are also tensile but typically only 30–60% of the longitudinal magnitude.  
   • To satisfy force equilibrium, balancing compressive stresses develop in the parent metal some distance from the weld.  
   • Through‐thickness profiles often show tensile peaks at the surface, a reduction (or even slight compression) toward mid-thickness, and sometimes compressive “root” stresses on the weld’s backside (for single‐sided welds).  

2. Laser glazing (surface remelting)  
   • A very shallow (tens to a few hundred microns) compressive layer forms at the surface, often in the –200 to –800 MPa range, owing to rapid cooling and the constraint of the colder substrate.  
   • Immediately beneath that layer is a tensile “balancing” zone (typically +50 to +300 MPa) that decays back to near zero within a few melting‐depths into the bulk.  

In both cases the overall stress distribution is self-equilibrating: a surface zone of one sign (tension in welding, compression in glazing) is offset by an opposite sign zone deeper in the material.

Cold spray achieves dense, low-oxide coatings for three principal reasons:

1. Solid-state deposition  
   – Particles never melt; they remain below their liquidus.  
   – On impact (500–1 500 m/s) they undergo intense plastic deformation, fracturing and jetting out surface films and entrapped gases rather than entrapping them as pores.

2. Minimal in-flight oxidation  
   – Gas temperatures in cold spray (typically < 600 °C) are well below the melting point, so the oxygen uptake rate on particle surfaces is extremely low.  
   – Often inert or low-O₂ carrier gases (He, N₂) are used, further suppressing oxidation.

3. Absence of solidification defects  
   – Thermal sprays (APS, HVOF, plasma) use molten or semi-molten droplets that re-solidify, trapping gas, shrinkage voids, and forming oxide lamellae at splat boundaries.  
   – Cold spray bypasses melting/solidification altogether, eliminating these oxide- and pore-generating mechanisms.

Together, the high‐velocity solid‐state impact bonds powder into a highly consolidated deposit with far fewer voids and oxides than you see in conventional, high‐temperature thermal sprays.

Varying the tool–workpiece rotational speed (ω) in friction‐stir processing (FSP) of face‐centered‐cubic (FCC) alloys has two competing effects on the nugget (stir) zone microstructure:

1. Heat generation  
   – Q ∝ μ·F·ω (μ = friction coefficient, F = normal force)  
   – Higher ω → higher peak temperature → more thermal softening and dynamic recovery  

2. Strain rate and deformation per revolution  
   – Effective strain rate ε̇eff ∝ ω/traverse speed  
   – Lower ω (at fixed traverse) → smaller total heat input but higher strain per unit heat → promotes severe plastic deformation, high stored energy  

Putting these together:

• Low ω (insufficient heat)  
  – Peak temperature may lie below or just above the DRX threshold  
  – Deformation is highly localized, grains are elongated and subdivided into high‐angle subgrains but many retain unrecrystallized lamellar structure  
  – Overall recrystallized fraction is low (partial DRX), and the “apparent” grain size is large and heterogeneous  

• Moderate ω (optimum heat/strain balance)  
  – Peak temperature exceeds the critical DRX onset, but not so high as to drive extensive grain growth  
  – Zener–Hollomon parameter Z = ε̇ exp(Q/RT) remains high enough for continuous dynamic recrystallization (cDRX)  
  – Fully recrystallized, fine equiaxed grains (typically 1–5 μm in 2xxx–7xxx series Al alloys)  
  – Maximum recrystallized fraction (often approaching 100 %)  

• High ω (excessive heat input)  
  – Nugget temperature may approach solvus or even melting thresholds locally  
  – Dynamic recovery dominates over DRX; growth of new grains outpaces formation of new boundaries  
  – Grain coarsening sets in: equiaxed grains grow (5–20 μm or more, depending on alloy and dwell)  
  – Recrystallized fraction can still be high but the average grain size is larger and the size distribution broader  

Typical trends reported in Al‐alloys (e.g. AA6061):  
– ω = 400–600 rpm → incomplete DRX, mixed lamellar/subgrain structures, ~10–20 μm effective grain size  
– ω = 800–1200 rpm → full cDRX, uniform fine grains ~2–5 μm  
– ω > 1500 rpm → over‐aging and grain growth, grain size increases to >10 μm

Key takeaway: there is an optimal intermediate rotational speed at which the balance of strain rate and heat input maximizes continuous dynamic recrystallization and minimizes final grain size. Both too low and too high speeds lead to coarser and less uniform microstructures.

Within an individual cold-sprayed splat you almost always find a strong grain‐size and deformation gradient from the point of impact outward.  In very rough strokes you can divide the splat into three regions:

1.  Bonding/shear-instability zone (right at the particle–substrate or splat–splat interface)  
    •  Plastic strains are highest here (strain rates >10^6 s–1)  
    •  Adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization produce very fine, often sub-micron or even nanocrystalline grains  
    •  High dislocation density, strong lattice rotation and sometimes refined oxide dispersions  

2.  Lateral‐flow or “rim” zone (the region of lateral spreading)  
    •  Grains are severely elongated in the flow direction, but less refined than the impact core  
    •  A strong crystallographic texture can develop along the flow direction  
    •  Intermediate hardness and dislocation density  

3.  Un- or lightly-deformed core (center of the particle away from the immediate bond area)  
    •  Largely retains the original powder grain size and morphology (tens of microns)  
    •  Lowest dislocation density and hardness  

Because these subregions coexist side by side in every splat, you get significant mechanical heterogeneity on the length scale of a few microns:

•  Hardness variation:  the recrystallized impact zone can be 30–50 HV higher than the core.  
•  Yield strength and work‐hardening rates are highest in the ultrafine‐grained interface region and lowest in the core.  
•  Local residual stresses: compressive in the bond zone, tensile in the lightly deformed core and along splat boundaries.  
•  Elastic modulus and plastic anisotropy: the textured rim zones deform differently than the nearly equiaxed recrystallized grains.  

All of these lead to nonuniform load sharing, preferential sites for crack initiation (often at core–rim or intersplat boundaries), and a macroscopically anisotropic stiffness/strength response in the deposit.

When you assemble a perfectly‐bonded multilayer curved beam and stay in the elastic regime, two things happen almost immediately:  
 1. “Plane sections remain plane’’ in the circumferential (θ–) direction, so that at any given radius r all layers share exactly the same εθ there, and  
 2. Each layer’s σθ is just Eᵢ·εθ, so the stiffer plies carry more load than the soft ones.  

Below is the classical outline of how one computes the actual ε(r) and σᵢ(r):

1. Geometry and kinematics  
   – Let the beam occupy a ring‐sector between inner radius a and outer radius b.  
   – Suppose it is bent through an angle Φ about the centre of curvature.  
   – By definition the neutral‐radius Rₙ is the unique radius at which the circumferential strain εθ = 0.  
   – A material fiber at radius r lengthens from r·Φ to Rₙ·Φ, so the engineering strain there is  
       εθ(r) = (r·Φ – Rₙ·Φ)/(Rₙ·Φ) = r/Rₙ – 1.  

2. Force‐equilibrium to find Rₙ  
   – No resultant axial force ⇒ ∫ₐᵇ σθ(r) ·dA = 0  
   – But σθ(r)=Eᵢ·εθ(r) on that layer.  Splitting the cross‐section into layers i, one shows  
       0 =  ∑ᵢ ∫_{layer i} Eᵢ (r/Rₙ – 1) dA  
         = (1/Rₙ) ∑ᵢ Eᵢ ∫_{Aᵢ} r dA  – ∑ᵢ Eᵢ Aᵢ  
   – Hence  
       Rₙ = [ ∑ᵢ Eᵢ ∫_{Aᵢ} r dA ]  /  [ ∑ᵢ Eᵢ Aᵢ ]  
     or, if each layer is thin so r≈constant = r̅ᵢ,  
       Rₙ = (∑ᵢ Eᵢ Aᵢ r̅ᵢ)/(∑ᵢ Eᵢ Aᵢ).  

3. Stress in each layer  
   – Once Rₙ is known, the strain field is εθ(r)=r/Rₙ–1 throughout.  
   – In layer i at radius r:  
       σθ⁽ⁱ⁾(r) = Eᵢ [ r/Rₙ  – 1 ]  
     (and σr is zero at the free inner/outer faces in the usual curved‐beam approximation).  

4. Small‐curvature (slender beam) limit  
   – If the total thickness t=b–a is small compared with Rₙ you may set r/Rₙ ≃ 1+(r–Rₙ)/Rₙ.  Then  
       εθ(r) ≃ (r–Rₙ)/Rₙ  ≡ –κ y  ,    κ=1/Rₙ,   y=r–Rₙ  
     and  
       σθ⁽ⁱ⁾(y) = Eᵢ (–κ y)  
     just as in straight‐beam bending, with the neutral axis at y=0.  

Key take‐aways  
 • Strains are continuous across perfectly bonded interfaces and depend only on the radius r (or y) and on Rₙ.  
 • Stiffer layers carry proportionally more σ because σᵢ=Eᵢ·ε.  
 • The neutral radius Rₙ shifts toward the stiffer side according to ∑EᵢAᵢ r̅ᵢ.  
 • In the limit of small curvature you recover the familiar linear ε(y)=–κ y, σ(y)=E (–κ y) of straight‐beam theory.

Particle–substrate bonding in cold spray is fundamentally a solid‐state, high‐strain‐rate phenomenon driven by four interrelated effects:

1. Severe plastic deformation  
   - Upon impact at velocities typically above a material-specific “critical velocity,” both particle and substrate undergo extremely high strain rates (10^6–10^8 s^–1).  
   - The powder particle flattens into a thin “splat,” conforming to substrate asperities and generating a high density of dislocations.

2. Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) and localized heating  
   - Plastic work is converted into heat faster than it can be conducted away, producing localized temperature spikes at the particle–substrate interface.  
   - If the shear stress exceeds a threshold, ASI initiates: the interface softens and flows, promoting dynamic recrystallization of ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains that lock the two bodies together.

3. Oxide‐film disruption and metallic jetting  
   - The extreme pressures (several GPa) and associated “jet” of surface material forcibly eject and fracture native oxide or contaminant films.  
   - This cleaning action exposes fresh metal surfaces, enabling true metal–metal contact.

4. Mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding  
   - Mechanical interlocking arises as the deformed particle edge “nails” itself into substrate valleys.  
   - The intimate contact and high dislocation density at the interface allow metallic bonds (interatomic bonding and short‐range diffusion) to form even below the bulk melting point.

Key parameters controlling these mechanisms are impact velocity (must exceed the critical velocity), particle and substrate hardness and ductility, gas temperature/pressure (which govern particle velocity and substrate temperature), and substrate roughness (which affects interlocking). Together, these effects yield a coating with near‐bulk density and strength without ever melting the feedstock.

In cold‐spray the single most useful “lumping” variable for predicting coating build‐up, microstructure and bonding is the particle’s total specific energy – i.e. the sum of its kinetic and thermal energy per unit mass.  In its simplest form one writes:

   E* = ½ v²  +  Cp ΔT

where  
 •  v  = particle impact velocity  
 •  Cp = particle’s heat capacity  
 •  ΔT = (particle temperature − reference temperature)  

By plotting deposition efficiency or coating porosity against E* (or the closely related spray‐power‐density parameter, mass flux×E*), one obtains a single “process map” in which both velocity and temperature effects are simultaneously accounted for.

Cold‐sprayed coatings are produced by accelerating metal powders to very high velocities (300–1200 m/s) and impacting them onto a substrate.  The particle/substrate bonding and coating build‐up rely almost entirely on severe, very high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation rather than melting.  Here’s why they end up so highly dislocated, and what happens when you heat‐treat them:

1.  Origin of very high dislocation densities  
    •  Adiabatic shear at particle interfaces – At impact, strain rates exceed 10^6–10^9 s⁻¹ in micron‐scale shear bands.  Plastic work is locally adiabatic, so there’s little time for thermal diffusion, and nearly all the deformation energy is stored as dislocations.  
    •  Intense strain and strain gradients – Particles flatten, jet, and flow plastically to fill gaps.  Every increment of shear generates new dislocations (Frank–Read sources, cross‐slip, etc.), and high strain gradients (between the unmated core of a particle and its deformed rim) force forest hardening and dislocation multiplication.  
    •  Subgrain formation without recovery – There is essentially no time or temperature for dynamic recovery or recrystallization in flight, so the dislocations accumulate to levels of 10^14–10^16 m⁻².

2.  Effect of post‐spray heat treatment  
    When you heat a cold spray deposit (typically 0.3–0.6 Tm of the alloy), three thermally‐activated processes progressively reduce dislocation density and residual stress:  
    a.  Recovery  
       – Dislocation rearrangement and annihilation at jogs, junctions and low‐angle boundaries.  
       – Reduction of internal stress fields and formation of well‐defined subgrain structures.  
       – Modest softening, but grain morphology remains largely as‐sprayed.  
    b.  Static recrystallization  
       – Nucleation of new, dislocation‐free or low‐dislocation‐density grains at highly strained regions (particle interfaces, shear‐band intersections).  
       – Growth of these nuclei at the expense of the deformed microstructure, drastically reducing dislocation density (often by an order of magnitude or more).  
       – Significant drop in hardness and residual stress, with improved ductility.  
    c.  Grain growth and precipitation (at higher temperatures or longer times)  
       – Grain coarsening further lowers dislocation density per volume.  
       – In age‐hardening alloys, precipitates may form or coarsen and can pin residual dislocations, preventing full recovery and stabilizing a portion of the as-sprayed hardening.  

Net result: heat treatment converts the heavily work-hardened, dislocation-rich as-sprayed microstructure into a softer, more stable one with larger, recrystallized grains and far fewer mobile dislocations—trading some strength and hardness for reduced residual stress, improved ductility, toughness, and dimensional stability.

Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) in cold spray refers to a localized, runaway plastic‐deformation event that occurs at the high strain rates (>10^6 s–1) and impact pressures generated when a supersonic powder particle strikes a substrate or previously deposited layer. Under these conditions:  
• Plastic work is converted to heat faster than it can be conducted away (“adiabatic” heating).  
• Thermal softening locally overcomes strain hardening, so deformation focuses into very narrow shear bands (10’s–100’s of nanometers wide).  

Why it matters for bonding  
1. Oxide‐layer disruption and fresh‐metal exposure  
   • The intense shear-band flow mechanically jets away surface oxides and contaminants, exposing clean metal surfaces on both particle and substrate.  
2. Enhanced plastic flow and interlocking  
   • Within the shear bands the metal can flow almost like a superplastic or even quasi‐liquid medium, filling asperities in the counterpart surface and creating a high‐area mechanical interlock.  
3. Metallurgical bonding  
   • The combination of intimate atomic contact under high pressure, freshly exposed surfaces, and rapid cooling can then promote true metallic bonding across the interface (no intervening oxide).  

In practice, achieving ASI requires reaching a critical impact velocity (depends on material, particle size, temperature). Below that threshold, particles may simply rebound or cold weld poorly; above it, ASI yields the fine‐scale, high‐strength bonds characteristic of dense, coherent cold‐spray deposits.

Adding a few volume % of hard ceramic nanoparticles (Al₂O₃, SiC, TiO₂, etc.) into a polymer cold‐spray powder has two principal, coupled effects on build‐up rate (coating thickness per pass) and deposition efficiency (DE = mass deposited/mass sprayed):  

1. Enhanced Interparticle/Particle-Substrate Bonding  
   • The hard nanoparticles act as “micro-anchors” or asperities on each polymer particle’s surface.  Upon impact they protrude through the soft polymer shell, increasing local friction, mechanical interlocking and surface roughness.  
   • This lowers the critical velocity for adhesion of the polymer binder and raises the fraction of particles that stick, boosting DE.  

2. Improved Momentum Transfer into the Polymer Binder  
   • At moderate loadings (typically 3–15 wt %), ceramics stiffen the polymer particles just enough to transmit more of the spray jet’s kinetic energy into plastic deformation rather than elastic rebound.  
   • That deeper, more uniform deformation leads to denser, faster build-up of the polymer layer per pass.  

3. Pore-Filling and Matrix Densification  
   • Nanoparticles fill voids between deformed polymer lobes, lowering porosity in the growing coating.  
   • The result is a higher “deposited mass per pass,” i.e. faster thickness growth.  

4. Limits at High Ceramic Loading  
   • Beyond roughly 15–20 wt % the powder’s flowability degrades, particles tend to agglomerate, and nozzle clogging or turbulent entrainment can occur.  
   • Excessive stiffness of the mixed particle embrittles the matrix on impact, leading to microcracking, bounce-off and overall lower DE.  

Practical takeaway  
– Loading in the 5–15 wt % range typically maximizes both deposition efficiency (up to +20–50% versus pure polymer) and build-up rates.  
– Above ~20 wt % ceramic the negative effects on powder handling, nozzle wear and particle rebound outweigh the adhesion benefits, so DE and growth rate fall off.

Adiabatic shear instability (ASI) in cold spray is the dynamic, localized softening and runaway shear‐banding that occurs when a high-velocity powder particle impacts a substrate (or another particle) at strain rates on the order of 10^4–10^6 s^–1.  Key points:

1. Mechanism  
  • Under impact, almost all plastic work is converted into heat in a very thin region (shear band) faster than it can conduct away—hence “adiabatic.”  
  • Temperature rises locally, reducing flow stress (thermal softening) faster than material can harden by strain work or recover dynamically.  
  • Once softening outpaces hardening, shear localizes catastrophically into a narrow band (typically microns thick).

2. Role in Bonding  
  • The intense shear and local heating generate a high-velocity “jet” of surface material that cleans oxides and asperities, bringing fresh metal surfaces together.  
  • ASI thus fosters intimate metallic contact and metallurgical bonding without reaching bulk melting.

3. Critical Conditions  
  • Requires sufficiently high particle impact velocity (“critical velocity”), material that exhibits thermal softening (e.g. Cu, Al alloys), and high strain rate.  
  • Below critical velocity no jet forms and bonding is weak; above it, ASI enables good coating adhesion and density.

4. Microstructural Effects  
  • Produces ultrafine grains in the shear band due to dynamic recrystallization.  
  • Can, if excessive, introduce porosity, voids or particle fragmentation from over‐localized failure.

In summary, adiabatic shear instability is the self-accelerating, thermally driven localization of plastic deformation at the particle–substrate interface that underpins cleaning, jetting and bonding in cold spray deposition.

Dynamic recovery in the context of severe plastic deformation (SPD) of high–stacking-fault-energy (SFE) face-centered-cubic metals (e.g. Cu, Al, Ni) is the continual in-situ rearrangement and annihilation of dislocations that competes with their rapid multiplication under very large strains.  Because high-SFE materials readily cross-slip and (to some extent) climb even at room temperature, new dislocations do not simply pile up indefinitely but instead reorganize into lower-energy configurations as deformation proceeds.

Key points  
1. Mechanisms  
  • Cross-slip of screw segments allows opposite-sign dislocations to meet and annihilate.  
  • Dislocation climb (vacancy- or interstitial-assisted) helps remove edge components.  
  • Formation of dislocation walls/cell boundaries (incipient subgrains) reduces stored energy.  

2. Effect on Dislocation Density  
  • At small strains in SPD, dislocation density ρ rises steeply due to intense multiplication.  
  • As strain continues, dynamic recovery kicks in: annihilation and rearrangement rate grows with ρ.  
  • A dynamic equilibrium (saturation) is reached when generation ≈ annihilation.  
  • Typical saturation levels in high-SFE FCC metals under SPD lie in the 10^14–10^15 m–2 range, rather than diverging to 10^16–10^17 m–2.  

3. Microstructural Consequences  
  • Subgrain/cell structures form and refine toward ultrafine grains.  
  • Flow stress levels off according to τ ≃ α μ b √ρsat, where ρsat is the dynamically stabilized density.  
  • Further refinement to nanograins often requires additional mechanisms (e.g. continuous dynamic recrystallization) once subgrains rotatate toward high‐angle boundaries.  

In summary, dynamic recovery under SPD in high-SFE FCC metals is the high-rate, strain-driven process of dislocation annihilation and rearrangement (via cross-slip and climb) that limits and eventually stabilizes the dislocation density, enabling the transition from a tangled dislocation network to a refined subgrain/grain structure.

In cold spray, bonding is achieved by extreme‐velocity impact of metal particles onto a substrate, producing intense, localized plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at the interface. Preheating either the powder or the substrate (or both) influences that process in several interrelated ways:

1. Reduction of Material Strength  
   – Raising particle temperature lowers its yield strength and flow stress. On impact, particles deform more readily, promoting higher flattening ratios and intimate contact with the substrate.  
   – Heating the substrate similarly softens its surface layer, allowing deeper indentation by the incoming particle and increasing the real contact area.  

2. Lowered Critical Velocity  
   – The “critical velocity” (minimum particle speed for bonding) scales with material flow stress. Preheating can typically reduce critical velocity by ~5–15 % per 100 °C of particle or substrate heating, enabling deposition at lower propellant gas pressures or higher deposition efficiencies.  

3. Enhanced Interfacial Jetting and Shear Instability  
   – Softer materials at elevated temperature facilitate the lateral “jetting” of oxide and contaminant layers out of the impact zone, improving metal‐to‐metal contact.  
   – Adiabatic shear bands—which drive most of the bonding—form more readily when both particle and substrate have reduced work‐hardening resistance.  

4. Improved Deposition Efficiency and Coating Quality  
   – Because more particles stick on first impact (fewer rebounds), overall powder utilization goes up and porosity goes down.  
   – Layer adhesion strength and cohesion between successive passes are both enhanced, yielding denser, higher‐performance coatings.  

5. Thermally Activated Diffusion (to a Limited Extent)  
   – Although cold spray is nominally a solid‐state process, modest preheat (up to ~200–300 °C) can promote a thin diffusion-aided bond zone without causing bulk grain growth.  

6. Practical Considerations and Trade­offs  
   – Excessive preheat risks oxidizing powder or substrate, leading to embrittlement and poor bonding. Controlled atmospheres or vacuum preheating may be needed for highly oxidation‐sensitive alloys (e.g., Ti, Cu).  
   – Overly soft substrates can suffer from rebound erosion or excessive roughening. Optimizing preheat temperature (often 150–300 °C for steels, 200–400 °C for Ni‐alloys) is critical.  

In summary, preheating in cold spray reduces the flow stress of both particles and substrate, lowers the velocity threshold for bonding, enhances jetting of surface films, and ultimately improves deposition efficiency and bond strength—so long as temperatures are kept below levels that induce unwanted oxidation or excessive substrate softening.

Oxygen diffusion into a cold‐sprayed Ti or Ti‐alloy coating during a post‐spray thermal oxidation step almost always raises its surface and near‐surface hardness—but only up to a point—through two related mechanisms:  

1. Interstitial solid‐solution strengthening (“α‐case” formation)  
   • Oxygen atoms, small enough to occupy octahedral sites in the hexagonal α-Ti lattice, distort the Ti unit cell.  
   • These lattice strains strongly impede screw and edge dislocation motion.  
   • Typical as-sprayed Ti coatings (200–250 HV) can climb to 350–450 HV in the oxygen-enriched zone.  

2. Formation of hard titanium oxide phases  
   • At the coating surface and along splat boundaries, TiO, Ti2O3 or TiO2 scale nucleate and grow.  
   • TiO2 (rutile) in particular has a Vickers hardness in the 800–1 200 HV range.  
   • A thin, adherent oxide film “seals” pores and stiffens the outer few microns.  

Key points on kinetics and limits  
• Diffusion and scale growth follow a parabolic law:  x^2 = k·t,  so thickness of the α-case and oxide layer grows as the square root of time (and exponentially with temperature).  
• Hardness profiles therefore show a steep drop from the oxidized surface (400–1 000 HV) back to the as-sprayed core (200–300 HV) over a few to tens of micrometers.  
• If you over‐oxidize (excess time or temperature), the oxygen-rich α-case thickens and becomes brittle. Subscale microcracks or oxide spallation can actually reduce the effective hardness and compromise adhesion.  

In practice:  
– A moderate oxidation (e.g. 500–600 °C for 2–5 h in air) produces a ~5–20 µm hard α-case + oxide layer, boosting surface hardness by 50–100 %.  
– Longer times or higher T deepen the brittle zone, so there’s a trade-off between maximum hardness and mechanical integrity (toughness, adhesion).

During cold spray, particles impact the substrate (or previously deposited particles) at high velocity but well below their melting point.  Bonding occurs almost entirely in the solid state by a combination of the following mechanisms:

1. Severing of surface films and oxide fragments  
   • The very high‐strain‐rate impact locally fractures/removes oxide and adsorbed films on both particle and substrate surfaces.  
   • Fresh, clean metal surfaces are exposed over micron‐scale contact areas.

2. Severe plastic deformation and mechanical interlocking  
   • Impact pressures exceed the yield strength of the metal, causing intense plastic flow in both particle and substrate.  
   • The particle flattens (“pancakes”), plastically conforms to substrate asperities and engenders mechanical interlocking.

3. Adiabatic shear and interfacial jetting  
   • Localized, high‐strain‐rate shear instabilities produce narrow shear bands at the interface.  
   • Material is ejected laterally as a “jet,” flushing away residual oxides/contaminants and promoting intimate metal–metal contact.

4. Solid‐state metallurgical bonding  
   • Once oxides are displaced, metallic bonding (essentially atomic‐level cohesion) forms across the interface.  
   • In many alloys, the extreme strain rates induce dynamic recrystallization in the interfacial zone, refining grains and enhancing bond strength.

5. Multiple‐impact build-up and work‐hardening  
   • Subsequent particles repeatedly plastically deform earlier deposits, closing any remaining gaps and increasing dislocation density.  
   • This work hardening further raises local yield stresses, promoting stronger bonds upon each new impact.

Key point: no bulk melting occurs.  Instead, high‐velocity impact → oxide removal + severe plasticity → intimate, recrystallized metal–metal contact = a robust, fully solid‐state bond.

Deposition of very hard or brittle materials (e.g. ceramics, high-strength tool steels, WC, TiB₂) is intrinsically difficult in conventional cold spray because:

 1. Bonding in cold spray is driven by extreme particle-substrate shear and adiabatic‐shear instabilities in the impacting particle.  Hard materials have very high yield strength and low ductility at the high strain‐rates imposed, so they  
    – require unrealistically high gas pressures or temperatures (and hence particle velocities) to reach the critical velocity for bonding  
    – tend to fracture or rebound rather than plastically deform and weld  

 2. Without sufficient plastic flow at impact you get little metallurgical weld and poor deposition efficiency.

General strategy for expanding the material palette  
 ------------------------------------------------  
Instead of trying to cold‐spray bare hard particles, you engineer the feedstock so that a ductile phase carries (and bonds) the hard phase.  Common realizations are:

  • Ductile-shell or core–shell powders  
    – Coat hard‐phase cores (e.g. WC, TiB₂, SiC) with a thin ductile metal shell (Cu, Ni, soft steel).  The metal shell deforms and bonds at achievable cold‐spray velocities, trapping the hard core in a coherent coating.  

  • Composite/cermet powders or co‐spraying  
    – Mix hard reinforcement powders with a ductile binder powder (e.g. 5–25 vol % WC + Ni or Co binder).  The binder plastically deforms and welds to substrate and itself, locking in the hard particles.  

  • In‐flight or in‐situ alloying  
    – Use reactive or mechanically activated powders that soften (alloy, amorphize, microcrystallize) under impact, lowering their dynamic yield strength just enough to bond.  

  • “Warm” or hybrid cold spray  
    – Raise gas temperature (or preheat particles/substrate) without melting, to reduce particle flow stress and critical velocity for hard phases.  

By always retaining a ductile, plastically deformable component in the impacting mixture (whether as a shell, matrix, binder or transient soft phase), you can lower the overall critical velocity for bonding and thus cold‐spray materials that would otherwise be too hard or brittle to deposit.

Cold spray (also called cold gas dynamic spray) is a solid-state coating/deposition process in which fine powder particles (typically 5–50 μm) are entrained in a high-pressure, high-temperature gas stream (N₂ or He, 300–800 °C) and accelerated to supersonic velocities (500–1 200 m/s) through a converging–diverging (“De Laval”) nozzle. Upon impact with the substrate, particles undergo extreme plastic deformation and mechanically interlock to form a dense, adherent coating—without melting the feedstock.  

Materials successfully deposited by cold spray include:  
1. Pure metals  
  • Aluminum, copper, nickel, titanium and their oxides (e.g. Al2O3-reinforced Al)  
  • Precious metals such as silver and gold (for electronics)  
2. Alloys and superalloys  
  • Stainless steels (304, 316L), Inconel®, Hastelloy®, Ti-6Al-4V  
  • High-entropy alloys (CoCrFeNi, etc.)  
3. Metal matrix composites (MMCs)  
  • Hard particles (SiC, Al₂O₃, TiC) in a ductile metal matrix  
  • Functionally graded coatings (e.g. corrosion‐resistant outer layer + wear‐resistant inner layer)  
4. Cermets and intermetallics  
  • NiAl, TiAl, WC–Co, Cr₃C₂–NiCr for wear and corrosion protection  
5. Ceramics (under special conditions)  
  • Partially stabilized zirconia, alumina, hydroxyapatite (often assisted by ductile metal “carriers”)  
6. Polymers and biomaterials (emerging)  
  • Thermally sensitive polymers or blends with metal binders for biomedical or flexible electronics  

Because there’s no bulk melting, cold spray preserves feedstock microstructure (no oxidation or phase transformations), enables repair of heat-sensitive parts, and produces coatings with high bond strength, low porosity (<1–2 %), and controlled residual stresses.

The term “critical‐velocity ratio” in cold spray is simply the particle’s actual impact velocity divided by the material’s critical (minimum) velocity for adhesion:
  
  critical‐velocity ratio R = Vimpact / Vc  

  • Vc (the “critical velocity”) is the lowest speed at which a given particle–substrate pair will plastically deform and adhere rather than rebound.  
  • R < 1 means the particle arrives too slowly, rebounds elastically or only slightly plastically deforms, and the bonding probability is essentially zero.  
  • R ≈ 1 is the threshold for the onset of significant plastic flow. At R just above 1 you get limited jetting and relatively low but rising probability of adhesion (say 10–50 %).  
  • R in the range 1.1–1.3 is typically where plastic deformation and interfacial jetting are sufficient to expose fresh metal, so bonding probability climbs above 80 – 90 %.  
  • R ≫ 1.3–1.5 can lead to excessive deformation, particle break-up or substrate erosion, which again drives down net deposition efficiency.

Qualitatively, you can think of both the particle’s peak strain and its contact pressure scaling strongly with (Vimpact–Vc).  Once Vimpact just exceeds Vc, plastic flow localizes at the leading edge, triggers a high‐speed lateral jet of clean metal, and allows intimate contact at the interface.  As you increase R above 1, the volume of plastically deformed material grows, the interfacial jet becomes more pronounced, and the statistical likelihood of a “good” metallic bond rises steeply—up to the point where over-deformation introduces new failure modes.  

In practice most cold‐spray systems aim for R≈1.1–1.2 to maximize deposition efficiency while avoiding substrate damage or particle erosion.

Key microstructural features of cold‐sprayed metallic coatings and their origins can be summarized as follows:

1. Lamellar, Layered Morphology  
   – Coatings build up as overlapping “pancake” or flake‐like particles.  
   – Each particle retains much of its original shape, producing a strongly anisotropic, layered architecture.

2. Narrow, Highly Deformed Interfacial Zones  
   – At every particle–particle and particle–substrate contact there is an ≈1–5 μm‐thick band of ultra–highly strained material.  
   – Within these bands you find:  
     • Very high dislocation densities (10^14–10^16 m–2)  
     • Nano‐ to submicron‐sized grains or subgrains (dynamic recrystallization)  
     • Evidence of adiabatic shear instabilities (“shear‐lip” formation and jetting)  

   Origin:  
   – When particles impact at 300–1200 m/s, local strain rates of 10^5–10^6 s–1 and adiabatic heating drive severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization just at the interface.

3. Largely Undeformed Particle Cores  
   – Away from the immediate contact zones the interior of each particle remains close to the feedstock microstructure (original grain size and dislocation density).  
   – A sharp gradient in grain size and stored energy exists between the deformed rim and the core.

4. Oxide/Impurity Fragments at Interfaces  
   – Native oxide layers on powder surfaces become fractured into fine debris during impact.  
   – Some debris is entrapped at boundaries, forming oxide‐rich stringers or pockets that can act as cleavage or crack initiation sites.

5. Residual Porosity and Unbonded Regions  
   – Incomplete particle interlocking or insufficient local deformation leads to micron‐scale pores, especially at “triple‐particle” junctions.  
   – Porosity is typically 1–5 vol% in well‐optimized Cu or Al coatings, higher in harder alloys.

6. Texture and Crystallographic Anisotropy  
   – The severe uniaxial compression during impact imposes shear‐type texture in the deformed bands (e.g. rolling‐type textures in Al or Cu).  
   – This can lead to anisotropic mechanical or thermal behavior in the coating.

Why these features arise in cold spray:  
• Mechanical bonding, not melting: particles must plastically flow, fracture their oxides, and “jet” material outwards to weld, all at near‐ambient bulk temperatures.  
• Very high strain rates generate extreme dislocation densities and local heating, but only over microns, so particle cores stay “cold.”  
• Successive impacts build up a stacked‐flake structure in which bonding quality and microstructure evolve layer by layer.

Induction heating is a contact‐free way to preheat or maintain the temperature of a metal substrate in many additive-manufacturing (AM) processes (laser/powder‐bed fusion, directed‐energy deposition, cold spray, etc.).  It works by the following steps:  

1. An AC power source drives a coil wrapped around or placed close to the substrate.  Because the current in the coil alternates (typically kHz–MHz), it produces a time-varying magnetic field.  
2. That changing field penetrates the conductive substrate and—via Faraday’s law—induces circulating “eddy” currents in the near-surface region.  
3. The eddy currents dissipate by resistive (Joule) heating: P = I²R, where R is the local resistance of the metal.  
4. If the substrate is ferromagnetic (e.g. steels), additional losses occur from magnetic hysteresis and domain‐wall motion.  

Key parameters are the frequency (which controls skin depth, δ ∝ 1/√f), coil geometry (which shapes the field), and power level (which sets the heat‐up rate).  By selecting frequency and coil design, you can tailor the heating zone so that the substrate (or the just‐deposited material) is uniformly brought to the desired process temperature—minimizing thermal gradients, reducing residual stress, and improving interlayer bonding.

1. Definitions  
  a. Rebound velocity (v­r): the lowest impact speed at which a particle just begins to deform plastically on collision with a substrate.  Below v­r the collision is essentially elastic (coefficient of restitution ≈1) and the particle rebounds with negligible shape change.  Above v­r plastic flow consumes part of the kinetic energy, but typically still leaves the particle bouncing off.  
  b. Critical (bonding) velocity (v­c): the minimum impact speed at which a particle undergoes such intense, localized plastic flow and adiabatic shear at the interface that oxide films are jet‐stripped away, fresh metal meets fresh metal, and a metallurgical bond forms.  For most metals v­c lies in the 300–1200 m/s range (depending on material, particle size, gas, nozzle design, etc.).  

2. Governing deformation mechanisms  
  a. Elastic–plastic transition (governs v­r)  
  – At low speeds (<v­r) contact pressures never exceed the dynamic yield strength σd of the particle or substrate, so deformation is entirely elastic.  
  – The threshold for irreversible plastic flow can be estimated by equating the maximum Hertzian contact pressure to σd, or by setting the local strain rate–dependent yield condition σ(ε̇) = ρ·v­r²/2.  
  b. Adiabatic shear localization and jetting (governs v­c)  
  – Above v­r but below v­c, the collision produces distributed plastic strain without sufficient local heating or shear instability to break oxides or create a clean interface—the particle still rebounds (albeit plastically deformed).  
  – At v ≥ v­c, the impact strain rate (typically 10⁵–10⁷ s⁻¹) drives rapid, nearly adiabatic temperature rise in a narrow shear band.  Thermal softening overtakes strain hardening and the flow localizes into an interfacial jet that ejects surface films.  The ensuing dynamic recrystallization and high interfacial pressures (>1 GPa) allow true metallic bonding.  

In summary, the rebound velocity marks the onset of plastic deformation controlled by the dynamic yield strength and strain-rate sensitivity of the metal.  The higher critical velocity marks the point at which adiabatic shear instabilities, jetting, and oxide removal occur, enabling particles to weld to the substrate rather than rebound.

In cold spray the dominant driving force is the particle’s kinetic energy (KE ≈ ½ m·v²), which at typical gas‐jet velocities (300–1,200 m/s) is high enough that upon impact the local stresses far exceed the weak interparticle bonds in powder agglomerates.  Two key effects follow:

1. Agglomerate break-up  
   – When a cluster of primary particles (“agglomerate”) strikes the substrate or an already‐deposited layer, the compressive and shear stresses in the particle are transmitted through the agglomerate.  If those stresses exceed the agglomerate’s cohesive strength, the cluster fragments into smaller sub‐agglomerates or individual grains.  
   – This de-agglomeration is beneficial: it promotes more uniform deposition of single particles, minimizes trapped voids, and leads to higher inter‐particle contact area.

2. Particle flattening and surface roughness  
   – Once de-agglomerated, the freed primary particles undergo extreme plastic deformation (“splatting”), driven by the same KE.  They form disk-like lamellae that weld together under “adiabatic shear” and high strain-rate conditions.  
   – If KE is too low, many agglomerates survive intact and embed only partially, producing large surface asperities—i.e. a rough, irregular topography.  
   – At an optimal KE window the agglomerates are fully broken, the particles flatten uniformly, and subsequent impacts (micro-peening) can even out residual peaks, yielding a relatively smooth coating.  
   – At excessively high KE the repeated high-energy impacts can erode or rebound fine fragments, generate micro-cracks, or re-scatter particles, which actually increases roughness or induces pitting.

In practice, controlling gas pressure, temperature and nozzle geometry to tune particle velocity—and matching that to the agglomerate strength and powder morphology—is the key to minimizing surface roughness by ensuring full de-agglomeration and ideal splat formation.

Ductile‐metal particles and ceramic particles behave very differently in a cold‐spray jet because the process of bonding relies in large part on the ability of the particles to plastically deform on impact.  Key contrasts are:  

1. Plastic Deformation versus Brittle Fracture  
   • Metals (Al, Cu, Ni, etc.)  
     – At typical cold-spray velocities (400–1,200 m/s) they undergo severe plastic deformation (adiabatic shear), flattening into “splats,” generating fresh metal–metal contact, and forming oxide-free metallurgical bonds.  
   • Ceramics (Al2O3, SiC, TiO2, etc.)  
     – Virtually no plasticity. Under the same conditions they tend to remain nearly rigid, fragment, crack, or simply rebound off the substrate. They cannot form true metallurgical bonds by themselves.  

2. Deposition Efficiency  
   • Metals: high efficiency (>80–90 %) once the critical velocity is exceeded, leading to dense, low‐porosity coatings.  
   • Ceramics: very low direct‐deposition efficiency unless velocities are pushed extremely high. Most particles either shatter on impact, bounce off, or embed only shallowly, producing high‐porosity, poorly adherent layers.  

3. Bonding Mechanism  
   • Metals: mechanical interlocking + dynamic metallurgical bonding (oxide disruption, local heating, shear instabilities).  
   • Ceramics: require a ductile “carrier” or binder phase (metal or polymer) to plastically deform around the hard particles and anchor them. In a metal–ceramic composite spray the metal matrix flows and bonds to substrate, carrying the ceramic fragments in suspension.  

4. Microstructure and Residual Stress  
   • Metals: equiaxed, heavily strained grains near particle interfaces, compressively residual stressed coatings of high density.  
   • Ceramics: highly fractured particles, irregular‐shaped fragments, wide crack networks, tensile residual stress; coatings risk spallation unless a compliant binder or post‐spray annealing is used.  

5. Practical Approaches for Ceramic Cold Spray  
   • Use a ductile metal or polymer binder (i.e. Al/Al2O3, Cu/SiC mixtures).  
   • Preheat substrate to lower thermal mismatch and reduce brittleness in ceramics.  
   • Optimize gas temperature and pressure to maximize kinetic energy without catastrophically fracturing the ceramic.  
   • In some hybrid processes, employ a second spray head or post‐spray consolidation (e.g. laser remelting) to densify and bond the ceramic phase.  

Bottom line: ductile metals bond through plastic deformation and shear‐induced metallurgical bonding; ceramics, being brittle, cannot plastically flow, so they either fracture or bounce. Successful ceramic coatings by cold spray almost always rely on a ductile carrier matrix to embed and lock in the hard particles.

Key cold‐spray parameters that drive up residual stresses in the deposited coating all boil down to accelerating particles to higher velocities, increasing per‐pass deformation, or building up thicker, more constrained layers.  In practice the most important levers are:

1. Gas pressure and pressure ratio  
   – Raising the compressed‐gas inlet pressure (or the pressure ratio P₀/Pₐ) boosts jet velocity and hence impact velocity, which increases plastic deformation and associated compressive stresses.  

2. Gas temperature and gas type  
   – Higher preheat temperatures reduce gas density and raise particle speed.  
   – Switching from nitrogen to helium (or using He-rich blends) further increases particle velocity and stress.  

3. Stand-off distance  
   – Operating at or slightly below the jet’s “shock‐free” focal point (i.e. a shorter stand‐off) produces the highest particle speeds—and therefore the greatest residual stresses—at the substrate.  

4. Traverse speed (torch dwell time)  
   – Slower traverse speeds (more overlapping passes per unit area) build up thickness more rapidly and give each layer less opportunity to relax, locking in higher stresses.  

5. Powder feed rate  
   – Increasing feed rate (for a constant carrier flow) raises the mass flux of impacting particles.  Thicker, more rapidly grown deposits accumulate higher residual stresses.  

6. Impact angle  
   – Near‐normal incidence (90° ± 5°) maximizes the normal component of particle momentum, intensifying plastic deformation and compressive stresses.  

7. Nozzle geometry  
   – Nozzles with higher expansion ratios and longer straight sections yield better gas acceleration and narrower jets—both of which increase particle velocity and stress.  

8. Deposit thickness (number of passes)  
   – Thicker coatings develop larger through‐thickness stress gradients.  Without intermediate stress relief (e.g. thermal annealing or peening), overall residual stresses grow with total thickness.  

9. Substrate temperature control  
   – Cold substrates tend to clamp the deposit more strongly, inhibiting stress relaxation.  Conversely, preheating above ~0.3 Tm can relieve some stress, so keeping substrate cool preserves higher residuals.  

By tuning these parameters toward maximum particle velocity, high layer‐build rates, and tight geometric control, you promote the intense plastic deformation and layer‐constraint that give rise to larger-magnitude residual stresses in cold‐spray coatings.

Cold‐spray additive manufacturing (CSAM) is a solid‐state, layer-by-layer build-up technique in which metal (or metal‐matrix) powders are pneumatically accelerated to high velocities (typically 300–1 200 m/s) and “cold” sprayed onto a substrate to form a dense deposit without melting.  

Key features and bonding mechanism:  
1. Powder acceleration  
   • An inert carrier gas (He or N₂), heated to a few hundred °C, expands through a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle.  
   • The pressure drop in the nozzle converts thermal energy to kinetic energy, accelerating the powder to supersonic speeds.  

2. Particle impact and plastic deformation  
   • Upon impact, each particle experiences extreme strain rates (10⁶–10⁹ s⁻¹).  
   • Severe plastic deformation generates adiabatic shear instabilities at the particle–substrate (and particle–particle) interfaces, locally removing surface oxides.  

3. Metallurgical bonding  
   • Fresh metal surfaces meet under high contact pressure, enabling atomic‐scale intimate contact.  
   • Mechanical interlocking and shear‐driven jetting promote cold welding rather than sintering or melting.  

4. Layer build-up  
   • By rastering the nozzle (or moving the part), successive layers are deposited and bonded.  
   • Because temperatures remain below the alloy’s melting point, microstructural coarsening, residual stresses, and thermal distortion are minimized.  

Applications span repair coatings, freeform builds of ductile alloys, and functionally graded materials where preservation of feedstock microstructure is critical.

At the deposit–substrate boundary in laser‐assisted cold spray (LACS) the net heat‐flux is not just “pure” conduction; it is the sum of several coupled mechanisms:

 1. Solid–solid conduction across the evolving contact area  
    • As particles deform and ﬂatten they establish new micro‐asperity contacts; heat conducts from the hotter partner (usually the substrate or the plastically heated particle) into the colder one.  
    • Interfacial contact resistance (determined by real contact area, gap conductance through any trapped gas, oxide films etc.) strongly modulates this term.

 2. Heat carried in by the particles (advection + conduction)  
    • Each particle brings its own thermal energy (from the laser preheat and/or prior impacts). Upon impact it dumps that energy into the near‐surface of the deposit/substrate by both direct conduction and internal diffusion from the impact zone.  
    • Because the particles are in motion, this can be thought of as a localized “advective” contribution to the boundary heat‐flux.

 3. Frictional and deformation (plastic‐work) heating  
    • High‐velocity impact generates intense, localized plastic deformation and friction in the very top layers of substrate and newly forming deposit. Up to 90 % of the particles’ kinetic energy can convert to heat in sub‐micron “adiabatic shear” bands at the interface.  
    • This heat is effectively a volumetric heat‐source that immediately conducts away from the shear zone into both deposit and substrate.

 4. Convective exchange with the process gas  
    • The supersonic or high‐pressure carrier gas jet cools (or, if preheated by the laser plume, warms) the near‐surface gas layer. Heat is swept away (or supplied) by gas‐side convection at the free surface of the deposit and substrate edge, which in turn alters the temperature gradient driving conduction at the buried interface.

 5. Thermal radiation  
    • The laser itself irradiates both substrate and powder plume; some of that radiative power is absorbed in the deposit/substrate region.  
    • At elevated temperatures the surfaces also radiate to the surroundings (and back onto each other in tight geometries), adding a small radiative‐exchange term to the overall boundary energy balance.

Putting them together, the instantaneous interfacial heat‐flux qtotal is typically written in an energy‐balance form as:

  qtotal  = qcond(contact)  
           + qadvective(particles)  
           + qmech(plastic/friction)  
           – qconv(gas)  
           – qrad  

where each term must be evaluated using local temperatures, contact area, flow conditions, material properties, and impact parameters.

Cold spray and spray‐forming both deposit copper particles in a “spray” mode, but the physics of consolidation are entirely different.  In brief, cold‐sprayed copper coatings end up nearly pore‐free because they never melt—‐there is no liquid‐state shrinkage, gas entrapment or inter‐dendritic porosity—and because the high‐velocity impacts mechanically weld and plastically flow the powder into a dense mass.  

Key reasons for minimal porosity in cold‐sprayed Cu versus spray form Cu:  
1. Solid‐state deposition  
   • Particles remain solid on impact; there is no solidification from the liquid state, so no shrinkage cavities, entrapped gas or dendritic porosity typical of spray‐formed (melt‐based) deposits.  

2. Extreme plastic deformation and jetting  
   • Impact velocities (300–1200 m/s) generate adiabatic shear at the particle–substrate and particle–particle interfaces.  
   • Surface oxides are fractured and expelled (“jetting”), exposing fresh metal and creating true metallic bonds.  

3. Mechanical interlocking and dynamic recrystallization  
   • The copper particles flatten and interlock under the shockwave, filling any gaps.  
   • Localized heating and dynamic recrystallization at the interface further eliminate residual voids and strengthen the bond.  

4. Absence of thermal‐cycle–induced porosity  
   • Cold spray operates at or slightly above room temperature, so there is little oxidation during deposition and no thermal contraction upon cooling.  

By contrast, spray forming (or plasma/thermal spray) melts the copper: droplets solidify on impact, sometimes entrapping process gas, forming inter‐dendritic voids, suffering shrinkage porosity, and relying on post‐deposition heat treatment or diffusion sintering to reduce but never fully eliminate pores. Cold spray’s “hit-and-hug” solid‐state weld mechanism closes voids in real time, yielding coatings with porosities typically < 1 %.

The softening of cold-sprayed Al alloys on annealing is overwhelmingly controlled by relief of their very high as-sprayed defect density and the attendant evolution of a more equiaxed, low-strain‐energy grain structure.  In practice three successive, partly overlapping microstructural processes are at work:

1. Recovery  
   • Dislocation annihilation (glide and cross-slip) and rearrangement into low-energy walls/subgrains  
   • Reduction of internal stresses without the formation of fully new (high-angle) grain boundaries  

2. Recrystallization  
   • Nucleation of strain-free grains (often at original particle–particle interfaces or regions with high dislocation density)  
   • Growth of these nuclei at the expense of the deformed matrix, producing high-angle boundaries and restoring bulk ductility  

3. Grain growth (at higher annealing temperatures or long times)  
   • Boundary migration driven by residual curvature/energy differences  
   • Coarsening of recrystallized grains, further reducing strength via the Hall–Petch relationship  

In commercial Al alloys (e.g. 2xxx, 6xxx, 7xxx series), you may also see concurrent changes in second-phase particles—coarsening or partial dissolution of strengthening precipitates—which further contributes to softening but is typically secondary to recovery and recrystallization in cold-sprayed material.

Deposition efficiency (DE) in cold spray is simply the fraction (or percentage) of feedstock powder that actually ends up adhering to the substrate rather than rebounding or blowing through the system.  Mathematically one usually writes it as

 DE = (mass of powder deposited on the part) / (mass of powder fed into the spray gun) × 100 %.

Although many parameters (particle size, gas temperature and pressure, stand‐off distance, substrate roughness, etc.) play a role, the single most critical factor controlling DE is the particle impact velocity relative to the material’s critical adhesion velocity.  Once the particle velocity exceeds this critical velocity, particles undergo the severe plastic deformation needed for bonding, and DE rises steeply.

Coatings rich in high‐angle grain boundaries (HAGBs, misorientation >15°) corrode along the boundary network far more readily than those made up mostly of low‐angle boundaries.  The main reasons are:

1. Higher boundary energy and atomic disorder  
   – A high‐angle boundary is a pronounced disruption of the crystal lattice.  Its higher excess energy makes it thermodynamically favorable for corrosion‐driving reactions (adsorption of aggressive ions, film breakdown) to initiate there.  

2. Fast diffusion and transport paths  
   – HAGBs provide “short‐circuits” for atomic and ionic transport.  Corrosive species (Cl–, H₂O, O₂) penetrate and diffuse along them much faster than through grain interiors, so localized attack advances rapidly intergranularly.  

3. Solute segregation and precipitate formation  
   – Impurities or alloying elements (e.g. S, P, Cr in stainless steels) preferentially segregate at HAGBs.  Where, for example, chromium carbides precipitate, they leave adjacent regions chromium‐depleted and unable to maintain a protective passive film—classic sensitisation—so the boundary itself becomes anodic and dissolves.  

4. Microgalvanic coupling  
   – The chemistry at a high‐angle boundary often differs from that of the surrounding grains (different oxide thickness, precipitate mix, or alloy‐depletion).  This compositional inhomogeneity creates tiny galvanic cells that drive selective dissolution at the boundary.  

By contrast, low‐angle boundaries contain only small arrays of dislocations and remain relatively continuous in their crystallography, so they are lower‐energy, less prone to segregation, and offer fewer fast‐diffusion paths.  As the fraction of HAGBs goes up, you increase the total length of “weak links” at which intergranular attack can start and propagate, hence a greater susceptibility to intergranular corrosion.

Cold spray operates at extremely high local strain‐rates (typically 10^4–10^7 s^−1) in the particle–substrate and particle–particle impact zones.  Two simple scaling arguments show why almost all of the plastic work must then appear as local heating (i.e. why the process is essentially adiabatic):

1.   Thermal-diffusion vs. deformation timescales  
     –  Thermal‐diffusion time across a characteristic deformation zone of size L is  
        t_th ≃ L^2/α_th,  
        where α_th ≃ k/(ρC_p) is the thermal diffusivity.  For L ≈ 10^−6–10^−5 m and typical metals α_th ∼ 10^−5 m^2/s, t_th∼10^−7–10^−5 s.  
     –  The mechanical deformation time is t_def≈1/ε̇.  At ε̇≳10^5 s^−1, t_def≲10^−5 s and can be 10–100× shorter than t_th.  

   Because t_def≪t_th, there is insufficient time for heat to diffuse away during the impact pulse, and the deformation can be treated as nearly adiabatic.

2.   Measured strain-rate dependence of heat dissipation  
     –  If one actually measures the fraction of plastic work converted to heat (the Taylor–Quinney coefficient η) as a function of ε̇, one observes that at low ε̇ a significant fraction of that heat is conducted away during deformation, but as ε̇ rises above 10^3–10^4 s^−1 the fraction dissipated through conduction drops sharply toward zero.  
     –  In other words, Q_gen≡∫σ dε grows with ε̇, but Q_cond (which ∼k∇^2T · t_def) cannot keep pace, so the generated heat stays where it is produced.  

Taken together, these observations show that at cold‐spray strain rates virtually all of the plastic work is trapped as a local temperature rise rather than being conducted away.  That rapid, locally confined heating—termed adiabatic shear heating—softens or even partially melts the metal at the impact interface, greatly enhancing bonding without bulk heating of the substrate.

In cold‐gas (or cold spray) deposition, particles are accelerated to high velocities (300–1 200 m/s) in a supersonic gas jet and impact a substrate well below their melting point. Because no melting occurs, the dominant bonding mechanism is solid-state bonding via severe plastic deformation and associated adiabatic shear instabilities at the particle–substrate (and particle–particle) interface.  

Key points on how this influences coating formation  
1. Critical Velocity Threshold     • Each alloy has a “critical velocity” above which particles deform sufficiently to break up surface oxides and establish clean metal–metal contact.     • Below that velocity, particles simply bounce or adhere weakly; above it, dense, well-bonded coatings form.  
2. Interface Jetting and Mechanical Interlocking     • Upon impact, material at the leading edge of the particle flows outward (“jetting”), scouring oxides and irregularities.     • The massive plastic flow creates mechanical interlocks and intimate contact that, given the high strain rates (~10⁷–10⁹ s⁻¹), mechanically weld together metal lattices.  
3. Microstructure and Properties     • Severe plastic deformation induces work hardening, ultra-fine or nanocrystalline grains, and high dislocation densities near interfaces.     • Low process temperatures minimize oxidation, phase changes, and thermal residual stresses.     • The resulting coatings are dense (porosity <2–5 %), exhibit high bond strengths (>300 MPa in many systems), and retain feedstock alloy chemistries.  

In sum, cold gas spraying relies on high‐velocity, solid‐state impact bonding—plastic deformation plus adiabatic shear—rather than fusion. This yields coatings with low oxide content, fine microstructures, and strong interparticle and particle–substrate adhesion without the drawbacks of high‐temperature spray processes.

Powder particle size is one of the single most important knobs for tuning both the in‐flight cooling rate of an atomized droplet and the scale and morphology of the solidification microstructure you end up with.  In inert‐gas atomized Al‐alloy powders the link goes roughly like this:

1.  Cooling‐rate vs. particle size  
   •  A molten droplet of diameter d in a high‐velocity inert gas stream sheds heat at a rate proportional to its surface area (∼d²), while its thermal mass scales with its volume (∼d³).  To a first approximation  
     cooling rate R ≡ dT/dt ∝ (h A ΔT)/(ρ Cp V) ∝ 1/d.  
   •  In practice you see R rise from 10²–10³ K/s in 100–150 µm powders to 10⁴–10⁶ K/s (or more) once you drop below 20–30 µm.  

2.  Effect on microstructure scale (primary dendrite/cellular arm spacing)  
   •  There is a well‐known empirical scaling of primary arm spacing λ with cooling rate:  
     λ ∝ R⁻ⁿ,  with n ≈ 0.3–0.5.  
   •  So if you halve the powder diameter (roughly doubling R), λ shrinks by ≈20–40 %.  
   •  In absolute terms:  
     –  Large powders (70–150 µm) → R∼10²–10³ K/s → λ of 2–10 µm, fully dendritic or mixed dendritic/cellular.  
     –  Medium powders (30–70 µm) → R∼10³–10⁴ K/s → λ of 0.5–2 µm, mostly fine cellular or feathery dendrites.  
     –  Fine powders (<30 µm) → R∼10⁴–10⁶ K/s → λ down to a few 100 nm, often entirely cellular or even nearly equiaxed “amorphous‐like” structures with heavy solute trapping.  

3.  Morphological transitions  
   •  Very small droplets cool so fast that nucleation density is high and growth is stunted → equiaxed or cellular structures with very fine spacing.  Solute partitioning is curtailed → you can retain supersaturated solid solutions or metastable phases.  
   •  Larger droplets cool more slowly, giving time for well-developed dendrites to grow and coarsen, and for solute to segregate into interdendritic channels.  

4.  Practical consequences for AM or cold‐spray feedstocks  
   •  Finer powder → higher hardness (from solute supersaturation and grain‐boundary strengthening), more uniform microchemistry, but also higher oxygen pickup and flowability issues.  
   •  Coarser powder → lower residual stresses in the deposit, but coarser, more segregated microstructure requiring more heat treatment to homogenize.  

In summary, reducing powder diameter raises the in‐flight cooling rate roughly in inverse proportion to d, which in turn drives the primary microstructural scale down via λ∝R⁻⁰․³–⁰․⁵, and pushes the morphology from coarse dendritic to fine cellular/equiaxed, with attendant effects on segregation, phase retention, and mechanical properties.

Increasing the ceramic‐particle fraction in your cold‐spray blend undermines their deposition efficiency for three interrelated reasons:

1. Reduced “metal‐binder” buffering and trapping  
   – In a ductile‐rich blend, metal particles plastically deform on impact and entrain the harder ceramics. When you dilute the metal fraction, fewer ductile particles are available to “cushion” and weld the ceramics in. Ceramics striking other ceramics simply rebound rather than embed.  

2. Increased particle–particle collisions and momentum loss  
   – At higher ceramic loadings the spray stream becomes “crowded’’ with hard, brittle particles. Rather than each particle racing into the substrate at or above its critical velocity, many knock into one another in flight. This lowers their net velocity and kinetic energy on impact, so fewer ceramics ever exceed the velocity threshold needed to overcome their brittleness and stick.  

3. Higher critical‐velocity requirement for ceramics  
   – Ceramics need a higher impact velocity than ductile metals to adhere (they cannot plastically deform to absorb impact energy). When you swap in more ceramic mass, the carrier gas’s total momentum is spread over more—and inherently tougher—particles. Average particle velocity drops and fewer ceramics reach their critical velocity, so the proportion of rebounded particles rises.  

Taken together, these effects—loss of ductile trapping, momentum sharing in collisions, and the higher velocity needed for ceramic bonding—explain why raising the ceramic content in a cold‐sprayed feedstock inevitably lowers its ceramic‐particle deposition efficiency.

Several groups have shown experimentally that if you spray a  “50:50” blend of A-powder and B-powder by weight you almost never end up with a 50:50 coating.  In fact the build-up of each phase in the deposit is a highly non-linear function of the feed ratio.  The root cause is that each component (A vs. B) has its own “deposition efficiency” curve that depends on:

 1. its critical velocity (Vc) for bonding,
 2. its particle size, density and shape (which set its acceleration in the gas jet),
 3. its ductility or hardness (which controls whether it deforms plastically, rebounds, fractures or erodes the substrate),
 4. and how it interacts in-flight and on-impact with the other phase (e.g. soft matrix particles can help “catch” brittle ceramic particles up to a point, but beyond that the ceramics simply abrade the growing coat).

If you denote by DE_A(R) and DE_B(R) the deposition efficiencies of A and B when the feed blend is R = [A]/([A]+[B]), then the actual coating fraction of A is

    X_A = R·DE_A(R)  
           ──────────────  
         R·DE_A(R) + (1–R)·DE_B(R)

Because DE_A and DE_B themselves change with R (through aerodynamic sorting in the nozzle, in-flight collisions, substrate peening, etc.), X_A(R) turns out to be a nonlinear function of R.  In practice this leads to:

 • At low R you may never reach A’s critical velocity so DE_A≈0 ⇒ almost pure B in the deposit.  
 • As R increases past A’s Vc threshold (possibly assisted by B’s soft peening), DE_A jumps up and the deposit suddenly “locks in” more A than the feed ratio.  
 • Push R too high and A particles start to interfere with the plastic metal matrix, etching rather than welding, so DE_A falls again.

The net result is a strongly non-linear deviation between feed composition and coating composition.

In cold‐gas spraying the minimum agglomerate size needed to deposit a brittle material is set by the requirement that the impacting cluster carries enough kinetic energy to overcome both the fracture toughness of the brittle constituent and the yield strength of any ductile ‘‘binder’’ phase in the agglomerate.  Since kinetic energy per particle (or agglomerate) scales as ½m·v², raising the particle velocity v lets you reduce the mass m – and hence the diameter – of the cluster that just meets the deposition threshold.

 In practice one finds experimentally (and by simple m·v² energy–balance arguments) that the critical agglomerate diameter d₍c₎ to achieve deposition approximately follows

       d₍c₎ ∝ (E₍crit₎ / ρ · v²)^(1/3)

where  
  • E₍crit₎ is the (fracture + plastic‐work) energy per agglomerate needed for bonding,  
  • ρ is the agglomerate density.

Thus:

  – If you double the particle velocity, v² goes up by 4, so d₍c₎ falls by about 4^(–1/3) ≃ 0.63.  
  – In mass terms m₍c₎ ∝ v⁻², so a higher v lets you use much smaller agglomerates to reach the same impact energy.

Caveats:

  • There is a lower‐size limit set by gas‐drag coupling and by the smallest agglomerates you can actually form without excessive fragmentation.  
  • Extremely high velocities can also induce surface erosion or embrittlement of the substrate.

But the bottom line answer is:  

  “Increasing particle velocity in cold spraying lowers the minimum agglomerate size required for depositing brittle materials, roughly following a d₍c₎ ∝ v^(–2/3) scaling (or m₍c₎ ∝ v^(–2) in mass).”

Applying a thin ductile‐metal sheath to otherwise “bare” ceramic powders fundamentally alters how those ceramics interact with each other, with the substrate, and with the cold-spray jet during impact.  In practice the benefits break down into three interrelated effects:  

1. Cleaner, higher-energy interfaces  
   – The metal coating buries any surface oxides, adsorbates or moisture on the ceramic, so that when particles hit the substrate or earlier-laid splats they are effectively “metal-to-metal” contacts.  
   – Under the extreme localized pressures of cold spray the metal shell plastically deforms and cold–welds both to the substrate and to neighboring shells, producing metallurgical bonds rather than weak, purely mechanical grips.  

2. Stress buffering and crack-deflection  
   – Ceramic–ceramic contacts are intrinsically brittle and prone to microcracking under impact or service loads. The ductile metal layer absorbs much of the shock, plastically flows around the ceramic core, and redistributes stress more uniformly.  
   – Any nascent cracks that form in the ceramic are blunted or deflected at the compliant metal–ceramic interface, suppressing crack coalescence and spallation.  

3. Synergistic hardness and wear resistance  
   – Once deposited, the coating becomes a continuous metal matrix in which hard ceramic islands are strongly bonded and encased. Under sliding or abrasive wear, the hard ceramics bear and redistribute the normal and tangential loads, while the metal matrix prevents catastrophic chipping by providing toughness.  
   – The result is a cold-sprayed composite whose macrohardness is boosted by dispersion strengthening (Orowan looping, load transfer to particles) and whose wear resistance benefits from both the high intrinsic hardness of the ceramics and the crack‐suppressing, energy‐absorbing action of the ductile sheath.  

In short, metal-coating ceramic powders turns what would otherwise be a brittle, poorly adhering particulate blend into a well-bonded metal–ceramic composite.  The metal sheath enables intimate metallurgical bonds during spray, cushions impact stresses, and locks the hard ceramic phase into a tough matrix—yielding coatings of enhanced hardness, cohesion, and wear resistance.

When a cold‐sprayed coating is annealed above its recrystallization temperature (Tr), several complementary metallurgical processes occur that turn the as‐sprayed, highly strained, partially bonded powder network into a more fully coherent, ductile metal:

1. Recovery and Recrystallization  
   – The extreme dislocation densities and subgrain structure inherited from the supersonic impact become the driving force for nucleation of new, strain‐free grains.  
   – These new grains grow at or across the original particle–particle interfaces, consuming the old, defect-rich microstructure and effectively “erasing” many of the weak splat boundaries.

2. Diffusion Bonding and Oxide‐Film Disruption  
   – At T > Tr, lattice and grain‐boundary diffusion rates rise sharply. Atoms can cross from one splat to its neighbor, healing microvoids and cold‐welded junctions.  
   – Any thin oxide or contaminant films that had survived the high‐velocity impact are thinned, ruptured or dissolved, allowing fresh metal–metal contact and atomic bonding.

3. Pore Closure and Stress Relief  
   – Internal stresses from impact‐induced plasticity are relaxed by recovery processes, reducing the tendency for interfacial crack opening.  
   – Small pores and microcracks at splat boundaries shrink or close as the metal creeps and diffuses under the heat-treatment stress state.

4. Net Effect on Tensile Ductility  
   – With inter‐splat boundaries replaced by newly recrystallized, equiaxed grains, the coating behaves more like a monolithic bulk metal rather than a stack of mechanically interlocked splats.  
   – The locus of tensile failure shifts from the former interfacial “weak links” into the bulk of the grains, and overall elongation rises dramatically even if ultimate strength may drop slightly due to grain growth.

In short, heat treating above the recrystallization threshold converts the cold-sprayed, highly strained, partially bonded microstructure into a more homogenous, fully bonded grain network, eliminating microvoids and weak interfaces and thereby restoring—or even enhancing—the ductile behavior of the coating.

Post‐deposition annealing of cold-sprayed coatings is essentially a sequence of thermally driven recovery, recrystallization and grain-growth (plus any alloy-specific phase transformations) that reorganize the heavily strained, high-dislocation‐density microstructure imparted by the high-velocity impact.  The net effect on microstructure and properties depends critically on both the absolute annealing temperature (often expressed as a fraction of the melting point Tm) and the intrinsic behavior of the substrate or alloy (stacking‐fault energy, precipitation‐hardening response, diffusion rates, etc.).

1. As-sprayed baseline  
   – Ultrahigh dislocation density in particle interiors and at particle–particle interfaces  
   – Nanocrystalline or heavily elongated “lamella” structure  
   – High residual compressive stress and strain hardening → high hardness, low ductility, limited cohesion at splat boundaries  

2. Low‐temperature annealing (~0.2–0.3 Tm) – Recovery regime  
   – Dislocation rearrangement into lower-energy subgrain walls  
   – Partial relief of residual stresses  
   – Minor grain‐size change  
   – Modest drop in hardness (10–20 %) and yield strength  
   – Small gain in ductility and interparticle bonding  

3. Intermediate‐temperature annealing (~0.3–0.5 Tm) – Recrystallization regime  
   – Nucleation and growth of new, strain‐free equiaxed grains  
   – Elimination of deformation‐induced lamellar structure  
   – Further residual‐stress relief  
   – Larger drop in hardness and strength (30–50 %), but substantial increases in ductility and toughness  
   – Significant improvement in cohesive interparticle bonding and through-thickness tensile strength  

4. High‐temperature annealing (>0.5 Tm) – Grain growth and interface healing  
   – Grain‐boundary migration coarsens recrystallized grains  
   – Lattice‐diffusion–driven pore shrinkage and healing of microvoids at particle boundaries  
   – Precipitation-hardened alloys may overage or dissolve strengthening phases (reducing peak strength) or reprecipitate upon cooling  
   – Hardness and yield strength often reach a minimum; elongation and fracture toughness maximize  
   – Risk of oxidation, excessive grain growth, intermetallic formation (especially in Ti, stainless steels)  

5. Role of material behavior  
   – High‐stacking‐fault‐energy metals (Al, Cu) recrystallize readily at lower temperatures and times; recovery and grain growth are fast.  
   – Low‐SFE metals (Ti, Ni alloys, stainless steels) require higher temperatures and longer times to recrystallize; may form deformation twins that slow recrystallization.
