   – Precipitation‐hardenable alloys (Al-Zn-Mg, Ni-based superalloys) demand careful temperature control to hit the optimal age-hardening window without overaging or dissolving precipitates.  
   – Diffusion rates (and thus pore healing and interparticle bonding) scale strongly with T; materials with sluggish diffusion (e.g. refractory alloys) may never fully densify without very high annealing temperatures.  

6. Net effect on mechanical properties  
   – Hardness/strength trade‐off: as-sprayed coatings are strongest but most brittle; annealed coatings trade some strength for greatly improved ductility, toughness and fatigue resistance.  
   – Residual stress relief lowers the risk of crack initiation and delamination.  
   – Improved interparticle bonding boosts through‐thickness tensile and cohesive strengths.  
   – Excessive grain growth or overaging can degrade hardness, wear resistance, and in some cases corrosion resistance.  

In practice, one selects an annealing temperature/time schedule that sits just high enough to trigger the desired level of recrystallization and interparticle diffusion (for cohesion and stress relief) but not so high as to induce detrimental grain coarsening, overaging or unwanted phase transformations.

Particle density enters the cold‐spray process in two interrelated ways: how fast a particle can be accelerated by the gas stream, and how much kinetic energy and momentum it carries into the substrate.  Because bonding in cold spray is driven by severe plastic deformation at impact, both of those factors feed directly into deposition efficiency (DE) and, in multi‐phase or blended powders, the eventual coating composition.

1. Acceleration and exit velocity  
  • Drag‐to‐inertia ratio.  The gas drag force Fd scales with particle cross‐sectional area (∼d²), while the particle’s inertia scales with its mass (∼ρ·d³).  Heavier (denser) particles require more drag force or a longer acceleration path to reach the same velocity as a lighter particle.  
  • Exit‐velocity window.  For a given spray pressure and temperature, lighter particles reach terminal velocity more quickly and can exceed the critical “bonding velocity” at shorter stand‐offs.  Denser particles may remain below that threshold unless conditions are raised (higher pressure, longer nozzle, higher temperature).

2. Impact energy, momentum and deformation  
  • Kinetic energy Eₖ = ½ m v².  At identical velocities, denser particles carry more impact energy and momentum, promoting greater plastic deformation of both the particle and substrate.  This is essential for jet formation at the interface and for metallurgical bonding.  
  • Critical velocity v_c ∝ √(σ_y/ρ).  Denser or harder materials generally have a higher critical velocity; if the spray gas conditions do not meet that, their DE falls off steeply.

3. Deposition efficiency (DE) trends  
  – Below v_c: almost no deposition.  
  – Near v_c: DE rises rapidly; lighter particles reach this regime earlier, but if too light they may lack momentum for good bonding.  
  – Above v_c: DE for denser powders can exceed that of lighter powders, provided they have been accelerated enough—because their higher momentum produces stronger interfacial jets and flatter splats.

4. Coating composition in powder blends  
  • Selective acceleration. In multi‐component feeds (for example Al + SiC, metal + polymer), the low‐density fraction accelerates more readily and can be “lead‐out,” resulting in coatings richer in the lighter phase unless gas parameters are tuned.  
  • Differential v_c. If one phase has a much higher critical velocity, it may under–deposit relative to its feed concentration.  This skews the final volume fraction away from the spray‐mixture ratio.  
  • Nozzle flow‐focusing. Denser particles tend to stay closer to the jet axis, while lighter ones spread more, causing radial composition gradients.

5. Practical implications  
  – To deposit a high‐density hard phase (e.g. WC or Ti), you typically need higher gas pressures, preheating or longer nozzles.  
  – To avoid “fractionation” in mixed feeds, you may have to stage the powder delivery or tailor carrier‐gas conditions so that all species cross their respective v_c roughly simultaneously.  
  – Understanding these density effects allows one to predict and control both DE and the uniformity of multi‐phase coatings.

In summary, particle density governs (a) how easily particles reach bonding velocity and (b) how much energy they carry on impact.  Those two effects together dictate the overall DE and, in blends, the departure of the coating’s phase composition from the powder‐blend recipe.

In cold spray additive manufacturing you deliberately keep the feedstock well below its melting point and instead rely on extremely high particle velocities (typically 300–1200 m/s) so that bonding arises from solid‐state plastic deformation rather than fusion.  The two key factors—and their synergy—are:

1. Sub-melting Temperature  
   • Particles never liquefy, so there is no solidification shrinkage or gas entrapment, and the ubiquitous porosity associated with weld pools or thermal sprays is avoided.  
   • Oxide layers remain thin and brittle; you don’t grow thick surface oxides that would inhibit bonding.  
   • Thermal gradients and residual stresses are kept low, minimizing crack formation and distortion.

2. High Impact Velocity  
   • Each particle carries high kinetic energy (Eₖ = ½ m v²). Upon impact, this energy is released in a very thin surface layer in the form of adiabatic shear and extreme plastic deformation (strain rates 10⁵–10⁷ s⁻¹).  
   • Oxide films on both the particle and the substrate fracture, exposing fresh metal.  
   • The localized, brief temperature spikes (but still below melting) promote dynamic recrystallization in a nanocrystalline interfacial zone, enabling true metallurgy (metal–metal bonding) in addition to mechanical interlocking.  
   • Each successive layer “irons out” any remaining gaps or voids, squeezing porosity down to below 1–2%.

Combined Effect  
Because particles never enter the liquid state, there is no shrinkage or gas-entrapped porosity. Because they hit so hard, they plastically deform and weld solid to solid, fracturing oxides and creating an ultrafine‐grained, strongly bonded interface. The result is a nearly fully dense (>98–99 %) coating with very high adhesion, minimal residual stress, and negligible porosity.

In cold spray deposits you almost always see a through‐thickness (and even within‐lamella) gradient in how badly particles deform, how many porosity defects survive, and how hard the material is.  All of it ties back to the fact that early particles hit a stiff, cold metal substrate, but later ones hit an ever‐more compliant, work-hardened “bed” of previously sprayed material.

1. Particle deformation  
  – Substrate interface (first few splat layers): “rigid‐backing” effect → very high local strain and adiabatic shear at the particle/substrate contact.  Splats pancake out strongly (high flattening ratio), develop extensive dislocation substructures, and weld intimately to the substrate.  
  – Mid‐thickness: subsequent particles still see some stiffness, but progressively less.  They deform less (lower flattening ratio), and cold weld mainly to earlier, already‐deformed splats rather than a rigid plate.  
  – Top surface: particles see the most compliant backing so they deform the least.  You may even see some rebound or incomplete lamellar bonding.

2. Porosity  
  – Near the substrate: very low residual porosity (< 1–2 %) because the high‐strain impacts crush oxides/voids and close emerging gaps.  
  – Mid layers: porosity rises modestly (2–5  %), as impacts are lower energy and oxide shearing isn’t quite as effective.  
  – Outer layers: the highest porosity (5–10 % or more in challenging alloys) survives here.  You’ll also find more continuous interlamellar pores and unbonded particles at or near the free surface.

3. Hardness (and work hardening)  
  – Bottom zone: hardest region.  Maximum plastic strain, highest dislocation density, sometimes nano‐grain formation in the shear zone → peak microhardness.  
  – Middle zone: intermediate hardness.  The backing is less rigid, so there’s less work hardening per particle, but repeated over‐spraying still contributes to moderate hardening.  
  – Surface zone: lowest hardness, since the final‐pass particles undergo the least strain.  In some systems you’ll also see slight thermal softening from adiabatic heating of the uppermost splats, further reducing hardness.

Additional fine‐scale effects:  
- Within each splat you’ll find the most severe shear (and hardness) near its periphery where it first hit, with a gradient to the lower‐strain core.  
- Grain size and residual stress also vary: compressive strains and grain refinement tend to be highest near the substrate.  

In practice, if you need a uniformly dense, hard coating throughout its thickness you either need very high particle velocities (to maintain high strain even late in the build) or post-spray treatments (hot isostatic pressing or shot peening) to homogenize the deformation, close pores, and equalize hardness.

Tungsten‐carbide (WC) particles behave very differently in cold spray versus HVAF largely because of differences in particle temperature, ductility, impact energy and bonding mechanism:

1. Plasticity vs. brittleness  
   – WC is a very high‐strength, high‐melting‐point ceramic that remains essentially brittle at the sub‐600 °C particle temperatures typical of cold spray. Under the extreme strain rates of cold spray (10^4–10^6 s^–1), WC cannot undergo appreciable plastic deformation, so instead of “splatting” it fractures or simply rebounds off the substrate.  

2. Thermal state and binder melting  
   – In HVAF the spray gas is hot enough (~1 800–2 500 °C flame) to at least soften—and in the case of WC–Co powders even melt—the metallic binder (Co or Ni). A partially molten binder wets the substrate and the carbide faces, absorbs impact energy, and flows around the carbides, locking them into the growing coating.  

3. Impact velocity and kinetic energy partitioning  
   – Cold spray velocities (600–1 200 m/s) are higher than HVAF (typically 400–800 m/s), so more of the kinetic energy goes into brittle fracture and elastic rebound rather than into local heating or binder flow. In HVAF the lower velocity plus high particle temperature directs more energy into plastic/binder deformation.  

4. Bonding mechanisms  
   – Cold spray relies purely on solid‐state plastic deformation of ductile metals to establish metallurgical joins; ceramics simply can’t partake.  
   – HVAF achieves a mixed “splat” bond: the molten/softened binder wets and metallurgically bonds to the substrate, mechanically trapping the WC particles.  

In short, cold spray keeps WC cold and brittle—so it bounces—whereas HVAF heats and/or melts its binder, enabling deformation, wetting and embedment of the carbide into the coating.

Post‐spray annealing and a follow‐up high‐temperature rolling step work together to convert the as‐sprayed, highly strained cold‐spray deposit into a more uniform, fine‐grained, and damage‐free metal matrix—and that in turn raises ductility.  The key transformations and the ductility gain come from:

1. As-sprayed condition  
   – Particles bond by severe local plastic deformation: you get ultra-high dislocation densities, nanolamella or subgrain structures around interfaces, oxide layers, micro-voids, pores, and strong residual stresses.  
   – The microstructure is very work-hardened and brittle, with interparticle defects that prematurely localize strain.

2. Post-spray annealing  
   – Recovery: dislocations annihilate or rearrange into low‐energy configurations, cutting stored strain energy and residual stress.  
   – Static recrystallization (if the anneal temperature is above the metal’s recrystallization threshold): new, strain‐free grains nucleate—often at particle boundaries—and grow, healing microcracks and reducing porosity.  
   – Grain coarsening is limited if the anneal is kept relatively short or at moderate temperatures.  You end up with a submicron to a few‐micron equiaxed grain structure and cleansed particle interfaces.

3. High-temperature rolling (thermomechanical processing)  
   – Dynamic recovery and dynamic recrystallization during deformation produce still finer, equiaxed grains (often <1 µm) and a high fraction of high‐angle grain boundaries.  
   – Rolling closes any remaining pores or microvoids and breaks up residual oxide networks at former particle boundaries, promoting full metallurgical bonding.  
   – Imparts a dislocation structure that’s balanced—enough to maintain strength, but low enough to allow strain to distribute homogeneously.

Why ductility rises  
  • Lower dislocation density and fewer stress concentrators let dislocations move more freely, reducing early strain localization.  
  • A fine, equiaxed grain structure with high‐angle boundaries encourages uniform grain‐boundary sliding and dislocation absorption, delaying necking.  
  • Fully healed interfaces and minimal porosity mean the material behaves like a wrought alloy rather than a particulate aggregate.  

In sum, annealing unlocks stored strain energy and initiates a strain‐free grain structure, and rolling refines that structure while eliminating defects.  The result is a cold-sprayed matrix whose microstructure approaches that of a ductile, wrought material.

Hard second‐phase particles under shear have two mutually reinforcing effects on the matrix microstructure and on wear resistance:

1. Microstructural refinement under shear  
   • Strain partitioning and particle–matrix mismatch concentrate shear strains around the particles.  
   • Particles act as “pinning” sites for dislocations, raising local dislocation density and promoting dynamic recrystallization (particle‐stimulated nucleation).  
   • The result is subgrain formation, grain‐boundary multiplication, and progressive fragmentation of the original grains, yielding a much finer, more equiaxed matrix grain structure in the particle vicinity.  

2. Impact on wear resistance  
   • Finer grains and higher dislocation densities raise the bulk hardness (Hall–Petch strengthening), so the matrix resists surface indentation and plowing under a tribological load.  
   • The hard particles themselves bear part of the contact stresses and inhibit macro‐scale plastic flow, reducing real contact area and suppressing adhesive wear.  
   • Debris formed by particle fracture often compacts into a protective tribofilm that further lowers wear rates.  
   • Caveat: Beyond an optimum particle volume fraction, clusters or poorly bonded particles can spall out, act as third‐body abrasives, and actually accelerate wear.  

Net effect: moderate loadings of well‐dispersed, hard second phases combined with shear‐induced grain refinement typically drive wear‐rate reductions by one to two orders of magnitude compared with the unreinforced matrix.

In cold spray you accelerate powder particles to hypersonic speeds and bond them to a substrate by severe plastic deformation rather than by melting. Two key thermal features of the process explain why the feedstock’s original phases end up “locked in” to the coating:

1. Low overall thermal input  
   • The gas temperatures used to accelerate the powder (typically 200 – 800 °C) are kept well below the powder’s melting point.  
   • Because no melting occurs, there is very little heat introduced into either the particles or the substrate. As a result, bulk temperatures in the deposit zone remain below the solid‐state phase‐transformation thresholds of the material.  

2. Extremely rapid local cooling  
   • Any heat that does arise—for example, in localized shear bands at particle–substrate or particle–particle interfaces—dissipates almost instantaneously into the cold mass of surrounding particles and into the substrate (thermal diffusivities of metals are high).  
   • Typical cooling rates in those shear‐deformation zones can exceed 10^5–10^6 K/s, far faster than diffusion‐controlled phase transformations can occur.  

Because the process stays entirely in the solid state and because any temperature excursions are quenched almost immediately, there is insufficient time or driving force for:  
  – Diffusional transformations (e.g. precipitation or eutectoid reactions)  
  – Grain growth or recrystallization beyond the very localized shear‐band regions  
  – Formation of unwanted equilibrium phases or intermetallics  

In sum, cold spray’s combination of sub-solidus processing and ultra-fast cooling “freezes in” the as-milled or as-atomized microstructure and any metastable or non-equilibrium phases present in the feedstock.

In cold‐gas spraying (CGS), “spray energy” is shorthand for the particle kinetic energy (½ m·v²) imparted by gas pressure, temperature and nozzle geometry. Because hydroxyapatite (HA) is a brittle ceramic, whereas the usual binders (Ti, Cu, Al, Ni) are ductile, changing the spray energy moves the composite through three distinct deposition regimes:  

1. Low spray energy (below HA’s critical velocity)  
   • Particle velocity v < v_c,HA (~500–600 m/s)  
   • Binder may plastically deform but cannot “trap” HA—very low deposition efficiency of HA (<10 %), high porosity (≥20 %), poor interfacial bonding.  
   • Coating is weak, powdery, dominated by loosely adhered flakes.  

2. Intermediate (optimum) spray energy (just above HA’s v_c)  
   • Binder reaches or slightly exceeds its critical velocity (v_c,metal ~300–400 m/s), and HA approaches its v_c,HA.  
   • Ductile binder splats around and anchors HA fragments into a lamellar matrix.  
   • Deposition efficiency rises to 40–70 %, porosity falls to 5–10 %.  
   • HA retains crystallinity (only mild fracture), interfacial shear and cohesive strengths peak.  
   • Residual stresses remain moderate, so delamination risk is low.  

3. High spray energy (well above HA’s v_c)  
   • v ≫ v_c,HA; kinetic energy becomes excessive for brittle HA.  
   • HA particles undergo severe micro-cracking or amorphization; local adiabatic heating at particle–substrate contacts can induce partial dehydroxylation or phase decomposition.  
   • Porosity may continue to drop, but internal tensile residual stresses climb, promoting microcrack networks and delamination.  
   • Adhesion strength often falls off as brittle fracture becomes the dominant failure mode.  

Key practical levers and observations  
• Gas pressure: raising from 3 MPa to 6 MPa typically pushes v from ~400 m/s to ~800 m/s.  
• Gas temperature: hotter gas reduces viscosity and boosts velocity but also edges up local heating.  
• Standoff distance: 15–25 mm is usually optimum—too close and nozzle wear/heat damage rises; too far and particles decelerate.  
• HA volume fraction: higher HA loading demands slightly higher binder deformation energy to achieve the same coating density.  

Bottom line: you want to tune your gas pressure/temperature and nozzle design so that your binder is well above its critical velocity (to form a cohesive scaffold) while HA is only just over its own critical velocity—this maximizes HA retention, minimizes porosity, and avoids high-stress, brittle failures or phase damage.

In cold spray, particles impact the substrate (and previously deposited particles) at hypersonic speeds (300–1 200 m/s), generating extremely high strain rates (10^6–10^9 s^–1) and localized adiabatic heating without bulk melting. That impact‐induced severe plastic deformation (SPD) drives grain refinement and boosts coating performance via the following chain of events:

1. Dislocation generation and interaction  
   - The collision imposes strains of several hundred percent in micro‐ to nano‐seconds, creating very high dislocation densities.  
   - Dislocations tangle, form cell walls and subgrain boundaries.

2. Dynamic recrystallization and subgrain rotation  
   - Localized heating plus the high strains trigger continuous dynamic recrystallization (cDRX).  
   - Subgrains rotate and break down into ultrafine (submicron to nanometer) equiaxed grains.

3. Hall–Petch strengthening  
   - Grain refinement raises the yield stress and hardness of the deposit, following σ = σ₀ + k·d^–½.  
   - A harder matrix resists plastic deformation under subsequent impacts, further refining grains in later layers.

4. Improved interparticle and substrate bonding  
   - SPD disrupts surface oxides at the particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces, promoting fresh metal contact and metallurgical bonding.  
   - The peening action closes pores and voids, yielding near‐full density (> 99 %) coatings.

5. Enhanced coating properties  
   - Higher cohesive and adhesive strength reduces spallation under load.  
   - Ultrafine grains impede crack initiation and propagation, boosting fatigue, wear and corrosion resistance.  
   - Homogeneous microstructure ensures uniform mechanical and thermal properties through the coating thickness.

In sum, impact‐driven SPD in cold spray refines grains by dislocation accumulation and dynamic recrystallization. The resulting ultrafine‐grained, nearly pore‐free structure delivers markedly higher hardness, strength, and bond integrity, and greatly improved wear and corrosion performance.

In thermal spray you can think of every powder‐particle as carrying two “fingerprints” into the coating:  
  1. A thermal fingerprint, how close and long it has been to or above its melting point – what we will call the melting index (M).  
  2. A fluid‐dynamic fingerprint, how fast it is and how big it is – which sets its particle‐Reynolds number (Re).  

Both M and Re vary from particle to particle in any given spray process, and it is their joint distribution that dictates whether a particle hits the substrate as an unbroken solid, a partially melted mush, or a fully molten droplet – and then how that droplet spreads, cools and solidifies into a “splat.”  Overlapping many splats then builds up your coating’s characteristic microstructure (lamellae, porosity, oxides, grain size, etc.).  

Below is a process‐by‐process outline of how M and Re control splat morphology and the resultant deposit:

 1. Plasma Spray (APS / VPS)  
    • Thermal side (M): gas temperatures up to 15,000 K drive almost all particles well above their melting point (M≫1 for most feedstocks).  Complete melting yields low viscosity droplets on impact.  
    • Fluid side (Re): velocities of 200–400 m/s on 20–100 µm particles give Re in the 10^3–10^4 range.  The boundary layer on a molten droplet is thin but still laminar–transitional.  
    • Splat morphology: thin (1–3 µm) pancake splats with rippled edges.  Fully molten droplets coalesce into smooth lamellae, but high surface temperature also oxidizes and re–solidified oxide strings between splats.  
    • Microstructure: stacked lamellae, interlamellar oxide networks, columnar or zone‐refined dendrites if cooling is slow, fairly high porosity (3–10 %) and oxide content.  

 2. HVOF (High‐Velocity Oxy‐Fuel)  
    • Thermal side (M): flame temperatures around 3000–3500 K melt only part of the powder or just bring it to the melt point (M≈1–1.2).  Many particles are in the “mushy” state.  
    • Fluid side (Re): velocities up to 800–1000 m/s push 20–40 µm particles into Re∼10^4–10^5.  Very high dynamic pressures on impact.  
    • Splat morphology: mucky, strongly flattened “pancake” or “splat‐stick” shapes with fringed rims.  Partially molten shells can fracture, entrapping pores or unmolten cores.  
    • Microstructure: dense, low‐oxidation deposits (porosity <1 %), fine lamellae, mixed fully and partially melted regions, fine equiaxed grains from rapid quenching of thin melt films.  

 3. Cold Spray  
    • Thermal side (M): intentionally kept below melting – M<1.  Particles remain solid to the point of impact.  
    • Fluid side (Re): very high gas velocities (500–1200 m/s) accelerate 1–50 µm powders to Re∼10^4–10^5 in a supersonic jet.  
    • “Splat” morphology: no splats – particles plastically deform on impact.  They form irregular “pancake‐like” deformations, but no melt‐recast features.  
    • Microstructure: bonding by severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear instabilities.  Grain refinement in the deformed zone, virtually no oxides, near‐zero porosity.  

General trends in any thermal spray  
  • As the melting index rises from M<1 toward M≫1, you move from solid‐state deposition to partially molten mush to fully molten droplet splatting.  
  • As Re rises, the convective heat‐transfer coefficient and impact dynamic pressure rise, both of which tend to increase M (via faster heating) and promote larger spreading ratios on impact.  
  • Heterogeneity in powder size → a spread in Re, and heterogeneity in heat‐transfer time → a spread in M.  That variance is why within one coating you often see a mixture of fully flattened splats, semi‐spheroidal remnants, unmelted cores, oxide islands and microcracks.  
  • The final microstructure (lamella thickness, grain size, oxide content, porosity) directly reflects that combined M–Re distribution.  

In practice, spray engineers tune gas temperature, flow rate (thus velocity), standoff distance, and powder feed rate in order to shape the particle M–Re distribution so as to achieve the desired splat morphology and hence the target deposit microstructure.

Cold‐sprayed coatings almost invariably carry a net compressive residual stress because the dominant “peening”‐type deformation stresses overwhelm any opposing thermal stresses.  In practice you can group the active mechanisms into two broad categories—intrinsic (deformation‐induced) and extrinsic (thermal‐mismatch)—and then superpose them:

1. Intrinsic (deformation‐induced) compressive stresses  
  a. Particle peening: each high‐velocity particle plastically flattens against the substrate and underlying deposit, imparting a compressive “hammer–anvil” stress field in both the new layer and the near‐surface of the substrate.  
  b. Work‐hardening and dislocation generation: severe plastic deformation in an extremely thin interfacial zone produces very high dislocation densities.  These dislocations introduce local compressive back‐stresses as the lattice tries to accommodate the imposed strains.  
  c. Elastic rebound of the substrate: the substrate material under the impact zone elastically “springs back” around the plastically deformed surface.  That rebound squeezes the deposit, adding to the compressive field.

2. Extrinsic (thermal‐mismatch) stresses  
  a. Gas and particle heating: typical cold‐spray gas temperatures (300–800 °C) warm both particles and a shallow substrate layer.  
  b. Cooling‐induced tensile stress: as the coating/substrate cools to ambient, any mismatch in coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) generates tensile stress in the coating if its CTE is higher than the substrate’s.  

Net compressive stress = (sum of intrinsic compressive stresses) – (thermal‐mismatch tensile stress)

Since the plastic‐deformation (“peening”) stresses are very large—often several 100 MPa of compression in the first few micrometers—they easily exceed the modest tensile stresses induced on cooling (typically a few tens of MPa).  Thus the overall residual‐stress state in a well‐bonded cold‐sprayed coating is compressive.

Below is a comparative outline of how the fundamentally different energy‐input regimes and deposition states in conventional thermal spray versus laser cladding drive differences in Ni‐based coating microstructure and defect populations.

1. Energy density & deposition state  
   • Thermal spray (e.g. HVOF, plasma):  
     – Energy densities on the order of 10^5–10^7 W/m²  
     – Powder particles are heated to a semi‐molten/molten state in-flight but do not form a continuous liquid pool  
     – Deposition occurs via successive “splat” impact, rapid solidification of individual droplets  
   • Laser cladding (e.g. powder‐fed laser):  
     – Energy densities of 10^7–10^9 W/m² concentrated into a small spot  
     – Powder and substrate fully melt, form a coherent melt pool  
     – Cladded track solidifies unbroken, metallurgically bound to the substrate  

2. Solidification kinetics & microstructure scale  
   • Thermal spray:  
     – Extremely fast solidification of each splat (10^3–10^6 K/s locally)  
     – Splat‐by‐splat solidification leads to a lamellar “pearl‐on‐a‐string” microstructure  
     – Typical grain size in individual splats: submicron to low‐micron range  
   • Laser cladding:  
     – Cooling rates lower than in-splat but still high (~10^2–10^4 K/s overall)  
     – Melt‐pool solidification governed by gradient G and growth rate R → planar/cellular → columnar dendritic  
     – Dendrite arm spacing typically 2–20 µm, grains may be epitaxial with substrate  

3. Defect types & formation mechanisms  
   • Thermal spray:  
     – Porosity (1–10 vol %) from gas entrapment at splat boundaries  
     – Oxide stringers and trapped unmelted cores (especially in plasma spray)  
     – Splat‐boundary debonding under thermal/mechanical load  
     – Tensile residual stresses at splat interfaces  
   • Laser cladding:  
     – Very low porosity (<1 vol %) if process parameters are optimized  
     – Risk of lack‐of‐fusion defects between adjacent tracks or layers if energy input is too low or travel speed too high  
     – Keyhole porosity or gas entrapment if energy density is excessive  
     – Solidification cracking due to high tensile residual stresses in the heat‐affected zone  

4. Bonding and dilution  
   • Thermal spray:  
     – Primarily mechanical interlocking + limited metallurgical bonding at micro‐asperities  
     – Negligible dilution of substrate because no bulk melting of the base material  
   • Laser cladding:  
     – Full metallurgical bond through a fusion interface  
     – Dilution levels typically 5–25 % (alloy pick‐up from substrate), affecting chemistry in the clad  

5. Consequences for performance  
   • Thermal spray coatings often exhibit higher hardness in‐splats, but lower through‐thickness cohesion and higher permeability to corrosives or wear particles  
   • Laser‐clad coatings have a more homogeneous, dense microstructure, superior adhesion, and predictable dilution—but require tighter control to avoid cracks or lack of fusion  

In summary, thermal spraying’s moderate energy input and sequential splat‐solidification produce a lamellar, somewhat porous coating with oxide entrainment, whereas laser cladding’s high‐density energy source produces a fully molten pool that solidifies into a dense, directionally solidified dendritic structure—trading off fewer pores and oxides for risks of fusion defects and solidification cracking.

Dynamic and static recrystallization play complementary roles in setting the final thermal conductivity of a cold‐sprayed metal coating.  In essence, the high‐strain‐rate impacts of cold spray drive dynamic recrystallization (DRX) that gives you strong, well-bonded, ultrafine/subgrain-rich interfaces but also a very high density of boundaries and dislocations that scatter heat carriers.  A subsequent post-spray anneal then invokes static recrystallization (SRX) to lower that defect density, grow the grains, heal pores/oxides, and thus reopen continuous, low-resistance pathways for electrons (in metals) or phonons.

1.    Dynamic recrystallization during cold spray  
    •    At each particle–substrate or particle–particle collision you get adiabatic heating + enormous local strains (strain rates ~10^6–10^8 s^–1), which nucleates new, very small, misoriented grains (often <100 nm).  
    •    These DRX grains weld particles together but introduce  
         –  A high density of high-angle grain boundaries and subgrain walls  
         –  Excess dislocation networks  
         –  Residual oxide fragments entrained at interfaces  
    •    All of the above act as strong scattering centers for conduction electrons (or phonons) and so depress thermal conductivity relative to bulk.

2.    Static recrystallization during post-annealing  
    •    Heating to 0.3–0.6 Tm (metal) supplies enough thermal energy for boundary migration, dislocation annihilation, pore/oxide re-diffusion, etc.  
    •    New strain-free grains nucleate and grow, consuming the DRX substructure and coalescing ultrafine grains into micrometer-scale ones.  
    •    Pores shrink or close and oxide films become thinner/continuous, yielding better metallurgical bonding.  
    •    Net effect: far fewer scattering sites → higher electron/phonon mean free path → boosted thermal conductivity.

3.    Interaction & optimization  
    •    If you under-anneal, too many DRX-induced boundaries remain and conductivity stays low.  
    •    If you over-anneal, you may excessively coarsen grains (dropping mechanical strength) or generate unwanted precipitates at high temperatures.  
    •    The ideal route uses DRX to achieve near-full density and strong interparticle welding, then a tuned SRX cycle to trim the boundary/dislocation density just enough to recover conductivity without losing needed hardness/toughness.

In short, cold-spray DRX builds a dense, strongly bonded, but highly defected/nanograined coating with poor conductivity; post-anneal SRX heals and coarsens that structure, removing the very defect structure that DRX created, and thereby restores thermal conductivity toward bulk values.

Key Points  
1. Build‐rate in cold spray is roughly proportional to (powder feed rate) × (deposition efficiency).  Raising substrate temperature boosts deposition efficiency and so increases net build‐rate, up to an optimum.  

Mechanisms Governing the Effect  
1. Yield‐Strength Mismatch Reduction  
   – Heating the substrate lowers its dynamic yield strength and hardness.  
   – This narrows the strength gap between particle and substrate, so particles penetrate and plastically deform the substrate more readily, improving bonding.  
   – Lower substrate strength also reduces particle rebound, so more particles “stick.”  

2. Enhanced Adiabatic Shear Instability (ASI)  
   – The critical velocity for ASI (the localized, high‐strain‐rate shear banding that underpins metallurgical bonding) drops when the substrate is preheated.  
   – As a result, more impacts exceed the threshold for jetting and clean‐surface formation, raising deposition efficiency.  

3. Oxide‐Film Disruption  
   – Plastic flow at the interface is easier when the substrate is warmer, so incoming particles are better able to fracture and displace surface oxides.  
   – Cleaner metal–metal contact yields stronger bonds and fewer rebounding particles.  

4. Localized Thermal Assistance  
   – The particle’s adiabatic heating during impact adds to the substrate preheat, pushing interfacial temperatures higher without bulk melting.  
   – This “thermal spike” aids in dynamic recrystallization or grain‐boundary sliding at the interface, strengthening the bond.  

Practical Consequences  
– Typical substrate preheat ranges are 100 – 400 °C for metals such as Al, Cu or Ni alloys. Within this window deposition efficiency can rise by 10–50%, translating directly into higher build‐rates.  
– Above the optimal temperature:  
   • Oxide growth accelerates, impairing bonding.  
   • Thermal softening can become so great that particles embed and smear rather than jet, creating porosity or laminar defects.  

Bottom Line  
Preheating the substrate in cold spray lowers the critical impact velocity, increases the fraction of particles that plastically bond rather than rebound, and promotes stronger mechanical and metallurgical bonds via enhanced adiabatic shear and oxide‐film disruption—hence a marked rise in build‐rate up to an application‐specific optimum.

In cold spray you can think of the mixed feed as a two-speed hammer set.  The fine metal powder carries relatively low momentum and, when it hits the growing coating surface, it plastically deforms, interlocks with its neighbours, breaks up oxide films and fills interstices—so wherever only little particles land you build up a rather dense, well bonded lamellar zone.  By contrast, the deliberately added hard “shot-peening” particles are much larger and stiffer.  When one of those heavier particles impacts:

 1. It locally hammers the spray substrate and the just-deposited metal, driving very high strain, adiabatic shear and oxide‐film disruption in a small “crater” zone.  That can actually hyper‐compact the metal immediately under the shot, producing a tiny ultra-dense nugget.  
 2. Immediately around that crater the shot often bounces or even spalls out fragments of the softer metal, so it leaves behind a ring of voids or poorly filled cavities until the next fine powder arrives to refill them.  

If you continuously spray a blended feed, the deposition history at any one spot alternates between (a) runs of fine‐particle impacts (building smooth, dense layers) and (b) intermittent “hit‐and‐run” impacts by the hard shot (forging a super‐dense core and spalling out a porous halo).  Microscopically that sequence shows up as alternating dense lamellae (where only fine powder welded) and more open, porous zones (where shot peening excavated or rebounded), giving you the characteristic stripe-or band-pattern of dense/porous regions in the final CSAM coating.

In cold‐spray you shoot solid particles at high velocity (300–1 200 m/s) so that upon impact most of the kinetic energy is dissipated in plastic deformation, frictional sliding at the particle–substrate interface, and the creation of fresh metallic surfaces that weld together. When the particle and substrate are made of different materials (“mismatch”), three of the most important consequences are:  

1. Contact pressure and yield strength partitioning  
   •  Hertz‐type contact models show that the peak normal pressure under impact scales with an effective yield strength Y_eff ≃ 1.1·(Y_p·Y_s)/(Y_p+Y_s) (Y_p, Y_s = yield strengths of particle, substrate).  
   •  If the particle is much harder (Y_p≫Y_s), Y_eff→≈Y_s so the substrate yields first, producing deep craters, higher local strains in the substrate, and more opportunity for mechanical interlocking.  
   •  Conversely, if the substrate is harder (Y_s≫Y_p), the particle “mushrooms” preferentially: it spreads out, flattens, and slides, but the substrate stays mostly elastic.  

2. Interfacial friction coefficient μ  
   •  μ in cold spray is not a simple Coulomb constant but depends on the local shear yield strength τ_y and the contact pressure P.  A common approximation is μ≈τ_y/P_hardness or μ≈c·(τ_y/Y), where Y is a representative yield stress and c≈0.6–1.0.  
   •  A hard‐on‐soft impact gives higher local P relative to τ_y of the substrate, so μ is lower (the hard particle “plows” through) but total frictional work μP·Δs is large because P is high and the sliding distance Δs is long.  
   •  A soft‐on‐hard situation yields relatively lower P but larger Δs in the spreading particle, so μP·Δs can still be substantial but is concentrated in the particle rather than the substrate.  

3. Energy dissipation partitioning  
   Total kinetic energy E_k = ½m v² is partitioned into  
     a) Plastic work in particle, W_p = ∫Vp σ_p dε_p  
     b) Plastic work in substrate, W_s = ∫Vs σ_s dε_s  
     c) Frictional work at interface, W_f = ∫A μ P d(Δs)  
     d) Surface‐creation/bonding energy, W_b  
   •  For hard‐particle/soft‐substrate impacts, W_s≫W_p, whereas for soft‐particle/hard‐substrate, W_p≫W_s.  
   •  W_f scales roughly with μPcontact×contact area×sliding distance; since Pcontact and sliding distance both depend on hardness ratio, the mismatch sets how much energy is “burned up” in interfacial shear versus bulk plastic flow.  

Illustrative examples  
  – Aluminum particles impacting steel: Y_p≈100 MPa, Y_s≈250 MPa → substrate supports higher pressure, particle deforms and spreads; friction and plastic work are concentrated in the aluminum mushroom.  
  – Tungsten carbide particle on aluminum substrate: Y_p≈1 500 MPa, Y_s≈100 MPa → substrate yields deeply, crater forms; friction and shear heating occur mainly in the substrate, promoting mechanical interlocking.  

Bottom line: The greater the disparity between particle and substrate yield strengths (and hardnesses), the more skewed the energy dissipation will be toward whichever partner is softer.  This controls not only how deep or wide the deformation zone is, but also the magnitude of interfacial frictional work (hence heating and fresh‐metal exposure), which in turn governs bonding efficiency in cold spray.

Cold spray’s unique combination of low thermal input and very high particle impact velocity produces coatings whose microstructure and defect population are fundamentally different from those made by thermal‐spray or fusion processes.  In essence:  

1. Low Temperature ⇒ Minimal Oxidation & Phase Change  
   • Particles never heat above ~0.6–0.7·Tₘ, so surface oxides and intermetallics do not form or grow.  
   • Initial feedstock microstructure (including any alloying phases or amorphous structure) is largely retained.  
   • No high–temperature residual tensile stresses (“quench cracks”) develop, and the substrate is not heat‐affected.  

2. High Velocity ⇒ Solid‐State Bonding & Severe Plastic Deformation  
   • Particles striking at 300–1200 m/s undergo adiabatic shear at their leading edge.  This produces dynamic recrystallization and ultrafine (often nanocrystalline) grains in a narrow interface jet.  
   • Violent plastic flow collapses voids and oxides at particle–particle and particle–substrate boundaries, yielding >98 % theoretical density.  
   • A strong metallurgical bond forms by finely mixed interfacial material rather than by melting and solidification.  

Consequences for Mechanical Properties  
  – High hardness and strength from work‐hardened, ultrafine‐grained material.  
  – Low residual tensile stress; often a net compressive stress that retards crack initiation and propagation.  
  – Excellent adhesion and cohesion give superior fatigue, wear, and impact resistance.  

Consequences for Corrosion Performance  
  – Extremely low porosity and no oxide networks provide a nearly impermeable barrier to corrosive species.  
  – Absence of high‐temperature oxidation avoids embedded oxide inclusions that can act as local galvanic cells.  
  – Compressive near‐surface stresses further inhibit stress‐corrosion cracking.  

By preserving feedstock chemistry, eliminating high‐temperature defects, and creating a dense, ultrafine‐grained, strongly bonded matrix, cold spray coatings routinely exhibit both superior mechanical robustness and outstanding corrosion resistance.

Key points  
1. Powder‐size ↔ amorphous fraction link  
   – Smaller powders (e.g. < 15 µm) cool fastest on gas‐atomization, so tend to be ≥ 95 % amorphous.  
   – Larger powders (> 30 µm) cool more slowly, often crystallize partially (10–30 % nanocrystals).  

2. Amorphous fraction controls mechanical response at impact  
   – Fully amorphous particles have very high yield strength (GPa‐level), low work‐hardening and limited plasticity. Under impact they localize strain in shear bands, tend to fracture or rebound unless impact velocities are very high.  
   – Partially crystalline powders contain ductile nanocrystals that blunt shear bands, promote more homogeneous flow, and lower the critical velocity for deposition.  

3. Particle size sets kinetic energy and deformation mode  
   – Fine, highly amorphous powders carry less momentum (mV), so even though they hit at high velocity they often fail to spread (high spring‐back) and can fracture, raising porosity.  
   – Coarser particles, even if only partly amorphous, have higher momentum and deform more readily—flattening into “splats” that fill voids.  

4. Net effect on coating porosity  
   – Small/high‐amorphous powders → poor interparticle bonding, frequent fracture/shear‐band debonding → porosity often > 5–10 vol %.  
   – Large/partially crystalline powders → better flattening, more metallurgical contact → porosity can fall below 2–3 vol % at the same spray conditions.  

5. Practical trade‐offs and strategies  
   – To exploit the corrosion‐ and wear‐resistance of the glassy phase without excessive porosity, one often uses a bimodal feedstock (e.g. 15–25 µm + 30–50 µm) or heats the carrier gas to boost the deformation of the finest, fully amorphous particles.  
   – Alternatively, slightly devitrifying (5–10 % nanocrystals) powders strike a balance: still predominantly glassy for high hardness, but deformable enough to give dense deposits at commercial spray pressures.

Key nanoscale features in copper coatings that improve Cu²⁺ generation and surface‐diffusion kinetics are all “defect”‐type or high‐energy sites that act as short‐circuit pathways or high‐reactivity anchors for ionization.  The most important are:

1. Nanocrystalline grain structure  
   • Grain sizes < 100 nm raise the fraction of grain‐boundary area.  
   • Grain boundaries have much higher diffusion coefficients (DGB ≈10³–10⁵ × Dlattice) and lower activation energies, so Cu²⁺ can migrate and dissolve more quickly along these interfaces.  

2. High dislocation density  
   • Severe plastic deformation (as in cold spray) leaves dislocation tangles and cells.  
   • Dislocations also provide rapid “pipe” diffusion paths for Cu atoms toward the surface and locally boost stress/strain‐driven dissolution.  

3. Nano-pores and sub-micron voids  
   • Interconnected nanopores (5–50 nm) trap electrolyte, increasing local wetting and sustaining ion transport.  
   • They raise the effective surface area and expose more high‐energy surface facets and edges to the solution.  

4. Surface steps, kinks and ledges on nanocrystals  
   • Atomic step edges (1–2 nm) and kinks on crystallite facets concentrate charge and create preferential ion‐release sites.  
   • These features lower the energy barrier for Cu atom detachment and diffusion along the surface.  

5. Twin boundaries and stacking faults  
   • Coherent twins (twin spacing ≲ 20 nm) are low‐energy but fast diffusion paths, combining the benefit of ordered structure with enhanced mobility.  
   • They also stabilize the nanocrystalline structure against coarsening.  

6. Nanoparticle aggregates and hierarchical roughness  
   • Assemblies of 10–100 nm Cu particles create a multi-scale roughness that both broadens the electrochemical double layer and sets up micro-galvanic cells, further promoting localized Cu²⁺ release and lateral surface migration.  

How these features work together  
• Short-circuit diffusion: Any high-angle boundary (grain, twin or dislocation pipe) gives an order-of-magnitude faster route for Cu atoms to migrate from the bulk to the outer surface compared with lattice diffusion.  
• Increased reactive area: Nanoscale roughness, pores and steps multiply the density of active edge‐ and corner‐sites where Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ is kinetically favored.  
• Electrolyte retention: Nanopores maintain localized hydration films and ion reservoirs, which sustain continuous diffusion rather than one‐time dissolution.  
• Lowered activation barriers: The high strain fields around defects weaken Cu–Cu bonds, making it easier for atoms to detach as ions.  

Taken together, coatings engineered to have grain sizes of 20–50 nm, high twin densities, abundant dislocations and a controlled nanoporous/stepped surface will exhibit markedly enhanced copper-ion diffusion rates and sustained antimicrobial or electrical performance.

In cold‐spray applications the carrier gas velocities are so high (often M > 0.3 and sometimes transonic or even supersonic near the nozzle exit/shock train) that simple “incompressible” correlations underpredict (or sometimes overpredict) the true heat‐transfer coefficient.  Two things happen as M rises:

 1.  Compressibility effects  
    – local density, viscosity and thermal conductivity no longer follow the low‐speed scalings assumed in the classic Ranz–Marshall form  
    – shock waves or expansion fans can steepen temperature and velocity gradients at the particle’s surface  

 2.  Unsteady relative motion  
    – the particle sees rapidly changing gas velocity and temperature along its trajectory  
    – the “thermal boundary layer” develops under non‐steady conditions and does not obey the steady Re^0.5 scaling alone  

To account for these effects one augments the Nusselt number with an explicit Mach‐number dependence.  A typical form might be  
   Nu  =  [2 + 0.6 Re^0.5 Pr^1/3 (μ/μ_s)^0.14] · (1 + a M^b)  
where the last bracket is an empirically derived compressibility correction (a, b ≈ O(0.1–1)).  

When the Mach number is low enough (M ≲ 0.3) and the flow can be regarded as quasi‐steady and incompressible, density and property variations are small.  In that regime the extra (1 + a M^b) term goes to unity, and you recover the familiar Ranz–Marshall or Whitaker form:  
   Nu  ≃  2  +  0.6 Re^0.5 Pr^1/3  
So, in practice:  
 • If your particle never “sees” local gas speeds above about one-third of the speed of sound and the temperature rise in the gas is modest, you may safely use the simpler form.  
 • If you have M > 0.3, strong shocks/expansions or rapid gas‐temperature transients, you should switch to a Mach‐corrected Nusselt correlation.

In cold spray, particles impact a substrate (or previously deposited layer) at velocities typically between 500 and 1 200 m/s. If the impact velocity exceeds a material‐specific critical velocity, the following sequence unfolds:

1. Ultrahigh strain‐rate deformation  
   • Upon impact, local strain rates of order 10^5–10^7 s^–1 develop in a thin interfacial zone (hundreds of nanometers thick).  
   • The material experiences intense plastic flow but, because the contact time (~100 ns) is so short, there is virtually no time for heat to diffuse away.

2. Adiabatic heating and thermal softening  
   • Nearly all of the plastic work is converted into heat locally, raising the temperature in the shear zone by several hundred degrees Celsius in microseconds.  
   • Thermal softening begins to compete with strain hardening, reducing the flow stress in the most‐deformed regions.

3. Onset of adiabatic shear instability (ASI)  
   • When thermal softening outpaces strain hardening, shear deformation localizes in narrow bands (tens of nanometers wide).  
   • These “adiabatic shear bands” accommodate most of the plastic strain, concentrating heat and deformation.

4. Grain refinement and dynamic recrystallization  
   • The combination of extreme strain and high temperature within the shear band drives dynamic recrystallization and the formation of ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains.  
   • The massive dislocation density and new grain boundaries further enhance diffusivity and promote mechanical accommodation.

5. Oxide/contaminant fracture and fresh‐metal exposure  
   • The shear bands fracture any adherent oxide or adsorbed layers on particle or substrate surfaces, exposing clean metal.  
   • This fracture is largely mechanical—there is still no bulk melting.

6. Metallurgical bonding  
   • The intimate atomic contact of fresh metal across the interface, plus high defect densities and nanograins, enable short‐range diffusion and the formation of metallic bonds.  
   • Grain‐boundary welding or “cold‐weld” junctions form, locking the particle in place with bond strength often approaching that of the parent metal.

In summary, impact→adiabatic heating→shear‐band localization→dynamic recrystallization→oxide disruption→atomic contact/diffusion, yields a fully metallurgical (non‐melt) bond in cold spray.

Cold‐sprayed coatings almost invariably pull off at the substrate–coat interface rather than through the bulk coating because the very first particle‐substrate contact simply cannot develop the same quality of metal‐to‐metal bond that successive particle–particle (interlayer) impacts do. The key reasons are:

1. Oxide and contamination on the bare substrate  
   • Even grit-blasting cannot remove every last oxide or absorbed contaminant, so the first layer of particles “cold weld” onto a partly oxidized surface.  
   • Subsequent particles repeatedly fracture and shed the thin oxide films on the already‐deposited coating, exposing pristine metal surfaces for true metallic bonding.

2. Lack of severe plastic deformation at the initial interface  
   • The bare substrate is cold, stiff and un‐work‐hardened, so the deformation zone under the first impacts is shallow.  
   • In contrast, each new layer of particles lands on an already work-hardened, heated and more compliant undercoat. That produces deeper jetting, adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization and mechanical interlocking, all of which strengthen interlayer cohesion.

3. Thermal and residual stress effects  
   • The substrate remains at ambient temperature for the first impact, limiting any local thermal softening that would assist bonding.  
   • High‐speed particle impacts generate residual tensile stresses at the substrate–coat interface (the “dead” cold‐sprayed surface), weakening the bond there. Meanwhile the interior of the coating often carries compressive residual stresses that reinforce particle–particle cohesion.

4. Absence of diffusion or metallurgical transitions  
   • Since cold spray runs below melting, there is no diffusion layer formed at the substrate interface unless special post‐heat treatments are applied. Particle–particle contacts, however, see repeated fresh welds under high‐strain‐rate conditions.

Net result: interlayer bonds formed under repeated oxide-breaking, high‐strain‐rate, adiabatic‐shear conditions become stronger than that first, mechanically restrained bond to the untreated, oxide-covered substrate. Under a tensile pull, the weakest link is almost always the substrate–coat interface, so delamination occurs there rather than through the coating.

When a cold‐sprayed metal is subsequently annealed its heavily work‐hardened, high‐dislocation‐density microstructure evolves in three overlapping stages—recovery, recrystallization and then grain growth—each with distinct signatures:

1. Recovery  
   • Temperature‐range: typically 0.3–0.5 T m (in Kelvin) for most metals (e.g. 200–300 °C for Al alloys, 300–500 °C for Cu/Ni).  
   • Mechanisms: dislocation annihilation and rearrangement into low‐energy cell or subgrain structures; reduction of tangled forests of dislocations.  
   • Microstructure: faint subgrain boundaries (misorientations <5°) appear inside the originally flattened, work‐hardened splats; no new grains.  
   • Effects: residual stress relief, modest softening, small gains in ductility and electrical/thermal conductivity.  

2. Recrystallization  
   • Temperature‐range: roughly 0.5–0.7 T m (e.g. 300–400 °C for Al alloys, 500–700 °C for Cu/Ni).  
   • Mechanisms: nucleation of strain‐free grains at high‐energy sites—particle/particle interfaces, oxides, severe‐shear zones—followed by growth of these nuclei into the deformed matrix.  
   • Microstructure: formation of new, equiaxed, high‐angle‐boundary grains (misorientations >15°) that consume the subgrain/deformed regions. Grain sizes typically in the submicron to a few‐micron range, depending on time/temperature.  
   • Effects: sharp drop in hardness and strength, marked increase in ductility and toughness, elimination of most work‐hardening features.  

3. Grain Growth  
   • Temperature‐range: above the recrystallization finish temperature or long times at recrystallization temperatures.  
   • Mechanisms: reduction of total grain‐boundary energy by migration of high‐angle boundaries, small grains shrink and disappear, large grains grow.  
   • Microstructure: progressive coarsening into fewer, larger grains; the grain‐size distribution broadens.  
   • Effects: further softening, possible loss of optimal strength–ductility balance; if excessive, can impair fatigue and toughness.  

In practice one often targets just past the completion of recrystallization to achieve a uniform, fine‐grained, strain‐free microstructure without entering the grain‐growth regime that would undermine mechanical performance.

Solution‐heat treating powder feedstock before cold spray significantly improves deposit quality by tailoring the powder’s microstructure and mechanical properties so that particles deform and bond more readily on impact.  The key mechanisms are:

 1. Dissolution of hard/brittle phases  
    – Heating into the single‐phase field (e.g. solutionizing Al-alloys above the β/(α+β) or β-transus region, or stainless steels above the γ-field) dissolves intermetallics, grain-boundary precipitates, and segregation networks.  
    – Quenching freezes in a supersaturated solid solution, so the powder is softer and more ductile.

 2. Grain‐structure homogenization  
    – Eliminates chemical and microstructural banding from rapid solidification in atomization.  
    – Breaks down coarse dendritic grains into finer equiaxed grains, reducing anisotropy and scatter in hardness.

 3. Reduced yield strength and increased ductility  
    – With fewer second‐phase obstacles and a more homogeneous matrix, the flow stress of the powder is lower.  
    – Particles reach the critical impact velocity for bonding at lower gas pressures/particle speeds.  
    – Enhanced plastic deformation on impact leads to stronger metallurgical bonding and fewer unbonded regions.

 4. Lower oxide fracturing and entrainment  
    – A more ductile, uniform matrix confines the oxide scale into thinner, more continuous films during impact, reducing oxide‐rich interfaces in the deposit.  
    – Results in lower porosity and higher interparticle cohesion.

 5. Better post‐spray properties  
    – Denser, more uniform deposits show higher as‐sprayed mechanical strength and corrosion resistance.  
    – Subsequent aging or precipitation treatments can then be applied to tailor final hardness without having to first break down as‐sprayed inhomogeneities.

In summary, solution heat treatment “softens” and homogenizes the powder—dissolving brittle phases and equalizing chemistry—so that during cold spray the particles deform more plastically, bond more thoroughly, and yield denser, higher‐performance coatings.

The “eggshell” model is a simple way to understand how cold-sprayed metal powders shed their surface oxides and achieve true metal–metal bonding without melting.  In this picture each powder particle is viewed as a ductile metal “yolk” surrounded by a thin, brittle oxide “shell” (much like an eggshell around the protein/albumen core).  During high-velocity impact:

1. Impact and plastic deformation  
   • A particle travelling at several hundred metres per second slams into the substrate (or previously laid splat).  
   • The metal core beneath the oxide shell undergoes very high, triaxial plastic strains and strain rates.  

2. Stress concentration and oxide fracture  
   • Because the oxide shell is stiff and brittle compared to the soft metal, local hoop and shear stresses concentrate at the metal–oxide interface.  
   • The shell cracks almost instantaneously, producing micro-spalls and flakes of oxide that are pushed outward into the inter-splat boundary.  

3. Peel-off of the oxide layer  
   • As the metal core “flows” outward (the classic bell-shaped splat), these oxide fragments are left behind in the growing coating’s pores and boundaries.  
   • What remains at the immediate impact interface is fresh, oxide-free metal.  

4. Metallurgical bonding  
   • The freshly exposed metal surfaces of both particle and substrate are pressed together under very high pressures (on the order of GPa) and remain at elevated—but sub-melting—temperatures due to adiabatic heating in the shear zones.  
   • This environment promotes intimate atomic contact, severe plastic flow, dynamic recrystallization, and even localized lattice defects—all of which drive true solid-state (metallurgical) bonding rather than mere mechanical interlocking.  

Key points of the eggshell model:  
– The oxide thickness (typically tens of nanometres) is small relative to particle size but stiff enough to fracture under impact stresses.  
– Removal of that brittle shell is purely mechanical, not thermal, so there is no melting or resolidification.  
– Once the oxide is stripped away, the underlying metal plastically deforms and bonds strongly to the substrate or previous splats.  

In short, the eggshell model explains how cold spray’s kinetic energy is used first to crack and peel off the oxide shell and then to forge clean-metal interfaces, yielding dense, well-adhered coatings in the solid state.

Improper cold‐spray parameters degrade particle deformation and inter‐particle contact, producing voids at three scales—micropores (sub-µm), mesopores (1–10 µm) and sometimes lamellar delaminations. Porosity then becomes a dominant source of ultrasonic attenuation, both by scattering and by changing the coating’s effective elastic properties.  

1. How bad parameters raise porosity  
  • Insufficient particle velocity  
    – Low gas pressure or temperature, excessive stand‐off distance or too large a powder size all reduce particle impact speed below the critical velocity for full plastic deformation.  
    – Particles “bounce” or deform only at their front edge, leaving unfilled gaps between them.  
  • Over‐ or under‐feeding  
    – Too high a powder feed rate causes particle crowding in the nozzle, turbulent flow and gas entrapment in the deposit.  
    – Too low a feed rate yields poor layer build‐up and poor overlap, so that voids form between passes.  
  • Excessive spray traverse speed or improper spray angle  
    – If the nozzle moves too fast or at an angle off normal, particles do not strike with uniform coverage or sufficient momentum, causing inter‐lamella gaps.  
  • Inadequate substrate preparation or temperature  
    – Roughness, oxide films or cold substrates can prevent intimate contact between the first few layers and the substrate, leading to interfacial porosity that propagates through the coating.  

2. Why porosity boosts ultrasonic attenuation  
  • Scattering losses  
    – Any pore whose diameter is comparable to—or larger than—the ultrasound wavelength (or its Rayleigh regime ∼λ/10) scatters energy out of the incident wave. The scatter‐loss coefficient grows rapidly with pore size and frequency (≈f⁴ in the Rayleigh regime).  
    – A high pore volume fraction means more scatterers per unit volume, driving attenuation up nearly linearly with porosity.  
  • Impedance mismatch  
    – Pores (essentially voids or trapped gas) have near‐zero stiffness and density compared to the metal matrix. Each pore boundary reflects part of the incident wave, reducing transmitted amplitude.  
  • Viscous and thermal absorption  
    – In open or interlinked porosity, the oscillating pressure drives fluid motion in the pores, dissipating acoustic energy as heat via viscous friction and thermal conduction at the pore walls.  
  • Effective‐media softening  
    – Porosity lowers the composite’s effective bulk and shear moduli. The resulting slower sound speed lengthens the interaction time, increasing the path over which other loss mechanisms act.  

As a result, even a few percent of porosity can double or triple the ultrasonic‐attenuation coefficient of a cold‐spray layer, degrading both wave transmission and the resolution of ultrasonic nondestructive tests.

Porosity in cold‐sprayed coatings almost always drives their electrical conductivity below the values you would predict by simply scaling bulk conductivity by the remaining metal fraction. Two key pore attributes control how big that drop is—and in what directions it occurs—namely pore morphology (shape and size) and pore distribution (location, connectivity and orientation). Here is how each factor plays out:

1. Pore volume fraction  
   – As a first approximation, if φ is the total porosity, many effective‐medium rules (e.g. Maxwell‐Garnett, Bruggeman) predict a conductivity σeff ≃ σbulk·(1–A·φ), where A is a constant of order 1.5–2 for random spherical pores.  
   – At low φ (< 5 %), the drop in σ is roughly linear in φ. Above ~10 % porosity, pore networks start interfering with each other and σeff falls off more sharply—sometimes precipitously if you pass a percolation threshold.  

2. Pore morphology (shape and size)  
   – Spherical/near‐equiaxed pores cause a modest loss in σ because the current lines splay around them smoothly. A can be taken ≃1.5 in many fits.  
   – Elongated, platelet‐like pores (often seen between splats or at particle interfaces) impose a much higher local field distortion. Perforations perpendicular to the current path can act like cracks, dramatically lowering σ. In effect A can rise to 3 or more.  
   – Microcracks (high‐aspect‐ratio), even at low volume fraction, can be more harmful than the same volume of closed, equiaxed pores. They introduce high‐resistance “bottlenecks.”  

3. Pore distribution and connectivity  
   – Closed, isolated pores simply reduce the effective cross section for conduction. Their impact follows the effective‐medium models quite well.  
   – Open or interconnected pores create tortuous pathways, force current to detour, and can lead to localized high current‐density spots. Once pores connect, you get percolation effects: σeff can collapse faster than linear with φ.  
   – Clustering of pores near particle boundaries elevates the interparticle contact resistance. Even if the bulk metal inside each splat is fully dense, the network of weak contacts around it dominates the overall σ.  

4. Anisotropy in conductivity  
   – Because cold spray builds up by flattening and overlapping “splats,” you often end up with pores aligned parallel to the substrate. In‐plane conductivity can be higher than through‐thickness conductivity by factors of 2–5 in coatings with the same φ.  
   – If pores are preferentially oriented perpendicular to the current flow, they act almost like a series of capacitive gaps—through‐thickness σ can be severely compromised.  

5. Deviation from bulk‐scaled predictions  
   – A naive bulk‐based estimate would say σcoat ≃ σbulk·(1–φ). In practice σcoat is typically 50 – 80 % of that value for φ ≈ 5 – 10 %, and can drop below 30 % when φ is 15 – 20 % or when cracks/interconnected channels exist.  
   – The mismatch grows with increasing pore aspect ratio and connectivity. Even coatings with the same φ can show σeff differences of a factor of two if one has mostly closed, equiaxed pores and the other a network of thin inter‐splat cracks.  

6. Modeling tools  
   – Effective‐medium approximations (Maxwell‐Garnett, differential Bruggeman) give you first‐order insight for low φ and isolated pores.  
   – Percolation theory and finite‐element/tomography‐based simulations are needed once pores connect or are highly nonspherical.  
   – Empirical fits of the form σeff/σbulk = (1–φ)n, with n between 1.5 and 4, are often used to capture both shape and connectivity effects in one exponent.  

Summary: The more the pores are elongated, interconnected, clustered at splat boundaries or aligned across the current path, the more severely electrical conductivity falls below simple bulk‐scaled predictions. To approach bulk‐like σ, you must minimize total porosity, break up crack networks, and favor isolated, spherical pores that the current can more easily skirt.

In cold spray the relative hardness (or, more fundamentally, the yield strength) of the feedstock particle versus the substrate dictates where most of the plastic deformation—and hence where bonding “action’’—takes place.  Three idealized regimes emerge:

1. Particle much softer than substrate  
   – Plastic flow localizes in the particle.  
   – Severe shear and adiabatic‐jetting at the nose of the particle strip oxides and expose fresh metal.  
   – True solid‐state (metal‐to‐metal) bonding dominates.  
   – Critical velocity for deposition is comparatively lower than for hard‐hard combinations.

2. Particle much harder than substrate  
   – Plastic flow localizes in the substrate.  
   – Particle embeds like a cold “bullet,” but little jetting occurs and oxide remains largely intact on the particle surface.  
   – Mechanical interlocking (geometric anchoring) and mechanical adhesion (frictional/van der Waals) dominate.  
   – Critical velocity remains high but bonding quality is poorer unless the substrate is made very ductile.

3. Particle and substrate of similar hardness  
   – Plastic deformation is shared between particle and substrate.  
   – You get a mix of oxide removal/jetting at the interface plus mechanical anchoring.  
   – Both metallurgical bonding and mechanical interlocking contribute.

In practice, you can think of hardness ratios (HVparticle/HVsubstrate):  
• ≪1 → particle‐dominated flow → shear‐induced bonding  
• ≫1 → substrate‐dominated flow → mechanical anchoring  
• ≈1 → mixed‐mode bonding  

Finally, because harder materials require higher impact stresses to reach the adiabatic shear threshold, the critical spray velocity rises with increasing particle or substrate hardness.

In cold spray additive manufacturing the two most important knobs you turn to control particle impact velocity—and thus deposit density and porosity—are the processing‐gas stagnation temperature (T₀) and stagnation pressure (P₀).  Their influence can be understood in three interlinked ways:

1. Particle Acceleration (Impact Velocity)  
   • Raising P₀ increases the gas mass flow and the pressure drop through the nozzle throat.  A larger drive‐pressure ΔP gives higher exhaust Mach number, so particles accelerate to higher velocities.  
   • Raising T₀ increases the gas sound speed (a∝√T₀) and thus, for the same pressure ratio, boosts the jet Mach number.  Although gas density ρ₀ falls as T₀ rises (ρ₀∝P₀/T₀), the net effect is still a higher terminal particle velocity for typical nozzle geometries.  
   • Higher impact velocity (vₚ) directly correlates with deeper adiabatic shear instabilities in the particle, more intense plastic deformation, and better mechanical interlocking with the substrate and previously deposited layers.

2. Deposit Density and Porosity  
   • There is a critical “bonding” velocity vₙ for each material system.  Below vₙ you get poor adhesion, high rebound of particles, and interparticle voids (high porosity).  Above vₙ, porosity drops sharply as particles plastically flow, weld together and fill gaps.  
   • Further increases in vₚ (via higher T₀ or higher P₀) improve density—typically from 85–90% up toward 98–99% of bulk material—until you reach a point of diminishing returns or onset of erosion/damaging rebound.  
   • Typical numbers: increasing helium or nitrogen gas temperature from 300 °C to 600 °C can boost average particle velocity by 50–100 m/s, dropping porosity from ~7–10% down to ~3–5%.  Similarly, increasing stagnation pressure from 30 bar to 50–60 bar can yield a further 5–10% density gain.

3. Substrate/Particle Preheating and Material Softening  
   • A higher gas T₀ also preheats both particles in flight and the substrate surface.  Lowered yield strength and increased ductility promote more homogeneous, jet‐like plastic flow upon impact, further closing residual voids.  
   • But if T₀ is too high (especially with low‐melting alloys), you risk surface oxidation or incipient melting, which can trap gas, cause cavitation, or lead to non‐cohesive layered structures—raising porosity again.

Guidelines for Optimization  
– First ensure P₀ and T₀ produce vₚ just above the material’s critical bonding velocity.  This typically means 600–800 m/s for metals like Al and Cu, 800–1000 m/s for harder alloys or steels.  
– Increase P₀ in steps (e.g. 20 bar→30 bar→40 bar) until density plateaus or erosion appears.  
– Adjust T₀ in concert: moderate T₀ rise (200–400 °C above ambient) gains density via softening without excessive oxidation or particle soft‐landing.  
– Watch for diminishing returns: once >98 % density is reached, further gas-parameter increases mainly add utility costs and risk surface damage rather than eliminating the last few percent of porosity.

In summary, both higher stagnation pressure and higher gas temperature elevate particle impact velocities and enhance plastic deformation at impact, which closes interparticle voids, boosts deposition efficiency, raises coating density, and lowers porosity—up to the practical limits set by material softening, oxidation risk, and substrate integrity.

In cold spray the “tamping effect” refers to the way in which particles arriving later in the spray jet effectively hammer down and laterally confine the material deposited by earlier particles.  That confinement changes how the system partitions the incoming particle kinetic energy (KE) into other forms:

1.   Enhanced Pressure and Confinement  
     •  A lone particle impact on a rigid substrate can eject splat material radially, wasting some KE as ejecta kinetic energy and elastic waves.  
     •  Once you have even a thin layer of accumulated splats, subsequent impacts clamp or “tamp” that layer.  The splat can no longer expand freely, so more of the incoming particle’s KE goes into compressive work on that layer.  

2.   Greater Conversion to Internal (Plastic-Deformation and Thermal) Energy  
     •  Under tamping, elastic rebound is suppressed and radial flow is hindered.  As a result a larger fraction of the particle’s KE is channeled into high‐rate plastic deformation (dislocation generation, grain refinement) and localized heating (adiabatic shear).  
     •  That means hotter, more severely deformed interfaces, which in turn promote oxide‐film fracture, fresh‐metal contact, dynamic recrystallization, even localized melting in extreme cases.  

Why It Matters for Inter-Splat Bonding  
–  Higher local pressures and temperatures accelerate oxide disruption and expose clean metal surfaces, both prerequisites for true metallic bonding.  
–  Increased plastic straining at the interface raises real contact area and generates high‐energy defect structures that diffuse and metallurgically weld adjacent splats together.  
–  Overall, the tamping effect shifts the energy balance from particle rebound or heat loss into substrate toward internal work that produces the intimate, oxide‐free, high‐strain‐rate contacts needed for dense, well‐bonded coatings.

Mesh resolution in an Eulerian cold‐spray model exerts a first‐order influence on both the magnitude and the spatial distribution of plastic strain and the attendant adiabatic heating in the impacting particle.  In practice you will see the following trends as you refine or coarsen your mesh:

1. Peak‐strain and peak‐temperature magnitudes  
   – Coarse meshes tend to smear out shear‐band zones and underpredict the maximum plastic strain (εp) by 20–50 % (depending on mesh coarseness), and likewise underpredict the local temperature rise by 10–30 %.  
   – As you refine the mesh, you resolve the narrow deformation bands more sharply, so εp,max climbs and the hotspot temperature approaches the thermodynamic limit set by material properties and impact velocity.  

2. Gradient steepness and hot‐spot size  
   – On a coarse grid the deformation and thermal gradients are spread over multiple elements, producing overly wide shear bands (typically several tens of microns wide) and lower spatial peak-to-background contrasts.  
   – A fine mesh collapses these bands down toward their physical thickness (often on the order of a few microns or less) and produces steeper εp and T gradients.  

3. Mesh‐induced localization and convergence  
   – In Eulerian formulations plastic localization can be mesh‐sensitive; excessively fine meshes may spuriously intensify localization if your constitutive model lacks proper strain‐softening regularization.  
   – You should carry out a mesh‐convergence study (for example, halving the cell size around the impact zone until εp,max and Tmax change by <5 %) to identify a grid density that balances accuracy against run time.  

4. Practical guidelines  
   – Aim for at least 15–20 Eulerian cells across the particle diameter in the impact region.  
   – Use adaptive mesh refinement (if available) to focus resolution on the advancing plastic front and heat‐generation zone.  
   – Monitor both global (average) and local (peak) strain and temperature metrics as you refine to confirm convergence of the quantities of interest.  

In summary, coarse Eulerian meshes underpredict both plastic‐strain and adiabatic‐heating peaks and smear out deformation bands, while sufficiently fine meshes capture sharper, higher‐magnitude εp and T fields—provided you guard against artificial localization by verifying grid convergence.

In cold spray the only “glue” holding the coating together is the severe plastic deformation of particles on impact.  Carrier‐gas heating, high stagnation pressure and an optimized converging–diverging nozzle all work in concert to maximize that deformation, to close inter-particle gaps and thus drive porosity down into the low‐single-percent or sub-percent range.  Here is how each factor contributes—and why you really need them all together:

1. Carrier‐Gas Heating  
 – Raises the gas (and particle) temperature, which  
  • low ers the yield strength and work-hardening rate of the feedstock (Johnson–Cook behavior),  
  • increases the local sound speed (a = (γRT)½) so that for a given Mach number the particle velocity is higher, and  
  • promotes adiabatic shear instabilities on impact that help particles “weld.”  
 Without heating, you’d need an impractically high stagnation pressure just to hit critical velocity, and the particles would be too stiff to deform fully and interlock.

2. High Stagnation Pressure  
 – Drives the mass flow through the nozzle, setting up a high dynamic pressure  
  p_dyn ≈ ½ ρ_gas v²  
 that directly controls particle momentum (m v).  
 – A higher inlet pressure also raises the Mach number in the throat and exit, so particles spend more of the nozzle’s length at supersonic speed.  
 – The result is greater impact velocity (typically 600–1200 m/s), ensuring each particle exceeds its material’s critical velocity for bonding and plastic flow—and thus closes voids instead of merely bouncing or fracturing.

3. Nozzle Design  
 – A well‐tuned converging–diverging geometry (correct throat diameter and exit‐to‐throat area ratio) gives a uniform, high‐Mach core flow with minimal shock losses.  
 – Low boundary‐layer growth and tailored expansion prevent flow separation or oblique shocks, which would otherwise scatter particles and introduce “dead zones” of low deposition efficiency.  
 – Some designs incorporate a slight focusing (narrowing) of the jet downstream so particles strike the substrate at a closer to 90° impingement angle—maximizing normal stress and avoiding shear‐off or ricochet that can trap pores.

Synergy and Porosity Reduction  
– Heated gas reduces material strength so that upon impact the high‐pressure, high‐velocity jet forces powder particles to undergo extreme plastic deformation.  
– The nozzle’s supersonic, well‐focused jet ensures that virtually all particles reach and exceed critical velocity with the proper impact angle.  
– This combination collapses microscopic voids, achieves metallurgical bonding at each particle interface, and fills interstitial gaps with newly deposited, severely deformed material.
