Result: a coating with minimal entrained gas or unbonded interfaces—i.e. low porosity (often well under 1 vol %).

Replacing low-diffusivity (special) grain boundaries with high-diffusivity (random) ones in a polycrystal has three linked effects on the hydrogen concentration field:

1. Faster overall penetration and higher D_eff  
   • Special boundaries act as semi-blocking interfaces, so the effective diffusivity D_eff is dominated by bulk diffusion and by the slowest boundaries in the network.  
   • Swapping in high-diffusivity random boundaries raises D_eff (often by a factor of 2–10 or more, depending on the fraction of replaced boundaries), speeding up hydrogen ingress and egress.

2. Smoother, more uniform profiles  
   • With slow (special) boundaries, hydrogen piles up on the upstream side of those boundaries, creating steep concentration jumps at each interface.  
   • High-diffusivity boundaries let hydrogen flow more freely from grain to grain, flattening out those jumps and producing a more continuous c(x) curve through the polycrystal.

3. Lower boundary-peak trapping but higher net uptake rate  
   • Fast boundaries do not hold hydrogen as long at the interface (they have a lower “residence time”), so the local GB concentration peaks drop.  
   • Because the network is more permeable, the total flux through the specimen (and hence the rate of hydrogen entry or escape) increases.

In practical terms, if you plot c vs. depth or time:  
– The breakthrough time (time to reach a given concentration at depth) decreases.  
– Peak concentrations at individual boundaries shrink, and the intergranular concentration variation is reduced.  
– The curve approaches the classical Fickian form for a homogeneous medium with an elevated effective diffusivity.

Substrate thermal conductivity and deformability enter cold‐spray bonding in essentially the same way they do in any high‐strain‐rate impact process: by setting how much of the particle’s kinetic energy is converted into heat at the interface, over what volume that heat is released, and how fast it is conducted away.  In practice you can think of them as two knobs that tune (a) how much heat builds up at the moment of impact, and (b) how quickly that heat is “soaked” into the substrate bulk rather than sitting there and locally melting particle or substrate.

1. Substrate thermal conductivity (kth)  
  • Low kth: the interface behaves almost adiabatically during the few‐microsecond contact.  Heat generated by plastic deformation and friction stays near the contact, so the local temperature spike is high and can exceed melting.  
  • High kth: the substrate acts as a heat sink.  As soon as heat is generated it is drawn away into the bulk, reducing the peak interfacial temperature and making local melting far less likely.

2. Substrate deformability (i.e. yield strength, hardness, elastic modulus)  
  • High‐strength (hard, “rigid”) substrate: hardly any plastic flow occurs in the substrate, so most of the plastic work is confined to the much smaller volume of the particle.  That high‐energy‐density plastic flow produces a very hot, highly localized zone in the particle, which again can reach or exceed melting.  
  • Low‐strength (soft, “deformable”) substrate: a larger fraction of the impact energy drives substrate deformation.  The plastic work is spread out into a bigger volume, both in particle and substrate, so the peak temperature in any one spot is lower.  

Combined effect  
  – Hard + low‐kth substrate gives the highest interfacial‐temperature spikes and therefore the greatest risk (or benefit, if you want transient melting for welding) of local melting.  
  – Soft + high‐kth substrate gives the lowest peaks, so you rarely reach local melt—even though bonding may suffer if you don’t get enough adiabatic heating.  

In brief:  
  – Low thermal conductivity ⇒ higher interface temperatures for a given impact condition.  
  – High substrate strength (low deformability) ⇒ plastic work is confined to the particle ⇒ smaller hot‐spot volume ⇒ higher peak temperatures.  
  – The converse combinations suppress peak temperatures and melting.

Carrier‐gas choice in cold spray primarily controls particle exit velocity (via gas density and speed of sound) and hence the degree of plastic deformation, interparticle bonding and residual stress in the deposit.  In practical terms:

1. Helium (light, high acoustic velocity)  
   – Highest particle velocities (800–1 100 m/s for typical nozzles)  
   – Very high deposition efficiency, ultradense coatings  
   – Maximum work hardening and adiabatic shear bonding at splat interfaces  
   – Highest fracture strength (> 600 MPa in many alloys)  
   – Lowest fracture toughness (KIC often < 10 MPa·m½) due to embrittling residual stresses and very fine microstructure  

2. Nitrogen (intermediate molecular weight)  
   – Moderate velocities (500–800 m/s)  
   – Good density, somewhat less work hardening  
   – Lower residual stress levels  
   – Fracture strengths in the 300–500 MPa range  
   – Improved toughness (KIC ~10–15 MPa·m½) compared with He sprays  

3. Argon (heavier, lower acoustic velocity)  
   – Lowest velocities (400–700 m/s)  
   – Best for very ductile coatings where some porosity is tolerable  
   – Tensile strengths often 200–400 MPa  
   – Highest toughness (KIC > 15 MPa·m½), but more voids and weaker interparticle bonds  

Trade‐off summary:  
– He‐sprayed coatings = maximum fracture strength at the expense of toughness  
– N2 = balanced strength/toughness  
– Ar = highest toughness but lower strength  

By adjusting the gas, spray temperature and pressure, one tunes the kinetic energy per particle and thus tailors the strength vs. toughness balance.

Particle size influences the cold-spray critical velocity (Vc) through three interlinked mechanisms: acceleration in the carrier gas, heat generation (and loss) at impact, and the momentum/energy required to achieve the interfacial pressures and strain rates for bonding.  In practice one observes that Vc tends to rise with increasing particle diameter, although very fine powders can also suffer elevated thresholds due to rapid cooling.

1. Acceleration and drag  
   • Smaller particles (say < 10 µm) have a high drag-to-mass ratio, so they accelerate more completely toward the gas exit velocity under a given pressure drop.  
   • Larger particles (> 30 µm) have more inertia, accelerate more slowly, and may not reach the nozzle-exit speed.  

2. Impact pressure and strain energy  
   • Bonding in cold spray generally requires that the particle impact pressure exceed the material’s dynamic yield or shear‐instability threshold (often linked to the Hugoniot Elastic Limit).  
   • Impact pressure pimp scales roughly as ρp·Vc², so larger particles—despite carrying more total kinetic energy—must hit harder (higher Vc) to generate the necessary peak pressures over their contact area.  

3. Thermal softening vs. cooling  
   • Plastic deformation at the interface is aided by local adiabatic heating.  
   • Very small particles lose heat to the surrounding gas extremely quickly (high surface-to-volume ratio), which can raise Vc because you need extra kinetic energy (i.e. speed) to achieve the same softening.  

Empirically and by finite‐element models one finds, for a given material and gas condition, that  
   Vc ∝ D^α  with α typically in the 0.1 – 0.3 range.  
In other words:  
   – Going from 10 µm to 30 µm powders often pushes Vc up by 10 – 30 %.  
   – There is usually an optimum size (e.g. 15 – 30 µm for many metals) where Vc is minimized because the powder accelerates well, retains enough heat to soften on impact, and carries sufficient momentum to bond.  

Summary  
   – Larger particles require higher Vc to reach the same interfacial pressure and strain rate.  
   – Very fine particles, although easy to accelerate, can lose thermal softening and thus also show a modest rise in Vc.  
   – Mid‐sized powders strike the best balance, minimizing critical velocity.

Particle velocity in cold‐gas dynamic spray is the single most critical parameter controlling both how particles bond on impact and how dense the resulting coating becomes.  Below about 300–400 m/s (material‐dependent), particles simply bounce or erode the substrate; above a material‐specific “critical velocity,” they begin to adhere.  As velocity climbs further, bonding mechanisms and porosity evolve as follows:

1.  Sub-critical regime (<Vcrit)  
    –  Impact energy (½mv²) too low to cause significant plastic deformation or oxide‐film rupture.  
    –  No metallurgical bonding; deposit efficiency ≈0, coating does not build.  

2.  Near-critical regime (≈Vcrit to ~1.1 Vcrit)  
    –  Just enough kinetic energy to initiate localized plastic deformation at particle and substrate surface.  
    –  Partial jetting of surface oxides (“adiabatic shear instability”) begins, creating fresh metal-to-metal contact.  
    –  Deposit efficiency rises, but interparticle cohesion is still weak coatings contain 5–15 vol % porosity.  

3.  Optimum regime (~1.1 – 1.5 Vcrit)  
    –  High strain rates generate sustained adiabatic shear zones at the interface; dynamic recrystallization refines subgrains.  
    –  Oxide films are continuously dispersed into the jet, maximizing true metal‐metal bonding.  
    –  Coating porosity falls to <1–3 vol %; bond strength and hardness peak.  

4.  Over-velocity regime (>~1.5 Vcrit)  
    –  Extremely high impact stresses can cause particle fracture (especially for brittle or ceramic feedstocks), substrate erosion, or rebound of over-hardened particles.  
    –  Residual tensile stresses may rise, risking spallation or microcracking.  
    –  Further gains in density and adhesion are marginal or even negative.  

Typical critical velocities (steel substrate)  
–  Aluminum alloys: ~550–650 m/s  
–  Copper: ~600–700 m/s  
–  Nickel‐based alloys: ~750–900 m/s  

In practice, one tunes gas temperature, pressure and stand-off distance to achieve a particle impact velocity in the “optimum regime.”  That maximizes plastic deformation, oxide-film disruption, and localized heating (but stays below levels that cause substrate damage), yielding the highest deposit efficiency and the lowest residual porosity.

In low‐pressure cold‐gas spraying the gas accelerates particles by drag, but the very same drag in the expanding (low‐density) jet also decelerates them.  Because drag force scales with particle cross‐section (∼d²) while inertia (mass) scales with volume (∼d³), the net particle acceleration a≡Fdrag∕m goes roughly like 1∕d.  This simple scaling immediately tells us two things:  

  1.  Small particles (small d) have large drag‐to‐mass ratios, so in the high‐density part of the nozzle they accelerate almost “instantly” toward the gas velocity.  Unfortunately, once they leave the nozzle and encounter the lower‐density jet and ambient air, that same large drag‐to‐mass ratio causes them to decelerate just as quickly.  They simply cannot carry their nozzle‐exit velocity all the way to the substrate.  

  2.  Large particles (large d) have small drag‐to‐mass ratios, so they “ride through” the free jet without much deceleration, but in the confined, higher‐density section of the nozzle their inertia is too great—their drag acceleration is too weak and their residence time in the accelerating flow too short—so they never reach very high speeds in the first place.  

Because of these two opposing trends there is a narrow band of diameters for which  
  • the drag‐acceleration time constant τaccel≃m∕(C ρgA) is shorter than the gas‐residence time in the nozzle (so the particle nearly reaches gas speed before the throat), and at the same time  
  • the drag‐deceleration time constant τdecel≃m∕(C ρambientA) is longer than the flight time from the nozzle exit to the substrate (so it does not slow appreciably in the jet).  

That matching of acceleration and deceleration timescales produces a peak in achievable particle velocity versus size.  Particles smaller than that optimal size accelerate fast but lose it again; particles larger than that size hold onto what little velocity they gain but simply never accelerate enough.  The result is a well‐defined “sweet spot” in diameter where the net final particle velocity is maximal.

In cold spray deposition the key to whether you get mostly “locking‐in” of particles or true metal–metal bonding is simply which side (particle or substrate) takes up most of the plastic work on impact.  That partitioning is governed to first order by their relative hardness (or yield strength):

1.  Particle much harder than substrate (H​p ≫ H​s)  
    •  On impact the soft substrate “gives.”  It deforms around the rigid particle, forming a crater or undercut into which the particle embeds.  
    •  Because the particle hardly plastically flows, there is little jetting of surface oxides or adiabatic‐shear‐instability at the interface.  You end up with a mechanically interlocked particle, bound chiefly by geometric anchoring and friction, not by metallurgical bonds.  

2.  Substrate equal‐to or harder than particle (H​s ≳ H​p)  
    •  The stiff substrate resists deformation, so most of the impact energy goes into plastically deforming the particle.  
    •  Intense shear at the interface generates a high‐velocity “microjet” that strips off oxide films and brings fresh metal faces into intimate atomic contact.  Local adiabatic heating, dynamic recrystallization, dislocation generation, etc., all promote solid‐state (metallurgical) bonding.  

3.  Intermediate cases  
    •  If hardnesses are comparable you get a mix: both particle and substrate deform, giving partial mechanical interlock plus some degree of metallurgical bonding.  

In practice this also shows up as a shift in the “critical velocity” needed for adhesion.  Softer substrates require higher particle velocity to reach the strain‐rate and shear‐stress needed to plastically deform the particle (and jet oxides), whereas with very hard substrates particles begin to bond metallurgically at lower velocities—provided they don’t shatter on impact.

Particle‐scale properties exert a first‐order control over how cold-sprayed particles deform, bond and pack, and thus directly set the coating’s porosity level and its fine‐scale structure.  In practice you adjust the feedstock distribution (size, shape) and material ductility/toughness to hit a “sweet spot” where impact velocities exceed the bonding threshold but avoid excessive particle fracture or rebound.  

1. Particle size  
  • Momentum and kinetic energy: larger particles (tens of microns and up) carry more momentum at a given gas velocity, so they can more easily exceed the “critical velocity” for bonding.  However, they are harder to accelerate and often do not deform uniformly, leaving unfilled gaps between splats.  Those voids show up as interlamellar porosity.  
  • Packing and filling: a broad bimodal or multimodal size distribution is often used.  Fine particles (< 5 µm) fill the interstices between coarser flattened splats, reducing open porosity, while coarse particles (20–50 µm) supply the bulk of the mass flux.  Very fine powders on their own, though, have too little momentum, tend to rebound or form loose agglomerates, and can oxidize more readily—raising porosity.  
  • Strain‐induced grain refinement: smaller particles are more uniformly strained on impact, producing a finer subgrain and ultrafine‐grain layer through severe plastic deformation.  Excessive fragmentation of very small or embrittled powders can create microcracks that raise closed‐cell porosity.  

2. Particle shape  
  • Spherical or near-spherical particles accelerate most efficiently in the carrier gas and deform into regular pancake-like “splats,” promoting tight, uniform lamellar stacking.  The result is lower interlamellar porosity and more homogeneous deformation‐induced grain refinement.  
  • Irregular or angular feedstock supplies mechanical interlocking and higher as-sprayed green strength, but the asperities and sharp corners can trap voids and impede the conformal collapse of neighbouring splats.  Fragmentation at sharp edges can further elevate porosity.  
  • Platelets or flakes (e.g. Mo, W alloys) may orient in-flight to give strong in-plane bonding but leave large planar gaps out of plane, unless a tailored size distribution forces folding and overlap.  

3. Material ductility and work‐hardening behavior  
  • High‐ductility metals (Al, Cu, Ni) readily undergo adiabatic shear and splat formation, producing metallurgical bonding via intimate atomic contact and even localized jetting that expels oxides.  This typically yields coatings with sub-1 % open porosity and strong interlamellar cohesion.  
  • Low-ductility or high-strength alloys (Ti alloys, stainless steels, Ni superalloys) require higher impact velocities (and hence higher gas temperatures/pressures) just to reach the same level of plastic deformation.  Inadequate deformation leads to poor bonding, more interparticle voids, and laminar cracks.  Conversely, if you exceed certain velocities you may cause particle shattering or severe work hardening at splat edges, also increasing porosity.  
  • Pre-heating to lower yield stress or tailoring the gas temperature/pressure can mitigate brittleness—but the fundamental limit remains the material’s capacity to deform at the cold-spray impact strain rates (10^5–10^6 s^–1).  

Net effect on coating microstructure and porosity  
  • Optimal feedstocks are usually spherical powders with a controlled bimodal size distribution in the 5–30 µm range for Cu- or Al-based systems, and slightly coarser for harder alloys.  That gives a dense, well-bonded lamellar microstructure, minimal open porosity (< 1 %), and a strongly work-hardened interfacial zone with ultrafine grains.  
  • Deviations—too coarse, too angular, or too brittle—lead to incomplete particle consolidation, higher interlamellar void fractions (2–10 % or more), and a correspondingly weaker, more permeable coating.  
  • Microstructurally, you observe:  
     – a highly deformed “skin” on each cold-sprayed splat, with grain‐refined zones tens to hundreds of nanometers thick;  
     – un-deformed cores in the largest particles (if size is excessive);  
     – dark, oxide‐rich pockets or microcracks at poorly bonded interfaces in the case of angular/brittle powders.  

By carefully tuning size, shape and selecting alloys with adequate ductility (or combining them with process heating), you push more of the feedstock into the well‐bonded, finely deformed regime, minimizing porosity and maximizing mechanical/metallurgical properties.

In cold spray, particles carried in a high‐pressure, high‐velocity gas jet must impact the substrate with sufficient kinetic energy and momentum to undergo intense plastic deformation, form an adiabatic shear instability at the interface, and bond without rebounding. Both particle size (d) and impact velocity (v) enter critically into that picture—and their “cross–talk” largely governs whether you build a dense deposit or end up with a porous, poorly adhering coating.

1. Critical velocity and deposition windows  
 • Critical velocity (Vc) is the minimum v at which a given material will plastically deform and weld rather than rebound. Vc is set by its yield stress, strain‐rate sensitivity, thermal softening behavior, etc., and is only weakly size‐dependent in the sense of material response. Typical Vc’s run from ~350–700 m/s for Al alloys up to ~800–1,100 m/s for steels.  
 • Below Vc: particles rebound or erode the substrate → little or no deposition and very high porosity.  
 • Above Vc but below an erosion threshold: good deposition, interparticle filling, low porosity.  
 • Far above Vc: you can get substrate erosion, reverse jetting, microcracking, or unwanted work-hardening that can raise final porosity.

2. Effect of particle size on acceleration and impact dynamics  
 • Acceleration in the gas: smaller particles accelerate more rapidly (drag ∝ d^2 vs. mass ∝ d^3), so very fine powders (< 5 µm) can exceed Vc easily. But once at velocity, their low mass → low momentum (m·v) and low kinetic energy (½m·v²) → insufficient energy per particle to create the full plastic flow and interfacial shear‐instability → limited bonding and high porosity.  
 • Larger particles (20–50 µm and above) carry far more momentum at the same v, so each impact can plastically deform more metal and fill voids. But large powders are harder to accelerate to Vc in a given gas set‐up. If they arrive < Vc, they simply ricochet or produce erosion. If they do reach very high v, their impacts may cause substrate damage or subsurface cracking, which again raises porosity or degrades adhesion.

3. Porosity trends with v and d  
 • At fixed d, porosity falls sharply as v is raised from below Vc to ~Vc + 50 m/s. Beyond that, additional v still improves interparticle bonding but with diminishing returns and rising risk of erosion ­– so a “sweet‐spot” window exists near Vc+10–30 %.  
 • At fixed v near Vc, there’s also a “Goldilocks” size: too small → insufficient impact energy → incomplete flattening → voids; too large → sub‐Vc impacts or substrate damage → porosity spikes. Typical optimum is in the 10–30 µm range for most metals.

4. Practical implications and optimization  
 • Powder selection: choose a PSD (particle size distribution) that maximizes the fraction of particles that can both reach and just exceed Vc. Narrow distributions avoid having too many fines (wasted gas energy) or coarses (poor acceleration).  
 • Gas conditions: higher pressure, lower gas molecular weight (e.g. He vs N₂) can raise particle velocities, letting you push larger sizes into the deposition window.  
 • Nozzle design and stand‐off: longer/nozzle or higher pressure raise v; too close leads to blast erosion; too far and you lose v by drag.

In sum, deposition efficiency, adhesion strength, and final coating density all hinge on getting each particle’s v safely above its material‐dependent Vc while also packing enough mass (i.e. choosing the right particle size) to drive full plastic flow and void‐closure on impact. Deviate in either direction and you pay in porosity, poor bonding, or substrate damage.

The core idea of the phase‐field method for brittle fracture is that instead of representing cracks by infinitely thin discontinuities in the displacement field u, you introduce a smooth auxiliary “damage” or “phase” field φ(x) ∈ [0,1] whose transition from φ≈0 (intact material) to φ≈1 (fully broken material) spreads the crack over a small length scale ℓ.  The crack geometry then emerges from the φ–field rather than being tracked explicitly as a moving set of surfaces.  

1. Variational energy functional  
   You postulate a total energy  
     E[u,φ]  =  
       ∫Ω g(φ) ψ⁺(ε(u))  +  ψ⁻(ε(u))  dV  
       +  Gc ∫Ω  (φ²/(2ℓ)  +  ℓ/2 |∇φ|²) dV  
   • ε(u) is the small‐strain tensor.  
   • ψ⁺/ψ⁻ split the elastic energy into tension‐driven (fracture‐promoting) and compression‐driven parts.  
   • g(φ) = (1−φ)² + k regularizes stiffness degradation (k≪1).  
   • Gc is the critical energy release rate, ℓ is the phase‐field length scale.  
   The first integral is the degraded elastic energy; the second is a diffused approximation of the Griffith surface energy ∫Γ crack Gc dS.  

2. Euler–Lagrange equations  
   Taking variations δu and δφ leads to two coupled PDEs, typically solved in a staggered or monolithic scheme:  
     – div [ g(φ) σ⁺(u) + σ⁻(u) ] = 0   (mechanical equilibrium)  
     Gc (φ/ℓ – ℓ Δφ)  – 2(1–φ) ψ⁺(ε(u))  = 0   (phase‐field evolution)  
   plus boundary and irreversibility conditions (φ̇ ≥ 0 or a history field H = max ψ⁺ over time).  

3. Natural crack initiation, propagation, branching, merger  
   • The φ–field diffuses cracks over ℓ but, as ℓ→0, recovers the sharp‐crack energy.  
   • New cracks nucleate wherever the energy release density 2ψ⁺ exceeds Gc/ℓ.  
   • Crack fronts advance along the steepest descent of the energy functional, automatically satisfying Griffith’s criterion.  
   • Because φ is a continuous field, complex events such as branching, kinking, or coalescence occur without special handling of crack surfaces or re‐meshing.  

4. Advantages of the variational framework  
   – Guarantees thermodynamic consistency (energy is nonincreasing after fracture).  
   – Provides a single global minimization principle rather than ad hoc crack‐growth rules.  
   – Easily couples to multi‐physics (plasticity, thermal effects, fluids) via additional energy terms.  

In summary, by casting fracture as the minimization of an energy functional over (u,φ) and regularizing the crack as a diffusive field, the phase‐field method automatically captures the nucleation, path deviation, branching, and merging of cracks as part of the same variational solution.

High‐pressure shockwaves in laser shock peening (LSP) generate ultrahigh strain rates (10^6–10^7 s^–1) and peak pressures of several GPa in the near-surface layer. The sequence of events is roughly:  
1. Laser pulse vaporizes an ablative coating or surface layer, producing a high-pressure plasma.  
2. The plasma expands against a confining overlay (usually water or transparent tape), launching a shockwave into the metal.  
3. That shockwave induces very large, localized plastic strains in nanoseconds, causing:  
   • Dislocation multiplication and pile-ups  
   • Dislocation cell and subgrain formation  
   • Intense adiabatic heating and rapid cooling in the deformation zone  
   • Continuous dynamic recrystallization (CDRX) or strain-induced boundary migration  

Together, these mechanisms break down coarse grains into ultrafine‐grained (UFG) and even nanocrystalline zones (100–500 nm), often with high‐angle boundaries.

Why ultrafine grains boost tribocorrosion resistance:  
1. Increased hardness and yield strength—UFG surfaces better resist mechanical wear and micro-ploughing, so passive oxide films suffer fewer mechanical breaches.  
2. High grain‐boundary density—grain boundaries act as fast diffusion paths and preferential sites for rapid repassivation, so once the passive film is damaged it reforms more quickly and uniformly.  
3. More uniform microstructure—reduced local compositional or microstructural heterogeneity minimizes microgalvanic couples that can accelerate localized corrosion under sliding or fretting.  
4. Reduced crack and pit propagation—high‐angle boundaries impede subsurface crack and pit growth under cyclic mechanical and electrochemical loading.  

In combination, these effects suppress the synergistic acceleration of wear by corrosion (and vice versa), raising both the wear life and the corrosion‐fatigue endurance of LSP‐treated components.

During plasma‐electrolytic oxidation (PEO) the nature of the surface discharges controls not only the rate of oxide growth but also what happens to any pre‐added ceramic particles.  When you switch from the relatively few, high‐energy B‐type discharges to a regime dominated by D‐type microdischarges, four key things happen to the dispersed ceramic particles:

1. Lower per‐pulse energy but much higher pulse frequency  
   – D‐type events last only micro‐ to nanoseconds and occur thousands of times per second, whereas B‐type microarcs last milliseconds at higher current densities.  
   – The peak temperature in each D‐type channel is still enough to locally melt or at least soften particle fragments, but the total heat input per event is much smaller.

2. Repeated thermal shock and rapid quenching  
   – Each D‐type event heats a tiny plasma channel to ~2 000–4 000 °C and then collapses almost instantly.  
   – Particles caught in these channels experience numerous cycles of rapid heating, fragmentation and quenching, driving them toward submicron size or even into an amorphous state.

3. Enhanced mixing and partial dissolution in the molten oxide  
   – The high frequency of discharges generates intense local fluid flow (turbulent eddies) within the molten oxide pool.  
   – Ceramic fragments are sheared, partially dissolved into the oxide melt, and then redeposited as very fine crystals or amorphous blobs as the channel solidifies.

4. Homogenization into a fine‐grained inner sublayer  
   – Because each D‐type discharge is so spatially confined and the cooling so rapid, any surviving fragments become too small and too well‐mixed with the surrounding alumina or titania to retain their original shape.  
   – The end result is a nanocrystalline/amorphous composite in the inner oxide sublayer where you can no longer distinguish discrete ceramic particles under conventional SEM or optical microscopy.

In short, by trading a few long, hot arcs for many ultra‐short, lower‐energy microdischarges you drive the particles through repeated melt–quench–shear cycles.  That process fragments, dissolves and reprecipitates them so thoroughly that they lose any recognizably “particle‐like” morphology in the inner oxide.

An NTC (negative‐temperature‐coefficient) ceramic’s total infrared emissivity ε(T) is the sum of two competing effects as you heat it:

 1. Phonon (molecular‐vibration) contribution  
    – At low T, the ceramic’s optical‐phonon modes are only weakly thermally excited, so ε is small.  
    – As T rises, those IR‐active lattice vibrations become more strongly populated according to the Bose–Einstein/Planck distribution.  That raises the phonon‐absorption coefficient and thus ε.  

 2. Free‐carrier (electronic) contribution via Hagen–Rubens  
    – NTC ceramics are semiconducting oxides whose resistivity ρ(T) falls exponentially with T (ρ∼ρ₀ exp(Eₐ/kT)).  
    – In the far‐IR the Hagen–Rubens relation gives   
         ε ≃ 1–R ≃ 2 √(ωε₀/σ)  ∝ √ρ  (since σ=1/ρ)  
      so as ρ decreases the emissivity governed by free‐carrier absorption also decreases.  

Putting these together:

  • At low‐to‐moderate T, the rising phonon emission dominates, so ε(T) climbs.  
  • Above a characteristic temperature the semiconductor conductivity has become large enough that the Hagen–Rubens (free‐carrier reflectivity) term wins, and ε(T) falls ∝√ρ(T).  

Thus ε(T) exhibits a maximum at the crossover between phonon-dominated increase and carrier-dominated decrease.

The derivation is trivial once you equate the average impact‐induced stress S to the quasistatic yield strength σ_y.  Starting from

 S = ρ v²/6

we demand S ≥ σ_y in order to plastically yield the particle (or the substrate).  Thus

 ρ v_c²/6 = σ_y

and so

 v_c = √(6 σ_y/ρ).

In other words, as long as your particle speed exceeds

 v_c = (6 σ_y/ρ)^(1/2)

the impact stress will reach the yield strength and plastic deformation (and hence bonding) can occur.

1. Cold‐spray occurs well below the melting point (Tm) of Al (typically 0.3–0.5 Tm) and each particle’s high‐velocity impact lasts only micro‐ to milliseconds. Although the severe plastic deformation generates very high dislocation densities, the temperature–time combination is far too low to enable long‐range diffusion of Mg and Si.  

2. During impact, Mg and Si atoms are dragged to and “parked” at high‐energy sites (dislocations, subgrain and adiabatic‐shear‐band boundaries). This segregation produces only extremely small, noncoherent clusters (if any), because the activation energy and diffusion distance required to form a stable β″ nucleus (critical radius r* ≈ 1–2 nm) are not met.  

3. Quantitatively, diffusion distance l≈√(Dt) with DMg ~ 10⁻²⁰–10⁻¹⁹ m²/s at 300–400 K and t < 10⁻³ s gives l ≪ 1 nm—insufficient to collect enough solute into a nucleus of stable β″.  

4. Consequently, the as-sprayed coating retains a supersaturated solid solution with solute‐enriched defects but no plate‐shaped β″ precipitates.  

5. In a subsequent solution treatment (e.g. 500 °C, 1–2 h), any coarse intermetallics or tiny GP‐type clusters dissolve. High‐temperature volume diffusion (D ~ 10⁻¹⁶–10⁻¹⁵ m²/s) homogenizes Mg and Si in the Al matrix.  

6. Rapid quenching “freezes” this homogeneous supersaturated solution in place, still loaded with a high density of dislocations from cold spraying.  

7. During artificial aging (e.g. 160–180 °C), DMg and DSi rise again (vacancy‐ and dislocation‐pipe diffusion), giving diffusion distances of tens of nanometers over hours. Solute atoms now can reach and coalesce at defects into nuclei exceeding r*.  

8. The dense network of dislocations and subgrain boundaries from the spray process acts as abundant low‐energy nucleation sites, sharply reducing the nucleation barrier (ΔG*). Mg–Si clusters grow into the coherent, needle-shaped β″ precipitates on {100}Al planes.  

Thus, only after the high‐temperature dissolution (to reset and redistribute solute) and controlled aging (to give solute atoms time and mobility to reach critical nucleus size) do the characteristic β″ precipitates form in cold-sprayed Al alloy coatings.

1. Impact and high-strain-rate plastic deformation  
   • Coating particles (0.5–50 μm) strike the substrate at 300–1200 m/s.  
   • The collision zones experience strain rates of 10^5–10^8 s^–1, generating intense shear and compressive stresses localized in ~1–5 μm thick interfacial jets.

2. Dislocation generation and multiplication  
   • The extreme shear instantly produces very high dislocation densities (10^14–10^15 m^–2).  
   • Dislocations accumulate, tangle, and form dense networks and cell structures in both the particle and substrate at the impact site.

3. Adiabatic heating and recovery processes  
   • Although bulk temperature remains below melting, local adiabatic heating (up to 0.3–0.5 Tm) occurs in shear bands.  
   • This moderate temperature rise enhances dislocation mobility, enabling dynamic recovery (annihilation and rearrangement of dislocations into subgrain boundaries).

4. Nucleation of new grains (dynamic recrystallization)  
   • In regions of highest stored energy (shear bands, particle–substrate interface), subgrain boundaries absorb dislocations and gradually rotate.  
   • Once a critical misorientation (~10–15°) is reached, these subgrains become high-angle grain boundaries, nucleating strain-free recrystallized grains.

5. Grain refinement via continuous dynamic recrystallization (cDRX)  
   • Further deformation drives progressive misorientation increases across subgrain boundaries, converting them into new grain boundaries.  
   • The process repeats as successive layers of particles impact, refining the grain size progressively down to the ultrafine (100–500 nm) or even nanocrystalline (<100 nm) regime.

6. Consolidation into a fine-grained deposit  
   • Multiple overlapping impact events and recrystallization cycles lead to a bulk deposit composed of equiaxed, strain-free grains.  
   • The resulting microstructure exhibits high hardness, strength, and often improved ductility due to Hall–Petch strengthening.

Summary: The ultrahigh strain rates of cold spray produce massive dislocation generation and localized heating that drive continuous dynamic recrystallization, converting dense dislocation structures into fine, equiaxed grains and thus refining the microstructure of the coating.

Below is a step-by-step outline of how heating the spray gas and accelerating metal powders to supersonic speed produces solid-state bonding in cold spray.

1. Powder feed and carrier gas selection  
   • Metal powders (typical size 5–50 µm) are metered into a high-pressure carrier gas line (N₂, He or H₂).  
   • The choice of gas affects sound speed, density and required operating pressure (2–6 MPa).

2. Gas heating  
   • The carrier gas is resistively or combustively heated to between ~200 °C and 800 °C—well below the powder’s melting point.  
   • Heating raises the gas’s total enthalpy, which can later be converted into kinetic energy in the nozzle.

3. Nozzle acceleration (de Laval nozzle)  
   • The heated, pressurized gas expands through a converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle.  
   • In the converging section the gas accelerates toward Mach 1 at the throat; in the diverging section it expands further to supersonic speeds (Mach 1.2–3).  

4. Particle acceleration  
   • Powder particles entrained in the gas accelerate along with it.  
   • By the nozzle exit they reach velocities typically in the 300–1200 m/s range, carrying high kinetic energy (½mv²).  
   • Because the gas temperature is below the powder’s melting point, particles remain in the solid phase.

5. Impact and severe plastic deformation  
   • Supersonic particles impinge on the substrate (or previously deposited layer) at near‐normal incidence.  
   • The enormous impact pressure (often several GPa) induces extreme localized plastic deformation in both particle and substrate surfaces.

6. Oxide fracture and jetting  
   • At these pressures and strain rates (>10⁶ s⁻¹), the thin native oxide/lubricant layers fracture and eject (“jet”) outward from the interface.  
   • This exposes fresh, oxide‐free metal surfaces in intimate contact under pressure.

7. Adiabatic shear heating and dynamic recrystallization  
   • Plastic work is partly converted into heat in a very thin interfacial zone, raising its temperature but still below melting.  
   • This promotes dynamic recovery/recrystallization, locally softening the metal and facilitating atomic diffusion across the clean interface.

8. Solid-state bonding  
   • Under the combined action of high contact pressure, intimate contact of fresh metal, and enhanced diffusivity, a metallurgical bond forms without any bulk melting.  
   • Subsequent particles build up layer by layer into a dense, cohesive coating or component.

Key take-aways  
   – Gas heating does not melt the powder; it simply raises the gas enthalpy so it can efficiently convert to particle kinetic energy.  
   – Supersonic impact produces plastic deformation, oxide removal, local heating and atomic contact—all in the solid state.  
   – The result is a high-density, low-oxidation, residual-stress-reduced coating or part made by solid-state welding rather than fusion.

During a progressive scratch test with a conical tip the frictional force is almost entirely a ploughing/shear‐strength effect.  In the simplest model one writes

  Fₚ ≃ τ·A_proj

where τ is the (coating) shear strength and A_proj is the projected contact area of the cone.  For a perfect cone of half‐angle θ penetrating to depth h

  A_proj  ∝ h²

so if τ were constant you would predict

  Fₚ  ∝ h² .

In cold‐sprayed coatings, however, τ (or equivalently the hardness H) is not constant but falls off with increasing penetration depth—largely because of an indentation‐size effect (and in many cases a substrate‐compliance effect at higher h).  Empirically one finds over the range of interest

  H  ∼ 1/√h

(sub‐surface strain‐gradient hardening, geometrically necessary dislocations, etc.).  Inserting that into the ploughing model gives

  Fₚ  ∼ H(h)·h²  ∼ h^(–½)·h²  =  h^(3/2) ,

i.e. the F ∝ h^1.5 scaling you observe.  In short, the cone geometry would alone give h², but the size-dependent hardness of the coating reduces the exponent to ≃1.5.

In laser‐based cladding or coating, everything ultimately comes back to how much energy you deliver to a given piece of substrate per unit time and per unit area.  By deliberately choosing your laser power (P), beam diameter (d), and scan speed (v), you fix two key energy‐density parameters:

  1.  Power density I = P / (π·(d/2)²)   [W/cm²]  
  2.  Linear energy density ED = P / v     [J/mm]

Once you know I and ED, you can predict:

  A.  Deposition mode  
     •  Conduction‐mode cladding (I ∼10⁴–10⁶ W/cm²; moderate ED):  
        –  Heat is absorbed and conducted into the surface without vaporizing metal.  
        –  Melt pools are shallow, nearly hemispherical; wetting is steady and bead shape is well controlled.  
     •  Keyhole/welding mode (I >10⁶ W/cm²; high ED):  
        –  Vaporization and recoil pressure open a “keyhole.”  
        –  Melt pools become deep and turbulent, often leading to porosity, undercut, or balling.  

  B.  Dilution  
     Dilution D ≃ (melted‐substrate mass) / (total clad mass).  In practice,  
     •  Low ED → shallow melt, D ≲ 5–10 %  
     •  Moderate ED → moderate melt‐through, D ∼10–20 %  
     •  High ED → deep penetration, D >20–30 % (often undesirable if you’re trying to preserve the substrate chemistry)  

     Roughly speaking, D increases monotonically with ED because a larger, hotter pool melts more substrate.  If your target is minimal dilution (e.g. a wear‐resistant overlay), you deliberately run at the low‐to‐mid ED of conduction‐mode cladding.  

  C.  Microstructure refinement  
     The final grain size or primary dendrite arm spacing (PDAS) is controlled by the solidification cooling rate, CR ≃ G·R  
       •  G = thermal gradient in the melt ahead of the solid–liquid interface (K/mm)  
       •  R = interface growth rate ≃ scan speed (mm/s)  

     Key trends:  
       –  Higher ED (high P, slow v, large d) → large melt pool, low G, low R → coarse columnar grains or long‐arm dendrites.  
       –  Lower ED (low P, fast v, small d) → small pool, high G, high R → planar or cellular growth transitioning quickly to very fine equiaxed or dendritic microstructure.  

     Empirically PDAS ∝ (G·R)^(–¼) to (G·R)^(–½) depending on alloy, so doubling R or G refines the microstructure by 20–30 %.  

In practice you tune P, d, and v to hit the “sweet spot” where you:  
  •  Stay in conduction‐mode (for stable, low‐porosity beads),  
  •  Achieve just enough ED for metallurgical bonding but not so much as to over‐dilute your powder chemistry, and  
  •  Generate a small, fast‐freezing melt pool to lock in the finest possible microstructure and maximize hardness or wear resistance.

In a typical cold‐spray jet the particle exit speeds follow a Gaussian‐shaped profile in the radial direction: highest in the center, tapering off toward the edges.  Superimposed on that is a material‐specific “critical deposition velocity” Vc, below which particles will not adhere but instead simply impact, plastically deform the surface, or rebound.  As a single beam scans across a substrate, each point on the surface sees that Gaussian profile in time—first the slow rim, then the mid‐speed annulus, then the fast core.  Because each velocity band interacts differently with the substrate, the beam in one pass effectively “prepares → builds → finishes” the coating.

1. Outer (sub‐critical) region—substrate preparation  
   • Particle velocity < Vc  
   • No net deposition. Particles plastically deform or abrade the very surface, breaking oxide films, dislodging contaminants, and introducing a controlled roughness/strain‐hardening peen.  
   • Result: a clean, work‐hardened, high‐surface‐area substrate ready for adhesion.

2. Mid‐radius (near‐critical) region—coating formation  
   • Particle velocity ≈ Vc (just above or just below)  
   • Particles begin to adhere, nucleating small splats that mechanically lock into the roughened surface. Adhesion is modest but continuous growth of a thin, porous underlayer occurs.  
   • Result: the first coherent layer of deposited material, with plenty of interparticle boundaries for subsequent consolidation.

3. Central (super‐critical) region—coating finishing and densification  
   • Particle velocity ≫ Vc  
   • Particles undergo intense plastic deformation on impact, fracturing oxides on the particle surface and welding both to the substrate nuclei and to each other. The high strain rates close residual pores and voids from the mid‐region.  
   • Result: a dense, well‐bonded, peened final‐pass microstructure with low porosity and high cohesive strength.

Thus, in a single traverse of the spray gun each patch of substrate is first cleaned and roughened by the slow periphery, then seeded with an undercoat by the moderate‐velocity annulus, and finally consolidated and smoothed by the high‐speed core.

In cold spray, the particle’s exit‐velocity vₚ is set almost entirely by how fast the carrier gas is moving in the nozzle (u_g) and how effectively that gas drags the particle along.  Three primary gas parameters control u_g and thus vₚ: stagnation (carrier) pressure P₀, gas molecular weight M, and gas temperature T₀.  In turn, vₚ dictates the impact kinetic energy and plastic deformation at the substrate, which control the interfacial bonding and ultimate adhesion strength of the coating.

1.   Nozzle gas velocity u_g  
     Under (quasi)­isentropic expansion from chamber pressure P₀ to back­pressure P_b, the axial gas velocity at the nozzle exit is  
     u_g ≃ √[2 k/(k–1) · R·T₀ · (1 – (P_b/P₀)^((k–1)/k))]  
     •  k = specific‐heat ratio (c_p/c_v)  
     •  R = R_u/M (so lighter gases have larger R)  
     •  T₀ = stagnation temperature  
     •  P₀/P_b = expansion ratio (higher P₀ ⇒ higher Mach ⇒ higher u_g)  

     – Raising P₀ increases the pressure ratio P₀/P_b and pushes the flow deeper into the supersonic regime, boosting u_g.  
     – Using a lighter gas (smaller M) raises R and celerity of sound a = √(kRT₀), so for the same P₀/T₀ you get a higher u_g.  
     – Increasing T₀ also increases a and the available enthalpy drop, so u_g scales approximately as √T₀.

2.   Particle acceleration and terminal velocity  
     As particles traverse the nozzle, they accelerate under the drag force:  
     F_d = ½·C_d·A_p·ρ_g·(u_g – vₚ)²  
     Newton’s law gives  
     dvₚ/dt = F_d / mₚ  
            = [3·C_d·ρ_g / (4·ρₚ·dₚ)] · (u_g – vₚ)²  

     •  ρ_g = local gas density (falls as velocity rises; roughly ρ_g∝P₀/T₀)  
     •  ρₚ, dₚ = particle density and diameter  
     •  C_d = drag coefficient (~0.5–1 for spherical or irregular particles)  

     Because u_g itself depends on P₀, M, T₀, all three gas parameters imprint on vₚ.  In general:  
     – ↑P₀ ⇒ ↑ρ_g and ↑u_g ⇒ ↑drag acceleration ⇒ ↑vₚ  
     – ↓M ⇒ ↑u_g (for constant T₀,P₀) ⇒ ↑drag ⇒ ↑vₚ  
     – ↑T₀ ⇒ ↓ρ_g (slightly) but significantly ↑u_g ⇒ net ↑drag ⇒ ↑vₚ  

3.   Particle velocity vs. coating adhesion  
     Adhesion strength σ_a in cold spray correlates strongly with the particle impact velocity vₚ relative to a material‐specific critical velocity v_c.  Below v_c particles tend to rebound or form weak, powdery deposits; above v_c they undergo intense, localized plastic deformation that:  
     a) breaks surface oxides, exposing fresh metal  
     b) generates high dislocation densities and grain‐refinement at the interface  
     c) causes mechanical interlocking and metallurgical bonding  

     Empirically, σ_a rises steeply once vₚ exceeds v_c and then begins to plateau or even decrease if vₚ becomes so large that it induces substrate erosion or severe heating.  A simple phenomenological relation is sometimes used:  
     σ_a ∝ (vₚ – v_c)^n    for vₚ > v_c,   n ≈ 1–3  

     Key points:  
     – Raising P₀, choosing a light carrier gas (He>H₂>N₂), or pre­heating the gas all raise vₚ, thus improving deposition efficiency and adhesion strength—up to the point where damage or excessive residual stresses set in.  
     – Increasing vₚ not only increases the number of particles that stick (deposition efficiency) but also enhances the true shear‐bond strength by driving stronger, more uniform plastic flow and metal–metal contact.  
     – The optimal velocity window depends on the material system: e.g. Al alloys v_c≈400–600 m/s; Cu alloys v_c≈600–800 m/s; steels v_c≈800–1200 m/s.

Summary  
•  Carrier‐gas pressure P₀ ↑, molecular weight M ↓, or temperature T₀ ↑ ⇒ higher gas Mach number and sound speed ⇒ higher gas velocity u_g.  
•  Higher u_g and gas density ⇒ stronger drag force ⇒ particles accelerate more rapidly and reach higher terminal vₚ.  
•  Particle impact velocity vₚ must exceed a critical value v_c to achieve good plastic deformation, oxide disruption, and intimate metal bonding—so adhesion strength climbs rapidly above v_c and then plateaus or degrades if vₚ is too high.

Below is a concise, step-by-step outline of how supersonic laser deposition (SLD) bonds metal particles to a substrate by combining kinetic (cold-spray-type) and thermal (laser-assisted) effects:

1. Powder feeding and gas acceleration  
   • Metal powder (typically 5–50 µm) is entrained in a high-pressure gas (He or N₂ at 2–5 MPa).  
   • The gas–particle mixture expands through a converging–diverging (De Laval) nozzle, accelerating particles to supersonic speeds (600–1 200 m/s).

2. In-flight laser pre-heating/softening  
   • A focused CW or pulsed laser (wavelength ~1 µm, power density ~10⁵–10⁶ W/cm²) intersects the particle stream upstream of the substrate.  
   • Particles absorb laser energy, raising their temperature to a fraction of melting (typically 0.3–0.7 Tm), which lowers their yield strength and increases ductility without causing bulk melting.

3. Impact and plastic deformation  
   • Supersonic particles strike the substrate at high strain-rates (10⁶–10⁷ s⁻¹).  
   • Even though thermally softened, the particle still undergoes severe plastic deformation on impact, generating compressive stresses and high local strains at the interface.

4. Adiabatic shear and jetting  
   • The combination of high strain-rate and thermal softening triggers localized shear instabilities at the interface (“adiabatic shear bands”).  
   • Material jets form at the leading edge, physically expelling surface oxides and contaminants.

5. Surface activation and mechanical interlocking  
   • Jetting and plastic flow produce fresh, oxide-free metal surfaces in intimate contact.  
   • Deformed particles embed into surface asperities, creating a tight mechanical interlock.

6. Metallurgical bonding via dynamic recrystallization and diffusion  
   • The adiabatic heat spike at the shear bands (locally approaching or briefly exceeding Tm) promotes dynamic recrystallization and formation of ultrafine grains.  
   • High dislocation densities and the transient local heating accelerate solid-state diffusion across the interface, establishing true metallurgical bonds.

7. Layer consolidation and build-up  
   • Subsequent particles impact both the substrate and already-deposited layers.  
   • Reheat and deformation of underlying layers further drive diffusion and stress relief, yielding a dense, fully bonded coating or near-net-shape build.

Key synergistic roles of kinetic + thermal effects:  
– Kinetic impact provides the plastic deformation and jetting needed to break oxides and achieve mechanical anchoring.  
– Laser-induced thermal softening reduces required impact velocity, lowers substrate damage, and by raising local temperatures enhances diffusion and dynamic recrystallization for strong metallurgical bonding.

Below is a step-by-step rationale for why cold‐sprayed Al‐alloy deposits always end up with similarly high flow stresses, insensitive to the feedstock’s initial microstructure or the precise spray pressure (so long as you’re above the critical deposition velocity).

1. Supersonic impact and extreme strain rates  
   – Particles strike the substrate/previous layer at high velocity (typically 600–1200 m/s).  
   – Local strain rates of order 10^5–10^7 s^–1 develop in the interfacial zone.  

2. Adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization (DRX)  
   – The impact produces highly localized plastic work and a transient temperature spike (“adiabatic shear band”).  
   – That thermal‐mechanical spike drives DRX in a thin layer (1–3 µm) around every particle boundary.  
   – Grain sizes in that layer refine to the submicron or even nanocrystalline scale, regardless of the parent powder grains.  

3. Erasure of the feedstock’s original microstructure  
   – Whatever dislocation content, precipitate state or grain size you started with in the powder, it is over-ridden by the new, impact-driven DRX microstructure.  
   – Any coarse precipitates tread a fine line: small ones can be sheared and redistributed, large ones can fragment, but they play only a secondary role in strengthening.  

4. Convergent strengthening mechanisms in the deposit  
   – Hall–Petch strengthening from ultrafine DRX grains at all particle interfaces.  
   – A very high forest‐dislocation density frozen in by the rapid quench following impact.  
   – Residual compressive stresses and subgrain boundaries from incomplete recovery.  
   – (Minor) Orowan or solid‐solution contributions from any retained solutes or finely dispersed second phases.  

5. Insensitivity to spray pressure (above critical velocity)  
   – Once particle velocities exceed the critical deposition threshold, the peak local strain, strain rate, and temperature in the shear bands all lie in a narrow band.  
   – Raising pressure (and hence velocity) further gives diminishing returns in local peak temperature and strain, so the DRX grain size and dislocation saturation level plateau.  

6. Net result: a “universal” cold‐spray microstructure  
   – Interfacial nanograins (100–500 nm) surrounded by a high‐dislocation‐density matrix.  
   – Equiaxed subgrains in the particle interiors, partly recovered but still much smaller than original powder grains.  
   – This structure always yields a similarly high flow stress (typically 200–350 MPa in compression or micro‐pillar tests), irrespective of powder history or modest changes in spray pressure.  

Bottom line: cold spray’s extreme, localized plasticity and rapid DRX forge a new, fine and heavily strained microstructure that dominates strength, effectively erasing any “memory” of the starting powder or small increases in spray pressure.

Below is a step‐by‐step, qualitative outline of how gas temperature (T₀) and particle mass (mₚ) govern particle velocity in cold spray and hence deposition efficiency.

1. Nozzle expansion and gas exit speed  
   – For a given stagnation pressure p₀ and exit pressure pₑ, the gas Mach number Mₑ and exit speed v_g are set by compressible‐flow relations:  
     v_g ≃√[2γ/(γ–1)·R·T₀·(1–(pₑ/p₀)^((γ–1)/γ))]  
   – At constant pressure ratio p₀/pₑ an increase in T₀ raises the local speed of sound √(γRT₀) and thus v_g roughly ∝√T₀.

2. Drag force on the particle  
   – As particles ride in the supersonic jet, they are accelerated by the drag:  
     F_d = ½·C_d·ρ_g·A_p·(v_g–vₚ)²  
     where ρ_g ≃p_g/(R·T_g), A_p=πd²/4.  
   – Increasing T₀ lowers ρ_g (ρ_g ∝1/T₀) but boosts (v_g–vₚ)² ∝T₀. To first order the net drag grows with the higher velocity difference.

3. Particle acceleration and residence time  
   – Newton’s law: mₚ·dvₚ/dt = F_d. Thus the acceleration aₚ≃F_d/mₚ.  
   – Heavier particles (larger mₚ∝ρₚ·d³) experience smaller dvₚ/dt under the same drag.  
   – The available acceleration time is set by the nozzle length L and v_g: t_res ≃L/v_g.

4. Exit particle velocity vₚ,out  
   – Integrating dvₚ/dt over t_res gives vₚ,out≈v_g·[1–exp(–t_res/τ)] with τ=mₚ/(C_d·ρ_g·A_p·v_g).  
   – Higher T₀ reduces τ (through higher v_g and drag), raises t_res/τ and pushes vₚ,out closer to v_g.  
   – Lower mₚ likewise reduces τ, making vₚ,out trail v_g less and thus grow.

5. Deposition efficiency  
   – Cold spray requires vₚ,out above a critical velocity v_c for adhesion.  
   – Raising T₀→higher vₚ,out→more particles exceed v_c→higher deposition efficiency.  
   – Increasing mₚ→lower vₚ,out→fewer particles surpass v_c→reduced deposition efficiency.

Summary:  
• Higher gas temperature → higher gas‐jet speed and drag → faster particle acceleration → higher exit particle velocity → improved deposition.  
• Larger particle mass → lower acceleration for given drag → reduced exit velocity → poorer deposition unless compensated by higher T₀ or longer residence time.

Below is a qualitative sketch of what happens when you move your powder size below, through, and above the “optimum” size for a given cold‐spray system.  Here d is the particle diameter and d_opt is the size at which you get the highest deposition efficiency (DE) under your chosen gas and spray conditions.

1. d < d_opt (“too fine”)  
   • Acceleration and impact velocity (V_imp) are high (drag∕mass ∼1/d).  
   • The particle’s critical velocity V_c actually rises as d→small (smaller particles need higher strain‐rate to achieve the same plastic work, and they have less kinetic energy per particle).  
   • V_imp may exceed the material’s bulk V_c, but the absolute kinetic energy and momentum (∼m·V_imp) are low, so particles tend to rebound or be deflected rather than plastically deform and bond.  
   • Net DE falls off sharply below optimum size.

2. d ≈ d_opt  
   • Acceleration is still strong, and V_imp reaches its maximum for that system.  
   • The bulk‐material V_c is essentially size‐matched: plastic deformation and adiabatic shear instabilities are triggered most easily.  
   • Kinetic energy and momentum are enough to exceed V_c by a good margin, but not so high as to cause particle fracture or excessive substrate erosion.  
   • DE peaks (you get the highest fraction of particles sticking and building up the coating).

3. d > d_opt (“too coarse”)  
   • Acceleration (and hence V_imp) falls off as d grows (drag∕mass ∼1/d).  
   • The bulk critical velocity V_c falls only modestly with size (larger particles carry more inertia, but their lower V_imp means they often cannot reach V_c).  
   • Below a certain size‐dependent V_imp, particles neither deform sufficiently nor bond—they may erode the substrate or simply embed poorly.  
   • DE again decreases, often even more steeply than on the fine side.

In summary:  
– Small powders accelerate fastest but carry too little momentum (and actually demand a slightly higher V_c), so DE is low.  
– At the optimum size, impact velocity and critical‐velocity conditions line up to give maximal DE.  
– Large powders cannot pick up enough speed to reach the critical‐deformation regime, so DE again drops off.

Under high‐current pulsed electron beam (HCPEB) treatment, each microsecond‐duration pulse deposits enough energy in the top few hundred nanometers of a metal to melt or near‐melt that layer, then allows it to cool almost as fast.  Three key consequences of these extreme thermal rates (heating rates of 10^5–10^7 K s^–1 and cooling rates up to 10^6–10^8 K s^–1) are:

1. Ultrafine (even nanometric) grain formation  
   • During resolidification the degree of undercooling can exceed several hundred kelvins.  Nucleation rates scale approximately with exp(–ΔG*/kT), so huge undercoolings drive nucleation densities to 10^20–10^24 m^–3.  Grain‐growth time is limited to microseconds, so grains impinge while still very small (tens of nanometres to a few hundred nanometres).  
   • Repeated pulses remelt and resolidify the same zone, further refining grains by cyclic nucleation–growth arrest.

2. Non‐equilibrium and metastable phase trapping  
   • Diffusional transformations (e.g. equilibrium precipitates) require seconds to hours—far too long.  The microsecond‐scale solidification “freezes in” supersaturated solid solutions.  
   • If the melt undercools enough, diffusionless transformations (martensitic or amorphous) can occur, yielding intermetallics or metallic glasses not stable under equilibrium cooling.  
   • Very high cooling rates prevent coarsening of any incipient second‐phase particles, so metastable nanoscale precipitates and solute‐clusters persist.

3. High internal stresses and defect densities  
   • The rapid thermal expansion and contraction of the melted layer against a cold substrate induces steep thermal gradients (10^6–10^8 K m^–1) and shock‐like stresses.  
   • As each layer solidifies, it shrinks; mismatch strains between successive “frozen” layers accumulate residual compressive or tensile stresses on the order of 10^2–10^3 MPa.  
   • The solidification front itself, especially under large undercooling, generates high dislocation densities (10^14–10^16 m^–2), and subsequent thermal cycling locks in those dislocations.

In combination, the ultra‐fast melt/resolidification cycles maximize nucleation while suppressing growth and diffusion, producing an ultrafine‐grained, metastable, highly stressed surface layer with an exceptionally high defect density.

Below is a simplified, step‐by‐step outline of how the repeated impacts in cold spray, together with the modest thermal excursions they induce, drive down microstrain and dislocation density while coarsening crystallites in Al coatings.

1. Particle acceleration and impact  
   – Feedstock Al powders are accelerated to supersonic speeds.  
   – Upon impact they undergo severe, very high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation against the substrate or previously deposited layers.

2. Generation of high dislocation density and microstrain  
   – Plastic deformation nucleates huge numbers of dislocations (edge and screw).  
   – Dislocations tangle, pile up and form dense networks, producing high internal stresses (microstrain) and subgrain structure.

3. Localized adiabatic heating  
   – Each high‐velocity impact converts a fraction of kinetic energy into heat in a very thin surface layer (adiabatic shear bands).  
   – Although peak temperatures stay below melting, they can reach a few hundred °C for microseconds.

4. Dynamic recovery (DRV)  
   – Aluminum’s high stacking‐fault energy promotes dislocation climb and cross‐slip even at modest T.  
   – Under the combined effect of high dislocation density and transient heating, dislocations annihilate in pairs or rearrange into low‐energy configurations.  
   – This reduces the net dislocation density and relieves some microstrain.

5. Formation and coarsening of subgrains  
   – Rearranged dislocations outline subgrain boundaries (low‐angle boundaries).  
   – Continued transient heating (from subsequent impacts) and stored energy drive subgrain boundary migration and coalescence.  
   – Subgrains grow into larger, more equiaxed “crystallites.”

6. Continuous (dynamic) recrystallization (cDRX)  
   – If local strains and temperatures are high enough, new high‐angle grain nuclei form within the deformed matrix.  
   – These nuclei consume the deformed microstructure, producing strain‐free grains.

7. Grain growth and stabilization  
   – As the build‐up proceeds, repeated DRV and cDRX steps progressively reduce stored elastic energy.  
   – Larger grains/thumb‐rule crystallites prevail because they lower the total boundary‐energy of the coating.

8. Final microstructural result  
   – Net dislocation density falls (dislocation annihilation + subgrain formation).  
   – Microstrain drops (relief of internal stresses).  
   – The average crystallite (grain/subgrain) size increases relative to the heavily deformed zone created by a single impact.

In sum, cold spray’s unique combination of severe plastic deformation and very short, repeated thermal pulses in a high-SFE metal like aluminum drives dynamic recovery and recrystallization in situ. That sequence of dislocation generation → transient heating → recovery/recrystallization ultimately lowers dislocation density and microstrain while coarsening the crystallite structure.

Hot rolling after cold‐spray repair promotes a true metallurgical bond at the deposit–substrate interface by a sequence of coupled mechanical and thermally activated events.  In practice one typically heats the spray build to 300–600 °C (below melting) and then applies a high‐reduction roll pass.  The key steps are:

1. Substrate/deposit softening  
   – Heating lowers yield strength and critical shear stress in both the original substrate and the cold‐sprayed layer.  
   – This makes them much more susceptible to uniform plastic flow under rolling loads.

2. Macro- and micro-scale densification  
   – Under the normal and shear stresses of rolling, splats plastically flatten and spread, collapsing inter-splat and deposit–substrate voids.  
   – Average porosity in the near‐interface zone drops dramatically (often from 5–10 % down to <1 %).

3. Oxide‐film rupture and fresh‐metal contact  
   – The high local strains fracture thin native oxides at splat boundaries and on the original substrate surface.  
   – Micro-asperity interlocking and microshear then exposes fresh metal–metal patches over the entire interface.

4. Mechanical mixing and short‐range diffusion  
   – Intense shear at the interface effects a mechanical “stirring” or brush‐type mixing zone, typically a few hundred nanometers thick.  
   – At the rolling temperature, short‐range atomic diffusion across these freshly exposed metal contacts begins almost immediately, further bonding the two sides.

5. Dynamic recovery and recrystallization  
   – The combination of large strains and elevated temperature drives dynamic recovery of dislocation networks and nucleation of fine recrystallized grains.  
   – These new grains span across the former interface, effectively removing the last vestiges of a two‐phase boundary.

6. Residual‐stress relaxation and homogenization  
   – Remaining cold‐spray tensile residual stresses (in the deposit) and compressive stresses (in the substrate) partially relax under heat and creep during or immediately after rolling.  
   – This eliminates crack‐driving stresses, closes any tiny tertiary voids, and yields a narrow‐transition, stress‐free diffusion zone.

The net result is a continuous, pore‐free transition region—often only a micron or two thick—where original substrate, new recrystallized grains, and deposit metal are metallurgically joined.  Roll-post-treatment typically boosts lap‐shear strength by 30–50 % over as-sprayed repairs and raises fatigue life by eliminating interface crack-initiation sites.

In cold‐sprayed metal–matrix composites the so-called mechanically mixed layer (MML) at a particle–matrix interface is born of two coupled phenomena:  
  1. high‐strain adiabatic shear that fragments and disperses the native oxides on both the metal matrix and on any oxide‐forming reinforcement, and  
  2. mechanical blending of metal and oxide fragments under the severe plastic flow around the impact periphery.  

Two key parameters control how thick that mixed layer grows and how stable it is under service loading: (a) the size of the reinforcing particle, which sets the local stress–strain and heating field during impact, and (b) the strength of the particle–matrix bond, which governs whether oxide fragments are entrapped or squeezed out of the interface.  

1. Oxide critical-thickness mechanism  
   • Every metal powder carries a thin native oxide (Al₂O₃, TiO₂, etc.) whose thickness δox typically lies between 10 and 200 nm. Under a sufficiently high shear stress τ imposed by the cold‐spray jet, that oxide can no longer deform plastically: it cracks and spalls once τ exceeds a critical value τcrit. At that point oxide fragments are blown into the metal’s shear‐localized zone around the impact edge, forming the MML.  
   • The maximum oxide that can be fractured in a single impact—the “critical oxide thickness,” δcrit—depends on the peak shear stress generated, which in turn scales with the impact pressure P and local strain rate γ̇.  

2. Effect of reinforcement size  
   – Small particles (submicron to a few microns)  
     • At a given plume pressure they achieve higher particle velocities and generate more localized shear and higher strain rates. That elevated τ more readily overcomes τcrit even for relatively thick oxides, so oxide fragmentation is efficient.  
     • The high local temperatures from adiabatic heating aid dynamic recrystallization of the metal, which tends to heal interface voids and limits the mixed layer to roughly the fragment size plus a few microns of plastically strained metal. In practice you see MML thicknesses of order 0.1–1 μm.  
     • However, because small particles present a much larger total oxide area per unit volume, you do introduce more oxide fragments overall—so if the particle–matrix bond is weak (see below), those fragments can accumulate into thicker, defect-rich MMLs.  

   – Large particles (tens of microns and up)  
     • Lower peak strain rates and reduced local heating mean that only the very thinnest oxides can be fractured. If δox > δcrit, no well-defined MML ever forms—oxide can simply roll up and be squeezed out of the interface, or remain intact and block bonding altogether.  
     • When an MML does form, it tends to be thinner (few tens to few hundreds of nanometers) and patchy, because the local shear zone is broader and stresses are lower.  

3. Role of interfacial bonding  
   • Strong chemical or metallurgical bonding (e.g. Al–Ti intermetallic formation, diffusion‐promoted wetting) helps strip oxide fragments cleanly out of the joint, leaving behind a thin but highly adherent mixed zone. Such interfaces resist fatigue crack‐initiation and shear‐delamination, and the MML rarely grows beyond the minimal oxide fragment size.  
   • Weak bonding (pure mechanical interlock only) allows oxide debris to lodge at the interface and “build up” over successive impacts. This not only increases the apparent MML thickness—often to several microns—but also introduces microvoids and stress concentrators that undermine both the mechanical stability and the load‐transfer efficiency of the composite.  

Summary  
  – Smaller reinforcements promote higher local shear stresses and hence more efficient oxide fragmentation, but because of their high specific‐area of oxide they can produce thicker MMLs if bonding is poor.  
  – Larger reinforcements produce lower stresses, so only very thin oxides ever crack—resulting in ultrathin or even absent MMLs—but they also risk incomplete bonding if oxide cannot be broken.  
  – Strong particle–matrix adhesion curtails the mechanical‐mixed layer to essentially the oxide‐fragment size, whereas weak adhesion allows oxide buildup, leading to a thicker, less stable MML.

In a cold‐spray gun you almost never get the “text‐book” one‐dimensional, inviscid, isentropic expansion.  In reality  

 1. two‐dimensional expansion (an axisymmetric or planar slit nozzle) and  
 2. wall friction (viscous boundary layers and any shock–boundary‐layer interactions or flow separation in the diverging section)  

both conspire to reduce the peak Mach number and to distort the cross‐sectional Mach profile that you would predict from  
   Mₑ  = f( Aₑ/A* , p₀/pₐ )  
in a lossless 1-D model.  

Key points on how the real flow differs:  
• Boundary‐layer growth “eats into” the throat and exit area, so the core flow sees a smaller effective expansion ratio.  In practice this lowers Mₑ by 5–10 % (depending on pressure ratio, nozzle length, divergence angle).  
• Viscous shear in the supersonic portion does two things: it dissipates total‐pressure (stagnation‐pressure) and it raises static temperature, both of which reduce local Mach.  
• In a 2-D (planar) or finite‐aspect‐ratio axisymmetric nozzle you get side‐wall boundary layers, corner vortices, and if the diverging angle is too large, local flow separation with oblique shocks—each of which further depresses M locally and shaves off useful nozzle area.  
• The net result is that the area‐ratio that you designed into the nozzle must be “bolstered” (i.e. made larger) to achieve the same Mach number in the core that your 1-D isentropic calculation predicted.  

Implications for cold-spray nozzle design:  
 1. Contoured, gradual divergence angles (5 °–15 °) help delay separation and keep boundary layers thinner.  
 2. Longer nozzles (within practical length limits) give more gentle acceleration and reduce shock‐layer interactions—trading off mechanical size for higher usable exit Mach.  
 3. You must include a boundary‐layer thickness allowance when defining throat and exit areas.  A common rule of thumb is to increase the geometric area ratio by about 10–15 % over the ideal 1-D value to offset viscous and 2-D losses.  
 4. For planar slit nozzles, keep the slot height small enough that the boundary‐layer displacement thickness remains a small fraction (<10 %) of the slot height even at peak pressure ratios.  
 5. Finally, you should validate with 2-D or 3-D CFD including a suitable turbulence or transition model.  This lets you see how shocks, viscous layers, and corner effects will actually limit the Mach in the core, and thus ensure your powder particles will be accelerated above the critical velocity for bonding.  

By acknowledging and designing around these two-dimensional and viscous effects you arrive at a nozzle that really does deliver the high particle velocities (often 600–1200 m/s) that cold spray requires, rather than the over-optimistic values a purely 1-D isentropic model would suggest.

In nanocrystalline or heavily milled powders, each Bragg peak in an X-ray diffraction pattern is broadened by two main “size‐strain” effects:  
 1. Finite crystallite size (D) broadening, which scales roughly as 1/D and gives a Cauchy‐type broadening that varies as 1/ cos θ.  
 2. Microstrain (ε) broadening, which comes from distributions of lattice spacings Δd/d and scales roughly as ε tan θ.  

The Williamson–Hall uniform‐deformation model (UDM) provides a simple way to disentangle these two contributions. The recipe is:

1. Data collection and peak fitting  
   • Measure the powder XRD pattern and fit each diffraction peak (hkl) to obtain its full width at half maximum β_meas in radians.  
   • Measure (or obtain from standards) the instrumental broadening β_inst for each θ and correct each measured width via  
     β = sqrt(β_meas² – β_inst²).  

2. Williamson–Hall equation in UDM form  
   For each corrected peak width β, apply the relation  
     β cos θ  =  (K λ / D)  +  (4 ε sin θ)  
   where  
     • θ is the Bragg angle,  
     • λ is the X‐ray wavelength,  
     • K is the shape factor (≈0.9 for roughly spherical domains),  
     • D is the volume‐averaged crystallite size,  
     • ε is the root‐mean‐square microstrain.  

3. Construct the Williamson–Hall plot  
   • On the horizontal axis plot 4 sin θ.  
   • On the vertical axis plot β cos θ.  

   Because the equation is linear in 4 sin θ, the data for all peaks should lie approximately on a straight line.

4. Extract D and ε  
   • The y-intercept of the linear fit = K λ / D.  ⇒  D = K λ / (intercept).  
   • The slope of the line = ε.  

That way, you obtain a single “size” term from the intercept and a single “strain” term from the slope. The UDM assumes that strain is isotropic (uniform in all crystallographic directions) and that both size‐ and strain‐broadening are purely Cauchy‐type; in practice you may refine the analysis by using Voigt deconvolution to separate Cauchy and Gaussian components if anisotropic or Gaussian‐type broadening is suspected.

Cold spray penetration depth ends up scaling almost linearly with particle density simply because at fixed particle size and impact speed the kinetic‐energy budget grows in direct proportion to mass, while the work required to carve out a cavity in the substrate grows roughly in direct proportion to penetration depth.  A back‐of‐the‐envelope derivation looks like this:

 1.  Particle kinetic energy  
    Eₖ = ½·m·v²  
    m = ρ·Vₚ  ⇒  Eₖ = ½·ρ·Vₚ·v²  
    (Vₚ = particle volume, ρ = particle density, v = impact speed)

 2.  Substrate deformation (plastic work)  
    Wₚₗₐₛₜ ≈ Y·Vₕ  
    Vₕ ≈ A·d  
    (Y = characteristic yield stress or hardness of substrate, A = contact cross‐section area, d = penetration depth)

    ⇒  Wₚₗₐₛₜ ≈ Y·A·d

 3.  Equating the available kinetic energy to the work of deformation  
    ½·ρ·Vₚ·v² ≈ Y·A·d  

    ⇒  d ≈ [½·Vₚ·v²/(Y·A)]·ρ  

At fixed geometry (Vₚ, A) and impact speed v, the bracketed term is a constant, so  
    d ∝ ρ  

In plain terms: double the density, double the mass → double the kinetic energy at the same speed → roughly double the plastic work you can do in the substrate → roughly double the penetration depth.  All other things being equal (particle diameter, speed, substrate hardness), you recover an almost linear d vs. ρ trend.

Using a lighter inert propellant gas (e.g. He instead of N₂ or Ar) changes the cold‐spray process in three interrelated ways:

1. Particle impact velocity and bonding  
   • Sound‐speed effect: lighter gases have higher ratios of specific heats (γ) and higher specific‐gas constants (R), so the maximum achievable jet velocity at a given stagnation pressure and temperature is larger.  
   • Increased acceleration: for a fixed nozzle geometry and inlet conditions, particles experience a larger drag force and thus accelerate to higher exit velocities.  
   • Enhanced bonding: once particle impact velocity exceeds the material’s “critical velocity,” the degree of adiabatic shear and plastic deformation on impact rises sharply. That boosts oxide‐film disruption, fresh‐metal intimate contact, and metallurgical inter‐particle bonding.  

2. Porosity reduction  
   • Denser packing: higher‐velocity impacts flatten and “splat” particles more completely, filling interstitial voids and reducing macro‐ and micro‐porosity in the deposit.  
   • Fewer void‐forming rebounds: a larger fraction of particles stick on first impact, rather than ricocheting and redepositing imperfectly.  

3. Deposition efficiency  
   • More particles ≥ critical velocity: because the velocity distribution shifts upward, a greater percentage of feedstock particles actually stick, raising overall deposition efficiency (mass of coating deposited ÷ mass of powder consumed).  
   • Broader operable pressure/temperature window: with helium you can achieve sufficient velocities at lower pressures or lower preheat temperatures, or spray harder‐to‐bond alloys that would not bond in N₂/Ar at the same conditions.  

Trade-offs to keep in mind:  
– Helium is more expensive and in many systems can raise running‐costs substantially.  
– Light‐gas jets may be more prone to divergence, requiring careful nozzle design to maintain focus.  

In summary, switching to a lighter propellant gas boosts jet velocity, which drives stronger impact‐induced deformation and bonding, fills gaps more completely (lower porosity), and lifts the fraction of powder that actually adheres (higher deposition efficiency).

The quickest way to see where a power‐law size dependence of the form  
    u_c ∝ D^n  
comes out of the “spall‐based” cold‐spray model is to write down three ingredients:

  1. the shock (or back‐stress) pressure generated on impact as a function of impact velocity u,  
  2. the temperature rise in the particle as a function of u and particle diameter D, and  
  3. the fact that the spall (or dynamic tensile) strength falls off with that temperature.  

If you then set “shock‐pressure = spall‐strength,” take logarithms, and pick off the coefficient of ln D, you immediately read off your exponent n.

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
1)  Shock (or back‐stress) pressure  
   
   A simple linearized Hugoniot for a metal gives  
     P_s(u) ≃ ρ_0 c_0 u  (1)  
   or, if you like a quadratic correction,  
     P_s(u) ≃ ρ_0 c_0 u + s u^2  
   but for scaling we will write schematically  
     P_s ∼ K_u u^b  .  

2)  Temperature rise in the particle  
   
   The particle warms by a combination of adiabatic plastic work and shock dissipation.  In the simplest “lumped‐capacitance” model one may write  
     ΔT ≃  (η u^2)/(c_p ρ D^a)  
   where η is the fraction of kinetic energy that ends up as heat, c_p the heat capacity, ρ the density, and a is typically 1 if you assume the entire particle heats uniformly or  “1/3” if you allow some 1D conduction out of a heated skin.  In scaling form:  
     T − T_0 ∼ A_u u^b / D^a  .  

3)  Temperature‐dependent spall strength
