   Empirically (and from Zener‐Hollomon‐type arguments) one often writes  
     σ_sp(T) = σ_0 exp[−Q/(R T)]  
   or in a power‐law approximation  
     σ_sp(T) ≃ σ_0 (1 − c T/T_m)^m  
   but to first order in T you may linearize  
     σ_sp(T) ≃ σ_ref exp(−α T)  .  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
4)  Equate P_s to σ_sp at u = u_c  
   
   P_s(u_c) = σ_sp[T(u_c,D)]  
   
   K_u u_c^b  =  σ_ref exp[−α (T_0 + A_u u_c^b / D^a)]  

5)  Take logs and isolate the D‐dependence  
   
   ln u_c^b  + ln K_u  =  ln σ_ref  − α T_0  − α A_u u_c^b / D^a  
   
   ⇒ b ln u_c  =  const  +  (α A_u u_c^b)/D^a  

   Now for large enough D the last term on the right is small, and ln u_c ≃ const.  But at small D the temperature‐softening term dominates the D‐dependence.  To leading order one may then balance  
   
     b ln u_c  ≃  (α A_u u_c^b)/D^a  
   
   or rewriting u_c^b on both sides  
   
     u_c^b  ∝  D^a  ⇒ u_c  ∝  D^(a/b)  

6)  Read off the exponent  
   
   n  =  a/b  

   •  If you take the Hugoniot as linear in u, then b = 1.  
   •  If you take the heating as uniform in D, then a = 1.  
   ⇒ n = 1.  In practice one finds instead that conduction into the particle core or a quadratic Hugoniot correction reduces n to something between 0.1 and 0.5.  

––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––  
Concrete example:  

  •  P_s ≃ ρ c u  ⇒  b = 1  
  •  ΔT ≃ η u^2/(c_p ρ D)  ⇒  a = 1, b = 2 for the heating law  
  •  σ_sp ∼ σ_0 exp(−α T)  

One actually solves  
  
  ρ c u_c  ≃ σ_0 exp[−α (η u_c^2/(c_p ρ D))]  

⇒  ln u_c  + ln (ρ c)  = ln σ_0  − α η u_c^2/(c_p ρ D)  

For small particles the right‐hand heating term dominates the D‐dependence, giving  
  
  u_c^2 ∝ D  ⇒  u_c ∝ D^1/2  

or if you allow 1D conduction into a layer you get a ≃ 1/3 ⇒ n ≃ 1/6.  

In short, once you have  
   
   P_s ∼ u^b,    ΔT ∼ u^b/D^a,    σ_sp ∼ exp(−α T)  

then imposing P_s(u_c)=σ_sp[T(u_c,D)] and letting the “−α ΔT” term carry all of the size‐dependence immediately yields  

   u_c ∝ D^(a/b)  

as your particle‐size‐scaling exponent.

You can think of a cold‐sprayed splat as a heavily work-hardened “particle” whose strength is dominated by its very high dislocation density ρ.  The classical Taylor hardening model then gives you an easy back‐of-the-envelope estimate of its yield or flow stress:

   σy ≈ σ0  +  M · α · G · b · √ρ

where  
 • σ0  is the friction (Peierls-type) stress of the pristine metal (often 10–50 MPa for Al, Cu, Ni…),  
 • M      is the Taylor (or polycrystal) factor (≈ 3.0 for FCC),  
 • α      is an empirical constant (≈ 0.2–0.5),  
 • G      is the shear modulus,  
 • b      is the Burgers vector,  
 • ρ      is the total dislocation density measured in the splat (e.g. by X-ray line‐broadening or TEM).  

1.  Measure or estimate ρ in your splat.  Cold spray splats routinely reach 10^14–10^16 m⁻².  
2.  Plug in G and b for your alloy phase, choose α≈0.3 (mid‐range), and M≈3.  
3.  Compute Δσdisl = M α G b √ρ and add the intrinsic σ0.  

Example (Al splat):  
 G≈26 GPa, b≈0.286 nm, ρ≈5×10^15 m⁻² →  
 Δσdisl ≈3·0.3·26×10^3 MPa·0.286×10^−3 mm·√(5×10^15 m⁻²)  
           ≃340 MPa,  
 σy ≃σ0(≈25 MPa)+340 MPa ≃365 MPa.  

When people have actually measured single‐splat or micropillar / nanoindentation flow stresses and compared to the Taylor‐predicted value they find:  
 – The Taylor estimate typically falls within 10–30% of the experimental flow stress.  
 – The experimental values are often slightly higher, implying there are extra strengthening contributions not in the simple Taylor term (grain-boundary or oxide reinforcement, residual stresses, strain‐gradient effects, solute or precipitation hardening, porosity closure forces, etc.).  
 – Conversely, if you include a Hall–Petch grain-boundary term (kHP·d^−1/2) or a residual‐stress correction, the agreement can tighten to a few percent.  

In short, the Taylor model captures the lion’s share of the strength rise in a cold-sprayed metallic splat and, by comparison with flow‐stress data, confirms that dislocation hardening dominates—though a small “extra” hardness always remains from microstructural and interfacial effects that lie outside the pure Taylor law.

1. Define known quantities  
   • ρm = density of the matrix phase (kg/m³)  
   • ρs = density of the secondary (reinforcement) phase (kg/m³)  
   • Ws = mass fraction of the secondary phase (wt% divided by 100)  
   • Wm = 1 – Ws = mass fraction of the matrix phase  

2. Compute the theoretical (zero‐porosity) composite density, ρth, by the rule of mixtures in its reciprocal form:  
   1/ρth = (Ws/ρs) + (Wm/ρm)  
   ⇒ ρth = 1 ÷ [(Ws/ρs) + (Wm/ρm)]  

3. Measure the actual (bulk) density of the sprayed deposit, ρbulk  
   – e.g. by Archimedes’ method:  
     • Weigh sample in air, ma  
     • Weigh sample immersed in fluid (water), mb  
     • Volume V = (ma – mb)/ρfluid  
     • ρbulk = ma/V  

4. Calculate total porosity, P (vol.%):  
   P = [(ρth – ρbulk) / ρth] × 100%  

5. Interpretation  
   – If ρbulk approaches ρth, P→0 (dense)  
   – Larger gaps indicate higher P (more pores)  

Example (numbers for illustration only):  
   ρm = 2700 kg/m³, ρs = 3500 kg/m³, Ws = 0.20  
   ⇒ Wm = 0.80  
   1/ρth = 0.20/3500 + 0.80/2700 = 5.714e-5 + 2.963e-4 = 3.535e-4  
   ⇒ ρth ≈ 1 / 3.535e-4 = 2828 kg/m³  
   Suppose ρbulk measured = 2600 kg/m³  
   P = [(2828 – 2600)/2828]×100% ≈ 8.0% total porosity.

Thermal softening in cold spray—whether by heating the substrate, the feedstock, or both (“synchronous” or in-line particle/substrate heating)—has a very reproducible effect on the hardness of the as-sprayed deposit.  In essence you are trading off some of the extreme work-hardening that you get in a fully “cold” impact for better particle deformation/bonding and lower post‐spray residual stress.  The principal observations and mechanisms are:  

1. Reduced Flow Stress → Lower Work Hardening  
   • By elevating the particle and/or substrate temperature (often 200–400 °C for common metals), the yield strength of the deposit material drops.  
   • Each particle impact then induces less plastic strain (lower strain hardening) than in a purely adiabatic, room-temperature spray.  
   • Net effect: dislocation density in the deposited splats is smaller, so the Hall–Petch and Taylor hardening contributions are reduced and microhardness goes down.

2. Partial Recovery/Recrystallization  
   • At sufficiently high in-spray temperatures you can activate dislocation recovery and even static recrystallization in the as-deposited layer.  
   • This coarsens ultrafine or nano–grain structures formed by severe plastic deformation, again lowering hardness but also reducing brittleness.

3. Residual Stress Relaxation  
   • Cold spray typically traps very high compressive residuals that boost apparent hardness.  
   • Introducing thermal energy during or immediately after spraying lets some of those stresses relax, which also subtracts from the measured microhardness.

4. Improved Cohesion vs. Hardness Trade-Off  
   • A modest reduction in microhardness (often 5–20% compared to a fully cold spray) is usually offset by significantly better interparticle and particle-substrate bonding, higher deposit ductility, and lower crack susceptibility.  
   • In many alloys you find an optimum pre-heat or synchronous-heat window where you still retain most of your strength but gain a more damage‐tolerant coating.

Typical data examples  
• Al alloys: substrate heated to ~300 °C → Vickers hardness drops from ~120–130 HV (cold spray) down to ~100 HV.  
• Cu: pre-heat ~200 °C → hardness moves from ~130 HV down to ~110 HV.  
• Ni‐based powders: 300–400 °C synchronous heating can reduce microhardness by 15–25% but improve cohesion by 30–50%.

Bottom line  
If your application prioritizes maximum hardness and wear resistance you may choose a purely cold spray.  If you need a tougher, better-bonded coating with fewer internal stresses, a controlled amount of thermal softening via synchronous heating will lower the as-sprayed microhardness but deliver a more robust final part.

In CSAM‐built metal‐matrix composites loaded in compression you will almost always see two competing “damage” modes around your hard, brittle particles: (1) interfacial debonding (the particle shears or “pulls out” of the softened interface zone) and (2) particle cracking.  As you drive the compression rate up, the balance between those two shifts very systematically:

1.  Rate-sensitive matrix/interface strengthening  
    –  The cold‐spray “interphase” is formed by ultra–high‐strain-rate plastic flow during deposition and is already quite strong; when you reload it faster in a mechanical test, its apparent toughness goes up (viscoplastic drag in the nanoscale grains and any residual strain‐rate hardening in the matrix both rise with \dotε).  
    –  In practice that means it takes more local energy/demanding Gc to decohere the interface at high \dotε than at low.

2.  Particle brittleness and stress‐wave focusing  
    –  The ceramic or hard second phase is essentially rate‐insensitive (it can’t flow to relax stress concentrations), so when you hit it with a sharper impulse the hoop‐tension around the inclusion skyrockets almost elastically and leads to rapid crack initiation and propagation through the particle.  

Net result as \dotε increases:  
  • The interface “holds” longer (debonding fraction goes down)  
  • Cracking inside the particles becomes the dominant damage sink

If you map damage volume fractions vs. strain rate you typically see debonding dominate at quasi-static rates (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹), a mixed regime in the 10⁻¹–10² s⁻¹ range, and particle fracture taking over beyond 10²–10³ s⁻¹.

Key points to pull ductility information out of a shear-punch curve for a cold-sprayed coating are (1) the points at which pure elastic response ends and yielding begins, (2) the maximum load (i.e. ultimate shear strength), and (3) the displacement at which the load collapses (onset of through-thickness cracking or plug-out).  From those you extract a “plastic” displacement and then normalize it to get an effective strain.

1.  Elastic limit and yield point  
    – On the load–displacement trace the end of the initial straight-line (elastic) region marks the shear yield load.  The corresponding punch displacement δy is taken as the onset of plasticity.  

2.  Peak (ultimate) load  
    – As the punch pushes on, the load rises into the plastic-hardening regime up to a peak Fmax.  The displacement at Fmax (δmax) still contains both elastic and plastic contributions.  

3.  Failure or plug-out displacement  
    – Beyond the peak the coating begins to crack or shear out and the load drops.  Define δf as the displacement where the load has fallen, say, 15–20% below Fmax (or the first inflection on the descending branch).  δf is taken to represent the displacement at “fracture.”  

From those three landmarks on the curve one defines a plastic (i.e. ductile) displacement Δδ:

    Δδ = δf – δy

If t is the local coating (or substrate+coating) thickness through which the shear plane runs, one then defines an effective (or equivalent) shear ductility γeff as

    γeff  =  Δδ  /  t

That is often reported as a percent.  In other words, γeff is simply the incremental punch‐displacement from first‐yield to failure, normalized by the gauge thickness, and represents the shear strain capacity of the coating.  If one wishes to convert to an equivalent uniaxial tensile strain εeff under von Mises assumptions, one can multiply γeff by √3∕2.

In virtually every study of rapidly‐solidified Al–Mg–Si (and similar) powders you will see the same three–step hardness trend:

1.  As‐atomized state (“as-spray” or “gas‐atomized”)  
   – Very fine cellular/dendritic microstructure, high dislocation density and microsegregation of strengthening solutes.  
   – Typical Vickers microhardness: 80–120 HV (depending on alloy).  

2.  After solution treatment and quench (e.g. 540–560 °C/1–2 h + water quench)  
   – Dissolution of Mg‐ and Si‐rich particles, relief of internal stresses, removal of fine subgrain structure.  
   – Hardness drops sharply to ~40–70 HV.  

3.  After artificial aging (precipitation hardening, e.g. 160–200 °C/8–48 h)  
   – Re‐precipitation of GP-zones and b′/β″ (Mg₂Si) or other strengthening phases.  
   – Hardness rises again, often exceeding the original as‐atomized value, to ~120–160 HV at peak age.  

In summary: hard (as‐atomized) → softest (solutionized) → hardest (aged/precipitation-hardened).

Cold‐sprayed deposits as built are almost always very strong but quite brittle.  The reasons can be grouped into microstructure, bonding and residual‐stress effects:  

1. Severe work‐hardening and high dislocation density  
   – Each powder particle suffers extreme plastic flow on impact (adiabatic shear) and traps enormous numbers of dislocations.  
   – Grains in the shear‐band bonding zones can be ultrafine or even nanocrystalline, which raises strength but collapses ductility.  

2. Weak, oxide‐contaminated or partially bonded interfaces  
   – Native oxide films on the feedstock particles seldom mix fully out, so many inter‐particle boundaries have only limited metallurgical cohesion.  
   – Any microscopic gaps or inclusions serve as crack initiation sites under tensile or bending loads.  

3. High residual stresses  
   – The build‐up of cold work and the mismatch in plastic flow between successive layers injects high internal stresses (often tensile at interlayer boundaries).  
   – These stresses lower the effective fracture toughness and promote crack propagation along particle boundaries.  

4. Lack of stress relief or annealing  
   – In the as‐sprayed condition there has been no heat treatment to recover or recrystallize the heavily deformed microstructure or to oxidize‐free boundary regions.  

Taken together, you end up with a deposit that is ultra-hard and high‐strength but whose ductility and toughness are crippled by (a) work‐hardened, nanostructured zones and (b) weak, oxide‐rich interfaces.  Under load it therefore defaults to brittle fracture through those interparticle or interlayer weak links.

Ion implantation modifies surface topography through two competing effects—collision-cascade mixing (which can smooth) and sputter/defect-driven roughening—and both the ion fluence (dose) and energy shift the balance between them.  In broad terms:  
1. Fluence dependence  
  • Low fluences (≲10^15–10^16 ions/cm²)  
    – Collision cascades induce viscous flow and selective sputtering of high-points, tending to smooth out pre-existing asperities.  
    – Net roughness change ΔRq is often negative.  
  • Moderate fluences (≈10^16–10^17 ions/cm²)  
    – Smoothing saturates as sub-surface damage accumulates; ΔRq approaches a minimum.  
    – If the coating can amorphize, a dense “near-amorphous” layer forms and roughness stabilizes.  
  • High fluences (≫10^17 ions/cm²)  
    – Defect clusters, micro-bubbles or blistering develop, and stochastic sputter-erosion creates pits and hillocks.  
    – Roughness grows rapidly—ΔRq becomes positive and may scale roughly with √(fluence) depending on sputter yield fluctuations.  
2. Energy dependence  
  • Low energies (<10 keV)  
    – Cascades are very shallow; sputter yields peak, so even modest fluences roughen if the original surface is hard to amorphize.  
    – Smoothing is limited to very low doses.  
  • Intermediate energies (10–100 keV)  
    – Collision cascades extend a few tens of nanometers in; sputter yield drops, so a wider dose window for net smoothing appears.  
    – Peak smoothing fluence shifts upward.  
  • High energies (>100 keV)  
    – Most damage is sub-surface (hundreds of nm), with minimal direct sputtering; the surface either remains essentially unchanged or undergoes minor densification (light smoothing).  
    – To roughen appreciably requires very high fluences to produce voids or bubble‐driven blistering from inert-gas implants.  
3. Practical guideline  
  – To polish or smooth a coating by ion implantation, choose an energy that deposits cascades just beneath the surface (10–50 keV) and keep fluence in the 10^15–10^16 ions/cm² range.  
  – To introduce controlled roughness (e.g. for adhesion or diffusion barrier structuring), push fluence above 10^17 ions/cm² or use low-energy implants at moderate fluence to maximize sputter roughening.

Compared with aluminum, titanium is substantially more difficult to cold-spray form. The main reasons are:

1. Higher critical velocity  
   • Aluminum alloys bond at particle velocities of roughly 400–600 m/s; titanium and Ti-alloys typically require ≥900 m/s to achieve the severe plastic deformation needed for metallurgical bonding.  
   • Hitting those velocities usually means using higher gas pressures, higher gas temperatures, and often helium rather than nitrogen or air.

2. Lower room-temperature ductility  
   • Aluminum is very ductile at ambient temperature and work-softens readily on impact, creating extensive interfacial jetting and mechanical interlock.  
   • Titanium is much stiffer, work-hardens quickly, and cracks more easily if the particle velocity or temperature aren’t high enough.

3. Narrower process window  
   • Aluminum cold spray tolerates a broad combination of pressures (15–35 bar) and gas temperatures (300–600 °C) with decent deposition efficiencies (60–90 %).  
   • Titanium usually demands 30–50 bar plus gas preheat in the 650–900 °C range (and often He), otherwise efficiencies drop below 50 % and porosity/oxidation rise.

4. Lower deposition efficiency and higher cost  
   • Aluminum powders achieve high build rates (1–5 kg/h per nozzle) with low nozzle wear.  
   • Titanium powders give lower build rates (0.5–2 kg/h per nozzle), accelerate nozzle erosion, and require more costly consumables (He, hardened nozzles).

5. Oxidation sensitivity  
   • Aluminum powders form a thin, easily disrupted oxide that helps bonding.  
   • Titanium’s oxide is hard and tenacious; if gas purity or temperatures aren’t tightly controlled, you get poor bonding and embrittled deposits.

In practice, cold spraying aluminum is a well-established, robust process with wide operating windows. Titanium cold spray requires optimized high-pressure/heated-gas setups (often with helium), a much tighter process window, and more attention to powder morphology and substrate preheating to approach even moderate deposition efficiencies.

Post‐spray annealing or ageing of cold‐sprayed deposits almost invariably alters their as‐sprayed microstructure—high dislocation densities, subgrains and intimate but strain-locked particle boundaries—and with that their mechanical behavior.  In broad terms you will see:

1. Residual‐stress relief  
   – Even a mild bake (e.g. 150 – 250 °C for Al or Cu) knocks down the gigantic compressive stresses trapped by impact work‐hardening.  
   – Tensile‐residual‐stress relief in the substrate/coating interface improves fatigue and adhesive strength.

2. Recovery, subgrain coalescence and recrystallization  
   – At moderate temperatures (again, a few hundred °C) dislocations rearrange into lower‐energy walls and cells.  You lose some of the as‐sprayed hardness (typically 10 – 30 % drop in microhardness) but gain ductility and toughness.  
   – If you push the temperature/time high enough you get full recrystallization and grain growth.  Hardness and strength continue to drop, but elongation climbs.

3. Interparticle diffusion and neck growth  
   – Annealing activates atomic diffusion across particle boundaries.  Voids shrink, boundaries “heal,” and cohesion/cohesive fracture strength rises (tensile strength up by 10–50 %, depending on alloy and cycle).  
   – Overall porosity falls, density goes up, and you often see a measurable gain in Young’s modulus.

4. Precipitation or phase changes (alloy‐dependent)  
   – In age‐hardening alloys (Al-Zn-Mg, Ni-Al, some steels) a tailored ageing step can actually increase hardness above the as‐sprayed level by precipitate formation.  
   – In pure metals (Cu, Al, Ti) no new strengthening phases form, so overall the hardness drop from recovery outweighs any work-hardening retention.

5. Net effect on mechanical properties  
   – Hardness/strength: usually down modestly unless you exploit precipitation;  
   – Ductility/elongation: up (crack‐resistance and toughness improve);  
   – Fatigue life: up (lower residual stress, fewer stress raisers at pores);  
   – Adhesion/cohesion: up (better interparticle and particle–substrate bonding);  
   – Wear resistance: often a trade-off—softer but tougher coatings can perform better in some wear modes (abrasive, fatigue), worse in pure adhesion‐type wear.

In practice one tunes the post‐heat cycle to the alloy system and target properties.  For instance, Al coatings often get a 250 – 300 °C “stress relief” bake; Ni-based alloys see a 500 – 800 °C ageing that promotes both stress relief and precipitation hardening; stainless or tool steels may need a controlled oxidation‐inhibiting ramp to avoid scale but to trigger carbide precipitation and boost hardness.

When an implant is much stiffer than the surrounding bone, it carries the lion’s share of the load and “shields” the bone from normal mechanical stresses. Bone remodels in response to stress (Wolff’s law), so under-loaded bone will resorb over time, weakening the interface and potentially leading to implant loosening or fracture.

Magnesium alloys have an elastic modulus on the order of 40–45 GPa, versus ~110 GPa for Ti-6Al-4V or stainless steels, and 15–25 GPa for cortical bone. By choosing or processing Mg-based materials so that their modulus more closely matches that of the host bone you:

  • Share load more evenly between implant and bone.  
  • Preserve physiological strain levels in the adjacent bone, maintaining normal remodeling.  
  • Reduce stress concentrations at the bone–implant interface.  
  • Minimize peri-implant bone resorption and the risk of stress-shielding-induced osteopenia.  

In short, a closer match in stiffness leads to more uniform stress transfer, healthier bone remodeling, and longer‐term stability of the implant.

In cold-sprayed coatings (as in most metallic or cermet coatings) the wear rate falls off as the coating’s hardness goes up.  In practice you will almost always see:  
• specific wear rate K_s ∝ 1/H (or more generally K_s ∝ H⁻ᵐ with m ≈1–2)  
• doubling the microhardness roughly halves (or better) the volume loss per N·m  
  
This behavior follows directly from Archard’s law (V = K·W·L/H), so when you plot K_s versus H on log–log axes you typically get a straight line with slope –1 to –1.5.  Of course porosity, adhesion, residual stress and the dominant wear mechanism can shift the exact exponent, but the inverse‐hardness trend is universal.

Adding Zn to Cu–Al₂O₃ cold‐spray feedstocks has three main, generally convergent effects:

1. Hardness  
   – Zn goes into solid solution in the Cu matrix (i.e. brass formation) and provides additional solid-solution strengthening.  Al₂O₃ still dominates the hardness, but at any given Al₂O₃ loading a Cu–Zn matrix is noticeably harder than pure Cu.  Typical hardness rises roughly linearly with Zn content up to ~30 wt % Zn.  

2. Adhesion (deposit/substrate bond strength)  
   – Zn lowers the alloy’s melting range and critical velocity, so particles deform more readily on impact, fill surface asperities better, and form tighter metallurgical bonds.  As a result, adhesion or pull-off strength of the coating usually increases with Zn addition (again up to an optimum Zn level, beyond which poor cohesion/deposition efficiency can set in).

3. Electrical conductivity  
   – Zn has only ~28 % the conductivity of Cu and Zn atoms in solution scatter electrons.  Accordingly, electrical conductivity of the composite falls nearly linearly with Zn content (on top of the conductivity drop already caused by the dispersed Al₂O₃).  

In practice one often sees an optimal Zn addition (e.g. 10–30 wt %) that maximizes hardness and adhesion gains before conductivity (and sometimes toughness or cohesion) becomes unacceptably low.

In cold spray the particles never melt.  Instead, their supersonic impact on the substrate (or previously‐deposited splats) subjects them to very high strain rates and adiabatic shear.  This does three things in concert:  
1. Fractures and expels surface oxides, exposing fresh metal.  
2. Drives severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization at the interface.  
3. Produces mechanical interlocking (micro-forging) and true metal-to-metal contact (“cold welding”).  

It is this high-velocity, solid-state plastic deformation (often called adiabatic shear bonding) that is the primary adhesion mechanism in cold spray coatings.

Typical nanoindentation‐depth hardening trends observed in cold‐sprayed metallic splats can be summarized as follows:

1. Indentation‐size effect in both splat types  
   – Both amorphous and crystalline splats show increasing hardness H as the penetration depth h is reduced below a few hundred nanometers, owing to geometrically necessary dislocations (in the crystal) or constrained shear‐transformation‐zone activity (in the glass).  
   – At very shallow depths (< 20–50 nm) surface oxides, roughness and tip artefacts dominate, so data there are usually discarded.

2. Crystalline splats  
   – Plateau (bulk) hardness Hbulk typically 2.5–4 GPa (depending on alloy).  
   – Below ≈ 500 nm, H rises steadily, by 20–50 % by h ≈ 50–100 nm.  
     • e.g. H(h=500 nm) ≈ 3 GPa → H(h=50 nm) ≈ 4–4.5 GPa.  
   – The slope dH/d(log h) is relatively steep, reflecting dislocation‐mediated ISE.

3. Amorphous splats  
   – Higher bulk hardness Hbulk ~ 6–8 GPa (for typical metallic glasses).  
   – Size effect is milder: H increases only 5–20 % when h is reduced from a few hundred nanometers down to ≈ 50–100 nm.  
     • e.g. H(500 nm) ≈ 6.5 GPa → H(50 nm) ≈ 7–7.5 GPa.  
   – At very low h (20–50 nm), H may rise further (up to ~8–9 GPa) but measurements are often dominated by surface layers.

4. Comparative summary  
   – H’amorphous(h) > H’cryst(h) at all depths.  
   – Crystalline splats exhibit a stronger indentation‐size hardening (larger dH/d(log h)).  
   – Amorphous splats show higher absolute hardness but a flatter hardening curve.

These trends are routinely fit with models of the form  
   H(h) ≃ Hbulk·√[1 + h*∕h]  
where h* (a characteristic length) is much larger for crystalline (≫100 nm) than for amorphous splats (≲50 nm), reflecting the different plasticity mechanisms.

Porosity in a cold‐sprayed coating almost always drives its measured hardness down.  The reasons are:  
1. Reduced load‐bearing area.  Every void within or between splats diverts indenter stress into the pore instead of the metal matrix, so less actual material resists deformation.  
2. Stress concentrations.  Pores act as crack‐nucleation sites under an indenter, so the coating yields or fractures at a lower applied load.  
3. Weaker interparticle bonding.  Porosity is usually associated with incomplete particle deformation or poor splat–splat contact; that lowers both local work‐hardening and the cohesion that contributes to hardness.  

Empirically one often sees hardness H vary with porosity fraction p roughly as  
 H ≃ H₀·(1–p)ⁿ  
where H₀ is the fully dense hardness and n is 1–3 depending on pore shape and distribution.  In practice, reducing porosity by optimizing spray parameters or applying a brief sintering/anneal step increases density, closes microvoids, and typically raises hardness by 10–50 % (or more if the original porosity was very high).

In WC–Co cermet coatings the WC phase is the “hard”, wear‐resisting component and the Co is the “tough,” crack‐arresting binder.  Qualitatively one observes:

1.  As the WC (carbide) fraction rises, bulk hardness goes up and abrasive or two‐body wear resistance improves—wear rates fall roughly in line with Archard’s law (wear ∝ 1/hardness).  
2.  At the same time, fracture toughness and ductility drop because there is less cobalt to bridge cracks, so under impact, erosion or cyclic loading the coating becomes brittle and may spall or crack.  
3.  There is therefore an optimum carbide‐to‐cobalt ratio (often in the 60–75 wt% WC range for HVOF or cold-sprayed coatings) at which you get maximum wear resistance in a given service regime.  Below that you’re too soft, above it you’re too brittle.

Key effects of increasing the deposition (pre‐heat) temperature in laser-assisted cold spray Al coatings are:  

1. Porosity  
   – Up to an optimum (~300–500 °C substrate/preheat) porosity steadily drops.  Higher local temperature softens Al, promotes adiabatic shear and particle flattening, closes interlamellar voids and breaks up oxide films, so you go from 5–8 vol % porosity at room temperature down to ≲1–2 vol %.  
   – Above ~500 °C you can still get very dense coatings, but diminishing returns set in—oxide re–growth and slight recoil of previously bonded particles can stabilize a residual ~0.5 vol % porosity.  

2. Hardness  
   – As you raise the deposition temperature to ~300–450 °C the coating hardness climbs (e.g. from ~35–45 HV up to 80–95 HV).  This is driven by:  
     • Greater plastic deformation/work-hardening in the impact-shear zones  
     • Finer “shear‐induced” subgrains and high dislocation densities at particle boundaries  
     • Build-up of compressive residual stresses  
   – Past ~500–550 °C the hardness begins to fall off (down to ~65–75 HV) because:  
     • Thermal recovery and static recrystallization relieve dislocations  
     • Grain coarsening in the hot substrate–coating interface softens the metal  
     • Any retained high‐temperature oxide pockets can act as weak spots  

Bottom line: there is a “sweet spot” (~300–450 °C preheat) where you maximize densification and work-hardening.  Below that range you suffer high porosity and low hardness; above it you gain density but lose peak hardness to thermal softening.

In virtually every aluminum alloy sprayed by cold‐gas deposition you start out with an “over–cold–worked” microstructure: very high dislocation densities, sub­-micron grains, residual stresses – all of which boost hardness.  A post-spray anneal almost invariably softens the deposit by the following sequence:

1. Recovery (≈100–200 °C)  
   – Partial annihilation and rearrangement of dislocations  
   – Modest drop in hardness (10–20 %)  

2. Recrystallization (≈250–350 °C, alloy‐dependent)  
   – Nucleation and growth of strain‐free grains  
   – Major loss of hardness (often 30–50 % of the as-sprayed value)  

3. Grain growth/coarsening (>350 °C)  
   – Further softening as grains coarsen  
   – Hardness approaches that of conventionally cast or cold-rolled feedstock  

For non-heat-treatable alloys (3xxx or 5xxx series) you won’t regain any strength past recovery/recrystallization – you simply soften the part.  For precip­itation-hardening alloys (6xxx or 7xxx series) a full solution‐treatment + quench + artificial‐age cycle (T6, T7, etc.) must follow if you wish to restore or exceed the original cold‐sprayed hardness.

In HVOF‐sprayed oxide‐dispersion‐strengthened (ODS) coatings the hardening comes almost entirely from the finely and uniformly distributed oxide particles (Al₂O₃, Y₂O₃, TiO₂, etc.) that are introduced into the metal matrix during spraying.  The key mechanisms are:

1. Orowan (particle‐bypass) strengthening  
   – Dislocations moving on slip planes are forced to bow between and loop around the oxide particles.  
   – The stress required to bow (and eventually shear or bypass) increases with decreasing inter‐particle spacing, raising the yield strength and hardness of the coating.

2. Grain‐boundary and subgrain‐pinning  
   – Nano‐ to sub‐micron oxide particles sit at grain and subgrain boundaries, inhibiting boundary migration during the brief thermal exposure of HVOF.  
   – This “Zener pinning” effect refines the matrix grain size and maintains that fine grain size on cooling, invoking a Hall–Petch increase in hardness.

3. Thermal‐mismatch dislocation hardening  
   – Differences in coefficients of thermal expansion between the oxides and the metal create high local dislocation densities around each particle during rapid cooling.  
   – Those geometrically necessary dislocations further impede mobile dislocations in service.

4. Load sharing  
   – Under an applied load or indentation, the stiff oxide particles bear part of the load, reducing the stress on the softer matrix and effectively raising the composite hardness.

By combining all of these, an HVOF‐sprayed ODS coating achieves significantly higher hardness, wear resistance, and thermal stability than a spray‐deposited matrix alone.

Both laboratory and industrial experience show that post-spray thermal treatments—whether simple anneals, age-hardening cycles or full hot‐isostatic pressing—tend to close or shrink the pore network in cold‐sprayed deposits and to improve their load‐bearing continuity.  In broad strokes:  

1. Heat treatment (no pressure)  
   • Stress relief and boundary diffusion—At temperatures of 0.4–0.6 Tm (metal’s melting point), lattice diffusion activates at particle–particle interfaces.  Small voids shrink, and dislocations rearrange, so interparticle bonding tightens.  
   • Porosity reduction—Typically 20–60 % of as-sprayed porosity can be eliminated, depending on alloy, time and temperature.  Because there is no external pressure, large or entrapped pores may remain.  
   • Mechanical‐property trends—Residual tensile stresses drop, ductility and impact resistance rise.  For pure or age-soft alloys (e.g. Cu, Ni), hardness often falls slightly.  For heat-treatable alloys (e.g. Al-Si, Al-Mg-Si, Ti-6Al-4V), a properly sequenced solution-treatment plus ageing can restore—or even exceed—the as-sprayed strength by precipitate hardening.  

2. Hot isostatic pressing (HIP)  
   • Pore closure under pressure—Typical HIP cycles (100–200 MPa, 0.7–0.9 Tm) collapse virtually all internal and open pores by creep and plastic flow.  Densities >99.9 % are routinely reported.  
   • Grain‐boundary healing—High‐temperature pressure also heals microcracks and cold‐spray‐induced splat boundaries, producing a near‐wrought microstructure with continuous grain structure across the formerly discrete particles.  
   • Mechanical‐property enhancements—Ultimate tensile strength and yield strength approach or match those of conventionally cast/forged stock.  Fatigue life rises by one to two orders of magnitude over the as-sprayed condition.  Residual stresses all but vanish; elongation-to-failure can double or more.  
   • Trade-offs—If held too long or at too high a temperature, grain growth or over-ageing may slightly reduce peak hardness in precipitation-strengthened alloys.  

In summary, simple heat treatments improve bonding and relieve stress but leave some porosity behind; HIP is the most effective way to eliminate pores and microcracks entirely and to recover bulk‐metal mechanical performance in cold‐sprayed coatings.

In virtually every study of thermally‐ or cold‐sprayed hydroxyapatite (HA) coatings that has mapped mechanical properties by depth (normally by nanoindentation), both the hardness (H) and the elastic modulus (E) turn out to be highest in the splat‐dense zone immediately adjacent to the substrate (or bond coat) and then fall off steadily toward the free surface.  In rough numbers you will see:  

 1.  Interface (first ~5–20 μm):  
    •  Highest density of strongly deformed, well‐flattened splats  
    •  H in the range of 4–7 GPa (thermal spray) or even 7–10 GPa (cold spray)  
    •  E in the range of 70–120 GPa  

 2.  Mid‐thickness (~20–80 μm in a 100–200 μm coating):  
    •  Slight loss of thermal exposure/plastic deformation → a few % porosity  
    •  H drops to ~75–85 % of the interface value  
    •  E drops to ~80–90 % of the interface value  

 3.  Near the free surface (last ~10–30 μm):  
    •  Least splat flattening, highest microcracking and interlamellar porosity  
    •  H down to 60–70 % of the interface layer (e.g. 3–4 GPa for plasma spray; 4–6 GPa for cold spray)  
    •  E down to 65–80 GPa (thermal spray) or 80–100 GPa (cold spray)  

The drop in H is typically 20–40 % from interface to surface; the drop in E is of order 15–25 %.  The root cause in all cases is the progressive decrease in particle temperature/strain during deposition (fewer fully‐flattened splats, more pores/cracks) as you move away from the heat‐sink provided by the substrate.

In cold spray the single most important “knob” you have for controlling how well particles bond (and thus how dense and how strong your build is) is the particle’s impact velocity.  In broad‐brush terms the effect breaks down like this:

1.  Below the “critical velocity”  
    •  Particles simply ricochet or embed poorly.  
    •  Deposition efficiency is essentially zero; deposits are extremely porous and weak.  

2.  Near and just above the critical velocity  
    •  Plastic deformation of the particle (and a thin layer of substrate) begins.  
    •  “Jetting” of oxide and adsorbed films at the interface creates metallurgical bonding.  
    •  Deposit density climbs steeply (porosity falls), and you see rapid gains in hardness, yield strength and tensile strength as you approach ~90–95 % of theoretical density.  

3.  As you increase velocity further (up to some material‐specific optimum, typically 700–1 200 m/s for metals in high-pressure systems)  
    •  More severe plastic deformation ⇒ finer sub‐grains (even nano-scale) through adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization.  
    •  Continued increases in deposit density (often 98–99+ % of bulk), hardness, yield and ultimate strength, fatigue resistance and wear resistance.  
    •  Ductility may initially improve versus lower‐velocity builds because interparticle bonding is more uniform and voids are closed out.  

4.  Beyond the optimum velocity  
    •  You begin to see diminishing returns or even degradation—substrate erosion, particle fragmentation, excessive residual tensile stresses, microcracking.  
    •  Mechanical properties (especially ductility and fatigue life) can suffer if you over‐shoot the velocity window.  

In practice you therefore tune your gas pressure/temperature (or carrier conditions, nozzle design, standoff) to get just above critical velocity for your powder/substrate combination.  That maximizes density and strength without introducing erosion damage or high tensile residual stresses.

Annealing a cold-sprayed Cu coating has two principal effects on microstructure and properties: it relieves the high dislocation density and residual stresses built up during the severe plastic deformation bonding process, and it activates solid‐state diffusion/recrystallization at the particle–particle interfaces.  The net result is stronger metallurgical bonding and much higher post-deposition ductility, at the expense of some hardness and strength.  

Summary of what happens on annealing:  
 1. Stress relief and recovery  
    • The extremely high dislocation density in as-sprayed Cu (10^14–10^15 m^–2) drops dramatically once you exceed about 200–250 °C.  
    • Residual tensile stresses around inter-particle boundaries relax, reducing the tendency for interfacial microcracks to open under load.  

 2. Recrystallization and interface healing  
    • Between ~250 °C and 400 °C new, strain‐free Cu grains nucleate and grow, first at high–energy sites (particle boundaries), then into the bulk of each particle.  
    • Grain‐boundary diffusion across formerly distinct particle interfaces “welds” them together, closing pores and microvoids.  
    • Typical closed porosity falls from ~4–6 % in the as-sprayed state to <1–2 % after a 1 h anneal at 300 °C.  

 3. Grain growth versus strength–ductility trade-off  
    • Modest annealing (200–300 °C, 1 h) yields a fine‐equiaxed microstructure (grain size ~1–3 μm), a 20–40 % increase in interfacial bonding strength, and a 2–3× gain in uniform elongation (from ≈3–5 % up to 8–12 %).  
    • If you push to higher temperatures (≥400–450 °C) or longer times, grains coarsen (5–20 μm), hardness drops further, strength falls (Hall–Petch), but ductility can approach that of bulk annealed Cu (>20 % elongation).  

In practice you choose an annealing window (often 250–350 °C for 30–60 min under inert or reducing atmosphere) to maximize tensile elongation and interparticle bond strength while retaining adequate hardness and yield strength for your application.

In cold‐sprayed coatings the “damage” you introduce by ultra‐high‐strain‐rate impacts is in fact the source of most of your strengthening.  In practice the most beneficial defect structures are those that impede dislocation motion and subdivide the metal into ever‐smaller regions.  Key examples include:

 • Dislocation tangles and networks  
   – At impact, extremely high dislocation densities are generated, especially at particle–particle interfaces.  These tangled forests of dislocations raise yield strength by traditional Taylor‐hardening.  

 • Dislocation cells and subgrain boundaries (low‐angle grain boundaries)  
   – With continued deformation, dislocations organize into cell walls or walls of misorientation 2°–15°.  These walls act like low‐angle grain boundaries and contribute to Hall–Petch–type strengthening.  

 • High‐angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) and ultrafine/nano-grains  
   – In many cold‐spray systems a combination of dynamic recovery and localized dynamic recrystallization at extreme strain rates produces grains < 1 μm or even in the 100–200 nm range, separated by HAGBs (> 15°).  These are among the strongest barriers to dislocation glide.  

 • Nano-twins and stacking faults  
   – Particularly in high-stacking‐fault‐energy metals (e.g. Cu alloys, certain stainless steels), deformation twins and dense stacking‐fault packets add an extra level of barrier to dislocation motion.  

 • Vacancy clusters and nano-voids (controlled porosity)  
   – Small, well‐dispersed vacancy clusters or sub-micron voids at the particle boundaries can contribute to strain hardening via constraint of local plastic flow.  (Large pores are detrimental, but a fine dispersion can raise work hardening.)  

 • Compressive residual stresses  
   – Although not a crystallographic “defect,” the high‐strain‐rate impacts lock in compressive stresses near the surface and at interparticle interfaces; these retard crack opening and improve fatigue and fracture toughness.  

In combination, these defects subdivide the microstructure and vastly increase the number of obstacles to dislocation glide—delivering higher hardness, yield strength, fatigue resistance, and often improved wear performance in cold‐sprayed coatings.

In virtually every ball‐ or attritor‐mill study you will find the same qualitative trend: as you increase the *total mechanical energy* imparted to the powder (by increasing milling time, impact energy or frequency, ball–to–powder ratio, etc.), the powder particles accumulate more dislocations, their grains or subgrains refine, and their hardness rises.  Quantitatively, this can often be rationalized by combining:  

 1.  Hall–Petch grain‐size strengthening  
      H ≃ H0 + kHP·d–½  
 2.  An empirical grain‐size vs. energy law  
      d ≃ d0·Etotal–n   (n typically 0.2–0.5)  

 ⇒  H ≃ H0 + k·(Etotal)n/2  

So you observe:  
 • At low Etotal: rapid hardness rise (large grain refinement per joule input)  
 • At higher Etotal: diminishing returns (grain sizes approach a lower bound, defect‐density saturation)  
 • Beyond a critical Etotal: hardness may plateau or even drop slightly if amorphization, cold‐welding/agglomeration, or dynamic recovery/recrystallization set in.  

Bottom line:  powder hardness grows roughly as a sub‐linear power of the total milling energy (often ≈Etotal½) up to a saturation point.

In cold‐spray impacts the “bounciness” of a powder particle – quantified by its coefficient of restitution (CoR = rebound-speed/impact-speed) – falls off rapidly as you push the impact velocity up.  Physically, more of the initial kinetic energy is being consumed in irreversible plastic deformation, jetting at the interface, heat and friction, and less is left over for elastic rebound.  

A useful way to think about it is in three regimes:

 1.  Low‐velocity (purely elastic) regime  
    – v ≪ v₁ (often < 0.2–0.3 vcrit)  
    – Plastic work is negligible, CoR is high (≈ 0.7–1.0).  

 2.  Intermediate (elasto-plastic) regime  
    – v ~ 0.2–1 vcrit  
    – Plastic deformation begins to dominate.  Experiments on Al and Cu powders typically show CoR dropping from ~ 0.6–0.8 at 200 m/s to ~ 0.1–0.3 at 400–500 m/s.  A simple scaling from energy balance (plastic work ∝ v5/3 vs. kinetic energy ∝ v2) gives CoR ∝ v–1/3 or, empirically, CoR ≃ 1 – (v/vcrit)^n (n ≈ 1–2).  

 3.  High‐velocity (adhesion) regime  
    – v ≥ vcrit  
    – Essentially all kinetic energy goes into plastic flow and interfacial jetting.  CoR→0 and particles stick (no measurable rebound).  

In summary: as impact velocity rises toward the material’s cold‐spray critical velocity, CoR falls monotonically from near unity in the elastic regime, through a steep decline in the elasto-plastic regime, to effectively zero once you exceed the deposition threshold.

Cold spray deposits typically show much higher strength and hardness than their wrought‐or cast counterparts—but at the expense of ductility.  Two main microstructural factors are responsible:  
  1. Extreme severe plastic deformation in each particle upon impact, producing very high dislocation densities and nano- or sub-micron grain sizes (Hall–Petch strengthening plus work hardening).  
  2. Residual tensile stresses and incomplete bonding/closed porosity at particle boundaries, which act as crack‐initiation sites.  

As a result, cold-sprayed coatings often fracture at low strains (few percent elongation) and exhibit reduced toughness.  

Restoring ductility is almost always done via a post-spray thermal treatment (anneal or stress‐relief):  
  • Stress relief anneal (just below recrystallization temperature) to remove residual stresses and reduce dislocation density. Typical cycles are 300–500 °C for Al alloys, 400–700 °C for Cu, up to 900 °C for steels, held for 1–4 h then furnace or controlled‐cool to minimize new stresses.  
  • Full recrystallization anneal (above or near recrystallization T) to achieve new, equiaxed grains and close sub-micron porosity. This recovers 70–90 % of wrought‐metal ductility but lowers yield strength.  

Alternatives / complements:  
  • Laser or induction surface annealing (rapid, localized heating) can soften the deposit without heating the entire part.  
  • Friction-stir or ultrasonic surface treatment can induce dynamic recrystallization in situ.  

In practice you choose the lowest‐temperature, shortest cycle that: (1) relieves stress, (2) coarsens grains just enough to restore required elongation, and (3) does not overgrow grains to the point of losing too much strength.

Preheating the feedstock particles in a cold‐spray process is found almost universally to reduce the final coating porosity.  The mechanisms at work are:

1. Lowered flow stress at impact  
   – Raising the particle’s temperature (even by a few hundred °C) drops its yield strength and work‐hardening rate.  
   – On impact, the warmer particle plastically deforms more readily and flattens out into a thinner, wider “splat,” filling the gaps between neighboring particles more completely.  

2. Increased critical velocity window  
   – Because preheated particles require slightly less gas-jet velocity to achieve the critical impact pressure for bonding, more particles land in the “good‐bonding” regime and fewer rebound or leave unfilled voids.  

3. Reduced thermal mismatch and residual stress  
   – A smaller temperature jump between particle and substrate cuts back on thermal‐elastic mismatch, which otherwise opens microcracks or intersplat porosity upon cooldown.  

Quantitatively, several studies report that preheating powders by 200–400 °C (on top of the usual gas heating) can halve the pore volume fraction—from, say, ~8–12 vol.% down to ~3–6 vol.% in common metals such as Al, Cu or Ni.  Beyond ~400 °C additional benefits diminish and risks of surface oxidation or particle agglomeration begin to counterbalance the gains in densification.

In cold‐sprayed metal–ceramic composites (e.g. Ni–SiC, Al–Al₂O₃, Cu–SiC), the wear response is governed by a handful of interacting damage modes.  In rough order of importance you will typically see:

1. Micro-abrasive wear  
   – Two-body micro-cutting and micro-ploughing of the metallic matrix by the hard ceramic particles that protrude from the surface.  
   – At higher sliding stresses, fractured ceramic fragments act as hard third bodies and aggravate three-body abrasion.

2. Particle fracture and pull-out  
   – Brittle ceramics crack under local stress concentrations at the matrix–particle interface.  
   – Once they debond, pulled-out particles become loose abrasives, or leave pits that become initiation sites for further damage (fatigue, delamination).

3. Delamination fatigue  
   – Repeated shear at the particle–matrix interface leads to microcrack coalescence and flaking of subsurface layers, especially if interfacial bonding is poor.

4. Adhesive wear (to a lesser extent)  
   – In areas where the metal matrix contacts the counterface directly, junctions can form and then shear out, carrying entrapped ceramic fragments.

5. Oxidative wear (minor in low-temperature cold spray)  
   – Thin tribo‐oxide films form on the metal matrix and can either protect or embrittle the surface, depending on load and temperature.

Overall effect on wear behavior:  
• Hard ceramic particles raise surface hardness, reduce real contact area, and so dramatically cut the depth of plastic deformation under the same load—typically reducing steady-state wear rates by an order of magnitude versus the unreinforced matrix.  
• However, if ceramic volume fraction is too high, or if particle–matrix bonding is weak, you see a crossover to brittle fracture–dominated wear (large‐scale delamination, spallation of particle‐rich islands) and a sharp rise in material loss.  
• Optimizing particle size, volume fraction and interfacial strength yields a coating in which the metal matrix “backs up” the ceramics, minimizing particle pull-out and keeping the dominant mode as low-severity micro-abrasion rather than catastrophic delamination.

In cold spray, particle impact velocity (v) is one of the single most important parameters controlling the microstructure—and hence the hardness—of the deposited coating.  Its influence can be broken down into three regimes:

1. Sub-critical velocities (v < v_c)  
   • v_c is the “critical velocity” below which particles rebound rather than bond (typically 300–500 m/s for Al alloys, 800–1000 m/s for steels/Ti).  
   • Little or no coating builds up. Any weakly adhered material has a low-density, porous structure and exhibits very low hardness.

2. Just above critical (v ≈ v_c to ≈1.2 v_c)  
   • Particles plastically deform on impact, creating intimate metal–metal contact.  
   • Strain rates of 10^6–10^9 s⁻¹ generate high dislocation densities and—in many alloys—adiabatic shear instabilities that lead to dynamic recrystallization in a thin interfacial layer.  
   • Grain sizes refine to sub-micron or even nanometric scale in the impact zone.  
   • Porosity falls and interparticle bonding strengthens.  
   • Result: hardness rises markedly over the as-powder and as-substrate values (often +20 – 50 HV or more, depending on alloy).

3. Over-critical or excessive velocities (v ≫ v_c)  
   • Further velocity increases continue to refine the microstructure only up to a point. Beyond an “optimum” (≈1.1 – 1.3 v_c) you begin to see:  
     – Erosive wear of the growing coating or substrate  
     – Excess tensile residual stress or microcracking  
     – Entrapped oxide fragments or micro‐voids from particle shattering  
   • These defects can offset the benefits of additional grain refinement, so hardness may plateau or even decrease.

Quantitatively, most cold‐sprayed Al alloys show a steady hardness increase as velocity climbs from ~400 to ~700 m/s, after which improvements level off. Harder alloys (Ti, Ni, steels) require higher v but follow the same trend.  

Key take-aways:  
• You must exceed the material’s critical velocity to get a coherent, hardened deposit.  
• In the “sweet spot” above v_c you maximize work hardening, grain refinement, and bonding quality—hence peak hardness.  
• Pushing velocities much beyond the optimum introduces defects that can reduce the net hardness or damage the coating/substrate interface.

Cold-sprayed coatings are prized in industry largely because the high‐velocity, solid-state deposition process imparts very favorable mechanical properties without the heat-related drawbacks of fusion sprays.  In broad strokes the principal advantages are:

1. Very High Bond and Cohesive Strength  
   • Intense plastic deformation of particles on impact creates metallurgical bonds to the substrate (adhesions often 20–100 MPa or higher) and excellent interparticle cohesion.  
   • Absence of a melt means no splat‐related defects or poorly adhered oxide interlayers.

2. Near-Fully Dense Microstructure  
   • Porosities typically <1–3 vol % versus 5–20 vol % in conventional plasma or HVOF coatings.  
   • Low oxide content—particles never exceed roughly 0.2–0.4 Tm, so oxidation is minimal.

3. Retained Feedstock Hardness and Work Hardening  
   • Particles undergo severe strain‐hardening on impact, boosting microhardness 20–50 % above the original powder.  
   • Fine, cold-worked subgrains contribute to high coating hardness and wear resistance.

4. Compressive Residual Stresses  
   • The shot‐peen–like effect of thousands of high-speed impacts leaves the coating (and near‐surface substrate) in a compressive stress state.  
   • Improves fatigue life and resistance to crack initiation and propagation.

5. Superior Wear, Erosion and Fretting Resistance  
   • High density, high hardness and low oxide content give excellent abrasive and erosive wear performance—often 2×–10× better versus thermally sprayed equivalents.  
   • Good fretting and galling resistance due to strong metal-metal bonding.

6. Minimal Thermal Distortion or Heat Affected Zone (HAZ)  
   • Substrates see only modest temperature rises (< 0.3 Tm of the metal), so there is no phase transformation, grain coarsening or substrate softening.  
   • Critical when coating heat-sensitive alloys or precision components.

7. Good Corrosion-Fatigue Performance  
   • Low porosity and oxide content limit pathways for corrosive media.  
   • Compressive residual stresses further slow crack growth under cyclic loading in corrosive environments.

8. Retained Ductility and Toughness (Material Dependent)  
   • Because no melting occurs, many alloys (e.g. titanium, aluminum, copper) retain much of their native ductility and toughness—even after work hardening.  

Taken together, these features make cold-sprayed coatings especially attractive for applications demanding high bond strength, exceptional wear/erosion resistance, enhanced fatigue life and minimal thermal impact on the substrate.

Similarity in key mechanical and physical properties of the feedstock powder and the substrate—most importantly their flow stress (yield strength), hardness, elastic modulus, thermal expansion coefficient, and thermal conductivity—helps maximize bonding strength in cold spray for several reasons:

1. Matched deformation behavior  
   • When powder and substrate have similar yield strengths and work‐hardening rates, both materials plastically deform in a compatible way upon impact.  
   • This yields a large, continuous “adhered” area, maximizes oxide‐layer disruption, and generates the adiabatic shear instability that forges the particles into intimate metal–metal contact.

2. Reduced interfacial stress concentrations  
   • If one material is much harder (or stiffer) than the other, plastic strain localizes in the softer material, creating stress concentrations at the interface.  
   • Such concentrations can lead to microcracking, void formation, or debonding under service loads or thermal cycling.

3. Minimized residual thermal stresses  
   • Cold spray is nominally a solid‐state process, but the high‐speed impacts still generate localized heating.  
   • Similar coefficients of thermal expansion ensure that any heat input or environmentally induced temperature swings impose balanced strain in coating and substrate, rather than tensile stresses that weaken the bond or cause delamination.

4. Optimized critical velocity and spray efficiency  
   • When the flow stress ratio powder/substrate is well matched, the particle critical velocity for bonding is lower—fewer particles rebound, and more deposit successfully.  
   • This improves build rate and uniformity without having to push gas pressures (and impact stresses) to damaging levels.

In contrast, large mismatches in strength or thermal properties force either (a) higher impact velocities—risking substrate erosion or substrate‐side cracking—or (b) poor interfacial conformity and low bonded area, both of which degrade adhesion and cohesion of the spray deposit.

Key reasons why cold-sprayed coatings almost always fall short of bulk tensile strength and ductility are:  

1. Porosity and entrapped voids  
   • Cold spray cannot fully collapse every interparticle gap; residual pores act as crack‐initiation sites under load.  
   • Entrapped carrier gas or debris further compromises local cohesion.  

2. Incomplete particle bonding  
   • Bonding is purely solid-state and relies on extreme plastic deformation at particle interfaces.  
   • Oxide films or surface contaminants on powder particles inhibit metallic bonding and leave weak interfacial layers.  

3. Microcracks and entrapped oxides  
   • High‐strain rate impacts can fracture hard or brittle particles, creating microcracks.  
   • Oxide fragments dragged into the spray stream become agglomerated at interparticle boundaries.  

4. High residual stresses  
   • Intense, localized plastic deformation introduces both compressive and tensile residual stresses.  
   • Tensile residuals near the coating surface facilitate early crack opening under external load.  

5. Anisotropic, work-hardened microstructure  
   • Grains near particle boundaries are heavily distorted, elongated, and ultra-fine but not fully recrystallized.  
   • Very high dislocation densities locally increase hardness but drastically reduce ductility.  

6. Limited diffusional healing  
   • Operating temperatures (typically 400–1000 °C) aren’t high enough for significant solid‐state diffusion or recrystallization across all interfaces.  
   • Interfaces remain mechanically bonded rather than metallurgically “welded,” lowering cohesive strength.  

In bulk wrought or annealed materials, by contrast, high‐temperature processing and full melting/recrystallization eliminate pores, dissolve oxides, and promote uniform grain structures—yielding higher tensile strength and ductility.

Cold spray (CS) and laser‐powder bed fusion (LPBF) both can produce near‐full‐density builds, but because the underlying physics are so different, the as‐fabricated microstructures—and therefore hardnesses—differ markedly even for the same alloy.  The key reasons CS deposits are typically harder than LPBF “as‐built” parts are:

1. Deformation vs. melting route  
   • Cold spray is a solid‐state, high‐velocity impact process. Particles bond under severe plastic deformation, but never fully melt.  
   • LPBF melts the powder locally, then rapidly re‐solidifies each layer in a laser‐scanned melt pool.

2. Work hardening & dislocation density  
   • In CS each particle impact generates extremely high localized strains (strain rates ~10^5–10^6 s⁻¹) and adiabatic shear at the interface.  
   • This floods the deposit with dislocations and sub‐grain boundaries that remain locked in (no anneal‐out), raising hardness via classic strain‐hardening.  
   • In LPBF, although the rapid solidification can refine the grain size, the repeated local re‐heating during layer‐by‐layer scans partially anneals out dislocations, so the net dislocation density is lower.

3. Ultrafine grain/sub‐grain structure  
   • Cold‐sprayed zones undergo dynamic recrystallization in the interfacial shear bands, producing sub‐grains on the order of 100–500 nm.  
   • LPBF grains often grow epitaxially through successive melt pools into columnar structures (1–10 µm), punctuated only by finer cellular features at the melt‐pool boundaries.

4. Residual stress state  
   • Cold‐sprayed deposits typically end up with compressive residual stresses in the near‐surface/substrate region, which can elevate hardness readings.  
   • LPBF parts accumulate tensile residual stresses from rapid heating/cooling, which can locally reduce hardness (and promote stress relief cracking).

5. Porosity and defect type  
   • Well‐optimized cold spray can achieve >99 % density with only nano‐ or sub‐micron voids at particle interfaces.  
   • LPBF sometimes traps keyhole pores, lack‐of‐fusion voids or gas pores that act as “soft spots” under indentation, lowering apparent hardness.

Putting it all together, an as‐sprayed Al or Ti alloy deposit will typically show 15–30 % higher Vickers hardness (HV) than its as‐built LPBF counterpart purely because cold spray “locks in” massive work‐hardening and ultrafine substructure without the counter‐acting thermal anneal cycles inherent in laser melting.

Friction‐stir processing (FSP) of a cold-sprayed (CS) metallic coating normally drives its hardness up—often by 20 % to 100 %—for three principal reasons:

1. Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement  
   - The severe plastic deformation and adiabatic heating under the FSP tool break the as-sprayed lamellar splats and ultrafine oxides into much finer, equiaxed grains (e.g. down from 10–30 µm in the as-sprayed material to 0.3–1 µm in the stir zone).  
   - According to the Hall–Petch relationship, smaller grains raise the yield strength and hardness.

2. Porosity reduction and inter-splat bonding  
   - FSP “stirs” and forges the coating in situ, collapsing residual pores and oxides and welding the neighboring splats into a near‐fully dense microstructure.  
   - The stronger metallurgical bonds across prior splat boundaries eliminate weak interfaces that would otherwise plastically deform at lower stresses.

3. Work hardening and dispersion strengthening  
   - The intense shear and torsion impart high dislocation densities, and any retained second‐phase (oxide or carbide) particles become more uniformly dispersed, adding further obstacle strength to dislocation motion.

Typical reported numbers (Al‐ and Cu‐based CS coatings)  
• Al 7075 CS: as-sprayed hardness ≈ 50–60 HV → FSP stir zone ≈ 80–110 HV  
• Pure Cu CS: as-sprayed ≈ 90–100 HV → FSP ≈ 130–160 HV  

Notes on hardness profiles  
• The peak hardness coincides with the fully developed stir zone beneath the tool shoulder.  
• Toward the thermo-mechanically affected zone (TMAZ) and heat-affected zone (HAZ), grain coarsening or over-aging may reduce hardness somewhat, giving a characteristic “hard center” tapering off to the as-sprayed base.  

In short, by dynamically recrystallizing, densifying and work-hardening a CS coating, FSP typically produces a much harder, more wear-resistant surface than the original cold-sprayed deposit.

Cold‐spray coatings stick so well to polymers mainly because of what happens when micro‐particles slam into a “soft” substrate at very high speed:

1. Extremely high local pressures (often >1 GPa) and strain rates (~10^6 s–1) on impact cause  
   – Severe plastic deformation of both the metal particle and the polymer surface  
   – Adiabatic shear at the interface that breaks oxide films and brings clean metal into atomic‐scale contact with polymer chains  

2. The low yield strength (and often low glass-transition temperature) of the polymer means it also flows or “pops out” under the impact, producing  
   – Plastic craters or pits in the substrate  
   – Mechanical undercuts and interlocking as particles hammer in  

3. Localized heating from the high‐velocity impact can soften or even partially melt the polymer surface, allowing  
   – Polymer chain flow into particle asperities  
   – A thin, interdigitated region where polymer and metal are intermixed (mechanically and, to some extent, entangled)  

4. The result is an interface with  
   – Large real contact area  
   – Mechanical anchoring via craters and undercuts  
   – Strong interfacial friction and van der Waals bonding at atomic‐scale contact spots  

By combining extreme kinetic‐energy impact with the deformability of polymers, cold spray achieves bond strengths on plastics that rival or exceed those on metals—yet without bulk heating that would damage temperature-sensitive substrates.

Cold-sprayed coatings never “get harder forever” as you pile on more material – instead their microhardness rises quickly over the first few hundred microns of build‐up and then levels off at a plateau that is typically 20–50 % above the annealed feedstock value but still below the hardness you could achieve in a bulk material that had been severely cold-worked or age-hardened.  

Mechanistic origin of the plateau  
1. Impact-driven severe plastic deformation at each particle–substrate and particle–particle interface generates very high dislocation densities and refines grains or subgrains (often into the submicron or even nanometer range) via adiabatic shear instabilities (“jetting” zones).  
2. At the same time, dynamic recovery and continuous recrystallization processes set in locally, so that once a critical dislocation density/subgrain size is reached additional impacts add very little net hardening.  
3. In effect the structure “saturates” – you’ve reached the maximum work‐hardening and grain-boundary strengthening that this high-strain-rate deposition route can deliver, and further thickness simply reproduces the same hardened microstructure rather than pushing hardness up toward the levels attainable in bulk materials subjected to much larger overall strains or thermal treatments.

Cold‐sprayed coatings almost invariably end up harder than the original powder simply because the supersonic impact process imparts very high strains at very high strain rates without melting, producing a very heavily deformed, ultrafine‐grained, highly dislocated microstructure plus residual compressive stresses.  In more detail:

1. Severe cold work and dislocation strengthening  
   • Particles impacting at 500–1 200 m/s deform plastically in a very thin “jet” zone at their periphery.  
   • Dislocation densities soar (10^14–10^15 m–2), locking up further glide and raising hardness (Taylor hardening).

2. Grain refinement (dynamic recrystallization/subgrain formation)  
   • The extreme shear strains and adiabatic heating in the impact zone drive continuous dynamic recrystallization or subgrain subdivision.  
   • Typical grain sizes in the bonded coating can fall into the submicron or even nanometer regime, invoking a strong Hall–Petch effect.

3. Residual compressive stresses  
   • The build‐up of successive, plastically deformed layers generates through‐thickness compressive stresses, further impeding crack opening and dislocation motion.

4. Porosity elimination and strong interparticle bonding  
   • High particle velocities collapse most pores and oxide layers, producing a near‐fully dense coating that offers uninterrupted load transfer and fewer “soft” zones.

5. Oxide/impurity dispersions (in some systems)  
   • In alloys or powders with intentionally added fine oxides (e.g. ODS‐type powders), these dispersoids survive the cold‐spray process and further pin dislocations.

All of these factors—ultra‐high dislocation densities, nanometer‐scale grains, compressive pre‐stress and oxide pinning—combine to give cold‐sprayed coatings a hardness often 20–50 % (or more) above that of the feedstock powder.

As-sprayed cold‐spray deposits are typically extraordinarily dense by thermal‐spray standards (often 95–99 % of theoretical density, i.e. 1–5 % residual porosity) but their metal particles bond by severe plastic deformation, so the as-deposited microstructure carries very high dislocation densities, locked‐in residual stress and limited elongation (ductility often in the single‐digit percent range).  In practice one almost always follows cold spray with a post‐deposition thermal consolidation step—either a conventional anneal/aging cycle (for Al, Cu, Ni alloys, etc.) or, where maximum pore closure and strength are required, hot‐isostatic pressing (HIP).  That treatment relieves residual stress, promotes recrystallization, closes or shrinks remaining pores, lowers hardness to a more ductile level, and markedly improves both mechanical toughness and wear resistance.

Grain refinement in cold-sprayed cermet coatings almost invariably raises their fracture strength and toughness.  In essence, breaking the metal (and to some extent the ceramic) phases down to sub-micron or even nano-scale yields three synergistic benefits:

1. Hall–Petch strengthening of the ductile binder  
   • As the metal‐matrix grains shrink, yield and ultimate strengths climb roughly with d–½.  Typical cold-sprayed Ni‐ or Co-based binders refined from 1–2 µm to 0.2–0.5 µm show 25–50 % higher tensile strength.  
   • Higher matrix strength postpones plastic collapse around a propagating crack tip, so the composite can sustain higher overall stresses.  

2. More tortuous crack paths and increased interface area  
   • Finer carbide or oxide particles dispersed in the binder force cracks to weave, branch, and bridge more often.  Each boundary or particle interface absorbs fracture energy and blunts crack tips.  
   • The increased length of metal–ceramic interfaces also improves mechanical interlocking and residual compressive stresses around hard phases, further raising the critical stress intensity for crack growth.  

3. Reduced porosity and improved cohesion  
   • Smaller grains deform more readily during particle impact, closing inter‐particle voids and producing a denser, better‐bonded deposit.  
   • Lower porosity means fewer crack‐nucleation sites, so the coating fails at a higher applied load.  

Taken together, these effects can double (or better) the fracture strength relative to a coarse‐grained counterpart.  In practice, one sees fracture-limit stresses climb from a few hundred MPa for micron-scale grains to well over 1 GPa when the binder and ceramic phases are refined into the sub-micron regime.

Laser cladding produces a true fusion bond, whereas cold‐spray relies almost entirely on high-velocity mechanical interlocking and solid-state plastic deformation.  In laser cladding the laser beam locally melts both the substrate surface and the injected feedstock powder, creating a metallurgical (weld-type) bond with interdiffusion, dilution of alloying elements, and epitaxial grain growth across the interface.  That fusion zone—with its chemical bonding and virtually zero interfacial porosity—is what gives laser‐clad layers their generally higher adhesion strength.

In cold‐sprayed metals and alloys the as‐sprayed microhardness is almost always well above that of the bulk feedstock.  Two principal factors are at work:  

1. Severe plastic deformation at impact  
   – Each particle striking the substrate or an underlying, already-deformed layer undergoes extremely high strain rates (10^4–10^6 s^–1).  
   – This engenders very high dislocation densities (10^14–10^15 m^–2), tangling and pile-ups at subgrain boundaries, and in many materials localized dynamic recrystallization to ultrafine or nanocrystalline grains (50–500 nm).  
   – The net effect is classic work‐hardening plus grain‐boundary hardening (Hall–Petch effect).  

2. Locked-in residual stresses and fine interfaces  
   – Cold spray produces predominantly compressive residual stresses and a large density of high‐angle boundaries and dislocation walls.  
   – Pores, oxides or other entrained second-phase particles (if present) also act as hard second‐phase obstacles to dislocation motion.  

As a result, typical as‐sprayed microhardness values for Cu, Al or Ti alloys can be 20–100 % higher than their conventional annealed or cast counterparts.  

What happens when you anneal?  

• Recovery (T ≲ 0.3 Tₘ)  
  – Dislocation annihilation and rearrangement into lower‐energy subgrain structures.  
  – Modest drop in hardness (10–20 %) as the dislocation density relaxes.  

• Recrystallization (0.3 Tₘ ≲ T ≲ 0.5 Tₘ)  
  – Formation of new, strain‐free equiaxed grains.  
  – Sharp reduction in hardness as the ultrafine, cold‐worked microstructure is replaced by coarser grains.  

• Grain‐growth and stress‐relief (T > 0.5 Tₘ)  
  – Continued grain coarsening and relief of residual stresses.  
  – Hardness approaches (or even falls below) that of fully annealed conventionally manufactured material.  

In some precipitation‐hardening alloys (e.g. Al–Zn–Mg) a low‐temperature “aging” step after spray can actually increase hardness again by precipitate formation in a strain‐supersaturated matrix.  But for most commercially pure or minimum-alloy cold‐spray deposits, any anneal softens the coating by removing dislocations and growing grains.

Cold‐sprayed coatings often exhibit higher surface hardness than the as-received substrate even though bonding is achieved entirely in the solid state. The key hardening mechanisms are:  

1. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) and work-hardening  
   • Each particle impact imparts very high strain rates (10³–10⁵ s⁻¹), generating large dislocation densities in the deposit.  
   • The accumulation and interaction of these dislocations raises yield strength via Taylor hardening.  

2. Adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization (DRX)  
   • Localized heating at the particle–substrate and particle–particle interfaces can trigger DRX, producing ultrafine‐to-nanocrystalline grains.  
   • Grain‐boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect) further boosts hardness.  

3. Residual compressive stresses  
   • Repeated peening impacts lock in compressive stresses in the coating, impeding dislocation motion under subsequent loading.  

4. Built-in second phases or oxides (in composite or alloy systems)  
   • In some feedstocks, dispersed oxides or hard intermetallics are fragmented and uniformly distributed, providing additional dispersion strengthening.  

5. Inherent material contrast  
   • If the spray material is intrinsically harder or more highly alloyed than the substrate, the deposited layer naturally exhibits superior hardness.  

Together, these solid-state phenomena—work hardening, ultrafine grain formation, compressive stress fields and potential dispersion strengthening—deliver the marked hardness improvement of cold‐spray coatings over their substrates.

In cold‐spray AM the “secret sauce” is the massive, high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation that each ductile metal particle undergoes on impact.  That deformation plays four interlocking roles in strengthening the final coating:

1. Surface cleaning and metal–metal bonding  
   • Impact pressures (hundreds of MPa) and adiabatic shear strip away oxides and contaminants.  
   • Localized jetting at the particle/substrate (and particle/particle) interface forces fresh metal into intimate contact, enabling pressure‐induced “cold welding” without melting.  

2. Work hardening via dislocation multiplication  
   • Strain rates of 10^5–10^7 s⁻¹ generate very high dislocation densities (10^14–10^15 m⁻²).  
   • Those dislocation forests raise yield strength and hardness by classical Taylor dislocation strengthening.  

3. Grain refinement through dynamic recrystallization  
   • Adiabatic heating at shear bands and subsequent rapid quench produce new, ultrafine (sub‐micron to nanocrystalline) grains.  
   • Hall–Petch grain‐boundary strengthening further boosts hardness, toughness, and fatigue resistance.  

4. Porosity reduction and mechanical interlocking  
   • Severe plastic flow collapses voids and draws particles into one another, increasing interparticle contact area.  
   • The resulting near‐fully dense deposit transmits load across many finely bonded interfaces rather than through weak, porous regions.  

Together, these mechanisms—oxide disruption/cold welding, dislocation strengthening, ultrafine‐grain formation, and pore collapse—transform a loose powder stream into a dense, high‐strength coating.

Ductile‐metal cold‐spray coatings (Al, Cu, Ni, etc.) deposit a 50 – 500 µm‐thick, hard/stiff shell onto an otherwise very soft and compliant polymer (Epolymer ≈1 – 5 GPa, Hpolymer ≈0.05 – 0.2 GPa).  The net result is:  
1. Near the surface the measured hardness and modulus jump to values characteristic of the metal coating (e.g. Hcoat ≈0.5 – 5 GPa, Ecoat ≈50 – 200 GPa).  
2. As an indenter penetrates deeper, the soft polymer substrate begins to contribute, and the apparent (composite) H and E fall off smoothly toward the polymer’s baseline.  

Key points  
•  Depth dependence:  – For indentation depths <≈10 % of coating thickness you essentially measure the metal.  – Beyond that the polymer “backs” the coating and lowers the composite modulus and hardness.  
•  Composite‐modulus models (e.g. Gao, Korsunsky, or a simple rule‐of‐mixtures weighted by coating thickness vs. penetration depth) accurately predict the H(h) and E(h) curves you’ll observe in instrumented indentation.  
•  Porosity/residual stress in the cold‐spray layer will reduce Hcoat and Ecoat somewhat below bulk‐metal values, but even a 90 %‐dense Al layer will still be an order of magnitude stiffer and harder than the underlying polymer.  

In practice you’ll see surface hardness rise from ~0.1 GPa (uncoated polymer) to 1–3 GPa (Al or Cu spray), and the elastic modulus from a few GPa up to tens or—even hundreds—of GPa near the top of the coating.  At larger depths the values revert back toward the polymer’s low modulus and hardness in a predictable, depth‐dependent fashion.

Increasing the particle impact velocity in a cold‐spray process has two primary effects on the coating microstructure and properties:

  1. Bond (adhesion/cohesion) strength rises sharply once you exceed the material’s “critical velocity” and continues to increase (then levels off) as velocity goes up.  
     – Below critical velocity: particles rebound, very little plastic deformation, almost no metallurgical bonding, bond strengths are low (<10–20 MPa typical).  
     – Above critical velocity: adiabatic shear instabilities at the particle–substrate interface produce fresh metal–metal contact, extensive plastic flow, mechanical interlocking and even local metallurgical bonding. Bond strengths can jump to 50–200 MPa or more (depending on material) as velocity increases from just above critical to an optimum range.  
     – Beyond an optimum velocity (~20–30% above the velocity giving maximum deposition efficiency) bond strength may plateau or even decline slightly if you start to erode the substrate or fracture incoming particles.

  2. Porosity falls as velocity goes up (again, until you reach an extreme‐velocity regime).
