     – Near and below critical velocity: poor particle deformation and low deposition efficiency leave interparticle voids; porosity can run 5–15 vol %.  
     – In the “good” velocity window: strong plastic deformation and high impact pressure squeeze out voids, close up pores, and achieve very dense deposits (porosity <1–2 vol %).  
     – At very high velocities, excessive impact pressure or particle fragmentation can introduce microcracks or localized damage that may arrest full densification—porosity can begin to creep up again or the microstructure can become overly stressed.

In practice you choose a gas pressure, temperature and nozzle geometry that give you just enough particle velocity above critical—this maximizes bond strength and minimizes porosity without running into substrate erosion or particle break-up.

In almost every case reported in the literature, introducing a hard ceramic phase (Al₂O₃, TiO₂, SiC, WC, etc.) into a cold-sprayed metal matrix drives the as-sprayed coating hardness up—often substantially.  You are essentially creating a metal-matrix composite (MMC) in which the hard particles act as dispersion-strengthening obstacles to dislocation motion, force load transfer, refine the metal microstructure, and inhibit plastic flow.  

Key points:  
1.   Hardness rises with ceramic fraction  
     – A rough rule‐of‐thumb is +20–40 % hardness per 10 vol % of well-dispersed ceramic, up to some practical limit (typically 20–30 vol %).  
     – Typical examples:  
        •  Al + 20 wt % Al₂O₃ jumps from ≈100 HV (pure Al) to ≈250–300 HV.  
        •  Ni + 15 wt % Al₂O₃ or TiO₂ rises from ≈200 HV to 400–500 HV.  
        •  SS + 10–20 wt % SiC or WC often doubles the hardness (≈250 → 500 HV).  

2.   Strengthening mechanisms  
     – Orowan looping: dislocations bow between hard particles.  
     – Load transfer: the stiff ceramic carries part of the applied stress.  
     – Grain refinement: deformation around particles refines the metal’s sub-grain structure.  

3.   Practical trade-offs  
     – Above roughly 30 vol % ceramics porosity and particle–particle contacts rise, which can actually reduce effective hardness and cohesion.  
     – Excessive ceramics can make the coating brittle, reduce inter-particle metal bonding, and increase spray pressures or temperatures needed for good embedment.  

In summary, you should expect anywhere from a 50 % to 200 % increase in macro-hardness by adding 10–30 vol % hard ceramics to a cold-sprayed metal matrix—provided the particles are uniformly dispersed and the total ceramic loading is kept below the point where porosity and embrittlement set in.

Hard reinforcing particles (e.g. carbides, oxides, nitrides) play several key roles in boosting the wear resistance of cold‐sprayed metal-matrix composite (MMC) coatings:

1. Load-bearing “skeleton”  
   – The hard particles embed in the softer metal matrix and carry a large fraction of the contact stress, reducing matrix deformation.  
   – By supporting high normal loads they limit penetration of abrasives or counter-bodies.

2. Obstruction of plastic flow and abrasion  
   – They act as micro‐“boulders” that interrupt plowing or cutting by abrasive particles.  
   – Their high hardness blocks dislocation motion in the surrounding metal, raising the composite’s overall hardness and yield strength.

3. Reduction of real contact area  
   – A harder, stiffer surface formed by the particles lowers the true area of metal–metal contact, which curbs adhesion and galling.  
   – Fewer adhesion sites translate into lower adhesive wear rates.

4. Crack-deflection and toughening  
   – Hard inclusions can deflect or blunt microcracks that form under cyclic or impact load, slowing their propagation.  
   – This increases resistance to fatigue-driven wear or spalling.

5. Formation of protective tribo-layers  
   – Under sliding, some oxides or in situ reaction products can smear across the surface, creating a low-shear tribofilm.  
   – This film further reduces friction and shields fresh metal from direct abrasion.

6. Three-body abrasion control  
   – Dispersed hard particles help to trap or “lock” loose abrasive debris, preventing them from freely rolling and cutting the surface.  
   – In some systems (e.g. graphite or MoS2 additives) a solid-lubricant effect lowers friction.

Example: A Ni–WC coating deposited by cold spray will have WC particles bearing most of the load, anchoring the harder phase in the Ni ductile matrix. This duality gives very high abrasion and erosion resistance compared with a monolithic Ni coating.

In sum, the hard particles transform the cold-sprayed coating into a composite that is both hard (to resist cutting and indentation) and tough (to resist crack growth), dramatically improving wear life in abrasive, erosive, and sliding applications.

Coating hardness is the single most important coating property governing two‐ and three‐body abrasive wear of ductile substrates.  In very broad terms, the harder the coating the lower the steady‐state wear rate—up to the point where other failure modes (chipping, fatigue, delamination) take over.  Key points:  

1. Archard’s Law and Hardness  
   •  Archard’s abrasive wear model predicts volume loss V ∝ (F·s)/(H·K),  
      – F = normal load, s = sliding distance, H = hardness of the contact surface, K = dimensionless wear coefficient.  
   •  As H↑  ⇒  V↓ (wear volume falls roughly in inverse proportion to hardness, for a given set of abrasives).  

2. Cutting vs. Ploughing Regimes  
   •  If coating hardness is less than or similar to abrasive particle hardness, the particles will cut or gouge -> high wear.  
   •  Once coating hardness exceeds abrasive hardness by ~20–30%, penetration is limited, particles tend to roll/plough shallowly, and the wear rate drops dramatically.  

3. Hardness Ratio (HR)  
   •  HR = Hcoating / Habrasive.  
   •  HR > 1.2–1.3 is usually the “sweet spot” for transitioning from cutting to ploughing‐dominated wear.  
   •  HR ≫ 1 may offer diminishing returns unless the coating also has sufficient toughness.  

4. Coating–Substrate Interaction  
   •  On a ductile substrate, very hard coatings (e.g. > 2000 HV) can cause high stress at the interface under load, leading to crack initiation or delamination.  
   •  Moderate hardness coatings (800–1500 HV) often deliver the best compromise of improved abrasion resistance and adhesion/toughness on steels, cast irons, and nonferrous alloys.  

5. Balancing Hardness with Toughness  
   •  Excessive hardness without fracture resistance can produce microcracks around abrasive contacts; these propagate under cyclic loading and lead to spallation.  
   •  Fine‐grained or nano‐structured coatings (e.g. nanocrystalline TiN or CrN) can push hardness higher while retaining enough toughness.  

6. Practical Guideline  
   •  Select a coating whose hardness exceeds that of the expected abrasives by at least 20–30%.  
   •  Verify via scratch or Rockwell adhesion tests that the substrate/coating pair can support the induced contact stresses.  
   •  Optimize thickness (usually 2–10 µm for PVD hard films, 30–200 µm for thermal sprays) so that the coating can arrest abrasive particle penetration without excessive brittleness.  

Summary  
Coating hardness directly lowers abrasive‐wear rate by resisting particle penetration and reducing micro‐cutting.  However, the best wear life in a ductile substrate comes from a balanced design: a coating hard enough to beat the abrasives yet tough and well‐bonded enough to avoid fracture and delamination under load.

Persistent inter-particle porosity in a cold-sprayed coating acts as a network of stress concentrators and weak interfaces, with the following consequences for ductility:  
1. Reduced load-bearing cross section.  Any pore removes metal from the load path, so for a given applied strain the local stress around pores is higher than in the fully dense regions.  
2. Early microvoid nucleation and coalescence.  Under tensile or bending loads, the pore edges become sites for void growth, link-up, and crack initiation long before the bulk metal matrix reaches its uniform elongation.  
3. Deco­hesion along splat boundaries.  Poorly bonded, porous interfaces open and slide instead of transmitting plastic strain, so the coating fails by inter-particle fracture rather than by homogeneous plastic flow.  

Net effect: a pronounced drop in both uniform and total elongation, a shift from ductile, work-hardening failure to brittle, interface-controlled fracture, and a lower apparent toughness. In practice even a few percent of residual porosity can cut ductility by tens of percent.

In nearly all cold‐spray systems you will find that, once you get past a “critical” first few hundred microns of build, further increases in coating thickness actually drive the overall (bulk) porosity up rather than down.  Two physical effects dominate:

 1. Loss of substrate constraint (“hammering”)  
    •  In the first few hundred microns of spray the substrate beneath the deposit behaves like a rigid anvil, so each new particle impact plastically hammers and closes pores very effectively.  
    •  As the deposit grows, that anvil‐like support recedes farther from the impacting particles.  Subsequent layers see less localized compressive back-pressure, so voids created by particle stacking and oxide entrapment are less efficiently closed.

 2. Cumulative work-hardening and roughness build-up  
    •  Each cold-spray impact work-hardens the nearsurface; once the coating is a millimeter or more thick the deposit itself has become quite hard and springy, so new particles tend to rebound or deform the deposit elastically rather than plastically.  
    •  Surface asperities (peaks and valleys) grow with each pass, trapping unmelted oxides or interparticle gaps that never get fully compacted.

Experimentally you often see something like:

  – At t ≲ 0.5 mm, porosity might be 0.5–1 vol %  
  – By t ≈ 1–2 mm it creeps up to 1–2 vol %  
  – Above 3–4 mm it can reach 3–5 vol % (or higher, depending on alloy and spray conditions)

In short, while the very first layers densify as you build up, once you exceed that substrate-constrained zone the bulk porosity rises steadily with further increases in coating thickness.

Coating thickness turns out to be a surprisingly strong “knob’’ for tuning the abrasive‐wear performance of cold-sprayed metals—and it does so in two competing ways:

1. Low‐thickness regime (≲ 50–150 µm)  
   – Incomplete substrate coverage and high open porosity.  
   – Insufficient work-hardening: each particle flattens on a soft substrate so you get low residual compressive stress and limited strain hardening.  
   – Poor interparticle cohesion/cohesion–substrate adhesion.  
   → These coatings wear through rapidly—substrate begins to contribute to the wear volume almost immediately.

2. Intermediate/thin-to-moderate thickness (≈ 150–400 µm, material‐dependent)  
   – Particles now impact onto a work‐hardened underlayer. Successive impacts produce higher local strains, higher residual compressive stresses, and reduced porosity.  
   – Hardness and elastic modulus rise, so according to Archard’s law (wear volume ∝ load × sliding distance / hardness) the volumetric wear drops.  
   – Coating thickness is now sufficient that the wear process stays entirely within the cold-spray layer, maximizing the benefit of its higher hardness.  
   → You achieve the lowest steady‐state wear rates in this thickness window.

3. High‐thickness regime (≳ 400–800 µm, depending on material and spray parameters)  
   – New layers no longer deform as plastically on top of an already‐hardened deposit.  
   – Interlamellar bonding can degrade, leaving more interfaces and oxide‐laden porosity.  
   – Coating self-stresses can turn tensile near the substrate or within the bulk, promoting crack initiation and interfacial delamination under abrasive loads.  
   – Effective hardness may drop or plateau.  
   → Beyond the “sweet‐spot” thickness you actually start to lose wear resistance: you see more microcracking, spallation, and ultimately higher wear rates.

Take-home rule:  
• In most systems (Cu, Ni-based alloys, steels, Al alloys) you find an optimal cold-sprayed coating thickness of a few hundred micrometers for minimum abrasive-wear.  
• Below that you haven’t built enough strain-hardened, low‐porosity material. Above it you introduce weak interfaces, residual‐stress problems, and rising porosity.  
• In practice you should map your wear rate vs. thickness curve, then spray just enough to sit in that plateau of maximum density, maximum hardness and maximum residual compression.

Residual stresses—both compressive and tensile—are invariably locked into a cold-sprayed coating by the high-velocity impact, plastic deformation and rapid cooling of particles. Those stresses influence virtually every performance attribute of the coating.  Key properties affected include:

1. Adhesion (bond strength)  
   – Tensile residual stresses at the interface promote decohesion and delamination.  
   – Mild compressive stresses can “clamp” the coating to the substrate and raise pull-off or shear strength.

2. Cohesive strength (interparticle bonding)  
   – High compressive stresses improve particle interlocking and bonding, boosting toughness.  
   – Excessive tensile stresses between splats can open microcracks along particle boundaries.

3. Fatigue resistance  
   – Compressive residual stresses retard crack initiation and early propagation, enhancing fatigue life.  
   – Tensile residual stresses accelerate crack nucleation and reduce endurance limits.

4. Wear and abrasion resistance  
   – Compressive stresses increase hardness and reduce micro-fracture under sliding or impact, improving wear life.  
   – Tensile stresses can embrittle the near-surface, promoting flaking and accelerated wear.

5. Corrosion and oxidation resistance  
   – Tensile stresses open up diffusion paths (microcracks, pore networks), accelerating localized corrosion.  
   – Compressive stresses tend to close porosity and slow corrosive ingress, but may also foster stress-corrosion cracking if too high.

6. Fracture toughness and crack-propagation behavior  
   – A compressive surface layer raises the threshold for crack growth under tensile loading.  
   – Residual tensile stresses lower fracture toughness and increase the risk of spalling under thermal or mechanical shock.

7. Dimensional stability and distortion  
   – Unbalanced stresses cause warping, bowing or curling of coated parts (especially thin or flat substrates).  
   – Upon post-heat treatment or in service, stress relaxation can lead to further distortion or loss of critical tolerances.

8. Microstructure, porosity and density  
   – Work-hardening and stress fields affect recrystallization during any subsequent heat treatment, altering grain size and hardness.  
   – Stresses influence closing or opening of pores and microcracks, thus changing effective density and permeability.

9. Thermal fatigue and high-temperature performance  
   – Mismatch in thermal expansion between substrate and coating, combined with locked-in stresses, drives microcracking under cyclic heating.  
   – High residual tensile stresses exacerbate creep and spallation at elevated service temperatures.

10. Functional properties (e.g. electrical or thermal conductivity)  
    – Crack networks and delamination caused by tensile stresses can interrupt conductive pathways.  
    – Compressive stresses that close porosity may improve conductivity, but excessive work-hardening may degrade it.

In practice you balance cold-spraying parameters (particle velocity, temperature, impact angle) and, if needed, apply post-deposition heat treatments or peening to tailor the residual stress state for optimal adhesion, fatigue life, wear and corrosion performance.

Incorporating hard particles or whiskers (e.g. carbides, oxides, nitrides or ceramic platelets) into a ductile metal matrix typically produces the following tribological effects:

1. Higher hardness and load‐bearing capacity  
   – Hard phases carry a disproportionate share of the normal load, reduce real contact area, and suppress plastic flow (plowing) in the metal.  
   – Result: markedly lower adhesive and severe‐plasticity wear rates.

2. Altered friction behavior  
   – In some systems (e.g. hard particles acting as micro-bearings or forming a stable tribofilm), the coefficient of friction can decrease.  
   – In others, surface roughness and particle protrusion can raise friction, especially under boundary lubrication.

3. Improved scuffing and galling resistance  
   – The hard phases interrupt metal-to-metal junction growth, limiting adhesive junctions, seizure and transfer film formation.

4. Generation of third‐body abrasives (if particles detach)  
   – Excessive volume fraction or poor interfacial bonding can lead to particle pull-out and three-body abrasion, which raises wear and friction.  
   – There is therefore an optimum reinforcement content, size and shape to balance toughness and wear resistance.

5. Enhanced tribofilm stability  
   – Some ceramics help stabilize oxide‐ or complex‐salt films under sliding, further reducing wear in oxidizing or lubricated environments.

In practice, you tune reinforcement type, size, morphology and volume fraction to maximize wear resistance while avoiding embrittlement or abrasive particle damage.

In almost every cold‐sprayed Al–alloy system that’s been studied, the in situ addition of a hard ceramic phase (Al2O3, SiC, TiC, B4C, etc.) drives the coating hardness up—often very significantly.  The key points are:

1. Hardness versus volume fraction  
   • 0 vol.% ceramic (pure Al or Al-alloy) → ~50–80 HV  
   • 5–10 vol.% ceramic → ~100–150 HV (≈30–100 % increase)  
   • 15–30 vol.% ceramic → 150–250 HV (sometimes 2–3× the unreinforced alloy)  

2. Why it gets harder  
   • Dispersion strengthening (Orowan mechanism): the sub-micron ceramics block and bow dislocations.  
   • Load sharing: stiff particles carry a larger fraction of the applied stress.  
   • Microstructure refinement: the very high strain rates around the particles during particle–substrate/substrate–substrate impacts fragment grains and stabilize fine subgrains.  

3. Practical limits  
   • Above ≈25–30 vol.% reinforcement you begin to see diminished deposition efficiency, poorer particle bonding and the onset of brittle cracking or higher porosity.  
   • Optimum hardness versus cohesion usually occurs in the 10–20 vol.% range.  

Bottom line: ceramic additions almost always boost the microhardness of cold‐sprayed Al‐alloy coatings, with the magnitude of the rise scaling (up to a point) with the volume fraction and fineness of the hard phase.

Compared with conventionally cast, wrought or powder‐metallurgy “bulk” metals, cold‐sprayed deposits and the substrates they are built on exhibit a number of distinctive microstructural and hardness features arising from the severe, high‐strain‐rate plastic deformation at particle impact:

1. Particle-level deformation and bonding  
   • Particles impact at 300–1 200 m/s and deform adiabatically, inducing shear instabilities at interfaces.  
   • Oxide layers are fractured and extruded, exposing fresh metal for metallurgical bonding without melting.  

2. Grain refinement and dislocation structures  
   • Impact zones undergo ultrahigh strain rates (10³–10⁶ s⁻¹), generating dislocation densities up to 10¹⁴–10¹⁵ m⁻².  
   • Localized adiabatic shear can drive dynamic recrystallization forming ultrafine or even nanocrystalline grains (100–500 nm) in the interface “white zones.”  
   • Away from interfaces the original feedstock grains are plastically elongated but retain a sub‐micron to micron size, producing a heterogeneous, bimodal grain‐size distribution.  

3. Residual stresses and substrate peening  
   • Each impact also plastically deforms the substrate surface, inducing compressive residual stresses in a “shot-peened” layer up to tens of microns deep.  
   • This peening effect further refines grains and raises surface hardness of the substrate beneath the coating.  

4. Hardness increases vs. bulk  
   • The combined effects of grain refinement (Hall–Petch strengthening) and very high dislocation densities typically raise hardness by 10–50% over annealed or even some heat‐treated bulk alloys.  
     – Example: Cold‐sprayed Cu coatings often measure 130–180 HV versus ~60 HV in annealed bulk copper.  
     – Al-based deposits can reach 100–140 HV compared to 70–100 HV in as-cast or annealed Al alloys.  
   • Substrate surface hardness likewise increases by 20–40% in the near-surface peened layer.  

5. Anisotropy and inhomogeneity  
   • Because deformation is directional, deposits can show anisotropic mechanical properties (parallel vs. perpendicular to spray direction).  
   • Small residual porosity or entrapped oxide films at splat boundaries can be stress concentrators, so hardness gains sometimes trade off against toughness or fatigue performance.  

Summary: Cold spray imparts very high plastic strain to both incoming particles and the immediate substrate surface without melting. The result is a strongly work-hardened, grain-refined, compressively stressed surface region whose hardness significantly exceeds that of conventional bulk metallurgy, albeit with a heterogeneous microstructure and potential anisotropies at the particle–particle interfaces.

Increasing the volume (or weight) fraction of hard nanoparticles in a polymer coating almost always raises its surface hardness—up to a point—by the following mechanisms:

1. Load-bearing inclusions  
   • Rigid particles (e.g. SiO₂, Al₂O₃, TiO₂, carbides) carry a share of the applied load and shield the softer polymer from indentation.  
   • In a simple rule-of-mixtures view, Hcomposite ≈ Hmatrix·(1–φ) + Hparticle·φ, so at low φ the increase is nearly linear.

2. Polymer chain immobilization  
   • Nanoparticles with high surface area restrict the mobility of nearby polymer chains, effectively raising the local crosslink density or glass-transition temperature and thus the hardness.

3. Percolation and particle networks  
   • Above a critical φ (often 10–20 vol %), particles begin to touch or form a semi-continuous network that can carry shear loads very efficiently, giving a steeper rise in modulus and hardness.

4. Diminishing returns and agglomeration  
   • Beyond an optimum loading (often 15–30 vol %, depending on particle size, surface treatment and mixing method) particles start to agglomerate.  
   • Agglomerates act as stress concentrators and create interfacial voids, which reduce effective load transfer and can actually lower hardness or embrittle the coating.

Typical hardness-versus-loading trends  
• 0 – 5 vol %: gradual, roughly linear improvement  
• 5 – 15 vol %: stronger gain, approach percolation  
• > 15 – 30 vol %: plateau or slight drop unless very well dispersed and surface-functionalized  

Key practical points  
– Ensuring good dispersion (e.g. by surface-treating nanoparticles or using high-shear mixing) pushes the plateau out to higher φ.  
– Too high filler content also raises viscosity, complicates application and can introduce defects.  

Bottom line: you get harder coatings by adding nanoparticles, but only up to the loading level where dispersion and matrix continuity can be maintained. Beyond that the hardness gain levels off or reverses.

Process‐gas temperature (T₀) is one of the primary “knobs” in cold spray for tuning particle impact energy, plastic deformation and hence final coating hardness.  In essence, raising T₀ tends to raise particle velocity and to preheat (and soften) the feedstock, both of which increase the severity of impact‐induced work‐hardening and grain‐refinement.  The trend and mechanisms can be summarized as follows:

1. Particle velocity and impact energy  
   – For a fixed pressure ratio, Vparticle ≃√[2·Cp·T₀·(1–(Pback/P0)^((γ–1)/γ))].  Raising T₀ both increases the maximum achievable Mach number and, because of the higher stagnation temperature, increases Vparticle.  
   – Higher Vparticle → higher strain rates at impact → more adiabatic shear, greater plastic deformation, more dislocation generation and finer subgrains → higher hardness.

2. Particle preheat and yield reduction  
   – Particles entering the supersonic jet at elevated temperature have lower yield strength, so they deform more readily and more uniformly upon impact.  This promotes intimate bonding, reduces porosity and activates more work‐hardening.

3. Microstructural refinement  
   – The combination of higher strain rates and repeated severe deformation at the interface refines grains (often into nano- or ultrafine regimes) and traps a high density of dislocations.  Both effects stiffen the lattice and raise microhardness.

4. Residual stress and thermal effects  
   – Up to an optimal T₀, residual compressive stresses add to hardness.  Beyond that, you may see partial recovery or even local oxidation (especially for Ti or Al alloys), which can relax strains and slightly soften or embrittle the deposit.

5. Empirical observations  
   – Typical metal systems (Cu, Al, Ni, Ti) show a steady increase in microhardness as T₀ is raised from ~300 °C to ~600 – 800 °C, often plateauing or even dropping if T₀ exceeds the point at which thermal softening or oxidation outweighs work‐hardening.

In practical terms, you tune T₀ to maximize impact‐induced hardening without triggering undesirable thermal recovery or surface oxidation.

Inclusion of a low-CTE (coefficient of thermal expansion) particulate phase (for example, SiC, Al₂O₃, WC, glass beads, etc.) in an otherwise conventional solder or braze alloy turns the filler into a CTE-tailored composite.  The two most important macroscopic consequences are:

  1.  Reduction in global CTE mismatch.  By “diluting” the metal’s relatively high CTE with a low-expansion ceramic, the overall composite CTE moves closer to that of typical electronic substrates (e.g. Cu, Al₂O₃, Si) or heat-sink materials.  On cooling from the bonding temperature this directly cuts the net shrinkage difference at the interface, so the magnitude of residual tensile or shear stresses in the joint is reduced.  Lower residual stress means less warpage, fewer interface cracks, and improved thermal‐cycling (fatigue) reliability.

  2.  Changes in joint mechanical properties.  
     – Young’s modulus (stiffness), yield strength and hardness of the filler rise because load is shared between the ductile matrix and stiff, strong particles.  
     – Creep resistance and fatigue life are improved:  
       • Particles act as load-bearing phases under constant stress and also serve as crack‐deflection/bridging sites in cyclic loading.  
       • The cyclic stress amplitude in the ductile matrix is cut because part of the thermal or mechanical strain is carried elastically by the particles.  
     – Ductility and toughness inevitably drop as particle volume fraction grows: too many hard inclusions make the joint brittle and can even interrupt wetting or produce voids around poorly bonded particles.  

At the microscopic level you actually generate a residual stress field around each inclusion because of the local CTE mismatch between particle and surrounding solder.  Typically a compressive “ring” develops in the metal matrix around each stiff particle (and a small tensile zone in the particle itself).  In moderation this can be helpful, since those compressive stresses oppose growing cracks.  If the particle–matrix interface is weak, however, you can instead nucleate microcracks there under load.

Designing a low-CTE composite filler thus boils down to picking the right:
  • Particle type (CTE, elastic modulus, thermal conductivity, chemistry),  
  • Size, shape and surface treatment (to promote good wetting/bonding),  
  • Volume fraction (to balance CTE tailoring and stress relief against loss of ductility).

When done properly you get a joint that  
  – warps and cracks far less on cooldown,  
  – endures more thermal–mechanical cycles,  
  – carries higher shear/tensile loads,  
  – but still retains enough plasticity to avoid catastrophic brittle failure.

Grain‐size strengthening in copper (and most crystalline metals) is dominated by the Hall–Petch effect: as the average grain diameter d falls, hardness H (and yield stress σy) rises roughly in proportion to d–½.  

  
1.  Hall–Petch law  
   σy = σ0  +  k·d–½  
   H   ≃ C·σy   ⇒   H = H0  +  kH·d–½  
   – σ0 (or H0) is the lattice friction (base strength of a single crystal).  
   – k (or kH) is the Hall–Petch coefficient (how strongly grain boundaries block dislocations).  

2.  Mechanism  
   – Grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion.  
   – Smaller grains = more boundaries per unit volume = more obstacles = higher stress (and hardness) required to propagate plastic flow.  

3.  Typical values for copper  
   – σ0 ≈ 20–30 MPa,   k ≈ 0.10–0.15 MPa·m½  
   – H0 ≈ 40–50 HV,   kH ≈ 5–10 HV·μm½  
   Thus:  
   • 100 μm grains → H ≃ 40 HV + 10·(100)⁻½ ≃ 40 + 1 = ≃41 HV  
   • 1 μm grains   → H ≃ 40 HV + 10·(1)⁻½   ≃ 40 + 10 = 50 HV  
   • 0.1 μm grains → H ≃ 40 + 10·(0.1)⁻½ = 40 + 31 ≃ 71 HV  

4.  Limits and deviations  
   – At ultra‐fine (nanocrystalline) sizes (< 20 nm) inverse Hall–Petch can appear: grain–boundary sliding or diffusion weaken the metal.  
   – Alloying and precipitation (e.g. in brass or age‐hardening Al alloys) superimpose additional strengthening.  

5.  Generalization to other metals  
   – The same d–½ scaling applies in steels, Ni‐based alloys, Al, Ti, etc., but σ0 and k vary with crystal structure, stacking‐fault energy, alloy content.  
   – Steels: k ≃ 0.6 MPa·m½, σ0 ≃ 150 MPa; Al alloys: k ≃ 0.07 MPa·m½, σ0 ≃ 30 MPa.  

Summary  
Reducing grain size increases hardness because more grain boundaries block dislocation motion.  Strictly, H(d)=H0 + kH·d–½ until very fine grains where other mechanisms (boundary sliding, diffusion) cause deviation.

Cold spray coatings almost invariably come out harder than their bulk‐annealed counterparts, with very little change in stiffness (elastic modulus).  The key reasons are

1. Severe plastic deformation and grain refinement  
   • At the particle–substrate interface and at particle–particle boundaries, adiabatic shear and high-strain-rate deformation drive dynamic recrystallization and build up very high dislocation densities.  
   • Typical grain sizes in the cold‐sprayed “splat” microstructure fall into the submicron or even nanocrystalline regime, so hardness goes up by 20–100 % over bulk.  For example, Al coatings often rise from ~25 HV (annealed bulk) to 60–100 HV, and Ni alloys can climb from ~150 HV to 300 HV or more.  

2. Elastic modulus remains near the bulk value  
   • Young’s modulus is a function of bonding stiffness and crystal structure, and it is relatively insensitive to microstructural features like dislocation density.  
   • In a fully dense spray deposit, E typically stays within 5 % of the bulk modulus.  Measured deviations (± 10 %) are almost always traced to residual porosity or interfacial pores, which act as compliance “soft spots.”  

3. Porosity and residual stress  
   • Even well‐optimized cold spray systems can leave 1–5 vol % closed porosity, which pulls the effective E down by roughly (1 − P), where P is the porosity fraction.  
   • Compressive residual stresses from peening can alter hardness readings (often boosting the apparent hardness) but have only a second-order effect on macroscopic elastic modulus.  

In practice you’ll see cold‐sprayed coatings that are markedly harder than bulk (thanks to work‐hardening/grain refinement) while their stiffness stays essentially the same as the parent metal, apart from small reductions due to porosity.

Softer metals and harder cold‐sprayed coatings simply live in two different tribological regimes.  The key lies in their relative hardness, real contact pressures and how the junctions between asperities behave under load:

1. Adhesive wear on soft substrates  
   • Low hardness ⇒ large real contact area at asperity tips  
   • Under sliding, asperities plastically deform, cold-weld to the counterface, then shear off  
   • Material transfer (“galling”) is easy because the substrate yields before fracturing  
   • Result: flat patches of material transfer, smearing and high adhesive wear rates  

2. Abrasive wear on hard coatings  
   • High hardness ⇒ small real contact area and very high local stresses  
   • Asperities on one surface (or hard debris) plow or cut into the opposing surface rather than weld  
   • Cold-sprayed coatings often contain hard phases or oxides that act as self-generated abrasives  
   • Fracture of brittle edges or micro-chipping produces abrasive third bodies  
   • Result: grooves, scratches and two- or three-body abrasion dominate  

In short, soft substrates deform and stick (adhesive wear) while hard, stiff coatings resist welding and instead cut or abrade their counterpart (abrasive wear).

Key microstructural factors in cold‐sprayed metal coatings that drive their superior wear resistance are:  

1. Grain refinement and subgrain formation  
   • Severe plastic deformation (“pancaking”) of high‐velocity particles generates ultrafine‐ to nano‐scale grains, especially at particle boundaries.  
   • Hall–Petch strengthening from the high density of grain and subgrain boundaries impedes dislocation motion.  

2. Very high dislocation density and work hardening  
   • Impact‐driven strain locking produces a network of tangled dislocations and low‐angle boundaries within particles.  
   • The resulting local hardening raises yield strength and surface hardness, reducing material removal under load.  

3. Dense, low‐porosity lamellar architecture  
   • Well‐bonded, tightly packed “splats” eliminate open pores and weak interfaces, enabling uniform load transfer across the coating.  
   • Remaining nanoscale interparticle voids are small enough to blunt crack initiation and hinder wear‐induced crack coalescence.  

4. Residual compressive stresses  
   • Plastic deformation and thermal mismatch during deposition impart compressive stresses, which close microcracks and raise resistance to fatigue‐assisted wear.  

5. Clean metallurgical bonding with minimal oxides  
   • Cold spray avoids bulk melting so interparticle oxides are fragmented into fine dispersoids rather than thick brittle films.  
   • These nano‐oxides can pin dislocations and crack tips, acting as dispersion strengthening without embrittlement.  

6. Textured, anisotropic hard zones  
   • Impact‐aligned crystallographic textures and elongated “pancake” zones create directional hardness gradients that deflect or blunt abrasive particles.  

Together, these features yield a coating with higher hardness, tougher grain-boundary networks, and suppressed crack growth—all of which translate into markedly improved abrasive, adhesive, and erosive wear resistance versus the uncoated substrate.

The single biggest hardening “knob” in cold‐sprayed metals is the ultrafine‐grained, high‐dislocation‐density substructure you get from the particle’s severe plastic deformation on impact.  In practice that means:  

 • Grain‐boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch):  you produce submicron or even nanocrystalline grains/subgrains so that the network of grain boundaries blocks dislocation glide.  
 • Dislocation‐density strengthening:  the impacts inject and tangle huge numbers of dislocations into the particles, further impeding slip.  

Of the two, the proliferation of new grain and subgrain boundaries (i.e. grain‐refinement/Hall–Petch strengthening) is normally the dominant contributor to the increased hardness.

Post‐heat treatment (annealing or aging) improves the ductility of cold-sprayed deposits by two main, interrelated mechanisms:

1. Recovery/Recrystallization and Grain Growth  
   – The as‐sprayed microstructure is heavily work-hardened, with very high dislocation densities and ultrafine, highly strained subgrains along particle boundaries.  A moderate‐temperature anneal allows these dislocations to annihilate (recovery) or reorganize into new, low‐energy grain boundaries (recrystallization), producing more equiaxed, strain-free grains.  As a result the hardness and yield strength decrease, while uniform elongation and toughness increase.  

2. Interface Healing and Diffusional Bonding  
   – At elevated temperatures, local diffusion across particle–particle interfaces and residual porosity can close microvoids, strengthen interparticle bonds, and reduce stress concentrations.  In some systems (e.g. Al, Cu) short‐time aging also precipitates fine second phases that may further toughen the matrix via Orowan looping.

Limitations and trade-offs you must keep in mind:

• Strength–Ductility Trade-off  
  – As you anneal out dislocations and coarsen grains, you inevitably lose some of the as-sprayed strength and hardness.  Over-annealing risks grain growth so extensive that both strength and fatigue resistance suffer.  

• Control of Temperature and Atmosphere  
  – High temperatures (or long hold times) can promote oxidation, decarburization, or formation of brittle intermetallics—especially in Ti, Ni alloys or steel coatings.  A controlled (inert or reducing) atmosphere is often required.  

• Substrate Compatibility  
  – If you’re heating a coated component, the substrate may have a very different coefficient of thermal expansion (CTE) or phase‐transformation temperature.  Thermal mismatch can induce warping, delamination or cracking during heating/cooling.  

• Incomplete Porosity Elimination  
  – Although heat treatment closes many microvoids, deep or interconnected porosity is often only partially healed.  Full densification may still require post-spray HIP (hot isostatic pressing).  

• Process Economics and Part Size  
  – Thick deposits require long soaks for uniform temperature, and large parts may need expensive furnaces or fixtures.  There’s a practical limit to how much heat treatment can cost-effectively improve ductility before alternate deposition or consolidation methods are preferable.

In practice, successful post-spray heat treatments are a balance: choose a temperature/time that maximizes recovery and interface healing without excessive grain growth, oxidation or detrimental phase changes, and be prepared to pair annealing with mechanical or HIP steps if ultimate densification and toughness are required.

In cold‐sprayed Al–ceramic composite coatings the embedded ceramic size exerts a first‐order control on steady‐state friction by (a) setting surface topography, (b) dictating the formation and stability of the transfer/tribo‐film, and (c) governing the prevailing wear mode (micro-ploughing vs. three‐body abrasion).  In broad terms you will observe:

1.  Smaller particles (submicron down to 50–200 nm)  
    •  Embed more uniformly in the Al matrix, filling interstices and yielding a smoother, denser surface.  
    •  Promote a more continuous, conformal transfer film of soft Al during sliding, which lowers the coefficient of friction (µₛₛ).  
    •  Suppress three‐body abrasive action because individual particles are too small to act as hard ploughing bodies.  
    Typical µₛₛ drop: from ~0.4–0.5 (micro‐SiC) down to ~0.3–0.35 for nanoceramics.

2.  Intermediate particles (0.5–5 µm)  
    •  Produce a mixed topography—some protruding grains generate mild abrasion, but there is still enough matrix cohesion for a semi‐stable tribo‐film.  
    •  Yield intermediate µₛₛ values (≈0.35–0.45), depending on volume fraction and particle distribution.

3.  Coarser particles (>5 µm)  
    •  Protrude from the Al matrix, become third‐body abrasives, and increase mechanical interlocking.  
    •  Generate a rougher running surface and tend to fracture out, producing hard debris that drives µₛₛ upward, often into the 0.45–0.6 range.  

Caveat:   
–  At very high loadings or if nanoparticles agglomerate, you can unintentionally reintroduce porosity/roughness, which may boost µₛₛ again.  
–  Optimum friction and wear resistance often occur in the submicron-to‐low‐micron regime where you balance surface smoothness, transfer‐film integrity, and sufficient hardness.

Bottom line:  
As you decrease the ceramic particle size (down into the nanometric range), you generally lower the steady‐state friction coefficient of cold‐sprayed Al–ceramic coatings—provided you avoid severe nanoparticle agglomeration and maintain good particle–matrix bonding.

Powder heat-treatment—whether simple annealing, solution‐treatment or artificial aging—serves to tailor the feedstock’s grain size, precipitate state and dislocation density, and in so doing has a very direct influence on the microhardness of the final cold-sprayed coating.  The key effects can be summarized as follows:

1.  Annealing (above recrystallization T)  
    ­– dissolves work-hardening dislocations, coarsens grains  
    ­– powder hardness drops (e.g. Al alloys from 110 HV to 50–70 HV)  
    ­– lower stored energy → less severe work-hardening and dislocation accumulation in the deposit  
    ­– as-sprayed coating hardness typically 5–15 % below that from as-received powder  

2.  Solution treatment + quench (T4 in Al alloys)  
    ­– dissolves strengthening precipitates, produces a supersaturated, low‐hardness but very ductile powder (≈70–90 HV in 6xxx/7xxx Al)  
    ­– during impact the combination of adiabatic shear bands, high strain rate and local heating stimulates dynamic precipitation and ultrafine grain formation  
    ­– yields coatings of intermediate as-sprayed hardness (≈100–130 HV) with good cohesion and density  
    ­– subsequent artificial aging (“in situ” or post-spray) drives hardness up into the  T6 range (≈150–180 HV)  

3.  Artificially aged powders (T6 in Al alloys, age-hardened Ni superalloys, etc.)  
    ­– feedstock is already hard and contains a high density of fine precipitates (→ powder ~140–180 HV)  
    ­– higher powder hardness normally gives a higher as-sprayed coating hardness (≈150–200 HV)  
    ­– but powder brittleness lowers deposition efficiency, can promote porosity or interparticle cracks  

General trends across most systems (Al, Cu, Ti, Ni alloys and some HEAs) are therefore:  
•  The harder and more heavily precipitated the feedstock powder, the higher the as-sprayed microhardness—but also the lower the ductility and deposition efficiency.  
•  The softer or more annealed the feedstock, the lower the as-sprayed hardness, but the better the interparticle bonding and coating density.  
•  Solution‐treated powders strike a compromise: they start soft for good build-up, then undergo dynamic recrystallization and precipitation during impact, giving coatings whose microhardness can be raised further by a subsequent aging step.  

By choosing the appropriate powder-treatment recipe you thus trade off “as-sprayed” hardness against deposition efficiency, porosity and post-spray heat-treatment requirements.

Solid‐state cold‐spray deposits almost invariably carry a net compressive residual stress, whereas conventional (molten) thermal‐spray coatings usually end up with net tensile stresses.  The reasons are:

1. Cold spray  
  – Particles impact at high velocity but at well below their melting point.  
  – Severe plastic deformation of the coating and substrate at each impact acts like a continuous peening process.  
  – The result is a layer in a state of locked‐in compressive stress (typically a few 10^2 MPa compressive).

2. Thermal spray (e.g. plasma, HVOF, flame)  
  – Particles solidify on the substrate from the melt, and large temperature gradients develop.  
  – As the coating cools, it contracts against a relatively “cold” substrate, generating tensile stresses.  
  – Typical net residuals are on the order of 10^2 MPa in tension.

In practice you’ll see, for example:  
• Cold spray: –100 MPa to –500 MPa (compressive)  
• Thermal spray: +100 MPa to +300 MPa (tensile)

The influence of intermetallics on the hardness of cold-sprayed coatings can be boiled down to three main factors: 1) the intrinsic hardness of the phase, 2) its morphology/distribution at the particle–substrate interface, and 3) the nature of the interface (coherent vs. incoherent).  

1. Intrinsic hardness of the intermetallic  
   • Different IMCs have very different bond characters and yield strengths.  For example, in Ni-based systems:  
     – Ni₃Al (L1₂) typically exhibits hardness in the range of 3–5 GPa.  
     – NiAl (B2) is harder, ≈5–7 GPa.  
     – NiAl₃ can reach 8–9 GPa.  
   • In Al-based systems:  
     – Al₂Cu (θ) ≈2 GPa, whereas Al₃Ti or TiAl₃ will be in the 6–8 GPa range.  

2. Morphology and distribution  
   • Continuous intermetallic layers at the interface give very high local hardness but can act as crack‐initiators under load, sometimes reducing effective toughness.  
   • Discrete, nano‐ to submicron‐sized intermetallic precipitates dispersed in an otherwise ductile matrix produce Orowan‐type strengthening without forming a grossly brittle film. This often yields the best combination of high hardness and retained fracture resistance.  

3. Interface coherency and strain fields  
   • Coherent or semi‐coherent precipitates generate strong lattice‐strain fields that impede dislocation motion more effectively than incoherent inclusions of the same chemistry.  
   • Incoherent, plate‐like or faceted IMCs still raise hardness by acting as hard obstacles, but they do not benefit from the additional coherency stress‐field strengthening.  

Net effect on the coating’s hardness curve  
   – Low or no intermetallic formation ⇒ hardness dominated by cold‐work and grain-refinement (typically 1–2 GPa for Al alloys, 2–4 GPa for Cu/Ni).  
   – Formation of relatively soft IMCs (e.g. Al₂Cu) ⇒ modest hardness bump (to ~2–3 GPa).  
   – Formation of harder IMCs (TiAl₃, NiAl, etc.), especially as fine dispersions ⇒ large hardness increases (5–8 GPa or more), at the expense of some embrittlement if present as continuous films.  

In practice, cold‐sprayed systems that form controlled, finely dispersed intermetallics at the particle/substrate junction tend to show the greatest hardness improvements without catastrophic brittleness.

Post‐spray heat treatment (HT) is widely used to turn the mechanically bonded, high-strain, highly defective microstructure of a cold-sprayed coating into a more fully metallurgically bonded, consolidated deposit with improved mechanical performance.  The key mechanisms by which HT improves inter-particle bonding and properties are:

1. Recovery and Recrystallization  
   • At typical HT temperatures (≈0.3–0.6 Tm of the spray metal), the very high dislocation density and subgrain structure produced by the supersonic impact begin to recover.  
   • Dislocations annihilate and rearrange, subgrains coalesce, and new, strain‐free grains nucleate and grow at the particle interfaces.  
   • This eliminates microcracks and voids at the former particle boundaries and restores a contiguous metal matrix.

2. Enhanced Atomic Diffusion (“Sintering-like” Neck Growth)  
   • Even well below melting, diffusion of metal atoms across intimate contact points grows and rounds the “necks” between particles.  
   • Oxide remnants and mechanically mixed layers at the interface become thinner or discontinuous, allowing metallic bonding to span larger areas.  
   • Pores shrink as atoms migrate into the voids, reducing overall porosity.

3. Stress Relief and Residual‐Stress Redistribution  
   • The extreme cold‐work of spraying leaves large residual compressive and tensile stress fields around particle boundaries.  
   • HT partially relaxes these stresses, lowering the risk of crack initiation under load or during subsequent thermal cycling.

4. Precipitation and Phase Transformations (in heat-treatable alloys)  
   • In Al‐, Ni‐ or Ti‐based alloys, solutionizing plus aging can re‐dissolve mechanically mixed or fragmented intermetallic phases and then re‐precipitate them in a fine, controlled dispersion.  
   • This adds a second strengthening mechanism on top of the densification and grain refinement.

Net Effects on Mechanical Properties  
– Tensile and Yield Strength: Often increases by 10–30 %, as inter‐particle bonds go from predominantly mechanical locks to true metallurgical bonds.  
– Ductility and Toughness: Can double or more, owing to elimination of stress‐concentrating defects at the interfaces.  
– Fatigue Life: May improve by an order of magnitude because crack‐nucleation sites (pores and microcracks) are healed or blunted.  
– Hardness: May drop slightly in work-hardened alloys (due to recovery) but can be recovered or surpassed if precipitation strengthening is applied.  

In practice, the exact HT schedule (temperature, hold time, cooling rate) is tuned to the alloy system and desired balance of strength vs. ductility.

Typical post‐spray vacuum anneals carried out at or above the alloy’s recrystallization temperature have two almost universal effects on a cold- or warm-sprayed metallic coating:

 1. Porosity drops (densification)  
    – At or above Trec substantial atomic diffusion and creep at particle–particle interfaces “heal” pores and micro-cracks.  
    – Neck growth between splats increases contact area and closes voids.  
    – Reported porosity reductions range from roughly 20–80 percent (absolute) depending on alloy, temperature, and soak time.  

 2. Hardness falls (annealing softening)  
    – The heavy work-hardening imparted by the high‐velocity impact is largely erased by recrystallization and grain coarsening.  
    – Dislocation density collapses, residual stresses relax, and any supersaturated precipitates coarsen or dissolve.  
    – Typical Vickers‐hardness drops of 20–60 percent are common unless a separate age or precipitation step is applied afterward.  

In short, vacuum heat treatment above the recrystallization point densifies the coating but markedly softens it by removing the cold-spray–induced defects that gave the as-sprayed deposit its high hardness.

Post‐deposition (i.e. post‐spray) heat treatments on cold‐sprayed metals are almost universally applied to improve interparticle bonding and relieve residual stress.  The principal effects on mechanical properties and porosity are:

1. Porosity Reduction and Densification  
   • Diffusion and localized plastic flow at particle boundaries close up micro‐voids.  
   • Porosity typically falls by 30–70 % depending on temperature, time and alloy (e.g. from ~5 vol.% to <2 vol.% in cold‐sprayed Al alloys after 300–400 °C/1 h).  
   • Oxide films and trapped gases at splat interfaces are disrupted and partially dissolved, enhancing interparticle contact area.

2. Bond Strength and Cohesion  
   • Metallurgical bonding replaces purely mechanical interlocking. Grain‐boundary and bulk diffusion weld adjacent particles together.  
   • Lap‐shear strength and tensile bond strength can increase by 20–100 % relative to the as‐sprayed condition.  
   • Fracture mode shifts from inter‐particle decohesion to particle or substrate fracture.

3. Hardness, Yield and Ultimate Tensile Strength (UTS)  
   • Low‐temperature ageing treatments (near glass‐transition or solvus) can precipitate or coarsen strengthening phases (e.g. Al–Si, Ni base), raising hardness and UTS by 5–20 %.  
   • At higher annealing temperatures, recovery and recrystallization soften the deposit: hardness and yield strength fall, but ductility rises.  
   • The balance of hardening vs. softening depends on alloy chemistry, prior work‐hardening (impact‐induced), and the chosen thermal profile.

4. Ductility and Toughness  
   • As‐sprayed deposits often fracture in a brittle, inter‐particle fashion. Post‐spray heat treatment restores plasticity by healing micro‐cracks and reducing stress concentrators.  
   • Elongation to failure can double or triple (e.g. from <5 % to ~10–15 % in cold‐sprayed Ti and Al alloys after 500–600 °C/1 h).

5. Residual Stress Relief  
   • Thermal cycles allow dislocation rearrangement and annihilation.  
   • Compressive or tensile stresses imparted by particle impact partially relax, reducing risk of crack initiation under fatigue or bending.

6. Microstructural Evolution  
   • Recrystallization at higher temperatures (>0.4–0.5 Tₘelt) erases the nanocrystalline layers imparted by cold spray, potentially coarsening grains.  
   • Sub‐grain coalescence can improve toughness but may lower strength.  
   • In alloys with metastable phases (e.g. Ni‐based superalloys), controlled ageing precipitates strengthening γ′ or carbides at interfaces, improving high‐temperature performance.

Key practical considerations:  
– Too low a temperature or too short a soak gives incomplete bonding.  
– Too high or too long a treatment can over‐anneal the deposit, sacrificing strength and hardness.  
– Optimal heat‐treatment windows are alloy-specific (e.g. 300–400 °C for Al, 500–600 °C for Ti alloys, 600–750 °C for stainless steels, and dedicated ageing cycles for Ni-alloys).

In summary, post‐deposition heat treatment transforms a mechanically interlocked, relatively porous cold spray deposit into a more fully bonded, less porous, and mechanically robust coating—but care must be taken to tailor the cycle to each alloy system to avoid undesirable grain growth or over‐softening.

Powder‐particle flattening is at the heart of wear resistance in cold-sprayed coatings because it directly controls coating density, bonding strength, microstructure and hardness.  In brief, the more effectively a particle “pancakes” on impact, the tougher and more wear-resistant the resulting coating:

1. Bonding and densification  
   – Upon impact at supersonic speeds the powder particle undergoes severe plastic deformation (“flattening” or splatting).  This creates a very large, intimate contact area with the substrate or prior splat, jetting off surface oxides and contaminants and promoting metallic (sometimes metallurgical) bonding.  
   – Better bonding and fewer unfilled voids mean fewer sites for crack initiation and material removal under abrasive or adhesive wear.

2. Strain hardening and grain refinement  
   – The extreme shear strains in the flattening process generate very high dislocation densities and often grain‐refined zones at or near the splat interface.  These work-hardened regions locally elevate hardness and yield strength, directly impeding plowing or micro-cutting wear mechanisms.

3. Reduced porosity and flaw population  
   – Well-flattened splats overlap and seal against one another, reducing lamellar voids and microcracks.  Lower porosity translates into higher load‐bearing cross-section and fewer stress raisers under sliding or impact.

4. Mechanical interlocking and load transfer  
   – Thin, wide “pancake” splats interlock like tiles.  This interlamellar anchoring helps distribute applied loads more evenly through the coating thickness rather than concentrating stress at isolated points, thereby slowing wear progression.

5. Surface morphology and friction  
   – A dense, well-flattened splat structure typically yields a smoother as-sprayed surface, which lowers real contact area with abrasives or counterfaces.  Less surface roughness often means reduced coefficient of friction and diminished third-body wear.

In contrast, under-flattened particles (due to insufficient impact velocity, too coarse a powder, or improper process parameters) leave a porous, weakly bonded lamellar structure rife with interfacial defects. Those coatings wear away rapidly because cracks easily nucleate at unbonded interfaces and pores, and the lower hardness offers little resistance to cutting or deformation. Thus controlling the degree of powder-particle flattening is central to optimizing the wear resistance of cold-sprayed coatings.

Nanocrystalline coatings (grain sizes in the 10–100 nm range) routinely out‐perform the same materials made with conventional (micron-scale) grains in almost every key mechanical metric.  The principal advantages stem from the Hall–Petch effect (grain-boundary strengthening), extreme microstructural refinement (low porosity, high density) and the deposition routes (e.g. PVD, HVOF, cold spray) that tend to leave compressive residual stresses and strong adhesion.  In practice you observe:  

1. Very high hardness and yield strength  
   – Grain-boundary density rises as d→10 nm, impeding dislocation motion; hardness typically doubles (or more) relative to coarse‐grained coatings.  
   – Yield (and ultimate) strength scale roughly as σy ∼ d⁻½ down into the tens-of-nanometers regime.  

2. Superior wear and abrasion resistance  
   – Lower steady‐state wear rates (often 1–2 orders of magnitude).  
   – Reduced friction coefficients (smoother, harder surface yields less adhesive/abrasive wear).  

3. Enhanced fatigue and contact‐fatigue life  
   – Crack‐initiation is delayed by the fine grain network, and cracks are deflected or arrested at dense grain-boundary regions.  
   – Typical fatigue limits are raised by 20–50 %.  

4. Improved scratch and indentation resilience  
   – Higher elastic limit and greater elastic recovery under point/contact loading.  
   – Indentation fracture toughness can actually increase because microcracks are blunted or pinned at grain‐boundary arrays.  

5. Often better corrosion/oxidation resistance  
   – Finer grains produce more uniform passive films and fewer fast‐diffusion paths.  

Caveat: if you push grains below ~10 nm you may enter the “inverse” Hall–Petch regime where grain‐boundary sliding reduces hardness.  But in the 10–100 nm window, nanocrystalline coatings deliver markedly higher strength, hardness, wear resistance and fatigue life than their conventionally crystalline counterparts.

Porosity in cold-sprayed deposits acts much like tiny cracks and voids in any metallic material—it reduces the effective cross‐sectional area carrying load, it concentrates stress at pore tips, and it breaks up the continuous metallic bonding that you would have in a fully dense billet.  The net effect is always a drop in hardness, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength relative to the fully dense parent metal.  A few of the key points are:

1. Effective area reduction  
   – If you have a volume fraction of porosity p, the solid metal fraction is only (1–p).  In simplest terms the “net” area resisting load is reduced by that same fraction.

2. Stress concentration at pores  
   – Pores (even sub-micron ones) act as crack‐like notches.  Under load they amplify local stress (stress‐concentration factor on the order of 2–3 for sharp voids), cutting into both yield and fracture strength.

3. Particle–particle bonding  
   – Cold spray relies on high-velocity particle impact and adiabatic shear bonding.  Porosity indicates spots where that shear‐bonding was incomplete.  Those interparticle interfaces are mechanically weaker than the bulk metal.

4. Empirical/analytical scaling  
   – A common first‐order approximation for many metals is  
     σ*/σsolid ≈ (1–p)^n  
     where σ* is strength of the porous deposit, σsolid is the fully dense strength, p is porosity (fractional), and n typically falls between 1.5 and 3.  For hardness H the same scaling often holds:  
     H*/Hsolid ≈ (1–p)^n.  
   – Example: n=2 gives σ*≈σsolid(1–p)^2.  At p=0.05 (5 % pores) you’d predict roughly a 10 % drop in strength or hardness; at p=0.10 roughly a 20 % drop.

5. Tensile strength vs. hardness sensitivity  
   – Hardness (a highly localized indentation measurement) often shows a smaller apparent drop than bulk tensile properties.  You might see a 5–15 % hardness decline at p≈5 %, but a 20–30 % loss in yield/UTS in the same deposit.

6. Pore size, shape and distribution  
   – Large “wormholes” or elongated voids between splats are worse than well‐distributed submicron pores.  Elongated pores aligned perpendicular to the load axis can knock strength down even more dramatically.

In practice, well‐optimized cold‐spray recipes can hold porosity below 1–2 %, at which point mechanical properties are within 5–10 % of the fully dense parent metal.  Once porosity climbs into the 5–10 % range, you routinely lose 15–30 % of your yield strength and a similar or slightly smaller fraction of your hardness.

Thermal‐spray metal coating hardness is quite sensitive to the kinematics and thermal state of the particles at impact.  Two “knobs” dominate the process:

 1.  Particle Impact Velocity (v)  
    –  Below a critical velocity (vc) there is little or no deposition.  Between vc and the “optimum” velocity (vo ≈ 600–800 m/s for HVOF Ni‐ or Co‐based alloys) hardness climbs sharply as you increase v, because higher v gives better splat flattening, lower porosity and higher work hardening.  
    –  In the steep‐slope region (v ≈ vc … vo) you typically see hardness rise by order of 1–2 HV per 1 m/s increase in v.  In practical terms a ±50 m/s swing around vo can change your as‐sprayed microhardness by roughly ±50–100 HV (i.e. ±5–10 % on a 1 000 HV coating).  
    –  Above vo further increases in v give diminishing returns (you approach a packing‐density plateau), and extremely high v can actually induce tensile residual stresses or microcracking that slightly soften the coating.

 2.  Particle Temperature (T)  
    –  The substrate‐surface temperature and particle temperature together control splat solidification, oxidation and intersplat bonding.  Too cold (<1 000–1 100 °C for most NiCr and CoCr feedstocks) yields poor metallic bonding, higher porosity and soft, brittle splats.  Too hot (>1 600–1 700 °C for many alloys) promotes excessive oxidation or carbide decomposition and again reduces hardness.  
    –  In the “sweet‐spot” window (ΔT ≈ 200–400 °C wide, depending on chemistry) you typically see a more gentle hardness dependence: on the order of 0.2–0.5 HV per 1 °C change in particle temperature.  That translates to about ±20–50 HV (±2–5 %) for a ±50 °C gas‐ratio (temperature) perturbation.

Putting it all together, in a well‐tuned HVOF or plasma‐spray run:

  •  A 10 % change in particle velocity (say ±70 m/s around 700 m/s) will typically shift microhardness by 5–10 %.  
  •  A 5 % change in particle temperature (say ±75 °C around 1 500 °C) will typically shift hardness by 2–5 %.  

Cold‐spray coatings show similar trends but even stronger velocity sensitivity near the deposition threshold (vc), since below vc no coating builds up at all.  Above vc, metal cold work and adiabatic shear‐induced grain refinement give an additional hardening contribution, so you often see hardness climbing steeply with v until it saturates.

The “flattening ratio” ε in cold spray is nothing more exotic than a geometric proxy for how much a single particle has plastically deformed (or “pancaked out”) when it hits the substrate or a stopping plate.  In practice one either  
  • sprays at very low coverage onto a polished catcher plate (or film) so that individual splats can be imaged by SEM, or  
  • takes a polished cross‐section of a real coating and measures the aspect‐ratio of a few near‐spherical remnants,  
and defines   
 ε = (lateral spread-diameter of the deformed particle)  
  (original particle diameter)  

Because ε is directly tied to the degree of high-strain-rate plastic flow in each droplet, it gives you a one‐number diagnostic of:  
1. Particle impact energy (i.e. how close you are to or above the “critical velocity” for that material).  
2. The local bonding quality—particles that deform a lot (high ε) make more intimate metal–metal contact, interlock mechanically, and weld better to both substrate and neighbors.  
3. Porosity and cohesion of the deposit—higher ε generally correlates with denser, stronger coatings.  
4. Work-hardening, residual‐stress levels and microstructural refinement—regions that flatten more also tend to exhibit the adiabatic‐shear bands and dynamical recrystallization kernels you see in fully deposited coatings.  

In short, by routinely measuring ε you can compare different gas pressures, temperatures, carrier gases, stand‐off distances, or even powder lots, and quickly see which set of parameters is driving you into the optimum high‐deformation, low‐porosity, high‐bond‐strength regime.

No.  In cold‐sprayed metal–ceramic composites abrasion resistance does not simply scale with ceramic loading.  Although adding hard ceramic particles raises the overall hardness of the coating, beyond a fairly modest volume fraction it begins to degrade the very features that give the coating abrasion resistance in the first place:

1. Binder continuity and toughness  
   • Cold spray relies on the plastic flow of the metal to form a ductile, load-bearing matrix.  If you overload the coating with non-deforming ceramics the matrix can no longer fully encapsulate each particle, so you lose toughness and the ability to blunt or bridge cracks around the hard phases.  
2. Interparticle and interphase bonding  
   • Ceramics don’t deform in flight, so they get trapped rather than welded.  At high ceramic fractions you tend to form “islands” of weakly bound ceramic that are easy to chip or pull out under abrasive contact.  
3. Porosity and defect content  
   • Very high ceramic fraction leads to increased pore volume (and microcracks) in the interstices between particles.  Those voids act as crack‐initiators under the high local stresses of two-body or three-body abrasion.  
4. Residual stresses and embrittlement  
   • Differential impact strains between the metal and ceramic phases introduce tensile residual stresses in the ceramic, promoting microfracture and premature spallation under cyclic contact.  

In practice you almost always see a maximum in abrasion resistance at an intermediate ceramic content (often 10–30 vol % depending on materials, particle size, spray parameters, etc.).  Below that point you simply don’t get enough hard phase to resist cutting, above it you sacrifice matrix integrity and adhesion.

Friction‐stir processing (FSP) of a precipitation–hardenable alloy typically (1) breaks up and dissolves the original coarse strengthening precipitates, (2) produces a very fine, recrystallized grain structure with high dislocation density, and (3) leaves the stir zone in a supersaturated, under‐aged or even essentially solution‐treated condition.  A tailored post‐process aging treatment then restores and optimizes hardness by the following sequence:

1. Supersaturation → Driving Force  
   – FSP’s frictional heating plus plastic flow re‐dissolves or coarsens the original precipitates, creating a high solute supersaturation in the new, fine‐grained matrix.  
   – The high dislocation density and grain‐boundary area act as fast diffusion paths and abundant nucleation sites.

2. Controlled Precipitation  
   – During aging (at a temperature below the solvus), fine, coherent or semi‐coherent strengthening phases (GP‐zones, metastable T′/θ′/T1 etc., depending on alloy system) nucleate homogeneously within grains and at dislocations.  
   – Because the grains are small, precipitate growth is constrained, giving a high number density of small (< 10 nm) precipitates.

3. Strengthening Mechanisms  
   – Coherency/Modulus‐Mismatch Strengthening: the lattice strain and modulus differences around the coherent precipitates increase the stress required to bow or cut them.  
   – Orowan (Bow‐Out) Hardening: dislocations must bypass the non–shearable precipitates, raising yield stress Δσ ∝ Gb/λ · ln(r/b) (where λ ≈ inter‐precipitate spacing).  
   – Grain–Boundary (Hall–Petch) Contribution: the fine grain size from FSP remains, so σ_y contains both Δσ_HP ∝ k·d^–½ and Δσ_precip.

4. Resulting Hardness Increase  
   – A dense, uniformly distributed population of nanoscale precipitates in a refined‐grain matrix produces a synergistic rise in hardness and strength compared to either the as‐processed (precipitate‐free) or the over‐aged/coarse‐precipitated condition.

In short, post‐process aging converts the FSP‐induced supersaturated, low‐hardness microstructure into one containing an optimized dispersion of nanoscale strengthening precipitates—leveraging both Hall–Petch grain‐boundary strengthening and precipitation hardening to maximize hardness.

Cold‐sprayed deposits commonly come out harder at the surface than the original powder or wrought stock for several interrelated reasons:  

1. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) at particle impact  
   • Particles striking the substrate at high velocity (300–1200 m/s) undergo extremely high strain rates (>10³–10⁶ s⁻¹).  
   • This generates very high dislocation densities and extensive work hardening in the near‐surface layers.  

2. Grain refinement and dynamic recrystallization  
   • The intense, localized shear can break up original grains into ultrafine or even nanometric subgrains.  
   • Hall–Petch strengthening from the reduced grain size raises hardness.  

3. Residual stress and peening effects  
   • Each particle impact plastically “peens” the surface, leaving behind compressive residual stresses that impede dislocation motion.  

4. Oxide/second‐phase fragmentation and dispersion  
   • Native oxide films are fractured and dispersed as fine oxide particles at splat boundaries.  
   • These act as Orowan‐type obstacles to dislocation glide.  

5. Work‐hardened interparticle boundaries  
   • The weld interfaces between particles are zones of even higher defect density and boundary area, which further block dislocations.  

Together, these mechanisms shift the microstructure to a heavily strained, ultrafine, and compression‐stressed state—resulting in markedly higher surface hardness.

Particle velocity is one of the single most important spray parameters in cold‐spray, because it controls impact energy (½m·V²) and thus the degree of plastic deformation, bonding quality and resulting microstructure—and that in turn governs hardness.  In broad strokes:  

1. Impact energy and deformation  
   • As particle velocity increases (typically from 300–1200 m/s), impact energy rises with V².  
   • Higher impact energy produces more severe plastic deformation at the particle–substrate and particle–particle interfaces.  

2. Work hardening & dislocation density  
   • Severe local straining drives dislocation multiplication and cell‐block formation inside particles.  
   • Increased dislocation density raises the as‐sprayed hardness via classical strain‐hardening mechanisms.  

3. Grain refinement & dynamic recrystallization  
   • Extreme shear at the interface can trigger continuous dynamic recrystallization (cDRX), breaking down initial grains into ultrafine or nanocrystalline subgrains.  
   • Finer grains (Hall–Petch strengthening) further boost hardness.  

4. Porosity reduction and interparticle bonding  
   • Higher velocities improve particle flattening and interlocking, closing pores and oxide layers.  
   • Denser, better‐bonded coatings have fewer crack‐like defects, so the measured hardness more closely approaches that of the work‐hardened bulk material.  

5. Optimum velocity window  
   • Below the critical velocity (Vc), particles merely ‘‘bounce’’ or lightly adhere—hardness is low and highly variable.  
   • Above Vc, hardness rises steeply with velocity, usually plateauing in an optimum range (e.g. 600–1000 m/s for many Cu‐ or Ni‐based powders).  
   • Too high velocities (>1.2 km/s, depending on material) can lead to excessive erosion, high residual tensile stress or adiabatic heating, which may promote recovery/coarsening and actually reduce hardness or cohesion.  

Summary: raising particle velocity increases coating hardness up to an optimum by (a) intensifying plastic deformation and work hardening, (b) driving grain‐refining dynamic recrystallization, and (c) producing denser, better‐bonded deposits. Beyond that window, erosion and thermal recovery effects can offset further gains.

Recovery is the first stage of annealing after cold (or other) work‐hardening. Its main effects on a deformed metal’s strength are:

1. Dislocation rearrangement and annihilation  
   • Mobile dislocations of opposite sign meet and cancel out.  
   • Dislocation walls and sub‐grain boundaries form, reducing internal strain energy.

2. Residual‐stress relief  
   • Internal stresses from cold work are relaxed, lowering back‐stress contributions to yield.

3. Point‐defect elimination  
   • Vacancies and interstitials diffuse to sinks (dislocations, grain boundaries), improving lattice order.

Net effect on strength and hardness  
• Modest softening: yield and tensile strength drop as dislocation density ρ falls (σy ∝ G b √ρ).  
• Hardness decreases accordingly.  
• The loss in strength is much smaller than in full recrystallization—typically a 10–30 % drop, depending on temperature and time.  
• Ductility and electrical/thermal conductivity rise slightly.

In short, recovery removes some of the work‐hardening “benefits” (high dislocation density and residual stress) and so lowers strength and hardness modestly, but without forming new strain‐free grains.

Heat‐treating cold‐sprayed coatings is almost always done to relieve the very high residual strains imparted during particle impact, to drive diffusion bonding at the numerous particle–particle interfaces, and—when dealing with age‐hardening alloys—to precipitate strengthening phases. The choice of atmosphere during that thermal cycle can make or break your final cohesiveness and strength.  In a nutshell:

1. Inert (Ar, N₂) or vacuum environments  
   • Minimize further oxidation of fresh metal surfaces  
   • Allow clean solid‐state diffusion across particle boundaries  
   • Promote recrystallization (grain‐boundary healing) without embrittling oxides  
   → Result: higher interparticle adhesion, higher tensile and fatigue strength, moderate softening (stress‐relief) or controlled hardness loss.

2. Reducing (H₂‐rich) atmospheres  
   • Chemically strip any nascent oxide films  
   • Encourage metal‐metal contact welding at lower temperatures  
   • Beware of hydrogen pick‐up if Fe or Ti alloys are involved  
   → Result: often the best cohesion and densification, with tensile‐strength gains of 10–30 %, though ductility can suffer if hydrogen embrittlement occurs.

3. Oxidizing (air, O₂) environments  
   • Grow thicker oxide (or even spinel) layers at particle interfaces  
   • Block diffusion welding and trap porosity  
   • Can spur brittle intermetallic or oxide‐stringer networks  
   → Result: reduced interparticle bonding, lower cohesive strength and ductility, higher fracture‐mode brittleness.

Quantitatively you often see a 20–50 % drop in room‐temperature tensile or adhesion strength when a spray is annealed in air versus vacuum/H₂, and fatigue‐crack growth rates can double under oxidizing anneals. Conversely, properly controlled vacuum or reducing atmospheres not only restore ductility (by recrystallization) but also recover or even boost ultimate tensile strength by eliminating the submicron‐oxide films that limit cold‐spray junction strength.

Typical as-sprayed austenitic stainless‐steel cold-spray coatings exhibit high hardness (often 250–350 HV) because of very high dislocation density plus strain-induced α′ martensite.  Subsequent annealing at moderate or high temperatures drives changes that almost invariably soften the coating:

1. Moderate‐temperature anneals (roughly 300 – 600 °C, 0.5 – 4 h)  
   • Stress relief and recovery – dislocation annihilation and partial rearrangement  
   • Reversion of α′ martensite to austenite (in metastable grades such as 304 or 316)  
   → hardness typically falls by 10–40 % (e.g. from ≈300 HV down to ≈180–240 HV)

2. High‐temperature anneals (> 650–700 °C, up to 900–1 000 °C)  
   • Full recrystallization and rapid grain growth  
   • Coarsening or dissolution of any fine precipitates formed at lower T  
   • At the upper end (≈700–900 °C) Cr‐carbide (M23C6) or σ‐phase may nucleate at grain boundaries – these can locally raise hardness but embrittle the coating  
   → overall hardness typically drops toward the annealed bulk value (≈120–170 HV), i.e. a 50 – 70 % reduction versus as-sprayed

In practice you end up trading dislocation- and martensite-induced hardness for better ductility and adhesion but at the expense of most of the strain hardening imparted by the cold‐spray process.

In virtually every metal–ceramic cold‐sprayed system (Al–Al₂O₃, Cu–SiC, Ni–WC, etc.) you will see that as you increase the hard (ceramic or intermetallic) fraction in the feedstock, all of the key coating metrics—porosity, cohesion (intra‐splat bonding), adhesion (substrate bond), and macrohardness—improve up to a point and then level off or even back‐slide.  In practical terms that “knee in the curve” almost always falls into the same neighborhood:    

  • 20–30 vol % (or roughly 25–40 wt %) hard phase is where you get most of the porosity reduction, cohesion/adhesion boost and hardness gain.    
  • Above ~30 vol %, deposition efficiency starts to drop rapidly, porosity begins to climb again, splats become more brittle (weaker cohesion), and bond strength at the substrate also suffers.  Meanwhile the incremental hardness gain per additional vol % hard phase becomes very small.    

If you push toward 40–50 vol %, you may still eke out a little harder coating—but you pay for it with much higher spray velocities (to exceed the critical velocity of the hard particles), poor build rates, rising porosity (>5 %), and low adhesion.  In short:    

  1. Up to ~20 vol % hard phase: rapid gains in porosity, cohesion, adhesion, hardness.  
  2. 20–30 vol %: you harvest the last of the “easy” improvements.  
  3. > 30 vol %: diminishing returns, often accompanied by lower deposition efficiency and mechanical integrity.    

Of course the exact breakpoint can shift by ±5 vol % depending on matrix toughness, particle size, gas temperature/pressure, and stand‐off, but in practice 25–30 vol % hard phase is a reliable rule‐of‐thumb for the onset of diminishing returns.

Cold‐sprayed deposits almost invariably come out harder than the same material in its “as-received” or bulk form.  Typical increases in Vickers or Knoop hardness range from 10 % up to 50 % (and in extreme cases even higher in the immediately deformed zones) compared with the feedstock alloy or wrought plate.  

Why?  The high-velocity impact of powder particles on the substrate subjects them to very large, very rapid plastic strains.  That impact-driven severe plastic deformation (SPD) produces:  
  • Very high dislocation densities  
  • Subgrain and nanograin formation (Hall–Petch grain-boundary strengthening)  
  • Localized dynamic recrystallization or shear‐instability zones  
  • Residual compressive stresses in the deposit  

All of these effects combine to “work‐harden” and refine the microstructure, so that the cold-spray coating is measurably harder than the starting bulk material.

Incorporating graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) into cold-sprayed metal coatings almost invariably lowers their dry sliding coefficient of friction by 20–60 %, simply because the platelets act as a solid-lubricant “third body” film.  A few representative findings from the literature are:  
• Ni–GNP coatings (1 wt % GNP) typically drop from μ≈0.60 (neat Ni) to μ≈0.30–0.35 under 5 N, 0.1 m/s sliding.  
• Al–GNP coatings (0.5–2 wt % GNP) go from μ≈0.50 (pure Al) down to μ≈0.10–0.25.
