• Increasing GNP beyond ∼3 wt % can induce platelet agglomeration and even raise μ again, so most researchers see an optimum in the 0.5–2 wt % range.  

Mechanism  
– Under load, the graphene flakes shear easily and form a thin, transfer film on both counterface and coating surface.  
– This film cuts down both adhesive and ploughing components of friction.  
– You also get a modest hardness increase and a reduction in porosity, which stabilizes the tribofilm.  

Bottom line: a small (∼0.5–2 wt %) GNP addition to a cold-sprayed metal coating typically pushes the coefficient of friction into the 0.1–0.3 window, versus 0.4–0.7 for the unmodified material.

The main “knob’’ for dialing in hardness in a cold-sprayed cermet is simply how much of the hard, non-deforming ceramic you load into the ductile metal matrix.  In rough terms the composite hardness Hc follows a rule-of-mixtures between the soft metal (Hm) and the hard ceramic (Hp):  
   
   Hc ≃ Vm·Hm + Vp·Hp  
   
where Vm and Vp are the metal and ceramic volume fractions.  In practice you see three regimes as Vp is raised:

1.  Low ceramic content (Vp < 20 vol %):  
    –  The metal matrix still dominates the deformation.  
    –  Hardness rises only modestly above the metal baseline.  
2.  Intermediate content (Vp ≈ 20–50 vol %):  
    –  Hard, well‐dispersed particles begin to bear load, block dislocation motion and introduce Orowan‐type strengthening plus local strain hardening in the metal.  
    –  Hardness climbs roughly linearly with Vp.  
    –  Coating porosity and interparticle bonding are still acceptable, so you gain hardness without undue brittleness.  
3.  High ceramic content (Vp > 50 vol %):  
    –  Deposition efficiency and particle–particle bonding suffer (insufficient metal to plastically “wet’’ and bond all the ceramics).  
    –  Porosity and microcracking rise, ceramic clusters form, and the interface cohesion drops.  
    –  Despite the large fraction of hard phase, the *effective* hardness can level off or even decrease because the coating becomes highly porous and brittle.  

In short, increasing the ceramic fraction raises hardness by increasing the volume of load-bearing, dislocation‐blocking particles.  Beyond an optimum (often 30–50 vol %), however, you pay a price in porosity, cohesion loss and brittleness, and the hardness gain stalls or reverses.

Annealing affects the tensile strength of cold‐sprayed metals mainly by changing their internal stress state, microstructure and interparticle bonding.  In broad outline:  

1. Stress relief and recovery  
   • Cold spray deposits are heavily work-hardened, with very high dislocation densities and locked-in residual stresses.  Low-temperature annealing (below or near the recovery regime) allows dislocation annihilation and relaxation of internal stresses without much grain growth.  
   • Result: a modest drop in yield/tensile strength but a substantial gain in ductility and toughness.  

2. Recrystallization and particle bonding  
   • At higher annealing temperatures (above the recrystallization temperature) new strain-free grains nucleate and grow at former particle boundaries and within heavily deformed regions.  Simultaneously, solid‐state diffusion across the particle–particle interfaces “welds” them more completely, closing pores and oxide films.  
   • Result: interparticle cohesion improves, which can raise the “effective” tensile strength of the bulk deposit, even though the matrix itself is somewhat softened.  There is an optimum temperature/time window where bonding gain outweighs softening.  

3. Grain growth and over-softening  
   • If annealing is too severe (too hot or too long), grains coarsen, residual porosity can reopen, and interface strength plateaus or decreases.  Tensile strength then falls off, and ductility may actually drop if pores or brittle intermetallics form.  

Net effect by alloy system:  
• Aluminum alloys often show a peak in tensile strength after anneals in the 200–350 °C range (better bonding + some stress relief), then strength falls beyond ~400 °C.  
• Steels and Ni‐based alloys typically need 500–800 °C to get good recrystallization bonding, but beyond the optimum they also soften.  

In practice one tunes the anneal temperature/time to trade off residual‐stress relief and interparticle welding against grain coarsening, thus hitting the highest tensile strength achievable for that alloy.

Surface skewness (Ssk) is the third statistical moment of a surface‐height distribution and measures whether a surface is “peak-dominated” (Ssk > 0) or “valley-dominated” (Ssk < 0). In sliding contacts this asymmetry has a very direct impact on how asperities interact and how lubricant films form.  Key points are:

1. Peak-dominated (positive skew, Ssk > 0)  
  • Most of the material lies above the mean plane in sharp asperities.  
  • At low loads or in boundary lubrication these peaks carry the load, giving high local contact pressures.  
  • Results in increased adhesive and ploughing friction and more rapid lubricant starvation.  
  • Under dry sliding you see higher µ, stronger stiction, and accelerated wear.

2. Valley-dominated (negative skew, Ssk < 0)  
  • The surface has more valleys below the mean plane and relatively blunt or fewer asperity peaks.  
  • Valleys act as micro-reservoirs for lubricant and debris, supporting a thicker hydrodynamic or mixed‐lubrication film.  
  • Real contact area grows more gradually with load, reducing peak pressures and ploughing friction.  
  • Typically yields a 10–30 % reduction in friction coefficient under mixed or boundary‐lubricated conditions.  
  • Can trap wear particles and promote local starvation if the texture is too deep or poorly distributed.

3. Mechanistic summary  
  • In boundary or mixed lubrication regimes, negative skew promotes film build-up and fluid entrainment, shifting the friction curve toward hydrodynamic behavior at lower sliding speeds or loads.  
  • In fully hydrodynamic regimes the effect of skewness becomes less pronounced, though slight negative skew still aids stable film support.  
  • Under dry or starved lubrication, positive skew intensifies asperity‐on-asperity contact and ploughing, whereas negative skew mitigates it.

Designers of engineered textures often aim for a mildly negative skew (Ssk ≈ –0.2 to –0.5) in combination with controlled kurtosis so as to optimize the balance between load support, lubricant retention, and debris entrapment. By tuning skewness and other higher‐order texture parameters one can systematically tailor friction and wear performance in sliding components.

Surface roughness is one of the primary surface‐geometry parameters controlling both friction coefficient (µ) and wear rate in coated contacts.  Its influence can be broken down into three interrelated effects:

1. Asperity Contact Mechanics  
   – Real contact area (Areal) at the interface is determined by the highest asperities.  Rougher surfaces have fewer, higher asperities, so Areal is small but local contact pressures are high.  High local pressure promotes  
     • plastic deformation and ploughing friction (µplough),  
     • micro‐cracking in brittle coatings,  
     • asperity fracture and generation of third‐body debris.  
   – Conversely, very smooth surfaces have a larger nominal real‐contact area, which tends to increase adhesive friction (µadhesive) but lowers ploughing.

2. Ploughing vs. Adhesion Balance  
   Friction at the macroscale is the sum of adhesive and ploughing contributions:  
     µ ≈ µadhesive + µplough  
   – As roughness (e.g. Ra, Rz) increases, µplough rises roughly in proportion to the ratio of asperity height to coating hardness.  
   – At the same time µadhesive tends to fall, because smaller contact patches reduce the total adhesive force.  
   – An optimum “medium” roughness often minimizes µtotal in boundary/lubricated regimes by balancing adequate lubricant‐film reservoirs in valleys against excessive asperity‐driven ploughing.

3. Wear‐Rate Dependence  
   Wear rate W (often expressed by Archard’s law: W = k · P · s / H) is strongly influenced by roughness through:  
   – Third‐body abrasion: Loose chips and spalled particles from tall asperities abrade the coating under sliding.  
   – Fatigue and crack initiation: Surface peaks concentrate stress, nucleating microcracks that grow under cyclic loading.  
   – Lubricant retention: Moderate valley depths (characterized by the Rvk parameter in the Abbott–Firestone curve) trap lubricant, reducing direct asperity contact and cutting down wear.  
   – Transfer‐film stability: Roughness dictates how well tribo‐films form and adhere; too smooth a coating may not anchor protective films, too rough a one will shed them as wear debris.

Key practical points  
 • Ultra‐smooth coatings (low Ra-Rz) can have low ploughing friction but risk high adhesive wear (galling).  
 • Highly rough coatings minimize adhesion but suffer high abrasive wear and friction spikes from asperity catch.  
 • An intermediate roughness or engineered bimodal roughness (micro peaks + valleys) often minimizes both µ and wear rate under specific load–speed–lubrication conditions.  

In designing or post‐treating coatings, it is therefore critical to specify not only an average roughness value but also profile parameters (skewness, kurtosis, valley depth) that control lubricant retention, asperity strength, and the balance between adhesion and ploughing.

Increasing particle velocity in cold spray has a first‐order effect on both how densely the powder consolidates and on the performance of the resulting coating or part.  In broad terms you see:

1. Improved Deposit Density (Lower Porosity)  
   – Particles impacting faster carry more kinetic energy (E ≈ ½mv²), deform more plastically on impact, “weld” more completely to neighboring particles and to the substrate, and squeeze out voids more effectively.  
   – As you go from just at/above the critical velocity (≈ 400–500 m/s for many metals) up into the 600–900 m/s range, porosity typically falls from several percent down to below 1 %.  Deposit efficiency (mass actually bonded) rises from 20–30 % at low velocity to 70–90 % at optimized velocities.  
   – Above an optimum (≈ 1,000 m/s for many systems), you can start to see substrate erosion, particle rebound, or even fatigue cracks in the deposit.  The density gains level off or reverse if you push the velocity too high.

2. Enhanced Mechanical Properties  
   a. Strength and Hardness  
      • Severe plastic deformation on impact generates a very fine, sub-micron or even nano-grain structure in the particle rims (dynamic recrystallization, high dislocation densities).  This gives Hall–Petch–type strengthening.  
      • Typical hardness increases of 15–30 % over the as‐sprayed low‐velocity case are common as you go from just‐depositing to fully densified coatings.  
      • Tensile yield and ultimate strengths similarly climb (10–25 % gains), and bond strength to the substrate typically doubles as porosity and interface flaws disappear.  

   b. Fatigue, Wear, and Toughness  
      • Compressive residual stresses from high‐velocity peening improve fatigue life.  
      • Denser, harder coatings show lower wear rates (20–50 % reductions) in sliding or abrasion tests.  
      • Fracture toughness can improve modestly because microcracks have less room to initiate/grow in a dense, well‐bonded microstructure.  

3. Diminishing Returns and Potential Drawbacks  
   – Once you exceed the material’s window of plastic deformation, additional velocity adds little to density and may cause excessive tensile residual stresses or substrate erosion.  
   – Each system (metal, alloy, powder size, nozzle geometry) has its own optimal velocity “sweet spot.”  In practice one tunes carrier gas pressure, temperature, and nozzle design to hit that window.

In summary, raising particle velocity from just above the critical threshold up toward the material-specific optimum markedly increases deposit density (porosity ↓), hardness and strength (via strain hardening and grain refinement), bond integrity, fatigue life and wear resistance. But above an upper limit these benefits plateau or reverse as erosion, rebound and crack formation set in.

A flat microhardness profile in the substrate all the way to the spray-metal interface simply tells you that the substrate’s bulk properties and microstructure have not been altered by the cold-spray pass.  In other words,

  •  There is no extended heat-affected zone (no thermal softening),  
  •  There is no measurable work/hard-peening of the substrate ahead of the interface, and  
  •  Plastic deformation is essentially confined to the very topmost layer (the actual impact zone), not the bulk substrate.

Put another way, cold spray places particles by localized, high‐strain‐rate impacts without generating enough heat or subsurface strain to change the bulk hardness of the substrate.

In almost every alloy system studied the as‐sprayed cold‐spray (CS) build sits at the “high‐strength/low‐ductility” corner of the strength–ductility map.  In practice this means:

 • Because particles undergo very large plastic strains on impact, the deposit ends up with an ultra-fine, heavily dislocated microstructure and very good particle–particle bonding.  Tensile strengths (or 0.2 % proof stresses) often meet or exceed wrought values.  
 • At the same time, the lack of recrystallization or recovery and the high density of dislocation walls and unmated interfaces means there is almost no strain‐hardening capacity.  Fracture strains (total elongation) in the as-sprayed condition are typically only a few percent (often <5 %).  

If you tune your parameters (higher gas temperature or reduced impact energy) to soften the deposit and open up ductility you invariably give up ultimate strength, and vice-versa.  Only by a post-spray heat treatment (which lowers dislocation density and coarsens the microstructure) can you partially recover ductility—at the expense of some of the as-sprayed strength.

Cold‐sprayed maraging steel as‐deposited is a highly work‐hardened, defect‐rich (porosity, weak particle–particle boundaries) microstructure.  A solution-aging cycle (typically solutionizing at 850–950 °C for 0.5–2 h + air or water quench, then aging at ~450–500 °C for 3–6 h) transforms its tensile response in two steps:

1. Solutionizing  
  • Recrystallizes the severely deformed splats and heals some interparticle voids/oxides  
  • Relieves residual stresses and dissolves coarse intermetallics  
  • Yields a relatively soft, ductile martensitic or reverted‐austenite matrix (YS drops to ~400–600 MPa, UTS ~600–800 MPa, elongation rises into the 8–12% range)

2. Precipitation aging  
  • Drives uniform precipitation of Ni₃(Ti,Mo), Fe₂Mo and related intermetallics on dislocations and lath boundaries  
  • Raises yield strength by Orowan‐ and coherency‐straining mechanisms to ~1.5–1.8 GPa and UTS to ~1.7–2.0 GPa  
  • Final elongation settles at 4–8%, a good compromise of strength and toughness  

In short, solution treatment restores ductility by recrystallizing and bonding the spray particles, then aging pumps up the yield and ultimate strengths via fine precipitates. After full solution + aging the tensile properties of cold-sprayed maraging steel approach those of conventionally processed material.

Cold‐spraying is a high-velocity, solid-state deposition process.  Unlike thermal sprays, the powder never melts, but each particle suffers very large plastic strains on impact.  That severe, localized deformation fundamentally alters the powder’s microstructure in the deposit and hence its mechanical properties:

1. Particle Deformation and Bonding  
   • Particles are flattened into “splats” and forge-bonded to one another by pressure of order 1–3 GPa.  
   • Original oxide films are broken up and dispersed as stringers or fine fragments at splat interfaces.  

2. Grain‐Scale Refinement  
   • Impact strains (true strains >1) drive dislocation multiplication and the formation of dislocation‐cell structures.  
   • At the highest‐strain loci (near particle boundaries) dynamic recrystallization or continuous subgrain rotation produces ultrafine (100 nm–1 μm) or even nano-scale grains.  
   • Original equiaxed, gas-atomized grains (10–50 μm) in the powder become highly elongated subgrains in the deposit.  

3. Residual Stress State  
   • The deposit develops net compressive residual stresses (−200 to −600 MPa in Al‐alloys, −300 to −800 MPa in steels), which improve fatigue and fracture resistance but can reduce ductility.  

4. Mechanical‐Property Changes  
   • Hardness and yield strength typically rise by 20–100 % over the feedstock (e.g. Al alloys from ~70 HV to 100–140 HV; steels from 200 HV to 300–400 HV).  
   • Ultimate tensile strength increases in proportion to hardness, but elongation to failure often drops by 10–30 % due to work hardening and strain‐induced damage at splat interfaces.  
   • Fatigue life and wear resistance are generally improved, owing both to the compressive stresses and the ultrafine grain structure.  

5. Phase and Chemistry Stability  
   • No bulk melting means minimal oxidation or phase‐transformation compared with thermal spray or fusion processes.  
   • Alloy chemistry remains essentially that of the original powder—though severe strain can promote precipitation in age-hardening alloys (for instance, Ni₃Al in Inconel).  

In short, cold spray transforms a relatively coarse, ductile gas‐atomized powder into a highly deformed, ultrafine‐grained, work‐hardened coating with elevated hardness and strength, beneficial residual compressive stresses, and generally enhanced fatigue and wear performance—all without the high‐temperature side effects of melting.

Heat treatment of a cold-sprayed metal coating rarely “creates” a new modulus the way it creates new yield strengths or precipitates; instead it tweaks the coating’s microstructure in ways that change its effective elastic stiffness.  In practice you will see changes of order 1–15 % in the effective (macroscopic) modulus 𝐸eff after annealing.  The main mechanisms are:

1. Porosity and pore‐shape evolution  
   – Cold spray deposits are never fully dense.  Open and closed porosity both reduce 𝐸eff roughly as (1–P)n (n≈1.5–2 for metal foams).  
   – Annealing at 0.3–0.6 Tm drives diffusion, sinters splat boundaries, closes submicron cracks and pores, and so raises 𝐸eff.  

2. Interparticle/interlamellar bonding  
   – At spray temperatures the particle–particle contacts are largely mechanical; there are oxide films and unmated asperities.  
   – Modest anneals (e.g. 300–500 °C for Al or 500–800 °C for Ni alloys) promote grain‐boundary and lattice diffusion across those interfaces, strengthening load transfer and lifting 𝐸eff by a few percent.  

3. Residual stress relief and recovery  
   – The high‐velocity impact in cold spray endows the coating with strong plastic‐strain gradients and locked‐in tensile/compressive stresses.  
   – Recovery/recrystallization reduces dislocation density.  Dislocations themselves can stiffen or soften a crystal (via kinks and forest interactions), so annealing can either rise or slightly lower the local modulus.  In most commercial alloys the net effect on bulk 𝐸eff is small compared to porosity effects.  

4. Grain growth and phase changes  
   – Below about 0.3 Tm little recrystallization occurs; above 0.5 Tm you get full grain growth, which slightly lowers the Hall–Petch contribution to stiffness (a very small effect on 𝐸bulk).  
   – In alloys that precipitate (e.g. Al-Zn-Mg, Ni-base), new phases or intermetallics can appear.  Since each phase has its own atomic‐bond stiffness, coarse precipitation can shift overall 𝐸eff up or down by up to 10 %, depending on volume fraction and spacing.  

Quantitative trends  
• A typical cold‐sprayed Al-Si coating may have 𝐸eff≈60–65 GPa as‐sprayed (bulk Al = 69 GPa); a 300 °C/1 h anneal can push it up to 66–70 GPa.  
• Ni-based coatings (bulk Ni ≈ 210 GPa) often go from ~180–200 GPa as-sprayed to 200–215 GPa after 600–800 °C diffusion anneals.  
• If you over‐anneal and induce coarse recrystallization or precipitate‐free zones, you can lose part of that gain.  

Modeling approach  
For many purposes you can treat the coating as a two‐phase composite of “metal” + “porosity” and apply an effective‐medium formula such as the Hashin–Shtrikman lower bound or  
  𝐸eff≈𝐸bulk·(1–P)^2.  
Then introduce a second correction (1+fB) for the bonded‐interface fraction fB that grows with anneal temperature/time.  

Bottom line  
• Heat treatment almost always raises the effective elastic modulus of a cold‐sprayed coating, primarily by densifying the deposit and improving splat‐to‐splat bonding.  
• Changes are generally modest (5–15 %), and the intrinsic elastic constant of the metal matrix remains essentially that of the bulk alloy.

Cold‐sprayed metal coatings almost invariably come out significantly harder than the same alloy deposited by conventional (e.g. plasma or HVOF) thermal sprays or even compared to the bulk wrought material.  The reasons are:

1. Severe plastic deformation (SPD) on impact  
   • Particles striking the substrate at 500–1200 m/s undergo intense shear and compressive strain.  
   • This generates a very high dislocation density, sub-grain formation and grain refinement down toward the sub-micron or even nano‐scale.  
   • In effect the spray jet “peens” the surface, producing work‐hardening.

2. Lack of high‐temperature softening  
   • Because the process temperature remains below melting, there is no solidification, little or no phase transformation and minimal oxide formation.  
   • You retain the strain‐hardened microstructure rather than annealing it out.

3. High density, low porosity  
   • Cold spray yields coatings ≥98 % theoretical density.  
   • Conventional thermal sprays have interlamellar oxides and porosity that both reduce hardness and act as crack‐initiation sites.

Quantitatively, typical hardness gains are:  
– Aluminum alloys: HV80–120 bulk → HV120–180 in cold spray (a +30–60 % rise)  
– Copper: HV55–75 bulk → HV80–100 in cold spray  
– Stainless steel and Ni alloys: often +20–40 % over their wrought or thermal‐sprayed values

Process tuning (gas pressure, temperature, stand‐off distance, nozzle design) lets you optimize the strain-hardening vs. build rate and residual stress. In short, cold spray’s ballistic, solid‐state deposition imparts high dislocation densities and fine grains that make the coating measurably harder than conventionally processed equivalents.

In cold spray the term “shot‐peening effect” refers to the fact that, after the first particle layer has been deposited, every subsequent particle impact behaves much like a miniature peening shot striking a metal surface.  Those repeated, high‐velocity impacts on the already-deposited layer (and on the substrate during the earliest stages) produce:  

 1. Severe localized plastic deformation and work hardening in the near-surface of both particles and substrate.  
 2. Dynamic recrystallization or grain refinement in the topmost microns of the deposit.  
 3. Disruption of residual oxide films and surface contaminants, continually exposing fresh metal.  
 4. Introduction of compressive residual stresses and closure of nano- and micro-voids at particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces.  
 5. Increased true contact area and mechanical interlocking (peening “hammer” effect flattens and forges particles together).  

Taken together these phenomena give rise to much stronger metallurgical and mechanical bonding than would occur simply by a single impact per particle.  Oxide removal plus the creation of fresh, highly strained, ultra-fine microstructures at the interfaces allow adiabatic shear bonding to proceed over a far larger contact area, dramatically improving adhesion (to the substrate) and cohesion (within the deposit), as well as reducing porosity and boosting fatigue and wear resistance.

Particle velocity in cold spray is one of the single most important knobs for tuning coating microstructure, hardness and hence wear resistance.  Below is a concise summary of the key effects and mechanisms:

1. Deposition efficiency and plastic deformation  
   – There is a material-specific “critical velocity” (Vc), typically 400–600 m/s for soft metals and 700–900 m/s for harder alloys.  
   – Below Vc you get poor flattening, low bond strength, high porosity and low work hardening.  
   – Above Vc particles undergo intense jetting and plastic flow, generating strong particle–particle and particle–substrate bonds and high dislocation densities.

2. Hardness evolution  
   – Impact strains of 10–100 and strain‐rates >10^6 s⁻¹ produce severe work hardening and often dynamic recrystallization or fragmentation of original grains.  
   – Hardness typically rises monotonically with velocity above Vc, plateauing when further velocity increments no longer raise strain levels.  
     • Example (Al-6061): from ∼60 HV at 500 m/s to ∼100 HV at 800 m/s.  
     • Example (Ni-based alloy): from ∼200 HV at 600 m/s to ∼300 HV at 1000 m/s.  
   – Mechanisms:  
     • Dislocation accumulation and cell structure formation  
     • Grain refinement (Hall–Petch strengthening)  
     • Elimination of pores (higher contact area)

3. Wear‐resistance trends  
   – Wear rate generally scales inversely with hardness if the coating is well bonded and dense.  
   – As velocity increases you get lower porosity and fewer crack‐initiating defects, so abrasive, adhesive and erosive wear resistance all improve.  
   – Typical improvements: a >50% drop in specific wear rate when raising velocity from just-above­-Vc to the upper practical limit.  

4. Limits of high velocity  
   – Above ∼1.2 × Vc, particle erosion of the growing coating or substrate can set in.  
   – Thermal and oxidation damage (from hotter carrier gas or shock‐heating on impact) may embrittle some alloys.  
   – Excessive residual stresses can cause delamination or spallation under service loads.

5. Practical guidance  
   – Identify Vc by parameter screening (pressure, temperature, nozzle design).  
   – Operate 10–20% above Vc for a good balance of deposition efficiency, hardness and low porosity.  
   – If maximum wear resistance is required, push toward the highest velocity that still yields a stable, crack‐free spray stream.

In summary, raising particle velocity above the critical threshold systematically increases coating hardness (via severe plastic deformation and grain refinement) and drives down wear rates—up to the point where erosion, oxidation or stress‐induced damage begins to counteract those gains.

Post‐deposition annealing of cold‐sprayed metals almost always strengthens the particle–particle interfaces and thereby raises the coating’s bulk mechanical performance, but the detailed outcome depends on alloy chemistry, time/temperature and whether you are simply stress‐relieving, annealing or carrying out a full solution‐plus‐age treatment.  In broad terms:

1. Interparticle bonding  
   • Thermal activation drives solid‐state diffusion across originally only “mechanically welded” contacts, gradually replacing high-energy asperities and nanocracks with true metallurgical bonds.  
   • Oxide films at particle boundaries tend to break up, become more discontinuous or even dissolve into the matrix, further improving intimate metallic contact.  
   • Residual compressive and tensile stresses (from adiabatic shear and work hardening on impact) relax, allowing interfaces to close up and reducing microvoid volume.  

2. Coating density and porosity  
   • Some of the remaining submicron pores and microcracks partially close as material plastically creeps or dif­fuses, increasing overall density by several percent.  
   • If a HIP‐style treatment is used, pores collapse almost completely, often achieving near‐bulk density.  

3. Mechanical properties  
   • Tensile and cohesive (interlamellar) strength generally rise by 10–30 % as linkage between particles goes from mechanical to metallurgical.  
   • Fatigue and fracture toughness improve markedly because crack‐arresting interfaces largely disappear and intrinsic ductility is regained.  
   • Ductility and elongation increase as residual hardening relaxes; in anneal‐only cycles you often trade some hardness or yield strength for improved toughness.  
   • In precipitation‐hardenable alloys (e.g. Al‐ or Ni‐base superalloys), a full solution + age schedule can actually increase hardness and yield strength beyond the as‐sprayed level by nucleating fine precipitates.  

4. Trade-offs and pitfalls  
   • If the anneal is too hot or held too long, grain growth near interfaces can oversoften the coating and reduce hardness below the sprayed condition.  
   • Too rapid or uneven heating may induce new thermal cracks along compositional gradients or at sharp corners.  

Summary  
A properly selected post‐spray heat treatment converts mechanically welded networks into diffusion‐bonded, low‐porosity structures with higher tensile strength, fatigue resistance and toughness.  Depending on the alloy and temper route, you may either lose some hardness (simple anneal) or gain it (precipitation‐hardening heat treat).

Particle impact velocity (v) in cold gas–dynamic spraying controls the kinetic energy available for plastic deformation, bonding and microstructure evolution—so it is the key “tuning knob” for hardness and residual stresses in the coating.  In broad strokes:

1. Bonding regime and microstructure  
   • Below the critical velocity (Vc, typically 300–500 m/s for metals):  
     – Particles rebound or lightly deform.  
     – Deposits are poorly bonded, highly porous, with coarse, largely undeformed grains.  
   • Near and above Vc (500–800 m/s):  
     – Severe plastic deformation at impact leads to adiabatic shear instabilities at particle interfaces.  
     – Oxide films are fragmented and dispersed; a dense, lamellar (splat‐like) microstructure forms.  
     – Extremely fine subgrains or dynamically recrystallized zones (100 nm–1 μm) develop at interfaces.  
   • Very high velocities (>800–1000 m/s):  
     – Further grain refinement and interface mixing may occur, but excessive velocity can promote particle rebound, microcracking or substrate damage.

2. Hardness  
   • Rises monotonically with v once you exceed Vc, for two reasons:  
     1. Work hardening – higher impact strain increases dislocation density.  
     2. Grain‐size strengthening – finer subgrain and recrystallized structures.  
   • Typical hardness increases of 20–50 % over the feedstock are reported as v increases from just above Vc to the practical maximum.

3. Residual stress  
   • Peening‐induced compressive stress:  
     – Each high‐velocity particle acts like a micro‐peening shot, imparting compressive stress in the deposit.  
     – Compressive residual stress magnitude increases with v (and mass flow) as impact energy grows.  
   • Thermal‐mismatch tensile stress:  
     – The gas preheat temperature and any localized adiabatic heating at impact can produce tensile stresses on cooling.  
     – In practice, at moderate v the peening‐induced compression dominates, but at very high temperature or velocity the tensile component can rise and partially offset the compressive stress.  
   • Net effect: moderate‐high v yields coatings with significant compressive stress (–100 to –400 MPa), which improves fatigue and wear resistance.

Summary of trends as v rises above the critical bonding velocity:  
  – Porosity ↓  
  – Interface bonding strength ↑  
  – Subgrain size ↓; dislocation density ↑  
  – Hardness ↑  
  – Net compressive residual stress ↑ (until thermal effects begin to counteract)

Ceramic particles (e.g. Al₂O₃, SiC, TiC or WC) boost the wear resistance of cold‐sprayed metal–matrix coatings by several synergistic mechanisms:

1. Load‐bearing “micro-balloons”  
   • Hard particles protrude from the softer metal matrix and directly carry the normal and tangential loads during sliding or abrasion.  
   • This reduces the real area of metal‐to‐metal contact and therefore cuts adhesive and plowing wear.

2. Matrix hardening and dispersion strengthening  
   • Well‐dispersed ceramics impede dislocation motion (Orowan mechanism) and refine the metal grain structure locally (particle‐stimulated nucleation), raising the yield strength and hardness of the composite.  
   • A harder matrix resists plastic flow and subsurface crack initiation under repeated contact loads.

3. Crack deflection and bridging  
   • Embedded ceramics deflect or blunt propagating cracks in the metal matrix.  
   • Particles behind a crack tip can bridge the crack faces, increasing the energy needed for crack growth and thus delaying coating spallation.

4. Formation of protective tribofilms  
   • Under sliding contact, some ceramics react (or generate oxide debris) that forms a thin, hard tribofilm on the sliding surface.  
   • This film lowers the friction coefficient and further shields the matrix from direct abrasive attack.

5. Microstructural tailoring at the interface  
   • Cold spray can embed particles just beneath the free surface or grain‐refine locally at particle–matrix interfaces, producing a graded hardness profile that optimally resists wear while retaining substrate adhesion.

Together, these effects turn the metal–matrix composite into a much harder, tougher, and lower‐friction surface than a neat cold‐sprayed metal, dramatically improving abrasion, erosion, and sliding wear resistance.

Post‐spray heat treatment of cold‐sprayed Ti deposits is typically carried out in two regimes: (1) low‐temperature “stress‐relief” anneals (≈300–600 °C) below the β‐transus, and (2) higher‐temperature anneals up to or above the β‐transus (≈800–1000 °C). In both cases the goal is to modify the highly strained, particle‐bonded as‐sprayed microstructure and thus tune strength, hardness and ductility.  

1. Microstructural evolution  
  • Recovery (300–600 °C):  
    – Partial annihilation of dislocations introduced by particle impact.  
    – Relief of compressive/tensile residual stresses.  
    – Slight coarsening of subgrains without full recrystallization.  
  • Recrystallization (≥600 °C):  
    – Nucleation of equiaxed α grains at particle boundaries and deformation bands.  
    – Growth of new strain‐free grains, elimination of high‐angle boundaries formed by severe plastic deformation.  
    – Reduction in inter‐particle porosity as diffusion‐controlled neck growth closes microvoids.  
  • α↔β phase transformations (approaching/transcending β‐transus):  
    – Above ~880 °C α→β transition, followed by controlled cooling to obtain refined α+β or Widmanstätten α.  
    – Tailoring of lamellar microstructure to balance strength and toughness.  

2. Mechanical‐property changes  
  • Hardness and strength:  
    – Stress‐relief anneals reduce microhardness (∼10–20 %) as dislocation density drops.  
    – Recrystallization further lowers yield and ultimate tensile strength by removing strain hardening.  
  • Ductility and toughness:  
    – Tensile elongation and reduction of area increase substantially (often doubling) after recrystallization.  
    – Fatigue crack‐initiation life improves due to lower residual stress and closed porosity.  
  • Bonding and cohesion:  
    – Enhanced inter‐particle diffusion bonding raises interlamellar cohesive strength, reducing interfacial decohesion under load.  

In practice, selecting anneal temperature/time trades off: lower T for modest stress relief with minimal strength loss; higher T for full recrystallization, maximum ductility and optimal fatigue performance.

Moderate‐temperature annealing of cold-sprayed Cu coatings (typically 150–400 °C for 0.5–2 h) drives recovery and the onset of static recrystallization in the heavily work-hardened, high–stored‐energy regions at particle–particle interfaces.  In practice you observe:

1. Microstructural changes  
   • Dislocation rearrangement and annihilation—cell structures and tangles formed during spraying begin to recover.  
   • Nucleation of new, nearly strain-free equiaxed grains (especially at prior particle boundaries).  Grain size coarsens from sub-µm fragments toward 1–2 µm (depending on time/T).  
   • Partial healing of micro-voids and cracks; oxide fragments at splat boundaries may “wet” adjoining Cu and improve metallurgical bonding.  
   • Relief of residual tensile stresses built up during impact.

2. Mechanical‐property changes  
   • Hardness/HV: drops by ≈20–40 % (e.g. from ~120–140 HV as-sprayed to ~70–100 HV after anneal).  
   • Yield/tensile strength: decreases by ~10–30 % as dislocation density falls and grain-boundary strengthening is reduced.  
   • Ductility/elongation: increases substantially (from a few % in the as-sprayed, very brittle state to 8–15 % or more, depending on anneal severity).  
   • Bond strength/cohesion: increases, shifting fracture mode from interparticle decohesion to more uniform ductile failure.  
   • Electrical and thermal conductivity: improve toward bulk Cu values as defects and micro-voids heal.

3. Trade-offs and optimization  
   • Too low a T or too short a time gives only partial recovery (hardness remains high, joint strength limited).  
   • Too high a T (≫400 °C) or long time leads to excessive grain growth, over-softening and possible oxidation.  

In summary, a moderate (200–350 °C, ~1 h) anneal is often chosen to strike the best balance: significant hardening relief and ductility gain, improved interparticle bonding and conductivity, with only a moderate sacrifice in strength.

Particle size in gas‐atomized powders controls the droplet cooling rate during solidification, and that in turn fixes the as‐atomized microstructure (dendrite/cell spacing, grain size, solute distribution, defect density) and thus the powder’s own mechanical strength—and, by extension, the behavior of cold‐spray deposits made from those powders.  The key points are:

1. Cooling‐rate vs. particle diameter  
   •  Approximate cooling‐time τ scales with the square of the droplet radius R (τ ∼ R²/α, where α is thermal diffusivity).  
   •  Small particles (say < 20 μm) cool at 10⁵–10⁶ K/s, large ones (50–150 μm) at 10³–10⁴ K/s.

2. Microstructural refinement  
   •  Higher cooling rates in fine droplets produce very fine cellular or dendritic substructures, with second‐arm spacings (SDAS) down in the hundreds of nanometers to low‐micron range.  
   •  Coarser droplets develop SDAS of several microns, pronounced microsegregation, and even shrinkage voids if solidification is very slow.

3. Solute trapping and supersaturation  
   •  Fine powders quench so rapidly that they retain solute in solid solution well beyond equilibrium limits—supplying solid‐solution strengthening.  
   •  Coarse powders allow more partitioning and precipitation, reducing that strengthening contribution.

4. Grain size and defect density  
   •  Ultrafine powders can form nanocrystalline or subgrain structures and accumulate high dislocation densities (quench strains), both of which raise yield strength via Hall–Petch and work‐hardening terms.  
   •  Larger powders typically show larger grains and fewer stored defects, so they are softer.

5. Resulting mechanical strength (powder‐intrinsic)  
   •  Hardness or yield strength of the powders themselves rises as particle size falls—for many alloy systems a twofold drop in diameter can boost hardness by 20–40%.  
   •  Small‐particle powders can be brittle or highly oxidized at the surface, a trade‐off for their higher strength.

6. Implications for cold‐spray deposits  
   •  Finer, harder particles deform plastically upon impact more readily (they start “cold‐welding” at lower particle velocities) and tend to produce denser, higher‐strength coatings—provided surface oxides and flow issues are managed.  
   •  Coarse, softer powders require higher spray velocities and often yield coatings with more porosity and weaker interparticle bonds.

Summary: decreasing gas‐atomized powder size raises quench rate, refines dendrite spacing and grains, increases solute supersaturation and dislocation density—all of which boost the powder’s intrinsic strength and improve cold‐spray deposit density and strength (up to practical limits set by oxidation, flowability, and embrittlement).

Rapid solidification during gas‐atomization typically imposes cooling rates on the order of 10^3–10^6 K/s in metal droplets.  The main consequences for powder microstructure and ensuing mechanical behavior are:

1. Grain/Cellular Refinement  
   • Submicron dendrite-arm spacing or fully cellular structures form.  
   • Very fine equiaxed grains (tens to hundreds of nanometers) dramatically increase grain‐boundary area.

2. Supersaturation and Metastable Phases  
   • Solute atoms are trapped in solid solution beyond equilibrium limits.  
   • Metastable intermetallics or amorphous pockets may form if alloy glass‐forming ability is high.

3. Reduced Segregation  
   • Short solidification times curtail macro­segregation; composition is more homogeneous across each particle.  
   • Microsegregation is confined to very narrow interdendritic channels.

4. Elevated Defect Density  
   • High dislocation densities, vacancy supersaturation, and residual stresses “freeze in” during fast passage through the solidus.  
   • These defects can act as nucleation sites for precipitation during downstream heat treatment.

5. Powder Morphology and Porosity  
   • Nearly spherical particles with smooth surfaces result from melt‐droplet reshaping under surface tension.  
   • Internal porosity is minimized—but any entrapped gas forms tiny closed pores.

Mechanical-Property Impacts

1. As‐Atomized Powder  
   – High microhardness from grain‐boundary strengthening and solid-solution hardening.  
   – Elevated yield strength (often 2–3× bulk values) but reduced ductility in the as-sprayed condition.  

2. After Consolidation (e.g. AM, Hot Isostatic Pressing)  
   – Retention of fine grains and supersaturated matrix enables higher strength and hardness in the consolidated part.  
   – Subsequent aging can precipitate nanoscale second phases more uniformly, boosting strength (precipitation hardening).  
   – Minimised segregation and refined microstructure improve toughness relative to conventionally solidified alloys of the same composition.

In sum, rapid solidification in gas atomization produces ultra‐fine, compositionally uniform, often metastable powders whose high defect density and fine grain size translate into superior as-atomized hardness/strength and excellent strengthening response after post‐processing heat treatments.

Below is a concise, technical summary of how successive high-velocity impacts in a cold-sprayed cermet coating affect crack density, deposition efficiency and hardness.

1. Crack density  
   • First few impacts on a bare substrate produce high local strain rates in the brittle ceramic fraction, nucleating micro-cracks at splat boundaries and along ceramic–metal interfaces.  
   • Subsequent impacts act like repeated miniature “hammers,” plastically deforming and cold-welding the metal phase around ceramic splinters. This mechanical forging tends to close or blunt existing micro-cracks (“crack healing”) even as it may generate new, finer cracks.  
   • Net effect: after an initial peak in crack density, further passes reduce macroscopic crack networks and porosity; residual cracks become smaller, better distributed, and more tortuous, improving toughness.

2. Deposition efficiency  
   • Defined as (mass of material retained in the coating)/(mass of powder shot).  
   • Early in the build, the roughened substrate and ductile metal binder promote high impact adhesion of both metal and ceramic particles.  
   • As the coating thickens:  
     – The surface impedance mismatch between incoming particles and an already-hardened layer grows, increasing particle rebound (erosion) and lowering incremental gain per pass.  
     – Local temperature rise (from repeated adiabatic shear) softens the metal binder, which can partially counteract the impedance rise and temporarily boost deposition efficiency.  
   • Net effect: deposition efficiency typically climbs over the first few tens of microns of build-up (because of work-softening and better base roughness), peaks, then gradually falls off as the coating stiffens and rebounds more particles.

3. Hardness  
   • Every particle impact drives severe plastic deformation into the metal binder, creating dense dislocation networks, refining grains to submicron size, and locking in compressive residual stresses.  
   • Ceramic splinters become more uniformly dispersed and better encapsulated, providing strong dispersion strengthening.  
   • As passes accumulate:  
     – The metal phase work-hardens rapidly at first, so hardness rises steeply.  
     – Once a steady-state balance of strain hardening vs. any dynamic recovery (from local heating) is reached, further passes yield only minor additional hardness gains.  
   • Typical profile: a steep rise over the first few hundred microns of coating thickness, then a plateau at or above the fully strain-hardened limit of the metal binder.

Summary  
– Early passes: high crack density + rising deposition efficiency + sharp hardness increase.  
– Mid-build: crack healing begins, deposition efficiency peaks, hardness approaches plateau.  
– Late-build: net crack density falls to a low, fine scale; deposition efficiency slowly declines; hardness stabilizes near its maximum.

Warm rolling a cold-sprayed Al-alloy deposit works like an in‐situ severe-plastic-deformation and light anneal in one step.  By rolling at an elevated but sub-recrystallization temperature (typically 150–300 °C) you:

 1. Mechanically close pores and cracks  
    – The compressive shear stress from the rolls collapses voids and forces particles into intimate contact.  
    – Oxide films at the particle boundaries are fractured or “smeared out,” exposing fresh metal surfaces.  

 2. Drive extensive plastic flow and oxide disruption  
    – Particles elongate and flatten, increasing the area of metal-metal contact.  
    – Strain at the interfaces causes high dislocation densities that cross originally discrete particles.  

 3. Activate dynamic recovery and local recrystallization  
    – The warm condition allows some dislocation annihilation and subgrain formation, reducing work-hardening and embrittlement.  
    – New, ultra-fine grains nucleate at the former particle boundaries and grow across them, creating a continuous, bonded microstructure.  

Taken together, these effects (void closure, oxide‐film degradation, subgrain bridging, and grain refinement) convert a brittle, porous cold spray build-up into a near-fully dense, fine-grained material.  The result is far stronger interparticle bonding and a substantial gain in ductility compared with the as-sprayed deposit.

In cold spray the overriding requirement for particle–substrate bonding is that, upon high-velocity impact, a very narrow shear zone forms at the interface in which plastic work is converted almost entirely into heat faster than it can be conducted away.  That localized heating drives adiabatic shear instability (ASI), which in turn produces the jetting, intimate metal–metal contact, and dynamic recrystallization that “weld” the particle to the substrate.  Three substrate properties enter into that picture:

 1.  Thermal conductivity (k) and volumetric heat capacity (ρ·cₚ)  
    •  They set the thermal‐diffusion time scale τ_th ≃ L²/(k/(ρcₚ)), where L is the effective shear‐band thickness.  
    •  High k or high ρcₚ → fast heat removal → lower peak temperatures → less softening → ASI suppression.  
    •  Low k and/or low ρcₚ → heat remains localized → rapid temperature rise → flow‐stress collapse in a narrow band → ASI onset at lower impact velocities.

2.  Yield strength (σᵧ) and strain‐hardening behavior  
    •  ASI is promoted when the flow stress is high enough to confine plastic deformation into a very thin zone.  Above a certain σᵧ, the shear‐band thickness shrinks, the strain rates within it climb, and more plastic work per unit volume is converted to heat.  
    •  If the substrate is too soft (low σᵧ), the deformation is distributed over a thicker zone, dilution of heating delays or prevents ASI, and the particle merely flattens without strong metallurgical bonding.  
    •  Conversely, a very high‐strength substrate may demand higher impact velocities to reach the threshold stress for ASI—but once that threshold is passed, localization is extreme and bonding is excellent.

3.  Density (ρ) via acoustic impedance and inertial effects  
    •  The substrate’s acoustic impedance Z = ρ·c controls how much of the impact pressure is transmitted into the particle vs. reflected back.  A higher‐ρ substrate generally produces a higher peak interface pressure and higher initial strain rates in the particle–substrate contact zone.  That accelerates plastic work‐to‐heat conversion.  
    •  Inertia (∼ρ) also sets how deeply the substrate “gives” under the particle.  A heavier (higher‐ρ) substrate moves less, focusing deformation—and hence heating—into a thinner region.

How they work together  
 •  The critical condition for ASI is that the heating rate via plastic dissipation, Ẇ ≃ σ·ε̇, outstrips the cooling rate via conduction.  Since ε̇ is driven by interface pressure (which scales with Z and impact velocity) and σ is the substrate’s flow stress, higher ρ·Z and σ drive Ẇ up.  Opposing them is the term k/(ρcₚ) in the thermal‐diffusion equation.  
 •  In practice, the most favorable substrates for ASI‐driven bonding in cold spray are those that have (a) moderate-to‐high yield strength so shear localizes, (b) high density to boost impact pressure and strain rate, and (c) relatively low thermal diffusivity so heat does not leak away.  Such substrates let you reach the ASI threshold at lower particle speeds and produce stronger, metallurgically bonded deposits.

During cold spray deposition, metal powder particles are accelerated to supersonic velocities and plastically deform upon impact.  The severe, high‐strain‐rate deformation that occurs in both the particles and the substrate leads to work hardening of the deposited metal matrix coating by the following sequence:

1. Severe Plastic Deformation  
   • Impact strains often exceed several hundred percent at strain rates on the order of 10^6–10^9 s⁻¹.  
   • Particles undergo flattening (“snowplow” or jetting) and bond by intimate metallic contact.

2. Dislocation Generation and Multiplication  
   • The high shear stresses at the impact interface generate very high dislocation densities (10¹³–10¹⁵ m⁻²).  
   • Dislocations multiply via Frank–Read sources and intersect to form tangles and cell structures.

3. Dislocation Interaction (“Forest Hardening”)  
   • Moving dislocations become pinned by forest dislocations, increasing the critical resolved shear stress.  
   • Pinning and pile‐up raise the yield strength (Taylor hardening).

4. Grain Subdivision and Refinement  
   • Dislocation walls evolve into subgrain and low‐angle boundaries.  
   • In some alloys, dynamic recrystallization at locally elevated temperatures refines grains to submicron sizes.  
   • Grain‐boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect) further elevates hardness and strength.

5. Layer‐by‐Layer Peening  
   • Successive particle impacts impart further plastic deformation, maintaining a high dislocation density throughout the growing coating.  
   • A hardness gradient often results, with peak hardness near the surface region of most intense deformation.

Overall, the combination of extreme strain, ultrahigh strain rate, and repeated “cold peening” produces a fine, highly dislocated microstructure.  This work‐hardened metal matrix resists further plastic flow, giving cold‐spray coatings their characteristic high hardness and strength.

In cold‐sprayed metal–matrix composite coatings, the addition of hard ceramic powders (Al₂O₃, SiC, TiC, etc.) raises the measured microhardness of the ductile metal matrix by three interrelated mechanisms:

1. Dispersion (Orowan) strengthening  
   • Each ceramic particle acts as an impenetrable obstacle to dislocation glide.  
   • Moving dislocations bow around the particles, leaving behind Orowan loops.  
   • The increase in shear stress required to bypass a given particle spacing Δ scales roughly with Gb/Δ (G = shear modulus, b = Burgers vector).

2. Grain‐refinement (Hall–Petch)  
   • At the high strain rates and plastic strains imparted by cold spray, new ultrafine grains nucleate preferentially at particle–matrix interfaces.  
   • The refined grain size d strengthens via σy ≈ σ0 + k·d⁻½ (k = Hall–Petch slope).

3. Residual‐stress and load‐bearing effects  
   • Thermal‐mismatch between metal and ceramic upon cooling induces compressive residual stresses in the metal around each particle—further hindering dislocation motion.  
   • Under an indenter (in a Vickers or Knoop microhardness test), the stiffer ceramic phase carries part of the load and constrains plastic flow in the surrounding metal, elevating the apparent hardness.

Taken together, these strengthening contributions can easily double or triple the as‐sprayed metal’s microhardness, transforming a relatively soft ductile spray deposit into a wear-resistant composite coating.

Stress‐relief and aging treatments play quite different roles in tailoring cold‐spray deposits. In broad terms, stress‐relief promotes recovery of the heavily deformed particle structure, whereas aging (in age‐hardening alloys) promotes precipitation of fine second‐phase particles. Below is a concise breakdown of each treatment’s microstructural effects and the corresponding changes in mechanical behavior.

1. Stress‐relief heat treatment  
   Typical cycle: 200–450 °C for Al‐based alloys (shorter times at the higher end), 300–600 °C for Ti, Ni or Cu alloys.  
   Microstructural changes  
     • Dislocation recovery and partial annihilation: the extremely high dislocation densities introduced by particle impact begin to rearrange into lower‐energy subgrain structures.  
     • Relief of residual tensile/compressive stresses at particle interfaces and across the deposit.  
     • Limited subgrain coarsening but generally no full recrystallization (unless held long or at the upper end of the temperature range).  
     • Healing of vacancy clusters and microvoids at some particle–particle interfaces.  
   Mechanical effects  
     • Yield and ultimate tensile strength decrease by 5–20 % (loss of dislocation‐hardening).  
     • Hardness drops typically 5–15 %.  
     • Ductility, fracture toughness and fatigue life improve by 10–50 %, owing to lower residual stresses and fewer stress concentrators.  

2. Aging (precipitation/phase-transformation) heat treatment  
   Applicable to alloys capable of precipitation hardening, e.g. Al‐Mg‐Si (6xxx), Al‐Zn‐Mg‐Cu (7xxx), some Cu and Ni superalloys. Typical cycle: solution-treat (if needed) + quench + 150–200 °C (Al) for 4–24 h.  
   Microstructural changes  
     • Nucleation and growth of nanoscale precipitates (e.g. GP zones, Mg2Si in Al‐6xxx; η′ or T phases in Al‐7xxx) on dislocations, subgrain boundaries and within subgrains.  
     • Possible coarsening of subgrain structure if aging is carried out at the high end of temperature or for extended times.  
     • Further annihilation of residual vacancy clusters from the as‐sprayed supersaturated state.  
   Mechanical effects  
     • Yield strength and hardness increase by 15–50 % over the as-sprayed or stress-relieved state, often approaching or exceeding wrought‐and‐age‐treated benchmarks.  
     • Ultimate strength rises similarly, but excess coarsening or overaging will reverse peak strength.  
     • Ductility typically decreases by 10–30 % relative to the stress-relieved condition; fracture toughness may also drop if overaging causes coarse precipitates and stress‐concentrating interfaces.  

Practical considerations  
 • For predominantly static or low‐cycle‐fatigue applications where ductility and crack‐arrest performance matter, a low‐temperature stress‐relief (without aging) is often preferred.  
 • For maximum hardness and yield strength in service, a full solution-treat/quench + aging schedule gives the best trade-off, provided overaging is avoided.  
 • The optimal cycle must balance recovery (to relieve spray‐induced stresses) against retention of a fine, heavily strained subgrain network that serves as a fast diffusion pathway for precipitate nucleation.

In cold spray you accelerate metal powder to supersonic speeds (500–1 200 m/s) and slam it onto a substrate without ever melting the feedstock.  The particles undergo extreme, very localized plastic deformation (strain rates 10^6–10^8 s⁻¹) on impact.  That deformation produces:

  • Dislocation multiplication and entanglement—work-hardening the material  
  • Dynamic subgrain formation and even partial dynamic recrystallization—generating ultrafine‐grained (100 nm–1 µm) zones at particle fronts and the interface  
  • A high density of grain boundaries (Hall-Petch strengthening)  
  • A compressive “peening” residual stress state that raises yield strength and impedes crack opening  

In addition, each particle impact jet erodes surface oxides, exposes fresh metal, and welds the particles together under high pressure.  The result is a fully bonded, near‐full‐density coating whose microstructure remains in the heavily strain-hardened, ultrafine‐grained state.  Because there is no post-deposition melting (and thus no grain growth or annealing), you lock in very high dislocation densities and fine grains—and therefore high as-sprayed strength and hardness.

Laser post-treatments of cold-sprayed cermet coatings typically take one of two forms: laser remelting (or re-melt annealing) and laser‐shock peening. Both routes can markedly raise near‐surface hardness and extend wear life, but they do so by somewhat different mechanisms:

1. Laser Remelting  
  • Pore- and Crack-Sealing: A focused laser beam locally melts the top 50–200 µm of the as-sprayed deposit. Rapid re-solidification “heals” inter‐particle porosity and microcracks, boosting the coating’s relative density.  
  • Microstructural Refinement: The ultra-fast cooling rates (10^4–10^6 K/s) during resolidification break up coarse carbides and binder phases into finer lamellae or globules. According to Hall–Petch, this grain refinement raises hardness by 10–30 %.  
  • Phase Transformations: In Co‐ or Ni‐based cermets, laser‐induced heating can partially dissolve carbides into the binder and then re-precipitate them in a more uniform, sub-micron dispersion—further hardening the matrix.  
  • Residual-Stress Adjustment: Thermal cycling can relax tensile residues left by cold spray and even introduce shallow compressive stresses, which hinder crack opening under load.

2. Laser Shock Peening (LSP)  
  • Shock‐Wave Hardening: Sub-nanosecond, high-power pulses generate elastic–plastic shock waves that impart deep compressive residual stresses (up to several hundred MPa, tens to hundreds of microns deep).  
  • Work-Hardening and Dislocation Multiplication: The passage of the shock front refines grains via mechanical twinning or dislocation cell formation, boosting hardness without melting.  

How these changes translate to wear performance  
– Higher microhardness resists abrasive particle cutting and plastic deformation under contact.  
– Fewer surface flaws and pores reduce crack initiation sites for spallation and delamination.  
– Compressive surface stresses from LSP suppress fatigue‐driven microcracking in sliding or rolling contacts.  
– A tighter, more uniform carbide distribution sustains a protective tribo-film during sliding, lowering the friction coefficient and retarding third-body abrasion.

In sum, laser remelting densifies and refines the microstructure via rapid melting/solidification and phase re-distribution, while laser-shock peening mechanically hardens and imprints compressive stresses via shock‐wave plasticity. Both effects synergistically enhance microhardness and markedly improve abrasive, adhesive, and fatigue wear performance of cold-sprayed cermet coatings.

In cold spray you are essentially building a metal–matrix composite coating, so every hard particle you add changes both the as-deposited microstructure and the coating’s properties in fairly predictable ways.  The key points are:

1. Particle embedding and matrix deformation  
   • At typical gas-jet velocities (500–1 200 m/s) the metal splats undergo severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization at their surfaces.  Hard ceramics (WC, SiC, Al2O₃, TiB₂, etc.) don’t deform but instead become “trapped” in the heavily worked metal.  
   • Around each ceramic grain you get an ultrafine or even nanocrystalline metal ring, with very high dislocation density.  That refines the matrix locally and creates high‐strain interfaces where load transfer takes place.

2. Effect on porosity and bonding  
   • Low to moderate ceramic loadings (10–30 vol %) can actually help fill intersplat voids and slightly reduce porosity if the particles nestle into the gaps.  
   • Above a certain fraction (often > 40 vol %), the lack of plastic metal to bond over and around particles drives porosity up and weakens splat–splat cohesion, so deposition efficiency and bond strength drop.

3. Strengthening mechanisms  
   • Orowan/pinning: ceramic particles block dislocation motion, raising yield strength and hardness.  
   • Load transfer: the stiff particles carry part of an applied load, further boosting strength and stiffness.  
   • Grain-refinement: the very fine recrystallized zones around particles elevate strength by the Hall–Petch effect.

4. Trade-offs in mechanical behavior  
   • Hardness, elastic modulus, abrasive- and erosion-resistance all go up, often dramatically.  
   • Tensile elongation and fracture toughness go down because you introduce brittle interfaces and reduce the amount of continuous ductile metal.  
   • Fatigue performance can suffer if particles agglomerate or if you introduce stress concentrators at poorly bonded interfaces.

5. Optimization guidelines  
   • Typical “sweet spots” in industrial practice are around 15–35 vol % ceramic—enough to get most of the wear resistance and stiffness gains while still maintaining a coherent, low‐porosity metal network.  
   • Process parameters (gas temp/pressure, stand-off, powder size) must be tuned so that the metal retains enough malleability to encapsulate the particles without shattering them or leaving them loosely bonded.

In summary, adding hard ceramics to cold-spray feedstock transforms a plain metal coating into a metal–matrix composite with much higher hardness and wear resistance, thanks to Orowan strengthening, load transfer, and local grain refinement—but at the expense of ductility, toughness, and potentially deposition efficiency if the ceramic fraction is pushed too high.

In cold‐gas‐spray (CGS) coatings almost all of the microstructural “driving force” comes from the severe plastic deformation that each particle undergoes on impact.  As a consequence, the harder and finer‐grained regions in a CGS deposit are almost always those that saw the highest local strains.  Conversely, lightly deformed particles or particle cores stay closer to their as-gas-atomized hardness.  In practice this gives rise to a fairly large hardness scatter—often tens of HV—within a single coating.

Key points on how plastic deformation governs local hardness in a CGS coating:

1. Work hardening and dislocation build-up  
   •  Impact strains in a single splat can easily reach true (“Hencky”) strains of 1–3 or more.  
   •  Dislocation densities jump from roughly 10^11–10^12 m–2 in the feedstock to 10^14–10^15 m–2 or higher in the most severely deformed zones.  
   •  The result is classic strain hardening—regions of high equivalent strain indent harder.

2. Adiabatic shear and dynamic recrystallization  
   •  At the very highest local strain rates/strains (typically near splat edges or twin‐jet collision interfaces) adiabatic heating can trigger dynamic recovery or even recrystallization.  
   •  This produces ultrafine—or in extreme cases nanocrystalline—grains in narrow bands, which show a further jump in hardness above what pure dislocation hardening would give.

3. Grain refinement scaling  
   •  Empirically one often sees a Hall–Petch–type relationship in these coatings: grain/subgrain size halves, hardness increases by 20–40 %.  
   •  Nanoindentation maps of many alloys (Ni, Ti, Al) show 20–100 % higher hardness in these ultrafine‐grained shear bands than in the mildly deformed particle interiors.

4. Spatial heterogeneity  
   •  Because each powder particle impacts with a slightly different velocity and angle, and because overlap between splats is never perfectly uniform, the local strain field is highly nonuniform.  
   •  Consequently, microhardness (or nanoindentation) maps through the coating thickness typically show hard spikes at particle–particle interfaces or splat edges and softer valleys in the middle of particles.

5. Process-parameter control  
   •  Raising gas temperature or pressure increases particle velocity, increasing flattening strain—and thus boosting overall hardness (and also increasing its variation).  
   •  Conversely, marginal parameters that only just exceed the critical velocity for bonding give lighter deformation and a coating hardness only slightly above the feedstock value.

In summary, the local hardness in a cold‐spray coating is almost a direct fingerprint of the local plastic strain experienced on impact.  The harder, finer‐grained shear zones mark the regions of greatest deformation, while the softer particle cores reflect zones of lower strain.

Wear under unidirectional sliding is almost always more severe than under oscillating (reciprocating) sliding for cold-sprayed metal coatings because the mechanics of material removal, debris handling, and tribolayer formation are fundamentally different:

1. Directional ploughing and cutting  
   – In unidirectional sliding the same asperities and reinforcement particles continuously gouge the counterface (and each other) in one fixed direction. That leads to deeper, aligned furrows and more efficient chip formation.  
   – In an oscillating test the reversal of motion tends to “polish out” shallow scratches, re-distribute debris, and reduce the net cutting depth per stroke.

2. Debris entrapment vs. protective glaze formation  
   – Unidirectional sliding generally ejects wear debris to the side of the contact, so there is little opportunity for a coherent third-body layer to form. Fresh metal and hard inclusions are constantly exposed to high local stresses and temperatures.  
   – Under reciprocation debris is more likely to be trapped in the contact, compacted, and sintered (or oxidized) into a semi-protective tribofilm. This glaze lowers local contact stresses and friction, and so reduces further material removal.

3. Temperature rise and adhesion  
   – A constant sliding direction produces a steadier heat buildup in the contact, promoting local softening of the spray-deposited lamellae, micro-welding at asperity junctions, and then more severe adhesive pull-out or delamination when those welds break.  
   – In reciprocating motion each reversal acts as a partial “reset” of the contact temperature and stresses, limiting the peak temperature and the size of adhesive junctions.

4. Microcrack nucleation and propagation  
   – Cold-sprayed coatings are built from a stack of heavily deformed metal lamellae with residual stresses and oxide films at interlamellar boundaries. Under unidirectional shear, microcracks that form at lamella interfaces propagate unchecked in the same shear sense, leading quickly to delamination.  
   – With oscillation, reversals tend to close or blunt propagating cracks, slowing down their growth and sometimes even welding them shut under cyclic compression.

Take-away  
Because unidirectional sliding combines continuous, aligned ploughing with poorer tribofilm formation, higher steady-state temperatures, stronger adhesive junctions, and unchecked crack growth in a cold-sprayed microstructure, it produces higher wear rates than oscillating-sliding tests.

Initial microstructure (grain size, dislocation content, boundary character) and the extreme plastic strains imposed during each particle’s supersonic impact work together to set the final hardness of a cold‐sprayed coating.  In essence, a coarse‐grained (“conventional”) powder and a nanocrystalline powder deform by very different mechanisms, so although both see very large local strains at the particle–substrate and particle–particle interfaces, the way they store that strain (and thus harden) is fundamentally different.

1. Initial microstructure sets the “hardness ceiling” and the dominant deformation mode  
  • Conventional (μm‐scale grains, relatively low starting dislocation density)  
     – Deformation is dominated by dislocation slip and multiplication.  
     – Large mean free path for dislocations ⇒ high work‐hardening rate.  
     – Under the several GPa transient pressure at the impact front, dislocation cells and subgrains form, and grains can refine down toward a few hundred nanometers in a heavily deformed zone.  
     – The combination of Hall–Petch grain‐refinement and Taylor‐type dislocation hardening can roughly double or triple the hardness locally.  

  • Nanocrystalline (10–100 nm grains, high boundary density)  
     – Starting hardness is already elevated by the Hall–Petch effect.  
     – Grain boundaries dominate plasticity (boundary sliding, grain‐rotation, Coble‐type diffusional flow) rather than bulk dislocation networks.  
     – The short dislocation mean free path saturates dislocation‐storage hardening almost immediately; further impact strain cannot increase dislocation density appreciably.  
     – Under adiabatic heating spikes, there is even a risk of boundary‐mediated recovery or slight grain growth, so net hardening can be very modest or even slightly negative.  

2. Impact‐induced plastic deformation determines how much additional hardening is possible  
  • In the coarse‐grained powder, each impact drives very large local strains (true strains of order 2–3 or higher in the bond zone).  That converts into:  
     – New dislocations stored in cell walls  
     – Subgrain formation and dynamic recrystallization into ultra‐fine grains  
     – A classic work‐hardening response that raises hardness from ~100–200 HV in the feedstock to 300–400 HV or more in the coating.  

  • In the nanocrystalline powder, each impact produces similarly high local strains but the mechanisms available for strain accommodation (boundary sliding, short‐circuit diffusion) neither store dislocations nor refine grains much further.  Instead:  
     – Grain boundary processes may lead to recovery or coarsening if the instantaneous temperature is high enough (softening).  
     – Net gain in hardness often tops out at a few tens of HV, sometimes less.  

3. Net result for final coating hardness  
  – Conventional CSAM coatings start “soft,” but gain 100–200 HV of work‐hardening and grain‐refinement from impact.  Their final hardness is thus predominantly set by the impact strain history (dislocation‐ and Hall–Petch hardening).  
  – Nanocrystalline CSAM coatings start already hard, but because they cannot store many more dislocations—and because dynamic boundary processes can partially undo hardness—impact adds little further hardening (and may even cause slight softening).  

Quantitatively one often sees:  
  • Coarse‐grained feedstock: ~150 HV → CSAM coating ~300–400 HV  
  • Nanocrystalline feedstock: ~350–400 HV → CSAM coating ~370–420 HV (or in some cases slight drop)  

In short, the interplay is that the larger‐grained material has “room” to accumulate dislocations and refine grains under the severe plastic deformation of cold spray, so it hardens dramatically.  The nanocrystalline material, already at a high hardness state set by its fine grains, cannot significantly increase its dislocation content and is more susceptible to boundary‐mediated recovery, so its final hardness is controlled almost entirely by its original microstructure rather than the spray‐induced deformation.

By combining cryogenic milling with pulsed‐gas‐dynamic spraying you marry two solid‐state, severe‐deformation steps that (1) produce ultrafine, high‐energy powder and then (2) forge it into a nearly pore‐free, nanostructured coating.  The mechanisms at work are:

1. Cryogenic milling  
   • At liquid‐N₂ temperatures repeated ball–powder impacts shatter and rewrite grains, driving them down to 10–100 nm, and pumping in very high dislocation densities.  
   • You end up with metastable, work‐hardened (and often oxide‐free) powders that store a huge amount of strain energy and that have vastly elevated yield strengths.  

2. Pulsed gas‐dynamic (cold) spraying  
   • High‐pressure gas is pulsed through a converging–diverging nozzle to generate a train of shock waves carrying powder particles at supersonic speeds (typically 500–800 m/s).  
   • On impact, each pulse delivers a “micro‐forging” step: particles undergo adiabatic shear, dynamic recrystallization at their interfaces, oxide‐film fracturing, and intense plastic flow.  
   • The pulsed nature (as opposed to steady flow) helps maintain high particle velocities, periodically breaks surface oxides, and gives brief “cool‐offs” so your ultrafine structure isn’t thermally overaged.  

Net effect on the coating  
   • Grain sizes remain in the ultrafine/nano regime because no bulk melting or slow cooling ever occurs.  
   • Each high‐velocity pulse progressively closes gaps and welds particles together in the solid state, driving residual porosity below 1–2 %.  
   • The final microstructure is a dense, nanocrystalline (or heavily dislocated) metal matrix whose Hall–Petch grain‐refinement and work‐hardening from impact give exceptionally high hardness and wear resistance.

In cold-sprayed Al-based composites (for example Al–SiC or Al–Al₂O₃) a modest post-spray anneal will almost always raise both hardness and wear resistance up to an optimum temperature, but if you push the temperature too high the coating softens and wears faster.  In rough terms you see three regimes:

1. Low‐temperature anneal (T < 200 °C)  
   • Recovery of cold‐work residual stresses and slight subgrain coarsening  
   • Very small change (often a slight hardness drop as some dislocations annihilate)  
   • Wear performance similar to the as-sprayed state  

2. Moderate‐temperature anneal (≈200 – 350 °C)  
   • Continued recovery plus the onset of discontinuous recrystallization in the ultrafine Al matrix  
   • Nucleation of nanoscale second‐phase/precipitate particles (for alloys with Si, Cu or Mg)  
   • Healing of interparticle porosity and improved interfacial bonding by solid‐state diffusion  
   • Net effect: peak hardness (substantially higher than as-sprayed) and lowest wear rate  

3. High‐temperature anneal (>350 – 400 °C)  
   • Full recrystallization and rapid grain growth in the Al matrix  
   • Coarsening of strengthening precipitates or potential dissolution of fine phases  
   • Loss of dislocation substructure and over-healing of pores  
   • Result: drop in hardness and an increase in abrasive/adhesive wear  

Microstructurally, the hardness and wear-resistance peak arises from a balance between  
– a high density of newly formed grain boundaries (Hall–Petch strengthening)  
– a dispersion of finely distributed hard second-phase particles or precipitates  
– a reduction in flaw size (closed porosity and healed micro-cracks)  
– sufficient retained dislocations to impede carrier motion but not enough to cause brittleness.

If you plot hardness or wear rate versus anneal temperature you will typically see a broad “sweet spot” around 250–350 °C where the coating is hardest and most wear-resistant. Beyond that, grain‐boundary and precipitate coarsening dominate, and the coating softens.

Increasing the laser‐scan speed in a laser-clad, in-situ combustion-synthesized ceramic composite has three main qualitative effects on both microstructure and hardness:

1. Reduced heat input, faster cooling → finer microstructure  
   • At low scan speeds the melt pool is deep and long‐lived: you get the classical planar–columnar–equiaxed sequence, coarse dendrite arms and large in situ–formed carbides/oxides.  
   • As scan speed goes up, energy per unit length falls, the pool becomes shallower and solidification rates rise.  Planar growth at the substrate interface is suppressed, columnar dendrites are shortened, and equiaxed grains plus very fine ceramic precipitates dominate the clad.

2. Lower substrate dilution → more uniform reinforcement distribution  
   • Slow scans allow extensive mixing with substrate metal: ceramic particles tend to segregate, giving clusters or a graded dispersion and a pronounced hardness drop toward the base.  
   • Faster scans shrink the dilution zone, lock in the reinforcements where they form, and yield a more homogeneous particle distribution through the thickness.

3. Hardness profile flattens (and may rise slightly)  
   • At low speeds you see a strong “high at the face, low at the interface” hardness gradient—coarser carbides + more dilution near the base give a softer region.  
   • With increasing speed the curve levels out as microstructural zones converge in fineness and phase distribution, so hardness becomes almost constant through the clad.  The overall peak hardness often ticks up a bit owing to finer precipitates and reduced dilution.  
   • If the speed is pushed too high, however, the melt pool may become discontiguous, reaction may be incomplete, porosity/voids appear and local hardness (and adhesion) will fall off.

In sum, increasing scan rate drives the coating from a coarse, graded, dendritic microstructure with a steep hardness gradient toward a thin, fine‐grained, equiaxed structure with a nearly uniform (often higher) hardness distribution—provided one stays below the threshold where melting and in-situ reaction become erratic.

Key factors by which cold‐spraying amorphous powders yields very hard, stiff coatings are:

1. Retention of the glassy (amorphous) state  
   • Cold spray is essentially a “solid‐state” process: particle temperatures remain below the glass transition/crystallization regime.  
   • No melting, so the parent amorphous structure—characterized by its dense, topologically locked atomic network and absence of dislocation‐based plasticity—is retained.  
   • Amorphous metals possess intrinsic hardness (5–9 GPa) and high elastic moduli (80–150 GPa) owing to the random but tightly bonded metallic matrix.

2. High‐velocity impact densification  
   • Particles are accelerated to 500–1200 m/s; upon impact they undergo severe plastic flow in localized shear bands, collapse porosity, and forge metallurgical bonds.  
   • Porosities can fall below 1–2%, so the coating’s properties approach those of fully dense bulk glass.

3. Work‐hardening of shear‐band regions
