   • Although the bulk of each particle stays amorphous, the extreme strain‐rates at interparticle and particle–substrate interfaces create very fine‐scale (nanometric) shear bands.  
   • These zones can locally crystallize or generate high dislocation densities, further boosting hardness without significantly lowering overall elastic modulus.

4. Minimal oxidation/intermetallic formation  
   • Cold spray avoids high‐temperature oxidation or brittle intermetallic phases that would otherwise embrittle the coating.

Combined, these effects yield a near‐fully dense, amorphous‐matrix coating, whose random atomic structure delivers high hardness and whose strong metallic bonds produce a high elastic modulus.

When a cold‐sprayed coating is struck by high‐velocity metal particles it ends up as a highly deformed “splat” matrix with  
  • ultrafine or even nanocrystalline grains,  
  • extremely high dislocation density and deformation twins,  
  • locked‐in residual stresses, and  
  • a network of subgrain boundaries that all act as strong barriers to dislocation motion.  

That microstructure gives cold‐spray deposits very high as‐sprayed hardness—but it is thermodynamically metastable. A brief laser scan over the surface (often with a CW or pulsed Nd:YAG or fibre laser at energy densities of 10^5–10^7 W/cm^2) induces a rapid thermal cycle:  

 1. Recovery. Dislocations rearrange into lower‐energy configurations (e.g. forming cell walls or disappearing at grain boundaries). Some vacancy clusters annihilate.  
 2. Recrystallization. Small subgrains consume the most heavily deformed regions and grow into strain‐free, equiaxed grains.  
 3. Grain growth. If the peak temperature approaches 0.4–0.7 Tm (Tm = melting point), recrystallized grains coarsen.  
 4. Stress relief and porosity reduction. Residual tensile/compressive stresses relax, and any micro‐voids or loose interfaces between splats partially close or even remelt and fuse.  

Each of those steps removes dislocation‐based strengthening, widens the average grain size (cutting back Hall–Petch hardening), and lowers internal stresses that previously impeded dislocation motion. The net result is a softened coating with lower Vickers microhardness, more ductile behavior, and often improved corrosion or fatigue resistance because of the healed interfaces and stress relief.

In cold spray you accelerate solid particles to high (often supersonic) velocities and “weld” them onto the substrate purely by impact, without ever melting either the feedstock or the base‐metal. That solid‐state nature is key to the unusually strong adhesion you can get when you spray ceramics onto metals:

1. No Melt ⇒ Minimal Oxide or Intermetallic Layers  
   • Because neither the particles nor the substrate ever cross their melting points, you avoid thick oxide films, brittle reaction zones or shrinkage cracks at the interface.  
   • You get far cleaner, more intimate contact at the particle–substrate boundary.

2. High‐Strain‐Rate Plastic Deformation of the Substrate  
   • Even though the ceramic particles themselves are brittle, they impact against—and locally “hammer”—the metal surface so hard that the metal plastically deforms.  
   • That deformation roughens and work-hardens the substrate, creating micro-anchors (undercuts, folds, shear‐lobes) into which ceramic fragments lock mechanically.

3. Particle Fracture and Mechanical Interlocking  
   • Ceramic particles shatter on impact, and their fragments wedge into the plastically deformed troughs and ridges on the metal.  
   • The result is a highly interdigitated interface—think tiny ceramic teeth biting into the metal.

4. Metallurgical Bonding under Adiabatic Shear  
   • The extreme local strain rates generate adiabatic shear zones at the interface, raising the temperature just enough (hundreds of °C locally) to promote atomic‐scale contact without bulk melting.  
   • Dislocation generation, subgrain formation and even very limited diffusion/recrystallization can occur, giving you a bond that is part mechanical-interlock, part true metallurgical weld.

5. Low Residual Thermal Stress  
   • Since the process runs 50–85% below the melting point of either material, thermal expansion mismatch is minimized.  
   • You end up with a dense, adherent coating and very little cracking or spallation driven by post‐spray cool-down.

Taken together, the solid‐state nature of cold spray delivers a “hammer‐and‐weld” effect: ceramics mechanically interlock into a plastically deformed metal surface while simultaneously forming oxide‐free, high‐strain‐rate metallurgical bonds—all without ever liquefying either partner. That is why cold-sprayed ceramic coatings on metals often exhibit adhesion strengths on the order of tens to hundreds of MPa.

In cold spray, powders accelerated to supersonic velocity impact a substrate and plastically deform without melting. Because the very first particles impinge on a rigid, hard substrate they experience the highest strain rates and most intense adiabatic shear; as you build up subsequent layers, each new particle impacts an increasingly compliant, already-deposited coating. The result is a through-thickness gradient in plastic strain and hence in microstructure and hardness:

1. Substrate–coating interface  
   – Highest impact strain rate and peak stresses.  
   – Adiabatic shear instabilities trigger dynamic recrystallization and ultrafine-grain (UFG) formation in both substrate surface and first layer of particles.  
   – Dislocation densities reach 10^14–10^15 m–2, dramatically raising hardness.

2. Mid-coating region  
   – Intermediate strain rates: still severe plastic deformation but less than at the interface.  
   – A mix of ultrafine and submicron grains, partial dynamic recovery; dislocation density somewhat lower.  
   – Corresponding drop in hardness relative to the interface.

3. Topmost (outer) coating  
   – Lowest strain rates—the incoming particles see a softer target and undergo less deformation.  
   – Grain sizes coarsen slightly; dynamic recovery dominates, reducing dislocation density further.  
   – Hardness is lowest here, though still above the bulk powder value if significant work-hardening occurred.

Key microstructural mechanisms driving the gradient:  
• Severe plastic deformation (SPD) and adiabatic shear at the interface produce ultrafine grains and high dislocation networks.  
• Dynamic recrystallization in the highest-strain zones refines grains to sub-100 nm.  
• As impact energy attenuates through the growing coating, strain energy falls below the threshold for full recrystallization, so grain growth and recovery become more prevalent.  
• Layered build-up on a progressively softer substrate means each successive stratum endures less deformation.  

Together, this evolving balance of strain, strain rate, work-hardening, recovery, and recrystallization yields a continuous hardness profile that peaks at the substrate–coating junction and tapers off toward the free surface.

In cold spray you build up coating thickness one “pass’’ at a time, and each pass both adds material and further plastically deforms (i.e. “peens’’) the layer beneath.  Two things happen as you increase the pass count:

 1. Global porosity falls, but with rapidly diminishing returns.  
    • Pass 1–2: you close the largest interparticle voids and achieve the biggest drop in total porosity.  
    • Pass 3–5: you progressively collapse smaller void networks trapped in prior passes.  
    • Beyond ~6–10 passes (depending on alloy and spray parameters) the curve flattens out—most pores that can be closed are already closed, and additional passes give only marginal gains.  

 2. The through-thickness porosity gradient becomes more uniform, but never quite vanishes.  
    • After the very first pass you already see a strong gradient: near the substrate the stresses are highest (back-pressure is greatest) so porosity is lowest there, while the free surface still contains uncollapsed voids.  
    • With each subsequent pass, the “high-pressure zone’’ moves up through the deposit and collapses pores closer to the free surface; porosity at mid-depth and near the top steadily falls.  
    • Eventually you end up with a low-porosity core and only a thin “skin’’ of slightly higher pore content at the very top.  

Key points to watch for:  
  • Diminishing returns in densification after a handful of passes.  
  • Build-up of residual stress (and even micro‐cracking) if you over-spray without stress‐relief, which can locally reintroduce voids.  
  • A maximum practical thickness set by how well fresh particles can weld into an ever-thickening, work‐hardened layer—past that you no longer reduce porosity effectively.

In cold‐sprayed coatings the as‐deposited microstructure consists of flattened “splats” that are held together largely by mechanical interlocking and very limited atomic bonding at their interfaces.  As you heat such a coating toward a temperature at which surface and grain‐boundary diffusion become active (the “splat‐sintering” window), three things happen simultaneously:

1. Neck growth between adjacent splats increases true contact area and welds previously weak interfaces.  
2. Closed‐pore formation and densification reduce the compliance contributions of voids.  
3. Grain‐boundary sliding and coarsening begin to occur at still higher temperatures, triggering the usual thermal softening.

Because of points (1) and (2), the elastic modulus E(T) no longer falls monotonically with rising temperature in the sintering range.  Instead it shows one of two characteristic deviations from the “as‐sprayed” behavior:

  • A plateau or even a modest increase in E  as you enter the splat‐sintering window, reflecting the sudden stiffening caused by interface welding and porosity reduction.  
  • A markedly reduced slope |dE/dT| as you pass through the sintering range—i.e. the coating retains a higher fraction of its room‐temperature stiffness up to the onset of extensive thermal softening.

After the sintering window closes and bulk diffusion/grain coarsening dominate, E(T) again trends downward with temperature in the conventional way, but from a higher baseline than would have been observed had you never sintered the splats.  The net result is an elastic‐modulus vs. temperature curve with an inflection or plateau centered on the splat‐sintering temperature, followed by the familiar softening at still higher T.

Cold spray (CS) and friction‐stir processing (FSP) are both severe‐plastic‐deformation routes, but they operate at very different temperatures and strain‐rates.  When you apply them sequentially to an Al alloy you typically see the following chain of effects on dislocation density, microstrain and micromechanical properties:

1. Cold Spray Deposition  
   • Extreme strain‐rate (~10^4–10^6 s^–1) particle–substrate impacts  
   • Localized shear at particle interfaces—dislocation densities jump into the 10^14–10^15 m^–2 range  
   • Significant local lattice distortion (“microstrain” from 0.5 up to 1 % by XRD line‐profile analysis)  
   • Work‐hardening: microhardness rises from  ~ 50–70 HV (bulk) up to 80–110 HV in the as-sprayed coating  
   • Microstructure: fragmented subgrains near interfaces, high residual stresses, poorly bonded boundaries and some porosity  

2. Subsequent Friction‐Stir Processing  
   • Temperatures in the stir zone typically 0.4–0.6 T_melt, combined with large plastic strains  
   • Dynamic recovery and continuous dynamic recrystallization reduce dislocation density by roughly one order of magnitude (e.g. down to 10^13–10^14 m^–2)  
   • Microstrain relaxes (XRD shows drop to ~0.2–0.4 %), residual stresses are largely removed  
   • Full consolidation of the coating—elimination of porosity and oxide films  
   • Grain refinement to submicron or low‐micron equiaxed structure (depending on alloy and tool parameters)  
   • Further hardening by grain‐boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch) can push hardness even higher (e.g. up to 100–130 HV) despite the lower dislocation density  
   • Micromechanical tests (e.g. nanoindentation, micro‐pillar compression) show:  
     – Higher yield and flow stresses (benefit from finer grain size)  
     – Improved uniformity of elastic modulus and hardness throughout the stir zone  
     – Often better ductility/toughness than as-sprayed because brittle interfaces have been healed  

Summary of Trends  
   – Dislocation density: very high after CS → reduced (but still above annealed) after FSP  
   – Microstrain: ~0.5–1 % (CS) → ~0.2–0.4 % (FSP)  
   – Hardness (micro): rises in CS step, then can rise further or remain high after FSP thanks to grain refinement and defect homogenization  
   – Micromechanical properties: CS gives high strength but poor cohesion; FSP yields a more uniform, high‐strength, damage‐tolerant microstructure.

In cold‐sprayed Al alloys the room‐temperature hardness is overwhelmingly a “cold‐work” effect (high dislocation density, fragmented powder particles with poor interfacial cohesion).  As you heat the deposit three things happen in parallel—each with its own T-dependence—and the net hardness is simply the sum of their hardening (or softening) contributions:

  1. Dislocation-annihilation (recovery)  
     • On heating, dislocations climb and annihilate, lowering the forest‐dislocation density ρ.  Since  
       ΔH ∝ α G b √ρ, removing dislocations causes softening.  
     • Becomes appreciable typically above 0.3–0.4 Tm of Al (≈150–200 °C) and accelerates rapidly with T.

  2. Inter-splat diffusion bonding (interface strengthening)  
     • Atomic diffusion across the original powder–powder interfaces welds splats together, eliminating microvoids and cracks.  This raises load-bearing area and interface cohesion, giving a modest hardness increase.  
     • The bonding rate follows an Arrhenius law, so it is negligible below ≈100–125 °C, then accelerates up to ≈300 °C before saturating once the interfaces are fully healed.

  3. Precipitate formation (precipitation hardening)  
     • Many Al‐alloys (e.g. 2xxx, 6xxx series) are sprayed in a supersaturated state.  On heating, solute atoms diffuse to form nanoscale precipitates (Mg2Si, Al2Cu, etc.) that pin dislocations (Orowan hardening).  The incremental hardness ΔHprecip ∝ f Gb/dp where f is precipitate volume fraction and dp is particle size.  
     • Nucleation and growth are active in a window (often 150–300 °C) and then coarsening (“overaging”) above ≈300 °C reduces their strengthening effect.

Putting it all together, the hardness H(T) can be thought of as  
H(T) = H0 + ΔHinterface(T) + ΔHprecip(T) – ΔHrecovery(T)  
where H0 is the cold‐spray–induced dislocation hardness at room T.  Typical behavior is:

  • Room T → ≈H0: very high, dominated by dislocations.  
  • Low‐intermediate T (100–150 °C) → slight drop as recovery begins but interfaces only slowly heal.  
  • Moderate T (150–250 °C) → ΔHprecip turns on and ΔHinterface grows faster than ΔHrecovery, often producing a hardness plateau or even a secondary peak.  
  • High T (>300 °C) → overaging/coarsening of precipitates plus runaway recovery (and in some cases grain growth) lead to net softening.

In practice an optimum post‐spray aging or heat‐treatment temperature can be chosen to maximize the sum of interface- and precipitate-strengthening while minimizing dislocation annihilation.

Laser remelting upgrades cold-sprayed coatings from a mechanically “stuck-on,” lamellar, somewhat porous structure to a fully dense, metallurgically bonded, fine-grained layer.  The key mechanisms by which it boosts wear resistance are:  

1. Pore and Oxide Elimination  
   – The laser heats the as-sprayed splats above their melting point, filling or “healing” inter‐splat voids and cracks.  
   – Any surface oxides are dissolved into the molten pool and dispersed or gasified, removing weak interfaces.  

2. Microstructural Homogenization and Refinement  
   – Rapid melting and subsequent chill‐rate solidification (10^3–10^6 K/s) produce very fine, often dendritic or equiaxed grains.  
   – Alloying elements or second-phase particles (e.g. carbides, intermetallics) become uniformly distributed, eliminating local soft spots.  

3. Metallurgical Bonding and Residual Stress  
   – The melted coating re-wets and metallurgically bonds both between splats and, in many cases, to the substrate.  
   – Upon solidification, beneficial compressive residual stresses develop, impeding crack initiation and growth under sliding or abrasive loads.  

4. Surface Smoothing and Hardening  
   – The liquid surface self-levels to some extent, reducing roughness and thus the contact stresses at asperities.  
   – The finer grain size and uniform dispersion of hard phases lead to significantly higher hardness (Hall–Petch strengthening + dispersion strengthening).  

Taken together, these changes—higher density, fewer defects, stronger bonds, finer grains, and a smoother, harder surface—mean that a laser-remelted cold‐sprayed coating resists plastic deformation, crack initiation/propagation, and adhesive or abrasive wear far better than its as‐sprayed counterpart.

Solid‐state deposition processes (cold spray, high‐velocity oxygen fuel with low heat input, friction‐based methods, etc.) impart very high plastic strains and strain rates to the feedstock particles without ever melting them.  This severe plastic deformation fractures and subdivides the original micrometer-scale grains into ultrafine or nanocrystalline sub-grains (10–200 nm).  The resulting coating microstructure and its superior wear behavior can be attributed to several interrelated factors:

1. Grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect)  
   • Nanocrystalline grains provide a very high density of high‐angle grain boundaries that impede dislocation motion.  
   • Hardness and yield strength rise sharply as grain size drops into the sub-micron or nanometer regime, directly reducing plastic deformation under tribological contact and thereby lowering abrasive and adhesive wear rates.

2. Enhanced toughness and crack‐arrest capability  
   • The fine, equiaxed grain network interrupts and blunts propagating cracks more effectively than the columnar or dendritic structures typical of fusion‐deposited coatings.  
   • Residual compressive stresses—induced by peening of high‐velocity impact—further inhibit crack opening under cyclic or impact loading.

3. Superior interparticle bonding and low defect content  
   • Since particles never melt, oxide films and micro-cracks that readily form during rapid solidification in fusion sprays are avoided.  
   • High‐strain, solid-state bonding closes porosity and welds particles metallurgically, yielding coatings with densities often above 99% of theoretical.  Lower porosity and minimized oxide‐rich interfaces translate directly into higher wear resistance.

4. Stable tribofilm formation  
   • Uniform, ultrafine grain surfaces oxidize in a controlled manner under sliding conditions, forming thin, adherent tribofilms that reduce direct metal–metal contact.  
   • In fusion-deposited coatings, coarse dendritic grains and entrapped oxides fracture more easily, spalling the protective film and accelerating wear.

By contrast, melting-based methods produce coarser dendritic microstructures, higher residual tensile stresses, entrapped oxides, and porosity.  These features combine to lower hardness, facilitate crack nucleation and propagation, and disrupt protective tribofilm stability, all of which degrade wear performance compared to nanostructured, solid-state deposits.

The key point is that in a cold‐sprayed metal deposit almost all of the electrical resistance in the “in‐plane” direction (i.e. parallel to the substrate) comes from particle–particle interfaces, and those interfaces are either metal‐to‐metal contacts or thin films of oxide trapped between particles.  How the original oxide scale on the powder evolves—either growing and remaining intact or fracturing and being expelled during impact—therefore controls how much of the inter‐particle contact area is true metal/metal (good conductor) versus oxide/metal or oxide/oxide (poor conductor).

1.  Initial oxide on the powder  
    •  Grown in the feedstock preparation (thermal exposure, air‐cooling, etc.) via the usual parabolic‐law oxidation.  
    •  Typically a few nanometers to a few hundred nanometers thick, depending on alloy, temperature and time.  

2.  What happens to that oxide in flight and on impact  
    a.  In–flight oxidation may add a very thin new layer, but it is the impact that dominates:  
       –  Particle surfaces are rapidly heated and plastically deformed.  
       –  The oxide, being brittle, cracks, delaminates, and is either ejected into the growing coating (as fine debris) or swept aside at the splat boundaries.  
    b.  Two limiting behaviors can occur at the splat interfaces:  
       1.  Brittle fracture + ejection of oxide fragments → exposes fresh metal at the interface → low contact resistance → high local conductivity.  
       2.  Partial spall but incomplete removal → a continuous or semi‐continuous insulating film remains trapped at the interface → high contact resistance → low conductivity.  

3.  Net effect on in‐plane conductivity  
    •  If most of the oxide is successfully fractured and expelled, the splats weld together metal‐to‐metal over large true contact areas.  The deposit then approaches the bulk metal’s conductivity (typically 50–70% IACS for a well‐consolidated cold spray copper or aluminum coating).  
    •  If the oxide is too thick, too adherent, or if the impact energy is insufficient to fully crack it, then oxide patches remain at many of the inter‐particle contacts.  Each patch acts as a tunnel barrier or an insulating inclusion, and the in‐plane conductivity can drop precipitously (often into the single‐digit %IACS range).  

4.  Practical implications  
    –  Lowering the initial oxide thickness (e.g. by annealing in a reducing atmosphere, or using powders with thinner native oxide) makes it easier for impact to clear the scale.  
    –  Raising particle impact velocity (higher gas temperature or pressure) increases the degree of plastic deformation and oxide fracture.  
    –  Post‐spray heat treatments can further break up residual oxides or promote diffusion bonding across thin oxide films, but they must be carefully controlled to avoid re‐oxidation.

In summary, the “evolution mechanism” of the oxide scale—from a coherent, load‐bearing film on the as‐received powder to a fractured, ejected debris layer during impact—governs how much of the interparticle interface is conductive metal/metal rather than insulating oxide.  That fraction of true metal‐metal contact directly sets the in‐plane electrical conductivity of the cold‐sprayed deposit.

In cold‐spray additive manufacturing, bonding of powder particles to the substrate (and to previously deposited layers) proceeds by the following chain of physical‐mechanical events:

1. Gas‐acceleration and impact  
   • Powder is accelerated to supersonic or high subsonic speeds (300–1,200 m/s) in a high‐pressure gas jet.  
   • Upon impact, a strong compressive shockwave is launched into both the particle and the substrate (or underlying deposit).

2. Extreme plastic deformation  
   • The shock stresses far exceed the yield strength → very high strain rates (10^5–10^7 s⁻¹) develop.  
   • The particle “pancakes” and spreads laterally; huge plastic work is done at and near the interface.

3. Adiabatic shear localization and jet formation  
   • Plastic‐work heating at the particle rim and interface leads to local softening (“adiabatic shear band”).  
   • Material at the periphery is expelled outward in a high‐velocity micro‐jet.  
   • This jetting action scrapes away surface oxides, adsorbates, and any entrapped gas.

4. Exposure of fresh metal‐metal contact  
   • With oxide and gas film removed, atomically clean surfaces are brought into intimate contact under high pressure (multi–GPa) and shear.

5. Metallurgical bonding and mechanical interlocking  
   • Under the combined action of pressure, shear, and high dislocation density, dynamic recrystallization or recovery can occur at the interface.  
   • Mechanical interlocking of the distorted crystal lattices plus atomic diffusion across the intimate contact area produces a metallurgical bond—without global melting.

6. Layer build‐up  
   • Successive particles impact and bond to the growing deposit, repeating steps 1–5 to build complex 3D geometries.

Key point: Bonding in cold spray is driven by extreme plastic deformation, adiabatic shear‐induced jetting (oxide removal), and intimate high‐pressure metal contact leading to solid‐state metallurgical joining.

Because each new particle impact plastically deforms not only the incoming powder but also the existing deposit, the bottom‐most layers—those pressed directly against the rigid substrate—see the most severe, constrained deformation. In effect:  
1. Substrate backing prevents free bulging, so bottom layers experience higher impact stresses and larger plastic strains.  
2. That intense, repeatedly imposed strain produces very high dislocation densities (and in some alloys even adiabatic‐shear‐induced grain refinement), boosting hardness by work-hardening.  
3. As the coating builds up, the growing deposit is more compliant and absorbs part of the impact energy, so the top layers are plastically deformed less severely (and may undergo more recovery), yielding a softer, lower-hardness surface.

Amorphous coatings made by cold spray routinely out‐perform their HVOF counterparts in thermal stability for three related reasons:  

1. Low Thermal Exposure  
   • Cold spray velocities (300–1200 m/s) deposit material almost entirely by plastic deformation rather than by melting.  
   • The powder and deposit never see high furnace‐type temperatures, so the feedstock’s fully amorphous structure is “locked in” with very little in‐process relaxation or crystallization.  

2. Minimal Oxidation and Heterogeneous Nucleation Sites  
   • HVOF’s 2,500–3,000 K flame partially melts particles and oxidizes them, creating fine oxides and nanocrystals that act as potent nucleation sites during subsequent heating.  
   • Cold-sprayed coatings remain largely oxide-free and single‐phase amorphous, so there are far fewer “seeds” on which crystals can grow.  

3. High Stored Mechanical Energy with Suppressed Diffusion  
   • The extreme strain rates at particle–substrate interfaces introduce high dislocation densities and free volume, raising the activation energy for long‐range diffusion.  
   • Compressive residual stresses locked into the deposit further inhibit atomic rearrangement.  
   • As a result, the glass-transition and crystallization onset temperatures (Tx) shift upwards, often by 50–100 °C relative to HVOF deposits of the same chemistry.  

In contrast, HVOF’s high thermal input both partially crystallizes the melt and embeds oxide inclusions, lowering the temperature at which devitrification begins. Cold spray’s “solid‐state” approach thus yields amorphous coatings that stay amorphous to higher service temperatures.

During cold‐spray deposition of nanocrystalline metals, each powder particle undergoes two very different deformation regimes: a largely undeformed core and an intensely sheared peripheral “bonding” zone.  This bimodal deformation pattern explains why the particle interiors retain their original hardness while the particle–particle interfaces become locally even harder.  

1.  Limited deformation in the particle cores  
   •  Subsonic/persistent gas flow conditions and the short (<μs) contact time prevent heat build-up or extensive strain beyond the outer shell.  
   •  As a result, the original nanocrystalline grain structure and dislocation density of the feedstock powder survive in the particle cores, preserving the feedstock hardness.  

2.  Extreme plastic deformation at interfaces  
   •  Upon impact, the contact zone experiences strain rates on the order of 105–107 s–1 and localized adiabatic heating.  
   •  This combination drives severe dislocation multiplication, dynamic recovery, and in many alloys dynamic recrystallization or continuous grain‐refinement to sub-50 nm dimensions.  
   •  The newly formed ultra-fine or nanograins at the interface exhibit Hall–Petch strengthening and a very high dislocation density, so the interface hardness markedly exceeds that of the original feedstock.  

3.  Residual stress and work‐hardening contributions  
   •  The high-strain‐rate shear zones lock in compressive residual stresses that further impede dislocation motion.  
   •  Accumulated geometric strain (grain boundary and Taylor hardening) in the interfacial nanograins adds yet another hardness increment.  

In sum, cold spray capitalizes on the “core–shell” nature of each bonded particle: an undeformed, feedstock-hard core surrounded by a highly refined, work-hardened, and strain-strengthened interfacial shell.

Substrate hardness enters cold spray in two principal ways—by controlling how the kinetic energy of an incoming particle is partitioned between particle and substrate, and by setting the ease with which that substrate can plastically flow at the impact site.  Both ultimately show up in (a) how the particle “flattens” and (b) how intimate the particle–substrate contact zone becomes.  

1. Strain partitioning and particle deformation  
 • Soft substrate (low hardness)  
   – A significant fraction of the particle’s kinetic energy is absorbed in substrate deformation.  
   – The substrate yields locally, forming a shallow “bowl” or crater into which the particle can embed.  
   – Particles exhibit extensive lateral spreading and jetting at the rim; adiabatic‐shear instabilities can develop at the interface.  
   – The high contact strain and fresh metal exposure promote both mechanical interlocking and localized metallurgical bonding (dynamic recrystallization, grain refinement, possibly even amorphous or nanocrystalline interfacial layers).  

 • Hard substrate (high hardness)  
   – The substrate barely plastically deforms, so most energy must be dissipated in the particle.  
   – Particle flattening is reduced, contact areas are smaller and more dome‐like, and jetting is minimal or absent.  
   – Achieving the critical impact velocity for bonding is harder—particles may rebound or only partially adhere.  
   – Bonding relies more on adiabatic shear within the particle itself and less on interfacial mixing or mechanical interlocking.  

2. Interface morphology  
 • On soft substrates you typically see  
   – Deep particle embeds with circumferential jetting.  
   – Wavy, highly convoluted interfaces with interdigitated flow lines (“onion rings” in the particle).  
   – A narrow but highly deformed interfacial zone (recrystallized grains, ultrafine structure).  

 • On hard substrates you typically see  
   – Shallow, flatter contacts with little to no jetting.  
   – Relatively smooth, planar interfaces.  
   – Thinner, less‐severe shear zones, lower dislocation density at the interface.  

3. Bond strength trends  
 • Bond strength (tensile or scratch tests) generally decreases as substrate hardness rises, all else equal.  
 • There is often an optimum substrate hardness range—if it is too soft, you risk substrate over‐deformation, subsurface cracking, or excessive residual stress; if it is too hard, you risk poor wetting and low coverage.  
 • In practice one raises particle velocity or uses softer interlayer coatings to compensate when spraying onto very hard substrates.  

In short, softer substrates facilitate deeper particle embedding, more severe interfacial plastic flow and thus stronger mechanical–metallurgical bonds, whereas harder substrates limit those effects, yielding smaller contact areas, reduced jetting, and weaker bonds unless spray parameters are pushed to much higher velocities.

In copper–aluminium bronzes (typically 8–12 wt % Al) the additions of Ni and Fe play two principal roles in tailoring the α+κ multiphase microstructure, and through it the strength‐ductility balance:

1. Stabilization and decomposition of the β phase  
   – Ni is a strong β-stabilizer (raises the β-transus), so in cast alloys you get a dual α+β field on cooling rather than a single‐phase α.  
   – On further cooling the retained β partially orders and decomposes into a suite of intermetallic “κ” phases (often labeled κ-I, κ-II, κ-III, κ-IV).  
   – Fe accelerates the β→κ decomposition kinetics and refines the κ precipitate size by raising the driving force for nucleation.

2. Solid‐solution and precipitation strengthening  
   – In the α (FCC) matrix both Ni and Fe dissolve to a few weight percent and contribute ≈20–60 MPa of yield‐strength increase per wt % by classic solid‐solution hardening.  
   – Most of the strength boost comes, however, from finely dispersed κ-II and κ-III intermetallics:  
     • Ni-rich NiAl (B2) type precipitates (κ-II)  
     • Fe–Al or Fe–Ni–Al (e.g. CuFe₂Al, Fe₃Al) phases (κ-III)  
   – A fine, semi‐continuous film of submicron κ-precipitates at α-grain boundaries plus an even distribution within grains can raise UTS by 50–150 MPa over the base Cu–Al–only alloy.

3. Grain refinement and morphology control  
   – Fe in particular tends to go into the early‐forming κ-I/κ-II phases, pinning α/β grain boundaries and limiting dendrite arm spacing in as‐cast structures.  
   – Ni assists by lowering the critical undercooling for κ nucleation, which gives a finer, more globular κ morphology rather than coarse, networked films.

4. Effects on ductility and toughness  
   – When the κ precipitates are fine (≤0.5 μm) and fairly uniformly distributed, you retain good elongation (20–30 %) and impact toughness, because cracks must cut through many small, closely spaced obstacles.  
   – If Ni+Fe are too high (Ni >10 wt %, Fe >4 wt %) or cooling is too slow, the κ phases coarsen and form continuous films at grain boundaries. Those become crack‐initiation sites under tension and drop elongation below 10 %.  
   – Optimum alloys (e.g. Cu–10Al–5Ni–2Fe) strike the balance: strong precipitation‐hardened matrix plus still-ductile α grains.

Summary of net effects:
– Strength ↑ by solid‐solution plus precipitation (κ) hardening; typical yield up from ∼200 MPa (Cu–10Al) to 300–450 MPa (with Ni+Fe).  
– Ductility maintained at ≈20–30 % if κ phases are fine and dispersed; falls below 10 % when they become coarse/continuous.  
– Control of Ni/Fe level, cooling rate, and any subsequent thermo‐mechanical treatment is therefore critical to obtain the desired α+κ microstructure and optimum strength–ductility combination.

In cold‐sprayed metal–matrix composites (MMCs), raising the volume fraction of hard ceramic particles (e.g. Al₂O₃, SiC, TiC) fundamentally alters the sliding‐wear regime in several interlocking ways:  

1. Real contact area is reduced  
   • Hard reinforcements protrude from the softer metal matrix, carrying a greater share of the normal load.  
   • The metal matrix between particles sees less plastic flow and welding to the counterface.  

2. Transition from adhesion-dominated to mild abrasive or “third‐body” wear  
   • With fewer large metal–metal junctions, adhesive shear plucking is suppressed.  
   • Detached ceramic fragments form a thin, hard “third-body” layer that (a) prevents direct metal–metal contact, (b) rolls or slides with a lower shear strength than bulk metal–metal adhesion, and (c) continually “refreshes” the contact surface.  

3. Suppression of subsurface deformation and crack initiation  
   • A higher ceramic fraction interrupts long shear bands in the matrix, localizing deformation into micro-chambers and reducing overall plasticity.  
   • Crack growth is pinned at ceramic interfaces, cutting down on spallation and delamination fatigue.  

4. Net effect on friction and wear rate  
   • Friction coefficient drops because the dominant shearing interface becomes ceramic/ceramic or ceramic/debris instead of ductile metal/metal.  
   • Wear rate falls as material removal shifts from deep plowing and adhesive pull-out to the much less severe slicing or micro‐rolling of hard particles.  

In sum, increasing ceramic volume fraction hardens and “armor-plates” the surface, promotes formation of a hard, self-limiting tribofilm, reduces plastic adhesion, and impedes crack propagation—all of which lower both friction and wear rates under sliding.

Graphene nanosheets (GNS) raise the fracture toughness of vacuum‐cold‐sprayed composite coatings almost entirely by mechanically “toughening” the metal matrix and creating a tortuous, energy‐absorbing crack path.  The principal mechanisms are:  

1. Crack deflection and branching  
   • A propagating crack encounters a stiff, plate‐like GNS and is forced to change direction (deflection).  
   • The crack front splits or branches around the sheet, lengthening the fracture path and raising the energy required for propagation.  

2. Crack bridging and pull-out  
   • GNS that span opposing crack faces carry part of the load even as the crack opens.  
   • Continued opening leads to interfacial sliding or pull‐out of the sheet, dissipating additional energy through friction and interfacial debonding.  

3. Interfacial sliding of graphene layers  
   • In multilayer or partially exfoliated GNS, the weak van-der-Waals interfaces allow shear sliding between graphene layers under stress, absorbing fracture energy without catastrophic failure.  

4. Grain refinement and residual‐stress effects  
   • Finely dispersed GNS act as heterogeneous nucleation sites during deformation or any post-spray thermal treatments, refining the metal grain size (Hall–Petch effect) and elevating yield strength and toughness.  
   • The thermal mismatch between graphene and the metal can introduce beneficial compressive residual stresses around the sheets, further inhibiting crack initiation and growth.  

By combining all of these effects—crack path tortuosity, load carrying by intact sheets, interfacial frictional dissipation, and microstructural refinement—graphene nanosheets significantly increase the energy needed to drive a crack through a vacuum‐cold‐sprayed composite coating, and thus raise its fracture toughness.

In cold‐spray additive builds the hardness you measure through a coating does not come from a homogeneous “as‐sprayed” microstructure but from the cumulative, high‐strain‐rate plasticity each new particle impact shares with all previously deposited material.  In practice this gives rise to a characteristic hardness gradient through the thickness:

1. Substrate/first‐layer region  
   – The very first cold‐sprayed layer is partially constrained by the stiff substrate, so much of the plastic flow is accommodated at the substrate–coating interface.  
   – You still get work‐hardening of the splats, but it is limited by the load‐sharing with the underlying bulk material.  
   – Measured hardness is higher than the bulk metal but lower than in subsequent layers.

2. Mid‐coating region (layers 2–n–1)  
   – Each newly sprayed particle peens the ones beneath it, inducing additional adiabatic shear bands, dislocation multiplication and very fine‐scale grain refinement.  
   – Residual compressive stresses accumulate.  
   – Hardness climbs with each pass because the same material volume receives fresh high-strain impacts over and over.

3. Near‐surface/top‐surface region  
   – Here the peening effect is strongest: there is no overlying layer to relieve the plastic strain, so you record the maximum work‐hardening and residual compressive stress.  
   – Often the top few tens of microns register the highest Vickers or Knoop numbers in the build.

4. Saturation or decay beyond a critical thickness  
   – Once the coating grows thick enough (typically a few millimetres in metals like Al or Cu), particle kinetic energy is partly spent bombarding earlier layers rather than directly deforming the newest splats.  
   – Hardness tends to plateau and can even dip slightly at the very outer surface if particle velocities have fallen below the critical velocity for full plastic bonding.

Typical hardness‐versus‐height curve (qualitative):

 Substrate  →  first layer (H↑)  →  mid layers (H↑↑)  →  top surface (H max)  →  ultimate plateau

Key take-homes:  
•  Multi-layer builds continually peen underlying material, so hardness generally rises from the substrate interface toward the free surface.  
•  Saturation of particle energy at larger thicknesses limits further hardening, producing a ceiling in the hardness profile.  
•  Interfaces between layers can also show local hardness variations if porosity or poor metallurgical bonding interrupts dislocation continuity.

When a spray particle (whether pure ceramic or ceramic–metal composite) strikes the substrate or a previously‐deposited layer at several hundred meters per second, the kinetic energy is converted almost instantaneously into extremely high localized pressures (on the order of GPa) and strain rates (10^5–10^7 s^–1).  This “cold” impact imparts several key microstructural changes that drive hardness up:

1. Severe Plastic Deformation (SPD) in any ductile binder phase  
   – The metal (or metal‐matrix) components undergo adiabatic shear, dynamic recovery and sometimes dynamic recrystallization.  Grain sizes collapse into the sub‐micron or even nanocrystalline regime, raising hardness via the Hall–Petch effect and high dislocation densities.  

2. Brittle Fracture and Fragmentation of Ceramic Particles  
   – At GPa‐level shock pressures the ceramics crack into finer fragments.  These fragments can fill pores, tighten packing and—and in composites—embed into the ductile matrix, increasing the effective load‐bearing cross section and suppressing microcrack propagation.

3. Mechanical Interlocking and Cold Welding  
   – High pressure forces intimate contact at particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces.  On metallic surfaces or binders this often leads to cold welding; on ceramics it promotes mechanical interlocks that resist indentation and crack growth.

4. Residual Stress and Strain Hardening  
   – Rapid unloading traps compressive stresses in and around each particle.  The high retained dislocation density in the binder or composite interfaces further elevates hardness by forest‐hardening incoming dislocations.

5. Pore Closure and Increased Density  
   – Repeated impacts crush and shear‐flow particles into any remaining voids, driving overall coating porosity down.  Denser coatings transmit load more uniformly, resisting localized yielding under an indenter.

By combining (1) grain‐size refinement and work hardening in metal/binder phases, (2) finer ceramic fragments that reinforce the composite, (3) strong mechanical and metallurgical bonding, and (4) compressive residual stresses, cold‐sprayed ceramic coatings exhibit markedly higher hardness than either loosely deposited powders or conventionally sprayed equivalents.

A simple way to think about what the pre‐diffusion bake does is that it turns your as‐sprayed, two‐layer “hard ceramic on soft metal” system with a razor-sharp, high‐mismatch interface into a more smoothly graded, nearly monolithic structure.  That grading both relieves built-in stresses and gives you a mechanically tougher interface—and as a bonus it can also precipitate or homogenize strengthening phases in your metal.  The net result is higher strength and preserved ductility (elongation) when you load at temperature.  

Here are the key mechanisms at work:  

1. Interfacial grading and toughening  
   • As-sprayed, the ceramic/metal interface is abrupt, with large CTE and stiffness jumps.  That sharp boundary is a ready site for cracks or delamination once you go to 800–1 200 °C.  
   • Holding the duplex coating at an elevated “pre‐diffusion” temperature for a few hours drives mutual diffusion of alloying elements from the metal into the ceramic top coat and vice versa.  You end up with a composition‐gradient zone a few microns thick instead of a knife‐edge interface.  This graded region:  
     – Smooths out elastic mismatch  
     – Raises the energy required to nucleate and run a crack across the interface  
     – Improves load transfer between the two layers.  

2. Residual stress relief  
   • All cold-sprayed or plasma-sprayed coatings carry locked-in stresses (tensile in the ceramic, compressive in the metal, plus step‐cooling stresses).  
   • A sojourn at high temperature allows partial stress relaxation in both layers, so you start your high‐T test with lower net stresses and fewer stress concentrators.  

3. Crack‐healing and pore‐infilling  
   • Tiny microcracks and spray‐induced pores in the ceramic can partially close or fill by creep of the metal infiltrating the ceramic’s open porosity.  
   • That densification reduces crack initiation sites under tensile load.  

4. High‐T precipitation and phase homogenization in the metal  
   • Many bond‐coat alloys (MCrAlY, Ni­based superalloy substrates, etc.) benefit from a homogenization step that dissolves coarse as‐sprayed phases and then re‐precipitates them in a fine, stable dispersion (e.g. β–NiAl, γ′ in a Ni matrix).  
   • Those fine, stable precipitates deliver real strengthening at service temperature (much like a Ni‐base forging would).  

Put together, these effects shift the failure mode from brittle, interface-controlled fracture toward bulk, ductile overload.  You end up with a duplex system that can carry higher tensile stresses at 900–1 100 °C and still stretch a bit before it finally gives way—just as you’d see in a single‐metal, well heat-treated alloy.

In cold‐spray AM, the single most important parameter controlling whether a particle bonds (and how well it bonds) is the ratio  
 η = vi/vcrit  
where vi is the particle’s impact velocity and vcrit is the material’s critical (or “bonding”) velocity.  By itself, η tells you if you’re above the threshold for adhesion (η > 1) and how “deep” into the bonding regime you are; taken together with your gas‐dynamic conditions (stagnation pressure P0, temperature T0, and gas molecular weight), it dictates both the degree of plastic deformation on impact (and hence interfacial cohesion) and the packing/densification of the deposit (porosity).

Key points:

1. Critical velocity and η  
 – vcrit is set by material properties: yield strength, hardness, fracture toughness, elastic modulus (i.e. the resistance to the plastic deformation needed for jetting and metallurgical bonding).  
 – If η < 1, particles simply rebound or erode the surface; no cohesive build‐up, porosity ≈ 100 %.  
 – As η passes unity (1 < η < ~1.2), you enter a “transitional” regime: weak bonding, large interparticle voids, tensile cohesion still poor.  
 – In the range ~1.2 ≤ η ≤ 2 you get vigorous plastic flow, material jetting at the interface, dynamic recrystallization—this is the sweet‐spot for high cohesive strength (comparable to wrought material) and low porosity (typically 1–5 %).  
 – Beyond η ≈ 2, you can get saturation of densification, a higher risk of substrate erosion/splashing, and elevated residual stress; porosity may no longer fall appreciably.

2. Role of process gas conditions  
 – P0 (stagnation pressure): higher P0 → higher gas density in the nozzle throat → greater drag force on the powder → higher vi (for a given particle size and gas temperature).  
 – T0 (stagnation temperature): higher T0 → lower gas density but higher sound speed → higher peak jet Mach number and reduced drag losses (particles accelerate more before the flow cools). You also get warmer particles, which plastically deform more readily (effectively lowering vcrit).  
 – gas molecular weight (N2 vs He): lighter gases (He) give higher exit Mach number and higher vi for the same P0 and T0, but at greater cost; heavier gases need higher P0 or T0 to reach the same vi.  

3. Coupling η and gas choice to deposit cohesion/porosity  
 – To hit the optimal η window (≈1.2–2), you adjust P0 and T0 (and/or switch gas) so that vi surpasses vcrit by the desired margin.  If you undershoot, you get a porous, mechanically weak spray; overshoot too far and you risk erosion, residual stress and possible re-deposition defects.  
 – Within the optimal η range, higher T0 or He can also raise particle temperature, promoting even deeper plastic flow and dynamic recrystallization—both of which tighten interparticle interfaces, driving porosity down toward a few percent and cohesion up to 80–100 % of bulk strength.  

In practice you characterize vcrit for your powder (often by hit-and-miss test sprays) then choose P0, T0 and gas type to achieve an impact velocity vi so that  
 η = vi/vcrit ≈ 1.2–1.8.  
That combination gives the best compromise of high interparticle cohesion (and hence mechanical properties) with minimal residual porosity.

Pre-heating the substrate before cold spray almost always gives you a stronger bond—up to a point.  In essence, by warming the substrate (typically 50–300 °C, depending on the alloy system) you:

1. lower its yield strength and hardness  
   – the softer substrate deforms more readily on particle impact, increasing the intimate contact area and mechanical interlocking  
2. promote interfacial plastic flow  
   – both the particle and the near-surface substrate shear, generate higher dislocation densities, and form fresh metal–metal contact  
3. enhance atomic diffusion (and even a very thin metallurgical bond)  
   – diffusivity climbs rapidly with temperature, so any nascent necks that form between particle and substrate can grow slightly during or immediately after impact  
4. reduce residual tensile stress  
   – because the temperature differential between the cold­sprayed feedstock and the substrate is smaller, you lock in fewer thermal stresses upon cooling  

In practice people see 10–30 % increases in bond strength (measured by pull-off or shear tests) for common material pairs (Al→Al, Ni→Ni, Cu→steel) when pre-heating in the 100–250 °C range.  Beyond ~300–350 °C the benefits level off or reverse, as you begin to grow oxides, anneal out the work-hardening you need for severe plastic deformation, or introduce excessive thermal mismatch.  

Bottom line: pre-heat ≈ +100–250 °C → stronger adhesion; pre-heat ≫ 300 °C → diminishing returns (oxide, grain growth, loss of plastic work).

In HVOF‐sprayed MCrAlY coatings, the deliberate introduction of a small volume fraction (typically 0.5–2 wt %) of CeO₂ nanoparticles produces two mutually reinforcing effects on the as‐deposited microstructure and, by extension, on the coating hardness:

1. Grain and lamella refinement via particle‐pinning  
   • During flight and impact, CeO₂ survives as discrete nano‐oxides that become trapped at splat boundaries and grain‐growth fronts.  
   • These particles exert a Zener‐pinning force, limiting recrystallization and blocking the coalescence of equiaxed γ/β grains and lamellae.  
   • The result is a finer, more homogenous “pancake‐splat” morphology with thinner inter‐splat oxide films.

2. Porosity reduction through pore‐filling and improved intersplat cohesion  
   • A fraction of the nanoparticles lodges in nano‐voids at the splat–splat interfaces, partially “healing” microcracks and mitigating oxygen‐induced oxide stringers.  
   • CeO₂ also scavenges residual O₂ in the spray jet, leading to fewer oxide inclusions and smaller, more spherical micropores.  
   • Typical porosity drops from ≈1.5–2 vol % in baseline MCrAlY to ≈0.5–1 vol % with optimized CeO₂ loading.

How this translates into higher hardness  
   a. Hall–Petch and Orowan strengthening. Finer grains and a high density of nano‐oxides increase the stress required for dislocation motion.  
   b. Reduced porosity and stronger splat bonding decrease soft, crack‐like defects that would otherwise concentrate stress.  
   c. At an optimum CeO₂ content (usually around 1 wt %), one sees hardness increases on the order of 10–20 % (e.g. from ≈450 HV₀.₂ to 500–540 HV₀.₂).  

Caveat: beyond the optimum loading (>2–3 wt % CeO₂), nanoparticle agglomeration and the formation of brittle oxide clusters can actually raise porosity and microcracking, reversing the hardness gains.

In most cold‐sprayed metallic systems (e.g. Al, Cu, Ni alloys) you will see essentially the same “rise‐and‐fall” of interface stripping resistance (adhesion) as you increase annealing time at a fixed temperature:

1. Short‐time anneal (minutes to tens of minutes)  
   – Resistance rises sharply.  
   – Why?  
     • Recovery/recrystallization in the deformed splats and at the substrate interface relaxes lethal tensile residual stresses and unlocks dislocations.  
     • Newly formed low-angle and high-angle subgrain boundaries accelerate atom transport across splat–splat and splat–substrate contacts.  
     • Grain‐boundary migration at the interface closes nano‐voids and drives metallurgical bonding (interdiffusion).  
     • Mechanical interlocking is “locked in” by stress relaxation, so the coating can sustain higher peel/strip loads.

2. Intermediate‐time anneal (optimum point)  
   – You hit a maximum in stripping resistance.  
   – Here recovery/recrystallization is essentially complete, interfaces are fully bonded, but deleterious coarsening has not yet begun in earnest.

3. Long‐time anneal (hundreds of minutes, depending on alloy and temperature)  
   – Resistance falls off.  
   – Why?  
     • Grain growth in the bulk coating and at the interface reduces grain‐boundary density and hence the number of “diffusion highways” and dislocation‐trapping sites.  
     • Precipitate coarsening (or formation of brittle intermetallics, in multiphase alloys) embrittles the interface region.  
     • Oxide or brittle intermetallic layers can thicken at the interface (especially if not run in vacuum or inert gas), acting as lateral crack‐separation paths.  
     • Complete stress relaxation removes the residual compressive “clamping” that had been partially holding splats against the substrate.

In sum, short anneals drive the microstructure toward a highly defect-engineered, fine‐grained, strongly bonded interface; longer anneals undo that refinement, coarsen precipitates and grains, and allow brittle phases or oxides to grow—so the stripping resistance peaks at an intermediate dwell time and then declines.

Mixed hard–soft blends exploit a synergistic interplay between a deformable ductile phase (“soft” particles) and a high‐hardness phase (“hard” particles) to boost cold‐sprayed bond strength.  The key steps in the mechanism are:

1. Impact–induced adiabatic shear instability (ASI) in the soft phase  
   – When the blend strikes the substrate at supersonic velocity, the soft particles (e.g. Cu, Al, Ni) undergo extreme plastic deformation.  
   – Localized shear bands form at the particle–substrate and particle–particle interfaces.  This ASI cleans oxides and breaks up surface films, exposing fresh metal for metallurgical bonding.  

2. Stress concentration by hard particles  
   – Embedded hard particles (e.g. WC, TiB₂, Al₂O₃) remain largely undeformed but act as micro-peening “stress concentrators.”  
   – They locally amplify stresses in the surrounding soft metal, triggering more extensive ASI and plastic flow in the soft matrix and at the interface.  

3. Mechanical interlocking and void filling  
   – Soft material plasticizes and flows around hard particles and into substrate asperities, creating a mechanical interlock.  
   – This flow also fills microvoids behind the hard particles, eliminating weak spots and increasing coating cohesion.  

4. Binder‐mediated consolidation  
   – The soft phase acts as a “kinetic energy buffer,” absorbing part of the impact energy and reducing particle rebound (critical velocity) for both phases.  
   – It binds hard particles into a dense, well‐bonded composite layer and ensures load transfer between hard particles and substrate.  

5. Final microstructure and bond strength  
   – The result is a bimodal microstructure: a ductile, heavily deformed matrix (full of high‐angle grain boundaries and nanocrystalline shear bands) reinforcing metallurgical bonds, and a dispersion of hard particles that sustain high abrasion resistance.  
   – Combined chemical bonding (from cleaned metal–metal contact) plus mechanical locking yields higher overall adhesion and cohesion than either phase alone.

Thermal post-treatment (e.g. annealing, hot isostatic pressing, diffusion bonding) improves interfacial adhesion in cold-sprayed coatings primarily by closing pores and fostering metallurgical bonding. Key mechanisms are:  

1. Pore closure and neck growth  
   • Driving force for sintering: elevated temperature activates surface and grain-boundary diffusion, leading to neck formation between particles and between the coating and substrate.  
   • Reduction of voids increases the real contact area at both particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces, so load is transmitted more uniformly.  

2. Metallurgical bonding via diffusion and recrystallization  
   • Enhanced atomic interdiffusion across previously separated splat boundaries and across the coating–substrate interface builds true metal-to-metal bonds rather than just mechanical interlocks.  
   • Recrystallization and grain growth across interfaces “bridge” former pores and collapsed oxide films, turning weakly adhered splats into a coherent polycrystalline network.  

3. Residual stress relaxation and homogenization  
   • Thermal exposure relieves impact-induced tensile‐type residual stresses and strain gradients that tend to open interfacial flaws.  
   • A more uniform stress state further discourages crack initiation and delamination at the interface.  

By transforming a discontinuous, porous assembly into a nearly pore‐free, diffusion‐bonded structure, thermal post‐treatment elevates the shear and tensile strength of the coating–substrate bond and markedly improves adhesion.

To assess whether a cold-sprayed fin array will survive the shear forces imposed by a flowing coolant or process gas, you essentially need to compare the shear stress that the fluid flow tries to impose on the coating–substrate interface with the shear‐adhesion strength you have measured for your cold‐sprayed material.  If the flow‐induced shear is everywhere below the adhesion strength (divided by a suitable safety factor), the fins should remain intact; if it exceeds the adhesion, delamination or spallation will occur.

Here is a step‐by‐step recipe:

1. Characterize the service flow  
   • Measure or specify the fluid density ρ, viscosity μ, and free‐stream velocity V∞.  
   • Decide whether the flow over your fins is laminar or turbulent (compute Reynolds number Re = ρV∞L/μ, L = characteristic fin length or chord).

2. Compute the local wall‐shear stress τw on each fin  
   a) For a flat‐plate–type fin in laminar boundary‐layer:  
      Cf(x) = 1.328/√Reₓ   with Reₓ = ρV∞ x/μ  
      τw(x) = ½ ρ V∞² Cf(x)  
   b) For a turbulent boundary‐layer (empirical 1/7‐power law):  
      Cf(x) ≃ 0.0592 Reₓ^(-0.2)  
      τw(x) = ½ ρ V∞² Cf(x)  
   c) If fins are better approximated as cylinders or blades, you can also write  
      τw ≃ ½ ρ V∞² Cf_global  
      or use tabulated skin‐friction coefficients for your geometry.  
   d) Integrate τw(x) over the coated area A to get the total drag force Fdrag if you need global loads:  
      Fdrag = ∫A τw(x) dA.

3. Measure or obtain the coating–substrate adhesion (shear) strength τadh  
   • From lap‐shear tests, scratch tests, pull‐off tests, or microshear tests.  
   • Be sure you have the shear direction and temperature matched to service conditions.

4. Compare loading to strength  
   • Define a safety factor FS (e.g. 1.5–3).  
   • Require that at every point on the fin  
       τw(x) ≤ τadh/FS.  
   • Or in global form  
       Fdrag/A_eff ≤ τadh/FS  
     where A_eff is the effective interface area carrying shear.

5. Account for cyclic effects, temperature, erosion, etc.  
   • If your flow is unsteady or oscillatory, use the fatigue shear strength of the interface and perform a cycle‐counting analysis (Miner’s rule).  
   • At elevated temperature, experimentally determine τadh(T) and repeat the comparison above as a function of T.  
   • If particulates are entrained in the flow, include erosion‐induced weakening in your safety factor.

6. Map out a “survival envelope”  
   • On one axis plot flow velocity V∞ (or Reynolds number), on the other axis plot τadh (possibly reduced by temperature or cyclic damage).  
   • The region where ½ ρ V∞² Cf ≤ τadh/FS is your safe operating window.  

In practice you will:  
  – Pick your worst‐case service conditions (highest V∞, highest T, most cycles).  
  – Calculate the corresponding τw distribution.  
  – Verify with FEA or hand‐calcs that the maximum wall‐shear does not exceed your measured τadh divided by the chosen FS.  

If that criterion is met, the cold‐sprayed coating on your fin array is predicted to survive without delamination under the given fluid‐drag loading.

Below is a sketch of how one goes from the general NASGRO growth law to the Hartman–Schijve form, and then under what conditions it collapses to a Paris law.

1. The general NASGRO crack‐growth law  
   NASGRO is usually written in the form  
   da/dN = C · (ΔK)n  
            ———————————————————————  
            [ (1 – R)p · (1 – ΔKth/ΔK)q ]  
         · [ 1 – (Kmax/KIC)r ]  
   where  
   • ΔK = Kmax – Kmin  
   • R = Kmin/Kmax  
   • ΔKth is the threshold range  
   • KIC is the fracture toughness  
   • C, n, p, q, r are material constants.  

2. Hartman–Schijve re-parameterization  
   Hartman and Schijve showed that one can recast the three denominators into two more physically transparent limits—one at the lower bound (ΔK → ΔKth) and one at the upper bound (Kmax → KIC).  A common two‐parameter form is:  
   da/dN = A · (ΔK – ΔKth)m  
            —————————————————  
            [ 1 – (Kmax/KIC) ]p  
   with A, m, p fitted to small-crack data.  

   Here the physics is clear:  
   – As ΔK ↓ ΔKth the numerator → 0.  
   – As Kmax → KIC the denominator → 0, modeling the approach to fast fracture.  

3. Reduction to a Paris‐like law  
   If small cracks emanate from microstructural discontinuities, it is often found that:  
   (i) ΔK ≫ ΔKth  (so ΔK – ΔKth ≃ ΔK),  
   (ii) Kmax ≪ KIC (so 1 – Kmax/KIC ≃ 1),  
   (iii) the effect of R is weak or incorporated into A and m.  

   Under these assumptions the Hartman–Schijve form collapses to  
     da/dN ≃ A · (ΔK)m  
   which is nothing more than the familiar Paris law  
     da/dN = C′ · (ΔK)m.  

   In practice this simplification is valid in the mid-region of the crack‐growth curve (stage II, long‐crack regime), provided small‐crack closure and high‐ΔK nonlinearities remain negligible.

To estimate the coherent‐diffraction domain (i.e. “crystallite”) size in your cold‐spray powder from the broadening of its XRD peaks, you proceed as follows:

1. Measure the XRD pattern of your powder (usually with Cu Kα, λ = 1.5406 Å).  
2. Choose a well‐defined diffraction line (e.g. the (111) or (220) reflection).  
3. Determine the observed full‐width at half‐maximum (FWHM) of that peak in 2θ, β_obs (in radians).  
4. Correct for instrument broadening by measuring a large‐grained standard (e.g. LaB₆) to get β_inst. Compute the “true” sample broadening:  
   β = √(β_obs² − β_inst²)  
5. Convert β from degrees to radians if needed.  
6. Apply the Scherrer equation:  

   D = K · λ  
       ———  
       β · cos θ  

   • D is the mean crystallite size.  
   • K is the shape factor (typically 0.89–1.0; 0.94 for spherical domains).  
   • λ is the X‐ray wavelength.  
   • θ is the Bragg half‐angle of the chosen peak.  

Result: smaller crystallites give larger β and hence smaller D. Note that Scherrer analysis assumes that all broadening arises from finite domain size; if microstrain is also significant, you must separate its contribution (e.g. via a Williamson-Hall plot) before applying the Scherrer formula.

In the Nix–Gao picture the apparent “smaller‐is‐harder” effect in nanoindentation simply comes from the extra geometrically‐necessary dislocations (GNDs) you must store under a sharp tip as the indentation depth h shrinks.  Quantitatively one shows that the square of the hardness H obeys  
   
   H²(h) = H₀² (1 + h*/h)  

or equivalently  

   H(h) = H₀ √[1 + h*/h]  

where:  
 • H₀ is the “long‐range” or macroscopic hardness you would measure at depths ≫ h*.  
 • h* is a characteristic length scale at which the size effect sets in.  

For h ≫ h* → H→H₀ (bulk value),  
for h ≲ h* → H ≃ H₀·(h*/h)¹ᐟ² and so hardness grows roughly ∝ h^(–1/2).  

Key parameters buried in h* are:  
 1. Burgers vector b of the crystal (sets the GND size).  
 2. Shear modulus G (elastic stiffness controlling dislocation line energy).  
 3. Dislocation‐interaction coefficient α (∼0.3–0.6).  
 4. Indenter‐geometry factor (β or the equivalent conical half‐angle or the 3‐sided Berkovich‐to‐conical‐equivalence constant).  
 5. Poisson’s ratio ν (mildly enters the conversion from H to G).  

In most treatments one writes for a Berkovich (≈70° cone)  

   h* ≃ (const.)·(G b/H₀)²  

with “const.” ≃ 0.4–1 depending on how α and the detailed geometry are lumped.  Once you know H₀ and h* for your metal, the Nix–Gao equation gives you the full H vs. h curve.

Cold‐sprayed coatings arrive on the substrate as a stack of heavily deformed, high‐dislocation‐density particles that are cold‐welded at point contacts but still contain residual porosity, oxide films and work‐hardened interiors. Spark‐plasma sintering (SPS) transforms that metastable, porous microstructure into a fully dense, bulk‐like metal by the following multi‐step, synergistic sequence:

1. Particle‐Contact Preheating by Joule Effect  
   • As soon as a DC pulse is applied, the electrical current preferentially flows through the smallest cross‐sectional areas—i.e. the point contacts between sprayed particles.  
   • Local resistive heating rapidly raises the temperature at these junctions to a few hundred °C–1 000 °C in milliseconds, while the bulk remains cooler.  

2. Plasma‐Microdischarge and Oxide‐Film Removal  
   • At interparticle gaps (10–100 nm), the high local field strength triggers micro‐discharges (“sparks”).  
   • These microplasmas locally vaporize and eject thin oxide/contaminant layers, exposing fresh metal surfaces.  
   • Inert‐gas SPS atmospheres prevent re‐oxidation.  

3. Neck Formation by Plastic Flow and Early Diffusion  
   • Once oxides are cleared, clean metal–metal asperities instantly cold‐weld under the simultaneous action of temperature and uniaxial pressure (10–100 MPa).  
   • Severe local plastic deformation helps flatten surface roughness and grows metallic “necks” across former gaps.  

4. Pressure‐Assisted Pore Collapse (Viscoplastic Densification)  
   • The applied uniaxial load continues to drive viscoplastic flow of the now‐softened material, plastically closing residual pores.  
   • At the same time, the high dislocation density inherited from cold spray can enhance Coble‐type grain‐boundary diffusion.  

5. Current‐Enhanced Mass Transport (Electromigration)  
   • The electric field lowers the activation energy for vacancy and dislocation motion, accelerating both lattice and grain‐boundary diffusion.  
   • Silver‐ton diffusion–creep mechanisms can operate even below 0.5 T m (T = temperature).  

6. Dynamic Recrystallization and Defect Recovery  
   • As the temperature ramps to ~0.6–0.9 T_melt, the stored strain energy drives dynamic recrystallization in both particle interiors and across necks.  
   • Dislocation annihilation and subgrain coalescence produce equiaxed, fine‐grained domains.  

7. Grain‐Growth Control and Thermal Holding  
   • A short hold (minutes) at the consolidation temperature thickens necks and completes boundary migration without excessive grain growth.  
   • Rapid cooling “freezes in” the fine, homogeneous grain structure.  

End result: A near‐fully dense (> 99 %) coating in which the former particle boundaries have been welded and diffused away, pores and oxides removed, dislocations reduced by recrystallization, and grains refined to a size comparable to or finer than bulk conventionally cast/forged metal. The mechanical properties—strength, ductility, toughness and electrical/thermal conductivity—thus approach those of wrought or cast–and–heat‐treated solid metal.

In the simplest combined Hall–Petch/Taylor picture the yield stress of a cold‐sprayed deposit is written as  
σy ≃ σ0 + kHP·d^(–½) + α·G·b·√ρ  

where  
 • σ0 is the lattice/friction stress of the crystal  
 • kHP·d^(–½) is the Hall–Petch term (grain‐boundary strengthening, inversely proportional to the square root of the average grain diameter d)  
 • α·G·b·√ρ is the Taylor hardening term (dislocation–dislocation interaction, proportional to the square root of the dislocation density ρ)  
 • G is the shear modulus, b the Burgers vector, and α a dimensionless constant (~0.2–0.5).  

Cold spray deposits acquire very fine (sub-μm to nano) grains through dynamic recrystallization and extremely high dislocation densities (10^14–10^15 m–2) from the severe impact.  As a result:  
 • Cutting the grain size in half raises the Hall–Petch contribution by √2 (i.e. roughly +30–40 %),  
 • Doubling the dislocation density raises the Taylor contribution by √2.  

Typical numbers for a cold‐sprayed metal might be d ≈ 0.2 µm (→ kHP·d^(–½) ≃ 200–300 MPa) and ρ ≈ 10^15 m–2 (→ αGb√ρ ≃ 200–400 MPa), so that the two terms add to give yield strengths in the few‐hundreds‐of‐MPa range.

Cold spray coatings routinely reach millimetres‐to‐centimetres in thickness whereas most flame, plasma or HVOF thermal‐sprayed deposits top out at a few hundred microns.  The key reason is how residual stresses build up during and after deposition:

1. Thermal spray coatings  
   • Particles are heated to semi‐ or fully molten temperatures (Tparticle ≈ 1 000–3 000 K).  
   • Upon impact the splats cool rapidly to the substrate temperature (Ts ≈ 300–500 K), introducing a large temperature drop ΔT.  
   • This quench generates tensile “quenching” stresses in the coating σQ ≈ E·α·ΔT (E = Young’s modulus, α = coefficient of thermal expansion).  
   • Although there is some peening‐induced compressive stress, σQ usually dominates, so net residual stress is tensile.  
   • As thickness grows, tensile stress accumulates until the coating cracks or delaminates.  In practice that limits build‐up to a few hundred microns before failure.

2. Cold spray coatings  
   • Particles remain solid or only lightly heated (Tparticle < 0.3·Tmelt), so ΔT on impact is small.  
   • Thermal contraction mismatches are negligible; quench‐related tensile stress σQ ≈ 0.  
   • Bonding is achieved by high‐velocity plastic deformation (adiabatic shear), which plastically “peens” the underlying layer and develops compressive residual stress σC in the deposit.  
   • Net residual stress is compressive, actually helping to close pores and cracks as you build more layers.  
   • Because there is no growing tensile stress to crack or delaminate the coating, one can build up millimetres or even centimetres of deposit in a single run.

In short, thermal sprays are limited by tensile quench stresses from high ΔT, whereas cold spray—by keeping temperatures low—avoids thermal contraction stresses and instead locks in beneficial compressive stresses, permitting much greater coating thickness.

Below is a step‐by‐step outline of how cold spray–induced microstructural changes translate into reduced wear via the Taylor strengthening relation and Archard’s wear law.

1. High‐velocity particle impact and severe plastic deformation  
   • Particles strike the substrate at 500–1 000 m/s, imposing strains (ε_p) often >100 %.  
   • This creates dense networks of dislocations (ρ increases from ~10^10 to >10^14 m⁻²).

2. Dislocation hardening via the Taylor relation  
   • Taylor’s law: Δσ = M·α·G·b·√ρ  
     – M = Taylor factor (~3 for fcc metals)  
     – α ≈ 0.2–0.5 (interaction coefficient)  
     – G = shear modulus, b = Burgers vector  
     – ρ = dislocation density  
   • As ρ rises, yield strength σ_y and hardness H ≈ C·σ_y increase.

3. Dynamic recrystallization and grain refinement  
   • Local adiabatic heating + high strain rates trigger dynamic recrystallization (DRX).  
   • DRX breaks up coarse grains into ultrafine (<1 μm) or even nanograins.  
   • Additional grain‐boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch):  
     σ_y = σ_0 + k_HP·d^(-1/2) further raises H.

4. Steady‐state hard, dense coating  
   • Final microstructure: submicron grains, trapped high ρ, few porosities.  
   • Measured hardness H_coating often doubles or triples that of the cast alloy.

5. Wear reduction via Archard’s law  
   • Archard’s wear law: V = (K·F·L)/H  
     – V = wear volume (m³)  
     – F = normal load, L = sliding distance  
     – H = hardness, K = dimensionless wear coefficient  
   • As H↑ ⇒ V↓ linearly (for constant F, L, K).

6. Net effect  
   • Cold‐sprayed coating exhibits much higher H (from steps 2–3).  
   • Under identical tribological loading, its wear volume V is reduced in inverse proportion to H.  
   • Result: longer component life, better abrasion and erosion resistance.

In cold spray, “hotter” carrier gas does not merely add heat to the powder—it alters gas properties, particle kinematics, deformation behavior at impact, and ultimately the microstructure and hardness of the build.  The following chain of physical events links gas temperature to coating microhardness and explains why there is an optimum:

1.    Gas‐Property Changes with Temperature  
    •  Density (ρgas) falls as temperature rises (ideal‐gas ρ∝1/T).  
    •  Viscosity (μgas) rises moderately with T.  
    •  Speed of sound and Mach number in the nozzle change, shifting the optimum pressure ratio for choked flow.  

2.    Particle Acceleration and Exit Velocity  
    •  Lower ρgas at higher T reduces drag force per unit area on particles, so for a fixed pressure ratio the nozzle can accelerate them to higher absolute velocities.  
    •  However, past a certain gas temperature the drop in density outweighs the gain from reduced drag, so particle exit velocity actually peaks and then declines.  

3.    Impact Kinetics and Deformation  
    •  Particle kinetic energy (½mv²) at impact controls the degree of plastic deformation (adiabatic shear) and jetting between particle and substrate.  
    •  Sufficiently high impact velocity (above the “critical velocity”) is needed to generate localized adiabatic shear zones, break oxide films, and create metallurgical bonds.  

4.    Microstructural Refinement and Work Hardening  
    •  Severe plastic deformation injects a very high dislocation density into the particles’ near‐surface layers.  
    •  Dynamic recrystallization or recovery may occur in those shear‐heated zones, producing ultrafine grains.  
    •  The balance of work hardening (dislocations) and any dynamic recovery/recrystallization sets the final grain size and residual stress state.  

5.    Macro‐Scale Coating Hardness  
    •  Higher dislocation densities and finer grains → higher hardness (Hall–Petch and Taylor strengthening).  
    •  Poorer deformation (below critical velocity) → weak bonding, large porosity, less work hardening → low hardness.  
    •  Over‐acceleration (if particle v drops again at very high gas T) gives less plastic strain per impact → lower dislocation density and hardness.  

Why an Optimum Temperature Exists  
– At low gas T: density is large but sound speed is low, so maximum achievable particle velocity may be below critical. Coating is under‐deformed and soft.  
– As gas T rises: exit velocity and impact energy rise, deformation and work hardening maximize, so microhardness climbs.  
– Beyond the optimum T: gas density falls too far (and viscosity/pressure losses rise), so exit velocity and kinetic energy actually decrease. Plastic deformation lessens, dislocation generation and grain refinement drop off, and hardness falls.  

In practice, each powder material and spray system has its own “sweet spot” gas temperature that balances gas‐density–driven momentum transfer against viscosity and choked‐flow constraints to maximize deformation, bonding, and microhardness.

Below is a simplified, step-by-step outline of how the interplay of intense mechanical deformation (from supersonic particle impact) and rapid laser‐induced thermal cycling drives microstructure evolution and raises microhardness in a metal coating produced by supersonic laser deposition (SLD).

1. Powder Acceleration and Impact  
   • Metal powder is entrained in a supersonic gas jet (Mach 2–3).  
   • Individual particles strike the substrate at velocities of 500–800 m/s.  
   • On impact, very high strain rates (10^6–10^8 s⁻¹) and adiabatic shear localized in micron‐scale zones produce severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization seeds.

2. Simultaneous Laser Heating  
   • A co‐axial laser (typically 500–2,000 W, continuous‐wave) irradiates the impact zone.  
   • Surface and near‐surface regions are rapidly heated toward or above the solidus.  
   • Local substrate softening lowers the critical velocity for bonding and promotes metallurgical (fusion) bonding of successive layers.

3. Rapid Solidification and Thermal Gradients  
   • After particle impact and laser pass, the molten/softened zone cools at rates of 10^3–10^6 K/s, set by substrate conduction and spraying intervals.  
   • Very high cooling rates suppress grain growth, yielding fine equiaxed grains (sub‐micron to a few microns) in the melt‐pools.

4. Severe Plastic Deformation Effects  
   • Impact imparts high dislocation densities (10^14–10^15 m⁻²).  
   • Adiabatic shear bands fragment the original particle microstructure into ultrafine grains via dynamic recrystallization.  
   • Mechanical interlocking of particles at splat boundaries ensures 100% dense deposits.

5. Thermo-Mechanical Cycling  
   • Each new layer re-heats the underlying coating to sub-solidus temperatures (several hundred °C).  
   • This repeated thermal exposure can relieve some residual stresses, induce low‐temperature recovery or secondary recrystallization, and in alloys with precipitation‐hardening elements (e.g. Al, Ti, Ni systems) drive nanoscale precipitate formation.

6. Final Microstructure  
   • Topmost layers (highest deformation + fastest cooling): ultrafine‐grained (~200–500 nm) zones.  
   • Mid-layers (laser‐remelted but less deformed): fine equiaxed grains (0.5–2 μm).  
   • Substrate heat‐affected zone: coarser, partially recrystallized grains (>2–5 μm), lower hardness.

7. Resulting Microhardness Changes  
   • Grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch): σ_y ∝ d^–½, so reducing grain size from 5 μm to 0.5 μm can raise yield strength by several hundred MPa.  
   • Dislocation strengthening: high residual dislocation densities add ∼50–150 HV.  
   • Precipitation hardening (if applicable) adds another 50–200 HV.  
   • Typical hardness map:  
      – Impact/splat boundaries: 450–600 HV  
      – Melt‐recast zones: 350–450 HV  
      – Near‐substrate HAZ: 250–350 HV (depending on base alloy)

Summary  
Supersonic laser deposition couples extreme—yet localized—plastic deformation from high‐velocity impacts with rapid, controlled melt/solidification from laser heating.
