The result is a hierarchical microstructure of ultrafine and fine grains, high dislocation density, and, where thermally allowed, nano-precipitates. Together these give coatings markedly higher microhardness (often +50–200 HV) versus conventionally processed or cold-sprayed materials.

Starting from  
  H≡F/A   with   A=2πR h_c  
we immediately get  
  H=F/(2πR h_c)   (1)

In a purely elastic (Hertzian) contact one also has  
  F=(4/3)E* √R · h_c^(3/2)  
where E* is the reduced modulus.  Substituting into (1) gives  
  H = (4/3 E* √R · h_c^(3/2))  
        —————————————  
        (2π R h_c)  
     = (4E*/3)^(2/3)  
       --------------------------------  
       2π     · R^(–2/3) · F^(1/3)  

or more transparently  

  H ∝ F^(1/3) R^(–2/3).  

Thus in the elastic–plastic transition regime (small loads) the apparent hardness *rises* as F^(1/3) and *falls* as R^(2/3).  Equivalently one may write in terms of contact depth  
  H ∝ (h_c/R)^(–1/2),  
so that very shallow indents on a “blunt” sphere give an artificially high H.

Once plastic flow dominates, F scales roughly with h_c^2 and one recovers a plateau hardness (the true flow hardness of the material), independent of F and only weakly dependent on R.

Implications for thin‐film testing  
1.  Tip‐shape effects and the indentation‐size effect (ISE) force you to indent *deep enough* (>> tip‐rounding radius) before H stabilizes. 2.  Substrate influence forces you to indent *shallow enough* (<10 % of film thickness) if you want to measure the film alone.  
3.  In practice there is only a narrow “window” of loads and depths where neither tip‐rounding nor substrate‐mixing dominates.  Outside that window the measured H will be systematically too high (at low loads) or too low (when the substrate is felt).

A quick way to get a first‐cut estimate of a composite‐coating hardness Hc is simply to weight the hardnesses of the two phases by their volume fractions.  In its simplest (Voigt) form the linear rule of mixtures says  
   
   Hc ≃ Vm·Hm + Vr·Hr  
   
where  
  •  Vm , Vr are the volume fractions of the metal matrix and the hard reinforcement (e.g. ceramic) respectively,  
  •  Hm , Hr are their individual hardnesses.  

You can also write a “lower‐bound” (Reuss‐type) rule by taking the harmonic mean  
  
   1/Hc ≃ Vm/Hm + Vr/Hr  

or more elaborate interpolations (Hirsch, Halpin–Tsai, Gurland, etc.) if you know something about load sharing or the reinforcement geometry.

Why does the real, sprayed-on hardness usually depart from the simple mixture number?  The rule of mixtures assumes perfect, continuous, pore‐free bonding, uniform phase distribution, no interface zones, no residual stresses, and purely elastic contact under the indenter.  In practice:

  1. Porosity or oxide films around the splats lower the load‐bearing area and reduce apparent hardness.  
  2. Particles tend to cluster or align, so you don’t get a homogenous “parallel‐layer” or “series‐layer” structure.  
  3. Cold spray produces large residual stresses (often tensile at the surface) and work‐hardening around particle‐matrix interfaces.  That can either raise or lower the measured hardness, depending on sign and distribution.  
  4. Indentation size effects and pile‐up vs. sink‐in around hard particles distort the contact area, so the area–load curve is not the ideal one used in the rule of mixtures.  
  5. Substrate compliance if your test indentation is deeper than ≈10% of the coating thickness.  
  6. Interfacial reaction layers or debonding can locally soften or crack under the indenter.  

Any of those microstructural realities will make the true hardness higher or lower than the straight-line rule-of-mixtures prediction.

During cold spray deposition, metallic powder particles impact the substrate (and previously‐deposited splats) at supersonic velocities.  The result is extreme, localized plastic strain (strain rates on the order of 10^5–10^8 s^–1) concentrated in narrow shear zones at particle interfaces.  Two key consequences follow:

1. Work hardening by dislocation accumulation  
   – Each high‐velocity impact generates very high local stresses, nucleating and multiplying dislocations.  
   – Dislocations tangle into dense networks or low‐angle boundaries, subdividing grains into subgrains (often in the 100–500 nm range).  
   – The increasing dislocation density (up to ~10^15 m^–2) raises yield strength (Taylor hardening) but leaves virtually no mobile dislocations available for further uniform plastic flow.

2. Brittle as-sprayed microstructure  
   – The deposit is a mosaic of highly deformed, cold‐welded splats with very little strain‐softening ability.  
   – Tensile or bending loads concentrate at hard, dislocation‐rich interfaces, promoting cleavage‐like or interfacial fracture rather than ductile necking.  
   – As a result, as‐sprayed coatings and near‐net parts exhibit high hardness but low elongation-to-failure (often <2–3 %).

Post‐deposition annealing (generally 0.3–0.7 Tm, where Tm is the melting point, held for minutes to hours) reverses much of this embrittlement through two sequential microstructural processes:

A. Recovery  
   – At moderate temperatures, some dislocation annihilation and rearrangement occurs.  
   – Low‐angle boundaries coalesce and shrink; stored elastic energy is relieved without changing the overall grain topology.  
   – Residual stresses drop, and electrical/mechanical properties begin to soften.

B. Recrystallization (and controlled grain growth)  
   – Above a critical recrystallization temperature, new, dislocation‐free grains nucleate—often at the most heavily strained splat boundaries or particle interfaces.  
   – These nuclei grow into the deformed matrix, replacing subgrains with equiaxed, strain‐free grains typically in the 1–10 μm range (depending on temperature and time).  
   – Continued heating yields limited grain growth; if over‐annealed, grains coarsen and strength falls excessively, so times/temperatures are optimized for a balance of strength and ductility.

The outcome of proper annealing is  
– A dramatic drop in dislocation density,  
– Elimination of most high‐angle misorientations and microcracks at interfaces,  
– Transformation from a brittle, work‐hardened aggregate to a more homogeneous, recrystallized grain structure.  

Mechanically, this restores uniform slip capability and strain hardening capacity, raising elongation (often to 10–20 % or higher) while retaining moderate strength. If the alloy system permits it (e.g., age‐hardening aluminum or precipitation‐strengthened steels), a follow-up ageing or tempering step can re–introduce fine precipitates for regained strength without sacrificing the newly recovered ductility.

Low‐temperature (sub‐Tm) cold spray of amorphous ceramic powders onto metals produces adherent coatings even though no bulk melting occurs.  Their adhesion derives from three synergistic effects:  

1. Mechanical interlocking and peening  
  • Each particle impacts at several hundred m/s, generating local adiabatic shear and plastic flow in the metal substrate beneath it.  This both roughens and work‐hardens the surface, driving fragments of ceramic into surface asperities and “keying” the coating mechanically.  
  • The repeated peening also leaves a residual compressive stress field in the near‐surface metal—helping clamp the overlying ceramic layer in place.  

2. Interfacial atomic/microshear bonding  
  • Impact ruptures both the native metal oxide and the particle surface, momentarily exposing fresh, highly reactive surfaces.  Interfacial shear mixing at these micro‐jets produces zones of intimate atomic contact.  
  • In the case of silicate or aluminosilicate glasses this contact can be “frozen in” as metal–O–Si (or Al) type bonds once the shear‐heated region cools and reconsolidates.  

3. Chemical/condensation bonding (in amorphous powders)  
  • Amorphous ceramics prepared by sol–gel or spray pyrolysis often carry surface silanol (≡Si–OH) or aluminol groups.  Under the brief high‐strain, moderately elevated‐temperature conditions of cold spray these can condense across the interface (≡Si–O–Me or ≡Al–O–Me), further locking the coating down.  

How crystallinity changes these mechanisms  
– Amorphous→crystalline transformation (by post‐spray annealing or local overheating) lowers the internal free energy of the ceramic, collapses free volume and removes most surface –OH groups.  The outcome is:  
  • Higher hardness and brittleness in the coating reduce its ability to dissipate impact energy plastically, so mechanical interlocking and interfacial shear mixing are both diminished, giving lower bond strength.  
  • Fewer surface hydroxyls and a more ordered network sharply cut back condensation‐type bonding.  
  • In some oxide systems a thin epitaxial or semi‐coherent crystalline oxide at the interface can form, which locally improves chemical adhesion—but typically not enough to offset the loss of mechanical anchorage and silanol condensation.  

How humid ageing modifies adhesion  
– Moisture ingress into a cold‐sprayed amorphous coating or along its interface promotes:  
  • Hydrolytic attack of siloxane (≡Si–O–Si≡) and metal–O–Si bonds, reconverting them to less‐stable silanols (≡Si–OH), thereby chemically debonding the interface.  
  • Capillary‐driven crack opening in micro‐porosity and at the particle–particle or particle–substrate junction, which undermines the peening‐induced lock.  
  • Corrosion of the underlying metal (oxide growth, hydroxide formation), which roughens and volumetrically expands beneath the coating—further prising the ceramic away.  

Net effect:  
• As‐sprayed amorphous ceramics adhere by a potent combination of mechanical peening, shear‐induced atomic mixing and silanol condensation.  
• Crystallization removes the key chemical‐bonding component and stiffens the coating so that mechanical interlock is also impaired.  
• Humid ageing then chemically and mechanically degrades whatever interfacial bonds remain, leading to progressive strength loss and eventual delamination.

Cold‐sprayed Al deposits are born highly work‐hardened, with a nanolayered, subgrain‐cell structure, very high dislocation density and strong residual stresses, plus inter‐splat oxide films.  Annealing alters them in three overlapping stages—recovery, recrystallization, and grain‐growth—that in turn change both strength–ductility balance and fracture path:

1. Recovery (typically 0.3–0.5 Tₘ, or 150–250 °C for Al)  
   • Dislocation annihilation and rearrangement into lower‐energy cell/subgrain walls  
   • Reduction of internal stresses and stored energy  
   • Slight softening (↓ yield strength, hardness), modest ↑ in ductility  
   • Splat–splat oxide films remain largely intact; fracture still prefers interfacial decohesion, but cracks begin to be blunted by more mobile dislocations  

2. Recrystallization (≈0.5–0.6 Tₘ, 250–350 °C)  
   • Nucleation of strain‐free, equiaxed grains at high‐energy sites (particle boundaries, oxide‐decorated dislocation tangles)  
   • Growth of new grains consumes deformed subgrain structure and dissolves many low‐angle boundaries  
   • Sharp drop in dislocation density yields a pronounced loss in yield strength and hardness  
   • Major gain in uniform elongation  
   • Fracture mode shifts from inter‐splat decohesion to mixed or fully transgranular ductile dimple rupture  

3. Grain growth (above ~350 °C)  
   • Coarsening of recrystallized grains by boundary migration  
   • Further modest softening (Hall–Petch effect)  
   • Ductility may plateau or even fall if grains become excessively large  
   • Fracture remains ductile but with larger dimples and fewer small‐scale crack‐initiation sites  

In sum, annealing first “unlocks” dislocations and relieves stress (stage 1), then replaces the ultrafine, highly strained subgrain network with a coarser, strain‐free grain structure (stage 2), and finally coarsens that new grain structure (stage 3).  The net effect is a continuous trade‐off: strength and hardness fall as dislocation content and grain‐boundary density drop, while ductility and the ability to form ductile‐dimple fractures rise, and the dominant crack path moves from interfacial separation along oxide films to ductile transgranular rupture.

Cold‐sprayed (CS) coatings almost invariably return a lower elastic modulus in an indentation test than the same alloy in the bulk, and “recovery resistance” provides a unified way to see why.  Recovery resistance Rr is simply the fraction of the total indentation deformation that unloads elastically; if anything else (microcracking, sliding, interfacial opening) takes up strain at peak load, Rr falls and the apparent E (derived from the unload stiffness) comes down.

Three features of CS coatings drive Rr down relative to bulk:

1. Inter-splat boundaries are far weaker (and more compliant) than the intragranular lattice.  
   – Under a spherical or pyramidal indenter you impose a non‐hydrostatic, multiaxial stress field: a strong compressive zone beneath the tip and hoop‐tensile stresses in a ring around it.  
   – Those tensile components (and any shear tractions resolved along the boundary planes) readily trigger sliding, decohesion, or microcracking at splat interfaces.  
   – Every ounce of strain that goes into sliding or interface opening is permanently lost from the elastic unloading response.  

2. Residual stress heterogeneity in the coating  
   – Cold spraying leaves a patchwork of local compressive and tensile residuals.  Under the indenter they interact with the applied load to promote local plasticity and interfacial slip in non-recoverable ways, further diminishing the unloading stiffness.  

3. Porosity and oxide films  
   – Even very well‐built CS coatings carry nano‐to‐submicron porosity and thin oxide films at most splat boundaries.  These “weak links” collapse or debond early in loading and do not spring back on unloading.  

In a bulk, wrought or fully consolidated metal, virtually all of the indentation strain (up to the elastic limit) comes back as elastic unloading, so the unloading‐slope method recovers nearly the true modulus.  In a CS coating, a significant fraction of the displacement under load is soaked up by inter-splat slip, fracture of oxides, or irreversible plastic flow aided by residual‐stress gradients—none of which recovers—so the unloading slope is shallower.  Hence the apparent E from indentation is systematically lower than the bulk modulus, and the coating’s recovery resistance Rr (the ratio of elastic rebound to total indentation displacement) is reduced.

Grain‐coarsening in a metallic coating that has been subjected to a high‐temperature heat treatment weakens its shear strength through two closely linked effects:

1. Hall–Petch softening  
   • The Hall–Petch relationship states that the macroscopic yield stress σ_y increases with decreasing grain size d according to  
     σ_y = σ_0 + k_HP·d^(–1/2)  
     where σ_0 is a friction stress (for dislocation motion within grains) and k_HP is the Hall–Petch slope (a measure of how effectively grain boundaries block dislocations).  
   • As the heat treatment drives grain‐growth, d increases, so the term k_HP·d^(–1/2) shrinks.  In other words, there are fewer grain boundaries per unit volume to pin dislocations, so less stress is needed to initiate yield.  

2. Translation into shear strength via the von Mises criterion  
   • The von Mises yield criterion for an isotropic metal can be expressed in terms of an equivalent shear stress τ_eq.  In uniaxial tension σ_y it predicts yielding when the octahedral (or equivalent) shear stress reaches  
     τ_eq = σ_y/√3.  
   • Thus, any reduction in the tensile yield stress σ_y (via Hall–Petch grain‐size softening) produces a proportional drop in the shear yield stress τ_eq.  

Putting it all together: high‐T heat treatment → grain coarsening (↑d) → smaller k_HP·d^(–1/2) contribution → lower σ_y → lower τ_eq = σ_y/√3.  Fewer grain‐boundary obstacles also mean dislocations can travel longer distances before being halted, further reducing the critical shear stress for dislocation slip.  The net result is that the coating becomes easier to shear and thus exhibits reduced shear strength.

In the simplest linear “rule‐of‐mixtures” for yield strength one writes the composite yield as a weighted average of matrix and reinforcement contributions, modified by an interfacial load‐transfer efficiency ηint:  
   
   σc,y ≃ (1–V​r)⋅σm,y + ηint⋅V​r⋅σr,y  
  
where  
• V​r  = reinforcement volume fraction  
• σm,y, σr,y  = matrix and reinforcement yield strengths in isolation  
• ηint  (0<ηint≤1) = a factor that measures how effectively the matrix can hand stress off to the reinforcement.  
  
1.  Reinforcement Volume Fraction (V​r)  
–  As V​r→1 the composite strength tends toward the reinforcement’s strength σr,y; as V​r→0 it tends toward the matrix strength σm,y.  
–  In the absence of any interface weakness (ηint=1), the two constituents simply average in direct proportion to their volumes.  
  
2.  Interfacial Characteristics (ηint)  
–  Perfectly bonded, high‐shear‐strength interfaces (high τi) give ηint→1, so you fully harvest the reinforcement’s strength.  
–  Poor or compliant interfaces (low τi, presence of interfacial porosity or reaction‐layers) reduce ηint below unity.  Physically this represents early debonding or slip at the fiber/matrix boundary and slippage of dislocations, both of which cut back on the reinforcement’s ability to carry load.  
–  In more detailed micromechanical models ηint can itself be expressed in terms of the interfacial shear strength τi, fiber aspect ratio, and any graded “interphase” thickness t, for example via:  
     
     ηint ≃ 1 – coth(βt) / (βt)     or     ηint ∝ τi·(interfacial area)/(reinforcement cross‐section)  
     
  but in all cases higher τi (stronger bonding) and thinner, well‐adhered interphases drive ηint up toward 1.  
  
Net effect: increasing V​r raises the upper bound on σc,y, but only a high‐quality interface (large τi, good adhesion and minimal reaction‐layer thickness) allows the composite to actually reach that bound.

Cold‐sprayed coatings emerge from the spray gun in a highly non-equilibrium, heavily deformed state – in effect a “cold” severe plastic deformation (SPD) process – and this has three key consequences that give them unusually good hardness retention after high‐temperature annealing:

1. Extremely high dislocation densities and ultrafine/submicron grains  
   • During impact each powder particle fractures, cold–welds, and plastically flows, producing a network of tangled dislocations, deformation twins, and nanometric subgrains.  
   • Such a structure stores enormous strain energy, and the effective grain size is often tens to a few hundreds of nanometers.

2. Strong pinning of boundaries and inhibition of grain growth  
   • Native oxides, adsorbed surface films or process‐generated nanoscale oxide fragments become trapped at particle–particle interfaces and along sub‐grain boundaries.  
   • These oxides (and any residual alloying‐element clusters) exert a Zener‐pinning pressure on grain/subgrain boundaries, raising the activation energy for boundary migration and thus slowing both recovery and recrystallization.

3. Sluggish recovery/recrystallization kinetics  
   • The combination of high stored energy (driving force for recrystallization) and strong boundary pinning (opposing force) sets up a situation in which partial recovery occurs at moderate temperatures, but full grain‐coarsening or complete softening only happens at much higher temperatures than in cast, bulk, or thermally sprayed (melt‐based) microstructures.  

By contrast, bulk metals that are annealed from a relatively coarse‐grained, low‐dislocation‐density starting point, or thermal‐spray deposits that solidify from a melt (where many of the deformation defects have been “burned out” during melting/rapid solidification), enjoy little of this pinning and thus readily recrystallize and grain-grow when heated.  The result is a large drop in hardness.  Cold‐sprayed coatings, on the other hand, settle into a “plateau” hardness set by their residual ultrafine grains, remnant dislocation networks, and oxide‐pinning particles – all of which survive up to far higher annealing temperatures.

In cold‐sprayed metal coatings the most important “defect” is the network of inter‐splat cracks (or microvoids) that interrupt the load‐bearing metal.  Phenomenological “defect” or two‐phase models treat the coating as a composite of perfect metal (modulus E₀) and zero‐stiffness cracks (volume fraction φ).  From these models one finds immediately that the effective Young’s modulus E satisfies  

  – Upper (Voigt) bound (iso‐strain)  
    E/ E₀ ≃ (1 – φ)  

  – Dilute‐crack (first‐order, self‐consistent) expansion for small φ  
    E/ E₀ ≃ 1 – C·φ (with C ≃2–4 depending on Poisson’s ratio and crack shape)  

  – Differential effective‐medium (DEM) model  
    dE/E = –α·dφ/(1 – φ)  ⇒  E/ E₀ = (1 – φ)^α  

      where α is a constant of order 1–2 for penny‐shaped cracks.  

All of these predict the same qualitative trend: as the crack volume fraction φ grows, E/E₀ falls monotonically from 1 at φ=0 toward 0 as φ→1.  In particular, for modest crack densities (φ<0.1–0.2) the drop is nearly linear,  

  E/E₀ ≃ 1 – C·φ,  

whereas at higher φ the DEM model shows a stronger, power‐law dependence  

  E/E₀ ≃ (1 – φ)^α.  

Numerically, if φ=0.2 and α≈1.5, then E/E₀≈0.8^1.5≈0.72, i.e. a 28 % reduction in stiffness.

High-temperature heat treatment of cold-sprayed, carbon-reinforced metal coatings typically involves a sequence of overlapping metallurgical events—recovery, recrystallization, solid-solution homogenization, carbide/intermetallic precipitation and particle-matrix strengthening—that together drive the as-sprayed, highly strained structure toward a much harder, more stable microstructure.  A representative multi-step mechanism is:  

1. Recovery of cold-spray defects  
   • As-sprayed grains contain extreme dislocation densities, tangled subgrains and residual tensile stresses.  
   • Heating into the 0.4–0.6 Tm range (where Tm is the melting point) activates cross-slip and climb, reducing stored energy, annihilating the most mobile dislocations, and forming a network of low-angle subgrain boundaries.  

2. Recrystallization and subgrain growth  
   • Continued heating nucleates strain-free, equiaxed grains at triple junctions and along high-angle boundaries.  
   • These new grains grow until pinned by hard second-phase particles (see step 4) and by the embedded carbon reinforcements.  
   • The result is a finer, more uniform grain size controlled by Zener pinning, boosting hardness by the Hall–Petch effect.  

3. Solid-solution homogenization of carbon and alloying elements  
   • At or above the solution-treatment temperature, C (from the reinforcement surface or any dissolved graphitic phases) and other alloying elements (Cr, Mo, Ti, etc.) diffuse into the metal lattice, eliminating compositional gradients and dissolving coarse, as-sprayed carbides.  
   • A supersaturated solid solution is established, with carbon atoms in interstitial sites and solute atoms randomly distributed.  

4. Precipitation of nanoscale carbides/intermetallics (aging)  
   • On controlled cooling or an intermediate “aging” hold (often 400–600 °C), the supersaturated solutes exsolve as very fine (10–50 nm) carbides (Cr23C6, TiC, M7C3, etc.) or intermetallic phases.  
   • These precipitates form both within grain interiors and along boundaries, serving as ultra-fine obstacles to dislocation glide.  

5. Orowan and interface dislocation strengthening  
   • The embedded carbon fibers/graphene platelets/nanotubes themselves remain chemically stable but generate high local thermal mismatch stresses during cooldown.  
   • Those stresses nucleate “geometrically necessary” dislocation loops around each stiff particle, further elevating the dislocation density in their vicinity.  
   • Dislocations bow and loop around both the nanoscale precipitates and the larger carbon reinforcements (Orowan mechanism), requiring higher shear stresses for plastic flow.  

6. Grain-boundary pinning and final grain-size stabilization  
   • A balance is struck at the end of treatment: recrystallized grains are prevented from coarsening by the very precipitates whose formation contributed to precipitation hardening in step 4, plus by the insoluble carbon particulates.  
   • The stabilized, fine-grained microstructure maximizes boundary-area strengthening without excessive grain growth.  

Net Result on Hardness  
– Reduction of weak, as-sprayed porosity and elimination of stress concentrators during recovery/recrystallization.  
– Hall–Petch strengthening from a refined, equiaxed grain structure.  
– Precipitation hardening from high‐number‐density, nanoscale carbides/intermetallics.  
– Orowan looping and thermal-mismatch–induced dislocation forests around carbon inclusions.  
– Improved cohesion across particle–particle and fiber–matrix interfaces.  

Taken together, these steps transform the highly strained, metastable cold-spray deposit into a precipitation-strengthened, fine‐grained composite whose combined Hall–Petch, solid‐solution, precipitation and particle‐reinforcement mechanisms yield a significantly higher hardness.

At a constant carbide‐in‐matrix volume fraction the mean spacing between hard particles scales directly with their diameter, so the depth (and hence volume) of matrix gouged out by an abrasive scales roughly with carbide size.  In simple terms, if you make the carbides 4× larger you increase the wear rate by about a factor of 4.  Equivalently, the fine‐carbide coating will be roughly four times more abrasion‐resistant than the coarse‐carbide one.

Below is a stepwise outline of how adiabatic‐shear‐driven dislocation accumulation and grain‐boundary strengthening act in tandem to set the yield strength of a cold-sprayed Cu alloy, with direct reference to the Hall–Petch relation.

1. High-velocity particle impact and adiabatic shear   
   – Upon supersonic impact, intense localized strain rates (10⁵–10⁷ s⁻¹) generate narrow “adiabatic shear” bands at the particle/substrate or interparticle interfaces.  
   – Plastic work within these bands converts to heat faster than it can dissipate, promoting further localized deformation and extremely high dislocation generation rates.

2. Dislocation accumulation (forest strengthening)  
   – Within and around the shear bands, dislocation density (ρ) climbs to 10¹⁴–10¹⁵ m⁻².  
   – The resulting “forest” of tangled dislocations impedes further dislocation motion.  
   – This produces a strengthening increment Δσ ≈ α G b √ρ, where α is a constant (~0.2–0.5), G the shear modulus, and b the Burgers vector.

3. Dynamic grain refinement at interfaces  
   – Severe plastic straining and dynamic recrystallization in the shear‐band zones produce ultrafine grains (d ≈ 100–500 nm) along particle boundaries.  
   – Away from these bands, grains may remain coarser (1–10 µm), but the interfacial layer carries a disproportionately large fraction of load.

4. Grain‐boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch effect)  
   – The classical Hall–Petch law states:  
     σy = σ0 + k·d⁻¹/²  
     where σ0 is the friction stress for single crystals, k the Hall–Petch slope, and d the effective grain diameter.  
   – As cold spray refines grains at interfaces, d shrinks and σy increases.

5. Synergy and overall yield strength  
   – The net macroscopic yield strength can be approximated by superposing the two mechanisms:  
     σy ≃ σ0 + k·d⁻¹/² + α G b √ρ  
   – Adiabatic shear ensures high ρ (forest hardening) while concurrent grain refinement maximizes the k·d⁻¹/² term.  
   – In practice, cold-sprayed Cu alloys see yield strengths rise from ~100 MPa (annealed) to 200–350 MPa or more, depending on particle velocity, temperature, and alloying.

Summary  
– Step 1–2 generate a high dislocation density for “inside‐grain” hardening.  
– Step 3–4 produce ultrafine boundary grains for “inter‐grain” strengthening via Hall–Petch.  
– Combined by rule-of-mixtures or additive strengthening models, these contributions set the final σy of the cold-sprayed deposit.

The effect of ceramic‐particle volume fraction Vₚ on both the composite yield strength σᶜ and its abrasive‐wear resistance can be seen most transparently by invoking a simple isostrain (Voigt) rule‐of‐mixtures for yield strength together with Archard’s wear law.  

1.  Rule-of-Mixtures for Yield Strength  
   In the isostrain model (i.e. perfect load sharing, no strain‐partitioning) the composite yield strength σᶜ is  
   σᶜ = (1–Vₚ)·σₘ  +  Vₚ·σₚ  
   •  σₘ = yield strength of the metal matrix (e.g. ~300–600 MPa)  
   •  σₚ = “yield” or fracture‐strength of the ceramic (effectively the stress at which a hard particle fails, often in the GPa range)  
   As Vₚ increases from 0 toward 1, σᶜ rises linearly from σₘ up toward σₚ.  In practice σₚ≫σₘ, so even modest Vₚ yields a large boost in strength.  
   Example: σₘ=400 MPa, σₚ≈2000 MPa  
     – Vₚ=0.1 ⇒ σᶜ≈0.9·400 + 0.1·2000 = 560 MPa  
     – Vₚ=0.3 ⇒ σᶜ≈0.7·400 + 0.3·2000 = 920 MPa  

2.  Correlation with Abrasive Wear Resistance  
   Under abrasive wear control, Archard’s law says the steady‐state volume loss per unit load is inversely proportional to hardness H:  
     W ∝ L⁄H  
   Hardness H is roughly proportional to yield strength (H≈2.8–3.0·σᵧ for many alloys).  Hence as σᶜ increases with Vₚ, H rises and abrasive wear rate falls.  Thus higher Vₚ → higher σᶜ → higher hardness → better wear resistance.  

3.  Caveats and Practical Limits  
 •  Interfacial bonding, residual porosity or particle clustering reduces the effective load transfer below the ideal Voigt case, so the real σᶜ often falls below the straight line.  
 •  Beyond a critical Vₚ (~20–40 vol%), the coating can become brittle, microcracks form, particles pull out, and porosity spikes—any of which can undermine the wear resistance.  
 •  Optimal Vₚ therefore balances the linear‐rule‐of‐mixtures gain in σᶜ against the onset of defects and embrittlement.  

Summary:  
Increasing the ceramic‐particle volume fraction Vₚ in a cold-sprayed metal–ceramic coating raises its predicted yield strength roughly in proportion to Vₚ (per σᶜ=(1–Vₚ)σₘ+Vₚσₚ).  Since abrasive‐wear rate scales inversely with hardness (and hardness tracks σᶜ), higher Vₚ delivers better wear resistance—up to the point where particle pull-out, porosity and brittle fracture start to dominate.

The Hall–Petch law for a polycrystal reads  

   σy = σ0 + kHP·d–½  

where  
• σy is the yield strength,  
• σ0 is the lattice friction stress (all other strengthening sources at fixed dislocation density),  
• kHP is the Hall–Petch coefficient for copper (≈ 0.10–0.15 MPa·m½), and  
• d is the average grain diameter.  

Because grain boundaries act as barriers to dislocation motion (they “pin” dislocations and force them to pile up), reducing d increases the total boundary area per unit volume.  In the Hall–Petch term kHP·d–½ that extra boundary area translates directly into higher stress needed to move dislocations out of one grain and into the next.  

If the dislocation density ρ remains essentially unchanged by the cold‐spray process, σ0 and the strain‐hardening contribution stay the same, so the only change in σy comes from the kHP·d–½ term.  Thus grain refinement (smaller d) gives a higher kHP·d–½ increment and therefore a higher overall yield strength.
